title: CoalWire 526, August 15, 2024
excerpt: Indonesian biomass co-firing challenged; Indian regulator in spotlight; Glencore holds on to coal.
content:
August 15, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

As the transition to renewables has accelerated, Japan has stepped up its promotion of a suite of technologies aimed at extending the life of coal plants, especially in Southeast Asia. As the hype about carbon capture and storage on coal plants has faded, Japan and coal industry groups have promoted co-firing coal units with alternative fuels such as biomass and ammonia as a path to emissions reductions. A new paper in Nature dissects the likely implications of large-scale biomass co-firing in Indonesia. At best, a low ratio of biomass use from crop waste and sawdust would marginally reduce emissions. At worst, it would result in accelerated deforestation of primary forests, affect local communities and threaten biodiversity.

In a separate development, the Supreme Court of Indonesia has upheld the conviction of a former regional official accused of accepting bribes from a construction subsidiary of the South Korean company Hyundai. The company had the contract to build a Japanese-financed coal unit facing local community opposition. In India, a new report by Hindenburg Research has put the spotlight back on the corporate regulator tasked with investigating the ultimate beneficiaries of investors in Adani group companies.

Elsewhere, Glencore – the world's largest exporter of thermal coal – announced that it won't spin off its coal division. Last year, the company suggested that if it succeeded in taking over Elk Valley Resources, which holds Teck Resources Canadian metallurgical coal projects, it would offload its coal assets and focus on other commodities. The decision to keep coal puts a big question mark over the company's climate plan that previously backed winding down coal production.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Singapore's banks and regulators can do more to drive a regional coal phaseout

For a genuine coal phaseout, it is essential that private banks cease funding for any new coal expansion and redirect these funds towards investments in grid infrastructure, renewable energies and the decommissioning of coal assets, writes Danielle Koh in EcoBusiness.

 

 Pro-coal arguments in ASEAN are based on false assumptions and unproven solutions

Recent arguments against phasing out coal in Southeast Asia ignore that the volatility of the international coal price undercuts the viability of coal-based generation during global energy disruptions and reduces energy security, writes Christopher Doleman for the Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis.

 

 Even with hard work, a just transition needs long-term support

The gradual closure of what was once the 2310 megawatt (MW) Turceni lignite plant in Romania illustrates the difficulties faced by local authorities in coal-dependent regions. People are used to massive coal power plants and mines and find it hard to accept that equally gargantuan industries will not replace them, writes Pippa Gallop from CEE Bankwatch in Just Transition.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Indonesian NGOs call on Japan to cancel loan after bribery conviction: The Indonesian Supreme Court has confirmed the conviction of the former regent of Cirebon, Sunjaya Purwadisastra, who the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) charged over allegations he received bribes and gratuities worth up to 64.2 billion rupiah (US$4.1 million) from Hyundai Engineering & Construction (HEC) to support for the 924 MW Cirebon 2 coal unit. HEC was the construction contractor for a joint venture that includes Marubeni and JERA. The unit began operation in mid-2023. In the wake of the ruling, Walhi (Friends of the Earth Indonesia) and three other local community organisations and NGOs called on the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) to immediately suspend the loans for the project and require mandatory prepayment of loans for the unit, in line with the provisions of its anti-bribery policy. In May 2019, Purwadisastra was convicted in a separate bribery case and sentenced to five years in prison. (Friends of the Earth Japan)

 

 US utility pays US$19.5 million to settle case on bribery scandal: FirstEnergy has agreed to pay US$19.5 million to settle an Ohio state government investigation into corrupt payments made by the utility to 'dark money' groups controlled by the former Republican Speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives, Larry Householder, and to former Chairman of the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, Samuel Randazzo. As part of the agreement, Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost agreed to drop criminal charges and a civil case against the utility. Householder is currently serving a 20-year sentence for his role in the US$61 million bribery scandal, while Randazzo recently died. FirstEnergy had previously admitted in a federal case that it had bribed Householder and Randazzo and paid US$230 million as part of a settlement agreement. With FirstEnergy's support, Householder succeeded in passing legislation to bail out two of the utility's loss-making nuclear plants and two coal plants. Cases filed by Yost against former FirstEnergy executives are continuing. (Akron Beacon Journal, Ohio Attorney General)

 

 US seeks order against coal companies owned by Republican governor: A US Department of Justice attorney has requested a district court find 23 coal companies owned by West Virginia Republican Governor Jim Justice guilty of civil contempt over non-payment of penalties owing to the Mine Safety and Health Administration. The Department of Justice reached an agreement with Justice's Southern Coal Corporation and associated entities in 2020 to pay US$5.13 million in monthly instalments of US$102,442 to settle the debt on 2297 citations and civil penalties issued by federal mine inspectors between 2014 and 2019. The deadline for payment was March 1, 2024, but the companies still owe US$579,042. In May, the Republican party selected Justice as its candidate in the November 2024 election for a seat in the US Senate. Justice is considered likely to win the seat vacated by former Democratic Senator for West Virginia turned independent, Joe Manchin. The US Senate is currently finely balanced, with Republicans holding 49 of the 100 seats and Democrats holding 47. Four independents, including Manchin, caucus with the Democrats. (News & Sentinel, US Department of Justice [Pdf])

 

 Report challenges Indian regulator over link to Bermuda fund: Hindenburg Research, a US-based short seller, has released a new report accusing the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Chairperson, Madhabi Buch and her husband, of previously holding an investment in a Bermuda-based company, Global Dynamic Opportunities Fund. This fund also attracted investments from a company controlled by Vinod Adani, the brother of Gautam Adani, the Chairman of the Adani Group. After Hindenburg Research released a report on the Adani Group in January 2023, the Supreme Court of India ordered SEBI to investigate the Hindenburg allegations of potential breaches of disclosure rules for stock exchange-listed companies. One of SEBI's 24 investigations remains uncompleted. The Buchs rejected Hindenburg's latest report, but the company said their response raised more questions. (The Wire, BBC, Hindenburg Research, Livemint)

 

 Welsh parliamentary committee pans flaws in coal mine rehabilitation: A report by the Welsh Parliament's Climate Change, Environment, and Infrastructure Committee (CCEIC) criticised the poor management, public consultation and restoration standards for open-cut coal mining sites in Wales. The report called on the Welsh government to press the UK government to remove the Coal Authority's statutory duty to maintain and develop a "viable" coal industry and for increased funding for the restoration of disused coal sites. The committee cited the Ffos-y-Fran mine, where Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council delayed action on illegal mining activities after the mine's license expired in September 2022, as a "symbol of the system's failures". The original proposal of Merthyr (South Wales) was to mine about 10 million tonnes of coal and fund the restoration of the area to create open space for the community. Restoration of the site could cost up to 120 million (US$154 million) compared to the 15 million (US$19.3 million) held by the local authority for the work. The company is proposing a rehabilitation plan that leaves the mine void and is part-filled with water. (BBC, Climate Change, Environment, and Infrastructure Committee [Pdf], Coal Action Network)

 

 
 "It now appears that the site operator [at the Ffos-y-Fran mine] has no intention of fulfilling its restoration obligations as per the original plan. Like so many others, it has taken profits from the site, but now the money they promised for restoration is not there,"

stated [Pdf] the report by the Welsh Parliament's Climate Change, Environment, and Infrastructure Committee.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The High Court of Australia has declined to the Environment Council of Central Queensland's application for special leave to appeal against the decision of the Minister for Environment, Tanya Plibersek, to approve two large coal mine expansions.

 

 Australia: Officials from Resources Safety and Health Queensland raided the offices of Metarock, a coal mine contracting company. The raid follows the deaths of two coal mine workers, one at Sojitz Corporation's Crinum mine in 2021 and another at Anglo American's Moranbah North mine in March 2022.

 

 Canada: A coalition of First Nations and environmental groups has called on the Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Steven Guilbeault, to require federal assessment of Coalspur's proposed expansions of the Vista thermal coal mine in Alberta.

 

 India: The Damodar Valley Corporation has awarded a contract to BHEL for the construction of a 1600 MW expansion of the Koderma coal plant in Jharkhand.

 

 Pakistan: The state-owned Jamshoro Power has commissioned the 660 MW Unit 5 at the Jamshoro coal plant. The Asian Development Bank was the main funder of the new unit.

 

 US: The Energy Information Administration estimates the wind sector generated more electricity in March and April than coal power plants.

 

 US: The Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation estimates industry bonds available for coal mine reclamation are at least US$34.4 million below what is needed.

 

 "If the American people elect a conservative president, his administration will have to eradicate climate change references from absolutely everywhere,"

said Bethany Kozma, former deputy chief of staff at the US Agency for International Development, in a training video as part of Project 2025 for a new Trump administration.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Study finds Indonesian biomass plan could increase deforestation: A paper published in Nature estimates that biomass co-firing can only play a limited role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions from coal plants. Indonesia's state-owned power utility, PLN, set a target in 2022 for biomass co-firing at 52 coal plants to contribute 10 per cent of electricity by 2050. Most of the biomass currently used at 32 coal plants relies on rice husks and sawdust byproducts, but increased volumes would require forest plantations dedicated to supplying the energy sector. The study finds that co-firing at higher ratios causes fouling in existing boilers, the economics of biomass supply are challenging, and year-round supply is uncertain in eastern Indonesia, where coal use is expanding most rapidly. The Ministry of Environment and Forestry has designated 5.4 million hectares of forest for energy plantations and commenced allocating concessions to project developers. The study warns that converting intact primary forests for biomass plantations will never offset emission losses from deforestation and threaten local communities and biodiversity. (Nature)

Rules relaxed so Adani can sell export power into the Indian market: India's Ministry of Power has agreed to relax the 2018 rules on power exports to Bangladesh to allow generators also to sell electricity into the Indian market. Reuters reports that an internal ministry memo states that the government may allow a plant to sell electricity into the domestic market "in case of sustained non-scheduling of full or part capacity". The only Indian plant approved to export power to Bangladesh is Adani Power's 1600 MW Godda coal plant. The Godda project is underwritten with a high-cost contract with the Bangladesh Power Development Board and burns coal imported from Adani's Carmichael coal mine in Australia. Two Indian government-owned financial institutions, the Power Finance Corporation and Rural Electrification Corporation, provided the bulk of the finance for the plant. (Reuters, Global Energy Monitor)

Internal report finds major funding needed for South African coal railway: An internal report for the South African state-owned rail operator estimates that restoring the capacity of the main coal railway to the Richards Bay Coal Terminal requires the investment of 12.2 billion rand (US$670 million) over five years. The review suggests capacity could fall to as low as 38 million tonnes of coal a year in the absence of the required work. In 2023, Transnet carried 48 million tonnes of coal on the railway, with 53 million tonnes expected this year. Transnet's operations have been affected by the theft of cabling, a lack of locomotives and difficulty obtaining spare parts. The report proposes investments to increase capacity to 78 million tonnes a year. (News24)

Complaint against Philippines Energy Secretary over coal plant approval: The Power for the People Coalition (P4P Coalition) has filed a case with the Philippines Ombudsman against the Department of Energy Secretary Raphael Lotilla over his decision in 2023 to approve the 169 MW Unit 3 at the Therma Visayas coal plant in Bato. The complaint alleges Lotilla approved the expansion of the plant in violation of the moratorium on new coal plants instituted in December 2020. It also argues that Lotilla's decision favoured AboitizPower, a utility he was a board member of until he resigned in July 2022 when he was appointed Energy Secretary. The Philippines Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PCCI) has backed Lotilla's approval of the plant expansion, complaining the filing of the case risked deterring foreign direct investment. The PCCI argued the Department of Energy's December 2020 moratorium applied to greenfield projects, existing plants with "firm" expansion plans and "indicative" projects with approved permits and plans. However, P4P Coalition said as recently as late 2023 AboitizPower hadn't decided whether they were proposing a gas or coal-fired unit and was obviously not in the coal project pipeline in December 2020. (P4P Coalition [Facebook], BusinessWorld)

Glencore decides to keep its coal business: Glencore has decided to keep all its coal operations on the basis that cash generated will boost returns to shareholders and provide the opportunity to invest in other divisions of the company. Before it purchased 77 per cent of Elk Valley Resources (EVR), the Canadian metallurgical coal division of Teck Resources, Glencore had flagged the possibility that it would merge the Canadian mines and its thermal coal projects in Australia, South Africa and Columbia into an expanded coal unit and spin it off. Glencore said it will assess how the expansion of its coal production capacity with the purchase of EVR will affect its climate strategy. In April, Glencore released its 2024-2026 Climate Action Transition Plan but this does address the acquisition of the EVR mines. The Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility (ACCR)​, which has pressured the company to align its business with the goals of the Paris Agreement, said the purchase of EVR increases Glencore's potential saleable coal by over 30 per cent, with most of the newly acquired mines likely to operate beyond 2050. ACCCR said Glencore needs to urgently update its climate plan and provide investors with a plan to wind down its coal mines in line with the Paris Agreement. Days before Glencore's coal announcement, the Swiss attorney general's office announced it had fined the company US$152 million for failing to prevent a business partner from bribing a public official in 2011 over the sale of two Congolese copper and cobalt mines. The company has paid US$1.7 billion in the last few years to settle a range of bribery and corruption investigations affecting different divisions of the company. (Glencore, Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility, Mining.com)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Indonesia's expansion of clean power can spur growth and equality, Ember, August 2024. (Pdf) (An Indonesian version of the report is available here.)

This 28-page report reviews the potential for the government to facilitate the construction of new renewables projects in Indonesia's coal-producing regions to soften the impacts of the energy transition.

links.text: Climate Change, Environment, and Infrastructure Committee [Pdf],
Indonesia’s expansion of clean power can spur growth and equality

title: CoalWire 527, August 22, 2024
excerpt: Bangladesh suspends new fast-track power projects; Teck fined over Canadian pollution; residents protest coal dust pollution from Mozambique mine.
content:
Augist 22, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The announcement by Bangladesh's interim government that the Ministry of Power has suspended the assessment of new power projects under fast-track legislation is significant news. At this stage, it is not yet clear which projects are affected or whether coal projects will be cancelled. As India presses ahead with plans for a massive expansion of coal power generation, a new report models the potential of batteries paired with renewables as a viable alternative. India's heavy reliance on coal generation continues to impose a heavy air pollution toll on communities, with new mines threatening agricultural areas, forests and wildlife.

In North America, the International Joint Commission is launching a study of downstream pollution from Glencore's metallurgical coal mines in British Columbia. In a separate development, federal regulators fined Glencore's Canadian subsidiary C$220,750 (US$162,111) for 29 breaches of the Environmental Management Act. In Mozambique, residents near the vast open-cut pit of Jindal's Moatize mine have voiced concern about the impacts of dust pollution. In the Philippines, increasing demand for coal has created turmoil for an Indigenous community in South Cotabato province.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 From quiet place to coal hub: South Cotabato village awakens, but at what cost?

Seven years after the killing of a group of Indigenous community leaders, the mountain village of Ned in Lake Sebu town, South Cotabato, is now abuzz with earthmoving equipment and huge trucks heavy with coal, writes Rommel Rebollido in Rappler.

 

 A town in Colombia fights to keep coal companies out

The recent declaration of Colombia's first Protected Area for Food Production was a win for the residents of Canaverales in their long struggle to protect their land and water from the impacts of coal mining, writes Emma Banks in Nacla.

 

 

Adani's Mirzapur coal-power project could impact threatened wildlife

India's National Green Tribunal has initiated a case to investigate Adani's proposed 1600 megawatt (MW) Mirzapur coal plant in a forested area home to species including sloth bears and leopards, writes Ayaskant Das in Adani Watch.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Interim Bangladesh govt suspends assessment of new power projects: Dr M Fauzul Kabir Khan, the adviser to the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources, said the ministry has suspended all projects under consideration via the Speedy Power and Energy Supply (Special) Act 2010. The act allows government-backed energy projects to bypass normal tendering requirements. Details of which power projects are affected have not yet been made public. The Global Coal Plant Tracker notes that there are four coal plants with a combined capacity of 6250 MW in the pre-approval stage. Following mass protests, former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina fled the country in early August. After negotiations between the student leaders of the protests, the military and President Mohammed Shahabuddin, Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was sworn in as the head of Bangladesh's interim government. The rapid expansion of power projects, including coal plants, reliant on expensive imported fuel has led to rapid increases in national debt and power prices. (Business Standard, Business Standard)

 

 International commission starts work on pollution from Teck coal mines: The International Joint Commission (IJC) has called for public comments by August 27 on its planned investigation of transboundary water pollution in the Elk-Kootenai/y watershed in Canada and the US. The commission was established in 1909 under the Boundary Waters Treaty to resolve cross-border disputes. Canada and the US, along with the Ktunaxa Nation, agreed in March 2024 to refer water pollution from coal mine sites in the Elk Valley in British Columbia to the commission. The IJC study comes as the US Geological Survey published new data revealing that selenium pollution from the mines in Canada was transported downstream over 575 river kilometres and "may pose risks to aquatic life in the transboundary Columbia River". The study found concentrations of selenium at monitoring sites downstream of the mines increased between 35 per cent and 89 per cent between 2005 and 2021. No trend was detected between 2005 and 2017 at a monitoring site not affected by mine pollution. (International Joint Commission, Wildsight, Environmental Science and Technology)

 

 Teck fined over Canadian mine pollution: The British Columbia Ministry of Environment fined Teck Coal C$220,750 (US$162,111) for 29 breaches of the Environmental Management Act between February 2021 and November 2022. The ministry fined Teck C$167,750 (US$123,193) for the discharge of 109,000 litres of waste slurry and tailings onto the ground over 27 occasions. The ministry rated the breaches as 'moderate' as there was no evidence the waste affected surface water or the affected environment. The company was fined a further C$52,000 (US$38,188) over two other spills, one in early October 2021 and another in late January 2022, that resulted in 11,500 litres of slurry spilled onto the ground and into a creek at its Elkview metallurgical coal mine. In mid-July a Canadian subsidiary of Glencore completed the purchase of Teck Resources 77 per cent stake in the Elk Valley coal mines. In mid-July, Environment and Climate Change Canada laid five Fisheries Act charges against Elk Valley Resources for water pollution from the company's Line Creek mine in British Columbia. (CBC, British Columbia Ministry of Environment [Pdf], The Narwhal)

 

 Residents raise pollution concerns of Jindal's Mozambique coal mine: An open letter from residents of eight neighbourhoods in Moatize called on Vulcan Mozambique to control dust pollution from the mine. The letter to government agencies and civil society organisations included photos of dust clouds from the mine and instances of water pollution. The letter flagged that the residents reserved their right to "take all legal measures to protest" if the residents concerns weren't addressed within 30 days. An estimated 5000 people were displaced by the mine when Vale began construction work in 2008. Vale sold the mine and the associated 912-kilometer railway to the port of Nacala for US$270 million to Vulcan in April 2022. Vulcan is a subsidiary of Jindal, a major Indian company. The Moatize mine can produce about 22 million tonnes of thermal and metallurgical coal a year. (Carta de Mocambique [Portuguese], Club of Mozambique, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Study finds Australian 45-day mine fire aged residents lungs: A study published in Respirology found a statistically significant association between exposure to PM2.5 fine particles pollution from the 45-day long Hazelwood mine fire and decreased lung function. The study of 479 adults was undertaken four years after the fire in 2014, with 65 per cent of those surveyed exposed to smoke that blanketed the nearby town of Morwell. Those exposed to smoke demonstrated poorer results in one of four performance measures assessed by a lung function test. The study authors calculated the lungs of those exposed to smoke from the mine fire aged by about 4.7 years. The authors suggested that future town planning should account for the health risks associated with decommissioned coal mines. (Guardian, Respirology)

 

 Indian study finds rehabilitation standards lacking: A study published in Frontiers in Environmental Science estimates native vegetation cover declined by 25 per cent over 28 years at three operating coal mines in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. The authors tracked changes at the Sohagpur, Jamuna & Kotma and Bishrampur coal mines between 1994 and 2022 using satellite data. The study estimated between 7.32 per cent and 17.61 percent of forest cover, 5 per cent to 10 per cent of water bodies, and 3 per cent to 5 per cent of agricultural lands were lost due to coal mining. The authors classed between 25 per cent and 40 per cent of the area across the three mining sites as extremely vulnerable to land degradation. The authors argue that despite the establishment of tree plantations as part of rehabilitation work, the rate of land degradation remains high near mines and overburden dumps, indicating the need for better rehabilitation standards. (Mongabay, Frontiers in Environmental Science)

 

 
 We opened our windows the first year we were here And then we realised that we [kept] having this black dust in our house on everything—on the carpet, on upholstery, all of it. You get tired of cleaning everything on a daily basis and wiping down everything. So it came down to justwe don't open the windows anymore," 

said Angela ​Shaneyfelt, who lives near the Curtis Bay coal terminal in Baltimore.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The New South Wales Land and Environment Court upheld the approval for MACH Energy's proposed 444 million tonne expansion of its Mount Pleasant mine. The Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group had challenged the September 2022 approval of the project.

 

 Australia: Origin Energy has acknowledged the 2880 MW Eraring coal plant is prone to unplanned outages. In May, the New South Wales state government committed to pay Origin up to A$450 (US$303 million) million over two years to keep the plant online to cover periods of peak demand.

 

 Australia: Ember notes that Idemitsu's estimate of methane emissions from the proposed expansion of the Boggabri mine is 95 times lower than the New South Wales government's guidance.

 

 Bulgaria: Podkrepa TU, Bulgaria's peak union body, organised a rally for energy industry workers calling for the protection of lignite mining and power plants.

 

 China: Three mine workers died and another three are missing after an accident at a coal mine in Santao Township in Yunnan Province.

 

 Colombia: President Gustavo Petro signed a presidential decree banning coal exports to Israel.

 

 India: Jharkhand will impose a levy of 100 rupees (US$1.19) per tonne on coal and iron ore mined in the state.

 

 Mongolia: Coal exports to China over the January to July period reached 46.6 million tonnes, up 35.5 per cent on the year before.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Report says declining battery prices could cap Indian coal generation: A report by climate policy think tank Ember estimates Indian coal generation could plateau at near current levels until 2032 if the cost of batteries continues to decline and displaces new generation. Ember estimates the addition of 43,000 MW of new solar and wind annually and a seven per cent a year decline in the cost of batteries could undercut coal generation. The Indian government is currently pushing for a significant expansion in new coal capacity, the delayed retirement of old coal units and the expansion of new solar and other renewable capacity. The report estimates that if India added 375,000 MW of solar capacity by 2032, renewables would provide up to 83 per cent of generation during daylight hours, but this would fall to about 38 per cent outside solar hours. The report estimates that capping coal capacity at the 260,000 MW proposed in the current national electricity plan would require a 15 per cent annual decline in battery costs. (Times of India, Ember [Pdf])

Former board member says the position of Indian regulator is 'untenable': A former board member of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) described the position of chair Madhabi Puri Buch as "completely untenable" after Hindenburg Research revealed she earned income from a consultancy she owns. Buch has a 99 per cent shareholding in the India-based Agora Advisory, a consulting firm she said her husband used since he retired from Unilever in 2019. Since Buch joined SEBI in 2017, the consultancy has earned 37.1 million rupees (US$442,025) in revenue, but the clients are not public. There is no known link between the consultancy and any Adani-related firm. "There was no justification for her to continue to own the firm after she joined the board. She could not have been allowed even after making disclosures," said Subhash Chandra Garg, a former SEBI board member. After Hindenburg Research's January 2023 report into Adani-related companies, the Supreme Court directed SEBI to investigate the allegations. The Opposition Congress party has called on Buch to resign. (Reuters)

Sasol flags it might skip transition to a low-emissions business: Simon Baloyi, the CEO of the South African coal-to-oil producer Sasol, has flagged the company could decide not to pursue options to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. "It is not transition at any cost if we see that there are no projects or possible pathways, we will always maximise the outcome and return cash to shareholders," he said. Sasol emits about 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually from its 17 coal boilers. Salsol accounts for about 12 per cent of South Africa's greenhouse gas emissions. The company also produces about 40 million tonnes of thermal coal a year from its mines, with about two to three million tonnes exported via the Richards Bay coal terminal. At its January 2024 annual general meeting, 77 per cent of shares voted for the company's climate plan, down from 95 per cent in each of the two previous years. In April, the Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, Barbara Creecy, granted Sasol's appeal for a variation in the pollution standard for the company's Secunda coal-to-oil plant. Tracey Davies, the Executive Director of Just Share, said Sasol's preferred approach would reduce premature deaths and health impacts by only five per cent by 2030 compared to a 40-60 per cent cut if the company complied with the original Minimum Emissions Standard. (News24)

RWE share price tumbles over report of investment in US gas utility: The price of shares in the German power utility RWE tumbled after suggestions it was considering a possible investment in Calpine, a private equity utility. Calpine operates 76 power plants in the US, Canada and Mexico, with a combined generation capacity of about 26,500 MW mostly from gas-fired plants. RWE has a controversial history including opposition to the closure of its lignite power plants in Germany, the expansion of the Hambach lignite mine and its hard coal plant in the Netherlands. Bernstein, a major financial services firm, said RWE would be "losing the plot on capital discipline and ESG (environmental, social and governance) transformation" if it pursued a stake in Calpine. RWE has proposed spending 55 billion (US$61 billion) by 2030 to transform the company into a major global renewable energy utility. (Reuters)

Report finds Indian regulation on biomass co-firing largely ignored: A regulation requiring 5 to 10 per cent biomass co-firing at 11 power plants within 300 kilometres of New Delhi has mostly been ignored by affected utilities, according to a report by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE). In a bid to cut extreme air pollution levels in the capital, the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) announced biomass co-firing requirements in September 2021 and, in March 2023, increased the target level to at least 10 per cent by December 2023. CAQM proposed the co-firing standard to provide a market for pelletised straw as an alternative to farmers burning off stubble in areas around the capital. CSE found that two of the 11 plants targeted by the requirement have recently achieved two to three per cent co-firing, with most having made no progress. While the CAQM Act provides for fines and imprisonment for non-compliance, there has been no enforcement action to date. It is not the first time India's politically powerful electricity sector has ignored new regulatory standards, with many utilities still not in compliance with pollution control measures that came into effect in December 2017, with subsequent extensions to compliance deadlines. (Indian Express, Centre for Science and Environment)

Russian thermal coal exports climb with cut in export tariff: Russian thermal coal exports increased over the May to July quarter, driven in part by the decision of the Russian government to suspend the export tariff on coal between May 1 and August 31. Exports of Russian coal increased to China, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and India, buoyed by increased electricity demand for air conditioning during high summer temperatures. Egypt, Morocco and Turkey recorded minor increases in imports of Russian coal. Thermal coal imports of 37.3 million tonnes in the May to July period represents a 27 per cent increase over the preceding three months and a marginal increasing on the same period in 2023. The increase in imports of Russian coal came at the expense of Colombian and Australian exporters. Russian coal exporters have been struggling with higher production costs, constraints on railway capacity to ports serving the Asian market and high rail freight charges. (S & P Global)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

"Community voices regarding coal mining human health impact in Limpopo Province, South Africa", ResearchGate, August 1, 2024. (Pdf)

This paper collates the views of 81 people from three villages on the health and community impacts of the operation of Exxaro's Tshikondeni mine in Limpopo province.

title: CoalWire 528, August 29, 2024
excerpt: China slashes new coal approvals; court revokes permit for polluting Czech plant; court win for Canadian municipality; Polish coal company books US$305 write-off as renewables surge.
content:
August 29, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The latest data showing a significant slowdown in China's new coal plant approvals is welcome news. But, many analysts remain cautious about reading too much into the trend just yet. Once bitten, twice shy. One factor in favour of a prolonged downturn is the sheer scale of China's domestic renewables industry compared to even just a few years ago.

A court in the Czech Republic has revoked the permit for the highly polluting Pocerady lignite plant. The ruling puts the ball back in the court of regional officials to reconsider a limit on mercury emissions from the plant. In Canada, a court ruling has found that a municipality has strong enough grounds to warrant a full hearing against a regulator's decision to grant permits for a new coal mine. In Australia, Whitehaven Coal announced the sale of 30 per cent of its Blackwater mine to two Japanese steel companies. One of the companies, Nippon Steel Corporation (NSC), is facing investor pressure to move to cleaner steel production. The purchase of a stake in the Blackwater mine, which is seeking approval to operate for another 60 years, is a clear indication that NSC is willing to ignore investor pressure for now.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 China's emissions trading scheme may remain powerless in decarbonising thermal power sector

China's national compliance carbon market may not evolve into the country's primary tool to decarbonise its coal-fired power sector due to the government's reluctance to give free rein to market forces and resistance from influential bodies in the thermal power sector, writes Ivy Yin in S&P Global.

 

 Indonesian Islamic behemoth's entry into coal mining sparks youth wing revolt

Indonesia's second-largest Islamic organisation faces a growing backlash following a decision to enter the coal mining industry, writes Asad Asnawi in Mongabay

 

 Adani's Godda coal-power plant benefits from Modi rule change

Following the political turmoil in Bangladesh, the Modi government has changed the rules and allowed Adani to sell power from the Godda plant to consumers in India. This has prompted outrage from critics who say that Modi is bailing out Gautam Adani, writes Paranjoy Guha Thakurta in Adani Watch.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Court revokes permit for plant in Czech Republic: The Regional Court in Usti nad Labem has revoked the exemption from mercury emission limits for the 1000 megawatt (MW) of lignite capacity at the Pocerady plant. The plant is owned and operated by the privately owned utility, Sev.En. The Regional Authority of the Usti Region and the Ministry of the Environment approved exemptions from European Union pollution standards that came into effect in August 2021. While temporary exemptions were allowed from the standards, this was on the proviso that continued operation of the plant would not cause significant pollution. The Pocerady plant was allowed to emit four times more mercury than other plants. The continued operation of the Pocerady plant, the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the Czech Republic, was opposed by local NGOs, municipalities, Greenpeace Czechia, Friends of the Earth Czechia and the public interest law group Frank Bold. The court ruling requires local administrative authorities to review the permit and decide on a new emissions limit. (Frank Bold)

 

 Chinese coal plant approvals slow with renewables boom: Chinese government agencies approved 9000 MW of new coal projects in the first half of 2024, a fall of 83 per cent compared to the same period in 2023. However, a review of the latest data by Global Energy Monitor and Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimates construction of more than 41,000 MW of new coal capacity commenced in the first half of the year. The latest data also reveals new and revived projects are at a lower level than the two preceding years, suggesting proposals may be slowing. Chinese coal generation slumped by 7 per cent between June 2024 and the year before. Since the start of 2023, China has added over 400,000 MW of new wind and solar capacity, and this year hydro generation has recovered from drought conditions that prevailed in the last few years. The report calls for the government to end support for new medium and long-term coal supply contracts between mining companies and power plants, the adoption of coal reduction targets and the continued expansion of clean energy. (Guardian, Global Energy Monitor and Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 Canadian court grants appeal hearing against Alberta coal mine: Alberta Court of Appeal Justice Kevin Feth granted the Municipal District of Ranchland's application to appeal against an Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) decision granting three applications by Northback Resources for its proposed Grassy Mountain metallurgical coal mine. Northback Resources is a subsidiary of Australian mining billionaire Gina Rinehart's Hancock Prospecting. In November 2023, Alberta's Minister for Energy, Brian Jean, wrote to the AER arguing that the proposed mine was exempt from the government's ban on considering new coal mines in the Rockies as it was an advanced project. The District of Ranchland argues the AER shouldn't have considered the mine as an advanced project as the federal government rejected it in August 2021. Feth said the AER did not consider the possibility that the project was not exempt and "appears to offer no independent analysis of whether Grassy Mountain met this definition [of an advanced project] in arriving at its decision to accept Northback's applications." (Global News, Alberta Court of Appeal)

 

 Australian study finds damage to swamp from underground mining: A study by UNSW Water Research Laboratory published in the Journal of Hydrology has found that underground longwall mining at South32's Dendrobium metallurgical coal mine has damaged a permanent peatland swamp, causing losses to Sydney's water supply. The lead author of the study, Joe Cairns, said that after longwall mining began in August 2020, water discharges from the swamp dropped "significantly" as water went into the mine void. The study concludes that the impacts on the swamps "may be irreversible, with severe ecological implications". South32 said the changes in the peatlands did not breach its licence conditions. A spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure said licence conditions could not be varied once approved. The department said the purchase of a 598-hectare parcel of land at Maddens Plains offset the predicted impacts. Water scientist Dr Ian Wright said he was "deeply uncomfortable" with the offset condition. "In exchange for just a few years of coal supply, we've lost something forever." (ABC News, Journal of Hydrology)

 

 Regulator backs US$105 million for plants at the centre of Ohio scandal: The Public Utilities Commission of Ohio approved US$105 million in charges for the Kyger Creek coal plant in Ohio and the Clifty Creek coal plant in Indiana. House Bill 6, the legislation at the heart of the Ohio corruption scandal, included subsidies for the two loss-making coal plants. The Ohio Manufacturers Association estimates subsidies for the coal plants could cost more than US$1 billion by 2030. Documents released by the Ohio Consumers Counsel reveal two of FirstEnergy's top internal lawyers, Robert Reffner and Ebony Yeboah-Amankwah, along with the utility's current chief accounting officer, Jason Lisowski, agreed to a US$4.3 million payment to Sam Randazzo for the termination of his consultancy contract. The day before the three discussed the payment, FirstEnergy CEO Chuck Jones and senior vice president Mike Dowling met with the recently re-elected Governor Mike DeWine and Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted. Immediately afterwards, Jones and Dowling met with Randazzo to discuss his appointment to head the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio and the payment. Reffner and Yeboah-Amankwah were later "separated" from the company, while Jones and Dowling currently face charges over the payment. Both have pleaded not guilty. Randazzo was also charged but died shortly afterwards. In a deposition, Lisowski said he had no reason to question the payment as the company's two senior lawyers did not raise any concerns over it. FirstEnergy admitted in a settlement agreement with the Department of Justice that the payment was a bribe. (Cleveland.com, The Columbus Dispatch)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Resources Safety and Health Queensland has ordered the suspension of all heavy vehicles at QCoal's Byerwen metallurgical coal mine after a worker died in a collision between a haul truck and a car. Three weeks earlier, another worker died in a crane accident at the mine.

 

 Australia: Wollongong Resources, a subsidiary of Jindal Steel and Power, was fined A$38,000 (US$25,800) after discharging about 30 tonnes of coal into a waterway in April 2024 from its Russell Vale Colliery site in New South Wales. The mine has not been operating since mid-January.

 

 Bangladesh: An NGO has called on the new government to cancel the Phulbari coal permit granted to UK-based Asia Energy, drop the charges against community opponents of the mine and compensate the three families of those killed in 2006 protests against mining.

 

 China: Seven people died in a coal mine accident at a mine in the Wutongqiao district in the city of Leshan in Sichuan province.

 

 India: The National Company Law Tribunal has approved Adani Power's US$490 million purchase of Lanco Amarkantak Power, which owns the 600 MW Amarkantak coal plant. A 1320 MW expansion of the plant commenced in 2015 but is only part-built.

 

 India: The National Company Law Tribunal has approved Adani Power's US$490 million purchase of Lanco Amarkantak Power, which owns the 600 MW Amarkantak coal plant. A 1320 MW expansion of the plant commenced in 2015 but is only part-built.

 

 India: The National Company Law Tribunal has approved Adani Power's US$490 million purchase of Lanco Amarkantak Power, which owns the 600 MW Amarkantak coal plant. A 1320 MW expansion of the plant commenced in 2015 but is only part-built.

 

 New Zealand: Bathurst Resources aims to use the new conservative government's fast-track planning process for two new coal mines: one on the Buller Plateau and along with the Rotowaro Extension near Huntly.

 

 South Africa: Union members and civil society groups called on Glencore to stop selling coal to Israel.

 

 UK: A UK court has agreed to a South African request to extradite 77-year-old Michael Lomas to face 41 charges related to US$41.5 million paid in bribes between 2015 and 2017 for work on Eskom's 4800 MW Kusile coal plant.

 

 US: Jay Justice failed to appear at a federal court hearing on a lawsuit against Bluestone Coke over pollution from its mothballed coking plant in north Birmingham. Justice is the son of West Virginia governor and Republican Senate candidate Jim Justice.

 

 Zimbabwe: The Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Authority instituted power rationing after a technical fault cut the capacity of the Hwange coal plant.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Polish coal miner books US$305 million write-off as demand slides: Bogdanka has written off 1.17 billion zloty (US$305 million) from the value of its assets due to declining sales. Bogdanka, a coal mining subsidiary of the state-owned power utility Enea SA, attributed the decline in sales to the "clear trend" of increasing renewables capacity. Bogdanka's previous report for the first quarter of 2024 warned that the company's 66 per cent fall in profits was "significantly" affected by lower prices and reduced demand for thermal coal in both the domestic and export markets. About three-quarters of Bogdanka thermal coal sales are for the 3994 MW Kozienice Power Plant and the 1657 MW Polaniec plant, with the remainder sold to other coal power plants. The Polish government elected in late 2023 committed to accelerating the rollout of new renewables capacity but has not yet published its proposed energy strategy. (BNNBloomberg)

US adds sanctions to companies in Russia's coal and steel sectors: The US Department of State and the Department of the Treasury have added 400 businesses and individuals to the Russian sanction list, including entities involved in steel, iron, and coal sectors and firms providing specialised services to metals and mining companies. The Department of State said it included top coal producers and exporters on the list with the aim of limiting "Russia's revenue generation capacity" and to "degrade its military-industrial base". The sanctions include coal mining subsidiaries in the Stroyservis group, coal, iron ore and services companies that are part of the Mechel group and subsidiaries of the coal exporter SDS UGOL. (AP, US Department of State)

US legal challenge against regulator mandating level of coal plant use: The Sierra Club has filed a lawsuit against the Commissioners of the Public Service Commission of West Virginia (PSC) over for their 2021 directive requiring the Appalachian Power Company (APCo) and Wheeling Power Company (WPCo) to operate their coal plants in West Virginia at a capacity factor of 69 per cent. APCo owns and operates the 2932 MW Amos Plant and the 1300 MW Mountaineer Plant, while WPCo owns a 50 per stake in the 1632 MW Mitchell Plant. The lawsuit argues that the commissioners' directives seek to ensure a more significant role for the two utilities in the wholesale market, a matter they argue is solely the role of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The Sierra Club suit states that the seven-year average capacity factors for the APCo and WPCo plants are 55 per cent or lower and argues that requiring a higher capacity factor forces customers to pay higher prices. (WV Public Broadcasting, Sierra Club)

Pakistan looks to overhaul debt payments on Chinese power projects: Pakistan's Minister for Power, Awais Leghari, said the government wants to renegotiate the terms of debt repayment with Chinese independent power producers. The government also wants to rely less on expensive imported thermal coal and switch where possible to lignite from the Thar coalfields. Leghari said the review is a joint project with the Chinese government and aims to achieve "a win-win situation for everyone". (Pakistan Today)

Two US coal companies merge: Arch Resources and CONSOL Energy announced a merger agreement to form Core Natural Resources, a US-based coal company that plans to focus on exports into the Asian market. Consol CEO James Brock told analysts he expected more than 67 per cent of the company's production would be exported to Asian markets. In 2023, the two companies sold about 101 million US short tons (91.6 million tonnes) of thermal and metallurgical coal. The combined company will operate 11 mines and holds stakes in two eastern US coal export terminals that entitle it to export up to 25 million US short tons (22.7 million tonnes) a year. The companies aim to complete the merger in early 2025, subject to regulatory and other approvals. (Reuters, Arch Coal)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Japanese steel companies buy into Australian mine: Whitehaven Coal has entered into agreements to sell 20 per cent of its Blackwater metallurgical coal mine in Queensland to Nippon Steel Corporation (NSC) for US$720 million and a 10 per cent stake to JFE Steel (JFE) for $US360 million. As part of the deal, NSC and JFE have entered into long-term coal purchase agreements, but the details are not public. The Blackwater open-cut mine has operated since 1967 and has produced over 500 million tonnes of coal. BMA, a joint venture between BHP and Mitsubishi Development, sold the mine to Whitehaven in June 2024 for US$2.1 billion. The Blackwater deposit extends for almost 80 kilometres, and current raw coal production is 12 to 13 million tonnes per annum. Whitehaven Coal is seeking approval for its Blackwater North Extension Project, which could extend the life of the mine to 2085. Fiona Deutsch from the Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility said NSC and JFE should be investing in greener steel technologies "instead of doubling down on the highest-emitting part of the steel supply chain". (Mining.com, Whitehaven Coal [Pdf], Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility​)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Forging a sustainable future: Brazil's opportunity to lead in steel decarbonisation, Global Energy Monitor, August 2024.

This 17-page brief provides a concise overview of Brazil's steel sector and the potential to transition to green steel production. Brazil is the world's ninth-largest steel producer

Koalas or coal mines, how the federal government can help save Australia's most iconic species, Queensland Conservation Council, August 2024. (Pdf)

This 36-page report finds 26 proposed new coal mines in New South Wales and Queensland could clear about 1644 hectares of koala habitat. The coal produced from the mines would produce about 8.2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions when burnt.

links.text: Global Energy Monitor and Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)
