title: CoalWire 529, September 5, 2024
excerpt: Danish coal unit closes; South Korean court orders new emission target.
content:
September 5, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

At the height of the 2022 European energy crisis, regulators delayed the retirement of some coal units and brought some mothballed plants back online. Two years on and many of those coal units are now going offline for good. The latest are two of Orsted's coal units in Denmark. In South Korea, a court ruling ordering the legislature to adopt a binding emissions reduction target for 2031 to 2049 will increase pressure for the retirement of the country's fleet of coal plants.

In Poland, the new government is rethinking the previous government's plan to shift coal plants and mines into a new taxpayer-funded entity. The rethink comes as Polish coal generation has declined as renewables capacity increases. In South Africa, the Presidential Climate Commission has outlined potential options for economic diversification in Mpumalanga province, the country's dominant coal-producing region.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Just 15 countries account for 98 per cent of new coal-power development

The number of countries with coal power under development has nearly halved from 75 in 2014 to just 40 in 2024. Almost all of the coal-power capacity under development is concentrated in just 15 countries, with China and India alone accounting for 86 per cent, write Lucy Hummer, Jeanette Lim, Jelena Babajeva, Claire Pitre and Xing Zhang from Global Energy Monitor in Carbon Brief.

 

 Biden administration backs plastic as coal replacement to make steel. One critic asks: 'Have they lost their minds?'

The decision by the Department of Energy to provide a loan guarantee of up to US$182.6 million for a project to use plastic as a coal substitute in steel mills has stunned clean air advocates, writes James Bruggers in Inside Climate News.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Danish coal unit closed

Orsted closed the 407 megawatt (MW) Esbjerg combined heat and power plant in Denmark on August 31. The plant previously used about 500,000 tonnes of coal a year. The Danish utility also announced the closure of the 380 MW unit 4 at the Studstrup Power Station in Denmark. In October 2022, at the height of the European energy crisis, Danish regulators ordered Orsted to keep the Esbjerg plant operating and resume generation at the mothballed Studstrup unit. The 362 MW unit 3 at the Studstrup plant is still online. The unit currently uses coal as a reserve fuel, but this is likely to cease later this year after the rebuilding of the biomass storage silo after a fire caused significant damage. (Power Engineering, Orsted)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 US regulator proposes fence to cut coal dust pollution at export terminal: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) has released a draft permit to cut coal dust emissions from CSX Transportation's Curtis Bay coal export terminal in Baltimore. The draft permit proposes CSX Transportation build a barrier to "prevent coal dust from being transported from any coal storage piles on the site into the surrounding community". It proposes that if CSX doesn't build a roofed structure, then the coal stockpiles must be lower than the barrier. The permit proposes requiring CSX to spray water on all incoming coal wagons and upgrade the current water spray system in the coal unloading shed. The draft permit is open for public comment until October 10, 2024. The Community of Curtis Bay Association and South Baltimore Community Land Trust said they will review the draft permit. Community opposition to CSX grew after a December 2021 explosion at the terminal spread a plume of coal dust across neighbouring suburbs. (Baltimore Banner, Maryland Department of the Environment)

 

 Human Rights Watch urges Turkiye to reject the expansion of lignite plant: Human Rights Watch has encouraged Turkiye's Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change to reject the proposed addition of two new 344 MW coal units at the Afsin-Elbistan power plant. The Afsin-Elbistan lignite plant has operated since 1984, with a series of expansions lifting capacity to 2460 MW. A 2022 Greenpeace Mediterranean study estimated the existing plant had caused about 17,000 deaths from air pollution. A recent Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) report estimated the proposed expansion would cause an additional 1900 premature deaths. Residents, health, and environmental groups oppose the proposed expansion. Part A of the plant was privatised in 2018 and sold to Celikler Holding, which did not respond to questions by HRW on its pollution control measures. (Human Rights Watch, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Court orders South Korea set medium-term emissions reduction target: The Constitutional Court of Korea has unanimously ordered the South Korean legislature to amend the Carbon Neutrality Basic Act to set legally binding greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets for the 2031-2049 period. The court directed the new target must be in place by the end of February 2026. The current act sets the goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 but does not include any obligations for the 2031 to 2049 period. Youth 4 Climate Action argued that the current target under the act is insufficient and the absence of binding targets after 2031 violated the constitutional rights of future generations. The court agreed that the absence of legally binding targets for greenhouse gas reductions for the period from 2031-49 "would transfer an excessive burden to the future" but found the current 2030 target is sufficient. South Korea's 41,884 MW coal fleet generates about 40 per cent of its electricity. A further 1050 MW of coal capacity is under construction. (Guardian, Reuters)

 

 Hundreds protest forest clearing for Indian mine expansion: Villagers and tribal groups have resumed protests against the clearing of part of the Hasdeo Arand forest for the expansion of the Parsa East and Kete Basan (PEKB) coal mine in Chhattisgarh. Activists said that police detained over 100 villagers to allow the clearing of a large part of a 74-hectare block of forest allocated to state-owned utility Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Ltd (RRVUNL). A 2024 winner of the Goldman Prize, Alok Shukla from the Chhattisgarh Bachao Andolan, said local village councils have not given their consent for coal mining in the area. The Chhattisgarh assembly supported a 2022 resolution opposing mining in the Hasdeo Arand forest but the recently-elected Bharatiya Janata Party government has backed the project. Police claim none of the protesters were detained but confirmed they were removed to other areas. (Hindustan Times, ABPLive)

 

 South African agency directed to investigate Eskom contracts: President Cyril Ramaphosa has authorised the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), a dedicated anti-corruption agency, to investigate nine Eskom contracts, including agreements with the Gupta family company, Tegeta Exploration and Resources. The investigation includes Eskom's 659 million rand prepayment in 2016 to Tegeta Resources and Exploration and a contract to supply coal from the Brakfontein Colliery Mine to Eskom's Majuba and Matla power stations. Another contract referred to by the SIU was the 1.68 billion rand guarantee Eskom provided to Tegeta in late 2015 for coal from Optimum Coal Mine for the Hendrina Power Station. The guarantee allowed Tegeta to purchase the mine from Glencore. Three weeks before the transaction, the Guptas transferred about half the shares in Tegata to a company in which Duduzane Zuma, the son of then-President Jacob Zuma, held a minority stake. Following the Zondo Commission of Inquiry into Allegations of State Capture, the Gupta brothers fled South Africa and their coal interests were placed into administration and subsequently sold. (BusinessTech, Special Investigating Unit)

 

 German state elections cast a shadow over energy transition: Elections in two former East German states have seen record results for the far-right AfD, which topped the poll in the small state of Thuringia and ran second in Saxony. Other parties have ruled out forming a coalition with the AfD, which opposes the current German climate policy. The refusal of other parties to work with the AfD bolsters the negotiating position of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which came third in both states after receiving 15.8 per cent and 11.8 per cent of votes in Thuringia and Saxony, respectively. Sahra Wagenknecht was a former member of the federal parliament for The Left party until 2023 before launching BSW in January. Like AfD, BSW has embraced support for the continued operation of lignite plants and right-wing criticisms of other climate policies, such as phasing out fossil fuel cars. Voters in Brandenburg, the fifth largest state in Germany, go to the polls on September 8. The election result increases pressure on the federal government coalition of the Christian Democratic Union, the Greens and the Free Democrats ahead of the September 2025 national election. In Thuringia and Saxony, both the Greens and the Free Democrats failed to reach the five per cent threshold required to win seats. (Clean Energy Wire, Deutsche Welle)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Queensland government will fund Stanmore Resources' construction of a 20 MW gas plant to use methane from the Stanmore South Walker Creek metallurgical coal mine.

 

 Australia: Coal generation in the National Electricity Market, the electricity grid for the eastern states, has dipped below 50 per cent over a whole week for the first time.

 

 Australia: A district court judge overturned a three-month prison sentence for Laura Davey, who blocked access to equipment at a coal export terminal in Newcastle. The judge reduced her fine from A$1100 (US$738) to A$800 (US$537) on condition she did not commit further offences.

 

 India: Two thousand people staged a sit-in protest against plans by Coal India to establish a coal mine waste dump in a residential area of Margherita in Assam.

 

 Indonesia: Low Tuck Kwong, Indonesia's fourth richest person, transferred a 20 per cent stake in his coal company, Bayan Resources, to his youngest daughter Elaine Low. The stake is worth US$6.55 billion. Low Tuck Kwong retains a 40.15 per cent stake in the company which produced about 45 million tonnes of coal in 2023.

 

 South Africa: The Chinese company Kinetic Development Group has bought a 51 per cent stake in MC Mining, a company that has struggled to finance the development of the proposed Makhado metallurgical coal mine in Limpopo province. The mine received environmental approval in 2013.

 

 South Africa: The Supreme Court of Appeals has reserved its judgement in the 'Deadly Air' case brought by a groundWork and the Vukani Environmental Justice Movement over regulations to protect residents of the Highveld Priority Area.

 

 US: A federal judge has found Bluestone Coke, the company's manager, Donald Wiggins, and company president, James Justice, guilty of civil contempt. The judge ordered them to comply with discovery requests by Black Warrior Riverkeeper and Greater-Birmingham Alliance to Stop Pollution as part of a lawsuit over emissions from the mothballed coke plant.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Cost of outage mounts after fire at Japanese coal and biomass plant: JERA's 1070 MW Taketoyo No.5 coal and biomass-fired plant remains offline after a fire at the plant in late January 2024. JERA is a 50-50 joint venture between a subsidiary of Tokyo Electric Power Company and Chubu Electric Power. In a briefing on the fire, JERA outlined that the fire burned for over five hours with an explosion causing extensive damage to part of the boiler building. The briefing identified a series of design flaws that led to the blast in the wood pellet conveyor system and noted there were three other occasions where smoke was detected in the conveyor system after JERA commissioned the unit in August 2022. JERA said the aim is to resume generation at the unit "as soon as possible". JERA used biomass pellets from Vietnam and the US to provide up to 17 per cent of the fuel used at the plant. JERA estimates the cost of the fire in the 2024-2025 financial year at more than US$68.5 million, in large part due to higher fuel costs at other plants. (Argus Media, JERA [Pdf])

Report urges short-term jobs strategy for South African coal region: The Presidential Climate Commission has urged the South African government to support a short-term economic diversification strategy for Mpumalanga province ahead of the closure of coal mines and power stations. The report estimates between 12,000 and 24,000 coal sector jobs could be lost in Mpumalanga province by 2030. About 231 million tonnes of coal is produced in the province, 87 per cent of South Africa's total. The province also hosts 11 Eskom coal plants and Sasol's Secunda coal-to-oil plant. The current unemployment rate in the province is 38 per cent, but the report notes that there are about 1.16 million formal jobs outside the agricultural sector. The report estimates the rapid expansion of the region's wood processing, citrus and citrus-processing sector and tourism industry could create between 33,000 and 47,000 direct jobs by 2030. The report also suggests new activities such as the production and processing of industrial hemp, sustainable aviation fuel production and agrivoltaics in farming could create up to 60,000 additional jobs. (Moneyweb, Presidential Climate Commission [Pdf])

Germany seeks clarity from South Africa and delayed coal closures: Germany's state secretary and special envoy for international climate action, Jennifer Morgan, said she is hoping to gain a better understanding of the South African government's revised coal closure timetable and the impact on greenhouse gas emission reductions. Germany is part of the coalition of countries and institutions committed to funding the US$9.3 billion Just Energy Transition Partnership. In July, the government announced that it would extend the life of three coal plants until 2030 but suggested Eskom could make emission reductions at other plants. (Bloomberg)

Pakistan pursues a study on switching coal plants to domestic lignite: Pakistan's Ministry of Energy has established a four-person committee to review the feasibility of switching four coal plants that rely on imported coal to run on domestic lignite. The primary task of the committee is to prepare joint bankable technical and financial feasibility studies with the current independent power producers to convert three imported coal plants to Thar lignite. The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) financed three plants: the 1320 MW Sahiwal, Port Qasim and Hubco plants. About 7 million tonnes of coal a year is imported for the plants at a cost of about US$1.5 billion, with the Hubco and Port Wasim plants located at coal import terminals. In a meeting with Chinese officials, Pakistan suggested financing the plant conversions could be done by local banks and not affect current loan agreements with Chinese banks. (The Express Tribune, Business Recorder, Business Recorder)

Poland stalls coal plants spinoff plan: Poland's Minister for State Assets, Jakub Jaworowski, has revealed there is no allocation in the budget for the establishment of the National Energy Security Agency (NABE), a new agency proposed by the previous government to hold state-owned coal plants and associated mines. The original plan was to shift the coal assets of PGE, Tauron, and Enea to the taxpayer-backed NABE, allowing the plants to operate up to 2049 and letting the coal-free utilities raise international funding for wind and other projects. Jaworowski described the previous government's plan as "a nuclear option" and suggested different options are under consideration. He said the government's preferred option will be clarified "in less than a year". In April, the Minister for Industry, Marzena Czarnecka, suggested the new government was considering linking coal plants with specific mines. Poland has a 28,457 MW fleet of coal and lignite plants that generate about 60 per cent of its electricity. (Financial Post)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Nippon Steel plans for coal in the US: Nippon Steel Corporation, the world's fourth-largest steel producer, announced it will spend US$300 million to reline the No 14 blast furnace at its Gary Works in Indiana if it completes the takeover of US Steel. The project would extend the life of the coal-based blast furnace by up to 20 years. In December 2023, NSC announced it had reached an agreement to buy US Steel for US$14.9 billion. NSC expects to complete the purchase of US Steel later this year. Caroline Ashley from SteelWatch said NSC's announcement indicated that the company planned to "lock in high-emission steel production for decades". The Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility (ACCR) said NSC's decision signalled it wouldn't be a leader in the transition to green steel production. ACCR said NSC's current emissions reduction targets only apply to its Japanese steelworks, not overseas plants. Last week, the major Australian coal mining company, Whitehaven Coal, announced NSC had agreed to buy 20 per cent of the Blackwater metallurgical coal mine in Queensland for US$720 million. Whitehaven Coal is seeking approval for its Blackwater North Extension Project, which could extend the life of the mine to 2085. (Nippon Steel Corporation, SteelWatch)

 

 Report says deadly toll from ArcelorMittal's Kazakh steelworks: Pollution from ArcelorMittal's Temirtau steel plant in Kazakhstan is estimated to have caused 3000 deaths and 2600 cases of childhood asthma between 1996 and December 2023, according to a new report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). CREA estimates the health costs of damage from PM2.5 fine particle pollution, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides emitted by the plant at US$4.2 billion. After years of public alarm over pollution from the plant and the deaths of 140 workers, the government forced ArcelorMittal to sell the plant to a state-controlled entity, Qazaqstan Investment Corporation. ArcelorMittal is the world's second-largest steel producer. The company produced 58.1 million tonnes of crude steel in 2023. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Fossil Fuels are a Health Hazard, Doctors for the Environment, August 2024. (Pdf)

This 38-page report reviews the health hazards to Australians from the continued growth of the fossil fuel sector.

links.text: (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)
Fossil Fuels are a Health Hazard

title: CoalWire 530, September 12, 2024
excerpt: China dominates new coal mine proposals; South Korean mine closes; Indonesia offers coal concession to a third religious group; study downgrades CCS potential.
content:
September 12, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

A new Global Energy Monitor (GEM) report revealing China's domination of proposed coal mining capacity highlights the risk of massive methane emissions from new mines. The report also highlights how China is also sucking in large volumes of coal from Indonesia, Russia, Mongolia and Australia, supporting new mines and mine expansions in those countries.

Indonesia's outgoing President, Joko Widodo, has offered a coal concession to a third religious organisation. The move to support major religious organisations with income from coal has sparked dissent from some followers concerned about the impacts on the global climate and local communities. The closure of South Korea's largest coal mine moves the country one step closer to ending domestic coal production, with the last remaining mine set to close in 2025. In another significant development, a new study argues the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has significantly overestimated the realistic storage potential of carbon capture and storage, a technology promoted by the coal industry as a technical fix to carbon dioxide emissions in the power sector.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Rethinking coal: lessons from Vietnam's termination of the Song Hau 2 coal power project

Vietnam's recent termination of the Song Hau 2 coal plant is not an isolated case. The cancellations of the Vinh Tan 3 project in Vietnam, Cirebon 3 in Indonesia, Sual 2 in the Philippines, and Krabi in Thailand all tell the same story: coal is losing its investment case, writes Christina Ng in Eco-Business.

 

 Campaign money? Bribes? Lobbying? Your utility rates may include some, advocates say

Eleven US states this year are considering legislation to keep utilities from passing on political-related expenses to consumers, writes Medora Less in USA Today.

 

 Hwange's coal-mining horrors in Zimbabwe

Up to 2000 people in the village of Dinde face eviction from their homes if the Zimbabwean government presses ahead with a plan to allow a Chinese-owned company, Beifa Investments, to build a coal mine and thermal power station, writes Oscar Nkala in Oxpeckers.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Korea's largest coal mine closes as the country's coal production declines

South Korea's state-owned coal mining company, Korea Coal Corporation (KCC), has closed the Jangseong Coal Mine. The mine, which was the country's largest, first began production in 1936 when South Korea was under Japanese occupation. Production from the underground mine declined rapidly over the last decade to just 67,000 tonnes last year. In March 2022, the government reached an agreement with the union for KCC employees to close the loss-making Jangseong, Hwasun, and Dogye mines by 2025. The Hwasun mine closed in June 2023, and the Dogye mine will close in 2025. (Korea Times)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 China's proposed new coal mines dominate the global project list: A report by researchers from Global Energy Monitor (GEM) estimates China is developing about 1.28 billion tonnes of annual coal production capacity, accounting for nearly half of all proposed production from mines of more than one million tonnes a year. GEM estimates that almost 80 per cent of the proposed mines are greenfield projects. China currently produces about 3.9 billion tonnes of coal from mines producing more than one million tonnes a year. The provinces of Shanxi and Inner Mongolia account for more than half of China's current coal production and one-third of global capacity. GEM estimates China's coal mines emit about 52.7 billion cubic metres of methane a year, about 70 per cent of the worldwide total from mines over the one million tonnes a year threshold. China's domestic coal production was supplemented in 2023 by 474 million tonnes of imported coal, with Indonesia supplying 220 million tonnes and Russia 102 million tonnes. (Reuters, The Business Times, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Call to suspend hearing on Canadian mine while court hears challenge: The Municipal District of Ranchland, country music star Corb Lund and the Pekisko Group, a group of ranchers, have requested the Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) abandon a public hearing on Northback Holdings' proposed Grassy Mountain metallurgical coal exploration project while the Court of Appeal is considering a legal challenge. Alberta Court of Appeal Justice Kevin Feth recently granted the Municipal District of Ranchland's application to appeal against an Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) decision granting three applications by Northback Resources for the project. In a letter to the AER, the municipality stated that if the court rules in its favour, the Northback application will be void. In this case, the municipality warned, it would have wasted time and resources preparing written submissions and attending two weeks of hearings. The Municipal District of Ranchland said the AER had adjourned hearings on other projects when they could be affected by subject court proceedings. (CBC)

 

 Another Indonesian Islamic group ponders offer of a coal concession: The Indonesian Islamic Da'wah Institute (LDII), a religious group with about 15 million members, is considering the offer made by the outgoing President Joko Widodo of a coal concession. LDII Chairman Chriswanto Santoso said the group is assessing the proposal "to ensure that we don't become victims". LDII is the third Indonesian religious organisation to be offered coal mining permits by the government. Two other Islamic organisations, Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) and Muhammadiyah, have agreed to accept coal concessions. Some members of the groups have expressed alarm about the involvement in the coal trade, both for its role in fuelling climate change and significant impacts on local communities. Legal changes to allow the granting of coal permits to religious organisations came into effect earlier this year. (Indonesia Business Post)

 

 Study suggests IPCC has overestimated carbon capture potential: Researchers from Imperial College London estimate the potential for carbon capture and storage (CCS) is five to six times less than the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) estimate of up to 30 gigatons of carbon dioxide a year by 2050. The study, published in Nature Communications, reviewed the potential contributions from CCS across ten geographic regions that have active or planned projects and found the best-case scenario is the storage of about 5-6 gigatons a year by 2050, with the US contributing about one gigatonne a year. The study argues the IPCC includes "unrealistic" projections of CCS deployment, especially in Asian countries including China, Indonesia, and South Korea. (Mongabay, Nature Communications)

 

 Court challenge to Bangladesh coal supply contract: The Coal Power Generation Company Bangladesh (CPGCB) has warned that coal generation at the 1200 megawatt (MW) Matabari coal plant at Cox's Bazar could cease operating in about a month if a legal case over a coal tender is not resolved soon. In June three unsuccessful tenderers alleged that CPGCB awarded a three-year coal supply contract to a company disqualified during the tender process. The following month, the High Court suspended the contract for six months while the case was before the court. CPGCB said it has a stockpile of about 280,000 tonnes of coal, and Sumitomo had delivered the last shipment due under its now-expired contract. Bangladesh's Anti-Corruption Commission has launched an investigation into the allegations. (Dhaka Tribune)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Queensland Office of the Work Health and Safety Prosecutor has charged Mastermyne with industrial manslaughter over the 2021 death of a coal miner at the Crinum underground mine. The case is the first time a mining company has been charged with industrial manslaughter after legal changes came into effect in 2020.

 

 Bulgaria: Sofia's municipal government has banned the use of coal and wood for home heating in nine of the city's 29 districts from January 2025. The city will ban wood and coal heating from all districts by 2029.

 

 Canada: CTI Plus Resources has proposed the 1.75 million tonnes per year Rocky Creek metallurgical coal mine in British Columbia.

 

 Canada: Conuma Resources has restarted production at the Quintette metallurgical coal mine in British Columbia. The company bought the mine in 2022 from Teck Resources, which had mothballed the project in 2000 due to low prices.

 

 Netherlands: Activists project "Deny debt to Glencore" onto ING's headquarters in Amsterdam.

 

 Philippines: DMCI is lobbying for the December 2020 moratorium on new coal to exclude areas outside the main power grid.

 

 Philippines: Meralco PowerGen Corporation is seeking Department of Energy certification that the proposed 1200 MW Atimonan coal plant is not affected by the December 2020 moratorium on new coal plants.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Poland submits draft EU energy plan as solar installation surges: Poland's draft national energy and climate plan for the European Commission proposes achieving 56 per cent of electricity from renewables by 2030. Poland generated 61 per cent of its electricity from coal in 2023, with wind and solar contributing 21 per cent, according to data from Ember. The four parties in the governing coalition have differing views on the preferred pace of decarbonising the power sector, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk from the Civic Coalition previously backing the former conservative government's pledge to keep coal mines operating until 2049. The previous government instituted a quasi-ban on onshore wind farms and opposed European Union emissions reduction targets. Solar capacity has been growing rapidly in the last few years, with about 4600 MW added in 2023 and capacity reaching about 19,233 MW at the end of June 2024. In 2019, Poland had about 1000 MW of solar capacity. (Reuters, BNN Bloomberg, PV Magazine)

US govt unveils funding for clean energy projects for rural co-ops: The US government has announced US$7.3 billion in financing from the Empowering Rural America (New ERA) program for clean energy projects proposed by 16 rural electric cooperatives. The announcement included funding for 3723 MW of wind and 4733 MW of solar projects. In the 1930's the US government provided funding to rural electric cooperatives to provide rural customers with electricity. The cooperatives now account for about 13 per cent of national electricity generation. The National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NECRA), a lobby group for 896 rural electric cooperatives, estimates about 30 per cent of the electricity supplied by the sector is from coal plants. While renewables projects now supply cheaper electricity, many coops have resisted the transition to renewables in part due to the difficulty in accessing capital for new plants. NECRA remains a strong defender of coal and has recently filed objections to requirements for stricter pollution standards for mercury and other air pollutants and a rule to tighten the regulation of pollution for coal ash dumps. (Utility Dive, US Department of Agriculture)

US sanctions slow development of Russian coal project: Vladimir Kolmogorov, the CEO of the Russian aluminium smelting company En+ CEO, told a Russian news outlet that sanctions are affecting its plans to develop the open-cut Zashulansky coal deposit. Since 2012, the Razrezugol joint venture between En+ Group and China Energy Investment Corporation has encountered a range of delays. Razrezugol recently proposed commissioning a five million tonnes a year mine by the end of 2027 for sales to both the domestic and export markets. Kolmogorov said EN+'s Chinese partners are concerned about delays due to sanctions. The US government recently widened sanctions to include projects that could support the country's military manufacturing base. In April this year, EN+ said initial works on the mine were on schedule and that it planned to spend 50 billion rubles (US$554 million) on the project, including a new road, transmission line and rail connection. (Moscow Times)

Indian steel producer plans to double capacity at its Mozambique mine: The Steel Authority of India plans to double the capacity of its Benga metallurgical coal mines in Mozambique to about 4.5 million tonnes per annum over the next three to four years. The Chairman of SAIL, Amarendu Prakash, said coal from the mine expansion is for its use. SAIL owns a 47 per cent stake in International Coal Ventures Ltd (ICVL), the special-purpose vehicle owned jointly by Indian government-owned companies including Coal India and NTPC. ICVL has issued a tender for a mining company to operate the site. ICVL bought Rio Tinto Coal Mozambique's stake in the Benga project in 2014. ICVL mothballed the project the following year when international prices slumped but restarted exports in 2018. The mine has a capacity of 2 million tonnes a year, but in the financial year to the end of March produced about 1.24 million tonnes. (Hindu Business Line)

Pakistan banks wary of funding switch to local lignite: The Thar Coal and Energy Board, a Sindh provincial government agency promoting the development of Thar lignite projects, has lamented the lack of interest by Pakistani banks in financing the conversion of imported coal projects to Thar lignite. Previously, the chief minister of Sindh lobbied the federal minister to require the State Bank of Pakistan to mandate commercial banks provide up to three per cent of their deposits by 2027 to fund local energy projects. An anonymous bank official said banks are concerned about the pollution impacts of coal projects while the central bank prefers to finance renewables projects. Chinese banks financed the current imported coal plants through the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor. (The News International)

Germany seeking more details on emissions reductions by South Africa: A delegation of senior German government officials, including the state secretary for Germany's economic cooperation and development ministry, Jochen Flasbarth, met with the South African government and Eskom officials last week to clarify plans for the shift away from coal generation. Flasbarth said that while Eskom's proposed delayed closure of three coal plants until next decade is "not ideal", Germany will continue to support the US$9.3 billion Just Energy Transition Partnership. Eskom has previously suggested offsetting the increased emissions from retaining the three plants against reduced utilisation at other plants. Flasbarth said South Africa will provide details of intended emissions reductions to achieve the agreed targets. (Business Tech)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Deadly toll from Brazilian steel plant pollution: The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates air pollution from the Ternium Brasil Santa Cruz steelworks in Rio de Janeiro has caused about 1200 deaths between 2010 and 2023. The plant was initially commissioned in 2010 by a joint venture between the German steel group ThyssenKrupp and the Brazilian mining multinational Vale. The Luxembourg-based Ternium bought the plant in 2017. The steelworks can produce about five million tonnes of steel a year. CREA's health impact analysis of the plant estimates air pollutants, including sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxide and PM2.5 fine particle pollution, reach Sao Paulo, more than 300 kilometres away. CREA estimates the air pollution from the steelworks and the captive power plant has imposed an economic cost of US$1.8 billion between 2010 to 2023. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 US looks to block Nippon Steel's takeover of US Steel: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the US (CFIUS), a US government inter-agency committee, has written to Nippon Steel Corporation (NSC), flagging concern that its proposed US$14.9 billion takeover of US Steel could result in less domestic production. In a 17-page letter, the committee suggested a NSC-owned US Steel would be less likely to support tariffs on foreign steel imports, which would undercut local steel production. CFIUS cast reduced domestic steel production capacity as a national security issue. Unions oppose NSC's takeover. Vice-President Kamala Harris said she wants US Steel to be "American owned and operated" while Donald Trump has opposed the deal. NSC recently indicated it remains committed to coal-based steel production, announcing plans to reline the No 14 blast furnace at its Gary Works in Indiana and agreed to buy 20 per cent of the Blackwater metallurgical coal mine in Queensland, which could operate until 2085 if an expansion plan is approved. A coalition of US unions, sections of the steel industry, think tanks, and environmental groups has proposed the Modern Steel Act to promote low-emissions steel. The proposed legislation has the support of steel producer Cleveland-Cliffs and the American Iron and Steel Institute but not US Steel. (Reuters, Recycling Today)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

"Fossil fuel industry influence in higher education: A review and a research agenda", Wiley, September 5, 2024.

This paper explores the role of the fossil fuel industry in delaying climate action through its ties to higher education in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia.

Plugging the Leaks: Mapping Methane Regulation in Queensland, Environmental Defenders Office, September 2024. (Pdf)

This 50-page report finds that there is nothing in the Queensland Government's new emissions reduction laws to make companies rein in their fugitive methane emissions.

“Fossil fuel industry influence in higher education: A review and a research agenda”

title: CoalWire 531, September 19, 2024
excerpt: UK court overturns mine approval; US utility pays US$100 million to settle charges over bribery scandal; interim Bangladesh government plans to review Adani power imports deal; Pakistan sets new deadline for new Chinese-backed 300 MW coal plant.
content:
September 19, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The decision of the High Court to overturn approval for a new UK metallurgical coal mine is significant on a number of front. Notably, the judge rejected the argument that new coal would only substitute for coal produced elsewhere. The decision also signals that just because a mine produces metallurgical coal, it shouldn't get a climate policy free pass. In the US, the Securities and Exchange Commission has agreed to FirstEnergy's US$100 million offer to settle charges stemming from the US$60 million Ohio bribery scandal.

In Switzerland, a court has rejected an application to unfreeze US$310 million held by six Swiss banks federal prosecutors believe could be associated with investments in Adani shares. The company is in the news elsewhere, too. n Bangladesh, the interim government is keen to scrutinise the contract to buy power from Adani's controversial Godda project in India that the Modi government supported. In India, the Modi government has also just reapproved the proposed Gare Palma Sector-II mine that would affect over 13,000 people.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 South Africa's move to green energy was slowed down by government to protect coal mining

Policymakers across the just energy transition sector should work to understand the fear of any "transition" in a post-colonial, post-apartheid state. The legacy of colonialism means there is little trust in the global north, writes Thokozani Chilenga-Butao from the University of the Witwatersrand in The Conversation.

 

 Risky arsenic and radium levels found in coal ash near North Carolina daycare centre

Test results of the soil near a North Carolina daycare centre reveal "unacceptable levels" of carcinogens and radioactivity in the coal ash placed there decades ago as fill dirt, writes Nate Morabito in WCNC Charlotte.

 

 Philippine coal mine roars into production amid waves of complaints

The commencement of a new coal mine by the San Miguel Corporation has sparked complaints over truck traffic, the impact on displaced families and accusations the company has breached a provincial ban on open-pit mining, writes Bong S. Sarmiento in Mongabay.

 

 A coal plant bulldozed an Ohio town, displacing residents. Now, its owners include a big Trump donor

Faced with increasing pressure to reduce pollution from its Gavin coal plant, American Electric Power bought the entire town for US$20 million and bulldozed it. The current owner of the plant, Lightstone Generation, is partly owned by private equity firm Blackstone, whose CEO is a major backer of Donald Trump's re-election bid as US President, writes Oliver Milman in the Guardian.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 High Court overturns decision approving new UK coal mine: The High Court has overturned the December 2022 planning permission granted by former Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Levelling Up, Michael Gove, for West Cumbria Mining' (WCM) proposed Whitehaven mine. Mr Justice Holgate ruled in favour of the appeal brought by Friends of the Earth and South Lakes Action on Climate Change. Holgate rejected WCM's claim that coal from the Whitehaven mine would substitute for coal produced elsewhere and would not increase greenhouse gas emissions. He also agreed that Gove had unlawfully agreed the mine would be 'net zero' and would not affect the UK's compliance with its emissions reduction target as the company would purchase international carbon credits. WCM said it would consider the decision. The company could ask the Secretary of State, Angela Rayner, to reconsider the application. (The Guardian, Friends of the Earth, South Lakes Action on Climate Change [Pdf], Cornerstone Barristers)

 

 US utility pays US$100 million fine to settle bribery case: The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has agreed to accept FirstEnergy's offer of US$100 million to settle charges over its role in the Ohio bribery scandal. FirstEnergy acknowledged it paid about US$60 million to GenNow, a group controlled by Republican candidate Larry Householder, who was campaigning to be speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives. Householder routed some funding to other Republican candidates. Shortly after he was elected speaker in early 2019, Householder and FirstEnergy executives worked to pass House Bill 6, which provided a subsidy for FirstEnergy's loss-making nuclear plants. The final bill included subsidies for two coal plants. Householder is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for his role in the affair. The SEC also announced it is suing former FirstEnergy CEO Chuck Jones and accused him of committing securities fraud. In July 2021, FirstEnergy paid US$230 million to settle criminal charges over the bribery scandal. (Cleveland.com, US Securities and Exchange Commission)

 

 US regulator concerned over failure of CCS test well: The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has issued a violation notice to Archer-Daniels-Midland (ADM) over alleged breaches of its permit for a carbon capture and storage (CCS) site at its 335 megawatt (MW) coal-fired Decatur Power Plant in Illinois. The CCS injection well was funded mainly by the US Department of Energy and began commercial operation in 2017 with the aim of burying one million tonnes of Co2 per year. In a September 5 notice to the company, the EPA stated that the company did not monitor the well in line with permit conditions, had allowed the injection of Co2 into "unauthorised zones", and failed to follow the provisions of the emergency response and remediation plan. ADM confirmed that it had detected corrosion in part of one of its two monitoring wells. (Politico, US Environmental Protection Agency [Pdf])

 

 Modi government reapproves Adani mine: The Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate Change has reapproved the environmental permit granted to Maharashtra State Power Generation Company (Mahagenco) for the development of the Gare Palma Sector-II coal mine in Chhattisgarh. Mahagenco has appointed Adani Mining as the project operator and developer. In January 2024, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) overturned the environmental permit for the mine, stating that a September 2019 public meeting on the project, which was the focus of mass public protests, was "not in accordance with the law". The tribunal also noted the lack of studies on the potential hydrological and health impacts of the mine. In reapproving the mine, the ministry reported that the Entrepreneurship Development Institute of India undertook "focused group discussions" in seven of the 14 affected villages. The proposed mine would produce 24 million tonnes of coal a year with the project affecting farmland, forests and more than 13,000 people. (Adani Watch)

 

 Western Balkans coal plant pollution continues: CEE Bankwatch's annual review of coal plant pollution in the Western Balkans has found that Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Serbia emitted 5.7 times the permitted amount in 2023, marginally up on the year before. The Comply or Close report found that small, old coal plants in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Serbia that were due to close in 2023 continue to operate without any penalty imposed by the national government. The Energy Community Secretariat has launched investigations into the plants operating after the expiry of the opt-out deadline for plants not investing in pollution control upgrades. The largest emitter of sulphur dioxide in 2023 was the 300 MW Ugljevik lignite plant in Bosnia and Herzegovina operated by EPS. The utility invested in a desulphurisation unit but, after experiencing technical problems, no longer operates it because it is considered an "economic burden". (BNE Intellinews, CEE Bankwatch Network)

 

 North Macedonia flags 20-year delay to closing old lignite units: The Minister of Environment and Spatial Planning in North Macedonia's new centre-right government, Izet Mexhiti, has flagged delaying the closure of North Macedonia's two lignite plants until 2050. In late 2023, the previous centre-left government proposed replacing the coal plants with 1700 MW of capacity, as well as grid upgrades and energy storage projects as part of its 3 billion (US$3.3 billion) just transition plan. Mexhiti said the government wants increased financial and technical support from the European Union and the US. North Macedonia has the 699 MW REK Bitola lignite plant, comprising three units commissioned between 1982 and 1988, and the 125 MW REK Oslomej plant commissioned in 1980. The state-owned power utility Elektrani na Severna Makedonija (ESM) owns and operates both plants. (Balkan Green Energy News)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Canada: Crowsnest Pass municipal council has agreed to hold a non-binding vote of residents within 90 days on whether they support Northback Holdings' proposed Grassy Mountain coal mine.

 

 India: Residents call for fines for pollution from Goa's coal port operations.

 

 India: Coal India has called for expressions of interest in a proposed gasification project utilising coal from the Sonepur Bazari mine in West Bengal.

 

 India: The government is establishing a police station in Gondalpura in Jharkhand after villagers objected to Adani's proposed coal mine.

 

 Indonesia: PT Adaro Energy Indonesia will seek shareholder support for a plan to sell its 99 per cent stake in its coal mining unit, Adaro Andalan Indonesia. Adaro said spinning off the coal unit would increase the company's access to more sources of finance.

 

 Pakistan: Nine Afghani workers died from methane gas exposure in a mine near Shahrag in Balochistan province.

 

 Ukraine: As Russian troops inch towards Metinvest's Pokrovske mine, Ukraine's steel producers could be forced to import metallurgical coal. Ukraine's steel production has fallen by 70 per cent since Russia invaded in February 2022.

 

 US: The Department of Energy has granted US$6.55 million to the Navajo Transitional Energy Company for a feasibility study of a carbon capture and storage project to extend the life of the Four Corners coal plant in New Mexico.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Swiss court dismisses appeal to unfreeze bank accounts: Switzerland's Federal Criminal Court has rejected an appeal seeking the release of US$310 million held by six Swiss banks. Swiss prosecutors allege Taiwanese businessman Chang Chung-Ling potentially held the funds to invest in the stock of listed Adani companies. The court verdict does not mention Chung-Ling or Adani by name but refers to information in the January 2023 report by Hindenburg Research on the company. The decision indicates that Geneva's public prosecutor began an investigation in December 2021 into possible money laundering and forgery of documents. The decision states that "the appellant is clearly unable to provide the [federal prosecutor's office] with the explanations — in the form of supporting documents — which it should be able to provide in order to dispel the doubts legitimately raised". The Adani Group stated it had "no involvement" in any Swiss court proceedings. (Swissinfo.ch, Federal Criminal Court [Pdf in Swiss])

Interim Bangladesh government to review Adani power imports deal: The interim Bangladesh government, led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, will review the power purchase contract between the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) and the Adani Group. The Adani Group, with the support of the Modi government, reached an agreement to sell power from the 1600 MW Godda power plant in Jharkhand solely to Bangladesh but at a price criticised by clean energy groups as excessive. The plant burns coal imported from Adani's Carmichael coal project in Australia. The Adani Group claims that the BPDB owes the company US$800 million for power purchases. (Hindustan Times)

Pakistan sets new deadline for new Chinese-backed 300 MW coal plant: Shah Jahan Mirza, the Managing Director of the Private Power & Infrastructure Board (PPIB), has written to CIHC Pak Power Company (CPPCL), the company proposing to build a 300 MW coal plant at Gwadar port, setting a September 18 deadline for a response to its concerns about the project. In the absence of a response, the PPIB has warned the government will end its support for the imported coal project. PPIB approved the plant in August 2019 and set the deadline for financial close as April 23, 2020. Since then, the power purchase tariff for the project has been revised upwards three times and the financial close deadline six times. The PPIB says that even though CPPCL has been granted a higher tariff than other imported coal projects under the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor, the company wants a further increase but has not approached the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority's Appellate Tribunal. In 2022, the government, spurred by concern over the cost of electricity from imported coal projects, proposed a solar project as an alternative. CPPCL and the Chinese government rejected the proposal. (Business Recorder)

Underground fire forces Polish met coal producer to trim production: JSW, Poland's largest metallurgical coal producer, has cut forecast coal production in 2024 due to the inability to extinguish a fire in its KWK Pniowek underground mine. JSW informed shareholders that "there is no possibility of eliminating the fire" that began in early December 2023 and said there is no prospect of resuming longwall operations this year. The Polish Treasury holds a 55 per cent stake in JSW. The company forecasts it will produce 12.45 million tonnes in 2024, down from 13.5 million tonnes in 2023. (GMK Center, JSW)

Another Philippines utility seeks to revive a stalled coal plant proposal: Semirara Mining and Power Corporation (SMPC), the largest coal producer in the Philippines, has suggested it will revive its 700 MW expansion of the 900 MW Calaca power station in Batangas. SMPC says reviving the project is contingent on an expansion of transmission capacity. The project was estimated to cost US$1.4 billion in 2013. SMPC, a subsidiary of DMCI Holdings that the Consunji family owns, proposed the expansion a decade ago but the plan stalled due to financial and legal challenges. A 2019 ruling by the Supreme Court blocked power supply agreements between generators and distribution utilities that weren't the result of a competitive tender process. In the wake of the court ruling, DMCI shelved the expansion. SMPC's indication it may revive the project comes as Aboitiz Power has proposed a 169 MW expansion of its Therma Visayas plant, and Meralco PowerGen has proposed proceeding with the 1200MW Atimonan coal plant. (Manila Bulletin)

South African coal producer slashes jobs: The privately-owned Seriti Resources announced plans to cut 1241 jobs from its Middelburg Mine Services (MMS) and Klipspruit South-East mines. The job losses represent almost one-quarter of the workforce at the two mines. About two-thirds of the 7.8 million tonnes of coal from Klipspruit and over half of the 16.5 million tonnes produced at MMS are exported to the global seaborne market. The MMS mine also supplies about 6.5 million tonnes a year via a conveyor system to Eskom for the 300 MW Duvha power station. Seriti bought both mines from South32 in 2021 and was buoyed by the high export market prices, particularly after the European energy crisis of 2022 and 2023. The company said the two mines are "not currently commercially sustainable" due to "market volatility" and Transnet's inability to fully cater for potential exports through the Richards Bay Coal Terminal. The National Union of Mineworkers, which covers the bulk of the employees at the mines, has vowed to campaign against the job cuts. (Seriti Resources)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Public perceptions and attitudes relating to climate change and the just transition in South Africa, Presidential Climate Commission, September 2024. (Pdf)

This 52-page report provides detailed research into public opinions on climate change and a transition away from coal generation to renewables in South Africa.
