title: CoalWire 532, September 26, 2024
excerpt: UK’s last coal power plant set to close; ADB rejects Pakistan’s coal-to-lignite conversion pitch; report finds only four major car companies plan to buy any fossil-free steel by 2030.
content:
September 26, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The impending closure of the 2172 megawatt (MW) Ratcliffe-on-Soar coal plant in the UK marks the end of the country's coal power sector. The rapid decline of coal generation over the last decade was the product of many drivers, including community pressure, government policies and technological shifts. Equally notable is that the transformation of the sector occurred under a conservative government. As the recent election result in the German state of Brandenburg indicates, the transition of regions with well-established mines and power plants rarely runs smoothly.

In Asia, the Indonesian Coal Miners Association told an annual coal industry conference that demand from India and China is likely to peak in 2025, but expects growth in Vietnam and the Philippines markets could largely offset this. While both Vietnam and the Philippines have huge renewables potential, there is well-entrenched resistance to clean energy advocacy. In Vietnam, one environmental defender was released from prison this week, but other clean energy advocates remain in jail. The UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Development has urged the government to explore ways within their legal system to set them free. In the Philippines, protesting against the health impacts of coal power plants is enough to draw the ire of authorities.

In South Asia, the Pakistan government is under pressure to cut reliance on expensive imported thermal coal for power generation. Private mining interests have also lobbied the government to convert imported coal plants to run on domestic lignite. The Asian Development Bank, which initially financed the construction of the recently commissioned 660 MW coal unit at the Jamshoro Power Plant, has ruled out supporting its conversion to lignite.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Consigned to history: the UK delivers on its promise to phase out coal power

The closure of the 2172 MW Ratcliffe-on-Soar coal power plant at the end of September will mark the end of coal generation in the UK. Coal power generation declined from nearly 40 per cent of UK power in 2012, writes Sean Rai-Roche in E3G.

 

 Utilities have to itemize some political spending in other states. They want regulators to keep it secret in Colorado

Xcel Energy and other Colorado utilities are trying to keep detailed records of their political activity secret, which lawmakers and advocates say undermines a law intended to increase transparency and ensure customers aren't charged for their political spending, writes Ishan Thakore in CPR News.

 

 "It's the wild west": Zombie mines multiply in South Africa's opaque coal sector

South Africa's Department of Mineral Resources and Energy lists 200 coal mines in the country, including projects that were closed years ago and left unrehabilitated, writes Julie Bourdin in African Arguments.

 

 Climate-weary Filipinos push back against fossil fuel

Primo Lamela, a development worker, filed complaints over pollution against the power plants in Toledo near where he lives. His actions made him a target for the authorities, writes Ronald O. Reyes in UCA News.

 

 Forests, wildlife 'threatened' by Adani's Gondbahera coal project

Adani's proposal for an underground coal mine in the Singrauli district of Madhya Pradesh has sparked concern over the possible impacts on water, forests and wildlife, writes Ayaskant Das in Adani Watch.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 UN calls on Vietnam to free environmental defenders; one released: Vietnam has released climate advocate and environmental defender Hoang Thi Minh Hong after 15 months in prison for her role with Change, an affiliate of 350.org. Hong founded Change in 2013, but she shut it down in late 2022 as a crackdown on civil society groups gathered pace. She was arrested on May 31, 2023, and subsequently sentenced to three years imprisonment on 'tax evasion' charges, a legal tactic commonly used against civil society advocates. Hong was released a few days after the UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Development, Surya Deva, urged the government to pursue ways within its legal system to pardon or remit the sentences of all environmental human rights defenders who peacefully raised concerns about government policies. Civil society groups have called for the release of all environmental defenders, including environmental lawyer Dang Dinh Bach from the Law and Policy of Sustainable Development Research Center. Bach was arrested in June 2021 and later sentenced to five years in prison after advocating for a shift away from coal. (UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Development [Pdf], 350.org)

 

 Australian government approves three coal projects: Australia's Minister for Environment, Tanya Plibersek, approved three mines on the same day, projects that environmental groups argue will result in about 1.357 billion tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions. Lock the Gate said the approval would permit Whitehaven Coal to clear 457 hectares of habitat for the endangered koala for the expansion of its Narrabri Underground mine. The mine is now approved to operate until 2066. The minister also approved Mach Energy's Mount Pleasant Optimisation Project and Glencore and Yancoal's proposal to revive the closed Ravensworth underground mine. All three mines are in New South Wales. (Guardian, Lock the Gate, Environmental Justice Australia)

 

 Iranian coal mine blast kills at least 49 workers: An underground mine explosion has killed at least 49 workers and injured others at Madanjoo's Parvardeh coal mine in South Khorasan province. The mine has a capacity of about 200,000 tonnes a year. The governor of the province, Ali Akbar Rahimi, said the province produces about 75 per cent of the country's coal with about eight to ten significant operations. Madanjoo also operates the Darbidkhun and Hotkan Coal Mines, which have a capacity of about 100,000 tonnes a year. Iran's coal mines have a long history of major accidents, with 42 miners killed in a 2017 explosion. (ABC News, Al Jazeera)

 

 Election result in German lignite state forces political realignment: The ruling Social Democratic Party narrowly won the Brandenburg state election, recording 30.9 per cent of the vote compared to the 29.2 per cent achieved by the far-right Alternative for Germany. The SDP has led a coalition government in Brandenburg since 2019 with the centre-right Christian Democratic Union and the Greens. However, the Greens vote more than halved to just 4.1 per cent, below the 5 per cent threshold to win seats in parliament. With the SDP and CDU falling one seat short of an absolute majority, the government will negotiate a coalition government with the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which came third and won 14 seats in the 88-seat parliament. BSW has embraced support for the continued operation of lignite plants and right-wing criticisms of other climate policies. The state hosts two lignite power stations – the 2140 MW Janschwalde and 1600 MW Schwarze Pumpe plants – and the Janschwalde and Welzow-Sud lignite mines, all owned and operated by the energy company LEAG. (Financial Times)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Queensland government said its preliminary view is that Fox Resources proposed metallurgical coal mine near Bundaberg is not in the public interest. The company has until November 15 to respond to the government's initial position.

 

 Australia: Environmental groups are concerned that Alcoa's proposal to pump groundwater to fill its disused Anglesea coal mine pit will contribute to the acidification of the Anglesea River.

 

 China: Air quality improved in the first half of 2024, likely due to increased clean energy and reduced cement production for the construction sector.

 

 France: EDF has dropped a plan to convert the 1260 MW Cordemais coal plant to run on biomass. The plant will close in 2027.

 

 India: Adaro International has launched legal action over a 2020 agreement to supply high-calorific value coal for Tata Power's 750 MW Trombay plant in Maharashtra state. Adaro is seeking US$106 million, with Tata lodging a counterclaim for US$229.94 million.

 

 Mozambique: Grindrod has agreed to buy the remaining 35 per cent stake it does not own of TCM for US$77 million, subject to approvals. TCM owns a coal and magnetite terminal in Maputo.

 

 New Zealand: Six Extinction Rebellion protestors were convicted of trespass after a December 2021 protest blocking a shipment of coal to Fonterra's Clandeboye milk powder plant.

 

 South Africa: Former Eskom contractor Michael Lomas has been extradited from the UK to face charges over alleged bribes paid for contracts on the 4800 MW Kusile coal plant.

 

 Taiwan: The Taiwan Cement Corporation will cease imports of Russian coal. The company accounts for about 20 per cent of Taiwan's coal imports.

 

 US: Warrior Met Coal will pay US$250,000 as part of a settlement agreement to repair a coal waste dam and end wastewater pollution of a tributary of the Black Warrior River in Alabama.

 

 US: The Sierra Club has launched a digital advertising campaign aimed at Blackstone over its 2600 MW Gavin coal plant in Ohio. A digital projection on the company's office stated, "244 deaths per year, 0 plans to retire".

 

 US: The Environmental Protection Agency has argued before the Supreme Court against delaying the application of new pollution standards to the 1556 MW Colstrip coal plant in Montana. NorthWestern Energy and Talen Montana claim pollution controls would make the plant uneconomic.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Asian Development Bank rejects conversion bid for Pakistan plant: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has refused to support the Pakistan government's proposed conversion of the 1320 MW Jamshoro Power Plant in Sindh province to run on 100 per cent domestic lignite. An ADB official said that the loan and project agreements with the Pakistan government specify a fuel mix of 80 per cent imported sub-bituminous coal and 20 per cent lignite. "We neither support the fuel conversion plan nor will finance it," the ADB stated. The first 660 MW unit at the plant was ready to operate in August but is affected by the delay in building a 105-kilometre railway from the Thar lignite field to the existing national rail network. Another 660 MW unit has been proposed but remains uncertain. AsiaPak International, the new owner of utility company K-Electric and an investor in a Thar lignite mine, has lobbied the Pakistan government to convert Unit 5 to operate solely on domestic lignite. K-Electric has also expressed interest in developing Unit 6. (Dawn)

Indonesian coal lobby tips China and Indian demand to peak in 2025: The Indonesian Coal Miners Association (ICMA) Chairman Priyadi told the Coaltrans Asia conference that he expects the end of growth in the seaborne coal trade coal after imports by China and India peak in 2025. Priyadi said ICMA estimates demand from Vietnam and the Philippines will grow by three per cent a year from 140.9 million tonnes in 2023 to 170.9 million tonnes in 2030. A Vinacomin executive, Dinh Quang Trung, said he expects Vietnam will import 66 million tonnes in 2024, up from 47.8 million tonnes in 2023. He said he expects demand will likely peak at 86 million tonnes a year by 2035, with about three-quarters used in the power generation sector. (Reuters)

Two Indian states call for power tenders that suit Adani's interests: Maharashtra and Rajasthan have both issued tenders 25-year power supply agreement with nearly identical wording calling for bids based on new coal and solar capacity. The Maharashtra tender allows for coal and solar capacity anywhere in the country, while Rajasthan is seeking to source power from local projects. Adani won the Maharashtra tender that sought 1600 MW of coal capacity and 5000 MW of solar capacity from one bidder. Rajasthan's tender calls for bids on 3200 MW of coal capacity and 8000 MW of solar capacity, with Adani considered as the leading bidder. Adani is involved in both coal and solar projects and has three 1600 MW coal projects proposed in India that are potentially eligible for the Maharashtra contract. The company is also proposing a 3200 MW expansion of its existing 1320 MW Kawai Thermal Power Project in Rajasthan. The opposition Congress party alleged the Bharatiya Janata Party-led governments in the state tailored the terms of the tenders to favour Adani. The state electricity utilities did not respond to queries about the tender. (Reporters Collective)

Australian opposition's nuclear plan to prolong coal and gas: The leader of the Liberal-National Party coalition, Peter Dutton, has acknowledged that his plan for the construction of seven nuclear plants would require the continued operation of coal plants into the 2030s and 2040s. Dutton has proposed the construction of seven nuclear power plants, including both conventional reactors and the notional small modular reactors (SMRs), but has not released detailed costings. Australia has no commercial nuclear power plants. The Minerals Council of Australia, which represents coal and uranium mining companies, is lobbying for nuclear power projects. A report by the Institute of Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) estimated electricity from nuclear plants could cost between 1.5 to 3.8 times more than the current cost of electricity generation in eastern Australia and would result in household electricity bills increasing by A$665 (US$458) a year. (Australian Financial Review [paywall], Institute of Energy Economics and Financial Analysis)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Report finds only 4 major car companies plan to buy green steel by 2030: A report by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), an NGO tracking progress in reducing emissions from the transport sector, has found that only 4 of 17 major car manufacturers plan to buy any fossil-free steel by 2030. The global auto sector accounts for 12 per cent of steel consumption, with a 17 per cent share in the European Union and 26 per cent in the US. General Motors, Ford and Mercedes Benz dominate current commitments, with Volkswagen committing to buy a sliver of fossil-free steel for its plants. The total volume of fossil-fee steel commitments across all four companies accounts for only two per cent of the steel bought by the 17 surveyed companies. The report estimates steel produced via coal-based blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace technology in Europe results in 1.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions per car and about 1.9 tonnes in the US. The use of automotive steel with more recycled material produced by an electric arc furnace would, based on the average electricity mix, cut emissions to 0.8 tonnes per vehicle in Europe and 1.2 tonnes in the US. The use of fossil-free steel could cut emissions per vehicle to below 0.1 tonnes in Europe and the US. (International Council on Clean Transportation)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

The UK's journey to a coal power phase-out, Ember, September 2024. (Pdf)

This 17-page report provides an overview of the UK coal power phase-out since 2012.

links.text: (UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Development [Pdf],
Institute of Energy Economics and Financial Analysis)
The UK’s journey to a coal power phase-out

title: CoalWire 533, October 3, 2024
excerpt: Coal generation slumps across OECD; German coal unit closed; Polish utility announces closure of four units by the end of 2025; UK mine permit rejected.
content:
October 3, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

With the closure of its last coal plant, the UK is the fourteenth country in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development to generate electricity without coal. The end of coal power could have spillover effects on the country's mining policy, with the Coal Authority rejecting a conditional licence for the proposed Whitehaven metallurgical coal mine in Cumbria.

A new report by Ember highlights that coal generation in the OECD member countries has fallen by more than half since the collective peak in 2007. This week another coal plant in Germany also closed and a Polish utility announced plans to close four coal units at the Rybnik plant by the end of 2025. In Japan, the election of a new Prime Minister could offer the prospect that the country's next energy plan is more favourable towards renewables. In Indonesia, an application has been filed for judicial review of a regulation by President Joko Widodo opening the door for the allocation of coal mining concessions to religious organisations.

Correction: Last week, the Queensland government said its preliminary view is that Fox Resources proposed metallurgical coal mine near Bundaberg is not in the public interest. The word "not" was accidentally omitted from the initial version of CoalWire.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 How the UK became the first G7 country to phase out coal power

The UK's phasing out of coal generation occurred as a result of key shifts, including an end to the construction of new coal capacity, the availability of alternative sources of generation and setting a clear phase-out timeline a decade in advance, write Molly Lempriere and Simon Evans in Carbon Brief.

 

 How local campaigners won the battle to stop coal

The closure of the last coal plant in the UK is the result of a diverse movement of people using a wide array of methods. Coal really shows that together, we can address the climate crisis, writes Anne Harris from the Coal Action Network in Huck.

 

 In Chile, a 'sacrifice zone' waits for a better future

The city of Huasco has suffered in the shadow of the country's largest coal-fired power complex. As it faces closure or conversion, doubts remain over the road ahead, write Nicole Kramm and Alexandra Gonzalez in Dialogue Earth.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 German coal plant closes

Uniper has closed its 875 megawatt (MW) Heyden 4 coal plant in North Rhine-Westphalia. The 37-year-old plant was initially slated for closure after Uniper decided in late 2020 that the plant was no longer required. However, the Federal Network Agency directed Uniper to keep the plant operating until September 2022. Uniper extended the deadline for closure until September 2024. Earlier this year, Uniper announced it plans to build a battery energy storage system at the site. (Uniper)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 UK Coal Authority rejects application for Cumbria mine: In a further setback for West Cumbria Mining (WCM), the Coal Authority has refused to grant conditional underground coal mining licences for the proposed Whitehaven metallurgical coal mine. WCM, a subsidiary of the privately-owned Australian company EMR Capital Investment, applied in February 2023 for a three-year mining licence to extract up to four million tonnes of coal a year. In mid-September, the High Court ruled in favour of the appeal brought by Friends of the Earth (FOE) and South Lakes Action on Climate Change and overturned planning permission for the mine. WCM has not announced whether it intends to appeal that decision. FOE spokesperson Tony Bosworth said the Coal Authority decision "is surely the knock-out blow for this totally unnecessary coal mine". (Business Green, UK Coal Authority)

 

 OECD coal generation halved since 2007 peak: A report by Ember, a climate policy think tank, estimates that coal power generation has fallen by 52 per cent since 2007 in the 38 member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Ember estimates that wind and solar generation mostly replaced coal power. The report states that coal generation accounted for 17 per cent of electricity in OECD countries in 2023. With the closure of the Ratcliffe-on-Soar plant, the UK's last coal power station, 14 of the OECD countries now have a coal-free generation system, with a further 13 committed to phasing out coal generation by 2030. Of the OECD countries, only Turkiye has increased coal generation, while four countries – Japan, South Korea, Colombia and Mexico – recorded declines of less than 30 per cent from their peaks. (Ember)

 

 Polish utility announces plan to close remaining units at coal plant: PGE, a Polish state-owned power utility, will cease generating electricity at the four remaining coal units at the Rybnik power plant by the end of 2025 when capacity market contracts expire. Heat supply from the plant will end by August 31, 2026. The four units have a combined capacity of 875 MW. The two oldest units at the plant were retired in August 2021, and another two went offline in December 2023. The remaining four coal units were all commissioned in 1978. PGE has entered into a contract with Polimex Mostostal and Siemens Energy for the construction of a new 882 MW gas plant at the site. (Reuters, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Legal challenge against coal concessions for religious organisations: A coalition of religious, legal, and environmental organisations has applied for judicial review of President Joko Widodo's regulation that enables the allocation of mining permits to religious organisations. Since Widodo promulgated Government Regulation No. 25 of 2024 in May, three religious organisations – Nahdlatul Ulama, Muhammadiyah and the Indonesian Islamic Da'wah Institute – have agreed to or are considering coal concessions. The Chair of the Indonesian Legal Aid Foundation, Muhammad Isnur, said Widodo's regulation contradicts other provisions of the Mineral and Coal Mining Law that emphasises the priority for the allocation of Special Mining Business Permits to state-owned enterprises and regional-owned enterprises. (Tempo)

 

 New Japanese Prime Minister faces big energy policy decisions: Shortly after his election as Prime Minister, Shigeru Ishiba, has called a snap election for October 27 in the hope of cementing his leadership of the Liberal Democratic Party. Ishiba replaced Fumio Kishida, who was elected Prime Minister in October 2021 but suffered the loss of heartland seats in recent by-elections. Ishiba has a reputation as a moderate and called for a shift away from nuclear generation to renewables in the wake of the March 2011 disaster at the Fukushima nuclear power plant. Japan's 7th Strategic Energy Plan is due for release soon and will indicate whether the government intends to adopt measures consistent with its G7 commitment to phase out unabated coal generation in the early 2030s. Coal contributes 29 per cent of Japan's energy-related carbon dioxide emissions with its use in steel and other industrial plants contributing a further 12 per cent. Japan is currently a prominent advocate in the Southeast Asian region of carbon capture and storage, the construction of new coal plants and co-firing existing coal units with ammonia, hydrogen or biomass. (Guardian, Al Jazeera, E3G)

 

 Audit reveals US utility spent US$200 million on lobbying: A Public Utilities Commission of Ohio audit of FirstEnergy expenditure found the utility paid over US$200 million to 130 external vendors on political activities between 2015 and 2021. The audit revealed that of the US$75 million FirstEnergy paid on bribes and lobbying costs for the passage and defence of House Bill 6 (HB6), US$4.9 million came from its three subsidiaries servicing northeast Ohio. HB6 provided subsidies to two nuclear and two coal plants, However, the audit only included direct expenditure on HB6 and didn't include a similar campaign in 2017 and 2018. FirstEnergy also blocked the auditor's access to an internal investigation into the Ohio scandal undertaken by an external legal firm. While the nuclear bailout was repealed months after the arrest of former Republican Ohio House Speaker Larry Householder, the subsidies remain for the two coal plants. Ohio Consumers' Counsel said it is reviewing the PUCO audit but noted "limiting factors" affected its findings. (Cleveland, Public Utilities Commission of Ohio)

 

 Coal exploration bid over part of South African game reserve: A relatively unknown company, Chikopokopo Zibaa Construction and Projects, has applied for exploration rights over 19,800 hectares of land for coal and other minerals, including part of the Ndumo Game Reserve. The reserve is on KwaZulu-Natal's northern border with Mozambique and within five kilometres of the border with Eswatini (formerly known as Swaziland). Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife, the KwaZulu-Natal agency responsible for protected area management, said mining is not allowed within the boundaries of a nature reserve, and any permit must reflect this. The agency said the Pretoria-based Basia Environmental Consultants should have consulted with the Ramsar Convention Secretariat, national government agencies and organisations involved in trans-border environmental projects with Mozambique and Eswatini. A geological consultant hired by Ezemvelo argues that Chikopokopo's application is unlikely to find the target commodities, and even if it does, they "will be of low value or uneconomic to mine". (Daily Maverick)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Afghanistan: Coal exports have slumped from 771,000 tonnes to 529,000 tonnes in the six months from late March due to increased costs and border tensions with Pakistan.

 

 Australia: The federal government's approval of three coal projects sparked a blockade of a coal train near Newcastle and a protest in front of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's electorate office.

 

 Botswana: Minergy, which operates the Masama coal mine, has reported a US$14 million loss for the year due to production losses and higher finance costs. The company's CEO said the results "mirror the gloomy operational year" for the mine.

 

 Canada: The Alberta Energy Regulator has rejected a request from the Municipal District of Ranchland to delay a public hearing on Northback Holdings' proposed Grassy Mountain mine. The council had requested a delay until the Alberta Appeal Court ruled on a legal challenge against the exploration permit.

 

 India: Adani is seeking an order from the Supreme Court requiring the Gujarat State Electricity Corporation to enter into arbitration over the refusal to allocate a coal block to the company in Chhattisgarh.

 

 India: A Delhi court has convicted Rungta Project Ltd and five executives on charges of providing misleading information to the Ministry of Coal to win the allocation of the Hutar Sector C and Hurilong coal blocks in Jharkhand. Sentencing will occur on October 4.

 

 South Africa: Eskom is reusing coal ash in a short-haul road used by heavy trucks during the construction of a new coal conveyor system at its 4800 MW Kusile Power Station.

 

 US: A miner was killed in a rockfall accident at the Oak Grove mine owned by Crimson Oak Grove Resources. The Mine Safety and Health Administration has cited Oak Grove Mine for 204 safety violations after a March 8 methane explosion in a house that killed one man and badly injured another.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

New York pension fund switch cut portfolio emissions by 40 per cent: In a strategy designed to deliver "quick wins", the US$20 billion New York State Insurance Fund decided to exclude investments in any company or asset manager that received more than one per cent of its revenue from coal mining. This change "immediately reduced our carbon exposure in the equity portfolio by something like 40 per cent", said Rajith Sebastian from the fund. (Reuters)

Bangladesh coalition calls for rapid transition to renewables: The Just Energy Transition Network Bangladesh (JETnet-BD), an alliance of 75 Bangladeshi civil society groups, has called for the phasing out of all coal power plants by 2027 and the establishment of 5000 megawatts (MW) of new renewable electricity generation by 2025 and 10,000 MW by 2027. The coalition also wants an end to new import based LNG plants by 2027 and the rapid conversion of 60 per cent of the capacity of heavy fuel oil power stations. In early August, mass protests toppled the previous Bangladesh government, which had backed the rapid expansion of coal and gas generation and a controversial deal to import expensive electricity from Adani's Godda power plant in India. The country's increased reliance on costly imported fossil fuels has resulted in power tariffs far higher than the cost of electricity from renewables. (The Business Standard)

Indonesian bank refinances Chinese-backed coal plant: Bank Mandiri, Indonesia's largest bank, has agreed to provide PT Huadian Bukit Asam Power (HBAP) with US$1.27 billion to refinance the 1320 MW Sumsel-8 coal power plant in South Sumatra. (The plant is also known as the Bangko Tengah power station.) HBAP is a joint venture between China Huadian Group Corporation (55 per cent) and the Indonesian state-owned coal mining company PT Bukit Asam (45 per cent). The plant, which began commercial operation in October 2023, was funded with a US$1.26 billion loan from the China Export-Import Bank. The initial loan had a 15-year term from October 2018 with a grace period of five years until the first payments were due. (The Business Times [paywall], Bukit Asam [Indonesian])

Mongolia moved to overhaul management of state-owned coal company: Mongolian Prime Minister Oyun-Erdene Luvsannamsrai has directed government officials to launch a tender for international consultants to choose a new management team for the state-owned coal mining company Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi (ETT). Allegations of corruption associated with coal exports sparked sustained public protests in 2022 and prompted the establishment of coal sales via an auction process. ETT owns the bulk of the vast Tavan Tolgoi coalfield, apart from the Ukhaa Khudag concession allocated to the Hong Kong-listed Mongolian Mining Corporation. Mongolia has emerged as a significant metallurgical coal exporter after China, its primary market, eased border restrictions instituted during the COVID-19 pandemic. Mongolia has forecast coal exports of 78 million tonnes this year and 83 million tonnes in 2025. Mongolian metallurgical coal exports have a significant price advantage, especially for northern Chinese steel plants, compared to Australian coal. (BNE Intellinews, Montsame)

Polish coal miner books US$1.6 billion loss in a quarter: JSW, Poland's largest metallurgical coal producer, reported a second-quarter net loss of US$1.6 billion due to a 33 per cent slump in revenue and a US$1.8 billion write-down. The company has been affected by reduced demand, a slump in prices in the coal export market and increased mine infrastructure costs. The company said it had increased capital expenditure on items such as powered supports in underground mines and new coal transport equipment. The Polish Treasury holds a 55 per cent stake in JSW. In mid-September, JSW cut forecast coal production in 2024 due to the inability to extinguish a fire that began in early December 2023 in its KWK Pniowek underground mine. (XM, JSW)

Rise in South African solar capacity helped end load shedding: For the first time in five years, South Africa has gone through winter without any load shedding due to a decline in demand and increased availability of some coal units. An analysis of Eskom data indicates that between 2023 and 2024, the average demand for electricity dropped by 804 MW an hour, especially during the middle of the day, suggesting rooftop solar has been a significant contributor. Over the same period, generation Eskom's coal plants contributed on average 1012 MW an hour more in 2023/24 than the preceding year, with the energy availability factor increasing from 51 per cent in 2023 to 60 per cent in 2024 over the winter months. One significant factor behind the change in EAF is increased generation from the new 4800 MW Kusile plant after the September 2022 fire that damaged Unit 5 at the plant. In late 2023, South Africa's then Minister for Environment, Barbara Creecy, approved Eskom's application to bypass the flue gas desulphurisation plant until March 2025. (AmaBhungane)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Mythbusting: Metallurgical coal, Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis, September 2024. (Pdf)

This 2-page fact sheet critiques Australian coal industry claims that metallurgical coal is essential for global steel production.

Green Iron Corridors: Transforming the Steel Supply Chains for a Sustainable Future, RMI and Green Hydrogen Catapult, September 2024. (Registration required.)

This 36-page report reviews the prospects for locating green iron production in regions with renewable energy and access to iron ore and the concentration of steelmaking in areas with strong manufacturing capabilities that are close to demand.

links.text: Green Iron Corridors: Transforming the Steel Supply Chains for a Sustainable Future

title: CoalWire 534, October 10, 2024
excerpt: Cambodia rules out more coal plants; US Supreme Court rejects challenge to pollution rule.
content:
October 10, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

US environmental groups breathed a sigh of relief when the conservative-dominated US Supreme Court rejected a request from Republican-led states and fossil fuel industry groups to block the Environmental Protection Agency's new Mercury and Air Toxics Standards for power plants. The rule is one of the measures adopted by the Biden administration to cut pollution from the power sector. In Australia, the recent holiday long weekend saw coal generation cut to a record low with rooftop solar and wind generation accounting for nearly half of total demand. In South Africa, Eskom is seeking a 36 per cent increase in power tariff to cover unanticipated coal purchases caused in part by delays in a government agency issuing contracts for additional renewables. Cambodia has ruled out approval for new coal plants, albeit after the completion of two small units that are currently under construction.

While the greatest death toll from coal is associated with air pollution where it is finally burnt, every week there are news reports of deadly coal mine accidents. Many of the news stories report just one or two deaths, but it is likely that many more go entirely unreported. There is even less coverage of the spread of black lung disease, a preventable illness. Occasionally, there are major accidents where dozens of workers are killed, such as in Iran a few weeks ago. This week there were reports of deaths in coal mines in Australia, India, Russia and the US. Oddly, there seems to be precious little study or media coverage of the global scale of the health impacts of the coal industry on its own workforce.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 A West Virginia community is counting on a 'miracle' to keep their coal plant open

West Virginia is betting US$50 million on Omnis Energy's promise of a 'revolutionary' new energy production technique. But the company, which has a history of unrepaid loans and lawsuits, hasn't publicly shown its technology actually works, write Taylor Kate Brown from Floodlight and Sarah Elbeshbishi in Mountain State News.

 

 Residents say South African mining has brought misery not benefits

Community members protested at coal mining offices of Seriti Resources over damage to homes from blasting, writes Ihsaan Haffejee in GroundUp.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 US Supreme Court rejects plea to block EPA pollution rule: The US Supreme Court has rejected a request from Republican-led states and fossil fuel industry groups to block the Environmental Protection Agency's new Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) for power plants. The standards, which were unveiled in April, cut allowable mercury emissions from lignite plants by 70 per cent and a 67 per cent reduction in allowable metal emissions from all coal plants. In June, the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit unanimously rejected an appeal by Republican state attorneys. The Supreme Court decided the plaintiffs must exhaust their legal options before the lower courts before turning to the Supreme Court. (NPR, Sierra Club)

 

 Cambodia rules out more coal plants: Cambodia's Minister of Mines and Energy, Keo Rattanak, has ruled out the construction of new coal plants and instead emphasised support for new wind, solar and hydro capacity. Cambodia currently has 1500 MW of coal capacity with another two units, with a combined capacity of 265 MW, under construction at the Chinese-backed Han Seng power station near the northern border with Thailand. The current coal plants, along with fuel oil plants, generate about 48 per cent of the country's electricity. "There is a need for Cambodia to continue to use coal-fired power but not to allow new projects," Rattanak said. Two other proposed coal plants – the 700 MW Koh Kong plant and its successor the 700 MW Botum Sakor power station in the Botum Sakor National Park – appear to have been cancelled. (The Star)

 

 New Japanese PM promises more efficiency and renewables: Ahead of his election as Prime Minister, Shigeru Ishiba, supported a reduction in nuclear power and increased reliance on renewables. However, shortly after his appointment as the new Minister for Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), Yoji Muto, said the new government supported the continued recommissioning of nuclear plants shut down after the 2011 Fukushima disaster along with increased energy efficiency and deployment of renewables. METI, power utilities and industry groups have resisted calls for increased renewables capacity and supported nuclear, coal and LNG plants. The new Minister for Environment, Keiichiro Asao, emphasised in his first media conference that Japan would focus on closing "inefficient" coal plants by 2030. Ishiba has called a snap election on October 27 for the House of Representatives with his Liberal Democratic Party retaining a commanding lead in recent opinion polls over rival political parties. Japan's 7th Strategic Energy Plan is likely to be released by March 2025. (Reuters, Argus Media)

 

 Coal company expands mine before Australian government approval: The Australian government is investigating evidence that Vitrinite commenced clearing koala habitat for a coal mine extension before it had federal government approval. Vitrinite applied in 2022 for a 1.9 million tonnes a year expansion of its Vulcan South metallurgical coal mine, including clearing about 1000 hectares of koala habitat. Satellite data shows the company cleared about 47 hectares of forest within the proposed expansion area since April this year. The company defended its action as a "small testing operation" and claimed that it has approval from the state government for a "bulk sample pit" to extract up to 750,000 tonnes of coal. The Queensland Conservation Council called on the federal Minister for Environment, Tanya Plibersek, to immediately ensure an end to any illegal activity. The company could be fined up to A$$825,000 fine (US$561,000) if charged and convicted. (ABC, Queensland Conservation Council)

 

 Adani moves to on-sell auctioned coal block: Adani Enterprises revealed in its March 2024 quarterly report that the board of its MP Natural Resources subsidiary has decided to sell the Gondbahera Ujheni East coal block in Madhya Pradesh. The block is estimated to contain about 250 million tonnes of coal. MP Natural Resources won the rights to the block in late 2023 after a controversial auction process. Adani Enterprises' quarterly report stated that the sale is "subject to regulatory approvals from the concerned authorities". If approved, the sale would be the first occasion since the Modi government commenced commercial coal auctions in June 2020 that an area has been sold to another company. Former senior Indian government bureaucrat Dr EAS Sarma said the government must assess the proposed buyer against the same criteria that governed the original allocation, including the names of the beneficial owners. R Ravi, the chairperson of Mines, Minerals, and PEOPLE, said the transfer of coal block could open the door to speculators and adversely affect the rights of tribal communities. (Adani Watch)

 

 Duke Energy wants 3-year delay in closing Indiana's last coal plant: Duke Energy has backtracked on its plan to go coal-free by 2035, proposing to extend the life of two 668 MW units at the Gibson Generating Station in Indiana until 2038. The two units were previously scheduled to close in 2035. Duke Energy is proposing to convert the two units to allow them to run on both coal and gas. In its latest proposed 20-year resource plan, Duke proposes delaying the addition of the bulk of its proposed renewables capacity until the mid to late 2030s. The company forecasts increased electricity demand, including from data centres and electric cars. Megan Anderson from the Sierra Club's Beyond Coal campaign said delaying the closure of the plant would push up costs for customers. (Indiana Public Media)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Aboriginal community leaders were shocked to discover fracturing and associated rock falls beneath an overhang with important artworks. The site is subject to subsidence from Illawarra Metallurgical Coal's Dendrobium metallurgical coal mine.

 

 Australia: A miner was killed and another seriously injured after an accident at Glencore's Oaky Creek Coal mine in Queensland.

 

 Colombia: The Council of State, Colombia's highest administrative law court, has agreed to hear an appeal against President Gustavo Petro's ban on coal exports to Israel. Colombia exported three million tonnes of coal to Israel in 2023.

 

 India: Seven workers were killed and three injured transporting detonators for use at the West Bengal Power Development Corporation's Gangaramchak and Gangaramchak-Bhadulia coal mines.

 

 Mexico: The incoming president, Claudia Sheinbaum, announced a target of 45 per cent share of renewables in power generation by 2030, up from 24 per cent in 2023. Details of the energy policy have yet to be announced.

 

 Pakistan: Pakistan Railways will construct the 105-kilometre Islamkot to Chhor spur line to allow lignite from the Thar coalfield to be transported to the Port Qasim coal plant. The project is due to be completed by October 2025.

 

 Romania: The 100million (US$110 million) refurbishment of the 330MW Unit 5 at the Rovinari lignite plant has been completed.

 

 Russia: A miner was killed in a rock collapse at the Kolmar Group's Denisovsky Vostochny coal mine in Siberia.

 

 South Africa: The Pretoria High Court has heard a legal challenge brought by a coalition of environmental justice groups against government plans to procure 1500 MW of new coal capacity.

 

 US: A coalition of environmental and First Nations groups has filed a legal challenge against the Montana Department of Environmental Quality's approval of an expansion of Signal Peak Energys Bull Mountains coal mine.

 

 US: The Department of Energy has awarded US$4.2 million to Minnkota Power Cooperative for a front-end engineering and design study for carbon sequestration at a proposed carbon capture and storage project at the 705MW lignite-fired Milton R. Young Station in North Dakota.

 

 US: A coal miner died after he was seriously injured in a September 28 accident at Arch Resources Leer Mining Complex in West Virginia.

 

 "It's very challenging for us to raise any money for anything that's coal-related. It has been the case for the last few years,"

said Ray Gunara, the President-Director of Harum Energy, an Indonesian coal and nickel company.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Global coal market set to soften: The latest edition of Resources and Energy Quarterly, published by the Australian Government's Department of Industry, Science, Energy and Resources (DISR), estimates the seaborne prices for both thermal and metallurgical coal are set to decline over the next three years. DISR estimates seaborne thermal coal could decline from US$135 a tonne in 2024 to US$113 a tonne by 2026, with metallurgical coal tipped to fall from US$251 a tonne in 2024 to US$205 a tonne by 2026. Metallurgical coal demand is forecast to decline due to the fall in new construction activity in China's property sector. Reduced Chinese demand is partly offset by increased Indian demand as investment continues in new blast furnace capacity and the government's plan to build 30 million new homes. Strong thermal coal demand in the last quarter was underpinned by hot weather in some Asian countries driving increased power demand. The imposition of tighter sanctions on Russia, such as restrictions on the Moscow Exchange announced in mid-June, will further affect its exports, especially into the Asian market. (Australian Department of Industry, Science and Resources)

Russian coal industry hit by sanctions and taxes: Russia's coal industry has been hit by reduced demand by China, India and Turkey, with the Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) estimating that more than half of coal companies are now unprofitable. Exporters have also been affected by China's imposition of import duties and a Russian export tax imposed to address the central government's budget crisis, created in part by the war with Ukraine. The latest edition of Resources and Energy Quarterly, published by the Australian Government's Department of Industry, Science, Energy and Resources (DISR), notes that Russian thermal coal exports are down 24 per cent in the first half of 2024, mainly due to declines in shipments to South Korea, China, and India. Thermal coal production is estimated as down by 10 per cent over the same period, with DISR estimating exports are likely to plateau at around 110 million tonnes a year over the next three years, down from 133 million tonnes in 2023. However, DISR estimates that Russian metallurgical coal exports are likely to be stable at 44 million tonnes a year over the next three years. While acknowledging a potential risk from the impact of sanctions on Russia, DISR notes that 95 per cent of Russia's metallurgical coal exports are shipped to China and India and sold at a discount to other suppliers of similar quality coal. (The Moscow Times [Russian], Australian Government's Department of Industry, Science, Energy and Resources)

Study estimates US LNG exports have worse climate impact than coal: A study published in the journal Energy Science & Engineering, estimates that Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) exported from the US is 33 per cent worse than coal in terms of the greenhouse gas emissions from over a 20-year period. The study estimates that the greenhouse gas emissions of US LNG are equal to or exceed coal even when a 100-year timeframe is used. Since the ban on LNG gas exports was lifted in 2016, the country has become the world's largest exporter with producers promoting LNG as a 'bridge fuel' between coal and renewables. The study estimates the production and midstream processing, transport and storage account for 38 per cent of total LNG emissions on a 20-year timeframe, with the energy used to produce LNG adding a further eight per cent in emissions. Robert Howarth from Cornell University argues that even though the carbon dioxide emissions from burning coal are greater than from using gas, methane emissions from LNG production and transport "can more than offset this difference". (Guardian, Energy Science & Engineering)

Solar and wind crunch Australian coal generation: Coal generation in Australia's eastern states electricity market dropped to an all-time low of just 24.2 per cent on Sunday October 6 during the long weekend holiday. In 2018, the record low for coal generation in the National Electricity Market (NEM), which covers the eastern states grid, was 63 per cent. At one point over the long weekend, rooftop solar alone generated 49.3 per cent of electricity in the NEM, with a new record share for solar and wind of 74.4 per cent. The high share of renewables pushed residual demand from other sources to just 4710 MW. (RenewEconomy)

Eskom blames renewables delay as factor in bid for power price hike: The South African state-owned utility Eskom has attributed the largest part of its bid for 36 per cent power price increase in 2025/26 on delayed deployment of renewables. In its application to the National Energy Regulator of SA (Nersa), Eskom states it needs an 11.2 per cent tariff increase to cover increased expenditure on coal. The utility stated that delays in commissioning new renewables projects will require increased coal consumption with additional fuel bought at higher spot prices rather than under cheaper long-term contracts. Eskom attributed the delay in renewables on the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy (DMRE), which conducts tenders for new capacity, and a lack of transmission capacity. Eskom is also seeking an 11.8 per cent and 9.1 per cent increases for 2026/27 and 2027/28, respectively. (News24)

Polish power utilities confirm the decline of coal generation: Grzegorz Kinelski, the head of state-owned power utility Enea, said the older coal units at the 4000 MW Kozienice plant are nearing the end of their technical "and perhaps also economical" life. "Coal is being pushed out (of the market) sooner than any forecasts predicted," he said. The Kozienice plant includes eight old coal units, with half currently scheduled to close in 2025 and the remainder in 2027. Enea has scheduled the closure of the two newest 560 MW units for 2041 and 2042. PGE recently announced the closure of the four coal units at its Rybnik coal plant in 2025. The European Union recently approved the extension of capacity payments from mid-2025 until 2028 for old coal units emitting more than 550 kilograms of carbon dioxide per megawatt hour. However, payments are likely to be allocated to the winners of annual auctions between 2026 and 2028. Polish utilities have 41 old coal units with a combined capacity of 9000 MW that are not likely to be viable without subsidies. (Montel)

Indonesian coal miner touts diversification to duck coal funding drought: Harum Energy, a small Indonesian coal producer, said it has allocated profits from its coal mining business to invest in nickel mining and processing projects as part of its transition away from coal. Harum Energy has two coal mines in East Kalimantan and another in Central Kalimantan, which produced almost seven million tonnes between them in 2023. The company's coal production jumped by 29 per cent compared to 2022 with sales to both the domestic power sector and export sales to Asia and China in particular. While the company told the Financial Times that it could be out of the coal sector within six years, its annual report paints a rosy picture of future coal demand. Fitch Ratings said that it expects companies without diversification plans away from thermal coal will find it harder to attract finance over the next three to five years. (Financial Times)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

"Japan continues pushing ammonia, not so-called 'decarbonized fuel'", Japan Beyond Coal, September 30, 2024.

This article provides a concise overview of the problems with Japan's promotion of ammonia as a fuel for co-firing coal plants.
