Australian Government’s Department of Industry, Science, Energy and Resources)
“Japan continues pushing ammonia, not so-called ‘decarbonized fuel’”

title: CoalWire 536, October 24, 2024
excerpt: Turkiye lifts 2035 wind and solar target; US court backs insurer's refusal to cover oil company's legal costs.
content:
October 24, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Turkiye's announcement of a significant increase in its 2035 solar and wind target is welcome and makes the prospects for the construction of a raft of proposed coal plants more challenging. In the US, the Supreme Court has rejected a request to block the Environmental Protection Agency from implementing rules to cut greenhouse gas emissions from coal and gas plants. However, the rule still faces a legal challenge in a lower court. In Hawaii, a court ruling is likely to leave an oil company to bear the costs of defending two climate lawsuits by local government bodies. It is a ruling that could have far broader application as legal actions against fossil fuel producers increase.

A new report documents the health impacts of pollution from the seven steel mills and ten coke plants in the US. The report is significant for demonstrating the nationwide health impacts of the steel industry, which to date has not been subject to anywhere near as much scrutiny as coal power plants have. In India, a government think tank has proposed directing power utilities to suspend further orders of flue gas desulphurisation units, bizarrely claiming that sulphur dioxide emissions from coal plants are not adversely impacting air quality. Ever since India's environment ministry first unveiled new emissions standards in 2015, power utilities have resisted implementing measures that would save thousands of lives a year.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Solar surge will send coal power tumbling by 2030, IEA data reveals

The International Energy Agency forecasts global electricity generation from solar will quadruple by 2030 and help to push coal power into reverse, write Simon Evans and Verner Viisainen in Carbon Brief.

 

 What the data centre and AI boom could mean for the energy sector

Electricity demand for data centres is set to grow strongly by 2030 and could make meeting climate targets more difficult in some locations, write Thomas Spencer and Siddharth Singh from the International Energy Agency.

 

 US coal plant closes, but its 'pollution debt' lives on

Seven years after a federal judge ruled that Ameren Missouri violated the Clear Air Act by making modifications to its 1242 megawatt (MW) Rush Island coal plant that increased sulphur dioxide emissions, the plant has finally closed. Ameren has faced no significant consequences for its decisions, but its customers must pay off the remaining debt, writes Jeffrey Tomich in E & E News.

 

 Making steel with clean energy would curb health risks, report says

Speeding up America's shift to cleaner steelmaking would not only slow carbon dioxide emissions, but help reduce the toxic pollution from coal-based production, writes Maria Gallucci in Canary Media.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Turkish minister announces plan to accelerate solar and wind: Tukiye's Minister for Energy, Alparslan Bayraktar, announced a new 2035 target for wind and solar capacity of 120 gigawatts (GW), up from the 83.5 GW in the previous national energy plan. The latest target represents a 43.7 per cent increase. Bayraktar said the ministry will focus on reducing the permit processing time for the 34 GW of proposed solar and wind projects and increase investment in transmission capacity. Turkiye will also conduct a tender early next year for 2000 MW of solar and wind capacity with winning bidders guaranteed a floor price and offtake agreements. Turkiye's electricity consumption has tripled in the last two decades, which has been underpinned by rapid growth in coal and gas generation. The surge in imported coal and gas prices has boosted increased interest in new domestic lignite projects, but these have encountered strong local opposition due to impacts on air quality, agricultural production and forests. According to the Global Coal Plant Tracker, Turkiye has 4608 MW of coal plants in the pre-approval stage and 20,473 MW of operating capacity. (Reuters)

 

 US Supreme Court clears way for EPA greenhouse gas rule: The US Supreme Court rejected a request from a coalition of power utilities, industry groups and mostly Republican-led states to suspend the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) implementation of a rule to cut greenhouse gas emissions from coal and gas plants. The EPA rule requires utilities that plan to operate coal plants past 2038 to use carbon capture and storage technology (CCS) to cut emissions by 90 per cent by 2032. Justice Clarence Thomas said he would have granted the stay, while two other conservative judges said the utilities "are unlikely to suffer irreparable harm" before the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rules on the appeal. After promoting CCS over the last three decades, the utilities claimed that the technology is not commercially viable on large-scale plants. (Reuters, Scotus Blog, US Supreme Court [Pdf])

 

 Protests against Indian coal projects: Community protests have erupted at two coal mines more than 500 kilometres apart. In Odisha, hundreds of villagers protested against Gujarat Mineral Development Cooperation's plans to develop the Baitarani West coal mine near Chhendipada. In Jharkhand, thousands protested around the walls of the compound erected at BGR's coal project at Badam. The proposed mine is one of several allocated to companies in recent years, likely to affect up to 76 villages. Adani Mining's proposed Gondalpura coal mine is nearby. (New Indian Express, Adani Watch)

 

 Indian government think tank urges end to scrubbers for coal plants: NITI Aayog, an influential Indian government policy think tank, has recommended the Modi government suspend the requirement for coal-based power utilities to install desulphurisation units to cut sulphur dioxide emissions. The NITI Aayog document, seen by Reuters, cites a government study that claims sulphur dioxide emissions from coal plants are not adversely impacting air quality. Earlier this year, a study published in Air Quality, Atmosphere and Health estimated that the Indian government could have avoided between 220,000 and 720,000 deaths if all coal power units operating after 2010 had installed pollution control units to cut sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions. In 2015, India's Ministry of Environment adopted new pollution control standards to cut sulphur dioxide and Nox emissions, with an initial compliance deadline of December 2017. Opposition to the standards by power utilities has resulted in repeated delays, with many units still operating without pollution controls. The current deadline for the installation of desulphurisation equipment is 2026. (Reuters)

 

 US court ruling backs insurer over oil company claim on legal costs: The Hawaii Supreme Court ruled that AIG is not required to cover the legal expenses for Aloha Petroleum, a Sunoco subsidiary, to defend itself against lawsuits brought by the city and county of Honolulu and the county of Maui. The lawsuits allege that Aloha Petroleum, along with other major oil companies, contributed to environmental damage across the Hawaiian islands. Aloha Petroleum launched a legal challenge seeking to require AIG to cover its legal costs. The US District Court posed two questions for the higher court to clarify the extent of coverage under the policy. The Hawaii Supreme Court ruled in favour of Aloha Petroleum on one question but ruled in AIG's favour on the issue of whether greenhouse gases are a pollutant under a clause that excludes coverage for pollution. "This court respects climate science," wrote Justice Eddins. The ruling is likely to mean AIG will not have to cover Aloha Petroleums's legal fees, but the final decision will rest with the federal court. The ruling could have implications for other fossil fuel companies that are the subject of climate change litigation. (Hawaii Public Radio, JD Supra, Hawaii Supreme Court)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Queensland Conservation Council has warned that the proposal by the opposition Liberal-National Party (LNP) to operate the Callide B coal plant beyond 2028 could cost up to A$420 million (US$280 million) a year.

 

 Australia: Scientists have rejected Adani's criticisms of their study that found the Carmichael coal mine would likely divert water flows from the nationally important Doongmabulla Springs wetlands.

 

 Malawi: The reconstruction of the railway from Balaka to the capital of Lilongwe has reopened Malawi to thermal and metallurgical coal exports from Tete province mines in Mozambique.

 

 Pakistan: Clean energy advocates question the Federal Board of Revenue's decision to grant a 100 per cent tax credit to individuals involved in lignite mining projects in Sindh province.

 

 Russia: Coal miners from Inskaya's Inskoy mine in Kemerovo have launched a hunger strike over unpaid wages. The miners claim nearly 400 workers remain unpaid from July to October. The mine has a long history of financial troubles.

 

 Ukraine: The head of the steelmakers' association says Ukraine's steel production could halve if Russian forces succeed in capturing the Pokrovske metallurgical coal mine near the city of Pokrovsk.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Report finds significant banks still backing coal: A review by the Transition Pathway Initiative (TPI) of the lending practices of 26 major international banks found that 22 have committed to phasing out new coal capacity. But only four had policies committed to exclude new coal power capacity immediately and none were committed to phasing out support for coal in line with the Paris Agreement goal of a 1.5C target. The TPI, a project of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, found that climate policies commonly only covered a narrow part of the banks' financing activities, such as corporate loans or financing for specific loans. It also found that climate policies also had loopholes allowing fossil fuel financing in particular regions or to companies below certain revenue thresholds. TPI estimates the limited scope of the banks' policies means their decarbonisation targets cover only 22 per cent of the bank's revenues. The report also noted that some banks have backtracked on earlier commitments, such as Bank of America resuming lending for new thermal coal mines and the Bank of Montreal dropping any restrictions on loans for the coal industry. (Net Zero Investor, Transition Pathway Initiative [Pdf])

India receives 44 bids in the latest round of coal auctions: The Ministry of Coal announced that 44 bids were received on 67 coal blocks up for sale in the latest round of coal auctions. The blocks include six blocks left over from earlier auction rounds and are mainly in a handful of India's 28 states. Eighteen of the coal blocks for auction are in Odisha, with 17 each in Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh and a further 7 in Jharkhand. Only 16 of the coal blocks attracted bids. Four of the coal blocks – the Ulia Gamhardih coal mine and the Gare Palma IV/5 coal mine in Chhattisgarh, the Kerandari BC North block in Jharkhand and the Marwatola South coal block in Madhya Pradesh – accounted for just over half the 44 bids received. Major companies, including JSW Steel, JSW Energy, Jindal Steel and Power and NTPC Mining, were among the 31 bidding companies. (Hindu Business Line, Economic Times, Ministry of Coal [Pdf])

US regulator orders utility to refund customers over coal unit explosion: The Minnesota Public Utilities Commission has ordered Xcel to refund customers about US$58 million for costs incurred as a result of the November 2011 fire at the 939 MW Unit 3 at the Sherco plant in Minnesota. During the testing of safety equipment, an explosion damaged the turbine and caused a fire. The unit was closed for 22 months with its reconstruction costing US$239 million. While insurers covered most of the reconstruction costs, Xcel Energy passed on the additional costs of replacement electricity and fuel to customers. Earlier this year, an administrative law judge concluded the utility failed to operate and maintain the unit and ordered it to refund customers. Xcel Energy has 30 days to file details of the final refund. (MPR News, Minnesota Public Utilities Commission)

Eskom avoids blackouts, but flaws at new Medupi plant worry minister: South Africa's Minister for Electricity and Energy, Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, has welcomed a six per cent increase in the energy availability factor for Eskom's power plant fleet. He said Eskom is aiming for a 70 per cent energy availability factor in 2025, up from the current 63.9 per cent this year. South Africa has enjoyed 200 days without load shedding for the first time in five years. Ramokgopa described the ongoing problems at the 4800 MW Medupi coal plants as a "big concern". The 800 MW Unit 4 at the Medupi plant has been offline since August 2021 after an explosion caused extensive damage. The US$8.7 billion plant, which was fully commissioned in mid-2021, was funded by the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the New Development Bank. The two 930 MW units at the Koeberg nuclear plant are also both offline at present, one as part of an upgrade and the other after failing a test. The loss of the Koeberg plant's capacity reduces Eskom's reserve margin in case any of the large coal units suffer unplanned outages. (News24)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Report estimates heavy health toll from US steel industry: A report by Industrious Labs, a clean industry advocacy group, estimates the steel and coke plants in the US cause an estimated 892 premature deaths a year and more than 250,500 cases of asthma symptoms. The report estimates that US steel and coke plants cause about US$13.2 billion in health costs a year. The report notes that there are currently ten coke plants that convert metallurgical coal into carbon-rich coke, emitting nitrogen oxides, sulphur dioxide, PM2.5 fine particulate pollution, and hazardous chemicals, including benzene and lead. Some of the coke plants are co-located at or near the country's seven remaining steel mills. The coke and steel plants are all located in the Midwest states of Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Michigan, and Virginia. Many of the coke and steel plants rank in the top 10 emitters of key pollutants in their states. The report argues that regulators should enforce and tighten pollution standards in the operating permits for the plants while supporting a transition to clean steel production. (Industrious Labs, Industrious Labs [Pdf])

 

 European Commission approves subsidies for clean steel mill: The European Commission has cleared Sweden to provide a 128 million (US$138 million) to support SSAB's project to transition its coal-based Lulea steel mill to electric arc furnace production. The grant is for the installation of an electric arc furnace and other equipment at the plant, which aims to produce 2.5 million tonnes a year of low-emissions steel slabs in 2029. SSAB plans to convert the current 7.5 million tonnes per annum coal-based blast furnaces to a 100 per cent renewables-based hydrogen direct reduced iron and electric arc furnace facility. In late June, the European Commission approved Sweden's 265 million (US$286 million) grant to H2GS AB's green steel plant in Boden, Sweden. The plant includes a 690 MW electrolyser, a hydrogen-based direct reduction iron plant and two electric arc furnaces and other facilities. H2GS is aiming to commission the plant in 2025. (Reuters, European Commission)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Southeast Asia Energy Outlook 2024, International Energy Agency, October 2024. (Pdf)

This 200-page report provides a detailed overview of energy trends in Southeast Asia, where coal power provides half the region's electricity and accounts for 80 per cent of power sector emissions.

title: CoalWire 535, October 17, 2024
excerpt: Renewables to pass coal generation in 2025; mixed results in review of China’s overseas coal ban.
content:
October 17, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The latest International Energy Agency (IEA) report notes that renewable electricity generation will exceed coal generation for the first time in 2025. While solar and wind capacity is snowballing, the IEA notes that renewable electricity generation is still falling short of its Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario goal of 60 per cent share of electricity. The agency's new World Energy Outlook report points to higher than expected electricity demand growth, slowing the decline in coal generation to 2035. Another new report paints an encouraging picture of the rapid growth of renewables in the Global South.

While new solar and wind generation is cheaper or on a par with coal in China, a new review finds mixed progress on the implementation of President Xi's September 2021 pledge to end support for new coal plants overseas. While China has withdrawn support for many overseas coal project, more have either been commissioned, are under construction or are in the planning pipeline.

Recent policies aimed at cutting coal mine methane emissions are starting to impact coal mining companies. In Australia, Glencore and Yancoal have withdrawn a massive proposed expansion of a coal mine after state officials highlighted concerns over methane emissions from the project. In Romania, a new report highlights that the European Union's new methane regulation will force changes in the country's coal sector and better management of its abandoned coal mines.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Records reveal how a US utility secretly spent big to court favour with then-President Donald Trump

Recently released records have revealed that FirstEnergy, the US utility at the heart of the Ohio utility corruption scandal, secretly spent millions of dollars as it pursued a multi-billion-dollar federal bailout for its coal and nuclear plants during Donald Trump's presidency. It was a bailout Trump promised but failed to deliver, writes Dave Anderson from the Energy & Policy Institute.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Review finds mixed progress on China's international coal plant ban: A review by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) has found that Chinese-backed international coal projects continue to proceed despite President Xi's September 2021 pledge to end support for new projects. In its third review of the ban, CREA found that just 5600 MW of coal capacity was cancelled in the year to July 2024, bringing the total cancellations to 42,800 MW since Xi's pledge. However, 7900 MW of new coal capacity was commissioned in the year bringing the total operational capacity over the last three years to 26,200 MW. CREA estimates that 52 coal power plants with a combined capacity of 49 500 MW capacity remain either under consideration or in construction. The report notes that 3400 MW of previously unannounced projects entered construction over the last year, with another 4900 MW under consideration. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 Glencore and Yancoal backtrack on mine expansion, for now: Hunter Valley Operations, a Glencore and Yancoal joint venture, has withdrawn a proposal to extend the operation of two mines from the federal and state environmental assessment process after alarm over methane emissions from the projects. The production and burning of the coal from the expnsions would generate over 1.2 billion tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions. The New South Wales planning department had raised concern that the proposed mine would increase methane emissions from one section of the mine during the 2040s when the state was committed to achieving net zero emissions by 2050. The withdrawal of the application also resulted in the discontinuance of a legal challenge by Hunter Environment Lobby against the decision of the Minister for Environment, Tanya Plibersek, that the federal environment department did not have to consider the impact of the mine expansion on the Great Barrier Reef. The company said it intends to resubmit an application after it has completed additional modelling and mine planning. (Guardian, Lock the Gate)

 

 Australian coal company found guilty on four charges over massive blast: Justice Sarah Pritchard of the NSW Land and Environment Court has found Whitehaven Coal subsidiary Maules Creek Coal guilty on four charges of breaching its environment licence as a result of the excessive use of explosives in an August 2020 blast at the Maules Creek open cut mine. In late 2019, the company sought a change in the blasting procedure to ensure better fragmentation of the rock. Modelling for the August 2020 blast suggested the use of 850,000 kilograms (kg) of explosives, but the company used more than 896,000 kg. The magnitude of the explosion resulted in the evacuation of about 100 workers at Idemitsu Resources' Boggabri Coal mine two kilometres away with two miners taken to hospital for possible ear damage. Drone footage revealed a massive plume of dust from the blast fell over the nearby Leard Forest, which is home to an endangered woodland. Sentencing will occur on October 31, 2024. (North West Protection Advocacy, YouTube, New South Wales Land and Environment Court)

 

 State agency prepares to renew permit for US coal export terminal: Despite opposition from residents concerned about the health impacts of coal dust, the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) said it plans to renew the operating permit for CSX's Curtis Bay coal terminal. The MDE claims it doesn't have the power to close the coal terminal, even though a joint study between the community, regulators and universities detected coal dust in all eight community sampling locations in Curtis Bay. MDE is proposing to require dust control measures, including a fence around the coal stockpile. In December 2021, a methane gas explosion on a conveyor belt shattered windows and blanketed nearby houses in coal dust. Last week, a federal judge agreed to a US$1.75 million settlement of a class action against the company over the blast. In 2022, CSX was fined US$1500 by MDE for the accident and agreed to operational changes. (CBS News)

 

 Judgement reserved in South African case over new coal capacity: Pretoria High Court has reserved its decision on a constitutional challenge against the inclusion of 1500 MW of new coal capacity in the 2019 Integrated Resource Plan. The then Minister for Mineral Resources, Gwede Mantashe, and the National Energy Regulator of South Africa (Nersa) approved the proposed new coal capacity and are respondents to the action brought by youth activists and a coalition of civil society groups. The plaintiffs argued that the government failed to ensure adequate consultation with youth and other groups that are most vulnerable to the effects of coal plant pollution and climate change. The minister and Nersa argued the court could not intervene in what was a policy decision and insisted they did not breach the applicants' constitutional rights as no action had occurred to procure new coal capacity. The defendants also emphasised that the plan required 'high-efficiency, low-emission' (HELE) coal capacity. The Center for Environmental Rights, representing the applicants, dismissed the notion of 'clean coal' " as a myth as HELE coal plants still involve pollution in all stages of the supply chain, including greenhouse gas emissions and coal ash. (Daily Maverick, Center for Environmental Rights)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Queensland Liberal National Party (LNP) has pledged to scrap the state's renewable energy target and extend the operation of state-owned coal plants "indefinitely" if it wins the October 26 state election. Polling suggests the LNP could win the election in a landslide.

 

 Pakistan: At least 21 coal miners died when an armed group attacked several coal mines owned by the Junaid Coal Company near Duki in Balochistan.

 

 Turkiye: The Russian Ministry of Energy said the Turkish Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Alparslan Bayraktar expressed interest in working with Russian companies on coal power projects.

 

 US: Six workers were injured in an accident at Hallador Energy's Sunrise Coal Mine.

 

 Zimbabwe: Jindal Africa Investments has entered into a US$350 million joint venture with the Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Authority to refurbish six coal units at the 1590 MW Hwange power plant. The project aims to increase the capacity of the plant by 400 MW.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

IEA forecasts renewables to pass coal generation in 2025: In its Renewables 2024 report, the International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates renewable electricity generation will exceed coal generation for the first time in 2025. The IEA forecasts that renewables will increase from a 30 per cent share in 2023 to 46 per cent in 2030, with wind and solar accounting for nearly all of the growth. The agency forecasts solar capacity could triple and wind capacity double between 2023 and 2030, with global renewable electricity generation increasing by 90 per cent over the period. The IEA notes that power from wind and solar projects in China is now on par or marginally cheaper than coal generation, depending on the province. The agency estimates that despite the rapid forecast growth, renewables generation is likely to fall 14 per cent below the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario goal of 60 per cent share of electricity. (International Energy Agency [Pdf])

Romania faces coal mine methane challenge: Ember, a UK-based climate policy think tank, says Romania must rapidly address coal mine methane emissions from its operating and abandoned coal mines to comply with a new European Union regulation. In August 2025 the European Union's (EU) methane regulation came into effect and requires member countries and coal exporters to adopt strict standards for monitoring, reporting and verifying methane emissions. The new standards apply to both operating and closed coal mines. Ember found that three of Romania's four operating underground coal mines exceed the latest EU standards and must cut methane emissions or face penalties. Romania also has seven open-cut mines and produced almost 15 million tonnes of coal in 2023, making it the fifth-largest coal producer in the EU. (Ember)

Chinese coal company unveils US$24 billion plan for coal-to-oil project: China Energy Investment Corporation (CIEC) has announced a plan to spend 170 billion yuan (US$24 billion) on a coal-to-oil project in Hami City in Xinjiang province. The company is aiming to commission the first stage of the plant in 2027. The company said the plant will produce 4 million tonnes of oil products a year. China produced about 11 million tonnes of products in 2023 from existing coal-to-oil plants. While CIEC is the country's biggest coal miner and operates other plants, the proposal comes as Chinese oil consumption may have peaked. The China Petroleum and Chemical Industrial Federation estimates that profits in the coal-to-oil sector slumped by 53 per cent in 2023. (Mining.com)

US utilities lag on coal closures: The Sierra Club's annual The Dirty Truth report has found that many major US utilities have either made no progress over the last four years in phasing out coal generation or are ranked worse. The report reviewed the plans of 75 utilities that own half of all the remaining coal and gas capacity in the US, against the Biden administration's target of 80 per cent clean electricity by 2030 and 100 per cent by 2035. The utilities intend to retire 30 per cent of their coal generation by 2030, or 58,000 MW of the 148,000 MW they own. Only 20 of the utilities plan to exit coal generation by 2030. New Environmental Protection Authority standards require utilities that plan to operate coal generation beyond 2032 to meet new greenhouse gas emissions standards but many utilities do not detail how they intend to comply with the standards. The report found the 50 parent companies of the utilities plan to build 168,00 MW of solar capacity and 70,000 MW of wind capacity by 2035. However, the utilities also plan on building 93,000 MW of new gas capacity. (PV Magazine, Sierra Club [Pdf])

South African union leaders sceptical about clean energy transition: European Union diplomats and politicians from countries backing South Africa's US$11.6 billion Just Transition Energy Plan encountered scepticism from union leaders in meetings in the coal belt province of Mpumalanga. Denmark, Germany, Britain, France, the European Union, United States, Canada, Spain, the Netherlands and Switzerland are supporting the transition plan, but the government and Eskom have backtracked on coal plant closures initially planned by 2030, in part as a result of the political fallout of the poor planning for the October 2022 closure of the Komati plant. "When all speeches are said and done, we need to see the practical terms ... a real commitment to leaving no one behind," said Collen Mahlangu from the National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa. Stine Leth Rasmussen, the Deputy Director General of the Danish Energy Agency, said that the Esbjerg port in Denmark had traditionally provided low-skilled manual jobs providing support services for the oil industry and has not transitioned to supporting offshore wind projects. He said South Africa could become the leader in renewables on the continent. (Reuters, Eye Witness News)

Poland ordered to compensate coal company for coal mine cancellation: Green X Metals, formerly known as Prairie Mining, was awarded 252 million (US$329 million) in compensation from the Polish government over the Jan Karski coal mine. In June 2021, Prairie Mining launched legal action, arguing Polish government actions amounted to the expropriation of its rights to develop the Jan Karski and Debiensko mines and breached the Australia-Poland Bilateral Investment Treaty and the Energy Charter Treaty. The company initially sought 737 million (US$963 million) in lost profits and damages, but the Arbitral Tribunal in London rejected the company's claims over the Debiensko mine in Silesia. In 2018, the Ministry of Energy decided against granting mining approval for the Jan Karski project. Since the dispute, Prairie Mining has changed its name and is now pursuing a copper exploration project in Greenland. (BNE Intellinews, Green X Metals [Pdf])

Norwegian sovereign wealth fund reverses six coal exclusions: Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages Norway's Government Pension Fund Global (GPFG), has revoked the exclusions of six energy companies on the grounds that either their share of coal-based generation or revenue from thermal coal has fallen below the 30 per cent threshold. NBIM said US utility TXNM Energy, Brazilian utility Eneva, the Greek Public Power Corporation and Canadian companies Capital Power Corporation and TransAlta Corp all now generate less than 30 per cent of electricity from coal. NBIM also reversed the exclusion of the Polish coal mining company Jastrzebska Spolka Weglowa (JSW), as it earns less than 30 per cent of its revenue from coal. NBIM had the US utility Southern Company and Australian mining company BHP under observation. It has now revoked this status as both companies' share of generation and revenue, respectively, are below the trigger thresholds. (IPE, Norges Bank Investment Management [Pdf])

IEA says increased power growth is slowing the decline of coal: The International Energy Agency's (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2024 points to higher than expected electricity demand growth, slowing the decline in coal generation to 2035. The agency estimates the addition of more than 560 gigawatts (GW) of renewables capacity in 2023, with the sector on track to reach 10,000 GW by 2030. The IEA notes increased demand for air conditioning in heat waves, especially in India, as well as the growth of data centres and vehicle electrification. The report estimates coal use is likely to decline only gradually in its current policies scenario from 5986 million tonnes in 2023 to 4453 million tonnes by 2035. The IEA estimates that under current policies, dubbed STEPS in IEA jargon, the world is on track to a 2.4˚C temperature increase by 2100. (Climate Analytics, International Energy Agency)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 BHP lags peers on attachment to metallurgical coal: A report by the Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis (IEEFA) notes that of the five major global iron ore producers, BHP will soon be the only company producing both metallurgical coal and low-grade iron ore. The report notes that Vale, Rio Tinto, Fortescue and Anglo American are focussing on increasing production of high-grade iron ore suitable for direct reduced iron (DRI)-based steelmaking processes. Vale and Rio Tinto have sold their stakes in coal projects, Fortescue never had any and Anglo American is in the process of selling its Queensland metallurgical coal mines. In its latest Climate Transition Action Plan, BHP discounts the prospect of a switch to low-emissions steel production and continues to emphasise the possibility of retrofitting carbon capture and storage to coal-based steel plants. IEEFA notes that BHP's climate plan discounts the availability of hydrogen-based direct reduced iron technology until "the mid-2030s" despite the aim of Stegra, formerly known as H2 Green Steel, to commission the first commercial-scale plant in 2026. IEEFA argues that BHP risks underestimating the speed of the steel technology transition. BHP produced over 22 million tonnes of metallurgical coal in the year to the end of June 2024. The company is proposing to extend the life of its Peak Downs mine in Queensland, which produces 18 million tonnes of metallurgical coal a year, out to 2116. (Institute of Energy Economic and Financial Analysis)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Carbon Mapper, October 2024.

Carbon Mapper is publishing open-access methane and carbon dioxide emissions data from its Tanager-1 satellite. The data portal allows users to set filters on the data display, such as by the type of emissions, sector and date range.

Analysis: BHP's 2024 Climate Transition Action Plan, Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility (ACCR), September 26, 2024. (Pdf)

ACCR analyses BHP's latest climate plan and notes that the company proposes little investment in steel decarbonisation. ACCR also finds there is little detail on how BHP's metallurgical coal expansion plans align with its decarbonisation strategy.

Powering Up the Global South: The Cleantech Path to Growth, RMI, October 2024. (Pdf)

This 39-page report reviews the rapid growth of renewable electricity generation in the Global South and finds key factors in favour of accelerating deployment.

New South Wales Land and Environment Court)
(Institute of Energy Economic and Financial Analysis)

title: CoalWire 537, October 31, 2024
excerpt: Surprise Japanese election result; Indian government utilities opposed coal ash regulation.
content:
October 31, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The failure of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and an ally to win a majority in the Japanese election puts a big question mark on the country's energy policy. For the last 12 years, the LDP government has resisted domestic and international pressure to stop building new coal plants and phase out existing projects. Prime Minister Ishiba may be able to cobble together a minority government, but that is far from clear at present. The Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan (CDP), the largest opposition party, supports more ambitious targets for renewables and a transition away from coal but it too is well short of holding a majority of seats. In other election news, the pro-coal Liberal National Party comfortably won government in Queensland. In British Columbia, Canada's largest coal exporting province, the New Democratic Party has narrowly retained government.

In the US, a new report explains why coal plant closures will occur at a faster rate than the Energy Information Administration estimates. But there are two wild cards on the horizon. The first is the possibility that Donald Trump could win next week's election for US President and move to gut a range of environmental regulations that are pushing coal out of the generation mix. The other is the prospect that increased electricity demand for data centres could prolong the life of at least some old coal plants that are slated to close. The Sierra Club notes that while a high rate of demand growth in the sector is possible, some analysts are overstating the number of data centre projects.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Race for US President has no time for old 'King Coal' 

The 'war on coal' narrative that was a significant element in the 2020 election has faded from the national stage and has scarcely been mentioned by US presidential candidates Donald Trump and Kamala Harris, writes Taylor Kuykendall in S & P Global.

 

 Why you – and the planet – are paying for the Artificial Intelligence gold rush

The rapid growth of data centres for Artificial Intelligence applications is, in some locations in the US, slowing the closure of coal power plants and adding pressure for new gas capacity, writes Megan Wachspress from the Sierra Club.

 

 Shooting the climate change messenger in Vietnam

As Vietnam reels from the aftermath of Typhoon Yagi and the impact of rising sea levels, one of Vietnam's most prominent climate defenders, Dang Dinh Bach, is two weeks into a hunger strike – not from the frontlines of the climate struggle, but from behind prison bars, write Andrea Giorgetta from the International Federation for Human Rights and Maureen Harris from International Rivers in Asia Times.

 

 As coal plants shut in Romania, some miners transition to green energy while others are reluctant

As Romanian coal generation declines, there is a lack of incentives and guarantees for coal workers to equip themselves with new skills for a renewables-based energy system, writes Anca Gurzu in Cipher.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Japan's ruling party loses election: The October 27 election has resulted in a shock loss for the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) led by Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba. Just after Ishiba took office on October 1, he called a snap election in a bid to distance himself from a scandal over LDP MPs' slush funds. The LDP and its coalition partner, Komeito, won only 215 seats in the 465-member lower house, down from the 279 won in the 2021 election. The leading opposition party, the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan (CDP), increased the number of seats it holds from 98 to 148. The CDP supports 50 per cent of electricity from renewables by 2030 and increased energy efficiency and energy storage. It also supports transitioning away from coal generation and phasing out nuclear power. Ishiba could form a minority government coalition with one or both of the Democratic Party for the People (DPP), which has won 28 seats, or the Japan Innovation Party (JIP), which has won 38 seats. However, both the DPP and JIP have significant policy differences with Ishiba's LDP and have ruled out forming a minority government with the LDP and Komeito. Japan's 7th Strategic Energy Plan is due for release in early 2025 and will indicate whether the government intends to adopt measures consistent with its G7 commitment to phase out unabated coal generation in the early 2030s. (AP, Argus)

 

 Election results in Australian state and Canadian province: The Queensland Resources Council (QRC), the state's mining industry lobby group, has welcomed the election of the pro-coal Liberal National Party (LNP) at the Queensland state election. The LNP won 52 seats in the 93-seat single-house parliament, with the counting of ballots in a handful of seats still to be finalised. Queensland has 56 operating coal mines that produced 223 million tonnes of coal in 2023, including 102 million tonnes of metallurgical coal. The LNP pledged to scrap the state's renewable energy target and extend the operation of state-owned coal plants "indefinitely". The QRC wants the new government to lower coal royalties after the Labor government legislated higher rates in 2022 that reaped A$9.4 billion (US$6.2 billion) in two years. In Canada, the ruling centre-left New Democratic Party suffered a swing against it in the British Columbian provincial election but has won a one-seat majority, subject to a judicial recount in two seats. If the NDP loses the seat of Surrey-Guildford on a recount, it could form a minority government with the support of the Greens, which won two seats. Glencore has four major metallurgical coal mines in the Elk Valley in British Columbia. The NDP, which has been in government since 2017, resisted calls for several years for an International Joint Commission study of water pollution in the Elk and Kootenai River catchments. (The Guardian, Queensland Resources Council, CBC)

 

 US coal port backers fund ads in election campaign for Oakland City Attorney: SOS Oakland, a group backed by two executives associated with the proposed Oakland coal export terminal, is buying online ads supporting Brenda Harbin-Forte for Oakland City Attorney. SOS Oakland received US$20,000 from Jonathan Brooks, the founder of the hedge fund JMB Capital and US$4000 from Vikas Tandon, an executive with the fund. JMB Capital controls Insight Terminal Solutions (ITS), one of the companies that proposed the Oakland coal export terminal. The project has faced protracted opposition and legal challenges since 2015, with ITS suing the City of Oakland for about US$1 billion in damages after a dispute over the port development contract. Harbin-Forte declined a request from No Coal in Oakland to rule out accepting financial support from coal terminal interests or their agents. Her rival, Ryan Richardson, agreed to rule out financial support from coal interests. (Oaklandside, No Coal in Oakland)

 

 Trump ally talks up plan to defund EPA: Russell Vought, one of the architects of the Project 2025 policy agenda, told a May 2023 conference that a future Donald Trump administration should defund the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). "We want their funding to be shut down so that the EPA can't do all of the rules against our energy industry because they have no bandwidth financially to do so. We want to put them in trauma," Vought said. He said he also wanted public servants to be "traumatically affected" so that "when they wake up in the morning, we want them to not want to go to work because they are increasingly viewed as the villains". Project 2025 includes proposals to allow the removal of employment protections for government workers. The original proponent of the measure suggested that Trump could fire up to 50,000 federal employees. (ProPublica)

 

 Coal billionaire backs Czech climate sceptic think tank: Czech coal billionaire Pavel Tykac announced he will fund the Vaclav Klaus Institute (IVK), a right-wing think tank founded by former Czech President Vaclav Klaus that opposes environmentalism and dismisses global heating. Tykac's privately-owned Sev.en Group operate 1000 MW of lignite units at the 1847 MW Pocerady plant in the Czech Republic and has coal power stations and mines in the US, Australia and Vietnam. Alan Svoboda, the head of Sev.en Group's international business, said the company is considering investing in coal projects in India, Indonesia and Malaysia. (BNE Intellinews, BNN Bloomberg)

 

 Documents reveal Indian govt utilities opposed coal ash regulation: Two government-owned companies – Coal India and National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) – lobbied the Indian government between 2019 and 2023 to weaken regulations requiring the 100 per cent reuse of coal ash from power plants. After the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change introduced fines in 2021 for non-compliance with the regulation, both NTPC and Coal India urged the government to scrap the coal ash reuse requirement. NTPC, which generates about one-quarter of India's electricity, claimed that the potential fines for failure to excavate existing dams could "render large pit head thermal power stations commercially unviable" and cause a power crisis. The Centre for Science and Environment estimates that Indian utilities have more than 1.65 billion tonnes of fly ash stored in impoundments. The government reduced the potential fine from 1500 rupees per tonne (US$17.80 per tonne) to 1000 rupees per tonne (US$11.90 per tonne) in the final 2021 regulation and added a loophole that exempted "operational" dams from the 100 per cent reuse requirement. (Climate Home News)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 India: The Supreme Court of India dismissed an application by the former Jharkhand chief minister Madhu Koda to suspend his 2017 conviction for criminal conspiracy in the allocation of the Rajhara North Coal Block in Jharkhand. Koda wanted the conviction overturned to allow him to contest the Jharkhand state election in November.

 

 Mozambique: JSW Steel's proposed purchase of a 92.19 per cent stake in Minas de Revuboe (MDR) will be delayed pending government decisions after the recent election. MDR has launched legal action against the government in the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes over a mining concession. The case could take several years.

 

 Norway: Norges Bank Investment Management will vote against BHP's proposed Climate Transition Action Plan over the company's lack of detailed transition plans to cut emissions.

 

 Philippines: With the expiry of a 25-year build-operate-transfer agreement, the government has transferred ownership of the 1294 MW Sual power station to San Miguel Global Power.

 

 Philippines: A barge carrying 11,200 tonnes of coal from Semirara ran aground on a coral reef near San Salvador Island and spilled coal into the ocean.

 

 Philippines: The Department of Energy (DOE) has awarded a two-year coal exploration contract to Filipinas Systems over Kapai and Tagoloan II municipalities in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. DOE wants to boost domestic coal production and cut imports.

 

 South Africa: The South African government has launched the Just Energy Transition Partnership Funding Platform to link funding from the US$9.3 billion deal with specific projects.

 

 "Actually, getting these coal plants [in the US] retired has been thwarted by a pretty savvy effort to confuse policymakers that somehow we have this crazy demand growth, and we can't possibly meet it with clean energy," 

said Bruce Nilles, executive director of Climate Imperative.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Chinese coal generation increases as emissions flatten: Government data indicates that Chinese coal generation increased by two per cent in the three months to the end of September, with a decline in the construction-related sectors of steel and cement production keeping carbon dioxide emissions flat. Solar and wind generation were up by 44 per cent and 24 per cent, respectively, but were offset by increased air conditioning demand during heatwaves in August and September. Coal consumption by the coal-to-chemicals industry has risen by 18 per cent in the first eight months of 2024. The coal-to-chemicals sector has received strong backing from the National Development and Reform Commission, a powerful central government planning agency. (Carbon Brief)

Uncertainty around of US data centre load growth on coal power: Increased US electricity demand from data centres could vary between 2 to 20 per cent a year, according to estimates by government agencies, utilities and NGO groups. Some utilities estimate a base rate of two to three per cent a year in data centre load growth with the potential to increase to about nine per cent a year. The Sierra Club estimates data centre demand could rise between 5 per cent and 20 per cent a year. However, the group cautions that some high-end estimates overestimate demand by totalling demand from all proposed data centres without adjusting for companies approaching several regions. While some significant data centre users are seeking renewable power supply, others are seeking contracts from utillities with underutilised coal plants or units converted to burn gas. (Argus Media)

US coal retirements tracking faster than government agency projects: The Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis (IEEFA) estimates US utilities plan to close or convert to gas 68,789 megawatts (MW) of coal capacity between 2025 and 2030. The IEEFA estimate is almost double the 36,425MW the Energy Information Administration (EIA) said will close over the same period. IEEFA notes that the EIA does not treat the 12,273 MW of coal-to-gas conversions as the closure of a coal unit. The EIA also relies on information submitted by utilities but does not include announcements, data in resource plans provided to regulators or filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. IEEFA estimates US coal capacity could be about 175,000 MW by the end of the year, down from a peak of 317,600 MW in 2011. IEEFA notes that of the 115,300 MW of coal capacity that could be online at the end of 2030, closure dates have been announced for just over one-third by 2040. It also argues that some of the units will be 60 years old by 2030, with the remaining units likely to operate at reduced capacity factors or sit idled for long periods. (Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis)

Western Balkans power exports face carbon barrier: The Energy Community Secretariat has warned that no Western Balkan country is on track to win exemption from the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which will impose carbon costs on electricity imports from January 1, 2026. CBAM will impose a carbon cost on imports so that European Union producers, which pay a carbon price, aren't undercut by imports that are not subject to a carbon price. The secretariat said that a critical element in winning an exemption from CBAM penalties between 2026 and 2030 is coupling electricity markets of exporting countries to ensure harmonisation of electricity exchanges and to minimise price differences between markets. Serbia, which has initiated market coupling measures, would have incurred a 1.07 billion (US$1.17 billion) penalty if CBAM was in effect in 2023. Based on 2023 power exports, the combined penalties for Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and North Macedonia would have been 797 million (US$861 million). (Balkan Green Energy News)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Emissions Gap Report 2024: No more hot air please!, United Nations Environment Program (UNEP), October 2024. (The full report is here as a Pdf.)

This 100-page report provides UNEP's latest stocktake on progress to cut greenhouse gas emissions. UNEP concludes that current commitments by governments put the world on track for a temperature increase of 2.6-3.1C this century.

"How a coal polluter's new strategy for sustainability transformed its business", Harvard Business Review, October 23, 2024.

This 22-minute podcast reviews the transformation of Italy's state-owned power company, Enel, from one of Europe's largest coal users to a utility with a strong emphasis on renewables.
