title: CoalWire 538, November 7, 2024
excerpt: Trump wins US election; Japanese PM to lead minority government.
content:
November 7, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The full impact of the electoral victory of Donald Trump and the Republican party will take some time to discern. Domestically, his win, along with the new Republican majority in the Senate, is likely to have a significant impact on agencies regulating the power sector, such as the Environmental Protection Agency. After taking office next January, the new Trump administration may manage to slow the retirement of some coal plants and stall aspects of the US energy transition. However, it is worth bearing in mind that the last Trump administration failed to halt the decline of coal mining and generation and the power sector has changed profoundly over the last four years. The likely impact of the Trump administration on international climate and energy policy over the next four years is less clear at the moment.

In Japan, the recent election has delivered a minority government. The surprise twist is that the defeated Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba is likely to resume his role, albeit dependent on the support of other parties to progress legislation. Whether the LDP minority government changes tack on its support for coal and gas in the power sector, remains to be seen.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 What Trump got wrong on China, coal and climate

Republican candidate Donald Trump has cited China's coal plants as a reason for the US to stick with fossil fuels – but he fails to acknowledge China's massive clean energy industry, writes Christine Shearer from Global Energy Monitor in Climate Home News.

 

 Further decline in the coal industry gives rise to a new phenomenon: Zombie mines

As many as 1300 of these coal mining facilities across Appalachia shuttered for at least a decade without operators finishing cleanup, write Stephanie Sandoval, Carrie Cochran and Amy Fan in Scripps News.

 

 How Modi has supported Adani's global ambitions

The growth of the Adani Group outside India, including coal projects in Bangladesh and Australia, has been closely aligned with the diplomatic efforts of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, write Paranjoy Guha Thakurta and Ayush Joshi in Adani Watch.

 

 The energy capital powering India and poisoning its residents

Pollution from NTPC's 4760 megawatt (MW) Vindhyachal plant and nearby coal mines have heavily affected villagers living near one of the world's top 10 most polluting power stations, writes Bhasker Tripathi in Context.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Trump wins, Republicans flip Senate but House of Representatives outcome is unclear: While climate policy featured less prominently in the 2024 US Presidential campaign, Republican candidate Donald Trump regularly touted coal and fossil fuels and said he would withdraw from the Paris Agreement. US election results revealed Republic Donald Trump was elected as President, defeating Kamala Harris. The Republican party also won control of the Senate, picking up seats in West Virginia, Ohio and Montana to give it a clear majority. Initial counting indicates the control of the House of Representatives may not be clear for several days. Republicans held 220 seats in the 435-member House of Representatives, with the Democrats holding 212 seats and a further three vacant due to the death of two members and a retirement. At the time of writing, the Republicans have won 201 seats and the Democrats 184 seats. (Climate Home News)

 

 Japanese Prime Minister may lead a minority government: Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) leader Shigeru Ishiba is likely to be re-elected Prime Minister after tendering his resignation at the start of the four-day session of the parliament commencing on November 11. If Ishiba is re-elected Prime Minister, he will lead a minority government and is expected to reappoint the same Cabinet apart from replacements for two ministers who lost their seats at the October 27 election. The opposition National Democratic Party and Japan Innovation Party will provide support for the minority government but assess legislation on a case-by-case basis. On energy policy, the National Democratic Party and the Japan Innovation Party promote the development of next generation nuclear plants. The Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan, the largest opposition party, favours more ambitious renewables targets and phasing out coal and nuclear plants. Ishiba's government supports restarting nuclear plants that shut down after the 2011 Fukushima disaster, but the process has been far from smooth. TEPCO restarted one unit at the Onagawa nuclear power plant on October 27 but shut it down five days later after a fault was detected. A new report by Reclaim Finance and Kiko Network notes that Japan is the only OECD country without a coal phase-out deadline, with Japanese banks providing US$23.5 billion since 2021 for thermal coal projects. The groups want the new government to adopt an energy strategy based on phasing coal power out by 2030 and replacing it with renewables, grid upgrades and energy efficiency measures. (Straits Times, ABC News, Reclaim Finance)

 

 Doubt increase over future of troubled US CCS project: Archer-Daniels-Midland (ADM) has told the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that it has found two dozen additional wells that could pollute groundwater supplies with carbon dioxide from its carbon capture and storage (CCS) plant at the 335 MW coal-fired Decatur power station in Illinois. ADM said the wells could potentially allow sequestered carbon dioxide to affect drinking water supplies. The EPA said the latest results do not suggest "any immediate threat" to drinking water supplies. In September, the EPA issued a violation notice to ADM over alleged breaches of its permit for the CCS project and alleged the company had allowed the injection of carbon dioxide into "unauthorised zones" and failed to follow the provisions of the emergency response and remediation plan. ADM's CCS injection well began commercial operation in 2017 with the aim of burying one million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year. ADM suspended the injection of further carbon dioxide in early October. A coalition of 150 civil society groups has called on the EPA to cease approving new injection wells and halt current projects. (E & E News [paywall])

 

 South African groups raise alarm over proposed special economic zone: A coalition of environmental groups has expressed alarm that the public could be shut out of involvement in decisions on the proposed Musina-Makhado Special Economic Zone (MMSEZ) unless they register their interest by November 12, 2024. In September 2018, President Cyril Ramaphosa announced Chinese government support for the zone's development, including up to 3300 MW of coal plants to support mineral smelting and other industrial projects. Chinese backing for the coal plants was withdrawn in late 2021, with the local planning authority claiming the zone would be solar-powered. The coalition noted that the proposed 1000 MW solar project would require clearing 4000 hectares of indigenous vegetation but provide only one-quarter of the electricity for the proposed ferrochrome smelter, coal washery and other projects over the 60 square kilometre zone. One of the coalition members, Living Limpopo, argues the MMSEZ will include coal mining in the Vhembe Biosphere Reserve. Members of the public can register their interest either with Gudani Consulting, the consultancy for the proponents or join Living Limpopo. (Iol, Living Limpopo)

 

 State police try to block Australian coal port protest: New South Wales Police has applied to the Supreme Court to reject the permit for Rising Tide's 2024 proposed November 19-28 festival and protest against the Newcastle coal export terminal. NSW Police claimed the public assembly permit, which would protect participants from obstruction and unlawful assembly charges, should be rejected, claiming the proposed protest would create significant safety risks to participants and members of the public. Rising Tide is aiming to attract thousands to the combined festival and protest, with the culmination of a flotilla of boats blocking coal shipping. Rising Tide wants the NSW Labor government to commit to phasing out coal exports through Newcastle by 2030, cancel new fossil fuel projects and tax existing projects to fund the transition. In 2023, a flotilla of about 3000 people blocked coal ships for 32 hours, with 109 arrested after the permit expired. (Guardian, Guardian, Rising Tide)

 

 Zimbabwean utility to move 500 households due to pollution: The state-owned Zimbabwe Power Company (ZPC) has agreed with Hwange Town Council to relocate over 500 families due to air pollution from the 1590 MW Hwange power station. Five of the seven coal units at the plant do not have flue gas desulphurisation units to cut sulphur dioxide emissions. ZPC has agreed to relocate all its workers living in the suburb of Ingagula to new housing in the council's area. (NewsDay)

 

 Adani presses ahead with mine expansion, but request to abandon hospital project rejected: An Adani subsidiary is pushing ahead with the development of the 21 million tonnes of coal per annum (Mtpa) Parsa East and Kente Basan mine in the Hasdeo Arand forest, despite failing to meet the February 2024 deadline to build a 100-bed hospital for local communities. The requirement to build the hospital was a condition imposed as part of approval to allow the mine to expand from 15 Mtpa to 21 Mtpa. Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Limited (RVUN), a power utility owned by the Rajasthan state government, was allocated the coal block in Chhattisgarh in 2007. The Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate Change rejected a request by Adani to exempt the company from the requirement to build the hospital but relaxed other conditions, such as requirements to control dust from the mine. (AdaniWatch)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Anglo American has sold its 33 per cent stake in the Jellinbah Group to billionaire Sam Chong's Zashvin Pty Limited for A$1.6 billion (US$1.1 billion). The Jellinbah Group owns a 70 per cent stake in the Jellinbah East and Lake Vermont metallurgical coal mines in Queensland. The sale is part of Anglo American's plan to exit the metallurgical coal sector.

 

 Canada: Northback Resources, a subsidiary of Australian Gina Rinehart's Hancock Prospecting, is urging residents of Crowsnest Pass to vote Yes in a non-binding municipal poll on the Grassy Mountain coal project in Alberta.

 

 India: A report to the Meghalaya High Court by a committee headed by B P Katakey proposes blowing up the entrances of illegal coal mines and regular aerial surveys to detect the development of new unauthorised projects.

 

 New Zealand: The new conservative government is pushing ahead with fast-tracking major projects, including at least several coal mines.

 

 Philippines: Civil society groups have called for a full investigation into the pollution of the Masinloc-Oyon protected seascape with coal from a barge accident.

 

 Poland: Local officials and energy transition advocates want the post-closure planning for PGE's Belchatow lignite mine to focus on new energy projects rather than leaving it as a recreation zone.

 

 Serbia: The commissioning process of the 350 MW Kostolac B3 lignite plant is nearing completion. The unit, which is likely to be the last coal unit commissioned in Europe, was built by China Machinery Engineering Corporation.

 

 South Africa: A major fire occurred in the 475 MW Unit 6 at Eskom's 3000 MW Kriel Power Station. The utility is assessing the extent of the damage.

 

 UK: The government budget includes 25 million (US$32 million) for the rehabilitation of abandoned coal tips in Wales, but Plaid Cymru, a centre-left Welsh party, said the estimated cost of rehabilitation is about 600 million (US$777 million).

 

 UK: The new leader of the Opposition Conservative Party, Kemi Badenoch, described herself as a "net zero sceptic" and opponent of "radical environmental policies". Badenoch received 10,000 for her leadership campaign from Neil Record, the chair of Net Zero Watch, a project of the Global Warming Policy Foundation, a climate science denial group.

 

 US: Joe Craft, the billionaire CEO of Alliance Resource Partners, a major US coal mining company, contributed US$1.5 million to America PAC, Elon Musk's pro-Trump campaign group.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Review finds 376 companies with thermal coal plans: The annual update to the Global Coal Exit List by Urgewald and 51 other NGOs has found that 376 companies with thermal coal interests are planning to develop new thermal coal mines, coal-related transport infrastructure or power plants in 36 countries. The report found that 40 per cent of the 1579 companies reviewed plan to develop new thermal coal related projects. The proposed mines have a combined capacity of 2636 million tonnes per annum (Mtpa), with state-owned Coal India proposing 90 new mines with up to 556 Mtpa of thermal coal capacity. The countries with the largest proposed expansion in thermal coal capacity are India (947 Mtpa), China (873 Mtpa) and Australia (201 Mtpa). The report estimates coal power capacity increased by 30 gigawatts (GW) in the last year to 2126 GW. In 2015, the year the Paris Agreement was negotiated, coal power plant capacity was 1910 GW. (Urgewald)

Bangladesh plants power down due to lack of coal and funding crunch: Five coal plants reliant on imported coal have cut electricity generation due to a lack of coal, unpaid bills, maintenance and mechanical problems. Only the 1244 MW Payra plant continues to run at full capacity, with the 1150 MW Matabari and the 307 MW Barishal plants shut down entirely. The Matabari plant has exhausted its coal stocks, with a further delivery not expected until December, while the Barishal is offline for routine maintenance. Three other plants – the 1234 MW Rampal, 1224 MW SS Power and 444 MW Barapukuria plants – with a combined capacity of 2902 MW, have just 1205 MW online. Adani Power has curtailed electricity generation at its 1496 MW Godda coal plant in the Indian state of Jharkhand by shutting down one of its two units. Adani claims Bangladesh owes it US$846 million. Adani has threatened to shut down the other unit at the Godda plant if the outstanding debt is not paid by November 7. An adviser to the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus said Bangladesh paid US$100 million to Adani in October and is owed about US$700 million. (Daily Star, Financial Times)

Review finds fossil fuel donors backed candidates for US utility regulators: An analysis has found that more than one-third of campaign contributions to candidates running for office as public utility commissioners originated from fossil fuel and electric utility interests. Elections for commissioners were held on November 5. Floodlight analysed all donations of over US$250 in the last 10 years to the 54 candidates who ran in the nine states that elect commissioners that oversee private utilities. The investigation found fossil fuel companies and private utilities contributed more than US$13.5 million to campaigns for public utility commissioners. The states reviewed were Alabama, Arizona, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, Oklahoma and South Dakota. The analysis found that Alabama and Louisiana topped the list for fossil fuel and utility contributions, with 55 per cent and 43 per cent, respectively. The nine states with elected commissioners all have significant shares of gas and coal generation and in most of these, a smaller share of wind and solar than the national average. In other states, elected officials appoint utility regulators. (Floodlight)

German coal use slumps in 2024: In the first nine months of 2024, hard coal use in the power sector fell by 39 per cent and lignite generation by 14.5 per cent, according to an assessment of preliminary data by AG Energiebilanzen (AEGB), an energy consultancy established by German industry associations and energy institutes. AGEB estimates coal power now accounts for about 25 per cent of German electricity generation, down by more than half since 1990. The decline in coal generation in 2024 is due to a mix of factors, including a sluggish domestic economy, increased deployment of renewables and increased power imports. The last three German nuclear power plants closed in April 2023. German law requires the phase-out of remaining coal capacity by 2038 at the latest. However, the recent electoral success of far-right parties, which oppose the government's current climate policies, has cast a shadow over the prospect of earlier retirement of coal plants. One factor likely to drive the earlier retirement of lignite units is the rising cost of carbon under the European Union's Emissions Trading System. The current price is about 64 per tonne (US$83 per tonne) of carbon dioxide emissions, with most scenarios estimating a significant rise in prices later this decade. (Clean Energy Wire)

 

Polish city grapples with plant and mines closures slated for 2030s: The Polish city of Belchatow faces an uncertain future with PGE's 5030 MW lignite plant and associated mines set to close in the mid-2030s and energy transition projects just commencing. Research by Instrat estimates that by 2038, when the last of the coal pits is scheduled to close, almost three-quarters of the workforce will be eligible for their pension. A 2022 agreement between the government and unions will ensure that many of PGE's 7000 direct employees at the power plant and associated mines will qualify for severance packages, but this does not extend to an estimated 5500 contractors engaged in transport and maintenance. While the bulk of PGE's workforce is male, women in Belchatow's service sectors are likely to be adversely affected if economic diversification projects fail to gain traction. In recent national elections, Patryk Marjan, a candidate for the far-right Konfederacja party and a critic of the energy transition, was elected as Belchatow's mayor. (Mining.com)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Steel companies' slow to embrace emissions reduction targets: A review of the top 50 steel companies has found that only 20 of the top 50 steel producers have pledged to reach net zero emissions by 2050, an increase of three in the last year. The 20 companies account for 565 million tonnes a year of steel capacity. However, the Global Energy Monitor and the Leadership Group for Industry Transition found that half of those with 2050 commitments do not have a specific emissions reduction target for 2030, and only four include the full range of emissions spanning from coal and coke production, electricity inputs and downstream emissions such as transport. Twenty-one companies have not publicly disclosed climate targets and a further 14 companies have not defined the categories of emissions they intend to reduce. (Global Energy Monitor)

title: CoalWire 539, November 14, 2024
excerpt: Trump team takes shape; early German election likely; Indonesian captive power boom.
content:
November 14, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

A week after Donald Trump was elected US President, the shape of the next administration is becoming more apparent, but the impact on international climate is subject to much debate. The Trump Administration will withdraw from the Paris Agreement (again) and increase trade restrictions aimed at Chinese products. These measures alone are unlikely to make much immediate difference to the global coal mining and power sector and could actually boost China's dominance of clean energy products and technologies. Indian solar panel exporters are also likely beneficiaries. How will European leaders respond? Will the propspect of a Trump administration spur the growth of the grassroots climate movement? Will the Trump administration withdraw US support from the Just Energy Transition Partnership programmes supporting a coal-to-clean shift in Indonesia, Vietnam and South Africa? 

Trump's pick for the head of the Environmental Protection Agency has a brief to pursue deregulation to benefit the energy industry. High on the list of targets are environmental regulations affecting coal mining and power stations, environmental justice programs and weakening legal enforcement. These will shift environmental, health and social costs to local communities and may extend the life of some coal plants. But, as no new coal plants are under construction in the US, Trump's deregulation agenda is only likely to delay the day of reckoning. By the end of Trump's term, the US fleet of coal plants will be four years older and often even less viable. Whether coal communities will be better prepared for the inevitable transition is less clear.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Donald Trump can't stop global climate action. If we stick together, it's the US that will lose out

Donald Trump's re-election to the White House is a significant setback for climate action, but ultimately, it's the US that could end up losing out, as the rest of the world will move forward without it, writes Bill Hare, the chief executive of Climate Analytics in the Guardian.

 

 Trump 2.0 could make even the most optimistic climate observers cynical – but it's not the whole story

While the new Trump administration will affect the transition to clean energy in the US, the most consequential decisions affecting the climate over the next four years will not be made in Washington D.C., writes Adam Morton in the Guardian.

 

 Experts: What does a Trump presidency mean for climate action?

Climate scientists, researchers and experts have expressed concern about his election's impact on efforts to tackle climate change, writes Molly Lempriere in Carbon Brief.

 

 Who will limit Trump's climate wreckage?

Many of the national leaders who promoted climate action during the last Trump presidency are distracted by their own domestic or regional problems. But the last Trump presidency was also the era of the youth climate movement, with many of the big leadership decisions beginning on the streets, writes Karl Mathieson in Politico.

 

 How will another Trump presidency affect Southeast Asia's energy transition?

The US is the biggest state partner in Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) programmes with Indonesia and Vietnam, to support the transition from coal power to clean energy. The withdrawal of US funding could stall these projects, writes Liang Lei in Eco-Business.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Trump announces EPA pick as Republicans win control of Congress: President-elect Trump announced he will appoint Lee Zeldin, a former Republican Congressman, to head the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). A central part of Zeldin's brief is to cut government regulations affecting the energy sector. Key EPA rules affecting the coal sector include regulations on coal ash disposal, pollution standards, haze reduction and a range of environmental justice initiatives. The Bureau of Land Management, a part of the Department of Interior, oversees the leasing of public lands for coal mining. Trump has not yet announced his nominee for the agency. The future of two signature laws of President Biden, the Inflation Reduction Act and the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, is less clear as Republican states are beneficiaries of energy transformation projects such as battery manufacturing and renewable energy projects. At the time of writing, the Republican party will narrowly retain control of the 435-seat House of Representatives, winning 218 seats and leading in three more. A majority is 218 seats. The Democrats have won 208 and lead in three more, while the Republicans won control of the Senate 52-46 seats. New members of both houses will be sworn in on January 3, 2025, with Trump's inauguration later that month. (E & E News, Canary Media, Inside Climate News, New York Times [Paywall])

 

 Bangladesh monitoring report reveals pollution from Rampal coal plant: An environmental monitoring report on the 1320 megawatt (MW) Maitree Super Thermal Power Project states the plant has not taken steps to minimise coal dust pollution at the site and that the disposal of dredged material was harmful to the environment. The report for the February to April quarter by the Bangladesh government's Center for Environmental and Geographic Information Services is the first published since public protests in August toppled the repressive Hasina government. The report stated that coal dust and fly ash are not correctly managed and are hazardous to workers. It also disclosed that the sewage system for the workers' accommodation is inadequate and causing an environmental hazard around the camp area. The two 660 MW units at the plant were commissioned in December 2022 and April 2024. Waterkeepers Bangladesh coordinator Sharif Jamil said the revelations in the report "must be the tip of the iceberg". (Daily Star, New Age, Center for Environmental and Geographic Information Services [Pdf])

 

 Australian court rules against coal port protest: A Supreme Court judge has ruled in favour of a New South Wales Police request to reject Rising Tide's notice of intention to hold a protest against the Newcastle coal export terminal. Police claimed that a proposed water-based protest flotilla to block coal ships represented a safety risk to participants and police alike. In his decision, Justice Desmond Fagan wrote that he agreed with police that some people "may engage in group behaviour that threatens to become unmanageable". Without police approval, protesters can be charged with obstructing people, vehicles or vessels. Rising Tide said it plans to proceed with the November 19-28 festival and protest. (ABC News, Guardian)

 

 Groups challenge impacts of South African special economic zone: The Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment has approved the clearing of 1000 protected trees, including ancient boabs, as part of the development of the northern section of the Musina-Makhado Special Economic Zone. Living Limpopo, an NGO that opposes the industrialisation of the area, said documents supporting the proposed zone cite the development of the Greater Soutpansberg Coalfield as a critical locational factor. The zone is proposed to include a coal washery along with steel, petrochemical and other industrial plants. The Department of Mineral Resources and Energy has granted licenses for 12 new open-cut coal mines in the zone. The High Court will hear a legal challenge against the environmental authorisation for the project on December 6. (IOL, Limpopo Mirror)

 

 Indian agency finds mine approval based on forged documents: Chhattisgarh State Scheduled Tribe Commission, a government agency to oversee safeguards for designated tribal groups, has recommended cancelling the forest clearance for the Parsa coal mine after finding the approval was obtained with forged documents. The commission upheld a complaint by 41 residents from affected villagers who argued that documents submitted by Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Limited (RRVUNL), a state-owned power utility, misrepresented the approval of the local village council. The Parsa coal block in the Hasdeo-Arand forest was allocated to RRVUNL, which awarded the development and operation of the mine to a subsidiary of Adani Mining. Chhattisgarh Bachao Andolan, a civil society group supporting tribal rights and forest protection, called for the Chhattisgarh government to cancel the forest and environment clearances for the mine and to launch a criminal case against the government officials involved. In mid-October, villagers and police were injured at a protest against the felling of part of the forests for the mine. (The Hindu, Adani Watch)

 

 German election likely in early 2025: Chancellor Olaf Scholz announced he will fire Finance Minister Christian Lindner, triggering the collapse of the minority government between the Social Democrats, the Greens and the Free Democratic Party (FDP). A critical factor in the dismissal of Lindner, the leader of the FDP, was his proposal for tax cuts and reversing a suite of national climate policies. Scholz said a vote of confidence in his government will occur on January 15, and if it fails, an election will be called by March. Recent polling suggests that the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and its Bavarian partner, the Christian Social Union, are polling about 32 per cent, with the far-right Alternative for Germany party about 17 per cent. Support for the Greens has slumped to about 10 per cent, while Scholz's SDP attracts about 17 per cent support from voters. Existing legislation requires the closure of coal plants by 2038. (Politico, Clean Energy Wire)

 

 Photos reveal coal-covered beaches after Philippines coal spill: Former ACT Teachers party MP Antonio Tinio has called for the compensation of fishing communities affected by pollution caused by a barge carrying 11,000 tonnes of coal running aground. Photographs revealed coal-covered beaches in San Salvador Island Marine Sanctuary almost 2 weeks after a coal barge ran aground. The sanctuary is part of the Masinloc-Oyon Bay Protected Seascape and Landscape. A second barge carrying an unknown amount of coal capsized near Sorsogon City during Severe Tropical Storm Kristine. (ABS-CBN News, Inquirer)

 

 
 "If there is one person on Earth who stands as the embodiment of unbreakable tenacity, unshakeable grit, relentless determination and the courage to stay true to his beliefs, it is Donald Trump. Fascinating to see America's democracy empower its people and uphold the nation's founding principles. Congratulations to the 47th POTUS-elect,"

wrote Gautam Adani, the Chairman of the Adani Group, on X after the US election.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Federal government officials confirmed a criminal investigation is underway into illegal land clearing of 47 hectares of forest by Vitrinite. Despite the investigation, the government is continuing to assess Vitrinite's application for a 1.9 million tonnes a year expansion of its Vulcan South metallurgical coal mine.

 

 Bangladesh: The Ministry of Power has opened a letter of credit worth US$170 million to stave off power cuts from Adani's Gooda coal plant in India.

 

 Brazil: Coal imports in November are set to surge to a record monthly level as hydro generation has slumped to a three-year low. Hydro generation usually accounts for 65 per cent of the country's electricity supply.

 

 India: The Ministry of Coal has cancelled the allocation to JSW Steel of the Banai-Bhalumunda coal block in Chhattisgarh. The ministry said the company had failed to provide a 10 billion rupee (US$119 million) bank guarantee and has forfeited its 1 billion rupee (US$11.9 million) deposit.

 

 Montenegro: The directors of the Pljevlja Coal Mine announced the compulsory acquisition of 15 houses in Kalusici village to allow the expansion of the lignite mine.

 

 Poland: The Polish government has filed an appeal against the decision to award Green X Metals, formerly known as Prairie Mining, 252 million (US$329 million) in compensation over its dispute over the Jan Karski coal mine. The court found Poland had breached the Australia-Poland Bilateral Investment Treaty and the Energy Charter Treaty.

 

 Thailand: The state-owned Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand is undertaking a feasibility study on refurbishing units 8 and 9 at the Mae Moh lignite plant. The units, which both have 300 MW capacity, were scheduled for retirement in 2025.

 

 US: The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission has approved AES Indiana's plan to convert the two 671 MW coal units at Petersburg Generating Station to run on gas.

 

 US: Ameren has agreed to pay US$61 million for violating the Clean Air Act by not installing pollution controls when it upgraded the now-closed 1242 MW Rush Island Energy Center. The settlement proposes converting St Louis school bus fleets to electric and underwriting the purchase of air filters for more than 125,000 Missouri households.

 

 US: District Judge Robert C. Chambers found Lexington Coal in contempt of court for the third time since 2021. Chambers ordered the company to pay a US$50,000 fine and establish a US$100,000 fund to comply with orders to address pollution from two mines in Mingo County in West Virginia.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

US coal power sector looks to Trump for relief from coal closures: The chief financial officer of Duke Energy, Brian Savoy, told Bloomberg that it may delay coal plant closures if the Trump administration axes new power plant pollution rules adopted by the Environmental Protection Agency. In early October, the utility backtracked on its plan to go coal-free by 2035, proposing to extend the life of two 668 MW units at the Gibson Generating Station in Indiana until 2038. Power utilities have also launched legal challenges against a new rule requiring utilities to clean up coal ash dams. The likely effect of the Trump administration rollbacks comes as some utilities are facing increasing power demand from data centres and manufacturing plants. S & P Global estimates that 3000 MW of coal units will close this year, the lowest level of coal closures since 2015. The consultancy forecasts that 14,100 MW of coal capacity will retire in 2025, down from the 16,600 MW it previously estimated would close. (S & P Global, Courthouse News, Washington Examiner)

Report finds Indonesia's captive coal plant boom continues: A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air and Global Energy Monitor found that Indonesian coal capacity increased by 7200 MW or 15 per cent in the year to July 2024, with 4500 MW from captive coal plants for industry and the remaining 2600 MW built by independent power producers. Captive power plants cater for major energy intensive industrial plants such as nickel and aluminium smelters, along with pulp and paper and chemicals industries. The report finds that the rapid increase in captive coal capacity is likely to continue, with up to 11,040 MW of new coal capacity by 2026 from proposed or under-construction plants. Since 2020, Indonesia has banned the export of raw nickel ores in a bid to capture more of the economic value from downstream processing. However, the absence of high emission and environmental standards could cause up to 5000 deaths by 2030 in Central and Southeast Sulawesi and North Maluku provinces. Indonesia is also lobbying to exclude captive coal plants from its 2040 coal phase-out target agreed to as part of its US$20 billion Just Energy Transition Partnership. Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto, who took over from President Joko Widodo in October, has backed the expansion of the nickel industry. Prabowo founded the Nusantara Group in 2001, a company that expanded into coal, gas, agriculture and fisheries operations and reportedly retained major coal concessions in East Kalimantan. (Global Energy Monitor and Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

Adaro moves to offload thermal coal but keep its met coal projects: Adaro Energy Indonesia (AEI) shareholders recently approved spinning off the company's thermal coal business into a separate company, Adaro Andalan Indonesia (AAI. Adaro is the world's sixth-largest coal company, producing 66 million tonnes of coal in 2023. Adaro estimates the value of the new company at about US$2.45 billion. The Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis (IEEFA) notes that the company's thermal coal business accounted for about 53 per cent of the parent company's total assets and contributed 89 per cent of total revenue, raising questions about AEI's aim of transitioning to its green energy, including hydro, wind and solar projects. In 2023, Adaro set a target of generating 50 per cent of its revenue by 2030 from non-thermal coal projects, including an aluminium smelter, metallurgical coal sales, renewables and other mining projects. IEEFA questions whether current Adaro shareholders will take up options in AAI and, if so, whether they will maintain support for the current low-carbon goals. (Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis)

Taiwanese PM announces conversion of coal plant to gas: Taiwan's Premier Cho Jung-tai announced that all the coal units at the 5780 MW Taichung power station would be converted to gas by the end of 2034. The Taichung power station has ten 550 MW coal units, making it the world's largest coal plant. Two units commissioned in 1991 will close with the opening of new gas units at the plant. In January 2023, Taipower, which has faced strong community opposition to the plant due to pollution, flagged the option of placing two further coal units on standby and possibly closing them by 2030. It suggested the remaining six units would be decommissioned by 2035. Cho said that in 2032, the government would assess whether the six units are still required. He said that after 2034, they would be held in reserve to operate if needed in cases of national security or natural disasters. Opposition MPs have questioned the need to keep retired coal plants in reserve. (Taipei Times, Global Energy Monitor)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Indian solar PV exports surging, Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis, November 11, 2024. (Pdf; the Executive Summary is here.)

This 16-page report provides an overview of the exponential increase in exports of Indian solar panels, primarily to the US. However, higher profit margins on exports are pushing Indian manufacturers to prioritise the global market. On current plans, India will have less domestic supply than the 30,000 MW per annum required to meet India's 2030 renewable energy target.

title: CoalWire 540, November 21, 2024
excerpt: UK unveils ban plan for new coal licences; smog crisis hits India, Pakistan; Trump unveils pro-fossil fuel nominees.
content:
November 21, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The UK government's announcement that it plans to ban new coal mining licences garnered a lot of positive coverage ahead of the global climate conference in Azerbaijan. While civil society groups welcomed the announcement, important details of the policy are yet to be finalised. In the US, President-elect Donald Trump is going full speed ahead in the opposite direction, unveiling pro-fossil fuel nominees for key administration positions. A review of the likely impact of the incoming Trump administration on the US energy industry by Wood Mackenzie, a resources industry consultancy, suggests the benefits to the coal industry are likely to be relatively muted. WoodMac tips the US coal industry will continue to decline.

The United Nations Environment Programme announced it is extending its methane monitoring system to cover the metallurgical coal sector. In Australia, a report details how a change to the methodology of estimating coal mine methane emissions has created a new loophole allowing significant underreporting of emissions. In India and Pakistan, extreme air pollution has triggered restrictions on schools, construction and vehicle use. A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air highlights how India's ongoing failure to enforce new standards requiring the installation of flue gas desulphurisation units has contributed to the country's air pollution crisis.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 A miner's play to undermine Alberta democracy

The Alberta government is supporting Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart's proposed Crowsnest Pass coal mine even though the province's citizens, courts and regulators previously rejected it. It is a master class in how to undermine democracy, writes Andrew Nikiforuk in The Tyee.

 

 Mongolian herders fear a new coal highway to China

After years of resisting the construction of a new border crossing point into China, Mongolian herders remain fearful of impacts on their way of life from the rapid growth in coal exports to China, write Thomas White and Enkhbat Sainbayar in Dialogue Earth.

 

 In Chhattisgarh's Hasdeo, coal is driving humans and elephants to conflict

The rapid growth of coal mining in the Hasdeo Arand forest is not just affecting the ability of tribal groups to collect produce from the forest but is driving increased conflict with elephants, write Shubhanghi Derhgawen and Deepanshu Mohan in The Wire..

 

 Signs of trouble for critical mine cleanup fund in Virginia

An actuarial study commissioned by the Virginia Department of Energy reveals that bankruptcy of any one of nine coal companies could tank the state's mine reclamation fund within a decade, writes Willie Dodson in Appalachian Voices Front Porch Blog.

 

 PJM sees an 'easy button' to meet power needs, but Appalachians see higher bills and more pollution

The additional US$15 billion cost for customers from the latest capacity auction decision of PJM Interconnection, the largest US wholesale power market, highlights the failure to curb support for uneconomic coal plants and back clean energy solutions that don't impose health and pollution costs onto Appalachian communities, writes Marcia Dinkins, the executive director of Black Women for Change, in Utility Dive.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 UK government flags end to new coal mining licences

The UK government announced it intends to amend the Coal Industry Act 1994 to restrict the future licensing of new coal mines. The government said it would introduce the amendment "when parliamentary time allows" and that "limited exceptions" may "be required for safety or restoration purposes". Coal Action Network (CAN) said the announcement, which came just months after the last coal power plant closed, bolsters the UK's international reputation in moving beyond coal. However, CAN said it hoped to work with the government to ensure no loopholes are included in the bill. The group said most recent open-cut mine proposals were touted initially as restoration projects, such as the Ffos-y-fran project in Wales, which closed without providing sufficient funds to cover proper rehabilitation of the site. CAN also noted the proposed ban may exclude the thousands of coal tips across South Wales. Friends of the Earth said the policy must "surely be the end of the line" for West Cumbria Mining's proposed Whitehaven metallurgical coal project. (UK Government, BBC, Coal Action Network)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Trump appointees signal pro-fossil fuel agenda: President-elect Donald Trump announced he will nominate North Dakota Republican Governor Doug Burgum as the Secretary of the Department of Interior and the CEO of Liberty Energy Chris Wright as the Secretary of the US Department of Energy. The Department of Interior oversees the management and development of mining projects on 500 million acres (202 million hectares) of federal and tribal lands, while the Department of Energy plays a significant role in facilitating and supporting old and new energy technologies. Trump said both Burgum and Wright would be members of a newly-created National Energy Council which will pursue "US energy dominance by cutting red tape". Trump said his administration would support the expansion of 'baseload' power generation, a term commonly embraced by conservative utilities to mean coal, gas and nuclear, to support increasing data centre demand. The latest election counting suggests the Republicans may win 220 seats in the 435-seat House of Representatives, with the Democrats winning 215 seats. Trump has nominated three House members for roles in the administration, which, if confirmed, would leave the Republicans with a razor-thin 217-215 majority until the completion of by-elections in the safe Republican seats. The next mid-term election, where there is typically a swing against the administration, is scheduled for November 3, 2026. (Reuters, Guardian)

 

 US govt utility paid US$140,000 to group resisting pollution controls: Documents released to the Energy and Policy Institute under the Freedom of Information Act revealed that the US-government-owned Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) paid US$140,000 in membership fees in 2021 to Power Generators Air Coalition (PGen), a lobby group of power utilities opposing government pollution restrictions. PGen members include Southern Company, American Electric Power and the Ohio Valley Electric Corporation. PGen has opposed a range of the Biden administration's environmental measures, including stricter regulation of greenhouse gases, nitrous oxide, and particulate matter pollution. PGen emerged in 2021 after public revelations of the activities of the now-defunct Utility Air Regulatory Group and an investigation by the TVA Office of Inspector General into the utility's involvement in several industry groups. (Energy and Policy Institute)

 

 NSW government bans water access to stymie coal port protest: The New South Wales government has imposed a ban on public access to Newcastle harbour after a judge ruled in favour of police rejecting a permit for Rising Tide to hold a water-based protest against coal exports. Newcastle is the world's largest thermal coal export port. After the court decision, Rising Tide negotiated with police to allow protestors to paddle out onto Newcastle Harbour from November 22 to November 24 but not enter the shipping channel. Later that night, Transport for NSW issued a blanket ban on non-commercial watercraft in the core area of the harbour and within a nautical mile of the mouth of the port. Rising Tide organiser Zack Schofield described the decision as "an abuse of power". Schofield said if NSW Premier Chris Minns "is scared of families and kids paddling off a beach in protest, then he's not cut out for the job". (Guardian)

 

 Deadly smog blankets New Delhi and Pakistan: In response to extreme smog levels, the government of Punjab in Pakistan declared an emergency and shut down schools, the construction sector and universities. New Delhi also enacted restrictions on students, construction and vehicles after the city's 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) soared to 481, a level classed as 'severe plus'. A report on India's air pollution crisis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) noted that restrictions on stubble burning in the agricultural area around Delhi are enforced more strictly than standards for pollution from coal power plants. CREA estimates only eight per cent of India's 211,000 MW of coal capacity has installed flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) to control sulphur dioxide emissions. The government first announced new sulphur dioxide emission standards in December 2015, with a compliance deadline of December 2017. However, lobbying pressure from utilities has resulted in successive changes to the deadline. CREA estimates the introduction of FGD technology could cut sulphur dioxide emissions by 64 per cent from the power sector. The report urges the adoption of strict enforcement deadlines, penalties for non-compliance and the publication of progress reports to ensure accountability. (Guardian, Indian Express, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Canada: The International Joint Commission (IJC) has expanded to include six First Nations representatives on the Governing Council. The IJC's governance was previously comprised of equal numbers of US and Canadian government representatives. The IJC will begin a two-year study into the transboundary pollution of the Elk-Kootenai River watershed by coal mines in British Columbia.

 

 India: Northern Coalfields, a Coal India subsidiary, plans to relocate the entire 927-hectare village of Morwa, which has a population of 30,000 families. The relocation is to allow the expansion of the Jayant mine and access to an estimated 600 million tonnes of coal.

 

 Romania: The European Commission has approved the expenditure of 790 million (US$833 million) by the Romanian government up to December 31 2032 on the closure of the Lonea, Lupeni, Livezeni and Vulcan coal mines. The mines supply the 150 MW Paroseni power station in the Jiu Valley.

 

 Russia: The Elga Company has completed a trial coal shipment along its 531-kilometre railway connecting its Elginskiy mine to the Port Elga export terminal. Local news reported that a locomotive and four wagons derailed during the trip.

 

 US: Southern Company said it is considering delaying the possible closure of the 806 MW Unit 1 and 789 Unit 2 at Plant Bowen in Georgia due to potential data centre load growth.

 

 US: Hallador Energy informed [Pdf] investors it has signed a non-binding agreement with an unnamed data centre developer for "large portions" of generation for over a decade from the 1080 MW Merom coal plant in Indiana.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Consultant says Trump admin may do little to slow decline of US coal: Wood Mackenzie (WoodMac), a resources industry consultancy, estimates the impact of the second Trump administration on the coal sector may be relatively limited. WoodMac estimates the decline in coal generation may "experience a brief pause" due to possible increased demand growth from electrification and data centres. However, the consultancy noted that coal generation would continue to decline as it became less economic and domestic thermal coal demand would "irreversibly weaken in the years ahead". WoodMac estimates the new Trump administration will support the development of small modular nuclear reactors and continue subsidies for carbon capture and storage. The consultancy said the growth in solar capacity may slow, but it is still likely to increase by 243,000 MW between 2024-2030 "even in our delayed transition scenario". WoodMac suggested that the offshore wind and battery storage sectors are most at risk under the new administration. (Power Magazine, Wood Mackenzie)

Study reveals Australian methane reporting creates emissions loophole: Australian coal mines could be underreporting methane emissions from open-cut coal mines by up to 10 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year, according to a report by the consultancy firm Reputex. The consultancy notes that the previous methodology used by the government to estimate emissions gave companies the option of either using average emissions from coal production in each state or company-led estimates for each site. Reputex estimates coal mine emissions decreased by 65-70 per cent after some companies opted to switch to site-specific estimates. From July 1 2025, mining companies must estimate emissions based on a site-specific methodology but without the requirement of independent verification. The state-based emission factors relied on an analysis of methane emissions from thousands of borehole samples, while site-based estimates by companies rely on a smaller number of samples. Earlier this year, the UK-based climate think tank Ember noted that companies that opted to switch reporting emissions based on site-specific estimates reported a significant drop. Ember pointed out that the Adani subsidiary Bravus Mining uses an emissions estimate for its Carmichael mine that is 135 times lower than the Queensland state average. (Renew Economy, Reputex)

Bangladesh coal mine may suspend production due to excess stockpiles: The Barapukuria Coal Mining Company (BCMCL), a subsidiary of the state-owned Petrobangla, may suspend production at the Barapukuria mine as its coal stockpiles designed to store 50,000 tonnes currently hold about 250,000 tonnes of coal. BCMCL is presently producing about 5000 tonnes of coal a day, but its sole customer, the 525 MW Barapukuria coal plant, only requires half that volume as the 250 MW Unit 3 is shut down and requires a significant overhaul. The Barapukuria mine is Bangladesh's only operating coal mine and has long been a source of controversy with the local community due to the impacts of subsidence and the threat of displacement of thousands of families if the mine expanded with an open-cut mine. (Daily Star, Global Energy Monitor)

Vietnam estimates rapid electricity demand growth in 2025: Vietnamese government officials anticipate electricity demand could grow by 14 per cent in 2025 and require a high level of utilisation of the country's coal fleet, especially in the northern provinces. Officials anticipate coal plants will operate at a capacity factor of about 75 per cent in 2025. Data from the state-owned power utility EVN indicates that coal plants generated almost 49 per cent of Vietnam's electricity in the first 10 months of 2024. In a separate development, the state-owned coal company, Vietnam National Coal and Mineral Industries Group (Vinacomin) told provincial officials from Quang Tri Province that it wants to import five million tonnes of coal from Salavan province in Laos. Vinacomin said it intends to import the coal by truck via the border crossing at La Lay in Laos to a new coal terminal at My Thuy Port in Vietnam commencing early in 2025. In Salavan province in Laos, villagers are alarmed that the provincial government is considering granting a coal mining licence over 400 hectares of farmland to Zhongya Yuxi Cement Lao Sole Company, a Chinese company. Villagers in Laos commonly lose their land without compensation when new mining, hydro and other projects proceed. (Reuters, TuioTreNews, RFA)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 UN project extends methane monitoring system to met coal mines: The International Methane Emissions Observatory, a project of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), announced ahead of the COP 27 conference in Azerbaijan that it is extending the coverage of its Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) to include emissions from metallurgical coal mines. The MARS system uses satellite data to detect methane plumes and generates notifications to governments and companies. UNEP estimates that emissions of methane, which is 80 times more potent than carbon dioxide over 20 years, represent about 30 per cent of the short-term impact of steel production. UNEP notes that metallurgical coal has fewer sources of emissions than the coal and gas sector and that production is concentrated in a small number of countries. (Mining Weekly, International Methane Emissions Observatory [Pdf])
