title: CoalWire 541, November 28, 2024
excerpt: Confusion over Indonesian coal pledge; US agency seeks arrest of Adani executives.
content:
November 28, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The comments by President Prabowo Subianto that Indonesia would phase out coal power by 2040 garnered widespread international media coverage, but it seems it is one of those 'it seems too good to be true' moments. A media release by the government reiterated that Indonesia plans a significant expansion of renewables but made no new announcement on an accelerated coal phase-out. At the COP 29 conference in Azerbaijan, Saudi Arabia made clear it wouldn't accept wording on a fossil fuel phase-out, while agreements on carbon trading and climate finance remain deeply contentious. The German government also revealed that the proposed Just Energy Transition Partnership between India and a coalition of countries has collapsed, though a narrower version focussed on support for renewables may progress.

There was a flurry of other significant developments, not least the US Department of Justice indictment of Indian billionaire Gautam Adani and seven other Adani executives. While the case is over deals done by Adani's solar subsidiary, the implications for the whole Adani Group of companies are likely to be profound. In Australia, thousands protested coal shipments through the world's largest export port. In the US, a new study further documents the spread of coal dust over one kilometre from a coal terminal.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 'The air is killing us': why Delhi's pollution problem runs deeper than smog season

Delhi's air quality index recently went as high as 1700 in some parts of the city, over 30 times higher than deemed safe by the World Health Organization. While the government tends to focus on the seasonal burning of stubble by farmers, environmentalists point to year round pollution from coal plants, industry, cars and construction, writes Hannah Ellis-Petersen in the Guardian.

 

 Shutting high-emission coal mines is key to China's methane reduction

By focusing on shuttering mines with high gas contents, China could reduce future coal methane emissions by 26 per cent, writes Liu Qiang from Tsinghua University's Institute of Energy, Environment and Economics in Dialogue Earth.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Indonesian President flags earlier coal exit, but media release says otherwise: President Prabowo Subianto stated at the G20 leaders summit in Brazil that Indonesia planned to phase out coal-fired "within the next 15 years". Subianto, who became President in late October, said Indonesia could build more than 75,000 megswatts (MW) of renewable energy in the next 15 years. However, his comments are at odds with current government policies. The Coordinating Economic Minister Airlangga Hartarto said at the G20 that Indonesia planned only to cut the share of coal generation to 33 per cent by 2040 and increase renewables share to 42 per cent, figures reiterated in a government media release. In 2023, coal generation accounted for 40 per cent of generation and renewables 14 per cent. Indonesia currently has 52.31 GW of coal capacity, with a further 9.81 GW under construction, according to Global Energy Monitor data. The origin of the discrepancy between Subianto's comments and the government media release is not clear. (Government of Indonesia, Jakarta Post [paywall], ABCNews, Government of Indonesia [Indonesian])

 

 UN conference reaches an agreement on climate finance: The United Nations COP 29 conference in the oil-rich state of Azerbaijan made little progress on advancing the 2023 commitment to support a roadmap for "transitioning away from fossil fuels". During the latest conference, the head of the delegation from Saudi Arabia, Albara Tawfiq, bluntly stated said the Arab group "will not accept any text that targets any specific sectors, including fossil fuels". While Saudi Arabia was blocking action on fossil fuels, a coalition of 25 countries and the European Union announced their next Nationally Determined Contributions would include a commitment not to build any new unabated coal plants. Early on, the conference host pushed through rules governing the global trade of carbon credits, a controversial framework that critics argue includes significant loopholes that could undercut emissions reductions. The conference reached a late agreement on the provision of at least US$300 billion a year by 2035 to support the transition away from fossil fuels, meet the costs of extreme weather events and adapt to global heating. (Carbon Brief, E3G, The Conversation)

 

 Germany reveals scrapping of India's Just Energy Transition plan: Germany and other funding countries have agreed to abandon a proposed Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) originally intended to provide India with financial and technical support to transition away from coal. Jochen Flasbarth, state secretary in the German Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development, said India was not going to agree to a project predicated on a transition away from coal. Flasbarth said any future agreement would focus on financing renewable energy projects. Germany, the US and other G7 countries had initially proposed expanding the JETPs beyond the deal with South Africa to include Vietnam and India . It is unclear whether the Trump administration will continue to support the JETP's with South Africa and Vietnam. (Climate Home News)

 

 Thousands attended Newcastle coal port protest; 170 arrested: Several thousand people attended Rising Tide's November 22-24 'protestival' against coal exports from Newcastle port, with 170 arrested when a flotilla of watercraft attempted to block coal ships accessing the port. Newcastle is the world's largest coal export port. The New South Wales government tried to block the flotilla by designating a ban on all watercraft in the shipping channel and entrance to the harbour, but the Supreme Court overturned this decision. The court accepted the argument by Rising Tide lawyers that the Marine Safety Act was not intended to prevent events from occurring, only to ensure they proceed safely. Earlier, the Supreme Court had upheld a NSW police decision to reject an application from Rising Tide that would allow the flotilla to block the shipping channel without exposing participants to charges of obstruction and unlawful assembly or an on-the-spot fine of A$1100 (US$712). (Guardian, Guardian)

 

 Study confirms coal dust pollution from US coal port: A study published by Johns Hopkins University researchers detected coal dust using electron microscopy at two sample sites near CSX's Curtis Bay coal terminal. The study, which was published in Science of the Total Environment, was based on dust samples from two sites, one 345 metres and the other 1235 metres away from the coal terminal and found 13.2 and 3.4 coal particles per square millimetre, respectively. The study authors note that most studies on the health impact of coal dust exposure have focussed on coal miners, with little research on communities near coal mining areas or people living near coal handling and storage infrastructure distant from mining areas. The study found coal dust at schools and playgrounds. More than 90 million tonnes of coal were exported by the United States in 2023, with about 30 million tonnes through the Port of Baltimore's two terminals, with the CSX site handling up to 12 million tonnes a year. The authors said the study also provides a reliable and affordable approach other communities could adopt to measure coal dust exposure. (CBS News, Johns Hopkins University, Science of the Total Environment)

 

 Alberta pro-coal citizens group helped by PR industry consultant: Citizens Supportive of Crowsnest Coal (CSCC), a group supporting the development of Northback Holdings proposed metallurgical coal mine in Alberta, has close ties to a lobbyist for a Canadian coal and gas industry group. The privacy statement on CSCC's website provided an email contact for Energy United, an arm of the Maple Leaf Institute, a pro-oil and gas lobby group. Supporters of CSCC said Jarret Coels offered to support the group's website and email list. Coels is the principal of Lynx Strategy, a public affairs consultancy specialising in advocacy campaigns, and is the campaign manager for Energy United. After a request for comment, the CSCC website was amended to remove the reference to Energy United. Initially, Coels declined to comment, but after his ties to the CSCC were publicised, he said he had used the same website template created for Energy United. Northback Holdings is a subsidiary of Australian mining giant Hancock Prospecting, a private company owned by Australian mining billionaire Gina Rinehart. Residents of Crowsnest voted in support of the mine in a non-binding referendum, but other communities remain opposed to the mine. (St Albert Gazette, CBC, Financial Times)

 

 Coal waste landslide highlights underfunding for cleanup: Heavy rainfall associated with Storm Bert triggered a landslide from a coal tip, forcing the evacuation of some of the residents of the village of Cwmtillery in Wales. The tip is one of the 360 waste coal sites in Wales classed as representing a high risk to nearby communities and requiring biannual inspections. The Coal Authority inspected the Cwmtillery tip in August and found no significant issues. While the new Labour government allocated 25 million (US$31 million) for coal tip safety in its October 2024 budget, the total rehabilitation cost of the high-risk sites could be as much as 600 million (US$752 million). The need to remediate coal tips across Wales became a significant public issue after a landslide above Tylorstown in February 2020 prompted a survey that identified 2573 sites. In early 2023, the Welsh government promised to introduce a bill in 2024 to establish an organisation to manage the rehabilitation of coal tips. Phil Thomas from Clear South Wales Coal Tips said the government hasn't tabled the bill. "By the time a stability issue is known, it is too late," he wrote. More than half of the high-risk coal tips are on private land. (BBC, Aberdare Online)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The New South Wales government has granted planning approval for EnergyAustralia's proposed 500 MW, 2000 megawatt-hour battery storage project at the site of the 1390 MW Mt Piper coal plant.

 

 Australia: The Australian energy market regulator warned that extended outages at nearly half the coal units in NSW and the 750 MW Kogan Creek coal plant in Queensland put the east coast grid under stress during a heatwave.

 

 New Zealand: Bathurst Resources wants 25-year permits for fast-tracked coal mining projects on the Buller Plateau.

 

 Philippines: Displaced fisherfolk marked World Fisheries Day with a waterborne protest against the impacts of the 232 MW Mindanao Steag power station and the 405 MW Filinvest Development Corp FDC Misamis coal plant.

 

 Turkey: Nearly 500 coal mine workers have occupied the Cayirhan lignite mine in a protest against government plans to privatise the mine and associated 620 MW power plant.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

US Department of Justice seeks arrest of Adani executives: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) is seeking the arrest of Indian billionaire Gautam Adani and his nephew Sagar Adani over an alleged $US265 million in bribes paid between 2020 and 2024 to Indian officials to win above cost power purchase agreements in India for solar projects. The DOJ indictment also identifies five other Adani executives. The DOJ and the Securities and Exchange Commission allege Adani executives paid the bribes at a time that Adani Green Energy and subsidiaries were raising funds from US-based investors. An Adani Group spokesperson described the allegations as "baseless" and said the indictment was linked only to Adani Green Energy. In March 2024, the Science Museum in London opened its Energy Revolution: The Adani Green Energy Gallery despite protests by climate groups objecting to accepting funding from an Adani entity. The museum defended its financing on the grounds that Adani Green Energy is a renewables business separate from Adani Group businesses with coal mining and power projects. (Reuters, Financial Times, US Department of Justice, US Department of Justice [Pdf])

Japanese utility to return plant after a year offline following biomass fire: JERA announced it plans to resume coal-only generation at its 1070 MW Taketoyo No.5 coal and biomass-fired plant in January 2025, almost a year after a fire in the biomass conveyor system damaged the plant. JERA, which is a 50-50 joint venture between a subsidiary of Tokyo Electric Power Company and Chubu Electric Power, is Japan's largest power generator. JERA said it plans to resume biomass co-firing towards the end of the 2026 financial year, which ends in March 2027. JERA, which sources biomass pellets from Vietnam and the US for the plant, said it would initially limit the biomass co-firing rate to eight per cent, down from the 17 per cent initially intended. The fire on January 31, 2024, burnt for five hours, with an explosion causing extensive damage to part of the boiler building. (JERA)

Peabody Energy buys Anglo American's met coal mines: Anglo American has agreed to sell its Australian metallurgical coal mines to US-headquartered Peabody Energy for US$2.05 billion, with potential for the sale yielding up to US$3.775 billion. Peabody agreed to pay US$450 million if the mothballed Grosvenor underground mine in Queensland recommences production and operates for two years. The mine was closed after a significant fire that commenced in late June. In 2023, Anglo American's metallurgical coal mines – Moranbah North, Grosvenor, Dawson, Capcoal and Aquila – produced 16 million tonnes of coal. Anglo American is selling the Dawson mine to the Indonesian coal company PT Bukit Makmur Mandiri Utama for US$455 million. The completion of the purchase will make Peabody Energy one of the world's largest seaborne metallurgical coal exporters, with a projected production of 19 – 20 million tonnes in 2026. Peabody Energy currently has four metallurgical coal mines in Australia and the Shoal Creek mine in Alabama. The purchase of Anglo American's assets allows the company to diversify away from reliance on the declining US thermal coal market, where it owns nine operating mines, including three in the Powder River Basin with a combined production of 87.1 million US short tons (79 million tonnes) in 2023. (BNNBloomberg, Anglo American, Peabody Energy)

Chinese company pitches 600 MW coal plant in Zambia: Protracted power rationing in Zambia caused by a drought-induced decline in hydro generation from the 2010 MW Kariba hydro project has rekindled debate over increasing captive coal capacity for industrial users as well as solar generation. The Wonderful Group, a Chinese company that manufactures ceramic tiles and fertiliser, met with Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema to discuss its proposal for a new 600 MW coal plant. First Quantum Minerals, which operates the Sentinel copper mine as well as the Kansanshi copper-gold mine and an associated smelter, has turned to higher-cost electricity imports to offset reduced hydro generation. The company was also affected by the need for maintenance of a 150 MW coal unit at Maamba Collieries power station. In July, the Energy Regulation Board of Zambia approved a construction permit for the 300 MW expansion of the Maamba coal plant with its completion likely in 2026. (BNN Bloomberg, News24)

Mongolian coal displacing Australian exports in the Chinese market: Land-based Mongolian and Russian coal exports are displacing China's imports from the seaborne market, especially for metallurgical coal. China's coal imports accounted for 476 million tonnes in 2023, with 79 per cent thermal coal, predominantly from Indonesia. Imports have increased by eight per cent in 2024. However, there has been a pronounced 17 per cent decline in seaborne imports in the last two years. Analysis of customs data indicates China imported about 102 million tonnes of Russian coal in 2023, with recent increases via land. Imports of Russian coal have declined in 2024 as Chinese import duties and financial sanctions have affected international payments. Mongolian exports to China surged to 70 million tonnes in 2023 and increased by 27 per cent in 2024. About three-quarters of Mongolia's coal exports are metallurgical coal. In 2023, Mongolia accounted for 53 per cent of China's metallurgical coal imports, largely displacing Australian suppliers. The shift away from Australian seaborne metallurgical coal cargoes has undercut demand for Panamax ships that are capable of carrying about 52,000 tonnes of coal. The report suggests the election of Trump and his preference for restrictive trade polices may increase Chinese reliance on Russian and Mongolian coal. (Mining.com, Veson Nautical [Pdf])

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 European steel producer standoff over steel imports: ArcelorMittal announced that it won't proceed with investment in renewables-based hydrogen-powered plant at its Dunkirk steel plant unless European regulators ensure a more favourable Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and other protections against cheap imports. ArcelorMittal, the world's second-largest steel producer, was offered US$885 million in subsidies by the French government to assist its decarbonisation plan, including replacing two out of three blast furnaces at its Dunkirk plant with green hydrogen-powered facilities. A coalition of the European Steel Association (Eurofer) and the IndustriAll European Trade Union is lobbying for a range of measures to support steel producers, including lower electricity prices, minimising renewable levies and provision of incentives for the use of green steel in the auto and construction sectors. ArcelorMittal is a member of Eurofer, which is pressing the European Commission's new Executive Vice-President for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy, Stephane Sejourne, to release an action plan to support the steel industry within the first 100 days of his appointment. The European Commission's Director General for Tax, Gerassimos Thomas, said the CBAM measures will be reviewed in 2025 with the intention to propose changes in 2026. (Reuters, BNNBloomberg, Eurofer)

title: CoalWire 542, December 5, 2024
excerpt: Indonesian President’s 2040 coal exit requires major policy shift; coal power in Chile hits new low.
content:
December 5, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

When Indonesia's newly sworn-in President Prabowo Subianto stated at the recent COP29 conference that he wanted to close his country's fleet of coal plants by 2040, there was much head-scratching. Was it a translation error or perhaps a misstatement of a new leader? If it wasn't, why was there such a significant mismatch between the stated coal exit goal and the level of renewables generation he said is required to achieve it? There remain many unanswered questions. As the Institute for Essential Services Reform, an Indonesian energy think tank, and the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air note, translating Prabowo's words into action will require a significant energy policy shakeup and far more ambitious targets for new renewables capacity.

The latest annual survey of Chinese energy policy experts reveals increasing expectations that coal consumption in the country has or soon will hit its peak. The potential plateauing of coal consumption, combined with the rapid expansion of renewable generation capacity, underpins growing optimism that China's greenhouse gas emissions have peaked or will in 2025. In Chile, coal power generation continues to slide with the commissioning of new renewable projects.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 How big fossil-fuel-producing countries export emissions abroad

Coal-fired cement plants in Egypt and North Africa, such as the plant in Alexandria operated by a subsidiary of Greece's Titan Cement, are increasingly reliant on coal imported from the US, write Mohamed Ezz and Valerie Volcovici in Reuters.

 

 How US federal charges punctured the myth of Adani's invincibility

Despite the US Department of Justice arrest warrant against him, Gautam Adani is trying to put up a brave front with the help of his public relations machinery. But he probably realises that after this round of civil and criminal charges, things can never be the same again, writes Paranjoy Guha Thakurta in Frontline.

 

 Who's against transparent clean energy?

The Adani scandal in India is shining a spotlight on the entire energy sector, which is rife with overpayment, questionable deals, and lack of competition, all because of closed buying systems and secret contracting, writes Todd Moss, a former US Department of State official, in his Eat More Electrons Substack.

 

 Adaro's coal spin-off: growing a climate conscience or simple greenwashing?

Indonesia's coal giant Adaro is desperately trying to show itself as a leader in the energy transition, but investors should remain cautious of reputational and financial risks, write Apekshita Varshney from Eko and Camilla Perotti from BankTrack.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Indonesian President's 2040 coal exit target requires major policy shift: Achieving President Prabowo Subianto's stated goal of phasing out coal and other fossil fuel generation by 2040 will require significant policy changes and a major increase in renewables targets beyond the 75,000 megawatts (MW) of new renewables and 5000 MW of nuclear capacity proposed at COP29, according to Indonesian and other energy analysts. The Executive Director of the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR), Fabby Tumiwa, said meeting the target will require orders to relevant ministers and the state-owned power utility PLN to develop targets and detailed plans, as well as the retirement of the current coal fleet. IESR estimates reaching net zero emissions by 2050 requires reducing coal generation by 11 per cent by 2030, a 90 per cent reduction by 2040 and entirely phased out by 2045. Indonesia currently has 52,315 MW of operating coal capacity that generates 62 per cent of its on-grid and captive power. It also has 9815 MW of coal plant capacity under construction and a further 5240 MW proposed, according to the Global Coal Plant Tracker. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates the 79,000 MW of new renewables and nuclear would only amount to about 35 per cent of the projected national electricity demand. CREA estimates achieving Prabowo's goal would require more than doubling the target for new non-fossil capacity. CREA estimates Prabowo's goal could avoid a cumulative total of 182,000 air pollution-related deaths and health costs of USD 130 billion from 2024 until the end-of-life of all coal-fired power plants in Indonesia. The Indonesian Coal Mining Association said the transition away from coal is "understood by industry players" but would require more time. The Association of Indonesian Mineral and Coal Energy Suppliers said the transition "must be implemented in a well-planned, realistic way" and wants the government to accelerate coal gasification projects. (Jakarta Post [paywall], Institute for Essential Services Reform, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 Survey of Chinese officials finds coal peak near: A survey of 44 Chinese energy transition experts found that 36 per cent of those surveyed in 2024 believe that China's coal consumption has peaked, up from 15 per cent in 2023. With increasing investment in clean energy and electrification of transport, 44 per cent of the surveyed experts believe China's greenhouse gas emissions have peaked or will by 2025, up from 21 per cent in 2023. Coal use in the steel and cement sectors has declined in line with reducing construction sector activity. However, coal consumption increased rapidly in the coal-to-chemicals industry in 2024, with greenhouse gas emissions rising by 12.5 per cent compared to 2023. Forty-four per cent of those surveyed believe that lower economic growth will slow the energy transition, up from 34 per cent in 2023. (Guardian, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf])

 

 Chilean coal generation slumps to new low: Coal generation in Chile continues its rapid decline, accounting for 15.8 per cent of electricity in the first 10 months of 2024 and falling to a new monthly low of 11.7 per cent in October 2024. Data from Ember indicates coal accounted for 43.6 per cent in 2016. The rapid decline in coal generation began after the emergence of a strong social movement that demanded pollution standards for existing coal plants and a deadline to phase out coal plants. The rapid increase in solar and wind generation has underpinned the decline in coal, with the recent recovery of hydro driving a six per cent reduction in fossil fuel generation. The International Energy Agency estimates Chile is on track to achieve 90 per cent of its annual generation from renewables by 2030. (The Progress Playbook)

 

 Bishop calls for the cancellation of new coal plant: Negros Occidental Bishop Gerardo Alminaza called on Aboitiz Power Corporation to abandon plans for a 170 MW expansion of the coal-fired Therma Visayas Energy Project in Toledo City. Alminaza said the expansion would pollute the air and water and adversely affect fishing communities reliant on the Tanon Strait marine protected area. In a separate development, the CEO of Meralco PowerGen Corporation, Emmanuel Rubio, said the company is currently assessing the viability of the proposed 1200 MW Atimonan plant in Quezon and an 80 MW expansion of the Cebu Energy power station in Toledo city. Rubio said the projects could cost US$2 billion and, if the preliminary assessment suggests they are viable, could seek board approval in February to undertake the feasibility study and engineering works. (Inquirer.net, The Philippine Star)

 

 Analysts question decision of Bulgaria to restart two lignite units: Energy analysts have criticised the decision by Bulgaria's interim energy minister, Vladimir Malinov, to restart two 227 MW units at the Maritsa East 3 lignite plant during the first quarter of 2025. The minister said the units can "maintain the balance of the Bulgarian electricity system". However, Tsvetomir Nikolov from the local think tank CSD noted there is no economic justification for restarting the uneconomic plant owned by US-based private equity company ContourGlobal. Another unnamed analyst said that the influx of new solar capacity early next year will push prices down and displace power from the plant in the merit order. Generation from the Maritsa Iztok 3 plant declined rapidly early this year after the contract with state-owned National Electric Co. expired. Subsequently, ContourGlobal laid off 320 workers in two tranches, with the company stating that generation costs were too high for the plant to operate profitably. (Montel News)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The new Queensland government announced a five-year A$1.4 billion (US$910 million) "energy maintenance guarantee" for coal power generators.

 

 Bangladesh: A coal unit at the 1200 MW Matarbari coal plant has resumed generation after being offline since October 31 due to the failure to import fuel.

 

 Greece: The transmission regulator has extended the operation of the 330 MW Meliti lignite plant by three months to the end of March 2025.

 

 India: The Minister of Coal and Mines, G. Kishan Reddy, told parliament that Coal India plans to develop 36 new coal mines in the next five years. He said Singareni Collieries Company is planning to open seven new mines and NLC India two new projects over the same period.

 

 India: Villagers from Assolda in Goa have objected to the proposed construction of two new jetties to facilitate coal transport.

 

 Kosovo: Eight people were arrested after an explosive charge damaged a water canal supplying Kosovo's two coal plants. Power generation was not affected.

 

 South Africa: The state-owned rail operator Transnet is on track to freight about 50 million tonnes of coal to the Richards Bay coal export terminal in 2024, well below its target of 60 million tonnes.

 

 "Given the uncertainty of what the end use is going to be for each type of coal, a safe approach is to just restrict financing for any type The differentiated approach between met and thermal coal shouldn't exist,"

said Cynthia Rocamora from Reclaim Finance.

 
 

Companies + Markets

US agency ends new coal Powder River Basin coal leases: The US Bureau of Land Management (BLM) has finalised two new plans ending new coal leasing in the Powder River Basin states of Wyoming and Montana. The BLM stated that it would not consider new coal leasing applications "in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions as a proxy for climate change". The agency adopted the final rule after finding that there would be significant impacts on the climate, human health, and the environment from further coal projects. Current coal projects, which have sufficient resources to operate until about 2041, will not be affected by the change. Republican Governors in Wyoming and Montana are looking to the incoming Trump Administration to reverse the change. University of Wyoming Associate Professor Rob Godby said Trump has pledged to support the oil and gas industry, a policy that would further undercut coal generation. "Market conditions have been very challenging for coal, regardless of regulations," he said. (Cowboy State Daily, Daily Montanan, E & E News, Department of Interior [Pdf])

Bangladesh seeks to renegotiate Adani power deal: Bangladesh's power and energy adviser Muhammad Fouzul Kabir Khan said a court-ordered investigation into the 25-year power purchase agreement between the Bangladesh Power Development Board and Adani for electricity from its 1496 MW Godda coal plant in Jharkhand is likely to be completed by the end of February 2025. A panel of experts appointed by the government and headed by former High Court judge Justice Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury is reviewing all power purchase agreements between 2009 and 2024. Khan said that contracts found to include "anomalies" should be renegotiated while those found to have involved "corruption and bribery" should be cancelled. Electricity from Adani's Godda plant, which relies on imported coal, was 27 per cent more expensive than power from other Indian private power producers in 2023-24 and up to 63 per cent more than Indian state-owned utilities. (Reuters)

Gautam Adani breaks silence over US indictment: Ten days after US regulators accused Adani executives of involvement in the payment of US$265 million in bribes to win solar power contracts in India, the chairman of the Adani Group, Gautam Adani, issued a statement describing the charges as "baseless" and vowing to seek "all possible legal recourse". Executives of several banks have anonymously confirmed that a freeze has been placed on new funding for the Adani Group, as has France's TotalEnergies, which holds a stake of about 19.8 per cent in Adani Green. The share price of US-based GQG, a significant backer of Adani Group and which holds a 4.2 per cent stake in Adani Green, has slumped by 15 per cent after UBS reported the Australian Stock Exchange listed firm may have lost A$600 million (US$390 million) in funds under management after the Department of Justice released the indictment of the Adani executives. (Reuters, Reuters, Reuters)

Questions over Deutsche Bank loan for Peabody Energy's mines: Of the coalition of firms providing Peabody Energy with a US$2.1 billion bridging loan to support the purchase of Anglo American's Australian coal mines, only Deutsche Bank has a policy restricting coal lending. The bank's policy excludes support for thermal coal for heating and power generation but does not mention metallurgical coal. Anglo American's annual report excludes reporting on the amount of thermal coal produced at its sites. The Capcoal mine, one of the four Peabody Energy is buying, produces a mix of hard coking coal, pulverised coal injection coal and thermal coal. The chief executive of DBX Commodities, Alexandre Claude, said companies often sell lower grades of metallurgical coal into the thermal coal market. Resources industry consultancy Wood Mackenzie estimates metallurgical coal can be up to three times as polluting as thermal coal due to higher methane concentrations. A Deutsche Bank spokesperson said the bank's climate policy is considered in any coal transaction. Cynthia Rocamora from the NGO group Reclaim Finance said all types of coal are "extremely polluting and need to be phased out." (BNN Bloomberg)

Eleven Republican states sue US funds over coal shareholdings: Texas, along with 10 other Republican states, have launched antitrust action against BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street, alleging they used their combined shareholdings in publicly traded coal companies to "constrict the market for coal through anticompetitive trade practices". The lawsuit argues that the three largest US index fund managers held significant stakes in nine major publicly-traded coal companies, including more than 25 per cent of Peabody Energy, Arch Resources, CONSOL Energy, Alpha Metallurgical Resources, Black Hill Resources and Warrior Met Coal. The lawsuit alleges that the climate policies of the three financial firms reduced coal supply and increased prices, allowing the investors to "produce extraordinary revenue gains". The legal action – which has the support of coal-producing states including Wyoming, West Virginia and Montana – follows on from some states curtiling state agency contracts with firms that restrict the financing of fossil fuels and conservative campaigns against increasing scrutiny of investments against environmental, social, and governance policies. BlackRock rejected the allegation that it invested in firms to damage their viability. (Reuters, Financial Times, Attorney-General of Texas, State of Texas [Pdf])

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

J. Mijin Cha, A Just Transition for All: Workers and Communities for a Carbon-Free Future, MIT Press, December 2024. (Cha is Assistant Professor of Environmental Studies at the University of California.)

This 215-page book (US$35) analyses just transition policies that offer the prospect of large-scale energy transition in a way that advances the interests of people and not just of fossil fuel workers.

Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf])
A Just Transition for All: Workers and Communities for a Carbon-Free Future

title: CoalWire 543, December 12, 2024
excerpt: South African court overturns new coal plants decision; Indian court suspends forest clearing for mine.
content:
December 12, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

South Africa's High Court has ruled in favour of three civil society groups that launched a legal challenge against the decision of the then Minister of Mineral Resources, Gwede Mantashe, and the energy regulator to approve 1500 megawatts (MW) of new coal capacity. The court ruled the decisions violated the constitutional rights of children to an environment that is not harmful to health and wellbeing. In Wales, the government unveiled plans to establish a new agency to oversee old coal waste dumps and ensure their safety.

In Slovenia, the government has taken over the country's only coal plant and associated lignite mine as the state-owned companies operating them neared bankruptcy. In Australia, a Japanese company has finally backed out of at least the first stage of a costly project aimed at converting brown coal to hydrogen for export to Japan. The latest analysis of electricity generation costs by Australia's premier science agency reinforces that firmed wind and solar beat coal, gas and nuclear by a substantial margin. While the data is specific to Australia, it illustrates the broad trend.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Analysis: China's coal-to-chemicals growth risks climate goals

China's coal-to-chemicals sector is where energy security and emissions reduction priorities are most directly at odds, write Chengcheng Qiu and Belinda Schape from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air in Dialogue Earth.

 

 Why rich countries are "reluctant" on additional Just Energy Transition Partnerships coal-to-clean deals

Top officials from the UK and Germany have disclosed that they are hesitant to pursue additional Just Energy Transition Partnerships (JETPs) – an initiative launched at COP26 in 2021 to help developing countries leapfrog fossil fuels, especially coal, to renewables, writes Vivian Chime in Climate Home News.

 

 Incineration, coal, and Curtis Bay: why the South Baltimore community suffers like no other

The residents of Curtis Bay have been fighting the worst air pollution in the state of Maryland for half a century, writes Ron Cassie in Baltimore Magazine.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Landmark South African court overturns decision on new coal plants

South African High Court Judge Cornelius van der Westhuizen has ruled that the government's plan to add 1500 megawatts of new coal plant capacity is "unlawful and invalid" as the then Minister of Mineral Resources, Gwede Mantashe, and the National Energy Regulator of South Africa had failed to consider the constitutional obligation to consider the best interests of children. The judge found the government had failed to document its decision, as it is required to do, and noted that the record "is ominously silent on any considerations given to the effect that the additional 1500 MW new coal-fired power will have on the environment and health of the nation, in particular, that of children". Three civil society groups – the African Climate Alliance, Vukani Environmental Justice Movement and groundwork – argued that Mantashe had not adequately considered that pollution from coal power poses a direct threat to public health and drives climate change. The decision nullifies the section of the 2019 Integrated Resource Plan that provided for 1500 MW of new coal capacity and the minister and Nersa's 2020 decision to procure the allocated capacity. The groups argue the ruling sets a precedent by emphasising the importance of environmental and health impacts in government decision-making, the constitutional right to a healthy environment, including future generations, and the need for transparent and participatory decision-making processes. (Daily Maverick, African Climate Alliance, Center for Environmental Rights)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Indian court orders a halt to forest clearance for mine: In response to a public interest application by Prakurti, a Maharashtra environmental group, the Nagpur bench of the Bombay High Court has ordered Western Coalfields, a subsidiary of Coal India, to suspend forest clearance for part of its proposed Durgapur Deep Extension Opencast coal mine. Prakurti argues that 121 hectares of forest slated for clearance as part of the mine expansion is in the buffer zone of the tiger corridor of Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve. Prakurti argues that clearing the forest will intensify the conflict between tigers and people as well as cause pollution and the loss of the forests. Western Coalfields commenced forest clearance without having responded to Prakurti's legal action filed in April 2024. The court ordered Western Coalfields to file a response to Prakurti's public interest litigation. (Times of India)

 

 Pro-coal Alberta town proposes bid to takeover neighbouring municipality: In the wake of a non-binding referendum in which residents of Crowsnest Pass voted 70 per cent in favour of Northback Holdings' proposed Crowsnest Pass mine, Mayor Blair Painter said the council would consider annexing the adjoining Municipal District of Ranchland which opposes the project. The Municipal District of Ranchland, which has launched a legal challenge against the Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) opting to hold public hearings on the project, said the suggestion of the Mayor of Crowsnest Pass is simply an attempt to "to decide what happens in our municipality". At the first stage of the AER hearing, ranchers, landowners, First Nations members and environmentalists expressed concern about the impact of the proposed mine on watersheds and communities downstream. (CBC, Global News)

 

 Japanese-backed brown coal hydrogen project in Australia stumbles: Kawasaki Heavy Industries has pulled out of the first stage of the proposed Hydrogen Energy Supply Chain (HESC) brown coal to hydrogen project in the Latrobe Valley. The HESC consortium – which includes J-Power, Iwatani Corporation, Marubeni Corporation and Sumitomo Corporation – proposes gasifying lignite in the Latrobe Valley, transporting the gas to the Port of Hastings for liquefaction and then shipping it to Japan. The Victorian and Australian governments both contributed A$50 million (US$31.9 million) to the initial project that produced a small trial shipment of hydrogen that HESC exported to Japan in January 2022. While the Japanese government had agreed to provide US$2.1 billion towards scaling the project up to 225,000 tonnes of hydrogen per year, the consortium partners in the project were reportedly only willing to enter into hydrogen purchase agreements for less than five years and wanted the Victorian government to hold responsibility for the carbon capture and storage component of the project. Kawasaki says the demonstration stage will now proceed in Japan but that it remains committed to the commercial-scale project in Victoria. Wendy Farmer from Voices of the Valley and Friends of the Earth said she doubts the project will proceed and viewed it as "another money grab from the Latrobe Valley".(Sydney Morning Herald [paywall], Nikkei [Japanese], ABC News)

 

 Welsh government proposes new agency for coal waste dumps: The Welsh government has released a bill to establish the Disused Tips Authority for Wales to manage former coal waste dumps and other tips that could threaten communities. In the aftermath of heavy rainfall in February 2020 that triggered a 60,000-tonne landslip from a former coal tip near Tylorstown, the Welsh government undertook a comprehensive survey and identified 360 coal sites classed as representing a high risk to nearby communities. The proposed authority will have responsibility for the assessment, registration, monitoring and management of disused tips, including those on private land. Residents temporarily evacuated from the village of Cwmtillery after a recent landslide from an old coal tip say they want to move or for the council to buy their property. (Guardian, Welsh Government, BBC)

 

 Canadian government waves through thermal coal mine expansion: Canada's Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Steven Guilbeault, and the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC) have decided not to require a federal environmental assessment of Coalspur's proposed 2.6 million tonnes a year expansion of the Vista thermal coal mine in Alberta. Guilbeault and the IAAC announced their decision late on Friday afternoon, allowing the 630-hectare expansion of the mine to proceed. Environmental Defence, a Canadian legal NGO, said the decision "represents massive backtracking on Canada's efforts to move beyond thermal coal". The former Environment Minister Jonathan Wilkinson designated the proposed expansion for federal environmental assessment twice before, but legal appeals by Ermineskin Cree Nation and Coalspur overturned these decisions. Amendments to the Impact Assessment Act were passed in June 2024, potentially allowing for the redesignation of the mine expansion. (Government of Canada, Environmental Defence, Ecojustice)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 India: Adani Group's plan for the proposed 3200 MW Anuppur coal plant in Madhya Pradesh has triggered concern about the likely impact on tiger populations in a critical wildlife corridor.

 

 Russia: A fire in the Alardinskaya underground coal mine led to the evacuation of 120 miners and the hospitalisation of two workers. The mine has a long history of fires, accidents and safety violations.

 

 US: The Sierra Club has criticised the decision of Alliant Energy, Madison Gas and Electric and Wisconsin Public Service to delay the closure of the 1112 MW Columbia Energy Center by three years until 2029. The utilities are considering converting the plant to run on gas.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Slovenian government takes over ailing lignite plant and mine: The Slovenian government has agreed to pay 403 million (US$424 million) to take over the 945 MW Sostanj lignite plant and the associated Velenje mine from the state-owned power utility Holding Slovenske Elektrarne (HSE). Slovenia's latest draft of its 2030 energy and climate plan proposed an emissions reduction target of 55 per cent by 2033, at odds with the European Union's 2030 deadline due to the continued operation of the Sostanj plant. The government said that without the takeover, the HSE subsidiaries operating the plant and mine would be bankrupt in January 2025, as losses on the plant have been running at about 100 million (US$105 million) a year due to carbon prices. The government said that the plant would primarily provide district heating for the Salek Valley until April 2027 at a cost of 327 million (US$344 million). (Balkan Green Energy News)

Indonesian coal phase-out by 2040 would require accelerating closures: Ember, a climate policy think tank, estimates that Indonesia would have to close about 3000 MW of coal capacity a year to meet President Prabowo's recently announced goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 and phasing out fossil fuel plants by 2040. Ember said that using current government assumptions, Indonesia would need to add 8000 MW of renewable capacity a year and 4000 MW of battery capacity per annum until 2040. Indonesia's current energy plan assumes electricity demand growth of five per cent per year, 22,000 MW of new gas capacity by 2033 and 5000 MW of nuclear capacity by 2040. The current estimates are for solar and wind to account for 20 per cent and 11 per cent, respectively, with the balance made up of geothermal, hydro and biomass. However, there are significant economic and environmental impacts with biomass generation associated with clearing native forests and palm oil plantations. Indonesia currently has no commercial nuclear capacity, and over the last 20 years, plans for projects with Russian, Chinese and Japanese partners have floundered. Ember notes that, aside from the need to revise contractual obligations between PLN and private power producers to facilitate reduced coal generation, the government needs to include the likely 26,200 MW of captive coal plants operating by 2026 in its phase-out plan. (Ember)

Indian government announces plan to auction another 20 coal blocks: The Ministry of Coal will offer 20 coal blocks for auction along with another seven areas that failed to sell in previous rounds. The new coal blocks for auction are in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Arunachal Pradesh. Just half of the blocks are described by the ministry as explored, with the remainder referred to as partially explored. The ministry estimates the new blocks contain a geological resource of up to 11.2 billion tonnes of coal. (Ministry of Coal [Pdf])

Australian agency says firmed solar and wind beat coal and nukes: The draft of its 2024-25 Gencost report by CSIRO, the Australian government's national science agency, estimates the cost of electricity in Australia from batteries fell by 20 per cent in the last year, with solar declining by a further eight per cent. CSIR0 estimates the price of electricity from onshore wind farms increased by two per cent in 2024. CSIRO estimates that electricity from a black coal plant with carbon capture and storage in 2024 would cost between A$190-303 per megawatt hous (MWh) (US$121.2 – 193.3/MWh), far higher than solar and onshore wind. The conservative opposition Liberal and National parties support nuclear power as an alternative to renewables replacing Australia's fleet of aging coal and gas plants. CSIRO estimates the cost of electricity from a conventional nuclear reactor in 2024 at A$155-252/MWh (US$98.9 – 160.8/MWh) and from a small modular reactor (SMR) notionally at A$400-663 per MWh (US$255.2 – 422.9/MWh). Even allowing for firmed costs at a 90 per cent share of renewables, CSIRO estimates wind and solar would cost between A$106-150/MWh (US$67.5 – 95.6/MWh). CSIRO estimates that while the cost of SMRs could decline significantly by 2050 if they are deployed commercially, solar and wind generation will still be far cheaper. Tristan Edis from Green Energy Markets said the CSIRO's analysis doesnt account for the risk of construction cost blow outs for nuclear plants. He estimates the cost of a nuclear plant in Australia would be double the CSIRO estimate. (Renew Economy, CSIRO [Pdf], Renew Economy)

South African coal mining company suspends CEO: The board of Exxaro Resources, one of South Africa's largest coal producers, has suspended Nombasa Tsengwa from both her roles as CEO and a member of the board pending an investigation by a law firm "into allegations related to workplace conduct and governance practice". Tsengwa's suspension followed a news report that nine senior executives at the company had resigned, were fired or suspended since she took over in August 2022. Tsengwa suspended the company's head of coal operations in late November while he was on a work trip in Switzerland. Exxarro anticipates total coal production of 40 million tonnes in 2024, with sales of about 30 million tonnes of thermal coal to Eskom and about 6.8 million tonnes exported. Due to security problems, vandalism, and locomotive shortages on the rail network servicing the Richards Bay coal export terminal, Exxaro is trucking some coal for export to Maputo in Mozambique. (Business Live, News24, Exxaro Resources [Pdf])

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Report says risk that Indian steel sector opts for high emissions pathway: A report by Global Energy Monitor (GEM) estimates nearly 40 per cent of India's operating coal-based blast furnaces will require relining before 2030, presenting an opportunity for their replacement with green technologies. The report also notes that more than 86 per cent of India's proposed basic oxygen furnace capacity is not yet under construction, revealing another opportunity to shift to a lower emissions pathway consistent with the national goal of net zero by 2070. The Ministry of Steel's current plan does not propose to move away from reliance on coal-based blast furnace technology despite India's plans to double steel capacity by 2030. The Indian steel sector currently produces more than 240 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year, about 12 per cent of the national total. A further 258 million of steel capacity proposed or under development could add an additional 680 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions a year. (Reuters, Global Energy Monitor)

title: CoalWire 545, January 2, 2025
excerpt: US agency funds coops switch to clean power; OECD coal plant proposals keep falling.
content:
January 2, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Happy New Year.

A recent Global Energy Monitor report highlighted how dramatically the coal plant pipeline in OECD countries has withered over the last decade: from 142 projects in thirteen countries to just five projects in four countries. Even then, most of the remaining projects are struggling to progress. Over the last few months, there has been much debate about the potential impact of new data centres and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in delaying the transition to clean energy. Indeed, coal and gas utilities have talked up the need to postpone coal plant retirements and support new gas plants. A new analysis suggests that rapid data centre load growth in the US is affecting power system reliability for other consumers. Meanwhile, energy analyst Michael Liebreich argues the impact of data centres and AI load growth on decarbonising power generation is likely to be far less than some claim.

An episode titled 'Taking out the Trash Day' in the late 1990s US drama series The West Wing highlighted the government practice of trying to bury media coverage of bad news by releasing it on a Friday with a bundle of other announcements. A variation on this is dropping bad news just before Christmas. In Australia, the government announced its support for four coal projects late in the week before Christmas. In Canada, the Alberta government announced its support for the Grassy Mountain mine owned by Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart on the Friday before Christmas. The government sought to hype its policy as strengthening the regulation of coal mining in the province but committed to exempting the Grassy Mountain project from its application.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Generative AI – the power and the glory

The tech titans will find out that the best way to power AI data centres is by building the same generating technologies that are most cost-effective for other users, connecting them to a robust and resilient grid, and working with local communities, writes Michael Liebreich in BloombergNEF.

 

 AI needs so much power, it's making yours worse

AI data centres are multiplying across the US and sucking up huge amounts of power. New evidence shows they may also be distorting the normal flow of electricity for millions of Americans, write Leonardo Nicoletti, Naureen Malik and Andre Tartar in Bloomberg Technology.

 

 Utah's coal mines can't find enough workers

A mine just reopened in eastern Utah, but the industry can't recruit enough workers. Low pay and the dangers of underground mining make the sector unattractive to young workers, writes Brooke Larsen in High Country News.

 

 For decades, Alabama's mining regulator has left citizens unprotected

Alabama has long demanded it remain the primary regulator of coal mining within its borders. The result? Unmitigated risks for citizens and statutory benefits for coal companies, writes Lee Hudspeth in Inside Climate News.

 

 Alberta surrenders to the Australian coal lobby

The so-called coal mining modernisation policy announced just before Christmas by the Alberta government has cruelly ignored the economic interests of people who depend on fresh water from the mountains in southern Alberta, writes Andrew Nikiforuk in The Tyee.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 US agency funds projects to cut cooperative utilities' coal use and boost renewables

The US Department of Agriculture announced US$4.37 billion in clean energy investments for ten cooperative power utilities, including US$1.4 billion to convert San Miguel Electric Cooperative's 410 MW lignite plant in Jourdanton, Texas, to a 600 MW solar and battery facility. The agency also announced US$331.5 million to refinance outstanding loans for Oglethorpe Power Corporation's two 952 MW retired coal units at the Hal B. Wansley plant in Georgia. Other projects included support for purchasing new solar, wind, hydro and battery capacity and additional transmission projects. (Chron.com, Department of Agriculture)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 OECD coal plant pipeline dwindles: A report by Global Energy Monitor revealed that the number of proposed coal plants in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries has plummeted from 142 projects with a combined capacity of 111,000 MW in 2015 to just five with a combined capacity of 3000 MW in late 2024. Of the 38 OECD countries, only 13 had coal plant proposals in 2015. Turkey is one of the few remaining OECD countries with new coal plant proposals. Three Turkish coal projects were cancelled or shelved in 2024, leaving just two proposed 344 MW units at the Afsin-Elbistan power station remaining. The other remaining projects are proposed carbon capture and storage projects in the US and Japan and a stalled plant in Australia. (Carbon Brief, Global Energy Monitor, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 New York law requires fossil fuel companies to pay for adaptation costs: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed the Climate Change Superfund Act into law that will require fossil fuel companies to contribute to a new climate change adaptation fund. The law tasks the New York Department of Environmental Conservation to identify companies responsible for more than 1 billion tonnes of global greenhouse gas emissions between 2000 and 2018. The act is modelled on existing state and federal Superfund legislation that requires the owners of designated toxic pollution sites to fund clean-up costs. The law aims to recover about US$75 billion over 25 years towards the costs of upgrading and repairing existing infrastructure such as roads, water and sewage systems against climate impacts. Senator Liz Krueger, who initiated the legislation, said various government agencies estimate climate costs for the state at up to US$200 billion. The American Petroleum Institute opposed the law and hinted it may launch a legal challenge. (Reuters, Governor Kathy Hochul, New York State Senate [Pdf])

 

 Australian government approves four coal mine projects: Just prior to Christmas, the Australian Minister for Environment, Tanya Plibersek, approved four coal mine projects with an estimated combined 850 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions. Plibersek approved Jellinbah's Lake Vermont project in the Bowen Basin, BHP Mitsubishi's Caval Ridge mine in Queensland and Whitehaven Coal's Boggabri mine in New South Wales. Plibersek also cleared the way for the approval of Vitrinite's controversial Vulcan South coal mine in Queensland despite a current investigation into a potential breach of the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation (EPBC) Act. The company allegedly cleared 47 hectares of protected koala habitat and mining coal without approval. Plibersek sought to downplay the decisions on the grounds that three of the projects are "extensions of existing operations" and will predominantly produce metallurgical coal. Joseph Sikulu, from the 350.org said Plibersek's decision "makes a mockery of the 'family' they claim to call the Pacific". (Guardian, Queensland Conservation Council)

 

 Alberta flags new coal mining rules as protests grow: In the week before Christmas, Alberta Energy Minister Brian Jean and Environment Minister Rebecca Schulz announced the Alberta Coal Modernization Initiative would allow new underground coal mines. The ministers said the government will finalise a new coal mining policy in the first half of 2025, but some 'advanced' projects, such as the proposed Crowsnest Pass project, will be exempt from the plan. Northback Holdings, a subsidiary of a private company owned by Australia's richest woman, Gina Rinehart, is lobbying the local and provincial government for approval of the Grassy Mountain metallurgical coal project. Northback's CEO Mike Young said the announcement reflected "the need to provide clarity on regulatory processes and to provide certainty for resource investment in general". The District of Ranchland has launched a legal appeal against the decision of the Alberta Energy Regulator to treat the proposed mine as an advanced project. The municipality argues the federal government rejected the project in August 2021 and the regulator should not reconsider it. (CBC, Government of Alberta)

 

 
 "The existing regulations ensured that the Grassy Mountain project [in Alberta] was rejected by regulators in 2021. If you create a new regime that advocates and approves a project like Grassy as the current government is now doing, then you are weakening standards — not strengthening them,"

said Dr Bill Donahue, the former head of Alberta's environmental monitoring branch on the government's support for new coal projects on the slopes of the Rocky Mountains.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The United Firefighters Union has warned that a special fire truck allocated to control any summertime fires at coal mines in the Latrobe Valley is currently out of service.

 

 Canada: A fire has damaged a coal loader at the Westshore coal terminal in Vancouver.

 

 India: The Andhra Pradesh Mineral Development Corporation and Adani have applied to expand the Suliyari coal mine in Madhya Pradesh from 5 to 7 million tonnes per annum without a public hearing. Families displaced by the mine three years ago are still waiting for resettlement and compensation.

 

 India: Hundreds of villagers attempted to block the construction of a new coal dump near Mulong in Assam by a subsidiary of Coal India.

 

 US: PJM announced that NRG's 455 MW coal-fired Indian River Unit 4 in Delaware can retire by February 2025. NRG applied in June 2021 to close the plant but was requested to continue operating it until December 2026. With the early completion of a new transmission line, the unit is no longer required.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

China is on track to install more solar in 2024 than the year before: The China Photovoltaic Industry Association (CPIA) estimates the country could install between 230,000 MW and 260,000 MW in 2024. In 2023, China installed 217,000 MW of solar capacity. The association said key factors behind the record rate of installation include a strong rooftop market, declining module costs and the establishment of solar and wind energy megabases. Wang Bohua, the chairman of CPIA, said that in the first 10 months of 2024, exports of solar cells and modules grew by more than 40 per cent and 15 per cent year-on-year, respectively. Module exports are dominated by the European market, with increasing shares in South Asia, Latin America and the Middle East. Bohua said the largest export markets for batteries are India, Turkiye and Cambodia. BloombergNEF estimates solar module costs could remain in the range of 8-9 US cents per watt in 2025. (China Daily)

US government closes black lung liability loophole: The US Department of Labour issued a final rule to close a loophole that allows self-insured coal mining companies to avoid liabilities for black lung disease. The symptoms of black lung disease can emerge many years after exposure to mine dust. The new rule requires self-insured companies to cover 100 per cent of black lung liabilities with the coverage reviewable annually. The new rule aims to ensure coal mining companies cover the full costs of health liabilities rather than fall on the taxpayer-funded Black Lung Disability Trust Fund when a company goes bankrupt. The new rule, which comes into effect 30 days after its publication date in the Federal Register, also prevents the establishment of new tax-exempt black lung benefits trusts and allows for greater oversight of existing trusts. Civil society groups have raised concerns about the potential impact of the recently announced merger of Arch Coal and Consol Energy on their potential black lung liabilities of more than US$300 million. (Public News Service, US Department of Labor, Appalachian Voices)

US state provides renewable energy credits for plant burning met coal: Ohio has passed a bill providing renewable energy credits to SunCoke Energy for waste steam from its coke plant in Middleton. SunCoke Energy's Middleton plant comprises 100 ovens that convert metallurgical coal to 550,000 US short tons (499,000 tonnes) of coke for the neighbouring Cleveland-Cliffs steel plant. The bill extends renewable energy credits to SunCoke Energy for steam supplied to Altivia Petrochemicals, a neighbouring plant that produces phenol, acetone and other chemical products. SunCoke Energy argued that renewable energy credits should include steam that offsets gas generation. SunCoke Energy also has coke plants in Virginia, Indiana, Illinois and Vitoria, Brazil and produces about 4.2 million US short tons (3.8 million tonnes) of coke a year for use in blast furnaces for steel production. (Cleveland, SunCoke Energy [Pdf])

Report tips decline in price of seaborne thermal coal: The latest edition of the Australian government's Resources and Energy Quarterly notes that heatwaves in 2024 triggered spikes in power demand in key countries such as India, China, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan and supported steady demand for thermal coal from the seaborne market. The Department of Industry and Resources estimates thermal coal prices could fall to about US$114 per tonne in 2026 from US$136 a tonne in 2024. The assessment also flags uncertainty about the impact of new data centres and artificial intelligence on thermal coal demand. The report notes that Russian thermal coal exports declined due to the effect of sanctions and constraints on railway capacity when higher-value metallurgical coal has priority. The report notes that Russian Railways plans to increase rail tariffs by 13 per cent in 2025. Indonesian thermal coal exports increased by five per cent in the first eight months of 2024, buoyed by strong demand from India. (Department of Industry, Science and Resources [Pdf])

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Jarred Sullivan, Valley So Low: One Lawyer's Fight for Justice in the Wake of America's Great Coal Catastrophe, Knopf, October 2024. (A review of the book is here.)

This 384-page book details the legal attempts to gain compensation for those affected by the December 2008 coal ash disaster at the Tennessee Valley Authority's Kingston coal plant in Tennessee.

Investing in coal plant flexibility: a strategic approach for J-POWER's transition, Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility, December 2024.

This 18-page report argues that J-POWER needs to prioritise investment in initiatives that lower minimum load levels and increase the flexibility of domestic coal plants.
