title: CoalWire 544, December 19, 2024
excerpt: Report reveals coal methane hotspots; China announces coal methane regulation.
content:
December 19, 2024
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

A new Global Energy Monitor report ties 23 methane emissions events detected by satellites to specific coal mines. While the United Nations Environment Program's new methane alert system alerts mine operators and regulators to methane hotspots, it does not make the information public. Without ready public access to quality data, mining companies and regulators are under less pressure to act. China, which is not a signatory to the Global Methane Pledge, has announced new regulations to cut emissions from new mines from early next year and existing mines in 2027.

After much debate about Indonesian President Prabowo Subiantos statements on phasing out coal power within 15 years, his envoy for energy and the environment, Hashim Djojohadikusumo, insists the government is committed to a "phase down", not a phase-out. Hashim is Prabowo's younger brother, so he is well-placed to speak for the President. In the US, the amount of coal stockpiled at power plants suggests coal production will decline next year.

Thank you for your reading CoalWire in 2024. I will take a short break with the next edition out in early January.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Philippines struggles to break free from coal despite renewables pledge

The Philippines, which is highly vulnerable to climate change, is struggling to reduce its reliance on coal despite ambitious renewable energy pledges, writes Gaea Katreena Cabico in Dialogue Earth.

 

 Musician Corb Lund on Alberta coal mines: 'They're going to ruin our groundwater' 

The award-winning country and western singer-songwriter Corb Lund, who grew up on a ranch in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains, is a leading voice against the renewed push for new coal mines in Alberta, writes Sharon J. Riley in The Narwhal.

 

 'It was the poisoning of a workforce,' says widow of clean-up worker at Tenessee Valley Authority's coal ash spill

Ansol Clark and Tommy Johnson were some of the first to respond to clean up the Tennessee Valley Authority's coal ash disaster at the Kingston coal plant in Tennessee 16 years ago. Their wives say coal ash killed their husbands, writes Ben Hall in NewsChannel5.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Report reveals global coal mine methane hotspots: A report by Global Energy Monitor has revealed that an analysis of satellite data between January 1 2023 and April 1 2024 shows 23 "super-emitter" scale methane emissions detections at significant coal mines. The report identified major emissions events at mines in Australia, China, Mexico and Colombia, including Drummond's Pribbenow mine in Colombia, China Shenhua Energy's Baode mine in China and Altos Hornos de Mxico's Mimosa coal mine in Mexico. In Australia, three mines were associated with significant methane emission events: Mandalong Pty Ltd's Mandalong mine, Bulga Management's Bulga mine in New South Wales and Capcoal's Capcoal Mining Complex in Queensland. The report notes that while the United Nations Environment Program's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) sends alerts to mine operators and government agencies, it does not publicly release the information. The report states that a further 59 methane emission events could not be conclusively tied to specific coal mines, such as where there were multiple mines in close proximity or where the source could not be identified but may be from an abandoned mine. (Reuters, Global Energy Monitor [Pdf])

 

 China unveils new coal mine methane rules: China's Ministry of Environment has unveiled regulations that require new coal mines with a methane content of eight per cent or higher and total emissions of more than ten cubic metres per minute to capture the gas. The rule will apply to new mines from April 2025 and existing mines after April 2027. China is the world's largest emitter of methane, with about 40 per cent of the country's emissions originating from the country's 3000 coal mines. The European Union and 159 countries have committed to the Global Methane Pledge target of cutting methane emissions by 30 per cent below 2020 levels by 2030. China has not joined the pledge but announced it would cut methane emissions. (Reuters)

 

 Indonesian President's envoy retracts coal phase-out: At a COP 29 debriefing in Jakarta last week, President Prabowo Subianto's special envoy for energy and the environment, Hashim Djojohadikusumo, insisted Indonesia is committed to a coal "phase down" rather than phasing out coal plants within 15 years. Hashim is Prabowo's younger brother. "Indonesia has not committed to shutting down all coal plants by 2040. Instead, we will reduce their intensity and supplement the energy mix with renewables, nuclear, and natural gas," Hashim said. He also emphasised that Indonesia will not "disrupt newly built coal plants". (China Global South Project)

 

 Indian company convicted of using forged documents to win coal blocks: A special Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) court sentenced the former managing director of Abhijeet Infrastructure, Manoj Kumar Jayaswal, to a four-year prison sentence for the use of forged documents to win the allocation of the Brinda, Sisai, and Meral coal blocks in Jharkhand. Special Judge Arun Bhardwaj also sentenced Abhijeet Infrastructure's director, Ramesh Kumar Jayaswal to three years in prison on the same offences and fined the company three million rupees (US$35,335). The CBI alleged that the forged documents misrepresented support for the company's proposed steel plant and its claimed purchase of private land for the plant in Hazaribagh. Based on the forged documents, the Ministry of Steel recommended the Ministry of Coal allocate the three coal blocks to the company. The company was allocated the coal blocks in June 2005, with the CBI filing initial charges in 2016. (Business Standard, Economic Times)

 

 Germany set for election in February: The German government has abandoned its proposed Power Plant Security Act that included provision for tendering for new gas plants to support the closure of coal plants. The intention was to auction 5000 MW of new gas capacity by 2026 with the option of converting the plants use hydrogen at a later date. The Christian Democratic Union ruled out supporting the law proposed by the minority government of Chancellor Olaf Scholz's Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Green Party. Greens MP and Minister for Economic Affairs and Climate Action, Robert Habeck, said the government would only take coal plants offline after sufficient backup capacity is available to supplement increased renewables generation. In October 2022, the government reached an agreement with North Rhine-Westphalia, which has energy-intensive industries, to close coal capacity by 2030. The coalition agreement between SDP, the Greens and the Free Democrats stated coal should "ideally" be phased out by 2030 rather than the legislated date of 2038. In mid-November, the coalition collapsed when Scholz fired finance minister Christian Lindner of the Free Democrats. An election is expected to be held on February 23, 2025. (BNNBloomberg, BNNBloomberg, Clean Energy Wire)

 

 Major Ukraine coal pit closes as Russian forces near: Metinvest, Ukraine's largest steel producer, has suspended operations at one of its three coal pits at the Pokrovske mine in Donetsk Oblast as Russian artillery and ground forces advance. The Pokrovske mine produces metallurgical coal, with estimates that the loss of the mine could cut the country's steel production by half. The Ukrainian utility DTEK has also reported widespread damage to its coal and gas plants from a wave of Russian missile and drone strikes on December 12 and 13 across seven provinces. The mid-winter attacks on critical energy infrastructure are aimed at weakening Ukraine's position ahead of an anticipated decline in military and other support when President Trump is sworn in on January 20. (Kyiv Independent, Kyiv Independent, Institute for the Study of War)

 

 US regulator warns Alabama agency of licence breach: The Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement (OSMRE), a federal US regulatory agency, has warned the Alabama Surface Mining Commission that it must take action within 10 days after an inspection revealed that Crimson Oak Grove Resource had breached a licence condition for its underground Oak Grove Mine. The investigation found the company has failed to report all required information about subsidence and methane monitoring at the mine. In March 2024, a gas explosion killed a homeowner and seriously injured his grandson in a house above the mine. Following an investigation, the Mine Safety and Health Administration cited Oak Grove Mine for 204 safety violations. The family has launched a lawsuit alleging methane from the mine caused the explosion, a claim the company rejects. In mid-September, a rockfall accident at the mine killed a miner. (Inside Climate News, Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Afghanistan: The Ministry of Industry and Commerce reports that more than 654,000 tonnes of coal were exported in the first eight months of its current solar year. The main markets are Pakistan, China, Iran, India, and Turkey.

 

 Bangladesh: PowerChina has agreed to a one-year extension of its memorandum of understanding with GCM Resources for the potential development of the Phulbari coal mine.

 

 Chile: AES sold two coal units with a combined capacity of 539 MW at its Ventanas coal plant to Quintero Energa. Chile's 2024 decarbonisation plan states the units would close in or by 2025.

 

 India: A Delhi court has acquitted six people, including former government officials and executives of Navabharat Power Private, who were charged with cheating over the allocation between 2006 and 2008 of coal blocks in Odisha.

 

 Montenegro: The draft National Energy and Climate Plan prepared by the Ministry of Energy proposes delaying the closure of the 225 MW Pljevlja lignite-fired plant until 2041.

 

 Mozambique: Sparks from welding equipment caused a major fire at the coal processing plant at Vulcan Mocambique's Moatize mine.

 

 Serbia: State-owned power utility Elektroprivreda Srbije (EPS) has commissioned the 350 MW ownership Kostolac B3 lignite-fired power plant. In 2010, EPS contracted China Machinery Engineering Corporation to build the unit, but the commencement of construction was delayed until 2017.

 

 South Africa: A burst high-pressure steam pipe caused the explosion of a transformer at Eskom's 3600 MW Matla coal plant. Nine employees were injured, with one in a critical condition.

 

 US: The Supreme Court has declined an application by the East Kentucky Power Cooperative to freeze the implementation of the Environmental Protection Agency's legacy coal ash rule targeting sites at risk of leaching toxic metals into groundwater.

 

 US: A coalition of environmental groups has asked the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement to close an illegal coal haul road through the Monongahela National Forest in West Virginia. The road is used to transport coal South Fork Coal Company's Rocky Run mine to a processing plant.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Stockpiles mount at US plants as coal generation struggles to compete: The Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates that coal stockpiles at US coal power plants stood at 138 million US short tons (125 million tonnes) at the end of November. The Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis (IEEFA) estimates this is equal to about four months supply for the US coal fleet at recent utilisation levels. Increasing renewable generation and low gas prices have undercut the profitability of coal power. IEEFA estimates the current inventory is worth about US$6.5 billion with high levels likely to drive reduced coal production in 2025. The EIA estimates US coal production in 2025 could fall to 469 million US short tons (425 million tonnes), a nine per cent decline on 2024 levels. EIA data indicates that the US produced 1.1 billion US short tons of coal (1.02 billion tonnes) in 2001, of which only 48 million US short tonnes (43.5 million tonnes) were exported. (IEEFA)

Lead contractor bails out of US carbon capture project: TC Energy has abandoned the Project Tundra consortium proposing to retrofit a US$2 billion carbon capture and storage unit to the 705 MW lignite-fired Milton R. Young Station in North Dakota. The company did not explain the reason for its withdrawal beyond stating it would pursue projects "that align with our commercial preferences". TC Energy was the lead contractor in the project, leaving Minnkota Power Cooperative (MPC), Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Kiewit as the remaining project partners. MPC had previously said it would decide this year whether to proceed with the project. The US Department of Energy has pledged to allocate US$350 million to the consortium if the project proceeds. (Inside Climate News)

Russian government plans rescue package for coal sector: Russia's Minister for Energy, Sergey Tsivilev, announced the government will develop a financial support package for the country's coal sector "as soon as possible". Tsivilev specifically mentioned the need to support the Kuzbass region, the country's coal-producing heartland. President Vladimir Putin has backed support for the coal sector which has been hit by international sanctions, declining export prices and the high cost of long-distance freight costs from coalfields to export terminals. Russian coal companies reported combined losses of US$873 million in the first nine months of 2024. Russia's metallurgical coal exports are likely to remain stable in 2025 at about 44 million tonnes, with about 95 per cent sales to India and China, albeit sold at a discounted price. Russia's thermal coal exports fell by almost one quarter in the first half of the year, with demand from South Korea, China, and India. Exports to South Korea fell by 44 per cent in the first half of 2024 as the government urged utilities to avoid Russian coal. The Australian government's resources agency projects thermal coal exports to fall by 17 per cent to 110 million tonnes in 2024 and plateau at that level for the next few years. (Kyiv Independent)

Australian opposition's nuclear plan would boost power sector emissions: Analysts suggest that greenhouse gas emissions from Australia's power sector could be about one billion tonnes higher by 2051 under the opposition Liberal-National parties' recently announced plan to build nuclear plants instead of renewables and slow the retirement of coal and gas capacity. The powerful Minerals Council of Australia, which represents uranium mining companies, including BHP, backs the establishment of commercial nuclear plants and slowing the rollout of renewables. The current Labor government aims for renewables to supply about 82 per cent of electricity by 2030, with about 90 per cent of the country's coal capacity closed by 2035. The opposition's nuclear power plan assumes only about one-third of coal capacity will be closed by 2035. The Smart Energy Council, a lobby group for renewable energy, argues that for the grid to accommodate about 13,000 MW of nuclear capacity proposed by the opposition parties, the government would require the curtailment of rooftop solar systems. An Australian election is due in 2025 with current polling suggesting a close result or a minority government. (Guardian, Renew Economy)

Adani asked for customs duty exemption on coal for Godda plant: Adani Power is lobbying the Indian government to grant an exemption from customs duty on coal imported for the 1600 MW Godda plant in Jharkhand that was originally built for power exports to Bangladesh. Adani and the Bangladesh Power Development Board were in dispute in November over an estimated US$846 million in outstanding payments for electricity. Adani shut one unit at the plant down and threatened to cease exports altogether. Adani also won approval from India's Ministry of Power to sell power into the domestic market but, given its remoteness, is seeking a waiver on customers duty on imported coal to make it competitive with domestic utilities. Adani's head of investor relations, Nishit Dave, said the company would only look at domestic power sales if required. A panel of experts appointed by the government and headed by former High Court judge Justice Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury is reviewing all power purchase agreements between 2009 and 2024, including the one for Adani's Godda plant. (The Business Standard, Adani Watch)

(Inside Climate News, Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement)

title: CoalWire 546, January 16, 2025
excerpt: Thai cement company drops coal mine plan; Pakistan scraps funding for coal plant; US coal mine suspended.
content:
January 16, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

In Thailand, a coalition of residents and civil society groups has prodded the Siam Cement Group to announce it will abandon a proposed new coal concession and mine. In Pakistan, the government has finally clamped down on proposals for private power projects seeking lucrative power purchase agreements. The government scrapped funding for one coal project, and a separate Chinese-backed project appears unlikely to proceed. In the US, the state of West Virginia has finally suspended the permit for a coal mine owned by the former state Governor and now a newly-elected Republican Senator.

As with all actions under the outgoing Biden administration, there is uncertainty about what will unfold under the incoming Trump government. The latest data indicates US coal generation declined marginally in 2024 but the big wild card is the potential jump in power demand for new AI data centres. A review has found the delayed retirement of 30 US coal units due to rising power demand. Meanwhile, a Reuters investigation found that Berkshire Hathaway's 12 coal plants rank worst of all corporate fleets when it comes to emissions of nitrogen oxides.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Trump's pick for Energy Secretary is a longtime member of Charles Koch's political donor network

Chris Wright, the founder and CEO of the fracking services company Liberty Energy and Donald Trump's pick for Secretary of Energy, has long been a part of the Koch network that has promoted climate change denial, writes Dave Anderson from the Energy and Policy Institute.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Thai cement company rules out new coal mine bid

The Siam Cement Group has informed Greenpeace Thailand that the company has decided to cancel its application for the Maetha lignite mine in Lampang province in northern Thailand and requested government agencies end its concession over the area. The company has also ruled out purchasing coal from the Omkoi coal mine project in the neighbouring Chiang Mai province for use in its cement plants. Residents and a coalition of civil society groups, including Greenpeace Thailand, oppose the development of the mines due to concerns about pollution and climate change impacts. Greenpeace has requested the Siam Cement Group publish the letters to government agencies on its website and publicly disclose a plan to phase out the use of coal, including imports from mines in Indonesia. (Greenpeace Thailand [Thai])

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Montana Supreme Court upholds youth climate case: In a 6-1 ruling, the Montana Supreme Court upheld a district court decision that 16 youth plaintiffs have a "fundamental constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment", and that includes a stable climate. The court released the decision on December 18. The youth argued that Montana policies promoting the development of fossil fuel projects violated their constitutional right and challenged two laws adopted in 2023 by the Montana legislature to weaken the provisions of the Montana Environmental Policy Act. The Republican Montana state government appealed the district court ruling. The Supreme Court found that the plaintiffs had proved that climate change had damaged the state's environment and that changes to legislation aimed at preventing the assessment of greenhouse gas emissions in the environmental assessment process breached the youth's constitutional right. Montana is the sixth largest coal-producing state in the US. (PBS, Daily Montanan)

 

 US state suspends coal licence: The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection has suspended Bluestone Coal Corporation's mining permit for the Poca mine. In December, the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement (OSMRE), a federal US regulatory agency, requested the state agency revoke the permit for the mine. Investigations of the site found numerous failures by the company to comply with environmental protection and rehabilitation standards at the almost 600-acre (283 hectare) mountaintop coal mine. The family of former West Virginia Republican Governor Jim Justice owns Bluestone Coal Corporation. In the November 2024 US election, Justice won the race to replace former Democrat Joe Manchin as a Senator for West Virginia. Forbes estimates Justice has a net worth of "less than zero". (West Virginia Public Broadcasting, Appalachian Voices, WCHSTV)

 

 Polish energy transition gathers pace; miners protest closures: Katowice, the largest city in Poland's coal heartland, has joined the Powering Past Coal Alliance (PPCA) and vowed to phase out coal-fired power generation. The city aims to serve as an example for other cities navigating similar challenges. Katowice's membership of PPCA comes as thousands of coal miners protested in Warsaw against the decline of the coal industry. State-owned utility PGE announced in late 2024 that it would close the four coal units at its 875 megawatt (MW) Rybnik plant in 2027. The coal units at the 908 MW Dolna Odra plant will close later this year, and the 505 MW Laziska plant is likely to close within a few years. In September 2020, the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government agreed with miners' unions to phase out coal mining by 2049. The unions initially wanted the deadline set at 2060. The PiS lost government in October 2023 but President Andrzej Duda, a member of the PiS, has blocked parts of the legislative agenda of the Civic Coalition government led by Donald Tusk. Duda's second term expires in August with an election for President in mid-May, with the PiS-backed candidate trailing in recent opinion polls. (EuroNews, Notes From Poland)

 

 Romania stalls coal plant closures: Romania's Minister for Energy, Sebastian Burduja, said he would seek European Commission approval to delay the closure of the country's last coal plants by about three years, stating that there is insufficient replacement capacity available by 2026. Romania opened tenders for the construction of two gas plants, but these failed to attract any bids. The gas unit proposed at the Complexul Energetic Oltenia site has also been delayed. In early 2022, the European Commission agreed to provide 2.66 billion (US$2.73 billion) in aid to state-owned power utility CE Oltenia, the country's largest coal generator, to replace its lignite units with new gas and renewables capacity. Romania had proposed to close 2085 megawatts of coal capacity by 2026. Despite the proposed delay, Romania's National Recovery and Resilience Plan and Territorial Just Transition Plan with the European Commission include binding commitments to phase out coal generation by 2032. (Balkan Green Energy News)

 

 Investigation finds many Berkshire Hathaway plants lack scrubbers: A Reuters investigation has found that the 12 coal plants operated by Berkshire Hathaway rank poorly for nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions. The investigation found that the fleet of coal plants operated by three utilities owned by Berkshire Hathaway, a major diversified company, emitted more nitrogen oxides than any other corporate coal fleet in the country in 2023, according to an analysis of Environmental Protection Agency power plant data. Berkshire Hathaway has resisted the installation of selective catalytic reduction scrubbers at its plants, lobbying regulators and filing lawsuits against adopting the pollution control technology. Reuters found SCR scrubbers operating at plants that generated 62 per cent of US coal generation in 2023 but only 27 per cent of Berkshire Hathaway's coal generation came from units equipped with the technology. The company described SCR scrubbers as "an expensive technology for our customers" and said it plans to exit from coal generation by 2049. The company said it had reduced NOx emissions by closing old plants but did not address the issue of health impacts caused by pollution from the units without SCR scrubbers. (Reuters)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Oakey Coal Action Alliance has withdrawn a legal challenge against the Queensland government's approval of a water licence to allow New Hope Group's expansion of the New Acland coal mine.

 

 Canada: The Alberta Energy Regulator has fined CST Canada Coal C$22,000 (US$15,331) over the unauthorised release of about 107,000 litres of mine wastewater into the Smoky River on December 29, 2022.

 

 Canada: The British Columbia Environmental Appeal Board has upheld a C$140,000 (US$97,689) penalty against Teck Coal after a January 2019 explosion of a truck tyre caused "life-altering" injuries to a worker at the company's Greenhills mine. Elk Valley Resources, a subsidiary of Glencore, now owns Teck Coal.

 

 Iran: The Balochistan government has ordered charges against the owners of United Mineral Company Sanjdi after an explosion at the underground coal mine killed 12 workers.

 

 Ukraine: Advancing Russian forces have forced Metinvest, Ukraine's largest steel producer, to suspend coal production at its Pokrovske mine in Donetsk Oblast.

 

 US: The US Supreme Court denied a request to review a Hawai`i Supreme Court decision allowing a legal case alleging fossil fuel companies deceived the public about their products' role in climate change. The respondents in the case include BHP and Chevron subsidiaries with coal interests.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

India and Indonesia set coal production records in 2024: Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources preliminary estimate is that coal production increased to 831 million tonnes in 2024, up from 775 million tonnes in 2023. New Chinese customs data revealed that 542.7 million tonnes of coal was imported in 2024, up 14.4 per cent from 474.42 million tonnes in 2023. Indonesia is a key supplier to China with lower international coal prices spurring increased imports as an alternative to domestic production. The China Coal Transportation and Distribution Association estimates imports could fall to 525 million tonnes in 2025. In India, estimated coal production for 2024 was 1.04 billion tonnes, up 70.4 million tonnes from the year before. Data from India's Central Electricity Authority indicates coal generation was up by five per cent in 2024 to 1293 terawatt hours. A recent International Energy Agency report on the global coal sector estimated global coal consumption could hit a record high of about 8.77 billion tonnes in 2024 but forecast demand plateauing through to 2027. (Mining.com, Reuters, Argus, International Energy Agency)

Standoff between Pakistan and Chinese company over coal plant: The Minister for Energy, Awais Khan Leghari, announced that 10,000 MW of new private power projects would not proceed as they were too expensive. He said that new power contracts would be allocated based on competitive bidding and prioritise least-cost electricity. High power prices are a major political issue in Pakistan, with the government announcing that only well-advanced projects that have achieved financial close will proceed. CHIC Pak Power Company, a Chinese company proposing the 300 MW Gwadar coal plant, is lobbying Pakistan's Private Power and Infrastructure Board to increase the power tariff for the plant to make it viable. The latest standoff comes after numerous delays to the project that was first approved in August 2019 with a deadline for financial close as April 23, 2020. Since then, the power purchase tariff for the project has increased three times, and the deadline for financial close has been extended on six occasions. Pakistan had proposed cancelling the imported coal plant in 2022 and replacing the project with solar capacity, but the company and the Chinese government objected to the proposed change. In December 2024, the government revealed that it had terminated funding for the 660 MW Unit 6 at the Jamshoro power station in Sindh province. It appears the expansion has been cancelled. (Dawn, Dawn, Business Recorder, The Nation)

Report estimates rapid demand growth for US data centres: A report by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL) estimates demand for electricity for US data centres could increase from about four per cent in 2023 to between 6.7 per cent and 12 per cent by 2028. LBNL estimates the annual compound power demand growth for data centres was 18 per cent between 2018 and 2023 and could increase to between 13 per cent and 27 per cent over the 2023 to 2028 period. The report estimates that assuming an average capacity utilisation rate of 50 per cent, data centres could account for between 74 and 132 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity by 2028. The wide range of demand depends on the level of demand for powerful AI processing chips and their level of utilisation. The report also highlights that the cooling technology used at the centres will also have a significant impact on power demand with the use of liquid base cooling incorporated into the processing chips as a less energy intensive option to reliance on evaporative air conditioning. LBNL notes that estimating possible future power demand is limited by the availability of direct energy data for a sector with rapidly evolving technologies. The Sierra Club highlights data centres will drive an increase in greenhouse gas emissions and domestic power prices. In the final days of his administration, President Biden signed an executive order directing the Department of Defense and Department of Energy to lease land for gigawatt-scale AI data centres and associated power plants. (Reuters, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory [Pdf], Sierra Club, Utility Dive)

US coal plant owners review retirements as power demand increases: The owners or operators of more than 30 uneconomic US coal plants plan to delay their retirement, according to an analysis of power plant data. An analysis of the 30 plants by RMI, an energy policy think tank, found that between 2015 and 2023, the plants imposed more than US$5 billion in unnecessary costs on customers. Michael Goggin from Grid Strategies, an energy consultancy, says utilities may be dispatching uneconomic coal power into the grid to make a plant "look more used and useful than it actually is" to ensure its continued support from regulators. Goggin said that the continued generation by uneconomic coal plants occupies scarce transmission grid capacity, often in areas favourable for new wind and solar projects, and slows the transition to clean energy. (Floodlight News)

US coal mining and power sector emissions declined in 2024: Coal power generation declined by one per cent to 16 per cent in 2024, the lowest level since 1967, according to an analysis by the Rhodium Group, an energy sector consultancy. Declining coal demand, along with large stockpiles, led to coal production falling by 12 per cent in 2024, leading to lower methane emissions from the industrial sector. The share of electricity generation from solar and wind increased by two per cent to 16 per cent, exceeding coal generation's share in the energy mix for the first time. Compared to 2023, solar and wind generation increased by 32 per cent and 7 per cent, respectively. While wind and solar generation increased, electricity demand increased by three per cent, with residential demand accounting for the largest share of demand growth. Power generation from gas accounted for 42 per cent of electricity in 2024, according to the report. The Rhodium Group estimates greenhouse gas emissions in the US across all sectors declined by just 0.2 per cent compared to 2023 and are about 20 per cent below 2005 levels. (Canary Media, Rhodium Group)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 BNEF says electrolyser costs hit hydrogen competitiveness: BloombergNEF (BNEF) estimates green hydrogen produced with renewable electricity will only be competitive with its gas-derived counterpart in China and India by 2040. BNEF estimates green hydrogen produced in Texas, the cheapest US state, is estimated to fall from US$7.22 per kilogram to US$4.82 in 2030. The Biden administration set a hydrogen cost target of US$1 per kilogram by 2031 and proposed a tax credit of US$3 per kilogram. BNEF estimates that if the Trump administration proceeds with the tax credit, hydrogen costs could fall to below US$1 per kilogram in Texas by 2040. But there are other uncertainties such as the possible impact of Trump administration tariffs on imported electrolysers used to separate hydrogen from water. BNEF estimates green hydrogen could fall from a current range of US$3.74 to US$11.70 per kilogram to US$1.60 to US$5.09 per kilogram in 2050. BNEF tripled its 2050 cost estimate, in large part due to the increased cost of electrolysers. Lowering the cost of hydrogen is a critical step in shifting coal-based steel production to low-carbon technology. (Bloomberg)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

German parties' energy and climate policy positions for the 2025 election, Clean Energy Wire, January 2025. (Pdf)

This chart provides a concise overview of the key energy and climate policies of the major parties contesting the German election scheduled for February 23, 2025.

title: CoalWire 537, January 23, 2025
excerpt: Trump sworn in; US coal power to decline in 2025; complaint filed over Czech lignite plant.
content:
January 23, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The inauguration of President Donald Trump is undoubtedly the most significant story of the week, both for the specific decisions he announced and the spillover effects of his reelection on global politics and efforts to combat global heating. But it is worth remembering that the US coal industry is a shadow of its former self compared to when Trump first assumed office in January 2017. Since 2016, the US has commissioned no new coal plants. During Trump's first four-year term, coal production fell by about 31 per cent to 535 million US short tons (485 million tonnes), and more than 48,000 megawatts (MW) of coal power plant capacity retired.

The remaining coal plants are now almost a decade older, and the US coal mining industry faces significant challenges. The US Energy Information Administration, a government agency known for its cautious modelling, estimates coal generation will fall again this year. Trump signed a raft of executive orders this week aiming to unwind a range of Biden administration initiatives. Some of these will have an immediate effect, such as on communities that previously benefited from environmental justice initiatives. But other measures, such as restrictions on new renewables projects, will, at best, take time to have any effect in slowing the continued decline of US coal power generation. Despite all the policy setbacks announced and those yet to come, it is worth remembering that the Republicans hold a wafer-thin 220-215 majority in the House of Representatives, with the next mid-term elections due in early November 2026.

Finally, the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University has launched some handy trackers to help keep up to date with key Trump administration announcements.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Foreign investors could stall coal plant closures in Asia

Dozens of coal plant contracts require host governments in Indonesia, Pakistan, and Vietnam to compensate investors, especially foreign ones, for actions that would drive early plant closures — creating a significant disincentive for shifting to cleaner energy, write Ziyi Ma, Guanying Liu and Shuang Liu from the World Resource Institute.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 US agency tips continued decline of coal generation in 2025: The Energy Information Administration (EIA), a US government agency, estimates coal generation is likely to decline by one per cent in 2025 to just 15 per cent. The EIA estimates coal generation may marginally increase by 0.3 per cent in 2026 if gas prices increase. The agency forecast solar will supply almost all of the increased electricity demand with the addition of 26,000 MW in 2025 and 22,000 MW in 2026. The agency estimates renewables will account for 25 per cent of all generation in 2025, up two per cent from 2024. The EIA states electricity consumption grew by two per cent in 2024 and will grow at that rate in each of the next two years, driven mainly by the commercial and industrial sectors. (US Energy Information Administration)

 

 Trump signs orders to boost fossil fuels: President Donald Trump has issued executive orders withdrawing from the Paris Agreement and revoking 80 Biden administration initiatives, including environmental justice policies aimed at protecting communities from disproportionate pollution. Trump declared "an energy emergency" as justification for a wide range of measures aimed at expanding fossil fuel production from public lands. One executive order directs all agency heads to review all "regulations, orders, guidance documents, policies, settlements, consent orders, and any other agency actions" that "impose an undue burden on the identification, development, or use of domestic energy resources" including coal. One order blocks the leasing of new offshore wind projects and freezes permitting and funding for onshore and offshore wind farms. (Grist, Heatmap, Utility Dive, President Donald Trump)

 

 Complaint filed over Czech lignite plant: Greenpeace, Friends of the Earth and the legal group Frank Bold have filed a complaint with the European Commission seeking an investigation into whether the continued operation of the Pocerady lignite plant violates the EU Industrial Emissions Directive. In July 2024, the Regional Court in Usti nad Labem revoked the Czech government's exemption from European Union mercury emission limits for the 1000 megawatt (MW) of lignite capacity at the plant. The plant is owned and operated by the privately owned utility, Sev.En. The court ruling required local administrative authorities to review the permit and decide on a new emissions limit. The groups said that the Usti Regional Office is still considering new emission limits and that this could drag on for months. Vaclav Prais from Frank Bold noted the failure of the Czech authorities to crack down on pollution from the plant is "a fundamental violation of European law". (Frank Bold)

 

 Namibia freezes accounts allegedly linked to South African coal mine: The Namibian High Court has frozen 10 bank accounts holding 52 million rand (US$2.8 million) that South Africa's National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) alleges include the proceeds from illegal coal mining. The NPA alleges that funds in the frozen accounts of Jacobus Jordaan, his wife and his wife's sister include the proceeds from a large-scale illegal mine operated by GNJ Mining on a private farm in Mpumalanga province. The NPA alleges GNJ Mining operated the mine and produced about 270,000 tonnes of coal between November 2021 and September 2023. The NPA estimated the coal was worth about 264 million rand (US$14.2 million). The mine at the farm operated without the authorisation of the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy or the Department of Agriculture, Rural Development, Land and Environmental Affairs. Jordaan failed on two occasions to overturn the September 2023 seizure of equipment at the farm. (News24)

 

 Report charts path for Bangladesh to meet clean air standards: A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates that if Bangladesh met the World Health Organization's 2021 air quality guideline deaths from air pollution would fall by 79 per cent or more than 81,000 lives a year. Bangladesh had the world's worst air quality in 2023. CREA says meeting the global air quality standard would eliminate almost all asthma-related emergency visits and preterm births and avoid 262 million annual sick leave days. Meeting the less strict national air quality standard would cut deaths by 19 per cent. The report says the government's recent air quality plan sets out targets for key industry sectors but that reducing reliance on coal and diesel will be critical in slashing PM2.5 fine particle pollution. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 Alberta lifts coal exploration moratorium, allows new open-cut mines: When the Alberta government announced its Coal Industry Modernization Initiative in late December, the Minister for Energy and Minerals Brian Jean said that there would be no new mountaintop removal mines, and any new mines would be underground projects or use highwall mining technology with minimal surface disturbance. However, the regulations proposed as part of the policy allow a range of conventional open-cut mining approaches, including "contour mining" and "self-contained progressive reclamation mining". Jean said the government doesn't want selenium to leach out of overburden on new mine sites and is consulting with the mining industry on the issue. Dr Bill Donahue, the former executive director of science for Alberta Environment, said he doubts the proposed techniques will make much difference. "Because when you're doing it on the side of a mountain, water flows downhill. And I don't see how that's not going to end up being a huge selenium pump," he said. Jean also rescinded three executive orders, allowing new coal exploration projects to proceed over the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains. (St Albert Gazette, CBC, Globe and Mail)

 

 Collapse of coal bunker at Indian cement plant kills 3, dozens rescued: Three workers died following the collapse of a coal hopper at the captive power plant for the Dalmia Cement plant in Rajgangpur, Odisha. Local authorities rescued sixty-four workers from the plant. Plant workers said that management had ignored requests for a structural inspection of the coal hopper. Local authorities have prohibited the company from operating the two 27 MW coal units and ordered a structural inspection of the plant. (India Today, Times of India)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 India: JSW Energy has received approval to buy KSK Mahanadi's 3600 MW Akaltara coal plant in Chhattisgarh for US$1.8 billion. The controversial plant comprises 1800 MW of operational capacity, with another 1800 MW under construction.

 

 Serbia: Elektroprivreda Srbije plans to co-fire three lignite units at its Nikola Tesla A plant with municipal waste. The three units have a combined capacity of 998 MW.

 

 Slovenia: One coal miner was killed, and two are missing after an accident at the Premogovnik Velenje lignite mine. State-owned Slovenske Elektrarne Group operates the mine and supplies lignite to the Sostanj power plant.

 

 US: Republicans have re-launched the Congressional Coal Caucus with the aim of overturning Biden administration restrictions on coal mining and power generation.

 

 US: The Utah Inland Port Authority has added the Fossil Rock mine, which is owned by Wolverine Fuels, to its development plan. The addition would allow the authority to provide funds for the development of the mine.

 

 Vietnam: Vietnamese climate activist Hoang Thi Minh Hong, who spent two years in prison, is seeking political asylum in the US. She, along with her husband and son, arrived in the US on Christmas Eve.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Russian coal exports slump: Russian coal exports fell by 17.5 million tonnes to 195 million tonnes in 2024, according to data compiled by Argus. Russian coal exports have fallen to their lowest level in six years and now stand at 13 per cent below the peak of 223.4 million tonnes in 2021. The US government has sanctioned major coal exporters SUEK and Mechel. Exporters have also been affected by transport bottlenecks caused, in part, by Russian Railways shortage of locomotives and drivers. The decline of thermal coal prices, combined with key Asian buyers avoiding Russian cargoes, has undercut the profitability of the domestic coal industry. One analyst tipped coal exports could decline to as little as 163 million tonnes in 2025. (Moscow Times [Russian])

Russian coal and steel giant restructures debt, again: Russian coal and steel producer Mechel announced it plans to delay debt repayments due in 2025-27 until 2027-2030. At the end of the first half of 2024, Mechel's debt stood at 262.5 billion rubles (US$2.6 billion). Declining coal prices, high interest rates and international sanctions undercut Mechel's finances. In August 2024, the US government expanded sanctions imposed on Russia to include a wide range of companies involved in the steel, iron, and coal sectors and firms providing specialised services to metals and mining companies. Some of the sanctioned services companies are part of the Mechel group. (Reuters)

Canadian minister flags prospect of coal plant upgrades until new nukes built: Jeremy Harrison, the Minister responsible for state-owned utilities, said the government would undertake a "very, very serious examination" of the option of upgrading three coal units at the Boundary Dam Power and two 315 MW coal units at the Poplar River Power Station. Saskatchewan's state-owned power utility, SaskPower, owns the plants. Two of the lignite-fired units at the Boundary Dam plant are scheduled to retire in 2024 and 2028, with the 110 MW Unit 3, which is fitted with a troubled carbon capture and storage unit, not expected to close until 2044. The Poplar River Power Station, comprising two coal units, is scheduled to retire in 2029 in line with the federal government's December 2018 regulations requiring all coal-fired plants in Alberta, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia to close by December 31, 2029. Harrison said extending the life of the lignite units would allow time until the construction of small modular nuclear reactors, with the first mooted for Estevan, the city adjoining the Boundary Dam and Shand lignite plants. (SaskToday)

Indian industry group urges end of levy on coal: Assocham, India's peak industry lobby group that lists Adani as one of its key members, has lobbied the Modi government to abolish a tax on coal and lignite. The levy, referred to in India as a cess, was introduced in 2010 to fund renewable energy projects. Assocham argues that the levy of 400 rupees per tonne (US$4.62 per tonne) adversely affects the competitiveness of energy-intensive industries, such as aluminium smelting. The levy was initially introduced at a rate of 50 rupees per tonne as a 'clean energy' tax to fund research and renewable energy projects. The rate increased after the election of Modi in May 2014, with funds increasingly allocated to other budget priorities. (Business Standard)

Chinese coal imports surged in 2024: Chinese coal imports increased to 542.7 million tonnes in 2024, according to customs data. Chinese imports of thermal coal were up by 13 per cent in the January to November period, with metallurgical coal imports increasing by 23 per cent over the same period. Chinese coal imports accounted for 41 per cent of the global coal trade in 2024. Coal power generation increased by 1.5 per cent in 2024, but a spike in demand in January and February "masks a very significant breakpoint" later in the year, says Lauri Myllyvirta from the Asia Society Policy Institute. Argus estimates Chinese thermal coal imports could decline marginally in 2025 as the share of coal generation declines with increasing renewables capacity. China sourced an increased volume of thermal coal from Russia and Mongolia in 2024. Argus estimates any reduction in Chinese thermal coal imports will affect smaller Indonesian suppliers initially and then Colombian and South African exporters. (Reuters, Reuters)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Analysts forecast big falls in Chinese steel production: Leading analysts estimate Chinese steel production will decline substantially from the more than one billion tonnes produced in 2024. Chinese consultancy Mysteel estimates a decline to less than 900 million tonnes by 2030, while Bloomberg Intelligence estimates production falling to below 800 million tonnes by 2030 or, in its worst-case scenario, 525 million tonnes. Overcapacity has dogged the Chinese steel industry for more than a decade, but government stimulus packages for heavy industry and the property sector propped up production. China's statistics bureau estimates the steel industry lost money for most of 2024 and by November had a total debt of 5.1 trillion yuan (US$696 billion). (South China Morning Post)

 

 Swedish steelmaker drops US clean steel project: The Swedish company SSAB has withdrawn its bid for up to US$500 million in funding from the US Department of Energy's DOE's Industrial Demonstrations Program for its proposed direct reduced iron project in Mississippi. SSAB, which is one of the partners in the Hybrit green steel project in Sweden, proposed producing direct reduced iron using green hydrogen at a plant in Perry County, Mississippi. SSAB intended to ship DRI iron from the new plant to its steel plant in Montpelier, Iowa. As part of the project, SSAB agreed with Hy Stor Energy to supply green hydrogen and renewable electricity to the DRI plant. However, Hy Stor failed to win US government funding for the project and, in late 2024, cancelled its agreement with a Norwegian electrolyser manufacturer. Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs is continuing negotiations for up to US$500 million in funding allocated under the Inflation Reduction Act, but the future of the programme is uncertain under the new Trump administration. (Canary Media)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

"The Sabin Center for Climate Change Law to Keep Tabs on Trump-led Climate Rollbacks and Anti-Science Actions Starting on Inauguration Day 2025", Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, January 2025.

The Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University has launched three online tools: the Climate Backtracker, the Inflation Reduction Act Tracker and the Silencing Science Tracker.

Steel and Coal: Global, country-, and company-level analysis of coal consumption in the steel industry, Global Efficiency Intelligence, January 2025.

This 23-page report details coking and thermal coal consumption in the global steel industry, major steel-producing countries, and leading steel manufacturing companies.
