title: CoalWire 548, January 31, 2025
excerpt: Chinese AI models burst US bubble; clean energy boom cuts Chinese, European, Australian emissions.
content:
January 31, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Just days after President Trump touted the prospect of fast-tracking approval for new power plants to support booming power demand for Artificial Intelligence (AI) projects, a Chinese tech start-up has cast a shadow over the US sector. The claim by DeepSeek that its large language models can deliver similar results at a fraction of the cost and computational power triggered significant share price falls for key US AI companies. The possibility of lower AI power demand increases uncertainty over the continued operation of old coal plants and plans for new gas and nuclear projects. Less new polluting projects could allow civil society groups a better chance of dealing with Trump's suite of environmental policy rollbacks.

While the prospects for new utility-scale renewables projects in the US are uncertain, the rapid rollout in China continues. A new analysis highlights how China's greenhouse gas emissions fell in the last 10 months of 2024. A rapid increase in solar installations across the 27 European Union countries resulted in a 22 per cent increase in solar generation in 2024. In Australia, the continued rapid growth in rooftop solar has helped drive prices lower and – together with coal unit outages – reduced greenhouse gas emissions.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Analysis: Record surge of clean energy in 2024 halts China's carbon dioxide emissions rise

A record surge of clean energy kept China's carbon dioxide emissions below the previous year's levels in the last 10 months of 2024, writes Lauri Myllyvirta from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air in Carbon Brief.

 

 Three reasons why AI's momentum could stall in 2025

There are signs that artificial intelligence (AI) momentum may wane in 2025, as doubts about the profitability of AI companies, growing energy and water constraints, and limits of computing power, writes Dambisa Moyo in Project Syndicate.

 

 Workers blow the whistle on Adani's Carmichael coal mine

Twenty-one current and former staff members have spoken out about reportedly unsafe working conditions at Adani's Carmichael coal mine in Queensland, writes Kim Paul Nguyen in SBS News.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Solar eclipsed coal generation in Europe in 2024: Data for 2024 compiled by Ember, a climate policy think tank, found that solar generated 304 terawatt-hours (TWh) or 11 per cent of European Union electricity demand, outpacing coal generation for the first time. Coal generators supplied 269 TWh or 10 per cent of EU electricity in 2024. A rapid increase in solar installations across the 27 European Union countries resulted in a 22 per cent increase in solar generation in 2024. Coal generation has declined to be the sixth largest contributor to Europe's electricity generation, while renewables contribute 47 per cent of the region's electricity in 2024. Ember estimates that in the five years of the European Union's Green New Deal, increased wind and solar generation avoided the importation of 55 million tonnes of hard coal and, combined with displaced gas imports, saved about 59 billion (US$61.4 billion) on imported fuel. (Electrek, Ember)

 

 Wales upgraded 13 coal waste dumps to higher risk categories: Freedom of Information documents obtained by BBC Cymru Fyw revealed that the Welsh government upgraded 11 coal waste dumps to the highest risk categories since November 2022. The government upgraded the sites due to the increasing frequency of extreme rainfall events. Two more coal tips were upgraded but to categories that require less frequent monitoring. The Welsh government began tracking coal tips after heavy rain in February 2020 triggered a 300 metre landslide in Tylorstown. The accident revived memories of the 1966 Aberfan disaster when a coal tip landslide killed 144 people, including 116 children at the village primary school. In December, the Welsh government introduced a bill to establish the Disused Tips Authority to manage former coal waste dumps and other tips that could threaten communities. The government has classified 360 of the 2573 coal tips as Category C and D sites that have "the potential to impact public safety". (BBC)

 

 Trump admin drops funding freeze for energy programs, for now: The Trump administration has backtracked after ordering a freeze on a wide range of energy programs until the completion of reviews to assess whether they "impose an undue burden on the identification, development, or use of domestic energy resources". The programs affected include the US Department of Agriculture's Powering Affordable Clean Energy program, which has funded clean energy projects for coal-intensive cooperatives, the Department of Energy's energy efficiency program, the Department of Labor's coal mine workers' compensation fund, and the Department of Interior's support for Tribal energy development grants and the regulation of surface coal mining. The spending freeze also applies to the Biden administration's Inflation Reduction Act and the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, including the implementation of energy tax credits. Other programs affected include the Environmental Protection Agency's environmental justice programs. After a judge granted a restraining order, the White House rescinded the Office of Management and Budget memo oredering the freeze but insisted it would press ahead with implementing the recently issued executive orders. (Heatmap, Sierra Club)

 

 Republicans scrap US environmental justice programs: An executive order by President Trump includes the revocation of a 1994 Clinton-era directive for federal US agencies to address environmental justice issues affecting minority and low-income communities and a 2023 Biden order to upgrade consideration of issues by federal agencies. Federal agencies were required to consider the disproportionate impact of pollution on minority and low-income communities, such as from coal power plants. Alice Kaswan, a law professor at the University of San Francisco, said the incorporation of environmental justice into agency regulations could be far slower to reverse. (CNN, Bloomberg, The White House)

 

 US utilities press for repeal of coal ash regulations: A coalition of ten US power utilities, including Duke Energy, Gavin Power LLC and Vistra, are pressing the new Trump administration to abandon the enforcement of the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) coal ash regulations. In a January 15 letter to Lee Zeldin, Trump's nominee to head the EPA, the utilities said they want the agency to rescind the ban on spreading coal ash on land. The letter also called for the revocation of the EPA's November 2022 order that Gavin Power LLC cease dumping coal ash into an unlined dam at the 2600 MW Gavin Power Plant in Ohio. In June 2024, the US Court of Appeals rejected two legal appeals against the regulation preventing coal ash from contacting groundwater, with one of the lawsuits relating to the Gavin plant. Gavin Power LLC is a subsidiary of Lightstone Generation, a company part-owned by the private equity firm Blackstone. The CEO of Blackstone, Stephen Schwarzman, was a major backer of Donald Trump's re-election campaign. (Canary Media)

 

 Former government insiders turned Alberta coal lobbyists: Fourteen former government officials were hired by coal companies and industry associations to lobby for changes to Alberta's coal policy, according to a review of public records by Great West Media. The former officials included retired energy and environment ministers, an executive from the Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) and staff from major political parties. In late 2024, Alberta's United Conservative Party government announced significant changes to the province's mining policy, including overturning a moratorium on new coal projects in the Eastern Slopes of the Rocky Mountains. Northback Holdings, formerly known as Benga Mining, has been prominent in its efforts to win policy changes and approval for its proposed Grassy Mountain mine. Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart owns Northback. The Alberta government's policy backflip spurred a protest by hundreds of residents outside the provincial legislature. (St Albert Gazette, CBC)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 China: The National Energy Administration estimates solar capacity increased by 24.2 per cent in 2024 to 886,670 MW. Wind capacity increased by 18 per cent in 2024.

 

 Poland: Three miners died, and 13 were injured, in a methane explosion at JSW Group's Knurow-Szczyglowice underground coal mine in Silesia.

 

 Ukraine: Since the commencement of Russian attacks on Ukraine in 2013, metallurgical coal production has plummeted by 74 per cent and coke production for the steel industry has fallen by 85 per cent.

 

 US: The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved Duke Energy spending US$70 million a year on coal gasification at its 804 MW Edwardsport plant and agreed to the three-year life extension to 2038 for Units 1 and 2 at the Gibson coal plant.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

US AI bubble punctured by Chinese start-ups efficiency claims: The sharemarket values of US AI-related companies fell dramatically after the Chinese start-up DeepSeek claimed that it had developed an open-source large language model at a fraction of the cost and computing power required for OpenAI's GPT. US power analysts, regulators and utilities have been planning a significant expansion in grid capacity to cater for the AI sector and, in some instances, the continued operation of coal and gas plants otherwise slated for closure. While DeepSeek's claimed advantages are yet to be verified, the stock of companies in the AI supply chain, including power utilities, fell dramatically. Days earlier, President Trump proposed supporting the expansion of the AI sector by fast-tracking approvals for new power plants, including "good, clean coal" projects. The International Energy Agency estimated that by 2026, AI data centres would require more electricity than the UK currently consumes. The US Energy Information Administration estimated that increased electricity demand could lead to a marginal increase in coal generation despite the growth of solar and wind generation. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, a leading energy research agency, estimates data centres accounted for about 4.4 per cent of US electricity consumption in 2023 and, before the DeepSeek announcement, suggested it could increase to between 6.7 per cent and 12 per cent of power demand. (AP, Utility Dive)

Australian coal power slumps to a record low as solar surges: The Australian Energy Market Operator's (AEMO) Quarterly Energy Dynamics report for October to December 2024 reveals that coal generation fell below 50 per cent for the first time due to record low availability of coal units and rapid growth of solar power. AEMO said rooftop solar generation increased by 18 per cent compared to the previous year to an average of 4054 MW, with record levels across the five eastern states and the Australian Capital Territory that comprise the National Electricity Market (NEM). Utility-scale solar generation also set a new record and was up nine per cent on the previous year to an average of 2212 MW. The increase in solar generation increased the frequency of negative or zero prices across the NEM. Brown coal generation in Victoria fell to a record low, declining by 9.2 per cent in the quarter compared to the previous year. Black coal generation fell by 6.5 per cent over the quarter compared to last year. As a result of increased contribution from renewables, greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector declined by 1.7 per cent ow. (Renew Economy, Australian Energy Market Operator [Pdf])

US utility pays US$19 million over role in Ohio scandal: American Electric Power, one of the largest US power utilities, agreed to pay a civil penalty of US$19 million to settle Securities and Exchange (SEC) proceedings over its role with Empowering Ohio's Economy, a non-profit group it founded and funded. In July 2020, former Republican Speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives Larry Householder and a non-profit, Generation Now, were charged with federal racketeering and conspiracy offences over a US$60 million scheme to back political candidates in return for a $1.3 billion bailout of two nuclear plants and subsidies for two coal plants. After a news report revealing AEP had contributed to Generation Now, the utility issued a media statement insisting neither it nor any of its subsidiaries "made any contributions to Generation Now" and that Empowering Ohio's Economy's contributions were for "promoting economic and business development and educational programs" in Ohio. The SEC alleged AEP failed to disclose that it had contributed a total of US$1.2 million to non-profit groups associated with Householder, including US$350,000 at the time he was using funds to win support for HB6. The SEC also stated that Empowering Ohio's contributions were "primarily made" to organisations "associated with politicians that American Electric Power wanted to support". The SEC argued that AEP's statements were misleading and that it had failed to disclose the related-party payments to investors. The Ohio legislature repealed the subsidy for the nuclear plants, but consumers continue to underwrite the two coal plants. In late January, Ohio Republicans unveiled a bill proposing to rescind the subsidy for the coal plants. (Columbus Dispatch, American Electric Power [Pdf])

Increase in South African coal exports: Coal exports from South Africa's Richards Bay Coal Terminal (RBCT) increased by 10 per cent to 52.08 million tonnes in 2024, but rail capacity constraints remain a significant bottleneck. The state-owned rail operator, Transnet, said it was aiming to carry 60 million tonnes of coal to the RBCT terminal in 2024. Transnet's operations have been affected by the theft of cabling, a lack of locomotives and difficulty obtaining spare parts. Early last year, an internal Transnet report proposed a five-year investment plan to boost capacity to 78 million tonnes a year. A consortium of coal exporters owns RBCT. (Reuters)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Report reveals 160 companies planning 250 new met coal projects: Urgewald and 10 NGO partners, including Global Energy Monitor, have released the first Metallurgical Coal Exit List that identifies 160 companies planning 250 new metallurgical coal projects in 18 countries. Urgewald estimates that the projects could produce up to 551 million tonnes of metallurgical coal, expanding production by half. Most of the projects are in Australia, Russia and China. The largest corporate metallurgical coal developers are Russian billionaire Albert Avdolyan's A-Property, Coal India and BMA, a joint venture between BHP and Mitsubishi. The projects under consideration by the three companies could add up to 118 million tonnes of metallurgical coal production a year. Lia Wagner from Urgewald described the failure of most financial institutions to address metallurgical coal in their climate policies as a "gigantic blind spot". (Mining.com, Urgewald)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Rate of return equals cost of capital: a simple, fair formula to stop investor-owned utilities from overcharging the public, American Economic Liberties Project, January 2025. (Pdf)

This 23-page paper investigates excessive US utility rates of return allowed by utility commissions in setting customer prices.

links.text: Rate of return equals cost of capital: a simple, fair formula to stop investor-owned utilities from overcharging the public

title: CoalWire 549, February 6, 2025
excerpt: Trump casts shadow over international 'just transition’ plans; China imposes tariffs on US coal.
content:
February 6, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The blizzard of decisions by President Trump and Elon Musk has cast a shadow over both the domestic energy transition and US support for Just Energy Transition Partnerships (JETP) for Indonesia, South Africa and potentially Vietnam. The decision by the US to end its role as co-lead of the Indonesian JETP leaves Germany to head the project. Germanys ongoing support for the project is contingent on the outcome of the February 23 national election. Musk has backed a far-right party that opposes action on climate change. China has responded to Trump's imposition of tariffs on Chinese products by levying retaliatory tariffs on US coal imports.

The unveiling of Deepseek's reportedly energy-efficient AI model poses questions for countries and utilities assuming significant increases in electricity demand for new data centres. In mid-December, Japan released its draft energy plan assuming electricity demand growth of between 12 per cent and 22 per cent by 2040 compared to 2023, mainly due to data centres and semiconductor manufacturing. In the US state of Georgia, a subsidiary of Southern Company has proposed delaying the closure of several coal plants due to rapid load growth, again in part due to estimates of future data centre demand. The cost of sticking with what could turn out to be significant overestimates of electricity demand could be high and suggests careful reassessment is warranted.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Japan's draft energy plan fails to meet the clean energy transition imperative

Japan's recent draft of its energy plan fails to make the most of the country's renewables potential, putting the country off track for decarbonising its power sector, write Hanna Hakko and Yoko Mulholland in E3G.

 

 Texas's largest coal plant is right outside Houston. Now, the community wants it out

Nearly 400,000 people live within 12 miles (19 kilometres) of NRG Energy's 3953-megawatt (MW) W.A. Parish Generating Station. Pollution from the largest coal plant in the state has residents worried, writes Janet Miranda in the Houston Chronicle.

 

 Navigating a just transition for China's coal regions

During the transition away from coal, Chinese cities struggle with selecting new industries, overcoming talent shortages, coping with infrastructure deficiencies, and fierce competition from neighbouring cities, all of which can hinder the development of alternative industries, write Yingxia Yang, Wenjuan Dong, and Jiejie Hui in the Just Energy Transition in Coal Regions Knowledge Hub.

 

 Nature and people shouldn't be designated losers in the energy transition

If you are worried about climate impacts, you should worry about how to ensure the growth of wind and solar doesn't occur in a self-sabotaging and destructive way, writes Ketan Joshi, an energy and communications consultant.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Judge extends injunction on Trump administration spending freeze: Court rulings have temporarily suspended the Trump administration's freeze on payments under federal contracts. On January 31, US federal judge John McConnell in Rhode Island issued a restraining order on the freeze, but this only applied to recipients in the 22 Democratic states and Washington DC that sought the order. In Washington DC, District Court Judge Loren L. AliKhan extended an earlier injunction she granted blocking the Trump administration from suspending payments. Despite the court orders, states and non-profit groups reported that contracted funding from the Environmental Protection Agency remained frozen. Project developers, construction groups and unions are also alarmed about the potential impact on projects approved under the Inflation Reduction Act and Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. Days after Trump's inauguration, the acting secretary of the US Department of Energy, Ingrid Kolb ordered all work cease on projects that required community benefit plans. The requirement for the plans was a Biden initiative to ensure host communities gained from contracts and as an environmental justice measure. (Engineering News-Record, Heatmap)

 

 US ends role as co-leader of Indonesia's just transition project: The secretariat for the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) for Indonesia has confirmed that the US has withdrawn as co-leader of the project. The Secretary General of the JETP Indonesia Secretariat, Paul Butarbutar, said the US would remain a participant in the US$21.6 billion project aimed at retiring coal capacity and transitioning to renewables. The exit of the US leaves Germany to head the project. The project, which was announced in December 2021, aimed to provide US$11.6 billion from public agencies of the International Partners Group of countries including the US, Japan, Germany and the European Union. Late last week, Hashim Djojohadikusumo, the special presidential envoy on environment and climate and the brother of President Prabowo Subianto, said "I think we shouldn't expect the US$20 billion". The US is the largest funder in both the JETP's with Indonesia and Vietnam. Uncertainty about the funding has increased since President Trump anointed Tesla CEO Elon Musk to seize control of the US Treasury's payments system where he has pledged to terminate contract payments to cut costs. Germany's support for the JETP is likely to hinge on the outcome of the election on February 23 2025. Musk is actively backing the Alternative for Germany (Afd), a far-right party that is currently running second in opinion polls. The AfD's platform for the 2024 European Union election described climate change as "Co2 hysterics" and stated it wanted to "abolish all climate laws". Analysts suggest that if the US cancels its support for the project, Indonesia is likely to turn to countries such as Japan, South Korea and China. (Jakarta Post [paywall], Financial Times, The Business Times [paywall])

 

 Trump freezes all funding to South Africa: President Donald Trump announced a freeze on all future funding for South Africa until the completion of a "full investigation" of the South African government's support for land reallocation. His comments came as Elon Musk, who has the backing of Trump, said he plans to shut down USAid, the US government's international aid agency. Musk lived in South Africa before migrating to the US and has criticised South African government polices. The South African government said Trump misunderstands the recently passed legislation allowing expropriation of land without compensation in certain circumstances, including unused state-owned land and abandoned properties. The government has not expropriated any land under the new law. While neither Trump nor Musk has mentioned the US$9.3-billion Just Energy Transition Partnership announced in December 2021 to support South Africa's transition to clean energy, there are doubts the US will continue to support it. Trump has vowed to support fossil fuels and announced the withdrawal of the US from the Paris Agreement. (Guardian, News24, News24)

 

 Whistleblower reveals appalling working conditions at Eskom plant: A whistleblower has submitted a detailed report to the Special Investigating Unit, the South African government's specialist anti-corruption agency, revealing appalling working conditions at Eskom's 4116 MW Kendal coal plant. The whistleblower disclosed pictures and video taken inside the plant revealing deep coal ash deposits enveloping vehicles within hours. The whistleblower also alleged contractors were injured falling into ash-covered maintenance holes and trenches. The report also alleged that a contractor died when working on the 686 MW Unit 5, and another man suffered serious burns from hot ash. Eskom did not confirm or deny the reported death but confirmed the ash stacker "had been out of operation for several months" but was now repaired and working. News24 reported that some of the videos were from December 2024 and January 2025, appearing to contradict Eskom's claim that the conditions improved after the repair of the coal ash stacker and the appointment of a new power station manager. (News24)

 

 Smog blankets Balkan cities as slow energy transition hits residents: Cities across the Balkans have endured extreme levels of smog due to a heavy reliance on coal power plants, diesel vehicles and the extensive use of wood and coal for home heating. Wintertime air pollution in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, ranks alongside New Delhi and Lahore. In Sofia, Bulgaria's capital, and the nearby city of Plovdiv, PM2.5 fine particle pollution levels recently reached three times the World Health Organization's (WHO) recommended limit. The WHO recommended PM2.5 limit is 15 micrograms per cubic metre (g/m3) over 24 hours and 5 g/m3 averaged over a year. On January 22, public officials warned residents of Sarajevo, Bosnia & Herzegovina's capital, to remain indoors as PM2.5 levels hit 208.9g/m3. In North Macedonia, Skopje briefly ranked as the world's most polluted city, with PM2.5 fine particle pollution levels 37.7 times higher than the WHO guidelines. Civil society groups want Balkan countries to accelerate the conversion of coal power plants to renewables, increase the energy efficiency standards of housing and convert home heating to heat pumps. (BNEIntellinews)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Nature Conservation Council has called on the New South Wales government to reject Wollongong Coal's proposal to discharge up to 42 million litres of wastewater a day into Sydney's water supply catchment.

 

 Canada: A study board established by the International Joint Commission has proposed four technical working groups to build a "common understanding" of the pollution from coal mines in the Elk and Kootenay rivers in British Columbia.

 

 US: Appalachian Voices has requested the Environmental Protection Agency regulate coal dust emissions from trains that contaminate waterways and contribute to air pollution.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

US exits climate risk body; China imposes tariffs on US coal: In further fallout from the election of President Trump, the US Treasury Department announced it is terminating its membership of the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System, a global body of 113 central banks and financial supervisors collaborating to improve environmental and climate risk management in the financial sector. Trump's decision to enact a 10 per cent tariff on all imports from China has triggered retaliatory measures. China's Ministry of Finance announced 15 per cent tariffs on imports of US coal and liquefied natural gas, along with other measures. The investment bank Citi estimates that China imported about 3.4 million tonnes of thermal coal and 10.7 million tonnes of metallurgical coal from the US in 2024. US thermal coal accounted for only 0.8 per cent of Chinese imported coal in 2024. The US supplied nine per cent of Chinese metallurgical coal imports in 2024. (Reuters, Investing.com)

US utility cites data centre growth in a move to delay coal retirements: Georgia Power's draft integrated resource plan filed with the Georgia Public Service Commission proposes extending the life of old coal and gas plants to meet its estimated electricity load growth of 8200 MW by 2030. The utility, a subsidiary of Southern Company, increased its estimate of peak electricity demand in 2030 by 2200 MW on its 2023 plan. The utility attributes much of the seven per cent annual load growth to the expansion of energy-intensive manufacturing and the technology sector, including data centres, electric vehicles, battery production and solar panels. The utility plans to invest in 1400 MW of new gas and oil units at its Yates plant and 665 MW of battery capacity by 2027. The utility previously planned on retiring the 891 MW coal-fired Unit 3 at Plant Scherer and converting a 952 MW coal unit at Plant Gaston to run on gas by December 31, 2028. The utility now proposes operating the Gaston unit through to the end of 2034 and the units at Plant Bowen and Plant Scherer through to the end of 2038, with environmental compliance upgrades. However, the election of President Trump introduces significant uncertainty about the future of the Environmental Protection Agency's pollution regulations. (AP, Georgia Power)

Banks lagging on climate lending: A BloombergNEF analysis of lending by about 1000 banks found increased funding of clean energy projects in 2023 but was still well short of the level required to reach the Paris Agreement goal of a 1.5-degree temperature increase. BNEF estimates reached 89 per cent of that for fossil fuels in 2023. BNEF found that coal projects attracted 18 per cent of fossil fuel finance, a level it estimates is three times higher than required to reach the Paris Agreement goal. The consultancy estimated that Chinese banks accounted for about 66 per cent of the US$94 billion of coal finance in 2023. Of the top 10 banks reviewed, BNEF estimates BNP Paribas performed best in supporting clean energy projects compared to fossil fuel developments. (Bloomberg, BNEF, BNEF [Pdf)])

New Chinese AI model poses challenge to Japan's draft energy plan: Japan's draft energy plan released in mid-December abandoned the previous forecast of declining electricity demand and projected an increase of between 12 per cent and 22 per cent by 2040 compared to 2023. The draft plan attributed the change mainly to increased electricity demand for data centres and semiconductor manufacturing. However, the recent release of an allegedly more energy-efficient AI tool by the Chinese tech start-up Deepseek has prompted some analysts to suggest a review of the assumptions in the draft energy plan. Professor Andrew DeWit from Rikkyo University's School of Economic Policy Studies said it would be risky not to consider a lower impact on power demand for the AI sector, especially after the development of overcapacity in the 1980s and early 1990s. The draft energy plan proposes no timetable for the phasing out of coal plants. The government plans to finalise the draft plan in early 2025. (Reuters)

Pakistan province pitches for Siemens to invest in lignite gasification: A delegation of three executives from Siemens Energy reportedly expressed interest in investing in a proposed 350MW solar-wind hybrid project as well as the development of Thar lignite. The three executives met with Syed Nasir Hussain Shah, the Minister for Energy, Development, and Planning for Sindh province. Sindh province has partly developed massive lignite mines and power projects to the alarm of residents and civil society groups. Shah promoted the potential of coal gasification in Thar province to the Siemens executives. (The News International, Engineering Post)

Australian utility fined over generator explosion that triggered blackouts: A federal court judge has ruled in favour of the Australian Energy Regulator and fined Callide Power Trading A$9 million (US$5.6 million) for breaching national energy market rules and meeting performance standards after an explosion at CS Energy's 848 MW Callide C coal plant in May 2021 triggered blackouts. Justice Roger Derrington found that the incident resulted in "the destruction of valuable equipment, the potential for loss of life, loss of power to the grid, and significant, long-term and wide-ranging impacts on the National Electricity Market". A 302-page investigation report released in July 2024 revealed a chain of errors that resulted in the catastrophic failure of the rotor shaft and the destruction of the generator. The explosion threw a two-tonne section of the shaft five metres across the turbine hall and blasted a 300 kg piece of equipment 20 metres up through the roof of the plant. No one was injured. The report described state-owned CS Energy, a utility wholly owned by the Queensland state government, as an organisation that "did not value or practise effective process safety". (ABC, Federal Court of Australia)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

title: CoalWire 550, February 13, 2025
excerpt: BNEF says new solar, wind beat new coal almost everywhere; First Nation opposes new Alberta mines.
content:
February 13, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The latest estimates of the cost of electricity from new renewables point to the rapid pace of change in the sector in 2024: a dramatic fall in the cost of batteries and significant declines in the costs of power from onshore and offshore wind. The consultancy tips the cost of power from wind and solar is likely to fall by a further 25 per cent or so over the next decade.

In the US, the Trump administration's move to freeze funding has thrown a shadow over many announced energy transition projects, mainly in Republican districts. While two judges directed an end to the funding freeze, reports indicate that some agencies aren't yet complying with the court orders. Irrespective of Trump's directives, a key factor affecting the retirement of the remaining US coal units is likely electricity demand for data centres. A new report argues that flexible management of power centre demand could avoid over-investment in new power plants and transmission lines.

In Canada, the Chief and Council of the Kainai Nation, also known as the Blood Tribe, announced their opposition to new coal developments on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains in Alberta. In India, the government is pressing ahead with subsidies for coal gasification projects, a sector that is also expanding in China and Indonesia.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Coal gasification, an old technology, is quietly expanding across Asia

Despite the environmental and human rights impacts, India, Indonesia and China are pushing ahead with coal gasification plans, writes Nithin Coca in Mongabay.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 First Nation opposes new Alberta coal developments: The Chief and Council of the Kainai Nation, also known as the Blood Tribe, announced their opposition to further coal developments on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains in Alberta. The Kainai Nation, which is one of three nations in the Blackfoot Confederacy, said the government had not consulted with the groups in a meaningful way before announcing the lifting of the moratorium on coal developments on the Eastern Slopes. The Ranchland municipal district announced it had abandoned its legal challenge against exploration applications for the Grassy Mountain coal project due to the government's new policy. Ranchland chief executive Ron Davis said the government's decision to lift the moratorium on exploration undercut its legal arguments. Chelsae Petrovic, the United Conservative Party MP for the electorate that includes the proposed Crowsnest Pass mine, said she had cancelled further public forums after constituents raised concerns about her support for new coal projects. (Global News, CBC, CBC)

 

 Trump freezes US Department of Justice bribery prosecutions: An executive order by President Donald Trump directing the US Department of Justice (DOJ) to suspend prosecutions under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act could benefit the Adani Group, at least in the short term. The executive order stated that enforcing the law against US citizens and businesses "for routine business practices in other nations actively harms American economic competitiveness and, therefore, national security". The order directed US Attorney General Pam Bondi to review "in detail" all existing investigations and enforcement actions within 180 days and issue updated guidance on the future implementation of the act. In October 2024, the DOJ announced it was seeking the arrest of Indian billionaire Gautam Adani and his nephew Sagar Adani over an alleged $US265 million in bribes paid between 2020 and 2024 to Indian officials to win above-cost power purchase agreements for solar projects in India. The DOJ indictment also identified five other Adani executives. In September 2015, Hitachi reached a US$19 million agreement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission to settle charges brought under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act over alleged bribes paid to secure a contract for boilers at the new Kusile and Medupi coal plants in South Africa. (Indian Express, The White House)

 

 US coal retirements hinge more on politics than economics: An analysis of Global Energy Monitor data by the New York Times found that of the almost 400 US coal power station units remaining, about half have retirement deadlines scheduled. It also found that between 2017 and 2025, about one-third of scheduled retirement dates have been pushed back or cancelled. Power utilities argue that a rapid increase in electricity demand growth, especially for data centres and electric vehicles, is a significant factor in delaying coal plant retirements. The American Coal Council, a coal industry lobby group, said the prospect that the Trump administration may roll back coal plant regulations may allow old plants to operate longer. Michelle Solomon from Energy Innovation, a clean energy group, said that even without allowing for the incentives included in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, "we're far past the crossover point for most coal plants". (New York Times [paywall])

 

 Study finds nitrogen dioxide emissions hits Indian crop production: A study found that nitrogen dioxide emissions from Indian coal power plants reduced wheat and rice crop yield by between 5 per cent and 10 per cent within a 100-kilometre radius. The study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that in the most heavily polluted parts of West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh, crop losses due to nitrogen dioxide emissions exceeded 10 per cent. The study by a PhD student at Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability examined nitrogen dioxide emissions from 144 coal plants between 2011 and 2020 and mapped the likely effect on wheat and rice growing areas. The study assessed which plants it would be best to retire early if a cap of 10 per cent of coal generation was used. The study found that power stations in Punjab and Haryana had the most significant impacts on crops, while projects in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, and Gujarat had the highest health impacts. The study estimated the benefit of the early closure of these plants at US$2.02 billion per year. The author emphasised that he did not assess the impact on crop productivity from other air pollutants or factors such as additional water stress and heavy metal contamination. (New Indian Express, Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences)

 

 Chinese coal ship runs aground in Russia: The An Yang 2, a Chinese bulk carrier loaded with 1000 tonnes of coal, ran aground on February 8 on rocky shore reefs on the western shore of Sakhalin island in Russia. The crew of 20 are safe and local emergency authorities are planning on pumping 1000 tonnes of fuel oil off the ship when the storm abates. (Maritime Executive, AP)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Ukraine: The Ukrainian steel industry faces an uncertain future after advancing Russian military forces forced the closure of the country's last coking coal mine in Pokrovsk. Continued operation of the steel industry would require the importation of about 7.5 million metric tonnes of coking coal.

 

 US: President Trump announced a 25 per cent tariff on all imported steel and aluminium to take effect on March 4. The largest steel exporters to the US are Canada, Brazil, Mexico and South Korea. Canada accounted for about 80 per cent of the primary aluminium imported by the US in 2024.

 

 US: The governor of Puerto Rico Governor has filed a bill to scrap the territory's renewable energy target and extend the life of AES Puerto Rico's 510 MW coal plant in Guayama.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Consultancy tips new wind and solar cheaper than new coal: BloombergNEF (BNEF) estimates that electricity from new wind and solar projects are cheaper than new coal and gas plants "in almost every market globally". BNEF estimates the levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) from onshore wind could decline to US$37 per megawatt-hour (MWh) in 2025, with offshore wind falling nine per cent to US$79 MWh and fixed-axis solar by two per cent to US$35 MWh. The consultancy estimates that lower-than-anticipated electric car demand has resulted in a glut of batteries, driving the costs of battery storage down by one-third in 2024 to US$104 per MWh and could fall below US$100 per MWh this year. The consultancy forecasts that between 2025 and 2035, the cost of electricity from solar, onshore wind, offshore wind and batteries could decline by 28.6 per cent, 24.3 per cent, 15.2 per cent and 43 per cent, respectively. (BloombergNEF)

Poland set to unveil coal utilities spin-off plan: The Polish Ministry of State Assets will outline to parliament on February 13 its plan to spin off coal projects from state-owned power utilities. The previous conservative government proposed spinning off coal assets to a taxpayer-owned entity to allow power utilities to attract International finance for renewable projects. The coalition government elected in October 2023 shelved that plan to allow time to canvass other options. In November 2024, the government unveiled its National Energy and Climate Plan for 2030-2040, which included the aim of reducing coal generation from its 60 per cent share in 2023 to 22.5 per cent in 2030. Two key drivers in the need for the transformation are the carbon price, which is currently 82.95 per tonne (US$85.4 per tonne), and the European Union's 'Fit for 55' commitment to cut greenhouse gas emissions in 2030 to 55 per cent below 1990 levels. In a separate development, the CEZ Group, a privately owned Czech company, has finalised the sale of two hard coal power plants in Poland – the 330 MW Skawina plant and the 238 MW Chrzow power station – to ResInvest Group. CEZ first announced plans to sell the plants in 2020. (BNE IntelliNews, CEZ Group)

Trump freeze on energy projects hits Republican districts hardest: Despite two court orders directing an end to the suspension of grant payments imposed by the Trump administration on legislated energy programs, the New York Times and ProPublica report the funding freeze remains in place at several agencies, including the Department of Energy. Atlas Public Policy, a clean energy consultancy, estimates that tax incentives, loans and grants in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) have spurred plans for US$165.8 billion investment in plans for solar panel manufacturing, wind power technology, the supply chain for electric vehicles and other clean energy projects. It estimates that 80 per cent of the projects are in Republican congressional districts. Despite this, the Republican leadership is considering repealing the IRA legislation and has remained mute on the impact of the funding freeze. (New York Times [paywall]), ProPublica)

Indian ministry announces coal gasification subsidies: India's Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs has approved the establishment of a US$980 million scheme to subsidise coal gasification for both public and private sector companies. The Ministry of Coal has established a target of processing 100 million tonnes of coal a year for coal gasification and selected Coal India and Bharat Heavy Electricals as the winners in the public sector category. In the private sector category, the ministry selected Jindal Steel and Power, New Era Cleantech Solution and Greta Energy to receive funding. New Era Cleantech Solution has proposed a coal gasification project in Maharashtra requiring five million tonnes of coal a year. (PSU Watch, Deccan Herald)

Vietnamese thermal coal imports soared in 2024: Vietnam's thermal coal imports increased by 31 per cent to 44 million tonnes in 2024 compared to the year before. Data from Ember indicates that Vietnam's electricity consumption grew by 27 per cent between 2018 to 2023. According to Global Energy Monitor's Global Coal Plant Tracker, Vietnam's current coal capacity is 27,239 MW, with a further 4000 MW currently under construction. The imposition of tariffs on Chinese products in the first term of President Trump spurred the relocation of manufacturing capacity to Vietnam, leading to a surge in electricity demand. Vietnam's Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade, Nguyen Hoang Long, emphasised that the ministry has carriage of the Just Energy Transition Partnership announced in November 2021 and the Asia Zero Emissions Community Initiative announced in January 2022 with the Japanese government. The minister emphasised that Vietnam plans to cease the development of new coal plants after 2030, convert existing plants to biomass and ammonia after they have been in operation for 20 years and cease operating plants over 40 years old if conversion is not possible. (Reuters, Vietnam.Vn)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 South Korean car maker challenged over dirty steel supply chain: A coalition of international NGOs has challenged the South Korean carmaker Hyundai to clean up its global steel supply chain. A report by Mighty Earth and a dozen other NGOs, Tainted Steel, reviewed shipments from 196 steel suppliers to Hyundai, including some embroiled in controversy over labour and environmental standards. The report noted that Formosa Ha Tinh Steel Corporation, a Vietnamese steel producer that supplies Hyundai, was responsible for a devastating toxic chemical spill in 2016. Formosa bought US$450M worth of Russian coking coal between 2022 and 2024 from mines connected to JSC Stroiservis, a company sanctioned by the US government after the invasion of Ukraine. The report also found that Hyuandai also sourced metallurgical coal from BHP Mitsubishi Alliance's Saraji mine, a project with significant methane emissions, and thermal coal from Glencore's controversial Cerrejon mine in Colombia. The groups called on Hyundai to develop and implement a new due diligence system to ensure its supply chain met the highest human rights, labour and environmental standards. (Mighty Earth, Mighty Earth [Pdf])

 

 GFG coal mine mothballed as clean steel ambitions stall: Hundreds of workers at Tahmoor Coal, an underground metallurgical coal mine south of Sydney, have been stood down for four weeks after suppliers ended deliveries over unpaid debts. Tahmoor Coal is part of the sprawling GFG Alliance that is privately owned by British billionaire Sanjeev Gupta. The GFG Alliance emerged as a significant global steel producer after Gupta's Liberty Steel bought struggling steel mills around the world and sought government funding to transform them into producers of 'green steel' using renewables-based hydrogen. Liberty also bought the Whyalla steel plant in South Australia and an associated iron ore mine, but the project is currently unable to pay its debts, owing the state government tens of millions in unpaid royalties, with a further A$15 million (US$9.4 million) due to SA Water, the state-owned water utility. Liberty Steel plans to close or sell plants in the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary, Belgium, Luxembourg and Italy. Subsidiaries in the UK and the US have also been affected by uncertainty over the viability of the parent company. The GFG Alliance has struggled to pay mounting debts after the collapse in 2021 of Greensill, the company's leading financier. GFG Alliance or its subsidiaries are the target of a raft of legal actions in the UK courts seeking repayments of about US$973 million. (ABC News, ABC News)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Rethinking load growth: assessing the potential for integration of large flexible loads in US power systems, Duke University Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability, February 2025. (Pdf)

This 43-page study argues that far greater flexibility is possible to cater for electricity demand growth, especially for data centres, but without premature investment in additional power plants and transmission lines.

title: CoalWire 551, February 20, 2025
excerpt: Poll indicates opposition to Alberta coal projects; Bangladesh requests Adani lower coal price.
content:
February 20, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

As the conservative Alberta government pushes ahead with new coal projects, an opinion poll by local landowner groups suggests widespread concern about new coal mines. In the UK, documents obtained under the Freedom of Information Act reveal that Adani paid about US$5 million to sponsor a Science Museum exhibition. In Bangladesh, the government has requested Adani lower the cost of coal used in its calculations for the price of electricity exported from its Godda plant in India.

While US courts have attempted to stay some Trump administration decisions, such as cancelling funding approved by Congress, cuts to federal agency staff levels are gathering pace. In the same week that the new administration mistakenly sacked crucial nuclear weapons staff and bird flu experts, 200 positions were axed at the Bonneville Power Administration, including power dispatchers and transmission schedulers. Needless to say, those responsible for ensuring the stability of the Pacific NorthWest grid are alarmed. In Kentucky, Republican legislators are pushing ahead with a bill that would remove the headwaters of streams and groundwater from all state pollution control regulations, a change that will benefit coal mining companies and power utilities.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Sustainable economic growth in South Africa will come from renewables, not coal: what our model shows

When people think about moving away from coal, they worry about job losses in the coal industry. But historically, energy transitions have never been instant. African countries that embraced the change early on reaped the benefits. They became more industrialised and prosperous, writes Andrew Phiri, an Associate Professor of Economics at Nelson Mandela University, in The Conversation.

 

 Indian power giants' decade-long lobbying battle that stalled crucial pollution standards

The Modi government repeatedly pushed back the deadline since 2015 for coal-fired power plants to install devices for curbing noxious emissions after power producers lobbied the government, writes Shreegireesh Jalihal in The Reporters' Collective.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Opinion poll finds little support for coal exploration in Alberta's Rockies: An opinion poll of 1000 residents of Alberta found that only 23 per cent supported coal exploration on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains in Alberta, with 77 per cent agreeing with a statement that the environmental risks associated outweigh the economic benefits of coal mining. The poll was commissioned by two landowners groups, the Pekisko Group and the Livingstone Landowners Group, and undertaken by Leger, a major Canadian opinion polling company. The survey found that 55 per cent of respondents were unaware that coal exploration is now possible on the eastern slopes. Seventy-seven per cent of respondents expressed concern about possible selenium contamination in the watershed and 70 per cent were concerned with coal dust carrying downwind from the mine sites. The Alberta government imposed a moratorium on new mining projects in 1976, but this policy was abandoned in mid-January by the United Conservative Party government after lobbying by the coal industry. (GlobalNews)

 

 China's coal plant construction accelerated in 2024: A report by Global Energy Monitor (GEM) and the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates China began construction on 94,500 megwatts (MW) of new coal plants in 2024 and resumed building 3300 MW of suspended projects. The surge of new coal plant construction comes despite President Xi Jinping's commitment to "strictly" limit the growth of coal consumption in the five years to 2026. While new project proposals fell to 68,900 MW in 2024, the retirement of old coal plants declined to just 2500 MW in 2024, down from 13,000 MW in 2020. CREA and GEM argue that more than three-quarters of new projects are funded by coal mining companies or diversified energy utilities with coal mining arms. The rapid growth of coal capacity could drive increased curtailment of wind and solar generation, with regional power grids prioritising coal generation and the provincial government backing away from requiring that new power purchase agreements include a minimum share of solar and wind generation. China accounted for 93 per cent of all new coal plant construction commenced in 2024. (Carbon Brief, Global Energy Monitor/Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 Documents reveal Adani paid US$5 million for Science Museum exhibit: UK Cabinet Office documents reveal that Adani Green Energy agreed to pay 4 million (US$5 million) in October 2021 for a multi-year agreement to sponsor the Science Museum's power exhibition Energy Revolution: The Adani Green Energy Gallery. The exhibition opened in late 2024. The Cabinet Office released the documents in response to a Freedom of Information request by Culture Unstained, a group campaigning to end fossil fuel sponsorships. The records reveal that on the day that Gautam Adani signed the funding agreement with the Science Museum, he met then-Prime Minister Boris Johnston. A briefing note for Johnston suggested the UK government wanted to establish closer ties with the company but flagged, in an oblique reference to the company's role as the largest private developer of coal mines, that Adani's "natural resources business remains a challenge". At another meeting between the two in India in 2022, Adani said the company wanted to become the "BAE of India". (BAE is the largest defence contractor in Europe.) In October 2024, the Science Museum's chief executive, Sir Ian Blatchford, rejected calls to cancel Adani's sponsorship after the US Department of Justice (DOJ) sought the arrest of Gautam Adani and charged other executives over an alleged kickback scandal in India. The DOJ alleged that between 2020 and 2024, Adani companies paid $US265 million in bribes to Indian officials to win above-cost power purchase agreements for solar projects. Adani described the DOJ claims as "baseless". (Financial Times, Culture Unstained)

 

 Global coal lobby group establishes Southern African branch: FutureCoal, the coal industry lobby group previously known as the World Coal Association, has established a Southern Africa branch for coal producers in South Africa, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Botswana. Mike Teke, the CEO of Seriti Resources Group, is chair of the new group. Seriti Resources operates six thermal coal mines supplying Eskom's Kriel, Tutuka, Lethabo, Kendal and Duvha coal plants as well as exporting to the global market. FutureCoal stated that the new chapter has 13 inaugural members but does not identify them. (FutureCoal)

 

 Kentucky Senate backs looser coal water pollution standards: The Republican-dominated Kentucky Senate voted 30-to-5 to dramatically weaken water pollution standards, a change that would benefit the coal mining industry and power utilities. Republican member Senator Scott Madon's bill, which has yet to be voted on by the House of Representatives, redefines "protected waters" to exclude groundwater and "ephemeral headwater" streams. The Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet currently has responsibility for protecting all waterways in the state, with Madon accusing the agency of "unwarranted governmental overreach". The Kentucky Resources Council, an NGO, notes that more than 1.9 million residents rely on groundwater for their drinking water from public water utilities or their wells. The group also stated that the bill would remove the regulation of discharging pollutants into headwater streams and end the ability of the state's environmental agency to require permits, sampling or reporting of pollution in order to protect downstream water quality. Madon presented his bill to the Senate alongside representatives of the Kentucky Coal Association, an industry lobby group that represents companies including Alliance Coal and Blackhawk Mining. (Lexington Herald-Leader, Louisville Public Media, Kentucky Resources Council [Pdf])

 

 Drone surveys find illegal coal mining continuing in India state: Justice B.P. Katakey, who the High Court of Meghalaya appointed to investigate allegations of illicit coal mining, reported that drone surveys of illegal mines revealed increased coal stockpiles in six coal districts of the state. The unlawful mines, referred to as 'rat hole' mines, were banned by the National Green Tribunal in 2014 after civil society groups alleged environmental damage and labour exploitation. However, the court allowed the transportation of already mined coal. Katakey's most recent report to the court, noted the discrepancies between the amount of coal seized and government submissions to the court on stockpiles demonstrated illegal mining continued. Katakey recommended continued drone surveillance and ground patrols. (The Hindu)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Afghanistan: Three workers died in a methane gas explosion at a coal mine in Dara-e-Suf Bala district in Samangan province.

 

 Australia: Rooftop solar drove electricity demand to a record low of 2532 MW on February 16, about 484 MW lower than the record set in October 2024. Rooftop solar supplied 60 per cent of NSW electricity demand, a new record.

 

 Australia: The Mining and Energy Union (MEU) has launched an independent investigation into the cause of the methane explosion that has shut down the Grosvenor underground mine since June 2024. Anglo American wants to re-enter the mine this year, but the MEU has yet to decide its position.

 

 India: Adani has secured A$330 million (US$207 million) in loans from King Street Capital Management and Sona Asset Management for its North Queensland Export Terminal. Bravus Australia, a subsidiary of the Adani Group, exports coal from the Carmichael mine via the terminal.

 

 India: Thousands of Indigenous residents protested against the auction of the Namchik coal mining projects in Changlang district in Assam.

 

 Mongolia: China agreed to a new cross-border rail link that will increase Mongolia's coal export capacity by 30 million tonnes a year. Mongolia aims to export 100 million tonnes of coal to China in 2025.

 

 Philippines: Energy Secretary Raphael Lotilla is considering a possible extension of the 232 MW Mindanao Steag coal plant to allow for the rehabilitation of the Agus and Pulangi hydro projects. The coal plant is 85 per cent owned by Aboitiz Power Corporation, a part of the conglomerate owned by the billionaire Sabin Aboitiz and his family.

 

 Sri Lanka: The government has approved the establishment of a coal testing laboratory as part of the Industrial Technology Institute in a bid to cut testing costs.

 

 US: Appalachian Voices expressed alarm that the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection could release Keystone West Virginia from its obligation to treat ongoing acid mine drainage originating at the KD #1 Surface Mine.

 

 US: The Nature Conservancy, Sun Tribe Development and ENGIE announced plans to establish 14 solar energy projects and three battery projects on 17 former coal mine sites in Virginia, Tennessee and Kentucky.

 

 US: The Trump administration has suspended funding for state-based Abandoned Mine Lands rehabilitation programs authorised under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The program includes funding for coal mine clean-ups in Appalachia, West Virginia, Ohio and Virginia.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Study finds social costs of carbon capture are far higher than an all-renewables scenario: A study published in Environmental Science and Technology found that an energy strategy that relies on carbon capture and storage and direct air carbon capture results in higher energy costs, public health impacts, and greenhouse gas emissions. The study compared a strategy of transition to wind, water and solar with a scenario that prioritised fossil fuels, renewables, biomass and nuclear along with carbon capture technologies. The study evaluated the two scenarios across 149 countries through to 2050. Both scenarios assumed equal rates of energy efficiency gains, though the all-renewables strategy assumed reduced energy demand through increased public transit, telecommuting and active transport such as cycling. The study found that the all-renewables strategy reduced end-use energy requirements by 54.4 per cent, lowered energy costs by almost 59.6 per cent and avoided five million deaths and hundreds of millions of illnesses a year. The study estimated the scenario relying on high utilisation of carbon capture and storage would have a social cost between 9.1 and 12.1 times higher than the all-renewable scenario. The authors argued that while the all-renewables scenario is extreme, carbon capture increases emissions and social costs and governments should scrap policies promoting reliance on the technologies. (Clean Technica, Stanford University, Environmental Science & Technology)

Bandgalesh requests Adani lower coal import price: Bangladesh's Power Development Board (PDB) has verbally requested the Adani Group lower the coal price used to calculate the electricity cost for sales from the 1600 MW Godda plant in Jharkhand. Adani has reportedly requested a written proposal from the BPD. Controversy has raged over the 25-year power purchase agreement entered into in 2017 by the recently ousted Sheikh Hasina government. After the Hasina government fell in August 2024 following student-led protests, the BPD struggled to pay the outstanding debt estimated at US$846 million, with Adani threatening to end all power exports. In the 2023-24 financial year, the cost of electricity from the Godda plant was about 25 per cent higher than from the 1320 MW Payra in Bangladesh, which also relies on imported coal. Prothom Alo reported that PDB sources allege that Adani is seeking to charge US$15-20 per tonne more than coal imported for either the Payra or the 1320 MW Rampal plants. (Prothom Alo)

US power sector fears effect of Trump administration layoffs: The Trump administration's staff cuts at the Department of Energy have included the axing of 200 positions at the Bonneville Power Administration that manages three-quarters of the high-voltage transmission lines in the Pacific Northwest, along with generation from 31 hydro dams and a nuclear plant. Positions axed include power dispatchers, transmission schedulers and traders from federal agencies that market and transmit wholesale electricity. Together with those who opted for voluntary buyouts, BPA may lose 20 per cent of its staff. Scott Simms from the Public Power Council, a trade association representing consumer-owned utilities in the region, expressed concern that the sudden staff cuts posed an increased risk to the stability of the region's power grid. (Latitude Media, Latitude Media)

Study finds groundwater pollution at Iowa coal ash sites: An analysis of coal ash dams by Interdisciplinary Environmental Clinic and the Sierra Club has found widespread groundwater contamination from coal ash waste at five MidAmerican coal plants in Iowa. The plants disposed of coal ash in nine dams and six landfills, covering more than 700 acres (283 hectares). Data compiled by the company reveals high levels of elevated levels of heavy metals and pollutants, including arsenic, radium, and lithium. For example, at the 1480 MW at Walter Scott, Jr. Energy Center, the levels of arsenic and radium reported in 2023 were beyond the Environmental Protection Authority's maximum contaminant level. (Sierra Club [Pdf])

Vietnamese utility aims to revive cancelled coal plant: A subsidiary of Vietnam's state-owned power utility, Vietnam Electricity (EVN), wants to revive the cancelled 1320 MW Quang Tri coal plant that the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand is in the final stages of abandoning. The plant was first proposed in 2013 but stalled due to delays in obtaining financing and commitments by both the Thai and Vietnamese governments to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. Power Generation JSC 1 (EVNGENCO 1) informed Quang Tri provincial leaders of its interest in developing the project, though its preferred fuel is unclear. In late 2023 the province proposed increasing the capacity of the project to 1500 MW and switching from coal to LNG. (The Investor)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 South Australian government pushes GFG steel mill into administration: The South Australian government has forced the GFG Alliance's Whyalla steelworks into administration and appointed KordaMentha to run the plant. Premier Peter Malinauskas said advice provided to the government was that the finances of the steel plant would continue to deteriorate despite last week's announcement by Sanjeev Gupta, the owner of the GFG Alliance, of the intended sale of some or all of the company's stake in Tahmoor Coking Coal. Gupta said the sale could raise up to US$500 million, would help clear debts owing after the March 2021 collapse of Greensill Capital. The mine supplies GFG's Whyalla steel plant and the export market. GFG's proposed plan to settle debts of up to $US4 billion requires the approval of a court in the UK, with Justice Robert Hildyard allowing a further six weeks to finalise an agreement if possible. Gupta has promoted his aim to pursue green steel production in Australia, the UK and Europe but has made little progress to date. While GFG publicly promotes its green credentials, a representative from Liberty Steel attended a conservative conference organised by Jordan Petersen's Alliance for Responsible Citizenship. (ABC News, ABC News, Australian Financial Review [paywall], DeSmog)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Behind the Mask: Investigating EPH's coal exit claims, Re-Set and Beyond Fossil Fuels, February 2025. (Pdf) (The media release on the report is here.)

This 23-page report investigates the relationship between the sister companies EPH and EP Energy Transition (EPETr). EPH is shifting its coal assets across to EPETr, which the report argues appears designed to greenwash EPH's continued involvement in coal and fossil fuel exploitation. Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky owns both companies.

 "Guide to investigating fossil fuels", Global Investigative Journalism Network, February 10, 2025.

This guide comprises six articles by journalists on how to investigate the global fossil fuel industry.
