title: CoalWire 552, February 27, 2025
excerpt: Microsoft trims data centre deals; US Coast Guard highlights coal ship methane explosion risk.
content:
February 27, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

A cornerstone of President Trump's plan to boost the US energy sector and stall the retirement of old coal plants relies on the rapid expansion of data centres. Investors and energy analysts are wondering aloud if Microsoft's cancellation of some data centre contracts could be a sign of things to come. A slowing of data centre demand growth would force utilities to revisit plans to delay the retirement of old coal plants and expand the fleet of gas plants, especially as new wind, solar and battery projects come online.

Finally, an underreported aspect of the coal industry is the constant series of rail and shipping accidents. A new US Coast Guard report revealed that in November last year a coal ship had two explosions in its holds with dangerous methane levels detected in another five holds. While no one was injured, it illustrates the dangers of shipping coal around the world.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Utilities are flying blind on data centre demand. That's a big problem

How can utilities plan grid and power plant investments for the Artificial Iintelligence and data centre boom when forecasts are so speculative? asks Jeff St. John in Canary Media.

 

 Is Japan a friend in need or a friend indeed for Bangladesh?

Japan has locked Bangladesh into decades of pollution and plunged the economy into relying on expensive coal and LNG imports. But there's an opportunity for a change of direction, writes Munira Chowdhury in The Diplomat.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Microsoft pulls back on data centre contracts: An analyst report from the financial services firm TD Cowen revealed that Microsoft has cancelled leases for "a couple of hundred megawatts" of US data centre capacity, prompting share market uncertainty over the prospects of companies reliant on investment in Artificial Intelligence (AI). Microsoft plans to invest US$80 billion in AI and data centre capacity in 2024/2025. Projections of significant expansions in US data centre capacity underpin power utilities plans for new gas plants and delays in closing old coal capacity. However, many analysts fear hype about AI is fuelling an investment bubble affecting both the technology and power sectors. The recent claims that the Chinese tech start-up DeepSeek had developed an AI tool at a fraction of the cost and power consumption of rivals added to investor unease. Some analysts at the investment bank Goldman Sachs have expressed concern about the financial risks associated with the AI sector. "AI technology is exceptionally expensive, and to justify those costs, the technology must be able to solve complex problems, which it isn't designed to do," said Jim Covello, the head of Global Equity Research at the firm. (Reuters, Goldman Sachs [Pdf], Paul Krugman)

 

 US Coast Guard warns of explosive risk on coal carriers: A US Coast Guard investigation reports that a bulk coal ship had two explosions in forward cargo holds on November 27, 2024, when it was 100 nautical miles off the coast of Virginia. The report suggested the likely case was methane emissions from the coal, combined with poor ventilation. The investigation found five other cargo holds also had "highly elevated levels" of methane that were "an immediate threat to the safety of the mariners and the ship". The Coast Guard noted that the exporter did not provide the ship's captain with a declaration disclosing that the metallurgical coal was liable to produce methane. Coast Guard investigators also noted that the ventilation and the atmospheric sampling of the cargo holds did not comply with International Maritime Solid Bulk Cargo (ISMBC) Code standards. The Coast Guard did not disclose the name of the ship. (US Coast Guard [Pdf])

 

 Report says renewables a better plan for Indonesia: A report by Ember, a climate policy think tank, estimates that Indonesia's December 2024 National Electricity Master Plan envisages a rapid expansion of coal capacity with a peak in 2037, 62.7 per cent higher than current generation. The plan projects the commissioning of 26,800 MW of new coal capacity by the end of 2031, with 20,200 MW of that as the captive capacity to supply new energy-intensive plants such as nickel and aluminium smelters. Ember argues that the costs of electricity from new captive coal plants could reach 7.71 US cents per kilowatt-hour, about 36 per cent higher than the levelised cost of electricity of grid-connected coal plants based on data from the Institute for Essential Services Reform. Power purchase agreements for some new solar and wind projects have revealed significantly lower tariffs. While a Paris Agreement-compliant target would require coal generation to peak at 435 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2030, the master plan assumes a peak at 494 TWh in 2037. The Trump administration's withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and potential cuts to funding for the Just Energy Transition Partnership has increased uncertainty about President Subianto's November 2024 commitment to close most of the country's coal-fired power plants over the next 15 years. (Ember, Mongabay)

 

 German conservatives win election; minority government negotiations: The conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) emerged as the largest party following the German national election, winning 208 of the 630 seats. However, the CDU will have to form a coalition with one or more other parties to command a majority on the floor of the Bundestag. Prior to the election, the CDU ruled out forming a government with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). The CDU's leader Friedrich Merz has had preliminary discussions with the outgoing centre-left Social Democratic Party, which is on track to win 121 seats. Together, the two parties would have a narrow majority on the floor of parliament. The vote for the Greens declined, with the former coalition partner in the outgoing government winning 85 seats. The AfD, which opposes climate action, doubled their vote from the 2021 election and won 151 seats. The Afd won just over 20 per cent of the vote nationwide and topped the results in all five former East German states. The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) led by Sahra Wagenknecht, who split from the Left Party in late 2023, also campaigned against the former government's climate policies. BSW narrowly fell below the crucial five per cent threshold and will lose all of its current 10 seats. The Free Democratic Party, which triggered the early election by withdrawing from a minority government with the SPD and Greens over climate policy, lost all 92 seats after failing to reach the five per cent threshold. (Euractiv, Deutsche Welle)

 

 Mining company wants to weaken rehab plan for Welsh mine: Merthyr (South Wales) Ltd (MSW), the operator of the now-shuttered Ffos-y-fran open-cut mine in South Wales, has submitted a revised rehabilitation plan to Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council. The company is proposing to leave existing spoil dumps and the water-filled mine pit intact. The proposed amendment to the original 2011 rehabilitation plan would result in few rehabilitation works beyond limited re-profiling of waste dumps and planting with grass and native trees. MSW proposes that the mine void that has partially filled with water would remain, though with shallows around the shoreline. The original proposal of Merthyr (South Wales) was to mine about 10 million tonnes of coal and fund the restoration of the area to create open space for the community. Recent estimates suggested the restoration of the site could cost up to 120 million (US$154 million) compared to the 15 million (US$19.3 million) held by the local authority for the work. Coal Action Network has called on the Welsh Government to launch an inquiry into the company's finances and prevent the council from approving the downgraded plan. (Caerphilly Observer, Coal Action Network)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Argentina: President Javier Milei, a right-wing libertarian who has privatised public assets since his election in December 2023, has converted publicly-owned coal miner Yacimientos Carbonferos Ro Turbio into a public company.

 

 Canada: The Alberta Energy Regulator fined [Pdf] CST Canada Coal C$9000 (US$6315) for discharging mine wastewater over 17 hours into the Smoky River and failing to inform the regulator immediately. The wastewater contained about 8.9 tonnes of coal fines.

 

 Canada: Atrum Coal, an Australian-headquartered coal mining company, has filed an amended statement of claim against the Alberta government for compensation for the ban on open-cut coal mines on the Eastern Slopes of the Rockies. Atrum says its proposed Elan coal project would not be viable as an underground project.

 

 US: The Republican-dominated Kentucky House of Representatives has passed a bill that cuts the number of medical emergency trained coal miners on a shift of less than 10 from two to one.

 

 US: South Fork Coal Company and its parent entities filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, a move that has stayed legal action by the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and Appalachian Voices over water pollution and reclamation at the company's mines.

 

 US: A train travelling along the Yellowstone River in Montana derailed, with between 25 to 27 laden coal wagons involved. At least one wagon was reported submerged in the river.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Utility solar and battery projects boom in US as coal closures continue: The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates power utilities will retire 8100 MW of coal capacity in 2025, 4.7 per cent of the country's remaining coal capacity. While the closures represent a doubling of capacity shuttered in 2024, it is lower than the average of the last decade. The slated coal closures include the 1800 MW Intermountain Power Project in Utah, the 1331 MW J H Campbell plant in Michigan and the 1273 MW Brandon Shores plant in Maryland. The closures come as the agency estimates utilities will add 63,000 MW of new capacity in 2025, with 32,500 MW of utility-scale solar and 18,200 MW of battery projects. The EIA estimates the commissioning of just 7700 MW of new wind projects in 2025. One of the first actions of the Trump Administration's Secretary of Energy, former gas industry executive Chris Wright, was the publication of an order titled "Unleash Golden Era of American Energy Dominance". While the order did not specifically mention coal, the first section – "Advance Energy Addition, Not Subtraction" – argued net-zero emissions policies delivered "precious little in reducing global greenhouse gas emissions". Wright subsequently said states should stop the closure of coal plants. The Department of Energy has subsequently postponed the implementation of new energy efficiency standards for appliances. The Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 proposed eliminating appliance energy efficiency standards. (Utility Dive, Energy Information Administration, Department of Energy, Utility Dive)

China's largest thermal coal importer suspends spot buying: China Shenhua Energy, the country's largest coal producer and importer, has temporarily suspended spot purchases of thermal coal for the first time. Inventories at 55 major ports climbed to 72.92 million tonnes as of February 21, near the August 2019 record of 77.46 million tonnes. The decision is expected to affect only about one million tonnes a quarter and represents only a sliver of the 542.7 million tonnes imported in 2024. Sources told Reuters that the suspension of spot purchases of thermal coal could last at least a month. In a recent corporate filing, Shenua reported that the company's commercial coal sales declined by 21.6 per cent in January due to inventory levels and reduced heating demand as a result of higher than normal winter temperatures. Shenhua cut its January coal production to 24.9 million tonnes, a 8.6 per cent decline compared to the year before. (Economic Times)

Vietnam's Deputy PM wants agency to revise power plan: Vietnam's Deputy Prime Minister, Bui Thanh Son, said the country's latest draft power plan needs to be adjusted to cater for a growth rate of eight per cent in 2025 and double-digit rates between 2026 and 2030. Addressing an online conference, Son acknowledged the rapid changes in battery technology paired with deployment of renewable generation. Son said he wants the Ministry of Industry and Trade (MOIT) to develop a schedule of emergency power projects aimed to addressing the forecast electricity shortage with an emphasis on projects that can be built quickly. Son said he wanted MOIT to review all stalled coal power projects and propose solutions for addressing problems they have encountered with changing joint venture partners and accessing finance. (Viet Nam News, The Investor)

Sasol exits coal export market, reworks production plans: The state-owned coal-to-oil producer Sasol announced it will cease selling coal into the global export market as part of its strategy to lift coal quality and boost oil and chemical production. Sasol previously exported about two to three million tonnes of coal a year via the Richards Bay coal terminal. Sasol's coal mines produce about 40 million tonnes of coal a year with most used to feed the 17 coal boilers at its processing plants. The company has been the target of shareholder resolutions demanding the company develop and implement a strategy in line with the goal of the Paris Agreement. At its January 2024 annual general meeting, 77 per cent of shares voted for the company's climate plan, down from 95 per cent in each of the two previous years. Sasol executives said the company had amended its emission reduction roadmap to exclude consideration of reduced production. Sasol plans to increase production by about seven per cent to 7.2 million tonnes a year by 2030. The company has abandoned its previous plan to import LNG to displace coal and instead is aiming to increase renewables capacity from 1200 MW to 1500 MW. The emissions reduction plan assumes that the company meets pollution standards. However, in April 2024, the then Minister of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, Barbara Creecy, granted Sasol's appeal for a variation in the pollution standard for the company's Secunda coal-to-oil plant that Just Share estimated would cut pollution-related deaths by just five per cent compared to a 40-60 per cent cut if the company complied with the original Minimum Emissions Standard. (Reuters, Engineering News)

Renewed load-shedding in South Africa after Eskom coal plants fail: Eskom instituted Stage 6 load-shedding – equal to 6000 MW – after failures at the Camden, Majuba and Kusile coal plants. Under Stage 6 of loadshedding, customers electricity supply can be turned off up to 12 times over four days, including 6 times for 2 hours and 6 times for 4 hours. The latest load-shedding occurred after a generator transformer at one of the units at the 4113 MW Majuba plant overloaded, tripping five units at the plant and taking 3000 MW offline. The sudden change in grid supply caused a frequency disturbance in the transmission system, taking an 800 MW unit at the Kusile coal plant offline. Eskom upgraded the initial Stage 3 loadshedding to Stage 6 after another four 200 MW units at the 1600 MW Camden plant tripped due to a fault in the station's cooling water pumps. South African electricity consumers had 10 months without load-shedding up until the end of January. The Minister for Electricity and Energy, Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, said that the 800 MW Unit 4 at the Medupi plant is due back online in mid-March after an explosion in August 2021. Ramokgopa also said Eskom expects to commission the 800 MW Unit 6 at the Kusile plant by the end of March. (News 24, News 24)

Glencore writes down value of South African coal production: Glencore, the world's largest exporter of thermal coal, informed shareholders that it has written down the value of its South African coal mining operations by US$611 million. The company said the revaluation was due to lowering its long-term thermal coal price assumption from US118 per tonne to US$95 per tonne and constraints on Transnet's railway operations to the underutilised Richards Bay Coal Terminal. Glencore's South African operations produced 16.6 million tonnes of thermal coal in 2024, down seven per cent on the year before. The company's global thermal coal production fell by six per cent to 99.6 million tonnes with just over 52 million tonnes produced from its Australian mines. Glencore said part of the decline in thermal coal production was due, in part, to "a combination of permit delays, community blockades and unusually heavy rain" at the Cerrejon mine in Colombia. In July 2024, Glencore's Elk Valley Resources (EVR) completed the purchase of Teck's British Columbia metallurgical coal mines. EVR produced just over 12.5 million tonnes of metallurgical coal in 2024, with a further 7.4 million tonnes produced at Glencore's Australian mines. (Iol, Glencore [Pdf])

Ohio power consumers pay heavily for two 70-year old coal plants: Data released by the Public Utility Commission of Ohio (PUCO) revealed that the state's electricity customers paid almost US$172 million in 2024 to subsidise two old coal plants owned by the Ohio Valley Electric Corporation (OVEC). The subsidy in 2024 was up 15 per cent per cent on the US$149 million paid in 2023. PUCO estimates customers have spent US$679 million over the last 10 years to OVEC, a joint venture between American Electric Power, Duke Energy, and AES Ohio. OVEC runs the 1303 MW Clifty Creek plant in Indiana and the 1086 MW Kyger Creek coal plant in Ohio, both of which have been operating since 1955. Subsidies for the two plants are enshrined in House Bill 6, legislation at the heart of the US$61 million FirstEnergy corruption scandal. The Citizens Utility Board of Ohio, an NGO group, estimates the subsidy for the two plants could reach US$1.1 billion by 2030 unless legislative changes are passed. Two bills currently before the Ohio legislature would block OVEC from passing losses on the plants on to electricity customers. (Michigan Public, Cleveland)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Navigating risks to unlock 500 GW of renewables by 2030, Ember, February 2025. (Pdf)

This 63-page report investment risks in achieving India's target of building 500,000 MW of renewable energy by 2030 and outlines strategies to address risks to ensure access to low-cost capital.

title: CoalWire 553, March 6, 2025
excerpt: Last Bavarian coal plant closes; early Indonesian closures; Adani revives stalled Indian project.
content:
March 6, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The barrage of announcements by the Trump administration – regulations overturned, programmes axed, agencies gutted and tariffs imposed on allies and rivals alike – make it hard to discern the fallout of all these changes on the domestic and global energy sectors. The best summaries to date suggest a profound short to medium-term impact on US domestic policies and agencies involved in environmental regulation and climate policies. An additional factor is the ongoing debate over the energy demand for data centres, especially in the US. At this point, the effects of Trump's trade wars and hostility against former allies on the global energy sector are less clear.

Outside the US, the energy transition progresses unevenly. In Germany, the last coal plant in the German state of Bavaria was retired, albeit held in reserve. In Indonesia, the announcement of the early retirement of the Cirebon 1 plant and the rapid development of renewables in West Java offers hope that other polluting plants may also close early. But if there were two steps forward, there was one step back, with Adani trying to revive a long-abandoned coal plant in India.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia's richest woman takes on local environment laws in Canada coal power play

A push by Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart's corporate interests to open The Rockies in Canada to coal mining is facing growing resistance after the provincial government announced it is planning to rewrite environmental rules in consultation with industry, writes Royce Kurmelovs in Renew Economy.

 

 AI data centre power and glory - an update

If they have any sense, investors will wake up from their Midsummer Night's AI Dream within the next year or two and reject excessively ambitious data centre plans. If they don't, I strongly suspect they will live to regret it, writes Michael Liebreich, an energy analyst who founded Bloomberg New Energy Finance.

 

 How Trump is crushing US climate policy

President Trump has upended America's climate policies, cutting staff at key government agencies, terminating climate change grant programs and overturning regulations, write David Gelles, Lisa Friedman and Brad Plumer in the New York Times.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Indonesian minister announces closure schedule for Cirebon 1 plant: Indonesia's Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources, Bahlil Lahadalia, announced in early February that the 660 megawatt (MW) Cirebon coal plant in West Java will close in 2035, seven years earlier than the previous retirement date of 2042. The Cirebon 1 and the 1050 MW Pelabuhan Ratu power station were the two coal plants identified in Indonesia's Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) investment plan as pilot plants for early closure. Bahlil said renewables capacity will replace generation from the Cirebon plant. A new report by the Centre for Research Energy and Clear Air (CREA) estimates that the early closure of the Cirebon 1 plant will avoid about 6000 deaths between 2036 and 2042, with about 5409 deaths prevented between 2038 and 2043 if the Pelabuhan Ratu plant closes in 2037. CREA notes that the plants lack air pollution controls and urges the government to ensure full disclosure of emissions during the transition period. CREA also notes that West Java could exceed the target of 6800 MW of renewables capacity by 2030, supported by rapid changes in technology and declining costs. A mid-2024 report by CREA highlighted that there is 7400 MW of grid-connected coal capacity in Indonesia that should retired by 2035 based on a 30-year lifetime. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf])

 

 German state closes last coal plant: The 474 MW Zolling power station in Bavaria in southern Germany has ceased commercial generation and been placed into the country's strategic reserve. Onyx Power, a subsidiary of the US-based private equity firm Riverstone Holdings, was paid more than 46 million (US$49.7 million) after winning an October 2022 Federal Network Agency (BNA) auction for compensated closure of coal capacity. The plant will remain available as reserve capacity until 2031. Several years ago, the conservative Bavarian state government opposed the closure of the plant, arguing it would be required once the nearby 1485 MW Isar 2 nuclear plant closed in 2023. Despite the closure of the nuclear plant, the Zolling power station had a utilisation rate of only 24 per cent in 2024. (Clean Energy Wire)

 

 Bills propose to end coal plant subsidies embedded in tainted Ohio law: Two bills before the Ohio legislature would cut the duration of subsidies for two 70-year-old coal plants look likely to pass. The Ohio legislature passed House Bill 6 in mid-2019 to provide subsidies to two coal plants owned by Ohio Valley Electric Coalition and two FirstEnergy nuclear plants. The legislation also gutted the state's renewable and energy efficiency standards. The legislation was supported and defended by a flood of hidden donations from FirstEnergy, including payments to then-Republican House Speaker Larry Householder. The Ohio legislature repealed the nuclear plant subsidies after the Department of Justice filed charges against Householder and others but did not rescind the coal plant subsidies, which run through to 2030. House Bill 15 and the broadly similar Senate Bill 2, currently before the energy committees in the respective chambers, propose phasing out the coal plant subsidies by 2026 or 2028. The Ohio Manufacturers' Association, along with consumer and environmental groups, support the repeal of the subsidies. (Canary Media, Common Cause Ohio)

 

 Adani revives and expands long-stalled Indian power plant: A subsidiary of Adani Power has proposed to revive the long-stalled 1050 MW Nilanchal Thermal Power Plant in the state of Orissa. Adani bought Orissa Thermal Energy Private Limited in September 2024 for 100,000 rupees (US$1150), a company that won an auction for the power plant site in the bankruptcy proceedings against KVK Nilachal Power. The project site is near biodiverse forests and just a few kilometres from the Kapilash Wildlife Sanctuary set aside for elephants. Opposition to the plant by farmers and environmentalists, along with KVK's financial problems, saw construction of the plant grind to a halt in 2012. Adani has proposed establishing a 2400 MW coal plant on the site, with the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change approving the company's request to proceed to compile an environmental impact statement on the project. (Adani Watch, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Residents feel 'betrayed' by backtracking on Welsh mine rehabilitation: Residents and environmental groups want Merthyr Tydfil Council's Planning Committee to reject the application by Merthyr (South Wales) for a downgraded rehabilitation plan for the Ffos-y-Fran open-cut coal mine site. The company won approval in 2011 to mine coal at the site on condition that proceeds from mining would enable the funding of proper rehabilitation of the 285-hectare site affected by earlier mining. Nearby residents Alyson and Chris Austin said council approval of the company's proposed plan would be the "ultimate betrayal". "We've suffered the noise, the dust, and the only thing we were going to get out of it has been taken away from us," Alison said. The company has paid only 15 million (US$16.2 million) into the council's escrow account to cover the cost of rehabilitation. Coal Action Network (CAN) said the company should pay for the 75-110 million (US$81-119 million) for the rehabilitation of the site. CAN said the proposed plan would leave a mine void that can hold about 1 million cubic metres of water and is about 175 metres deep at one end. CAN has launched a letter-writing portal for residents to submit letters urging Merthyr Tydfil Council's Planning Committee to reject the companys revised rehabilitation plan. (BBC, Coal Action Network)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Canada: Environmentalists said a C$9000 fine (US$6274) for CST Canada Coal spilling 1.1 million litres of tailings into the Smoke River in Alberta is a "slap on the wrist".

 

 Canada: Bitfarms, a Canadian cryptocurrency company, announced it is on track to complete the purchase of Stronghold Digital Mining, a company that owns the 85 MW Scrubgrass and the 80 MW Panther Creek waste coal plants in Pennsylvania.

 

 Kenya: The Environment and Land Court will deliver its verdict on May 29 on Lamu Power's appeal against the 2019 National Environmental Tribunal decision to revoke an environmental impact assessment license for the 1050 MW Lamu coal power plant.

 

 US: Iowa has suspended work on the rehabilitation of old coal mining sites until it has confirmation that federal grants will be honoured.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Chinese coal industry groups call for production cuts, lower imports: Two powerful Chinese coal industry lobby groups, the China Coal Transportation and Distribution Association and the China National Coal Association, have urged coal producers to trim production to avoid a "severe" oversupply. The associations also want importers to reduce shipments of lower-quality coal. Domestic thermal coal prices fell 2.9 per cent in 2025 to the lowest level since April 2021. China imported 542.7 million tonnes of coal in 2024, accounting for just over 40 per cent of the global export market. The level of imports in 2024 was well in excess of the import cap of about 300 million tonnes that was in place until 2022. An analyst note from the financial services firm Morgan Stanley suggested that Chinese authorities could slow the level of imports by delaying inspections, a measure adopted in previous occasions of oversupply. Reduced imports, especially of lower-grade thermal coal, would primarily affect Indonesian exporters. (Mining Weekly, Financial Post)

Adaro restructures to win funding for coal-powered aluminium smelter: The completion of the corporate restructuring of Adaro Energy, an Indonesian country that is the world's sixth-largest coal mining company, may allow the new company to access financing from Standard Chartered and DBS Bank despite their restrictions on coal lending. Adaro Energy produced 66 million tonnes of coal in 2023. In early December 2024, the Adaro Energy Group spun its thermal coal assets off into Andalan but kept a 15 per cent stake in the new company. With a small stake, Adaro – now renamed PT Alamtri Resources – is no longer required to report revenue from thermal coal. Alamtri also holds its metallurgical coal mines in Kalimantan, its proposed aluminium smelter and renewables projects. Another entity, Adaro Strategic Capital (ASC), owns over 40 per cent of both Alamtri and Andalan. In early 2023, DBS Bank and Standard Chartered withdrew support for Adaro's proposed 1.5 million tonnes a year aluminium smelter with power supplied by an 1100 MW captive coal plant. The banks withdrew from supporting the project as it breached their respective environmental, social and governance policies. An analysis by the Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis (IEEFA) of the restructured Adaro suggests the two banks could meet the terms of their current ESG policies even if they finance the company's proposed coal-based aluminium smelter. IEEFA says that as ASC has significant stakes in both Alamtri and Andalan, the banks should amend their policies to assess coal revenue at the group level rather than the operating level. (Eco-Business, Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis)

Mongolia and China agree to dual gauge track to boost coal exports: The Mongolian and Chinese governments reached an agreement on extending the rail networks between the two countries to connect at the Gashuun Sukhait border crossing. Mongolia has invested in new rail links to boost its coal export trade to China and cut costs by reducing reliance on long-haul coal trucks from the Tavan Tolgoi coalfield. A bottleneck for exports existed because the Mongolian railway uses the Russian standard 1520 mm gauge while the Chinese rail connection on the other side of the border utilises the European 1435 mm standard. The two governments agreed to construct dual gauge lines that allow the interoperability of the rail fleet. The upgrading of the rail line will commence in April with the completion due by 2028. Mongolia exported about 84 million tonnes of coal in 2024, with the new rail connection expected to increase export capacity by 30 million tonnes a year. (Railway Gazette International)

Zimbabwe flags coal expansion plan in climate report to United Nations: Zimbabwe's climate plan submitted to the United Nations backs building a new 720 MW coal plant to offset the impact of the drought on the country's hydro capacity. The drought has cut the generating capacity of the 1050 MW Kariba South hydropower project to 185 MW. The hydro project accounts for about 40% of Zimbabwe's generation capacity. A joint venture between Jindal Africa and Zesa Holdings is also proceeding with a US$350 million refurbishment of existing coal units at the Hwange power plant that would increase the capacity of the plant by 400 MW. (Climate Home)

Indonesian sets floor price for coal exports: Indonesia's Minister for Energy, Bahlil Lahadalia, promulgated a regulation requiring coal exporters to only sell coal after March 1 above the official floor price referred to as Harga Batubara Acuan (HBA). Previously, the HBA was revised monthly based on sales price data submitted to the government for royalties owed. Ministry officials said that the HBA price will be updated on the 1st and 15th of each month, with new sales expected to be at or above the new floor price. The current HBA rate varies between about US$34 per tonne for the lowest quality coal and $124 per tonne for the highest grades. The ministry said companies could honour existing export contract prices. The government aims to maximise returns to the government rather than allow exporters to sell using other indices, which often have prices for Indonesian coal at lower rates than the HBA. The China Coal Transportation and Distribution Association warned the new policy could discourage purchases of Indonesian coal. Indonesia is the largest thermal coal supplier in the Asian market, with lower transport costs than Australia and South Africa. (Reuters, Mining Weekly)

Investigation finds JP Morgan sustainable funds invest in Glencore: JPMorgan Asset Management had more than US$260 million invested in Glencore shares and bonds via supposedly sustainable funds in the second quarter of last year, according to an investigation by three independent media groups. Glencore is one of the world's largest coal producers, with controversial mines in South Africa, Colombia, Canada and Australia. The investigation by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, Voxeurop and the Daily Maverick found that JP Morgan's "sustainable" funds are required to invest 51 per cent of funds in companies that have positive environmental and/or social features, with the remaining funds unrestricted by the policy. While JP Morgan's sustainable funds exclude investments in companies earning more than 20 per cent of revenue from thermal coal sales, Glencore's diversified commodities interests ensure it falls below that threshold even though coal accounts for almost half of its profit. Glencore also has significant interests in metallurgical coal production. (Bureau of Investigative Journalism, Guardian)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

"How Bosnian open-pit coal mines threaten farmer livelihoods", Deutsche Welle, February 27, 2025.

This 5-minute video documents the struggle of farmers against the encroachment onto their farmlands by a lignite mine near Sanski Most in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

links.text: (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf])
Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis)
“How Bosnian open-pit coal mines threaten farmer livelihoods”

title: CoalWire 554, March 13, 2025
excerpt: Zimbabwe parks agency objects to coal lease; US exits Just Energy Transition Partnerships.
content:
March 13, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The policy upheavals initiated by the Trump administration continue. As expected, the US has confirmed its withdrawal from the Just Energy Transition Partnerships with South Africa, Indonesia, Vietnam and Senegal. The administration is also reviewing how quickly it could lift economic sanctions on Russia's energy sector if Ukraine concludes a peace deal. The administration's imposition of tariffs on Canadian goods has escalated rapidly, with Ontario initially imposing a levy on electricity exports and Trump retaliating by doubling tariffs on Canada's steel and aluminium exports. The escalating uncertainty about the impact of the administration's policies and funding cuts has cast a shadow over US equity markets and sparked fears of a recession.

While there are significant changes in the costs of technologies supporting the transition to clean energy, such as wind generation and batteries, the rate of deployment in China this year is likely to slow following changes to financial incentives. If the deployment of renewables does slow significantly, will Chinese manufacturers of solar, wind and battery technologies focus on expanding their market share elsewhere?

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 China's 2025 wind and solar additions set to drop as policy backstops fade

New wind and solar capacity additions in China in 2025 are almost definitely going to decline compared to last year after a new renewables compensation policy comes into effect on June 1, writes David Fishman from The Lantau Group in LinkedIn.

 

 Philippine fishers struggle as China-funded coal projects expand

The development of two Aboitiz-owned coal plants in the Bataan special economic zone on Manila Bay has caused significant environmental damage to the local marine ecosystem, with local fishers hit by reduced catch and the health effects from pollution, writes Mavic Conde in The China Global South Project.

 

 The price of a village's anti-coal protest – 369 charges

Three hundred and sixty-nine villagers have had initial legal cases filed against them for their involvement in protests against Adani's proposed coal mine in the Gondalpura area of Jharkhand, writes a special correspondent in Adani Watch.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Zimbabwe National Parks agency calls for rejection of mining application: The Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority (ZimParks) has urged the Ministry of Mines to reject an application by a Chinese company for a 16,120-hectare prospecting permit that includes parts of Hwange National Park. ZimParks said the proposal by Sunny Yi Feng (Private) Limited for coal mining just eight kilometres from the Sinamatella Black Rhino Intensive Protection Zone represented a significant risk to the survival of the species. Environmentalists argue that coal mining would damage groundwater resources that are vital for the 65,000 elephants in Hwange National Park. (Zimbabwe Mail, Nehanda Radio)

 

 US withdraws from Just Energy Transition Partnerships: The Trump administration has confirmed it has withdrawn its financial support for the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) projects with Indonesia, South Africa, Vietnam and Senegal. The US government and a coalition of European countries announced the US$8.5 billion project with South Africa in December 2021. The US government committed US$1 billion to the project and played a lead role in facilitating pooled funding from governments, development banks and the private sector to support a transition away from coal power. The US had also committed a total of US$3 billion to Indonesia and Vietnam, with the projects announced in 2022. The US cancelled its US$4 billion commitment to the Green Climate Fund in February and this week withdrew as a board member of the United Nations Fund for responding to Loss and Damage. In an address to the Powering Africa summit in Washington DC, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright dismissed concern about African countries developing coal projects as "100 per cent nonsense". (Climate Home News, Reuters, Financial Times, E & E News)

 

 Indonesian minister's brother to head holding company for state-owned mines: Maroef Sjamsoeddin, the brother of Indonesia's Minister for Defense Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin, has been appointed as president and director of MIND ID, the Indonesian government's holding firm for state-owned mining companies. MIND ID subsidiaries include Bukit Asam, the state-owned coal company that produced more than 43 million tonnes of coal in 2024 and PT Aneka Tambang (Antam), which is the largest producer of nickel in the country. Maroef was previously the commander of the special forces section of the Air Force, defence attache to Brazil and, between 2011 and 2014, served as the director of 'counter-separatism' for the State Intelligence Agency (BIN). Indonesia's military has long sought to counter independence movements in provinces such as Aceh and West Papua. In a separate development, the Minister for Energy, Bahlil Lahadalia, said the newly created sovereign wealth fund Danantara Indonesia would invest in four proposed coal gasification projects in South Sumatra and East Kalimantan but did not provide further details. The Indonesian government has promoted the concept of processing low-grade coal into dimethyl ether to cut expensive LPG imports. However, companies have withdrawn from the projects, which the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis argues are not viable. (Jakarta Post, Reuters)

 

 South African study flags heavy health toll from coal plants: A study by the South African Medical Research Council has found that people living in municipalities with coal plants are six per cent more likely to die prematurely compared to those living in areas without coal power stations. The authors reviewed almost three million death certificates issued between 1997 to 2018 and compared the data with air quality readings. The study, which the UK Department for International Development funded, found that children are particularly vulnerable to coal plant pollution, with an increased number of cleft lip and palate anomalies in areas with coal plants. The study recommends phasing out coal plants, strengthening air quality standards while they continue to operate and ensuring communities are better informed of the health risks they face. (Daily Maverick, South African Medical Research Council, South African Medical Research Council [Pdf[)

 

 Canadian electricity exports to Canada caught in US trade war: The Trump administration's imposition of a 10 per cent tariff on energy imports from Canada has fuelled uncertainty by power system operators over whether the tariff applies to electricity bought from Canadian provinces and, if it does, who has responsibility for collecting and remitting it. The New York Independent System Operator (NYISO ) and ISO New England notified the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) seeking urgent clarification on the matter. New England ISO estimated that a 10 to 25 per cent tariff on electricity imports would cost between US$66 million and US$165 million a year. NYISO told FERC it imported 7.7 terawatt hours of Canadian electricity in 2024 through interconnections with Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator and Hydro-Qubec. In retaliation for US tariffs, Ontario Premier Doug Ford imposed a 25 per cent tax on all electricity exported from the province to Michigan, Minnesota and New York from March 10. Ford said Ontario sold about C$700 million (US$484 million) in electricity to the US a year and that the tax would remain in place until the US lifted all tariffs on Canadian goods. The Trump administration responded by doubling tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminium from 25 per cent to 50 per cent. After Ontario rescinded its levy on electricity exports, Trump reduced US tariffs on Candian steel and aluminium back to 25 per cent. (Utility Dive, The Narwhal, CNN)

 

 Interim Bangladesh government backs reviving Phulbari coal mine: The Hydrocarbon Unit of Bangladesh's Ministry of Power and Energy is promoting the development of the controversial Phulbari open cut coal mine owned by the UK-based Global Coal Management Resources. In response to a mass protest against the mine in 2006 by an estimated 50,000 people, police shot and killed three people and injured hundreds more. In an agreement with the local community, the then government agreed to abandon the proposed open-cut mine. Despite the agreement, the company has lobbied to revive the project. In 2010, a diplomatic cable published by Wikileaks revealed the US government also lobbying the government to approve the project, citing the interests of US investors in the company. The original project was estimated to require the relocation of between 50,000 and 130,000 people with water extraction to allow mining affecting a further 220,000 people. The Hydrocarbon Unit argues the mine is needed to supply domestic coal power plants. The interim government, which assumed power after student-led protests toppled the authoritarian Sheikh Hasina government in 2024, is tentatively supporting the GCM Resources project. (New Age, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Mineral Resources Tasmania has cancelled the mining lease for a proposed one-million tonnes a year coal mine after Paladin Hydrogen failed to pay the annual rent by the January 1 deadline.

 

 Australia: Nexa Advisory, a clean energy consultancy, said subsidies to keep unreliable coal plants like Origin Energy's 2640 MW Eraring plant operating beyond scheduled closure dates are unwarranted.

 

 India: Indian coal imports declined for the sixth month in a row as slowing manufacturing undercut electricity demand growth. Coal imports fell by 20 per cent in the sixth months to the end of February.

 

 India: Villagers in Margherita, Assam, fear that a plan by North Eastern Coalfields, a Coal India subsidiary, to establish a coal dump for the nearby Tikak Colliery could obliterate villages that are home to 1000 families.

 

 India: Reports that the Meghalaya state government is considering petitioning the High Court to seek the termination of Justice BP Katakey's investigation into illegal coal mining in the state.

 

 India: Two gunmen assassinated a senior NTPC manager on his way to work at the Keredari coal mine in Jharkhand. Two other NTPC officials associated with the mine have previously been killed.

 

 India: Three workers died when a roof collapsed in the Bagdona-Chhatarpur underground coal mine in Madhya Pradesh. Western Coal Fields, a subsidiary of Coal India, owns the mine.

 

 India: Assam's Minister for Mines, Kaushik Rai, revealed that at least 263 illegal 'rat-hole' mines operate in the state. The National Green Tribunal banned 'rat-hole' mines in 2014.

 

 US: A Kentucky Senate committee voted 7 to 4 to back a bill reducing the number of first-aid qualified workers from two to one in a shift of 10 or fewer workers. The vote came after Stella Morris testified that her husband died after a December 2005 accident when there was insufficient first aid to prevent him bleeding to death.

 

 US: A federal court has given Tams Management and Frontier Coal until May 1 to pay US$400,000 in outstanding mine safety penalties or face contempt charges. Republican Senator Jim Justice owns the two companies.

 

 "Without systematic changes to prevailing utility rate-making practices, the public faces significant risks that utilities will take advantage of opportunities to profit from new data centres by making major investments and then shifting costs to their captive ratepayers. The industry's current approaches of luring data centres with discounted contracts or lopsided tariffs are unsustainable,"

write [Pdf] Eliza Martin and Ari Peskoe from the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Bangladesh court committee urges renegotiation of Adani power deal: A committee appointed by the High Court of Bangladesh has recommended the government renegotiate the power purchase agreement with Adani Power for power imports from the 1600 MW Godda coal plant in Jharkhand. The committee found that the 25-year power purchase agreement entered into in 2017 by the Sheikh Hasina government included "one-sided" provisions such as tax exemption and coal pricing that favour the company. The committee also found that the power purchase agreement allows for the imposition of late payment surcharges of up to 27 per cent a year. The committee has directed the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) to renegotiate the tariff and problematic clauses with Adani Power. The committee is also investigating potential corruption associated with the power purchase deal. The committee suggested that if Adani refuses to renegotiate the key clauses of the agreement the government should pursue legal action in the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC). "If anything adverse happens, we bear the cost, but if it's favourable, Adani benefits - unless the Indian government instructs otherwise," said Zahid Hussain, a member of the committee and a former World Bank economist. (Business Standard)

The US looks to lift sanctions on Russian energy sector companies: The Trump administration is investigating options to quickly lift sanctions on Russia's energy sector if Ukraine reaches a settlement to end the war. Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the European Union, the US and other countries imposed sanctions on Russian oil, gas and coal companies, along with service companies in the supply chain for the energy sector. The US government has sanctioned major coal exporters SUEK and Mechel. The sanctions have resulted in reduced coal exports along with significant restrictions on everything from financial services to spare parts. Russian coal exporters have also been affected by state-owned Russian Railways' shortage of locomotives and drivers. The Trump administration has ratcheted up pressure on Ukraine to make significant territorial concessions to reach an agreement with Russian President Putin by suspending authorised weapons supplies and intelligence. Russian coal exports have fallen to their lowest level in six years and now stand at 13 per cent below the peak of 223.4 million tonnes in 2021. (Reuters)

US study finds utilities could push data centre costs onto ratepayers: A study published by the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative warns that existing ratepayers rather than technology companies could bear the costs of utilities investments in power plants and transmission lines required for new US data centres. The authors of the paper, Eliza Martin and Ari Peskoe, reviewed almost 50 regulatory proceedings setting utility rates for data centres and warned that there are significant risks that utilities will profit from investments by US technology companies such as Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft by shifting the costs onto other ratepayers. The paper notes that by the end of 2024, some analysts were projecting that 65,000 MW would be required for new data centres by 2030. However, the paper cautions that utilities have an incentive to overhype potential demand growth as data centre developers pitch projects to several utilities. The authors recommend that public utility commissions (PUCs) could better protect consumers by establishing guidelines for reviewing special contracts and shifting data centres to tariffs. They also suggested another measure PUCs could pursue is the development of "energy parks" that are not connected to any utility-owned network, thereby avoiding passing the costs on to other customers. They also proposed requiring utilities to provide more frequent demand forecasts and only allowing new data centres if they commit to flexible operations, thereby lowering costs during periods of expensive peak demand. (Utility Dive, Harvard Electricity Law Initiative [Pdf])

Japanese utility lobby group calls for delay in closing old coal plants: The Federation of Electric Power Companies of Japan (FEPC), the country's power industry lobby group, has objected to the Agency for Natural Resources and Energy's suggestion that additional measures may be required to accelerate the closure of old and inefficient coal plants. As part of the G7 countries, Japan agreed to phase out unabated coal plants by 2035. The FEPC objected in its submission to the agency to setting a deadline for closures and called for government measures to support the continued operation of inefficient plants even if they operate at lower capacity factors. The lobby group also called for a review of the capacity market and reserve power schemes. (Nikkei [Japanese])

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

"Can wind energy compete? Three key takeaways on its future", Columbia Business School, March 5, 2025. (Slide deck here as Pdf and Powerpoint).

This article provides a brief overview of key global and US trends affecting the development and deployment of wind power globally, including challenges with dispersed supply chains and the prospect of the declining cost of offshore wind projects.

"The future of energy storage: five key insights on battery innovation and the clean energy shift", Columbia Business School, March 5, 2025. (Slide deck here as Pdf and Powerpoint).

This article summarises a discussion on key trends affecting the role of batteries in the energy transition, including trends in production, battery chemistries, the possible impact of vehicle-to-grid technology and recycling.

What Japan's new Strategic Energy Plan means for J-POWER, Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility, February 2025.

Japan's new Strategic Energy Plan increases the target for renewables by 2040, but this report argues that J-Power, the country's largest coal power utility, should adopt more ambitious investment goals for renewables. J-Power currently assumes that it can decarbonise its coal plants by investing in hydrogen and ammonia co-firing and carbon capture and storage.

title: CoalWire 555, March 20, 2025
excerpt: UK requests clarification on mine; Zimbabwe Speaker opposes coal mining in National Parks.
content:
March 20, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

A few weeks back, senior US government representatives were extolling the prospects of coal in southern Africa. But on the ground, the picture is more complicated. The Speaker of Zimbabwe's parliament has voiced his opposition to the application by a Chinese tile company for a coal exploration permit in Hwange National Park, the country's largest reserve. In neighbouring Botswana, the government has called for proposals for up to 1500 megawatts (MW) of solar capacity. In South Africa, the government's anti-corruption agency told parliament about the number of Eskom staff with interests in companies supplying the state-owned power utility. The briefing of parliament came as a contractor extradited from the UK faced court on charges over contracts on the construction of the Kusile coal plant.

In Australia, a superannuation fund was fined A$10.5 million for claiming it did not invest in coal companies when it had interests in two major coal producers. In the UK, the government has given West Cumbria Mining a March 26 deadline to indicate whether it plans to continue with its proposal for the Whitehaven metallurgical coal mine. The company had claimed that metallurgical coal production is required to produce steel. Across the Atlantic, Boston Metal was celebrating its success in testing its technology for producing iron without coal.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Peruvian farmer takes Germany's RWE to court in landmark climate case

A Peruvian farmer who says German energy giant RWE's emissions have contributed to the melting of Andean glaciers, increasing the flood risk to his home, appeared at a German court in a hearing that could set a precedent for climate litigation, writes Riham Alkousaa in Reuters.

 

 Mongolia's children choke on toxic air pollution

Pollution from coal power plants and households blankets Mongolia's capital, Ulaanbaatar, in toxic smog each winter, with successive governments failing to address the problem, writes Rebceea Baily in France 24.

 

 Indonesia's coal gasification reboot faces backlash over economic and environmental risks

A renewed plan by the Indonesian government to turn coal into gas or liquid fuel has prompted a backlash from climate experts who say it will be ecologically and economically disastrous, writes Basten Gokkon in Mongabay.

 

 Adani literally doubles down on coal-power

Adani's expansion plans put the company on track to double its coal power generation capacity to 38,000 megawatts (MW) and burn about 155 million tonnes of coal annually, write Ayaskant Das and a special correspondent in Adani Watch.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Speaker of Zimbabwe's Parliament opposes mining in National Parks: The Speaker of Zimbabwe's Parliament, Jacob Mudenda, said he is opposed to the application by Chinese tile manufacturer Sunny Yi Feng for a coal exploration licence in the Hwange National Park. Mudenda noted other areas within the country are prospective for coal and that he "will not support mining in national parks". Last week, the Zimbabwe National Parks and Wildlife Management Authority urged the Ministry of Mines to reject Sunny Yi Feng's application for a 16,120-hectare prospecting permit. Hwange National Park is Zimbabwe's largest reserve and is known for its large elephant herds, lions, giraffes, impala and more than 400 bird species. (ZimLive)

 

 UK govt ask company to clarify intention with Cumbrian mine plan: The UK government's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has written to West Cumbria Mining (WCM) requesting clarification by March 26 on whether the company wants to continue with its planning application for the proposed Whitehaven coal mine. In September last year, the High Court overturned the December 2022 planning permission granted by former Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Levelling Up, Michael Gove, for WCM's mine. Mr Justice Holgate rejected the claim by WCM that coal from the Whitehaven mine would substitute for coal produced elsewhere. Holgate ruled that Gove had unlawfully agreed the mine would be 'net zero' and would not affect the UK's compliance with its emissions reduction target as the company would purchase international carbon credits. The ministry must reconsider the application as a result of the decision and gave interested parties until February 27 to respond. WCM failed to submit a reply. Friends of the Earth campaigner Tony Bosworth said it is time for the company to abandon the project. (BBC, Friends of the Earth UK)

 

 US cryptocurrency company ordered to clean up coal ash dump: In response to legal action by environmental groups, the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) has set a September 1, 2026, deadline for cryptocurrency company Stronghold Digital Mining to clean up the unpermitted coal ash dump at the 94 MW Scrubgrass Power Plant in Kennerdell. In 2022 an inspection of the site by the Pennsylvania DEP found the dump had exceeded its permitted size and gave the company four years to remove the unauthorised coal ash. The company estimated the dump contained 325,000 US short tons (295,000 tonnes) of coal ash. The Scrubgrass Creek Watershed Association and Citizens for Pennsylvania's Future challenged Pennsylvania DEP's decision and shortened the deadline by a year, with the company obliged to keep the groups informed of progress. (WESAFM)

 

 South Korean government abandons requirement to cap coal ash dumps: The South Korean Ministry of Environment announced it will revoke the requirement for power utilities to cap coal ash landfills with soil at least 60 centimetres thick. The ministry claimed that coal ash landfills present a low pollution risk and that sites that did not generate pollution during power station operation will be exempt from rehabilitation requirements. Major power utilities – Dongsuh Power, West Power, South East Power, South Power, and Central Power – propose to establish new LNG power stations on old coal ash sites. The companies claim that exemption from capping the coal ash landfills would save them about 370 billion won (US$255 million) and allow the commissioning of the proposed LNG plants one year earlier than if they had to comply with the current requirements. Allowing uncapped coal ash dams would allow water to move through the ash, which the US Environmental Protection Agency has documented the pollution of groundwater and streams with pollutants including arsenic, boron, cadmium, chromium, lead, radium and selenium. (Chosun)

 

 Australian coal lobby group promotes fundraiser for conservative party: Coal Australia, a lobby group for coal mining companies including Peabody Energy and Whitehaven Coal, encouraged members to attend a political fundraising event with David Littleproud, the leader of the conservative National Party. Coal Australia's flyer for the event said it would "provide an opportunity to discuss election strategy, policy priorities and insights from polling". Data submitted to the Australian Electoral Commission reveals that in 2023-24, the National Policy Forum Trust, a National Party-associated entity, received A$66,000 (US$42,000) from Adani Mining, A$38,500 (US$25,000) from the Minerals Council of Australia and A$25,000 (US$15,900) from Low Emission Technology Australia, a coal industry group promoting carbon capture and storage. (The Guardian)

 

 Johannesburg hit with rotten egg gas from Sasols coal-to-oil plant: A plume of hydrogen sulphide emissions from Sasol's Secunda coal-to-oil plant drifted through Johannesburg last Thursday night and Friday morning. Hydrogen sulphide is commonly referred to as rotten egg gas. Sasol won significant concessions from the government on compliance with pollution standards for the plant, the world's single largest source of greenhouse gas emissions. The head of the City of Johannesburg's Air Quality Unit, Musa Mahlatji, said plumes of hydrogen sulphide often occur in February and March due to specific weather conditions. Lauri Myllyvirta from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air said the city would continue to suffer from the odours until "the government requires Sasol to clean up its emissions". (News24)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: One hundred and thirty protestors arrested over an April 2024 protest against coal exports from Newcastle pled not guilty at a hearing before the NSW Supreme Court.

 

 Australia: AGL was fined A$30,000 (US$19,072) for discharging 10 cubic metres of coal ash into a creek near its 2665 MW Bayswater coal plant in New South Wales. The incident occurred in August 2024.

 

 Germany: RWE announced it plans to build a 600 MW/1.2 gigawatt-hour battery energy storage system on the site of the now-closed Westfalen coal plant at Hamm in North Rhine-Westphalia.

 

 India: JSW Energy has entered into a 25-year power purchase agreement with the West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company for a 1600 MW coal plant in Salboni, West Bengal. The plant is slated for completion by 2030.

 

 India: The Minister of Coal and Mines, Kishan Reddy, told parliament that 226 workers had died in the country's coal mines over the last five years.

 

 India: The Minister for New and Renewable Energy, Pralhad Joshi, said that one million rooftop solar systems have been installed since the February 2024 launch of a government scheme promoting the sector. The systems have a capacity of more than 3000 MW.

 

 Mozambique: Damage caused by Tropical Cyclone Jude caused the suspension of operations on the coal railway from the Moatize mine to the Port of Nacala.

 

 Mozambique: Damage caused by Tropical Cyclone Jude caused the suspension of operations on the coal railway from the Moatize mine to the Port of Nacala.

 

 US: The Kentucky House of Representatives voted 69-26 to confine environmental regulation of waterways to navigable waters only, a change supported by the state's coal industry.

 

 US: The Department of Interior has approved a 16-year life extension of the Spring Creek mine in Montana. The Navajo Transitional Energy Company owns the mine, with the modified mining plan allowing the production of an additional 39.9 million US short tons (36.2 million tonnes) of coal.

 

 US: The Sierra Club and the West Virginia Public Service Commission (PSC) have settled a legal challenge to the 2021 directive that Appalachian Power must operate its three coal plants at a 69 per cent capacity factor. The PSC agreed that 69 per cent is not a requirement but a target. Appalachian Power had stated that its three coal plants – John Amos, Mountaineer and Mitchell – have a capacity factor of about 40 per cent, the average of coal plants in the PJM Interconnection region.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Botswana calls for solar project, grants coal bed methane licence: Botswana's Minister for Mines and Energy, Bogolo Kenewendo, said the government will issue a request for proposals this month for 1500 MW of solar capacity as part of its goal to commission 8000 MW of solar capacity by 2030. Botswana currently has just 5.2 MW of renewable capacity and a domestic power demand of about 600 MW. The state-owned Botswana Power Corporation owns and operates the 600 MW Morupule coal plant, but the four units at the power station have proven unreliable and operate at a low capacity factor. Jindal Steel & Power is currently building the 600 MW Mmamabula Energy Project, with its four units scheduled to come online in late 2026 and 2027. While Botswana has low domestic electricity demand, it aims to export electricity to adjoining countries such as Zimbabwe and Zambia, where hydro generation has been affected by drought and South Africa, where old coal plants are often offline for maintenance. The Botswana government also recently approved the granting of a mining licence for Botala Energy's proposed Serowe coal bed methane gas project. The company intends to complete a bankable feasibility study for the project that aims to supply gas to the domestic market in Botswana and for export to southern Africa. (Financial Post, Botala Energy [Pdf])

South African anti-corruption agency flags staff ties to Eskom suppliers: The Special Investigating Unit (SIU), the South African government's specialist anti-corruption agency, told the Parliamentary Committee on Electricity and Energy that 334 Eskom employees had direct business interests with suppliers to the utility. The SIU found 180 million rand (US$9.9 million) in illegal payments to vendors tied to Eskom employees, with coal supply the most significant area of concern. The SIU said that 5464 staff, more than 10 per cent of the utility's employees, had not submitted conflict of interest declarations. In a separate development, former Eskom contractor Michael Lonas was granted bail after his extradition from the UK. Lonas and 11 others face 65 charges on the misappropriation of 1.4 billion rand (US$77 million) on contracts for the construction of the 4800 MW Kusile coal plant. Several days ago, Eskom announced a further six arrests over fraudulent equipment purchases at the plant, including more than US$47,000 spent for a pump that had the same serial number as one bought at a fraction of the cost a decade earlier. (Daily Maverick, Iol, Eskom)

Australian super funds fined for greenwashing coal investments: The Federal Court of Australia found Active Super "misled members and potential members by saying it had eradicated investments in gambling, coal mining and oil tar sands". The court found the fund made these claims in a range of communications with members and on its website at a time that it held investments in two coal companies, Whitehaven Coal and Coronado Global Resources. The fund also had investments in Russian companies Gazprom and Sberbank, as well as oil tar sands and gambling companies. Justice David O'Callaghan found Active Super breached the Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act of 2001 and accepted the commission's submission that "the real harm of greenwashing is not the harm to an individual investor, but rather the harm more generally to ESG [environmental, social, governance] programs as a whole and investor confidence in them". The court ordered Active Super to pay a penalty of A$10.5 million (US$6.78 million) and email members informing them of the court's finding and include the notice on its website for six months. (Australian Securities and Investment Commission, Federal Court of Australia [Pdf])

Indonesian Minister wants state companies to back coal gasification: The Deputy Energy and Mineral Resources Minister, Yuliot Tanjung, said state-owned enterprises will lead the development of coal gasification projects. The Indonesian government is promoting coal-to-dimethyl ether (DME) gasification projects with the intent of displacing imported LNG. However, private US and Chinese companies withdrew from joint ventures with Indonesian companies due to the poor economics of the projects. The state-owned coal company PT Bukit Asam and state-owned oil and gas utility Pertamina were part of earlier joint venture plans. Yuliot said that the state-owned companies may form new joint ventures if they don't have the required capital, though the government has also considered financing projects through its newly created sovereign wealth fund, Danantara. "If we do not increase the added value in the form of DME, our coal cannot be utilised," Yuliot said. (Jakarta Post [paywall])

Japan to subsidise biomass co-firing at Vietnamese coal plants: Japan's Agency for Natural Resources and Energy has agreed to subsidise plans by Japanese company Erex to trial biomass co-firing at coal power plants in Vietnam. Erex states on its website that it aims to establish 4600 MW of biomass co-firing capacity at Vietnamese coal plants by 2040 and a further 3400 MW of biomass power plants. Erex currently operates biomass plants in Japan with a capacity of about 269 MW. (Vietnam Investment Review, Erex [Pdf])

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 US steel producer completes test of new iron production technology: Boston Metal produced its first US short ton of steel from a reactor at its test plant in Woburn, Massachusetts. The start-up is pursuing the development of molten oxide electrolysis producing iron with minimal greenhouse gas emissions. The company's current test cell produced about one US short ton of steel in a month and trialled the use of multiple inert anodes. The next step in the company's development of the technology is commissioning a demonstration plant in late 2026 with a one-ton-per-day capacity. The company says the technology can process a wide range of grades of iron ore. The process aims to slash greenhouse gas emissions by avoiding the use of coal in steel production and bypassing steps in processing iron ore. (Boston Metal, Boston Metal [Pdf])

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Dineo Skosana, No last place to rest: Coal mining and dispossession in South Africa, Wits University Press, March 2025.

This book 224-page book documents the displacement of families in the Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal provinces of South Africa by the expansion of coal mining operations. The book includes chapters on the Tendele Coal Mine in KwaZulu-Natal and Glencore's Tweefontein mine in Mpumalanga.

"Coal pollution chokes Ulaanbataar – in pictures", The Guardian, March 17, 2025.

This photo essay highlights the pollution of the Mongolian capital from coal burnt in power stations and homes.
