title: CoalWire 556, March 27, 2025
excerpt: Glencore slashes Colombian mine output; Microsoft drops US$12 billion data centre option; Queensland minister flags likely decision to reject coal lease application.
content:
March 27, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The announcement by Glencore, the world's largest exporter of thermal coal, of a significant cut in production from its Cerrejon mine in Colombia is a striking development. As European coal demand has declined, Colombian exporters tested shipments into the Asian market when prices were high. But that requires either shipments routed through the Panama Canal to the Pacific Ocean or the long way around via southern Chile. With declining prices, expensive shipping options are not viable. Reports that President Trump is considering imposing a port levy on ships either built in China or a fleet with a significant Chinese component has backfired, with coal shippers reluctant to run the risk of substantial losses on future cargoes. Xcoal Energy & Resources has warned the Trump administration such a levy could undermine US coal exports.

The latest International Energy Agency report notes that the bulk of increased coal consumption in 2024 occurred in China and India as extreme heat waves drove power demand needed to cater for air conditioning. The report also notes that one of the drivers for increasing electricity demand is the rapid growth of data centres to cater for Artificial Intelligence applications. In an indication that high power demand projections for the sector may moderate, Microsoft abandoned an option to buy almost US$12 billion in data centre capacity.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Trump's love for coal is crashing into the market's economic reality

The US coal industry is once again enjoying support from the White House. Yet that's unlikely to quell the economic challenges that underpin a long-term decline for the dirtiest fossil fuel, writes Shoko Oda in Bloomberg.

 

 Trump administration moves to shutter mine safety offices in coal country

Miners and their advocates worry that the Trump administration's cuts to the Mine Safety and Health Administration will put them at risk, writes Katie Myers in Grist.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Queensland minister flags likely decision to reject coal application

Queensland's Attorney-General Deb Frecklington stated that her preliminary view is that it is "not in the public interest" to grant Fox Resources application for a mineral development licence for a potential metallurgical coal mine near Bundaberg. Fox Resources first applied for a licence in 2019 for over 7800 hectares of agricultural and residential land north of Bundaberg. The Bundaberg Council, farmers, and environmentalists opposed the proposal, and in April 2022, the then Minister for Resources, Scott Stewart, noted "significant adverse community sentiment" to the proposal and rejected the company's application. However, a court set aside the decision following an appeal by the company. The conservative Liberal National Party won government at the October 2024 state election, with Frecklington responsible for making a fresh decision. She said that the Department of Natural Resources and Mines is preparing a decision brief for her to consider. (ABC News, Queensland government)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 UN study says Glencore underreported methane emissions at Aust mine: A study based on data from plane-based surveys found that methane emissions are likely to be between three and eight times higher than Glencore reported for its Hail Creek mine in Queensland. Glencore reported 0.53 million tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent (CO2e) emissions from methane and other sources from the mine in 2023 using the Australian government's approved reporting methodology. The latest study, published in the American Chemical Society's journal Environmental Science and Technology Letters, relied on data collected from instruments mounted in two planes overflying the mine and estimated methane emissions alone of between 1.5 million tonnes and 4.2 million tonnes of CO2e per year from the mine. A team of researchers undertook the study for the UN Environment Programme's International Methane Emissions Observatory. Glencore said it had "significant doubts" about the study, but the researchers said the results highlighted the need for "a comprehensive review of the bottom-up reporting methods" used to assess methane emissions from the mine. (Guardian, Environmental Science & Technology Letters)

 

 Peabody Energy fined over coal sludge pollution of NSW National Park: The New South Wales Land and Environment Court has fined Peabody Energy A$196,560 (US$123,626) for incidents in September and October 2022 that resulted in coal mine sludge flowing into a tributary of the Hacking River that runs through the Royal National Park near Sydney. Major causes of the accident were the long delays by the company in excavating accumulated coal sediment from a storage dam and the blockage of a pump intake. The pollution of the river was discovered by a bushwalker and reported to the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA). The court ordered Peabody Energy to pay A$150,000 (US$94,342) of the fine to the NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service to fund a water quality monitoring program in the Royal National Park and Garawarra State Conservation Area. The maximum fine for each of the offences was A$1 million (US$629,000) at the time. Peabody Energy was also ordered to pay A$304,806 (US$191,707) to cover the EPA's legal and investigative costs. The Sutherland Shire Environment Centre described the fine as a "minor business expense" for Peabody that was "manifestly inadequate given the national significance of the environment" affected. (ABC News, Sutherland Shire Environment Centre [Facebook], NSW Environment Protection Authority, NSW Land and Environment Court)

 

 Alabama says mine methane the "likely" cause of fatal house blast: The Director of the Alabama Surface Mining Commission, Kathy Love, acknowledged in a letter to a federal agency that a fatal explosion was "likely" caused by the ignition of methane produced by underground coal mining. Love had declined to release a copy of her letter, but Inside Climate News obtained it after submitting a Freedom of Information Act request to a federal agency. In March 2024, a gas explosion killed 74-year-old homeowner W.M. Griffice and seriously injured his grandson in the house above the Oak Grove Mine. The Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement (OSMRE), a federal US regulatory agency, warned the Alabama Surface Mining Commission in early December 2024 that it must take action within 10 days after an inspection revealed that Crimson Oak Grove Resource, the mine operator, had failed to report all required information about subsidence and methane monitoring at the mine. A subsequent investigation by the Mine Safety and Health Administration cited Oak Grove Mine for 204 safety violations. The Griffice family has launched a lawsuit alleging methane from the mine caused the explosion, a claim the company rejects. (Inside Climate News)

 

 Indonesia says Germany and Japan to lead just transition project: The Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs, Airlangga Hartarto, said Japan and Germany will lead the group of nine nations supporting Indonesia's Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) after the US withdrew earlier this month. The US committed initially to provide US$2 billion in grants, concessional loans and guarantees from multilateral development banks. Indonesia proposes to increase the renewable share of its grid power to 44 per cent by 2030 and gradually retire old coal plants. However, the JETP does not include the rapid expansion of captive coal plants to power nickel and aluminium smelters, with Indonesia insisting the focus remains on grid-connected plants. In early March, the Trump administration announced it would no longer support the JETP projects for Indonesia, South Africa and Vietnam. (Reuters)

 

 Indian government celebrates passing billion tonne production mark: Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the production of more than one billion tonnes of coal in a single year for the first time as a "proud moment for India". He said the record highlighted a "significant commitment to energy security, economic growth and self-reliance". The announcement came as the Ministry of Coal completed the sale of 12 of 20 blocks on offer in the 11th round of coal auctions. Jindal Steel and Power and Coal India subsidiary Western Coalfields were among the winning bidders. The ministry estimates the 12 auctioned blocks contain geological reserves of about 5.7 billion tonnes of coal with an estimated peak production capacity of about 15.46 million tonnes a year. Of the other eight blocks offered, five attracted no bids, and three more drew only one bid, voiding the sale process for those blocks. (Prime Minister of India, Economic Times, Business Standard)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Europe: A draft agreement between the Christian Democrats and Social Democrats suggests a coalition agreement would retain the 2038 legislated phase out date for the country's remaining lignite plants. The previous government supported an ideal 2030 phase out date.

 

 Europe: A draft agreement between the Christian Democrats and Social Democrats suggests a coalition agreement would retain the 2038 legislated phase out date for the country's remaining lignite plants. The previous government supported an ideal 2030 phase out date, subject to negotiations with states and utilities.

 

 India: Villagers protested against evictions and environmental damage from the proposed Deocha-Pachami-Dewanganj-Harisingha coal mine in West Bengal.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Glencore slashes coal production at Colombian subsidiary: Glencore announced that it will cut coal production at its controversial Cerrjon mine in Colombia by between 5 and 10 million tonnes a year due to the decline in thermal coal prices in the export market. The company said production at the mine would fall to between 11 and 16 million tonnes. The President of Cerrejon Coal, Claudia Bejarano, told a recent conference that mine production was interrupted on 135 days in 2024 due to community blockades. Local communities have been profoundly affected by the mine, with villages displaced, the degradation of water sources and the effects of coal dust pollution near the mine and along the rail corridor to the Puerto Bolivar coal export terminal. The cost to ship coal from Cerrejon to the growing Asian market is about US$37 per tonne, about US$20 per tonne higher than the company's traditional markets of Europe and Turkey. "We are losing our competitiveness completely," Bejarano said. (Mining Weekly, BNAmericas, Argus)

Microsoft backs away from data centre power deals: Microsoft abandoned an option to buy almost US$12 billion in data centre capacity from CoreWeave, a US company that specialises in supplying cloud computing capacity to developers of artificial intelligence (AI) projects. While Microsoft has reiterated its plan to spend US$80 billion on AI in 2025, it cancelled leases in February for several hundred megawatts of new capacity and stated that it may "strategically pace or adjust" its plans for new data centres. Faced with the high costs of AI projects, Microsoft has increased the price of its 365 software by up to 45 per cent to cover the inclusion of the Copilot generative AI chatbot. A recent study by the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative warned that existing ratepayers could end up bearing the costs of investments in power plants and transmission lines for new US data centres rather than technology companies such as Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Meta. (Semafor)

US index funds file for dismissal of Texas lawsuit: The three largest US index fund managers — BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street — have filed a joint motion in the US Eastern District Court of Texas seeking the dismissal of a lawsuit brought by 10 Republican states that alleged the funds violated federal antitrust law by restricting support for coal companies. The November 2024 lawsuit by the states alleged the three funds held significant stakes in nine major publicly traded coal companies, including more than 25 per cent of Peabody Energy, Arch Resources, CONSOL Energy, Alpha Metallurgical Resources, Black Hill Resources and Warrior Met Coal. The lawsuit alleges that the climate policies of the three financial firms reduced coal supply and increased prices, allowing the investors to "produce extraordinary revenue gains". The three funds described the states' claim as a "farfetched theory" that claimed they "conspired (without speaking with each other) to decrease coal output (which increased) by controlling the production decisions of coal companies (in which they each never held more than small minority stakes)". (ESG Dive)

Texas legislators aim to slow solar and batteries and boost gas capacity: A bill has passed the Texas Senate that would require half of all new power generation capacity to be ​"dispatchable generation other than battery energy storage". SB 388, if adopted by the House of Representatives and signed into law by Governor Greg Abbott, would dramatically slow the construction of new solar and wind generation and favour gas projects. An earlier version of the bill explicitly mentioned natural gas plants. New projects in the grid served by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas are overwhelmingly battery and solar projects with few gas plants. Energy analyst Doug Lewin estimates about 1000 MW of new battery and solar capacity has been added to the ERCOT grid each month for the last year. Coal accounts for about 16 per cent of generation in the state. (Canary Media, Renew Economy)

Trump shipping tariffs hit US coal exports: Coal stockpiles have increased due to uncertainty about a draft executive order by the Trump administration suggesting imposing a levy on any ships docking at US ports that are part of a fleet that includes Chinese-built or flagged ships. The draft order does not detail the amount of the levy, but an earlier proposal by the US Trade Representative's office suggested US$1.5 million per ship. In a March 12 letter to US Department of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Xcoal Energy & Resources CEO Ernie Thrasher said that shipowners have declined to supply ships for US coal exports. Thrasher argued that the scale of the fees under consideration could add up to 35 per cent to the cost of US-delivered coal and could force the curtailment of US coal exports within 60 days. US Exports of coal were estimated at 82 million tonnes in 2024, split evenly between thermal and metallurgical coal. (Reuters, Reuters)

IEA says heatwaves in China and India drove 2024 coal demand increase: The International Energy Agency's (IEA) Global Energy Review estimates global electricity consumption increased by 4.3 per cent in 2024, almost twice the rate of demand growth of the last decade. The IEA states the increase is demand followed record global temperatures driving air conditioning loads, with a 20 per cent increase in cooling degree days in 2024 compared to the 2000-202o average. (Cooling degree days is a metric to track cooling needs above a selected temperature threshold.) Other factors driving increased electricity consumption include the electrification of transport, increased data centre demand and industrial growth. The IEA estimated global coal demand increased by one per cent in 2024, or about 123 million tonnes, with heatwaves in India and China accounting for 90 per cent of the increased consumption. The IEA estimates metallurgical coal consumption fell by 0.5 per cent in 2024 due to declining steel production but with an overall slight increase in other industrial sectors due to expansion of the nickel sector in Indonesia and chemical production in China. The increase in coal consumption in 2024 was half the rate of increase in 2023. Electricity generation grew by more than 1200 terawatt hours (TWh) in 2024. Solar generation increased by 40 per cent or 480 TWh, with wind generation increasing by 15 per cent or 180 TWh. (Climate Home News, International Energy Agency)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 European NGOs call for an end to permits and investment in new coal-based steel production: A coalition of NGOs has called on the European Commission to drive a shift away from coal-based steel production by ending permitting for or investment in new-build or existing coal-fired blast furnaces. A report by a coalition of 28 civil society organisations, The State of the European Steel Transition, argues the European Union also needs to increase green hydrogen and renewable-powered production, boost steel recycling measures, increase scrap-based output and ensure a just transition for steel industry workers. The European steel industry accounts for about five per cent of the region's greenhouse gas emissions. The report argues that Europe is currently a leader in near-zero emission steel innovation, but China is restricting new blast furnace approvals and backing hydrogen-based direct iron reduction projects. Governments in the Middle East and North Africa region are also pursuing green steel production. The European Commission recently released its Commission's Steel and Metals Action Plan but excluded civil society organisations from the drafting process. (E3G and Beyond Fossil Fuels, E3G and Beyond Fossil Fuels [Pdf])

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Coal, Power Production and Corruption in South Africa: An Analysis, Centre for Business Ethics (CfBE) at the University of Pretoria's Gordon Institute, August 2024. (Pdf) (The Executive Summary is available here.)

This 52-page report reviews the role of corruption and criminal activities in the dysfunction of South Africa's state-owned power utility, Eskom.

links.text: Coal, Power Production and Corruption in South Africa: An Analysis

title: CoalWire 557, April 3, 2025
excerpt: Chinese data centres sitting idle; South African govt grants Eskom pollution exemptions.
content:
April 3, 2025.
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The recommendation of a Queensland Land Court judge against the granting of a mining lease for the expansion of the Ensham thermal coal mine makes for fascinating reading. Underpinning the judge's recommendation was deep scepticism that Sungela and Bowen Investment were really committed to implementing the emissions reduction measures the joint venture has announced.

The boom in power demand to cater for new data centres has cast a shadow over most emissions reduction strategies. In China, an industry body estimates that by the end of 2024 about 150 data centres had been built, but local news reports suggest many now lay idle with their sponsors struggling to survive. In the US, civil society groups fear that cut-price power deals brokered between utilities and data centre developers could inflate the Artificial Intelligence bubble at the expense of residential ratepayers.

In South Africa, the new Minister for Forestry, Fisheries, and the Environment, Dr Dion George, insisted that he hadn't given Eskom everything they wanted in granting five and nine-year exemptions from emissions control standards for more than 30,000 MW of coal plant capacity. While George insisted the exemptions, together with other conditions, "ensure accountability", the sorry history of Eskom's refusal to meet standards first announced in 2010 provides little comfort to the millions of people exposed to air pollution from the utility's coal plants.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 The economics behind Indonesia's coal gasification push are hard to justify

Four coal gasification projects in Sumatra and Kalimantan backed by Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto are unlikely to be economically viable, writes Ghee Peh from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

 

 China Is no climate saviour

Behind all the promises and signalling, the numbers don't lie: China is not going to drive a rapid transition away from fossil fuels at home or abroad. It may well be the case that what is happening in China is simply what is happening everywhere else: slow, long-term decarbonisation, write from Seaver Wang and Vijaya Ramachandran from the Breakthrough Institute on Foreign Policy.

 

 Deep fear in coal country: Trump administration cuts put region's miners and families on edge

After years of investigating hundreds of mining deaths and injuries, the Trump administration has moved to cancel the lease at the Mount Pleasant office of the Mine Safety and Health Administration in western Pennsylvania, write Michael D. Sallah, Mike Wereschagin and Jimmy Cloutier in the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Queensland judge recommends against granting coal lease: The Queensland Land Court has recommended against the granting of a new 25-year mining licence to allow the expansion of the Ensham thermal coal mine "until the applicants show real and significant progress towards mitigating their greenhouse gas emissions". The mine is owned by a joint venture between Sungela, a majority owned subsidiary of South African coal mining company Thungela, and Bowen Investment. The companies applied for a mining lease over an area with an estimated 85 million tonnes of coal resources with the intention of producing coal for 20 years. The lease drew three objections, including one from the Lock the Gate Alliance. Judge Peta Stilgoe noted in her ruling that the company had not submitted an emissions reduction management plan to the court. "What, if any, of the 19 measures identified in the [company's] submissions have the applicants actually done?" the judge asked. The Queensland Minister for Natural Resources and Mines, Daryl Last, makes the final decision on the mining lease and any conditions. (ABC News, Queensland Land Court)

 

 South African govt grants pollution exemptions for Eskom coal plants: South African Minister for Forestry, Fisheries, and the Environment, Dr Dion George, has granted exemptions from the Minimum Emissions Standards for Eskom's 3000 MW Duvha and 3600 MW Matla coal plants until they close in 2034. George also granted five-year exemptions from the pollution control standards for Eskom's 3654 MW Tutuka, 4116 MW Kendal, 3708 MW Lethabo, 4143 MW Majuba, 3990 MW Matimba and 4768 MW Medupi coal plants. The plants must comply with the MES standards by April 1, 2030. George also announced Eskom must establish air quality monitoring stations within eight months and produce a data-free alert app within eight months. Eskom is also required to publish real-time emissions data from its existing monitoring stations and complete a revised cost-benefit analysis on the installation of flue gas desulphurisation on the recently commissioned 4768 MW Medupi plant. The MES was announced in 2010, with existing plants required to comply with the emissions standards by April 1, 2015, but the government allowed applications for one-off five-year exemptions. In May 2024 then Minister Barbara Creecy granted Eskom's request to permit the Hendrina, Grootvlei, Arnot, Camden and Kriel plants to operate at current weaker standards until March 31, 2030. Two civil society groups, groundWork Trust and Earthlife Africa, have filed an appeal against Creecy's decision, arguing that "stringent air pollution protections" must be adopted as the plants are in the Highveld Priority Area. (Engineering News, Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment)

 

 Ohio House of Representatives repeals coal plant subsidy: The Ohio House of Representatives has repealed part of House Bill 6 from 2020 that guaranteed subsidies to the 1303 MW Clifty Creek plant in Indiana and the 1086 MW Kyger Creek coal plant in Ohio. The two plants have been operating since 1955. The Public Utility Commission of Ohio recently estimated that the state's electricity customers paid almost US$172 million in 2024 to subsidise the plants owned by the Ohio Valley Electric Corporation (OVEC), a joint venture between American Electric Power (AEP), Duke Energy, and AES Ohio. The Ohio Citizens Utility Board of Ohio, an NGO group, estimated the subsidy for the two plants could reach US$1.1 billion by 2030. A similar bill recently passed the Ohio Senate. Representatives of AEP, Duke Energy, AES Ohio and the Edison Electric Institute, a power utility lobby group, all provided testimony opposing the bills. (Ohio Capitol Journal, Energy and Policy Institute)

 

 Trump invites utilities and steel plants to seek pollution exemptions: The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has invited power utilities, iron and steel works and coke oven operators to request a two-year exemption from air pollution standards. A narrow provision of the Clean Air Act allows an exemption from pollution control standards in a national emergency and where pollution control technology is not available. Companies have until March 31, 2025 to request an exemption. The EPA invitation specifically identifies the Mercury and Air Toxics Standard, which sets limits on mercury, arsenic, and other pollutants emitted from coal and oil power plants of more than 25 megawatts of capacity. While most power utilities already comply with the standard, the EPA provided an email template for applicants requesting a statement on why the technology is not available and why an exemption is "in the national security interests" of the US. Iron and steel companies may also seek an exemption from a rule that primarily regulates manganese and lead emissions, while the regulation affecting coke ovens limits pollution by benzene, mercury, lead and arsenic. The Sierra Club said the administration's attempt to bypass regulations designed to protect public health is "outrageous". (Guardian, Environmental Protection Agency, Sierra Club)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: EnergyAustralia, a subsidiary of the Hong Kong-based CLP Group, was convicted and fined A$170,000 (US$107,000) after a fire at Yallourn brown coal power station in Victoria put workers "needlessly" at risk.

 

 Bulgaria: The 908 MW Maritsa East 3 lignite plant has closed down, with Contour Global laying off 130 of the 160 workers at the site.

 

 Europe: Greenhouse gas emissions from the European Union power sector fell by 16.5 per cent in 2024 compared to the preceding year, with coal generation declining by 50 terawatt hours.

 

 India: Adani Power has recommenced supplying electricity to Bangladesh from both 800 MW units at its Godda power station in Jharkhand. Adani cut exports from one unit in October after the Bangladesh Power Development Board fell behind on payments.

 

 India: Hundreds of villagers from Malu village in Assam protested against plans by Coal India subsidiary North Eastern Coalfields to construct a new coal dump near the village.

 

 Kosovo: The Ministry of Energy of Kosovo confirmed that it intends to redevelop the 680 MW Kosovo B lignite plant, extending the life of the project by 20 years.

 

 Spain: Five workers died, and four were seriously injured, in a methane explosion at the Cerredo mine owned by Blue Solving in Degana.

 

 US: The two leading contenders for the April 15 election for Oakland Mayor, Loren Taylor and Barbara Lee, have pledged to oppose the proposed coal export terminal in West Oakland.

 

 US: A coal industry-backed bill removing the headwaters of all streams and groundwater from Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet regulatory control has become law. Governor Andy Beshear initially vetoed the bill but the Republican-dominated legislature overrode this.

 

 Zimbabwe: Residents protesting against coal dust pollution blocked the road to the Hwange power station.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Chinese data centre boom stalls: After the central government announced the construction of AI infrastructure was a national priority and pressed provincial governments to support the sector, about 500 new data centre projects were announced in 2023 and 2024. The China Communications Industry Association Data Center Committee estimates that by the end of 2024, about 150 data centres were built. Local news outlets report that up to 80 per cent of new data centres are now sitting idle, with industry sources telling the MIT Technology Review that many companies are struggling to stay afloat. In late 2024, the International Energy Agency (IEA) noted that large data centres have power demands of 100 MW or more, and estimated they account for between two and four per cent of total electricity consumption in China, the US and Europe. They also warned that the concentration of new data centres in specific states or areas could strain local power networks and jeopardise the ability of states to meet climate targets due to rapid growth in electricity demand. (MIT Technology Review)

US group wants data centres to pay rate that covers costs: The Southwest Energy Efficiency Project (SWEEP), a group promoting energy efficiency in six south-western US states, wants power utilities to utilities to require new industrial or commercial loads, including data centres, of more than 50 MW to commit to contract rates sufficient to cover the costs of generation and transmission. SWEEP also wants all data centres to contract to buy their power requirements from renewables or net-zero supplies to avoid the risk of significant new demand entrenching new fossil fuel generation and undermining greenhouse gas emissions goals. A December 2024 report by Synapse Energy Economics for the Sierra Club estimated data centre growth in the PJM Interconnection region, the largest US wholesale power market covering 13 eastern US states and Washington DC, could increase annual load by 2040 by 28 per cent above a base case. The report estimated data centres could increase the net present value of total system costs from 2025-2040 by US$160 billion and increase residential power bills by almost 10 per cent. (Utility Dive, Synapse Energy Economics [Pdf])

Eskom connects the final Kusile unit to the grid: Eskom has connected the last of six 800 MW coal units at its Kusile coal plant, more than 17 years after the February 2008 final investment decision. The plant was initially estimated to cost 80 billion rand, but the current estimate is almost 161 billion rand (US$8.74 billion). Eskom said the unit will be subject to further "testing and optimisation" over the next six months before commencing commercial operation later in 2025. Energy analyst Chris Yelland said the substantial cost overruns probably made Kusile "the most expensive coal-fired power station" ever built. (My Broadband, Eskom)

NGO calls on banks to rule out funding for Harita's coal-based nickel plans: Market Forces has launched a public campaign urging a dozen banks to suspend financial support for the expansion of the Harita Group's coal-powered nickel refinery and smelter on Obi Island in North Maluku province in Indonesia. The Harita Group's nickel plant is supplied by the 890 MW PT Halmahera Persada Lygend Nickel Smelter power station, with an additional 1200 MW under construction. Market Forces urged supporters to write to the banks, including BNP Paribas, DBS and China Eximbank, to withhold any further financing if the company continues to build new fossil fuel power plants for Harita's plan to expand smelter capacity. The plant currently produces 120,000 tonnes of ferronickel per year, and a refinery capable of producing 55,000 tonnes of mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP). Harita is planning to expand production to 350,000 tonnes of ferronickel and 120,000 tonnes of MHP. (The Business Times [paywall], Market Forces)

Bangladesh rejects coal cargo contaminated by soil: The Coal Power Generation Company Limited (CPGCL) has rejected a shipment of 63,000 tonnes of coal for the 1200 MW Matabara coal plat at Cox's Bazaar due to the high soil content. An Indian supplier sourced the coal from Indonesia. An anonymous Chittagong Port Authority official said that the conveyor system used to unload the coal broke down due to excessive soil content. Meanwhile, the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) remains in dispute with Adani Power Jharkhand Limited over the power utility's claim that it was owed US$771 million as of the end of December 2024. The BPDB says that it believes the amount owed at the end of 2024 was US$630 million and that Adani's coal pricing methodology is flawed, resulting in a US141 million overestimate. Two weeks ago, a government-appointed committee recommended renegotiating the agreement with Adani for power from the 1600 MW Godda coal plant in Jharkhand. (Business Standard, Business Standard)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Appetite for risk: Glencore's growing coal portfolio, Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility, March 2025. (Pdf) (The Executive summary is here.)

This 31-page report assesses the risks of Glencore's growing coal portfolio, including its recent acquisition of Elk Valley Resources metallurgical coal operations in British Columbia.

Australia's coal mining emissions paradox, Ember, March 2025. (Pdf)

This 28-page report delves into the recent decline in coal mine methane emissions, noting the closure of some 'gassy' mines and the recent use of unverified emissions estimates methodology. The report also warns that proposed mine expansions of methane-rich underground mines could reverse the downward emissions trend.

title: CoalWire 558, April 10, 2025
excerpt: Global coal power capacity inches up; UK mine proposal dropped; Finnish coal plant closes; US-China tariff war to hit coal sector.
content:
April 10, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Global Energy Monitor's latest annual update on the global coal plant fleet has mixed news: the rate of new coal capacity added to the grid is well below the long-term average, but China and India have lots of new capacity under construction and proposed. New coal capacity continues to outstrip retirements, such as the recent closure of one of Finland's last remaining plants. Two wild card factors overhang the prospects for new coal power plants: the trade war President Trump has launched against allies and rivals alike and the uncertainty over how much power data centres will require. In the last week, Trump's announcements of on-again off-again tariffs on imports have triggered a significant correction by share markets and increased the prospect of a global recession.

The uncertainty about how Trump's trade war will play out and the shocks on the global economy are likely to affect energy projects for years to come. New data on the rapid deployment of wind and solar in 2024 reveals renewables grew rapidly. As for data centres, project developers hawk proposals to multiple locations, seeking to entice utilities to enter into cut-price deals. The impact of Trump's trade war, the prospect of lower growth rates and the likely emergence of less energy-intensive technologies suggest data centre demand may moderate, at least in the short term.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Africa must shun Trump's push to resurrect coal

Clean energy can be Africa's greatest success story, which is why its leaders must not fall for the pro-coal lobbying of the Trump administration, writes Mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa in Al Jazeera.

 

 Trump's attempts to bring back coal will fail

Given the realities of the US electricity market, whatever President Trump tries to do to bail out the coal industry is likely to fail again, writes Christy Walsh from NRDC.

 

 US utilities grapple with Big Tech's massive power demands for data centres

Tech companies are approaching multiple power utility providers within the same state or across several states seeking multiple bids for the same data centre project, inflating power demand outlooks, write Laila Kearney and Seher Dareen in Reuters.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Company abandons UK metallurgical coal mine proposal

West Cumbria Mining (WCM), a subsidiary of the privately-owned Australian company EMR Capital Investment, has abandoned its proposed metallurgical coal mine. WCM applied in February 2023 for a three-year mining licence to extract up to four million tonnes of coal a year. In mid-September 2024, the High Court ruled in favour of the appeal brought by Friends of the Earth (FOE) and South Lakes Action on Climate Change and overturned planning permission for the mine. In the wake of the court decision, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government was obliged to reconsider the application but requested a response from WCM and other interested parties by February 27 on their continued interest in the project. FOE met the deadline, but WCM did not respond. The ministry then set a new deadline for the company of March 26. The company confirmed that it had withdrawn its application on March 30. In a statement, Tony Bosworth said FOE is "delighted" the company has abandoned the project. "Congratulations to all the brilliant local campaigners who fought so powerfully to stop this mine," he said. (BBC, Friends of the Earth UK)

 

 Finnish coal plant closes four years before coal exit date

Helen Oy, a major energy utility, has closed the 177 megawatt (MW) Salmisaaari B coal and biomass plant in Helsinki four years earlier than required under Finnish law. In 2019, the Finnish parliament set a deadline for the country's remaining coal plants to close by the end of 2029. In the aftermath of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the utility delayed the closure of the plant by one year to April 1, 2025. Since 2010, data from Ember indicates that coal generation fell by 73 per cent to less than 1 per cent of the electricity mix. Over the same period, wind generation grew by 143 per cent. Finland has two operating coal plants: the 238 MW Vaskiluoto 2 unit that uses coal for about 30 per cent of its fuel and the 80 MW Martinlaakso 2 unit where coal use will end in 2026. (Reuters, Power Magazine, Beyond Fossil Fuels)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Global coal plant capacity creeps higher: Global coal plant capacity increased by 18,800 MW in 2024, with 44,100 MW of new capacity outpacing the 25,200 MW of coal plant closures, according to data in Global Energy Monitor's (GEM) Global Coal Plant Tracker. New coal plant capacity was added in a dozen countries, with China accounting for 70 per cent. The 44,100 MW of new capacity commissioned in 2024 was well below the annual average of 72,000 MW commissioned between 2004 and 2024. New coal capacity currently under construction is dominated by China (204,200 MW) and India (29,500 MW), with the remaining eight largest countries – including Indonesia, Vietnam and Bangladesh – accounting for just 19,000 MW. In the European Union, coal plant retirements quadrupled in 2024 compared to the preceding year to 11,000 MW, with the UK becoming the sixth country to complete a coal power phase-out since the 2015 Paris Agreement. GEM estimates that coal plant retirements in the 18 OECD countries need to jump to 70,000 MW a year to align with the goals of the Paris Agreement. (Reuters, Bloomberg, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Trump throws rescue line to beleaguered US coal industry: President Trump signed four Executive Orders aimed to delaying the retirement of coal power plants and supporting continued operation of associated coal mines. The first order directs the Department of Energy to revise its processes for invoking the emergency provisions of the Federal Power Act based on assessments of reserve margins. The most likely outcome is discounting the role of wind and solar capacity in contributing to grid security and boosting the reliance on fossil fuels in the power sector. The second order directs Attorney-General Pam Bondi to block states enforcing local laws addressing climate change, greenhouse gas emissions, environmental justice, environmental, social, and governance polices and collecting carbon taxes or penalties for past pollution. The order specifically mentions laws in New York and Vermont making fossil fuel companies liable for the costs of past emissions and California's cap and trade carbon tax scheme. The third order exempts 47 companies operating 66 coal plants from the Environmental Protection Agency's Mercury Air Toxics rule. The fourth order directs agencies to support coal mining, including through identifying where coal plants are "suitable for supporting AI data centres". The order also directs the International Development Finance Corporation and the Export-Import Bank of the United States to rescind any policies and other measures that limit their ability fund coal mining and coal power plants. (Guardian, The White House, The White House, The White House, The White House, Sierra Club)

 

 US city backs pro-climate candidates opposing power contract extension: Pro-climate candidates won all four open seats on the Naperville City Council, a rebuff for the Illinois Municipal Electric Agency (IMEA). IMEA currently supplies electricity to Naperville, a city of about 150,000 people on the outskirts of Chicago, with about 80 per cent of it sourced from coal power plants in the region, including the 1766 MW Prairie State Generating Station in Illinois. IMEA wants the council to agree by April 2030 to extend its current wholesale power supply agreement. IMEA's current supply agreement runs until 2035, but the utility is pressing the council for an extension that could run to 2055. The four winning candidates all promised they would not agree to a contract extension. The Public Utilities Advisory Board has called a meeting on April 8 to hear from the Naperville Environment and Sustainability Task Force, a community-based group, on key factors for the city's energy supply. (E & E News, Say No to Coal)

 

 Investigation into Chinese mine accident lambasts company officials: An investigation has identified 43 company officials and staff allegedly responsible for the December 2023 accident at the Kunyuan Coal Mine in Heilongjiang province. A steel cable attached to a train hauling five rail cars up to the surface of the underground mine snapped, with the wagons hurtling back down the slope. Twelve workers died in the accident, and a further 13 were injured. The investigation report found that the winches and steel cable were not appropriate to haul the wagons, nor should workers and cargo be in the same train. The investigation report found that mine managers attempted to cover up the accident, transferred and hid the bodies of dead workers and destroyed evidence. Mine managers also decided to rely on their inexperienced rescue crew rather than call in the professional rescue team as required by its emergency management plan. Fourteen company officers and officials in the local district's coal mine administration bureau are the subject of criminal investigations. (China Daily)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Four men were injured after a roof collapse at the Appin mine in New South Wales operated by GM3, a joint venture owned by Golden Energy and Resources and resources trader M Resources. The NSW Resources Regulator is investigating the accident.

 

 Australia: The recently elected Liberal National Party government announced a five-year plan to refurbish 700 MW Callide B and the 1400 MW Tarong coal fired power stations, extend the life of other coal plants beyond 2035 and revise the state's legislated target of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 75 per cent by 2035.

 

 Iran: At least seven mine workers were killed in what the Red Crescent described as a carbon monoxide gas leak at a coal mine near the village of Damghan in Semnan province.

 

 Poland: Greenpeace occupied an excavator in PGE's Turow lignite mine and called on the national government to accelerate the transition for the region.

 

 Poland: ENGIE Polska announced it will end the use of coal in its district heating plants in Slupsk and Zlotow.

 

 South Africa: Dozens of people protested outside the offices of African Rainbow Minerals and called on the company to rule out coal exports to Israel.

 

 UK: Asthma + Lung Scotland has urged the Scottish government to ban the use of coal for home heating. An estimated 14,000 homes in Scotland rely on coal for home heating.

 

 US: A&G, a coal mining company that is majority-owned by Republican US Senator Jim Justice, is scheduled to appear in a district court over its failure to comply with a 2023 consent decree requiring the rehabilitation of three abandoned coal mines.

 

 "The data centre process is to have a competitive bid from three companies in many markets. That one-third, automatically, is going to win, and two-thirds are going to drop out,"

said James Richmond, CEO of e2Companies, an energy management system provider.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Solar surge dominates growth in generation capacity: Global solar generation grew by 29 per cent in 2024, making it the fastest-growing source of new electricity for the twentieth year in a row, according to Global Energy Review 2025 by Ember, a UK-based energy think tank. Global solar power capacity reached two terawatts in 2024, double the amount installed by the end of 2022. China installed just over half of all new solar capacity in 2024. Wind generation grew to 8.1 per cent and solar 6.9 per cent of electricity demand and remain the two fastest growing sources of new supply. Nuclear power slumped to its lowest share of power generation in 45 years, accounting for nine per cent of electricity. Nuclear generation has increased by just 9 per cent since the turn of the century. Hydro generation accounted for 14.3 per cent of electricity in 2024, an increase of just over two-thirds since 2000. However, existing hydro projects in some countries were affected by drought conditions. New large-scale hydro projects often encounter strong community opposition due to significant environmental and social impacts. Ember estimates electric vehicles, data centres and heat pumps increased global electricity demand by 0.7 per cent in 2024, a marginal increase on 2023. (Ember)

Trump tariffs carve out exemptions for coal imports: US President Donald Trump has exempted a range of coal products from new import tariffs, including thermal and metallurgical coals and coke. On April 2, Trump announced a range of "reciprocal tariffs" on a wide range of countries, triggering dramatic declines share values in many countries, prompting leading commentators to warn of slowing global growth rates or a recession triggered by a global trade war. Trump subsequently said he would suspend increased tariffs for 90 days for countries that had not retaliated, settling back on a blanket 10 per cent tariff. In a rapid series of announcements, Trump increased tariffs on Chinese goods, with China retaliating. The current state of play is that China has imposed tariffs of 84 per cent on US imports, with Trump increasing the tariffs on Chinese goods to 125 per cent. China imported US$1.52 billion worth of coal and about US$1 billion worth of iron and steel from the US in 2024, according to S&P Global data. China's tariffs will particularly affect US metallurgical coal exporters, with the share prices of companies such as Peabody, Core Natural Resources and Ramaco Resources falling more than the S&P 500 index. (Argus, S & P Global, The White House [Pdf])

Drummond cuts production at its Colombian coal mines: Drummond, a controversial US-headquartered thermal coal company, announced it is cutting production at its Pribbenow and El Descanso open cut mines in Cesar province in northern Colombia. Drummond said production cuts follow slowing demand, a low share of output contracted to customers in 2025 and growing stockpiles, including at its export terminal, Puerto Drummond. The port can export up to 60 million tonnes of coal a year and stockpile 1.5 million tonnes. Drummond, a privately owned company, disclosed limited information on its plans but warned that if current market conditions persist, it will announce further cuts later this year. Glencore announced two weeks ago that it plans to cut coal production at its Cerrejon mine in Colombia by between 5 and 10 million tonnes a year due to the decline in thermal coal prices in the export market. About 54 million tonnes of thermal coal was exported from Colombia in 2024. (BNamericas)

BHP pondered offloading met coal and iron ore divisions in the late 2020s: BHP considered spinning off its Australian metallurgical coal and iron ore divisions in a bid to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions exposure and focus on growth commodities of potash and copper, according to Reuters. Three sources that spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity said that CEO Mike Henry considered offloading the declining coal and iron ore businesses later this decade but decided against it, in part as major companies began to back away from moves to reduce their climate exposure. BHP Mitsubishi Alliance (BMA), a 50:50 joint venture between BHP and Mitsubishi Development operates five metallurgical coal mines in Queensland that it estimates will produce between 33 and 38 million tonnes in 2024-2025. BHP estimates it will produce between 13 and 15 million tonnes of thermal coal from its New South Wales Energy Coal division and between 255 and 165 million tonnes of iron ore from its West Australian mines. BHP has reduced its thermal coal capacity dramatically in recent years but downplayed the risk to metallurgical coal and iron ore from new approaches to steel production. (Reuters)

Greek utility unveils plans data centre for lignite plant site: PPC has unveiled a plan to establish a new 300 MW data centre by 2027 at the site of the Agios Dimitrios lignite power plant in Western Macedonia. PPC, which the Greek government holds a 34 per cent stake in, announced construction would begin "once agreements are in place with the hyperscalers who will operate it". PPC said the project could expand later to a 1000 MW data centre. Two 300 MW lignite units at the site were retired in August 2025 with the remaining three units with a combined capacity of 995 MW scheduled to retire this year. PPC said it will convert the 660 MW Ptolemaida 5 lignite plant to operate as a 350 MW open-cycle natural gas unit until the end of 2027. PPC said it will upgrade the Ptolemaida 5 plant to a 500 MW combined-cycle gas unit once the data centre project proceeds. PPC is investing 1.2 billion (US$1.3 billion) in 2130 MW of solar capacity on former lignite mines and 940 million (US$1 billion) in 860 MW of battery and pumped hydro energy storage projects. Coal accounted for less than six per cent of electricity generation in Greece in 2024, according to data collated by Ember. (CEEnergyNews, PPC)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Lethal landscape: cuts to Ffos-y-fran mine restoration puts community at risk, Coal Action Network, March 2025. (Pdf)

This 17-page report provides a detailed review of the Coal Action Network's objections to Merthyr Tydfil Council's proposed downgrading of the rehabilitation requirements for the Ffos-y-Fran opencast coal mine in Wales.

Resources and energy quarterly: March 2025, Australian Department of Industry, Science and Resources, March 2025. (Pdf)

This quarterly report includes detailed chapters on key trends in production and consumption of thermal coal, metallurgical coal and steel.

links.text: Lethal landscape: cuts to Ffos-y-fran mine restoration puts community at risk

title: CoalWire 559, April 17, 2025
excerpt: China opens the door for more coal plants; AI’s energy, water and funding challenges; Trump cuts eliminate health support for US coal miners.
content:
April 17, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The latest plan by China's National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration backing more coal power plant construction to at least 2027 reflects the power of the country's coal lobby and provincial governments. The Trump administration's onslaught on US climate policy, coal mining safety regulations and clean energy transition similarly reflects the policy wish list of the domestic fossil fuel industries. Trump has touted growing power demand for data centres as justification for propping up the declining fortunes of the coal power plants.

The International Energy Agency's (IEA) new report on the implications of Artificial Intelligence for the energy sector is remarkably upbeat about the technology despite its potentially significant impact on power demand and greenhouse gas emissions. The IEA acknowledges the rapid expansion of data centres will drive an increase in coal and gas generation, at least in the short to medium term. In many respects, the IEA's report is similar in tone to the agency's 2009 boosterish report that insisted there could be 100 large-scale carbon and capture plants built between 2010 and 2020. It didn't happen.

The IEA's report on AI assumes that the sector is financially viable. Technology writer Ed Zitrons analysis of the financial challenges facing OpenAI, a key player in the industry, warns of potential knock-on impacts for other major companies in the sector. His argument is undoubtedly a dissenting view on the future of some AI companies, but the US technology sector is well known for its ability to over-hype new technologies. One of the less discussed aspects of the AI boom is the high water requirements for data centre cooling and the likely impacts on host communities, especially in water-scarce regions.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 The power industry must oppose Trump's coal bailout ... again

The executive order threatens to conflict with existing methods for accrediting generators, assessing resource adequacy, securing sufficient generation and setting wholesale prices. It's also illegal, writes Ari Peskoe from Harvard Law School in Utility Dive.

 

 Reopening closed US coal plants makes no economic sense

The plan by President Trump to restart coal plants ignores the fact that most of the still-operating facilities are running far below their capacity. Restarting coal plants makes no economic sense, write Dennis Wamsted and Seth Feaster from the Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis.

 

 With US utilities quietly dismantling diversity, equity and inclusion programs, black households pay the price

Monopoly US utilities are retreating from racial justice pledges made in 2020, signalling, as one analyst said, 'Black lives mattered, briefly, as a marketing strategy', writes Adam Mahoney in Capital B News.

 

 OpenAI is a systemic risk to the tech industry

OpenAI has the only meaningful userbase in generative AI, and this entire hype-cycle has been driven by its success, meaning any deterioration (or collapse) of OpenAI will tell the market that generative AI is not the next hyper-growth market, and its underlying economics do not make sense, writes Ed Zitron in his technology newsletter, Where's Your Ed At.

 

 Big tech's new data centres will take water from the world's driest areas

Amazon, Microsoft and Google are planning hundreds of data centres in the US and across the globe, with a potentially massive impact on populations already living with water scarcity, write Luke Barratt and Costanza Gambarini from SourceMaterial in the Guardian.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Chinese agency clears path for more coal capacity: China's National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and the National Energy Administration (NEA), two powerful central government agencies, have released a new plan backing the continued construction of new coal capacity until at least 2027 but with some conditions. The agencies propose allowing new plants in regions where there is a shortfall of peak capacity, are required to stabilise the grid and have lower greenhouse gas emissions per kilowatt hour than the average of the current coal fleet. The previous plan backed reducing coal consumption in the 2026-2030 period. China currently has 204,000 megawatts (MW) of new coal capacity under construction, according to Global Energy Monitor's Global Coal Plant Tracker. A further 212,000 MW of proposed new coal capacity, including more than 120,000 MW already permitted but not yet under construction. Power generation from coal and gas fell by 4.7 per cent in the first quarter of 2025 and declined by 2.3 per cent in March, according to data from the National Bureau of Statistics. The decline in thermal generation, which is predominantly coal power, is due to increased solar, wind, hydro and nuclear generation. (Reuters, Reuters)

 

 Trump cuts eliminate health support for US coal miners: The Trump administration has terminated the roles of 25 people who ran the Coal Workers' Health Surveillance Program that provided free black lung screening services for coal miners, training for doctors and approved job transfers for miners with respiratory diseases. Congress established the program in 1969 with the aim of detecting black lung disease. The legislation also granted miners the right to work in roles with lower dust exposure. A West Virginia lawyer, Sam Petsonk, has filed a class action lawsuit against Robert F. Kennedy Jr, the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, seeking the reinstatement of the service. In a separate development, the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) announced a four-month delay in enforcement of the new silica dust rule for 60 coal mine operators. The rule aims to reduce miners' exposure to silica dust in coal mines. The "temporary enforcement pause" is in effect until August 18, 2025. (NPR, Mine Safety and Health Administration)

 

 Resident hospitalised after gas explosion linked to US underground mine: Kimberly Thomas was hospitalised with severe burns after the flame of a cigarette lighter triggered an explosion and fire in her house on April 5. Her family home sits above Leer Mine in West Virginia, which Core Natural Resources owns. The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection issued a "imminent harm cessation order" on the Leer Mine on April 7, forcing the company to suspend mining operations temporarily. Inspectors from the department said they detected methane "at explosive levels" when they visited the house on April 5. In March 2024, a gas explosion killed 74-year-old homeowner W.M. Griffice and seriously injured his grandson in the house above the Oak Grove Mine near Birmingham, Alabama. The Director of the Alabama Surface Mining Commission, Kathy Love, acknowledged in a letter to a federal agency that the explosion was "likely" caused by the ignition of methane produced by underground coal mining. In January, Love wrote to mining companies in the state requiring they submit plans by March 31 that included measures to monitor methane gas in and near houses above their mines. After a letter from the Alabama Mining Association, Love granted the companies a six-month extension until September 30 to submit their subsidence and methane management plans. (Inside Climate News, Inside Climate News)

 

 IEA estimates surging power demand for data centres: The International Energy Agency (IEA) forecasts that global power demand for data centres could more than double to about 3 per cent by 2030, mainly to cater for Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. The IEA estimates electricity demand for AI alone could more than quadruple. The agency estimates that the US accounts for about 45 per cent of current data centre power demand, followed by China with 25 per cent and Europe with a 15 per cent share. The agency estimates data centre demand has grown by 12 per cent a year since 2017, with future growth predominately met by renewables and gas. However, the IEA estimates coal generation currently provides about 30 per cent of data centre electricity demand and, in its base case scenario, could grow rapidly to more than 200 terawatt hours by around 2030. The agency extols the potential benefits of AI applications, including in the broad energy sector, and suggests data centre demand could accelerate the deployment of new small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) by 2030. Most analysts suggest SMRs are unlikely before the early to mid-2030s and that the economics are highly uncertain. The IEA acknowledges potential energy efficiency gains in AI technologies but that in a rapid growth scenario, coal would play a significant role in the short to medium term in supplying demand in the US and China. (Guardian, International Energy Agency)

 

 
 "The Trump administration can't force utilities to buy dirtier, more expensive fuels they don't want A flurry of executive orders won't save the coal industry,"

said Rob Jackson from Stanford University and chair of the Global Carbon Project.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Queensland state-owned CS Energy revealed that the 420 MW Callide C coal unit will be offline until the end of May after a blast caused the sudden shutdown of the unit. The accident came just days after the new conservative government said it would extend the life of the 700 MW Callide B plant by three to four years.

 

 China: Five workers were killed and nine others injured in a carbon dioxide outburst accident at a coal mine in Lanzhou in Gansu province. An outburst occurs when gas violently escapes from a coal seam, expelling coal, carbon dioxide and methane.

 

 China: Chinese imports of coal dropped by 0.6 per cent in the first quarter of 2025. Imports in January and February were up two per cent on the year before but fell by six per cent in March due to large stockpiles and low domestic prices.

 

 India: The Indian government commenced the auction process for three coal seam gas projects, two in West Bengal and one in Gujarat.

 

 Japan: The Japan Bank for International Cooperation has agreed to provide US$240 million in finance for JFE Steel's acquisition of a 10 per cent stake in the Blackwater coal mine in Queensland. A further US$400 million is being co-financed by Mizuho, MUFG and SMBC.

 

 Malaysia: BloombergNEF estimates that solar paired with batteries could become cheaper than new coal capacity by 2028 and more viable than co-firing coal units with ammonia.

 

 US: The US Environmental Protection Agency is planning to eliminate long-standing requirements for power utilities, coal miners and other polluters to report their greenhouse gas emissions.

 

 US: Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum visited two Warrior Met mines in Alabama, along with a Fox News crew, promoting President Trump's announcements supporting the coal industry. Burgum did not address the thousands of federal safety violations issued against the company.

 

 "New demand from data centres is a significant near-term driver of growth for natural gas-fired and coal-fired generation, through both higher utilisation of existing assets and new power plants",

states the International Energy Agency in its new Energy and AI report.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Trump administration cuts to hit funding for energy programs: About half of the staff at the Department of Energy's (DOE) US$400 billion Loan Programs Office has reportedly applied for voluntary redundancy packages. A Trump-appointed group headed by Elon Musk is implementing wide-ranging cuts to US government services, with DOE staff offered pay until the end of September if they stand down now. Sources suggest that about 2700 of DOE's 16,000 workforce have applied for redundancies, including about 100 from the loans office, which gained additional funding for new energy projects under former President Joe Biden. Anonymous sources said that up to 80 per cent of employees within the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations have applied for a redundancy. Trump's appointee as Secretary of Energy, Chris Wright, wants the agency to focus on support for coal plants and nuclear technology. (Bloomberg)

Peabody reconsidering Anglo deal after fire at Australian mine: Peabody Energy is reviewing its November 2024 agreement to buy four Queensland metallurgical coal mines from Anglo American after an underground fire at one of the mines. The agreement stated the intent to complete the transaction by mid-2025 but the outbreak of a fire has resulted in the temporary closure of the Moranbah North coal mine. Part of the original deal was for Peabody to pay an additional US$450 million if the mothballed Grosvenor underground mine recommenced production and operated for two years. The Grosvenor mine was closed after a significant fire in late June 2024. Following the most recent fire, Peabody stated that it is "reviewing all options" about the purchase of the mines. The completion of the purchase will make Peabody Energy one of the world's largest seaborne metallurgical coal exporters, with a projected production of 19 – 20 million tonnes in 2026. Peabody Energy currently has four metallurgical coal mines in Australia and the Shoal Creek mine in Alabama. (Mining.com, ABC News, Peabody Energy, Anglo American)

Polish coal utility racks up significant loss: Jastrzebska Spoka Weglowa (JSW), the 55 per cent Polish state-owned coal mining company, has reported an annual loss of 7.24 billion zloty (US$1.92 billion) for 2024 due to declining coal prices, a fall in production and a 6.4 billion zlotys (US$1.7 billion) write-off. JSW is the largest metallurgical coal producer in Europe and produced 12 million tonnes of metallurgical coal and 3 million tonnes of coke in 2024, down 9.3 per cent and 8.6 per cent, respectively. JSW reports that it experienced a 19 per cent decline in the price of hard coking coal and a 20 per cent fall in the blended thermal coal price compared to 2023. JSW recently applied for a new exploration licence over the Debiensko 1 coal deposit adjoining the company's Knurow Szczygłowice mine and has applied to extend its mining licence for the Borynia mine until 2042 and extract methane from the site. (Mining.com, Notes from Poland, JSW)

Indian state-owned utility plans to increase coal capacity target: A senior executive from the National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC), India's state-owned power utility, anonymously told media outlets that the utility intends to add a further 4000 MW of new coal capacity on top of the current aim of 26,000 MW of new capacity by 2031-32. NTPC currently generates about one-quarter of India's electricity and operates a fleet of 27 coal plants with a capacity of more than 53,000 MW. NTPC is also a joint venture partner in subsidiaries that operate another 10 coal plants with 9004 MW of capacity. NTPC, which produced more than 45 million tonnes of coal from its five mines in the year to the end of March, aims to increase production to 50 million tonnes in the current financial year. NTPC's renewable energy subsidiary is planning to have 19,000 MW of renewable projects by 2026-27 and rapidly expand into nuclear generation. (Financial Express, Economic Times)

Australian coal industry-backed group pulls election ads: Australians for Prosperity, a coal industry front group, has deleted a series of advertisements published on its social media accounts over the last two months after the Australian Electoral Commission contacted the group over unauthorised advertisements against pro-climate candidates. Under Australian electoral law, groups publishing political advertisements must include the name and address of the person who has authorised the material. The now-deleted advertisements included vox-pop interviews with residents on local issues. But several of those interviewed said they weren't told they were for advertisements and objected to how the group edited their comments. Coal Australia, a lobby group for coal companies including Peabody Energy, Whitehaven and Yancoal, has contributed A$725,000 to Australians for Prosperity. The Australian election is on May 3. (ABC News)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 UK government passes legislation forcing steel mill to remain operating

The UK government convened an emergency Saturday sitting of parliament to pass legislation granting the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, the power to order Jingye to continue operating the Scunthorpe steel mill. Reynolds told parliament that the government had negotiated with Jingye, a Chinese steel company, since it was elected in June 2024 and offered "substantial" support to keep Britain's sole remaining primary steel mill operating. However, he said Jingye intended to cancel existing orders for materials for the plant and unilaterally close it. The legislation provides for criminal penalties against company executives if they shut the plant. While the government said it hoped for private sector investment to keep the plant operating, it acknowledged the most likely option was nationalisation, with a decision likely within the next two weeks. Sangeeth Selvaraju from the London School of Economics said blast furnaces are not viable in the UK due to high energy costs and competition with Chinese and Indian steel imports. Jingye bought British Steel in 2019 and reportedly rejected a recent government offer of 500 million (US$658 million) in support. (Guardian, Guardian)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Satellite analysis identifies 40% more methane from Australian coal mines, Ember, April 2025.

This report draws on satellite data to estimate that Australia's coal mine emissions for the 2020 and 2021 financial years are about 40 per cent higher than official government estimates.
