title: CoalWire 560, April 24, 2025
excerpt: Vietnam boosts renewables role in power plan; high mercury levels found near Indian power plants; Trump grants pollution exemption to about one-third of the US coal fleet.
content:
April 24, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Vietnam's latest power development plan aims for a massive expansion of power generating capacity, with solar and wind accounting for the bulk of new supply. It is a marked shift from the 2023 draft of the plan. While the latest plan suggests a reduced share of coal-based generation, it estimates there will still be a marginal increase in coal capacity. The wild card factor is whether the target 10 per cent per annum increase in economic growth comes to pass, especially with growing uncertainty about the fallout from President Trump's tariffs and especially the trade war with China.

The suite of announcements by the Trump administration are reverberating across the coal and steel sectors. More than a thousand workers at steel mills and iron ore mines in the US and Canada have been laid off due to the tariff war and reduced auto sector demand for steel. Environmental groups are bracing for rumoured moves to strip some NGOs of their tax-exempt status. A raft of utilities were granted a two-year exemption from US pollution control standards for power plants, and looser rules on coal ash management are likely.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Trump's Environmental Protection Agency eyes looser rules for handling coal ash

Power utility lobbying of the Trump administration to weaken the regulation of coal ash disposal is beginning to gain ground despite risks to the environment and public health, writes Michael Phillis in the Associated Press.

 

 HBO's 'The Dark Money Game' spotlights FirstEnergy's Ohio scandal

The premiere of HBO's new documentary "The Dark Money Game" shines a spotlight on FirstEnergy's bribes-for-bailouts scheme in Ohio, writes Dave Anderson for the Energy and Policy Institute.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 US environmental NGOs brace for Trump move against nonprofits: Internal Trump administration sources have told journalists that the Department of Justice and White House officials are preparing an executive order targeting the tax-exempt status of nonprofit groups opposing the expansion of coal, oil and gas production. After President Trump announced plans to rescind the tax-exempt status of Harvard University, he said nonprofit status has been "abused" by other groups too, and, when pressed on whether he meant environmental groups, he said, "could be". Todd Paglia, the executive director of Stand.earth, said Trump's suggestion would fail to survive legal challenges. "You don't go after people that are having no impact," he said. Initial reports suggested that the Trump administration planned to announce an executive order on April 22, Earth Day. However, no announcement was made. A White House official told Politico that "no such orders are being drafted or considered at this time". (Bloomberg, Inside Climate News, Politico)

 

 Trump grants pollution exemption to about one-third of the US coal fleet: President Donald Trump granted two-year exemptions from the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) rule for about 71,000 MW of coal capacity, about 37 per cent of the capacity of the entire US coal fleet. The most recent MATS standards were unveiled in April 2024 during the Biden administration and cut allowable mercury emissions from lignite plants by 70 per cent and a 67 per cent reduction in allowable metal emissions from all coal plants. The US Supreme Court rejected a challenge against the rule by a coalition of Republican states and fossil fuel companies. In mid-April, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) invited power utilities, iron and steel works and coke oven operators to request a two-year exemption from air pollution standards. The EPA's publication of the list revealed that the largest beneficiaries of the exemption are Southern Company, with about 11,285 MW; NRG, with about 7100 MW exempted; and the government-owned Tennessee Valley Authority, with about 6660 MW exempted. The Sierra Club said the exemptions would have significant public health impacts on communities downwind from the country's dirtiest coal plants. (Utility Dive, Environmental Protection Agency [Pdf], Sierra Club)

 

 Former US Senator appointed coal company director: Ramaco Resources, a coal company that operates mines in West Virginia and Virginia, has appointed former West Virginia Senator Joe Manchin as an independent director. The company produced about 3.5 million tonnes of coal in 2024. Manchin originally won the Senate seat for West Virginia as a conservative Democrat but turned independent in early 2024 before deciding not to recontest the seat at the election last year. Republican coal baron Jim Justice won the seat. In a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Ramaco Resources stated that Manchin will earn US$125,000 a year plus 10,560 shares that will vest at the end of next year. The company disclosed it would enter into a US$10,000 per month consulting agreement with Manchin Partners, LLC, for "strategic advisory services to the Company including in public policy, energy, and technology matters". Manchin also earns income from Enersystems, a coal company he founded but which is managed by his son. Enersystems buys low-grade waste coal for resale to coal power plants. (Ramaco Resources, Ramaco Resources [Pdf])

 

 Report finds high mercury levels in water near Indian lignite mines: A report submitted to the National Green Tribunal (NGT) by the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board (TNPCB) reported mercury at up to 115 times more than allowable levels in water bodies and up to 62 times higher than permitted in groundwater samples taken near Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC)'s coal plants and lignite mines in Cuddalore district. TNPCB collected 17 water samples around the plants and mines on December 17, 2024. The NGT requested the report after Poovulagin Nanbargal and Manthan Adhyayan Kendra revealed pollution near NLC's 3640 MW Neyveli coal plant and the 1200 MW IL&FS Tamil Nadu Power Company plant and the associated mines. Of the 17 samples collected, 15 revealed mercury levels above the permissible limit. However, TNPCB said that as the water bodies are not classed for drinking water or irrigation use, the high levels of pollution were not breaches of licence conditions. Poovulagin Nanbargal challenged the TNPCB's view on the classification of the water sources, arguing that several of the water bodies are known as drinking water supplies and that the government should undertake a health assessment of residents. The final NGT hearing on the matter is scheduled for June 12. (The News Minute)

 

 Indian utilities sign MOU for 1600 MW expansion of existing coal plant: Coal India and the Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) announced a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding to establish a 50:50 per cent joint venture to develop a 1600 MW expansion of the Chandrapura Thermal Power Station in Jharkhand. DVC is a state-owned utility that operates both hydro and coal plants in West Bengal and Jharkhand. Coal India subsidiaries will supply coal for the plant expansion from nearby mines. The existing Chandrapura plant comprises two 250 MW coal units commissioned in 2011 with three smaller older units retired in 2017 and 2020. (Coal India [Pdf])

 

 Protest shuts down New Zealand coal mine: Seventy environmentalists occupied part of Bathurst Resources mothballed Escarpment metallurgical coal mine to protest against the company's plan to revive the mine. Protestors also occupied the bucket cableway system at the nearby coal transport buckets at the company's nearby Stockton Mine, an active mining site that the company wants to extend to include the Escarpment mine and produce about 20 million tonnes of coal over 25 years. The company has applied for fast-track approval of the project by the conservative National Party government. (Newsroom, Ministry of the Environment, 350 Aotearoa, 350 Aotearoa)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Africa: The Africa Solar Industry Association said about 9000 MW of is currently under development across the continent, up from 2500 MW in 2024. Algeria, Angola, Egypt, South Africa and Zambia account for 70 per cent of the new capacity under construction.

 

 Philippines: The Department of Energy has exempted Meralco's proposed 1200 MW Atimonan plant and the 73 MW Toledo project from the moratorium on the construction of new coal plants.

 

 South Africa: Sasol will cut coal production by two million tonnes to 28 to 30 million tonnes and increase imports as it completes the conversion of its Twistdraai export plant to a destoning unit. The destoning plant will process 10 million tonnes of coal a year to improve the quality of supply for the Secunda coal to oil and chemicals plant.

 

 US: West Virginia Republican Senator Shelley Capito wants Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. to reinstate funding for the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, which sacked three-quarters of its staff, including programs aimed at detecting and preventing black lung disease among coal miners.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Vietnam's revised power plan backs expanded role for wind and solar: Vietnam has finalised its Power Development Plan VIII (PDP8), significantly increasing the total installed capacity by 80,000 MW to 236,000 MW by 2030 and boosting the role of solar and wind. The plan assumes Vietnam achieves the target economic growth rate of 10 per cent per annum. The PDP8 sets of target of 73,000 MW of solar and 38,000 MW of onshore wind capacity by 2030. The 2023 version of the plan proposed 12,900 MW of solar and 21,000 MW of onshore wind by 2030, targets clean energy groups and international investors said were unrealistically low. The plan restates the aim of phasing out coal by 2050,. The plan proposes increasing solar and onshore wind capacity to 296,000 MW and 230,000 MW, respectively. The government has also endorsed plans for up to 6400 MW of new nuclear capacity by 2035 and a further 8000 MW by 2050, with Russia and Japan leading contenders to build the new plants. Under the plan, coal generation would account for between 13.1 per cent and 16.9 per cent of electricity generation. However, despite a decrease in coal's share of generation from the 2023 target of 20 per cent, total coal capacity would increase marginally from 30,127 MW to 31,055 MW by 2030. The plan also proposes the establishment of between 6000 MW and 17,000 MW of offshore wind capacity between 2030 and 2035. The plan proposes to cater for power imports of between 9,360 MW to 12,100 MW from Laos and increase imports from China. (Reuters, Vietnam.Vn, France24)

Asian thermal coal prices slump: The benchmark Newcastle thermal coal spot price has slumped to US$94.25 a tonne, the lowest level since May 2021. Thermal coal prices in the Asian market have been affected by warmer northern hemisphere winter weather, tempering power demand for heating and increased Chinese production, causing large stockpiles at coal import terminals. Steve Hulton from the energy consultancy Rystad Energy said prices were unlikely to fall further as "there are producers at the top end of the cost curve who are hurting at prices below $100 per tonne". Chinese coal prices are also near the long-term contract rates set by the government. However, Trump's punitive tariffs on Chinese exports have added to uncertainty about seaborne thermal coal prices. The Standard & Poor's 500 index, a benchmark of diversified US stocks, has declined by almost 10 per cent since the start of the year. (Mining.com)

New York state pension fund drops four coal companies from banned list: The New York State Common Retirement Fund, the superannuation fund for employees of the New York State government with more than US$267 billion under management, has removed four coal companies from its investment exclusion list. A spokesperson for the fund declined to detail the reasons for the change of status of the four companies. The four companies the fund is now eligible to invest in are Indonesian coal producers PT Adaro Energy Indonesia and PT Delta Dunia Makmur, South African coal miner Thungela Resources and Australian coal company Whitehaven Coal. The State Comptroller Thomas P. DiNapoli said that the changes followed the fund's annual review of fossil fuel exposure with the threshold for coal producers set at those that earn more than 10 per cent of revenues from thermal coal mining. However, the review has not been made public. The fund added eight fossil fuel companies to the list, including NLC India and Yancoal Australia. (Responsible Investor, Office of the New York State Comptroller)

BHP gains four-year extension to life of NSW mine: The New South Wales government has agreed to a four-year extension of mining to June 2030 at BHP's Mt Arthur thermal coal mine in the Hunter Valley. In 2021, BHP applied to extend the operation of the mine from 2026 to 2045 but later withdrew the request. In 2024, New South Wales Energy Coal, a 100 per cent BHP subsidiary, produced 15.3 million tonnes of coal from the Mt Arthur mine. BHP is liable for the cost of rehabilitating the sprawling 7000-hectare open-cut mine site that it has operated since 2002. BHP announced a one-year study by ACCIONA Energa on the option of converting part of the Mt Arthur site into a pumped hydro project. For BHP, the development of a pumped hydro project would provide short-term construction work for part of the company's current 2000-strong workforce, utilise part of the existing site infrastructure and reduce rehabilitation costs. (Mining.com, BHP)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 US and Canadian steel producers cut staff on tariffs fallout: US and Canadian steel and iron ore producers have announced production cuts and staff retrenchments as President Trump's tariffs on imports have hit the steel and auto sectors. In the US, Cleveland-Cliffs announced the retrenchment of 600 workers at its Dearborn steel plant in Michigan and a further 630 layoffs at two iron ore mines in Minnesota. The company said the cuts are a response to the "current market environment", which has seen a decline in car production. The company's Chairman, President and CEO, Lourenco Goncalves, is a supporter of Trump's tariffs and suggested steel production at Dearborn would resume when auto production increases in the US to avoid the increased cost of imports. In February, the Canada Metal Processing Group announced that it planned to retrench 140 staff due to the impact of US tariffs and expected lower steel demand. 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

SteelWatch Explainers, SteelWatch, 2025.

SteelWatch, an international NGO promoting the decarbonisation of the steel sector, has produced a handy series of briefing papers in English and Japanese on key issues facing the industry. The explainers are on hydrogen, auto-quality green steel, steel and climate, metallurgical coal and green iron.

links.text: Office of the New York State Comptroller)

title: CoalWire 561, May 1, 2025
excerpt: Amazon trims international AI plans; New York City comptroller puts fund managers on notice; Philippines agency withdraws coal plant exemption pending review.
content:
May 1, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

All is not well with some of the key companies catering for the rapid growth of the AI sector. This week, a US financial analyst reports that Amazon has trimmed its plans for leasing space in new data centres, especially outside the US. It is a move that comes as a major company supplying servers for AI clients reported slowing sales. Are these announcements a sign of things to come or just a temporary setback for the AI sector? At what point will utilities reassess plans for keeping old coal plants online and building new fossil fuel projects?

The New York City Comptroller, a key adviser to three pension funds for state civil servants, has put major fund managers on notice to expect increased scrutiny of their decarbonisation plans. Lander's announcement is a response to the successful campaign by President Trump and his supporters in pressing fund managers to retreat from pro-climate policies. RE100, which encourages corporate members to ensure they source all of their electricity requirements from renewables, has amended its technical standards to rule out electricity from coal plants co-fired with other fuels.

In India, some government officials are lobbying to scrap the requirement to install flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) units. A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air finds that, despite the announcement of the standards in late 2015, only 44 of the 537 coal units have installed FGD plants. Those with the technology, the report warns, emit sulphur dioxide at "dangerously high levels". Another report estimates that if India installed 33,000 MW of new renewable energy, it could avoid spending about US$826 million every year on thermal coal imports during the summer months.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 The hidden journey of Ukrainian coal stolen by Russia — and who profits from it

Over the past year, Russian occupation authorities transferred two dozen seized Ukrainian coal mines to five private companies, most of which have set up illicit exports of the stolen Ukrainian coal to the global market, writes Alisa Yurchenko in the Kyiv Independent.

 

 Indonesia defies global coal retreat with captive plant boom

Captive coal plants built for industry have tripled in capacity since 2019, exploiting a loophole in Indonesia's coal moratorium and undermining its climate pledges under the Paris Agreement and Just Energy Transition Partnership, writes Hans Nicholas Jong in Mongabay.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Philippines agency withdraws coal plant exemption pending review: The Philippines Department of Energy (DOE) has withdrawn the certification exempting Meralco PowerGen's (MGen) proposed 1200 megawatt (MW) Atimonan plant from the moratorium on the construction of new coal power projects just hours after notifying the company the project could proceed. DOE stated that the exemption was revoked "for further review, pursuant to government's policies and programs". MGen President Emmanuel Rubio said the company assumed the change was to review the conditions on the project. (Bilyonayro, Business Mirror)

 

 US coal state suffers fallout from Trump's tariffs: West Virginia, which supplies almost 30 per cent of US coal exports, is suffering the fallout from President Trump's decision to impose tariffs of 145 per cent on goods from China. In response to the US decision, China imposed tariffs on US coal and gas imports. Nick Messenger from the Ohio River Valley Institute said coal shipments to China have declined by 64 per cent. At both a state and federal level, the Republicans dominate West Virginia politics. Alliance Resource Partners, the fourth largest US coal producer, warned in its recent annual report that a trade war could affect demand for US thermal and metallurgical coal. (Mountain State Spotlight)

 

 "Dangerously high" pollution from Indian coal units without FGD units: Indian power utilities and key government agencies are pushing the government to abandon the requirement for the installation of flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) units on coal power plants. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) said that by the end of March, only 44 of India's 537 coal units had FGD plants installed or just eight per cent of the total. The Central Electricity Authority estimates that FGD equipment is on order or being installed at 230 coal units. While the Indian government announced the requirement for FGD in December 2015, the owners of 260 coal units have still not placed orders for the equipment. A study commissioned by the Indian government's Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser argues the government should scrap the requirement for the installation of FGD equipment except for units utilising imported high-sulphur coal. CREA says that 380 of the 493 units without FGDs, just 12 per cent comply with emission standards. CREA estimates that 77 per cent of the units exceed pollution limits. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has set different emission standards by location and age of the plant. CREA notes that plants without FGD units exceeded sulphur dioxide emissions limits by between five and ten times allowable levels. CREA noted that while farmers face strict penalties for seasonal stubble burning, power plants emit sulphur dioxide "at dangerously high levels" year-round "largely unchecked due to regulatory leniency and delays in enforcement". (New Indian Express, The Hindu, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf])

 

 Business group amends guidelines to exclude co-firing of coal plants: RE100 has amended its technical guideline on renewables to exclude electricity generated from coal plants co-fired with biomass or other fuels. RE100 is a business group supporting business members to voluntarily source 100 per cent of their electricity requirements from renewable generation. The change blocks the procurement of electricity from co-fired coal units from counting towards companies' renewables target. RE100 said coal co-firing "prolongs the damage coal does to our planet" and diverts finance away from greater renewable electricity generation. (RE100, RE100 [Pdf])

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The NSW Crime Commission has abandoned any attempt to recover $A30 (US$19.2 million) million former NSW Labor minister Eddie Obeid made from the granting of a coal exploration licence over the family farm in the Bylong Valley. In 2021, Obeid, his son Moses and the former Resources Minister were found guilty of conspiring over the granting of the licence a lucrative mine licence and jailed

 

 Cambodia: The Cambodian government has approved KP Cement's plan to build a new cement plant inside Prey Lang Wildlife Sanctuary. The plant will likely rely on imported coal.

 

 Germany: Greenpeace Germany told a recent Beyond Fossil Fuels conference that the corporate restructuring of the East German lignite company LEAG has created limited liability companies holding mines that face significant rehabilitation costs.

 

 India: The Ministry of Coal has halved the share of revenue payable to the government from coal produced from underground mines. The new level will be two per cent. The government wants to increase the share of underground coal production from 4 per cent to 10 per cent by 2030.

 

 India: Villagers from Varvand in Maharashtra protested against coal ash pollution from a dairy processing plant operated by the National Dairy Development Board.

 

 India: One coal miner died, and six were critically injured after a bus transporting workers rolled over in NTPC's Dulanga coal mine in Odisha.

 

 India: Solar and wind accounted for almost 72 per cent of the 13,495 MW of new generation capacity added in the first quarter of 2025. Coal and lignite accounted for 2843 MW or 21.1 per cent.

 

 Laos: Construction has commenced on the first 300 MW unit of Phonesack Group's 1800 MW Xekong coal power plant and associated transmission line to Cambodia. A Chinese company, Western Power Industrial, has won the design, procurement, and equipment contract for the plant.

 

 Spain: In the aftermath of a major blackout in Spain that also affected Portugal and parts of France, some commentators sought to blame renewables. Energy analyst Gerard Reid suggested the source of the crisis was the Spanish-French power interconnector.

 

 US: Following protests and a lawsuit, the Trump administration has temporarily rehired some of the Center for Disease Control staff responsible for lung disease screening and the job transfer program for affected miners.

 

 US: The Department of Interior announced it will fast-track the approval of new coal and other projects, cutting the assessment process from one to 2 years to "just 28 days at most". Earthjustice, an environmental law group, described the decision as "blatantly illegal" and said it would take legal action.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

US analyst says Amazon has suspended deals on some new data centres: The US financial services firm Wells Fargo stated in a research brief that Amazon has reportedly suspended negotiations on leasing capacity in several proposed new data centres. The note said the decision particularly affected international centres but that the company has not cancelled any existing contracts. Amazon Web Services and Microsoft are the dominant providers of cloud-based data infrastructure and launched a program of significant investment to cater for the boom in Artificial Intelligence applications. Several weeks ago, Microsoft announced it would trim its investment plans and had cancelled some options for new power plant capacity. The share prices of both Amazon and Microsoft have dropped since the start of the year by 25 per cent and 15 per cent, respectively. There are also significant concerns about the financial stability of OpenAI, the company that launched ChatGPT, an AI tool that contributed to expectations of a rapid expansion of the sector. Super Micro, a major supplier of servers using Nvidia's high-end AI processors, reported a slump in quarterly sales due to "some delayed" purchases by major customers. (NBC News, CNBC)

New York City Comptroller puts fund managers on notice over climate: The New York City Comptroller Brad Lander announced new climate action performance standards for financial services companies managing funds for the New York City Employees Retirement System, Teachers Retirement System, and Board of Education Retirement System. Lander said that President Trump and his allies have pressured investors into withdrawing from the Net Zero Asset Managers Initiative and Climate Action 100+ and backtracking on their net zero commitments. The three funds have directed their fund managers to submit net zero plans by June 30, 2025, including details of their engagement with companies and voting record on decarbonisation. Lander said that for any plans found below standard, his office would recommend the three funds "put the investment strategy out to bid". Lander, who is seeking Democratic Party endorsement in June to run as its candidate for Mayor of New York, said he would also recommend evaluating fund managers' corporate-level "climate behaviour and stewardship practices as part of our due diligence". (Financial Times, New York City Comptroller Brad Lander [Pdf])

Report says India could slash coal import costs with renewables rollout: A report by Climate Risk Horizons estimates that if India installed an additional 33,000 MW of new renewable energy, it could avoid spending about US$826 million every year on thermal coal imports during the summer months. The report notes that India imported about 206 million tonnes of thermal coal in 2023-24 at a cost of US$21 billion. Thermal coal imports account for about 20 per cent of coal used in the power sector. The report also notes that the volatile coal prices, combined with the depreciation of the Indian rupee against the US dollar, have resulted in the cost of imported thermal coal surging by 124 per cent even though the volume of coal imported has increased by 58 per cent between 2013 and 2023. (Carbon Copy, Climate Risk Horizons [Pdf])

Bangladesh power utility finds a wide range of fuel cost for coal plants: An analysis by the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) has revealed a wide variance of fuel costs per kilowatt hour (kwh) of electricity generated from the country's fossil fuel plants. The review found that the average fuel cost for coal plants, which accounts for about 20 per cent of generation, is 7.02 taka per kWh (US$0.058 per kWh). The first two 125 MW units of the BPDB's Barapukuria power plant cost 12.30 taka per kWh (US$0.10 per kWh), 75 per cent higher than the average of all coal plants and more than double the fuel cost of the 1200MW Matarbari plant. The plant with the second highest fuel cost is Adani's 1600 MW Godda coal plant in Jharkhand, which costs 8.01 taka per kWh (US$0.066 per kWh). Following the toppling of the Sheikh Hasina government in August 2024, the interim government has sought to renegotiate Adani's power purchase agreement and minimise expenditure on expensive imported fossil fuels. Bangladesh's coal fleet has also expanded recently, with the commissioning of the 1320 MW Patuakhali power station in April. (New Age, Weixin)

India urges companies to invest in overseas coking coal supplies: Sandeep Poundrik, the Secretary of the Ministry of Steel, has urged Indian companies to invest in overseas resources projects to supply commodities such as coking coal for India's growing steel sector. "Raw material securitisation is the most important aspect of steelmaking," he said. India imports the bulk of metallurgical coal for steel production, a trade dominated by Australian exporters. More recently, the Indian government has explored options to increase imports from Russia and establish trade ties with Mongolia. Fifteen years ago, the then Congress government promoted the need for Indian companies to invest in international thermal and metallurgical coal projects, but with mixed success. Some projects, such as Adani's Carmichael coal mine, became embroiled in long-running controversy, while others floundered, such as state-owned companies' investments in Mozambique. (Reuters)

Mozambique coal producers cut jobs as export prices decline: Vulcan International, a privately owned subsidiary of the Jindal Group, has informed the Mozambique government that it plans to axe 105 jobs at its Moatize coal mine due to declining export prices. Vulcan agreed to buy the Moatize mine from Vale in December 2021 for US$270 million after the Brazilian company decided to divest its coal interests. The Chair of Vulcan, Naveen Jindal, is an MP in the Indian parliament and a member of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. In mid-2024, residents of eight neighbourhoods adjoining Vulcan's mine complained about air and water pollution from the mine. Other companies in Mozambique's coal sector are also retrenching workers as prices decline and due to violent conflict after the October 2024 election. (Mining.com)

Chinese coal buyers shun new Indonesian coal price benchmark: Chinese coal buyers and Indonesian coal exporters have mostly ignored the Indonesian government's latest official floor price scheme, referred to as Harga Batubara Acuan (HBA), that came into effect on March 1. Most Indonesian coal exports to China are still using the Indonesian Coal Index (ICI), with coal traders arguing that the HBA price is more expensive and the floor price is only adjusted twice a month. The Indonesian Coal Mining Association, a coal industry lobby group, said most exporters were also using the old ICI. In February, the Minister for Energy, Bahlil Lahadalia, promulgated a regulation requiring coal exporters to only sell coal after March 1 above the official HBA floor price. The government wants to maximise returns to companies and the government rather than allow exporters to sell using other lower-priced indices. However, Chinese and Indian thermal coal imports have slowed. Indonesia is the largest thermal coal supplier in the Asian market, with lower transport costs than Australia and South Africa. (Reuters)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Carbon to Clean Tracker, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

This database is tracking the repurposing of more than 150 retired or retiring coal and other fossil fuel sites, including solar, wind, battery storage, biomass, gas and nuclear projects.

"What do more renewables mean for our electricity system?" ABC News, April 26, 2025.

This excellent explainer shows the impact of increasing renewable generation on prices and other electricity technologies as the transition away from coal generation gathers pace. While focussed on Australia, the broad principles are relevant elsewhere.

links.text: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf])
New York City Comptroller Brad Lander [Pdf])
“What do more renewables mean for our electricity system?”

title: CoalWire 562, May 8, 2025
excerpt: Only one proposed coal plant left in Latin America; Ohio legislature repeals coal plant subsidies.
content:
May 8, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Global Energy Monitor's latest analysis of new coal plant proposals indicates Latin America is on the verge of having no new coal power projects awaiting construction. Outside China and India, which account for most new coal plants, new projects announced in the first quarter of 2025 are in just five countries. While the US Export-Import Bank has revoked its ban on overseas coal lending, much of the world has moved on from when the US imposed the policy restriction 12 years ago.

While President Trump has championed support for coal plants and mines in the US, it is not all a one-way street. In Ohio, the legislature revoked scandal-tainted subsidies for two 1955 vintage coal plants. Without the financial props, the old plants are likely to close before too long. In India, the National Green Tribunal has blocked the authority of the Ministry of Power to allow coal power plants to change fuel sources without reassessing the environmental impacts. In another case, the tribunal is asking pointed questions about the lack of pollution controls on coal plants that surround the national capital.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Inside an Australian miner's brawl with Alberta regulators

When the Alberta Energy Regulator asked the Australian coal exploration company to improve selenium monitoring and uphold the law at a proposed mining site, the firm's CEO not only refused but threatened to sue individual members of the agency, writes Andrew Nikiforuk in The Tyee.

 

 Rocky Mountain coal mine in Alberta takes next step to expansion

In Alberta, a massive open-pit coal mine near Jasper National Park is hoping to expand the amount of coal it mines to be burned for electricity overseas, writes Drew Anderson in The Narwhal.

 

 The Deocha-Pachami coal mine in India is not development. It's dispossession in disguise 

The proposed Deocha-Pachami coal mine in West Bengal commodifies Adivasi land, flouts forest rights, and replaces dignity with surveillance, fear, and fragile jobs, writes Panchali Ray in Frontline.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Proposed coal plant pipeline shrinks outside China: A Global Energy Monitor review of all proposed coal plants outside China has found only one small coal plant proposal remains in Latin America, a 100 MW plant in Honduras. In 2015, there were 18 proposed coal plants in Latin America. The new or revived coal plant projects announced in the first quarter of 2025 are concentrated in just six countries: Botswana, India, Mongolia, Niger, Vietnam, and Zimbabwe. Vietnam's recently revised power development plan featured a pivot to new renewables capacity but also included the revival of the 1000 MW Quang Tri power station. In Africa, three Chinese-backed proposals emerged in Zimbabwe, a new project in Zimbabwe and a feasibility study on a 600 MW Salkadamna plant in Niger. In September 2021, President Xi Jinping announced that China would ban financial support for new international coal plants. In India, power utilities announced a further 10,400 MW of new proposals in the first quarter. India now has 91,200 MW of proposed new coal capacity. Global Energy Monitor, Global Energy Monitor [Excel sheet])

 

 US back backtracks on coal lending: The board of the US Export-Import Bank (Ex-Im) has voted unanimously to revoke a restriction on funding overseas coal projects. Last month, President Trump issued an executive order directing the band and the International Development Finance Corporation to support coal projects. The bank hasn't financed a coal project in over a decade. Jake Schmidt from the Natural Resources Defense Council said the change was a retrograde step that harks back to when the Ex-Im was one of the largest financiers of overseas coal projects in the world. (Mining Weekly)

 

 Ohio legislature repeals subsidies for scandal-tainted coal plants: The Ohio Senate has approved House Bill 15 that includes provisions revoking subsidies for the 1303 MW Clifty Creek plant in Indiana and the 1086 MW Kyger Creek coal plant in Ohio. The Ohio legislature passed the scandal-tainted House Bill 6 in 2019, legislation that guaranteed subsidies for the two coal plants and a nuclear plant. After federal prosecutors charged the then speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives and others over their roles in a US$61 million bribery scandal, the subsidy for the nuclear plant was revoked. However, subsidies for the 1955-vintage coal plants remained. The Ohio Citizens Utility Board of Ohio, an NGO group, recently estimated the subsidy for the two plants could reach US$1.1 billion by 2030. The Ohio Valley Electric Corporation (OVEC), a joint venture between American Electric Power (AEP), Duke Energy, and AES Ohio, owns the plants. HB15 has been sent to Governor Mike DeWine for his signature. He has previously stated he supports the repeal of the coal plant subsidies. (Cleveland, Sierra Club)

 

 Trump administration terminates mine safety workers: The Department of Health and Human Services has issued termination notices to staff of the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) responsible for the coal mine safety program. The department placed about three-quarters of NIOSH staff on administrative leave in February and shuttered agency offices and labs, including those implementing the legislated Coal Workers' Health Surveillance Program that provided free black lung screening services for coal miners. West Virginia Republican Senator Shelley Capito urged Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. to reinstate the black lung program, but the latest notices included at least two of the 40 temporarily reinstated staff. The United Mine Workers of America said it would campaign to reinstate the programs. (Reuters)

 

 Indian court orders assessment if coal plants changed fuel source: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) overturned Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change decisions allowing power utilities to change the source of coal burned without requiring fresh environmental assessment. The tribunal found that 'office memorandums' by the ministry were issued without any scientific review and effectively amounted to de facto exemptions from a regulation that required fresh environmental clearance if a change in raw materials results in increased pollution. (The New Indian Express)

 

 Indian court told most coal plants near New Delhi lack pollution controls: The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (CAQM), a state agency, told that National Green Tribunal that of the 35 coal power units at 11 coal power plants within 300 kilometres of the capital, only 13 units have flue-gas desulphurisation (FGD) technology fitted. FGD can cut sulphur dioxide emissions up to 95 per cent. The 35 coal units have a combined capacity of 13,575 MW. In an affidavit submitted to the court, CAQM said that "action is ongoing" to achieve compliance for the other 22 units. The tribunal initiated an inquiry into pollution controls in the New Delhi region after a news article mentioned a Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air analysis that suggested the installation of FGD technology on all the units would cut sulphur dioxide emissions by 67 per cent. (Hindustan Times)

 

 Study ties fossil fuel majors to climate damage: A study by Dartmouth College researchers estimates that the damage caused by the 111 most significant greenhouse gas emitters cost the global economy about US$28 trillion from 1991 to 2020. The study, which was published in Nature, ties company-specific emissions to their impact on extreme weather. The study authors, Christopher Callahan and Justin Mankin, argue that "the scientific case for climate liability is closed". The study estimates that the damage caused by heat alone from each one per cent of greenhouse gas emissions since 1990 cost the global economy US$502 billion. The costs of floods, droughts and other extreme weather events impose additional costs. The study relies on emissions data in the Carbon Majors database of 180 of the world's largest greenhouse gas emitters. The database identifies the leading coal emitters, including Coal India, CHN Energy, the British Coal Corporation, Peabody Energy and BHP. (CBS News, Dartmouth College, Nature [paywall])

 

 Australian coal company set to abandon proposed coal project: Bickham Coal has indicated that it has abandoned plans to develop a coal exploration lease in the New South Wales Hunter Valley that spurred opposition from landholders. The NSW government first granted the lease in 1997. The company proposed the development of an underground coal mine, a plan opposed by the powerful thoroughbred industry that was alarmed at dust pollution and the impact of the project on water supplies. While the exploration lease is due to expire on May 28 2025, Bickham said it wants to renew the lease so it can complete rehabilitation of the site prior to relinquishment "in the quickest possible time frame". The New South Wales government rejected the proposed mine in 2010 but the company has continued to renew the lease since. (ABC News)

 

 Welsh parliament backs bill to establish coal tips authority: Members of the Welsh parliament, the Senedd, unanimously endorsed the aims of the government's Disused Mine and Quarry Tips (Wales) Bill, but concerns remain about key provisions of the bill. The bill authorises the establishment of the Disused Tips Authority for Wales to protect communities from the risk of coal tips but does not address the problems of pollution from the sites and does not require management plans for each site. Amendments to strengthen key provisions of the bill have not yet been voted on. Public alarm at the stability of the 2573 coal tips in Wales was triggered after a 300 metre-long, 60,000-tonne landslip occurred near Tylorstown after heavy rain in February 2020. The Welsh government subsequently undertook a broader assessment of the risks to local communities from old coal tips, with 360 sites classified as having "the potential to impact public safety". In November 2024, residents were temporarily evacuated from the village of Cwmtillery after a landslide from an old coal tip swept into part of the village. The accident revived memories of the 1966 Aberfan disaster when a coal tip landslide killed 144 people, including 116 children at the village primary school. (Wales Online, Welsh Parliament)

 

 Coal-backed groups campaigned against Greens in Australian election: The Australian Institute for Progress (AIP), a lobby group that received A$613,500 (US$394,000) from a coal industry lobby group in last year's state election, launched last-minute advertisements against Greens MPs ahead of the May 3 general election. In an email, the AIP executive director sought donations to target sitting Greens MPs on housing issues. Two other groups - Australians for Prosperity (AFP) and Advance Australia - have also targeted sitting lower-house Greens MPs around the country. AFP has also received A$725,00 from Coal Australia, a lobby group for coal companies, including Peabody Energy, Whitehaven and Yancoal. The Greens appear likely to lose three of their four lower house seats but retain the balance of power in the Senate. The Australian Labor Party, which supports a transition of the domestic coal power sector to renewables and increased coal exports, was re-elected with an increased majority. (Guardian)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Queensland Conservation Council has filed a legal challenge against the expansion of Bowen Basin Coal's Lake Vermont Meadowbrook Project in the Queensland Land Court. The expansion would extract about 7 million tonnes per year of coal from the underground mine.

 

 Bangladesh: Civil society organisations have called for the scrapping of the Orion Group's proposed 635 MW in Matarbari, including the cancellation of finance, the power purchase agreement and leases of land.

 

 India: The Ministry of Power has directed coal plants reliant on imported coal to operate at full capacity until June 30 to cater for increasing power demand. Imported coal plants have a combined capacity of about 17,000 MW of capacity.

 

 Mozambique: About 200 workers for a company subcontracted by Vulcan, which operates the Moatize coal mine, have gone on strike for wages owing for February, March and April.

 

 US: Donations to Donald Trump's second presidential inauguration in January included [Pdf] US$500,000 from Alpha Metallurgical Resources, US$895,000 from United States Steel and US$100,000 from Southern Company.

 

 US: The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), a federal agency, is considering delaying the closure of at least part of its coal fleet after President Trump's recent executive orders aimed at supporting the coal industry. The TVA's current plan is to close its coal plants by 2035.

 

 US: Coal generation in March was just 15 per cent of electricity generation.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

NGOs question the impact of Indonesia's energy transition regulation: Civil society groups have urged the government to embrace more ambitious reforms than laid out in the recent Ministerial Regulation No. 10/2025 which took effect on April 10. The regulation tasks the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources with oversight of developing a coal phase-out plan, with access to finance given the greatest weight in the criteria used to assess closures. The regulation reinforces that new captive coal units can proceed if tied to the downstream processing of natural resources. It also allows new coal plants if the owner commits to reduce emissions by at least 35 per cent from a 2021 benchmark of average emission within 10 years from commencement. The regulation allows the use of carbon offsets, renewables and technology changes to count towards the 35 per cent emissions reduction target. Grita Anindarini from the Indonesian Center for Environmental Law said "the energy transition risks remaining stalled and largely symbolic" unless the government amends the electricity master plan to bring the coal end date forward from 2060. The Indonesian government also wants to install 10,000 MW of nuclear capacity by 2040. Past plans to establish nuclear power have failed. (Jakarta Post, Umbra, Reuters)

Bangladesh sets new tariff for new imported coal plant: The Bangladesh government approved a new tariff of 8.44 taka per kilowatt-hour (kWh) or US$0.076 per kWh for the 1200 MW Matarbari imported coal plant. Just over two-thirds of the tariff is the fuel cost, with the balance set as a capacity charge for the plant, assuming it operates at 85 per cent of rated capacity. The two units at the plant were commissioned in 2023 and 2024. The Bangladesh Working Group on Ecology and Development warns that the headline rate is misleading due to the exchange rate assumptions and expectation of a high level of capacity utilisation. The latest deal assumes an exchange rate of 110.25 takas against the US dollar. According to Bangladesh Bank, the current exchange rate is 122 per US dollar. (Daily Star, New Age)

Indian NGO files complaints against banks backing for JSW steel plant: Community members from the Anti-Jindal & Anti-POSCO Movement in India have called on the Australian bank ANZ, and Japanese banks Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC), Mizuho, and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG) to publicly rule out financial support for JSW Steel's JSW Utkal steel and coal project in Odisha. With the support of BankTrack, community members have filed complaints against the banks. JSW propose the establishment of a coal-based steel plant with an annual capacity of 13.5 million tonnes per annum and a 900 MW captive coal plant. The project has encountered strong community opposition due to impacts on water, the diversion of protected tribal forest land for the plant and government repression of project opponents. The South Korean company POSCO originally proposed the project in 2005 but it abandoned the plan in 2017. In early 2023, the National Green Tribunal and Odisha High Court overturned environmental approvals for the plant, but the Odisha government acquired the land for the project to facilitate JSW's proposal. (BankTrack)

Peabody flags prospect of dropping takeover of Anglo American mines: Peabody Energy has warned Anglo American that it may abandon its proposed US$3.78-billion purchase of metallurgical coal mines in Queensland due to concern about the Moranbah North mine. An underground fire occurred in the mine on March 31, 2025, and production has not yet resumed. Peabody said that the suspension of the mine has "created significant uncertainty" about the proposed deal as the mine accounted for a significant share of the offer price and "there is no known timetable for resuming longwall production". Part of Peabody's original offer was a payment of US$450 million if Anglo American's mothballed Grosvenor underground mine resumed production and operated for two years. The mine was closed after a June 2024 fire. The completion of the purchase would make Peabody Energy one of the world's largest seaborne metallurgical coal exporters, with a projected production of 19 – 20 million tonnes in 2026. Peabody Energy currently has four metallurgical coal mines in Australia and the Shoal Creek mine in Alabama. The purchase of Anglo American's assets would allow the company to diversify away from reliance on the declining US thermal coal market, where it owns nine operating mines, including three in the Powder River Basin. Anglo American said it re-entered the Moranbah North mine on April 19 and did not consider the delay in a resumption of production as a "material adverse change in accordance with the definitive agreements with Peabody". (Mining Weekly, Peabody Energy [Pdf], Anglo American)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Report says ArcelorMittal backtracking on decarbonisation commitment: A report by SteelWatch accuses ArcelorMittal of stalling investment decisions to progress new low-carbon steel projects while diverting billions to shareholders. The report states that ArcelorMittal spent US$800 million on decarbonisation projects between 2021 and 2024, compared to the US$12 billion allocated to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. SteelWatch notes that the company has not made a final investment decision on any of the five announced Direct Reduced Iron projects in Europe and Canada. Caroline Ashley, SteelWatch's Executive Director, notes that the company now refers to "competitive decarbonisation" and "economic decarbonisation". She said this is "language that signals climate action is conditional, to be pursued only when commercially convenient. This is not climate leadership – it's a strategic retreat". (SteelWatch, SteelWatch [Pdf[)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Trump coal pollution dashboard, Sierra Club, May 2025. (Media release is here.)

This interactive tool allows users to select one or more coal units in the US and assess how much pollution could be avoided if one or all five Environmental Protection Agency rules under threat from the Trump administration are retained.

title: CoalWire 563, May 15, 2025
excerpt: Indonesian coal exports slump; coal to clean transition credit unveiled.
content:
May 15, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Faced with the challenge of a young age profile of many coal plants, especially in Asia, the Rockefeller Foundation has backed the development of transition credits to underwrite the early retirement of coal plants and support investment in an equivalent amount of clean energy generation. Mitsubishi, a major Japanese trading company, has joined a consortium of companies aiming to benefit from the early retirement of a small coal plant in the Philippines. A shift away from coal generation in Asia would pose significant challenges for Indonesia, which has just reported a substantial decline in thermal coal exports in the first four months of 2025.

The draft US budget proposed by Republican legislators reflects the Trump administration's fulsome support for fossil fuel development and hostility to renewables. The draft budget proposes axing tax credits for renewable technologies, such as wind, solar and batteries, but retaining generous subsidies for carbon capture and storage projects. One provision in the bill opens the door for the removal of non-profit groups' tax-exempt status. The administration is also seeking to allow North Dakota to have prime management responsibility for coal ash dumps, along with considering granting a two-year exemption from federal pollution regulations to a US Steel plant in Pennsylvania.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Coal company lobbying Alberta government for lenient definition of open pit mine

As the provincial government finalises details of new rules for coal mining in Alberta's mountains and foothills, Westmoreland Mining is asking officials to pick a definition of open pit mining that won't interfere with its plans for its 20,660-hectare Coal Valley Mine, writes Brett McKay for CTV News.

 

 The latest Trump and DOGE casualty: energy data

The Energy Information Administration stripped its analysis out of a recent report on the latest energy data and scrapped a second one entirely amid sweeping job reductions and turmoil, writes Peter Elkind in Pro Publica.

 

 Warren Buffett's successor got his start selling clean energy. Now he defends coal

Warren Buffett has recommended that Berkshire Hathaway's board name Greg Abel as its new chief executive. At a recent meeting, Abel defended the company's continued operation of coal plants, writes Sammy Roth in the Los Angeles Times.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 US bill targets support for clean energy and alarms non-profit sector: A draft budget by Republican legislators proposes progressive reductions in the investment and production tax credits from 2028 for wind, solar, batteries, geothermal and nuclear projects and their elimination after 2031. The Biden administration's Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 allowed claims for the full value of the credit until 2032. The House Ways and Means Committee's draft budget retains the US$85 per tonne of carbon dioxide captured by carbon capture and storage projects and eliminates the credit for clean hydrogen production from the end of 2025. Other provisions propose limiting tax credits only to projects once they are "placed in service", restricting the use of components from foreign entities "of concern", preventing the transfer of credits to other entities and eliminating the residential clean energy tax credit. The 389-page bill also includes a provision that would grant Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent unilateral authority to revoke the tax-exempt status of non-profit groups designated by the Treasury Department as having provided "material support or resources" to a terrorist organisation. The definition of what constitutes a "terrorist organisation" is left to the discretion of the Treasury Secretary. The draft bill only requires a majority vote, with the Republicans holding a majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate. (Utility Dive, Evergreen Action, Non-profit Quarterly)

 

 US EPA proposes allowing North Dakota to regulate coal ash dams: The US Environmental Protection Agency has proposed accrediting the North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality's (ND DEQ) permitting of coal ash dams as equivalent to the requirements of the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. The proposal is open for a 60-day public comment period and will be subject to an in-person and online public hearing on July 8, 2025. Earthjustice, an environmental law NGO, noted that the 16 pits at eight coal plants contain about 70 million cubic yards (53.5 million cubic metres) of coal ash. Earthjustice said that groundwater monitoring data at seven of the state's coal plants revealed pollution of groundwater with hazardous chemicals at levels above federal safe drinking water standards. The group also noted that North Dakota's proposed accreditation is just the first, with Wyoming, Alabama, Indiana, and West Virginia all currently or likely to pursue the same path. Scott Skokos from the Dakota Resource Council said only half of the coal ash pits in the state have liners and that most North Dakota coal plants have emitted pollutants far above federal standards "for decades". (US Environmental Protection Agency, Earthjustice)

 

 US Steel applies for emissions exemption: US Steel has applied to President Trump for a two-year exemption for its Mon Valley Works from Clean Air Act rules on emissions from coke, taconite and integrated iron and steelmaking plants. In May 2024, the US EPA announced new emissions standards for coke ovens, which emit pollutants including mercury, arsenic, lead and benzene. Metallurgical coal is baked in the ovens to produce coke for use in steel production. The coke rule also required steel plants with coke ovens to monitor emissions at the fenceline of the plant and take action when pollution exceeds federal limits. Matt Mehalik from the Breathe Project in Pittsburgh said residents "need protection from these hazardous air pollutants". (Trib Live)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The New South Wales Premier, Chris Minns, has offered the NSW Crime Commission additional resources and support for legal changes to recover the A$30 million (US$19.4 million) former NSW Labor minister Eddie Obeid made from the granting of a coal exploration licence over the family farm in the Bylong Valley.

 

 Greece: PPC, the state-owned power utility, has commenced construction on the second 125 MW phase of building a 4980 MW solar farm on the former Megalopoli lignite mine.

 

 India: Adani Power said it will build a new 1600 MW coal plant to supply a 1500 MW contract with the Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation. Adani doesn't name the project, but it appears to refer to the controversial Mirzapur power station in Dadri Khurd.

 

 US: The Trump administration plans to fast-track the expansion of Warrior Met's Blue Creek mine in Alabama. The mine primarily sells coal into the export market.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Indonesian coal exports slump on decline in Indian and Chinese demand: Declining Chinese and Indian thermal coal demand has underpinned a 12 per cent decline in Indonesian coal exports over the first four months of 2025. Indonesian thermal coal exports over the January to April period fell by almost 20 million tonnes to 150 million tonnes. Chinese imports declined by 14 million tonnes or 20 per cent, and Indian shipments by 6 million tonnes or 15 per cent. Indonesian exports to Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia and Pakistan also declined compared to the same period in 2024. The decline in exports comes as the government is reviewing the benchmark prices it wants coal exporters to use in negotiating new export sales despite resistance from Chinese buyers. The government recently announced increased royalties when thermal coal exceeds US$90 per tonne. Civil society groups view the increased royalties on coal and other minerals as an opportunity for the government to fund the energy transition, discourage coal production and ensure the community reaps part of the windfall profits the coal industry earns from price spikes in the export market. (Reuters, Indonesia Business Post)

Carbon credits for coal closures: Verra, a non-profit certifier of carbon offsets, has released a methodology that assesses avoided emissions from coal plant retirements to allow the creation of "high-integrity transition credits" to finance early retirements. The methodology envisages the investment in new renewable generation capacity to "ensure real emission reductions". The standard was developed by the Coal to Clean Credit Initiative with support from the Rockefeller Foundation. The methodology defines eligible renewable projects as including wind, solar and battery projects. More controversially, the definition of renewables includes run-of-river hydro schemes, waste-to-energy incineration projects and provides qualified support for biomass plants. The standard calls for a monitoring plan to ensure that where a state-owned utility is retiring a coal plant, neither the utility nor the country announces or builds new coal capacity or expands existing projects. In the case of private utilities, the owners couldn't claim transition credits if they have new coal plants or expansions under development or construction "that are under their control". (Reccessery, Verra, Verra [Pdf])

Japanese company joins Philippines transition credits consortium: Mitsubishi has joined a consortium headed by Philippine energy firm Acen to retire the 246 MW Puting Bato power station in 2030 instead of 2040. Acen estimates the early retirement of the plant could generate carbon credits equivalent to 19 million tonnes of avoided carbon dioxide emissions. The two units at the plant were commissioned in 2015 and 2016. The consortium headed by Acen includes Mitsubishi, its Hong Kong-based subsidiary Diamond Generating Asia, GenZero and Keppel. Mitsubishi wants Japan's Joint Crediting Mechanism (JCM) to approve transition credits from the plant retirement. Mitsubishi wants some of the credits used to offset emissions from Japan's coal fleet to help meet its nationally determined contributions target under the Paris Agreement. (Argus Media)

Peabody Energy suspends fundraising for Anglo American's mines: Peabody Energy has temporarily suspended fundraising for its proposed US$3.78-billion purchase of metallurgical coal mines in Queensland after a March 31 fire at the Moranbah North mine. Anglo American suspended production at the mine, and there is no date set for resumption of operations. Peabody Energy's Chief Financial Officer Mark Spurbeck said investors "aren't willing" to underwrite the purchase of Anglo American's mines until there is greater clarity about the future of the mine. On May 5, Peabody Energy gave Anglo American ten days to respond to its view that the suspension of the Moranbah North mine amounted to a material adverse change to its agreement to buy the mines. Anglo American says it does not consider the suspension of mining a material adverse event. Part of Peabody's original offer was a payment of US$450 million if Anglo American's mothballed Grosvenor underground mine resumed production and operated for two years. The mine was closed after a June 2024 fire. (Australian Financial Review [paywall])

Norwegian sovereign wealth fund drops investment ban on RWE: Norway's US$1.8 trillion sovereign wealth fund has revoked its 2020 exclusion of RWE, a major European coal miner and power generator, from its investment list and instead placed the utility "under observation". Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages the fund, recommended the change after coal plant closures put RWW under the 10,000 MW of coal capacity threshold. RWE operates 7065 MW of lignite plant capacity and coal mines with a capacity of 56 million tonnes, according to the latest data from Global Energy Monitor's Global Coal Plant Tracker and the Global Coal Mine Tracker. The guidelines for the fund also state that companies with a capacity of over 20 million tonnes of coal a year will be excluded. "Coal mining will nevertheless remain above the threshold for some time to come," NBIM stated. The fund said that RWE plans to close all lignite power plants and mines by 2030 and is following a set schedule, along with increased investment in renewables. (Reuters, Norges Bank Investment Management)

Macquarie Bank loosens met coal lending policy: Macquarie Bank announced in its annual report for the year to the end of March 2025 that it has abandoned its policy of eliminating financial support for coal mining projects by the end of 2024. In its report, Macquarie stated that in light of "limited viable alternatives to metallurgical coal for steel making and industry", the bank's restrictions on coal lending would only apply to thermal coal projects. The report revealed the bank commenced easing its policy in April 2024 when it decided that "advisory transactions" for metallurgical coal projects were acceptable and expanded it in November 2024 to include lending and equity investments where the purpose was "the purchase, operation, development or expansion" of metallurgical coal projects. Market Forces, an NGO group that lobbies banks against financing fossil fuel projects, said that Macquarie's coal policy retreat occurred when other major Australian banks "have imposed stronger restrictions". In February, Macquarie became the first Australian bank to quit the Net Zero Banking Alliance, an approach mimicking the decisions of some US banks backtracking on climate commitments in the face of criticisms by Republican lawmakers. (Australian Financial Review [Paywall], Macquarie [Pdf])

World Bank funding for Bosnia and Herzegovina's coal transition: The World Bank has approved 79.90 million (US$88.8 million) loan and a 2.89 million (US$3.21 million) to support the closure of Elektroprivreda's loss-making Zenica lignite mine and redevelopment of the Banovici, Zenica, and Kreka mine sites. Elektroprivreda plans to repurpose the Banovici and Kreka mine sites to host renewables projects. (Intellinews, World Bank)

Analysts pan draft South African power plan: Leading South African energy industry analysts have criticised the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy's draft Integrated Resource Plan 2024 (IRP) released in December. Dr Grove Steyn from Meridian Economics said that the draft plan is "deeply flawed" and not based on the best analysis. Steyn said that the draft has "uneconomically forced" nuclear and gas projects into the plan and fails to detail the "energy mix costs or emissions for the modelled scenarios or the actual proposed balanced plan". The reference case in the draft plan assumes all coal plants operating after 2030 will have a 50-year operational life. In one scenario, the draft plan considers extending the life of five coal power plants – Kendal, Majuba, Lethabo, Matimba and Tutuka – by 10 years to 60 years. The five plants have a combined capacity of 19,611 MW. The current draft of the IRP is under consideration by the National Economic Development and Labour Council with Cabinet likely to consider the final draft later this year. The Minister for Electricity and Energy, Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, has promoted the potential for coal's long-term retention in South Africa's grid if coal plants are fitted with pollution controls. "If we have access to technologies that reduce emissions like sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides, then there's no issue with coal itself," he said. (Daily Maverick, JacarandaFM)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 US steel company retreats from hydrogen-based project: The Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs announced on an investor call that its 2024 plan to phase out the use of coke, build two electric arc furnaces and replace an existing blast furnace with a 2.5 million tonnes per annum "hydrogen-ready" direct reduced iron (DRI) plant "will be substantially altered" to "better align" with the Trump administration's energy policies. The company's Chairman, President and CEO, Lourenco Goncalves, a supporter of Trump's tariffs on imports, said changes to the Middleton plant in Ohio would not "assume [the] availability of massive amounts of hydrogen and would instead rely on readily available and more economical fossil fuels". In March 2024, the US Department of Energy announced it was considering providing up to US$500 million in funding to Cleveland-Cliffs towards the overhaul of the plant from a program under the Biden administration's Inflation Reduction Act. (E & E News, Cleveland Cliffs [Pdf]

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Glencore's methane risks a concern for shareholders serious about reducing Scope 1 emissions, Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, April 2025. (Pdf)

This 8-page briefing note provides a concise overview of the likely underreporting of methane emissions from Glencore's predominantly open-cut Australian coal mines. Glencore is the world's largest thermal coal exporter.
