title: CoalWire 564, May 22, 2025
excerpt: China’s power sector emissions declined in 2024; Philippines coal plants struggle to obtain insurance.
content:
May 22, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The data indicating China's greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector fell by two per cent in the year to the end of March 2025 is welcome news. The sheer scale of China's solar and wind industries offers hope that this trend will continue. If it does, China's coal sector faces a significant transformation. A recent survey of 10,000 residents of Shanxi province, China's largest coal-producing region, offers insight into public doubts that the area is ready for a decline in coal production.

The deployment of a fleet of 135 autonomous 90-tonne haul trucks at a mine in China is just the latest illustration that new, long-life mines are likely to involve increasing levels of automation. Over the last decade, the mining industry has deployed remote-controlled drilling rigs, haul trucks, trains and automated underground longwall mining. If the most significant social benefit of coal production is jobs, especially in regional areas, further automation will diminish local economic benefits. While it is unclear how much new automation will affect existing mid to late-stage mines, it is a topic that rarely rates a mention in reports discussing a just transition for coal workers and communities. Not only are there fewer jobs, but those supervising automated mining projects are often based in control rooms hundreds of kilometres away.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 China's carbon dioxide emissions went into reverse for the first time

For the first time, carbon dioxide emissions from China's power sector fell despite rapid power demand growth, writes Lauri Myllyvirta from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air in Carbon Brief.

 

 As Indonesia phases out coal, what happens to the people and environments left behind?

An analysis by the Indonesian Center for Environmental Law (ICEL) finds that the country's energy transition plans do not address the remaining impacts of coal plants, such as pollution, degraded ecosystems and lost livelihoods, writes Hans Nicholas Jong in Mongabay.

 

 We did the math on AI's energy footprint. Here's the story you haven't heard

The emissions from individual AI text, image, and video queries seem small—until you add up what the industry isn't tracking and consider where it's heading next, write James O'Donnell and Casey Crownhart in MIT Technology Review.

 

 A fraction of proposed data centres will get built. US utilities are wising up

One expert estimated that speculative interconnection requests were five to 10 times more than the number of actual data centres, but the scale of the problem remains elusive, writes Brian Martucci in Utility Dive.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Chinese mine deploys a fleet of 135 autonomous 90-tonne haul trucks: Zakhnuur Coal Company, which operates an open-cut coal mine in the Chinese province of Inner Mongolia, has expanded its fleet of autonomous haul trucks to 135. The company, a subsidiary of State Power Investment Corporation, began a trial of 33 autonomous 90-tonne haul trucks in early 2024. The company said there were no safety incidents with the fleet, fuel consumption was 20 to 30 per cent lower, and the trucks were almost as efficient as human drivers. Huaneng Ruichi, a subsidiary of China Huaneng Group, led the production of the trucks. The trucks operate without human controllers, with the role of operators confined to the management of the fleet. The operation of the fleet relies on the construction by Huawei of a dedicated 4G/5G private communications network and a cloud-based data control centre. (China Daily, Huawei)

 

 US court orders restoration of black lung program: US District Judge Irene Berger issued a preliminary injunction ordering the restoration of the National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety's Respiratory Health Division. West Virginia coal miners led by Harry Wiley filed a class action against the Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., arguing Congress established the black lung program and its cessation represented a threat to the health of coal miners. Sam Petsonk, a West Virginia labour attorney who filed the class action, said the ruling may also force the Mine Safety Health Administration to restore the new silica standard the Trump administration suspended without public notification. (In These Times, West Virginia Watch)

 

 Energy Australia apologises for carbon offsets scheme: EnergyAustralia, which operates two coal and four gas power plants and is one of Australia's largest energy retailers, has settled legal action brought by Parents for Climate with an acknowledgement that carbon offsets "do not prevent or undo the harms caused by burning fossil fuels for a customer's energy use". EnergyAustralia was the third-highest greenhouse gas emitter in 2023-2024 and operates the 1430 megawatt (MW) Mt Piper coal plant in New South Wales and the 1480 MW lignite-fired Yallourn plant in Victoria. In July 2023, Parents for Climate launched legal action in the Federal Court of Australia, arguing that EnergyAustralia's 'Go Neutral' carbon offset scheme with 400,000 customers amounted to misleading or deceptive conduct under Australian consumer law. Energy Australia, which is a subsidiary of the Hong Kong-based CLP Group, abandoned the 'Go Neutral' scheme in July 2024. In settling the legal case, EnergyAustralia stated that its focus has "now shifted its focus to direct emissions reductions". (Guardian, Energy Australia, Parents for Climate)

 

 Alberta approves new exploration program for met coal project: The Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) has approved the application by Northback Holdings for a 105-day coal exploration program at Grassy Mountain in southern Alberta. Northback is a subsidiary of Hancock Prospecting, a private company that Australian mining billionaire Gina Rinehart owns. The AER emphasised that it focused only on the exploration project and not any impacts of a future coal mine at the site. Northback's plan is for 11 drill pads with 14 boreholes on public land and a further 12 drill pads with 19 boreholes on land owned by the company. The District of Ranchland opposed the proposed exploration program on the grounds it would provide little information beyond the data from the previous 633 drill holes on the site used by Northback to support its previous mining plan. In August 2021, the Canadian Minister for Environment rejected Northback's proposed metallurgical coal mine because of likely damage to First Nations heritage and water pollution impacts on fish, especially from selenium emissions, but a court overturned this decision on appeal. At the public hearings on the project, ranchers, landowners, First Nations members and environmentalists expressed concern about the impact of the proposed mine on watersheds and communities downstream. The Piikani Nation supports the exploration project, including the potential economic benefits for members from contracting services, but signalled its position on a potential mine would be determined at a later point. The Alberta Wilderness Association said public pressure had forced the company to reduce the extent of the proposed drilling program and scrap plans for new roads on public land. (CBC, Alberta Energy Regulator [Pdf], Alberta Wilderness Association, Environmental Defence)

 

 Company owned by Republican Senator to face hearing on mine cleanup: The US District Court for the Western District of Virginia has granted three months for the discovery of documents held by the A&G Coal Corporation, a coal mining company majority-owned by Republican US Senator Jim Justice. The ruling centres on A&G Coal Corporation's failure to comply with a January 2023 consent decree requiring the company to rehabilitate the Looney Ridge Surface Mine #1, Canepatch Surface Mine and Sawmill Hollow #3 Mine that between them cover 4700 acres (1902 hectares) of land in Virginia. A court hearing will be held at the end of the discovery period with Southern Appalachian Mountain Stewards, Appalachian Voices, and the Sierra Club arguing that A&G missed deadlines for undertaking the rehabilitation work, illegally extracted coal at one site and failed to pay US$600,000 in penalties owing to the Upper Tennessee River Roundtable until just days before a contempt of court hearing. (Appalachian Voices)

 

 
 "It's not clear to us that the benefits of these data centres outweigh these costs. Why should we be paying for this infrastructure? Why should we be paying for their power bills?"

said Eliza Martin from the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard University.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 China: Three coal miners died at a coal mine in Baiyin in Gansu province when water flooded into the mine.

 

 Russia: A blackout caused the loss of ventilation in seven coal mines in Siberia's Kemerovo region.

 

 Poland: JSW has declared force majeure due to a fire on May 7 in a section of its Budryk mine. The company said production would decline as a result of the fire by 345,000 tonnes in 2025.

 

 Spain: The Minister for Energy, Sara Aagesen, said investigators had identified a sudden loss of generation at a substation in Granada as a key factor in the April 28 blackout that affected Spain and Portugal. Investigators have ruled out cyberattacks, an imbalance in supply and demand or insufficient grid capacity.

 

 US: Coosa Riverkeeper has filed a formal notice of intent to sue Alabama Power over groundwater pollution from a coal ash disposal at the site of the now-closed Gadsden Steam Plant in Alabama. The two 69 MW coal units were retired in 2016.

 

 US: 8 Rivers has contracted with the Navajo Transitional Energy Company (NTEC) to undertake a technical feasibility study on a proposed coal plant of up to 1000 MW at either the Navajo mine or in the Powder River Basin.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Philippines Energy Secretary bemoans coal plant insurance costs: The Philippines Secretary of Energy, Raphael Lotilla, said that utilities operating the country's coal fleet are struggling to obtain insurance even for the 7000 MW of plants that are less than 10 years old. Lotilla said premiums for existing coal plants have increased and that insurance companies are "reluctant to re-insure" existing coal plants. Lotilla told a media event that he recently met with an unnamed insurance company in the hope of convincing them "that the risks they associate with the Philippines are actually much less than what they are inputting now as part of their premiums". Lotilla also acknowledged that utilities face a challenge in gaining finance for new coal plants. (Inquirer.net, Philippines Star)

Powder River Basin mines keep on declining: Peabody Energy and Core Natural Resources (which merged with Arch Resources in January) reported that their five mines produced 32 million US short tons (29 million tonnes) of coal in the first quarter of 2025. While Peabody reported a US$38 million profit, Core racked up a US$62 million loss. The two companies produce two-thirds of all the coal produced from the Powder River Basin, which spans Wyoming and Montana. In 2024, the five mines owned by Peabody and Core produced 185.15 million US short tons (168 million tonnes), a 26.6 per cent decline on the 252 million US short tons (229 million tonnes) produced in 2014. In 2020, Arch Resources flagged its interest in potentially selling the massive Black Thunder mine, a deal that never eventuated. In 2024, the mine produced 44.5 million US short tons (40.2 million tonnes), an almost 56 per cent decrease from a decade earlier. Rob Godby from the University of Wyoming said Core would have to "make some significant investment" in the mine if they want to keep operating it in the long term. "I think they'll just run it until it doesn't make sense to run it anymore," he said. (Cowboy State Daily)

Russia plans to prop up ailing coal sector: Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak wrote to President Vladimir Putin in late April proposing a 12.8 per cent cut in rail fees for some coal exports and a 60 per cent reduction on long-distance transport costs. Novak stated that Russia's coal industry lost 112.6 billion roubles (US$1.4 billion) in 2024, with companies producing about 30 million tonnes of coal a year and employing 15,000 people at risk of bankruptcy. Russian coal exports have declined since the invasion of Ukraine due to the impact of sanctions and, more recently, declining prices in the export market. (Reuters)

Sasol pitches plan to increase coal-to-oil production: South Africa's state-owned coal-to-oil producer, Sasol, told investors that it plans to increase production from its coal gasification plant at Secunda by nine per cent by 2027. Sasol proposes increasing its renewables goal from 1200 MW to more than 2000 MW to displace coal power consumption and sell surplus generation back to the grid. The company currently has agreements to purchase electricity from 757 MW of renewable generation capacity. A new report by Just Share, a shareholder activist group, said that a series of meetings between Sasol executives and the National Treasury likely played a key role in the government agency abandoning most of its proposals on the implementation of the second phase of South Africa's carbon tax. (News24, Sasol, Just Share)

Report reveals Australian coal plants frequent breakdowns over summer: A report by three Australian environmental groups revealed that there were 128 unplanned breakdowns and 17 scheduled outages at coal fired power stations between October 2024 and March 2025. The report found that, on average, about 5100 MW of coal capacity was offline across New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland over the period, with 25 per cent of Queensland and NSW coal capacity offline at any given time. Coal plant outages, especially during peak summertime loads, can drive electricity prices higher. When 35 per cent of coal capacity was offline in NSW and Queensland in October 2024, wholesale electricity prices surged from A$70 per megawatt-hour (MWh) (US$45 per MWh) in both states to A$177/MWh (US$114 per MWh) in Queensland and A$220/MWh (US$142 per MWh) in NSW. A separate report by Nexa Advisory found that the 1450 MW Yallourn brown coal power station had an unplanned outage for at least one of its four generators 32 per cent of the time over 2024. The Yallourn plant emits about 12 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year, half of Victoria's emissions reduction target of 45-50% on 2005 levels by 2030. The plant is scheduled to close in 2028. The report urges the Victorian government to ensure the development of offshore wind projects, commission the 8000 MW of approved wind and solar projects and 4000 MW of large-scale battery projects. Nexa estimates that there is also about 6000 MW of potential rooftop capacity on commercial and industrial buildings in the state. (Renew Economy, RenewEconomy, Nexa Advisory)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 New report highlights challenges in steel sector transition: The latest Global Energy Monitor stocktake on the transition of the steel industry found that electric arc furnace production grew by 11 per cent since the turn of the decade, with a further 24 per cent increase proposed by 2030. However, the Pedal to the Metal 2025 report found that 303 million tonnes per annum of coal-based blast furnace capacity is under development. The completion of 259 relining projects in the last five years extended the life of another 372 million tonnes per annum of blast furnace capacity. GEM estimates that India now accounts for 57 per cent of new coal-based steel capacity under development. The report notes that only eight per cent of India's proposed steel projects have entered the construction phase, down from 14 per cent in the previous year. (Reuters, Global Energy Monitor, Global Energy Monitor [Pdf])

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

The Obstruction Playbook: How corporate lobbying threatens South Africa's Just Transition, Just Share, May 2025. (Pdf)

This 102-page report documents how companies and business lobby groups, such as Sasol, Business Unity SA and the Minerals Council, have compromised the effectiveness of South Africa's Carbon Tax Act and Climate Change Act.

Coals Health Impacts in Phola Report 2024, Center for Environmental Rights, May 2025. (Pdf) (The media release is here.)

This 17-page report reviews the results of a community health survey of people exposed to air pollution from coal mining operations near Phola in Mpumalanga Province. The report proposes community and government strategies to reduce pollution impacts on residents.

"Interview: What the people of China's coal-rich Shanxi think about climate change", Carbon Brief, May 15, 2025.

This interview discusses the views of the residents of Shanxi province, China's largest coal-producing region, on the country's climate policies, the impacts on their local economy and whether they felt prepared for the energy transition.

Gina: What does she want? Guardian, podcast. (The link to the whole series is here).

This podcast series reports on Gina Rinehart, Australia's richest person. Episode 7 touches on her backing of the proposed Grassy Mountain coal mine in Alberta, Canada.

title: CoalWire 565, May 29, 2025
excerpt: Bangladesh cancels one coal project, revives another; Honduras joins Powering Past Coal Alliance.
content:
May 29, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The decision of Honduras to join the Powering Past Coal Alliance likely signals the end of the road for the country's last proposed coal plant. Together with the lack of progress in the previous two years on a plant in Brazil, it seems likely that Latin America will have no more coal plants. A new report also highlights how China's Belt and Road Initiative is investing more in solar and wind power projects despite supporting coal projects already under consideration at the time of President Xi Jinping's September 2021 announcement of a ban on new overses coal plants.

Another report suggests that India is likely to have excess generation capacity to meet daily peaks if all the financially stressed coal plants are revived and projects under construction are completed. The completion of the pipeline of renewable energy projects will further undermine the need for new coal projects. In neighbouring Bangladesh, the government has cancelled a lease for one stalled plant but approved the expansion of another scrapped by the previous government. In Indonesia, the government's latest power plan includes an increased target for new coal capacity, along with an expanded role for renewables.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Alberta regulator set bar too low in coal exploration approval

The "mitigation" measures adopted by the Alberta Energy Regulator for Northback Holdings for Grassy Mountain coal exploration project tend to be untested, unproven and overly optimistic, writes Lorne Fitch, a past adjunct professor with the University of Calgary in the Edmonton Journal.

 

 In India's coal belt, a window into the challenges facing the energy transition

India's reliance on coal is tied to a complex set of economic, social, and energy security factors; any successful energy transition plan will have to address all of them, writes Rishika Pardikar in Drilled.

 

 Plagued by black lung, coal miners wage long battles for benefits to pay bills — and to stay alive

For workers in one of America's most dangerous jobs, the push for benefits is often the most formidable challenge they'll face before they die, write Anavi Prakash, Victoria Malis, Tianyi Wang and Jessie Nguyen in the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

 

 Kentucky's Bitcoin boom has gone bust

In Kentucky's coal country, crypto mining was supposed to bring renewal. Now mines are powering down, and investors are hoping AI-powered data centres will fill the void, writes Dina Temple-Raston in Wired.

 

 Some of the most polluted US cities are home to coal-based steel plants

Seven steel plants in the US still use coal-based blast furnaces — and worsen pollution in the cities they are located, according to an analysis by climate research group Industrious Labs, writes Alexander C. Kaufman in Canary Media.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 End of the line for Latin America's last two proposed coal plants

The Honduran government's decision to join the Powering Past Coal Alliance, an international coalition comprising 180 national and sub-national governments committed to phasing out coal, suggests that the 100-megawatt (MW) Puente Alto Energy power station will be cancelled. The plant is the last proposed coal plant in the country. A report by Global Energy Monitor (GEM) also noted that the 600 MW Pedra Altas coal plant in Brazil has not progressed since the company was granted a licence in 2023. GEM notes that with the likely end of the two projects, there are no new coal plants under consideration in Latin America. In 2015, there were 18 proposed plants with a combined capacity of 7300 MW. (Global Energy Monitor)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Bangladesh cancels land lease over site of proposed coal plant: Nazmul Haque, the managing director of the state-owned Coal Power Generation Company Bangladesh, announced the cancellation of a lease of 225 acres (91 hectares) of land for the Orion Group's proposed 635 MW in Matarbari. In early May, 144 civil society organisations called on government agencies to cancel the finance, power purchase agreement, and land lease approved by the previous Bangladesh government for the development of the controversial project. The government approved Orion's proposed plant in 2013. The Bangladesh Working Group on Ecology and Development welcomed the cancellation of the lease. The cancellation came as the interim government's Planning Commission revived the second 1200 MW stage of the Matarbari coal power project. The previous government cancelled the project in 2021. (New Age, Business Standard)

 

 Japanese NGOs call for loan suspension after Bangladesh charges official: Japanese civil society groups have called on the Japanese government and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) to suspend loans for the 1200 MW Matarbari coal plant in Bangladesh until the resolution of criminal charges against a senior official overseeing the plant. Bangladesh's Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) filed a case in mid-May against Jahangir Alam, the project director of the Matarbari project, alleging that he had amassed 290 million Bangladeshi taka (approximately US$2.38 million) beyond his known sources of income. The ACC also alleges that Alam engaged in suspicious financial transactions, transferring 1.27 billion Bangladeshi taka (approximately US$10.48 million) between 94 different accounts between 1999 and 2024. The ACC alleged the transactions were aimed at concealing the illegal origins of the funds, in breach of the Money Laundering Prevention Act. Three NGOs – the Japan Center for a Sustainable Environment and Society (JACSES), Friends of the Earth Japan and Mekong Watch – said JICA has entered into eight loan agreements for the Matarbari plant since June 2014, a project that Sumitomo Corporation, Toshiba, and IHI had the engineering, procurement, and construction contract for. The groups called for clarification on whether JICA funding was involved in the transactions referred to by the ACC. The groups stated that JICA's Guidelines for Environmental and Social Considerations provide for the suspension of loan funds or early repayment in the event of legal violations in a project it supported. (Dhaka Tribune, Japan Center for a Sustainable Environment and Society)

 

 Australian tribunal backs coal seam gas project despite Gomeroi pleas: To the distress of the indigenous Gomeroi People, the National Native Title Tribunal has ruled that the NSW government can lease approximately 65,000 hectares of land to Santos for the development of the Narrabri coal seam gas project. The tribunal accepted that the Pilliga "is an important cultural landscape" but rejected the Gomeroi's objections to the project and decided that the project "offers a net public benefit." Central to the tribunal decision was its acceptance of the company's argument that there would be a shortfall of gas in the domestic market without the project, a claim rejected by the Gomeroi. Australia is one of the world's largest exporters of natural gas. Santos has proposed drilling 850 new wells on up to 425 well pads to allow the extraction of gas from coal seams located between 300 and 1200 metres below ground. Gomeroi woman Polly Cutmore says the project will be "devastating" for her community. "We are here because of our ancestors, they fought, and we will continue to fight," she said. The project still requires other approvals, but the leases have been the subject of legal challenges since the NSW Independent Planning Commission approved the project in 2020. (SBS, ABC, National Native Title Tribunal [Pdf])

 

 Trump administration orders Michigan coal plant to remain online: US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright issued an emergency order directing the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) and Consumers Energy to delay the closure of the 1560 MW J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan. Consumers Energy decided to close the plant in 2021, but Wright's order came just eight days before the May 31 closure date. Wright said he ordered the delay "to minimise the risk of blackouts and address critical grid security issues". The Sierra Club and Earthjustice rejected Wright's claim, stating that the closure had broad support, including from Consumers Energy, regulators, the state Attorney General, and others. Bryan Smigielski from the Sierra Club described the decision as "a payday for the coal industry that leaves us with higher bills and dirtier air". The plant comprises three units, which were commissioned in 1962, 1967, and 1980. In his statement, Wright claimed that the closure was "15 years before the end of its scheduled design life". The youngest of the three units is 45 years old. (Michigan Advance, MLive, Secretary of Energy, Sierra Club)

 

 US designates metallurgical coal as a 'strategic' mineral: US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright has added metallurgical coal to the Critical Materials List created under the Energy Act of 2020. The designation of a mineral as critical imposes obligations on government agencies to facilitate increased domestic production, such as fast-tracked permitting, tax subsidies, and access to federal funding. The Department of Energy assessment concluded that the shared infrastructure and workforce producing both thermal and metallurgical coal "are under strain from declining investment and operational capacity" and that without government intervention, this will "jeopardise domestic steel dominance". DOE argued that "dramatic increases in domestic metallurgical coal production and use" are required to expand domestic steel production and reduce reliance on imports. The agency estimates an increase of 18 million US short tons (16 million tonnes) is required. However, about 70 per cent of US steel production is from electric arc furnaces, which use less or no metallurgical coal compared to blast furnace production. Government support for increased production could lower prices and lead to industry consolidation. Global metallurgical coal prices are declining, and some major US coal producers are already operating at or above their production costs. US metallurgical coal production is primarily concentrated in the Appalachian region, with exports totalling 56 million US short tons (50.8 million tonnes) in 2024. (Argus Media, Congressional Research Service [Pdf], US Department of Energy)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The New South Wales government approved a two-year extension to 2035 for Glencore's Ulan underground mine. The company proposes to produce approximately 19 million tonnes of coal from the expansion, which Lock the Gate estimates will result in about 42 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions.

 

 New Zealand: Forest and Bird has called for the designation of the Denniston Plateau as a scientific reserve to protect the area's unique species from open-cut coal mining.

 

 Vietnam: The Ha Tinh Maritime Port Authority reported that the Cong Thanh 07 ship, carrying approximately 4,900 tonnes of coal, sank on May 26. One of the crew was rescued by a fishing boat, but nine others are missing, believed drowned.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Report says India could avoid more coal plants with renewables surge: A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates that the 32,300 MW of coal capacity already under construction, along with 23,550 MW of existing but financially stressed plants, would result in national coal capacity of 271,000 MW by 2030. India's National Electricity Plan set 260,000 MW as the required coal capacity by 2030. India's electricity demand profile features a massive peak. CREA estimates that in the year to the end of March 2025, there were 256 out of 365 days when the daily peak occurred during solar hours, and peak demand outside solar hours is within the capacity of existing and under-construction coal, hydro and other sources. CREA notes that there are currently 234,000 MW of renewable energy projects proposed or under construction, which will ease pressure on coal capacity, especially during peak hours. Even allowing for integration and balancing costs, electricity from new renewables is already cheaper than coal power capacity. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

Indonesian power plan increases role for coal, backs modest solar target: Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources has released the 2025-2034 power purchase plan (RUPTL), proposing the addition of 6300 MW of new coal capacity with new plants slated for commissioning as late as 2033. In 2021, Indonesia announced its intention to gradually phase out coal plants, with the last new plant expected to come online in 2027 and be closed by 2056. The previous plan proposed 5300 MW of grid-connected coal capacity, 8600 MW of gas and 7900 MW of solar. "Coal should not be considered an illicit commodity," said the Minister for Energy Bahlil Lahadalia. Bahlil also referred to the possibility of carbon capture and storage as a means to reduce emissions. The ministry's electricity director general, Jisman Hutajulu, said details of the proposed fossil fuel plants could be released next week. The latest plan also increases the proposed new gas capacity to 10,300 MW and the solar capacity to 17,100 MW. While advocates welcomed the increase in the solar target, the slow target rate of deployment is significantly lower than the technology's potential. Tata Mustasya from the Indonesian Sustainable Welfare Foundation said the plan made it "impossible to achieve" the previous goal of moving away from reliance on fossil fuel plants by 2040. (The Straits Times, Jakarta Post [paywall], Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources [video of press conference, in Indonesian])

Chinese overseas investments are shifting to renewables: An analysis by Boston University's Global Development Policy Centre has found that in 2023, just over two-thirds of investments through China's Belt and Road Initiative went to solar and wind projects. Between 2000 and 2021, just 13 per cent of China's overseas power investment went to solar and wind projects. The analysis found that, to date, Chinese state agencies have not backed new overseas coal projects since President Xi Jinping's September 2021 pledge to end support for overseas coal power projects. The report also found that coal plants in the pipeline at the time of Xi's pledge have continued to progress, with 8000 MW of new capacity operational in 2022-23 and another 9000 MW planned or under construction. (Inside Climate News, Boston University Global Development Policy Center)

Report finds banks support for Glencore flows through policy loopholes: A report by Reclaim Finance found nine European banks have participated in 12 bonds that raised US$8 billion to finance Glencore's operations. Glencore is a diversified commodities and mining company with plans to expand its coal operations at 17 coal mines in Australia, South Africa, Canada, Russia, and Kazakhstan. Glencore is the world's largest thermal coal exporter and, following the purchase of Elk Valley Coal in Canada, accounts for nine per cent of the global metallurgical coal trade. Reclaim Finance found that all of the bonds issued were for general corporate financing, which allows the allocation of funds raised to any of the company's operations. The nine European banks are Barclays, BBVA, Commerzbank, Deutsche Bank, HSBC, ING, Santander, Standard Chartered and UBS. While all nine have policies restricting financing for thermal coal projects, loopholes allow funding of the broader company. HSBC, Standard Chartered, and Barclays policies exclude support for thermal coal mines but allow general corporate financing, while restrictions in the policies of Commerzbank and Santander only apply to new customers. Reclaim Finance wants European banks to exclude finance for all coal project developers. (Net Zero Investor, Reclaim Finance)

Mozambique govt reopens door for JSW Steel purchase of coal lease: President Daniel Chapo's cabinet has reinstated the mining concession held by Minas de Revuboe (MdR), a company owned by the estate of Ken Talbot, an Australian mining developer who died in a plane crash 14 years ago. Last year, JSW Steel, an Indian company owned by billionaire Sajjan Jindal, announced a US$74 million deal to buy a 92 per cent stake in MdR, but then-President Filipe Jacinto Nyusi cancelled the concession. The government subsequently proposed allocating the concession, which reportedly contains 280 million tonnes of coking coal, to Stonecoal SA, a company with five directors from Jindal Steel & Power, another Indian company led by Naveen Jindal, Sajjan's younger brother. Naveen Jindal heads the privately owned Vulcan International, which operates the adjoining Moatize mine that exports thermal and metallurgical coal. The reinstatement of the lease allows JSW to complete the purchase of MdR which had proposed producing 7 million tonnes of coal annually from the mine. (Bloomberg)

US agencies back lawsuit against index funds with coal holdings: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) filed a submission in support of a case brought by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton against the three largest US index fund managers — BlackRock, Vanguard Group and State Street over their holdings in coal companies. The November 2024 lawsuit alleged the three funds held significant stakes in nine major publicly traded coal companies, including more than 25 per cent of Peabody Energy, Arch Resources, CONSOL Energy, Alpha Metallurgical Resources, Black Hill Resources and Warrior Met Coal. The companies produce nearly half of US coal production. The Texas lawsuit, backed by nine other Republican-led states, alleges that the climate policies of the three financial firms reduced coal supply and increased prices, allowing investors to "produce extraordinary revenue gains". The submission by the DOJ and the FTC argues that the funds could breach competition laws if they engaged in "concerted efforts to reduce output". The three firms say that their investments in the companies track changes in the share market indexes and are not actively managed. They argue that their decisions about votes on climate-change policies were "incidental" activities that don't create an antitrust conspiracy. (Wall Street Journal)

(Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)
Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources [video of press conference, in Indonesian])

title: CoalWire 566, June 5, 2025
excerpt: Indian solar + batteries undercut coal; coal utilisation rates declining in key Asian countries.
content:
June 5, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The long-running legal challenge against RWE regarding the impacts of its greenhouse gas emissions came to a close with mixed results. While the court accepted the principle that major emitters could be held liable for the damage caused by historical emissions, it found that in the case of Peruvian farmer and mountain guide Saul Luciano Lliuya, the risk of flooding from a melting glacier was not sufficiently imminent or certain.

In the US, President Trump's intent to 'save' an old coal plant in Arizona could come with a US$1.9 billion price tag, according to the state's utility regulator. In Montana, Republican lawmakers are considering repealing a 2020 law that promotes carbon capture and storage for coal plants. The driving factor is the prospect of CCS costing about US$1 billion per coal unit.

In Asia, a new report notes that in South Korea, Japan, and Indonesia, coal plant utilisation rates have declined significantly since 2020 as new coal plants came online and renewables generation increases. Another report finds that in India, solar paired with batteries is cost-competitive with industrial tariffs in many states and new coal plants. In Russia, the government has decided to offer financial concessions to coal exporters as shipments pivot from the European to Asian markets. In Indonesia, a new report estimates that co-firing coal plants with biomass would only make a marginal difference to the country's power sector emissions.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 One lawsuit just helped melt the fossil fuel industry's defence against being held accountable for climate change

While a German court dismissed a claim against RWE filed by Peruvian farmer and mountain guide Saul Luciano Lliuya, it confirmed that private companies can, in principle, be held liable for their share in causing climate damages, writes Ben Franta in The Conversation.

 

 Bitcoin miner gets powerful perch at Department of Energy loan office

A former executive whose company had a track record of environmental permit violations from its coal-fired bitcoin operation is now operating at the highest ranks of the US Department of Energy, writes Brian Dabbs in E&E News.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Court decision spares RWE but opens the door to other climate litigation: The Higher Regional Court of Hamm has dismissed the legal case against the German energy giant RWE for part of the costs associated with reducing the flood risk to a Peruvian farmer's home. Peruvian mountain guide Saul Luciano Lliuya argued that as RWE had contributed about 0.4 per cent of the increase in greenhouse gases from its fossil fuel energy projects, it should pay about 17,000 (US$19,000) towards flood mitigation measures to protect his home. The judges ruled that the flood risk to Lliuya's home was not sufficiently imminent or certain to hold the company liable. Germanwatch, which supported Lliuya's case, said that the court accepted the principle that companies can be held liable for the impacts of their greenhouse gas emissions. The group stated that liability provisions exist in the statutes of other countries and that there are currently more than 30 cases in which fossil fuel companies are being sued. (Deutsche Welle, NPR, Germanwatch, Guardian, Hamm Higher Regional Court [Pdf])

 

 Polish election result casts shadow over energy transition: The election of right-wing populist Karol Nawrocki as Poland's next President will pose new challenges to the ability of Prime Minister Donald Tusk's centre-right government to implement its policies. Tusk was elected on a platform of promoting a transition to renewables but relatively little progress has been made. Nawrocki, who was backed by the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party and US President Donald Trump, will hold the position until 2030. While the role of is largely ceremonial, the President has a veto power over government legislation. Nawrocki, who has advocated more extreme policies than the PiS, could derail any moves by Tusk to progress his agenda ahead of the 2027 national election. After Nawrocki's election, Tusk announced a vote of confidence in his own government will be held on June 11. (BBC, Guardian, Notes from Poland)

 

 Indonesian anti-corruption agency revives power plant investigation: South Korean prosecutors successfully lobbied Indonesia's anti-corruption agency, the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK), to reactivate its investigation into allegations that a Hyundai Engineering and Construction official paid US$368,493 to Sunjaya Purwadisastra, a former regent of Cirebon, to help facilitate the construction of the 1000 MW PLTU Cirebon-2 coal plant. KPK investigators interviewed a South Korean citizen in the prosecutor's office in Seoul and the KPK subsequently interviewed Herry Jung, the then general manager of Hyundai Engineering and Construction, who was first named as a suspect in the case in 2019. Sunjaya was jailed in 2023 to serve a 9-year sentence on an unrelated bribery charge. (Jakarta Post)

 

 Coal ash overflow polluting Indian river: The Bokaro Power Supply Company Limited (BPSCL) has not paid the 20.5 million rupee (US$240,000) fine imposed in April by the Jharkhand State Pollution Control Board (JSPCB) for the pollution of the Darda River. Coal ash contaminated water from all six of the coal ash dams at the 500 MW coal plant continues to pollute the river. BPSCL is a joint venture between the Steel Authority of India and the Damodar Valley Corporation, a state-owned power utility. Two of the coal ash dam walls were breached in 2022 resulting in pollution downstream. (Times of India)

 

 Report says biomass not a viable solution to Indonesian coal use: A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates that Indonesia's proposed introduction of 10 per cent biomass co-firing at coal plants could result in increased emissions of pollutants such as mercury, lead and arsenic as well as carbon monoxide and hydrogen sulphide. The report states that the government's envisaged level of biomass co-firing would only reduce coal power sector emissions by between 1.5 per cent and 2.4 per cent. CREA estimates that biomass co-firing could reduce fine particle pollution by 9 per cent, nitrogen oxide emissions by 7 per cent, and sulphur dioxide emissions by 10 per cent. However, dedicated biomass power plants are allowed to emit higher levels of fine particle pollution, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides than coal units. CREA said that PLN promotion of biomass power by the state utility threatens to prolong the use of coal and derail a just transition away from reliance on fossil fuels. (Indonesia Business Post, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf])

 

 Arizona regulator warns reviving old coal plant could cost US$1.9 billion: The Arizona Corporation Commission (ACC), the state's utility regulator, said it would cost about US$1.9 billion to continue operating the 426 MW Cholla Generating Station in Arizona in line with President Trump's recent executive order. In early April, Trump signed an executive order aimed at reversing the decline of coal generation and announced he had ordered Energy Secretary Chris Wright to "save" Arizona Public Service's Cholla plant from closure. The two units at the Cholla plant were commissioned in 1962 and 1980 and retired in late March 2025. ACC Chair Kevin Thompson said that returning the two units to service would necessitate the installation of selective catalytic reduction equipment, along with major plant maintenance. In a statement, Thompson said he had met with Department of Interior officials in March "to outline the exorbitant cost that would be placed on APS ratepayers" to keep the coal units operating. (KJZZ, Arizona Corporation Commission)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Mongolia: Prime Minister Luvsannamsrain Oyun-Erdene resigned after failing to secure a majority of MPs support on a motion of confidence. His resignation follows weeks of protests over allegations of corruption.

 

 US: Core Natural Resources has told about 200 workers that the Itmann Mine No. 5 and associated processing plant in West Virginia will be idled in August.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

South African company to expand Mozambique coal export terminal: Grinrod, a South African company, announced it will spend US$80 million to expand the Matola coal export terminal in southern Mozambique. In January 2024, Mozambique extended the DP World and Grindrod's lease at the Port of Maputo until 2058. Grinrod proposed expanding the capacity of the coal export terminal from 7.5 million tonnes a year to 18 million tonnes a year but this has now been revised down to 12 million tonnes a year. Persistent problems with Transnet's rail operations to the Richards Bay Coal Terminal prompted some South African coal exporters to truck coal to the Matola terminal. Mozambican President Daniel Chapo said the government wanted to invest in rail links "so that we have fewer trucks and more rail wagons" transporting coal and magnetite. Mozambique has two other coal export terminals, one at the port of Beira on the central coast and the other at Nacala in the country's north. Both of these cater for exports from the Moatize coalfield in Tete province. (AIM)

Study says solar paired with battery storage in India undercuts new coal: A study by the India Energy and Climate Center at the University of California estimates that solar combined with battery storage can deliver electricity at over 95 per cent availability for less than 6 rupees per kilowatt hour (US$0.07 per kWh). The study is based on recent Indian auction bids for unsubsidised storage as well as bids for batteries paired with solar. Solar module prices in India now cost about 10 US cents per watt in 2024 due to a glut of module production capacity. Lithium-ion battery prices have fallen from US$165 per kWh in 2020 to US$100 kWh in 2025 while performance has improved substantially. The study estimates that solar plus battery storage can deliver electricity that is "comparable to or lower" than current industrial tariffs in most states and for power from new coal plants. "Unlike industrial tariffs, which typically increase with inflation, solar-plus-storage tariffs will remain fixed and inflation-proof for 25 years," the study concludes. (Economic Times, India Energy and Climate Center [Pdf])

Report highlights declining coal utilisation rates in key Asian countries: A report by the Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis (IEEFA) has found that coal plant utilisation rates in Japan, South Korea, and Indonesia have declined since 2020 as new coal plants were commissioned and renewable capacity increased. In China, the coal plant utilisation rate was four per cent higher in 2024 compared to 2020 but was still only at 50 per cent. Chinese coal generation has increased in part due to a drought-induced decline in hydro generation and some provinces prioritising the construction of new coal capacity. In Japan and South Korea, coal utilisation rates in 2023 were 15 per cent and 10 per cent lower, respectively, compared to 2020. In Indonesia, the utilisation rate of coal capacity fell 13 per cent between 2020 and 2023 as new coal generation capacity increased by 38 per cent. Typically, utilities aim to operate new ultra-supercritical coal plants at utilisation rates of 80 per cent or more and older plants above 65 per cent. IEEFA suggests that the low utilisation rates indicate "substantial room" to retire older and less efficient coal capacity. (Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis)

Trump administration doubles tariffs to 50 per cent on steel: Despite a court ruling that only Congress can set tariffs, President Donald Trump announced plans to increase tariffs on steel and aluminium imports from 25 per cent to 50 per cent on June 4. Trump said the increase is aimed at securing the US steel industry. He announced the tariff increase at an event in Pennsylvania to celebrate a potential takeover agreement between US Steel and Nippon Steel that proposes investing $14 billion, including expanding steel production at the Mon Valley steel works in Pittsburgh and upgrading other mills and mines. The expansion of domestic steel production could also increase demand for US metallurgical coal. If implemented, the tariffs will affect a wide range of steel and aluminium exporting countries, including Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Australia, and the UK. The increased cost of aluminium will also affect US auto producers. The European Union has flagged that it will impose countermeasures. (Time, ABC News)

Russia offers financial support to coal exporters: In a bid to support struggling coal exporters, the Russian government has agreed to defer the mineral extraction tax and insurance payment obligations of coal companies until December 1, 2025. Other measures include the possibility of debt restructuring and a reduction in the coal export tax for Siberian producers supplying coal to north-western and southern ports. The introduction in 2022 of European Union and US bans on buying Russian coal forced exporters to direct production to the Asian market, which now accounts for 80 per cent of the country's sales. Exporting via eastern ports to the Asian market also increased rail costs. (Reuters)

Republican legislators in Wyoming regret the law requiring CCS: Republican legislators in Wyoming are reconsidering a 2020 law they passed that mandated power utilities undertake feasibility studies on the use of carbon capture and storage (CCS) on existing coal units by 2030. The Arizona legislature passed the Reliable and Dispatchable Low-carbon Energy Standards Act to preserve coal generation and increase demand for coal. Since the bill became law in 2020, both Rocky Mountain Power and Black Hills Energy have estimated that it could cost US$1 billion to install CCS on a single unit. "I have a concern that we're continuing to implement something that does nothing but increases the rates of our ratepayers, number one, and drives up the price of coal-fired power, which then does lead to alternatives such as nuclear or wind and solar," said Representative Chris Knapp, a Republican representing the seat of Gillette, a city based on coal, oil and gas projects. The interim Joint Minerals, Business, and Economic Development Committee is considering repealing the law, although a recent attempt to do so failed. (Wyoming Public Media)

Glencore restructure consolidates coal projects: Glencore has transferred its coal mines in Canada, South Africa, and Colombia to its Australian subsidiary, Glencore Investment. The projects are valued at US$22 billion and also include a South African subsidiary focused on manganese, chrome, and vanadium. Early last year, Glencore decided against spinning off its coal assets, which generated more than a third of its earnings in 2024. It also floated the idea of merging with Rio Tinto but was rebuffed. Analysts view the restructuring as potentially allowing for merger discussions with BHP and Rio Tinto if Glencore Investment is sold. BHP has previously indicated that it doesn't want to operate in South Africa, and Rio Tinto offloaded its last coal assets in 2018. (Reuters, Mining.com)

title: CoalWire 567, June 12, 2025
excerpt: Pakistan’s solar boom hits coal plants; Chinese coal imports slump; Indian coal plants water woes.
content:
June 12, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

More than a decade ago, Indian NGOs and scientists warned that the rapid expansion of inland coal capacity would struggle to access water year-round in a rapidly heating world. With the commissioning of many new coal plants in recent years, competition between residents, farmers, and power utilities is intensifying over access to scarce water resources. In Pakistan, the astonishing growth in solar capacity, much of it small-scale, has undercut the viability of Chinese-backed coal plants that rely on expensive imported coal. In China, coal imports have slumped as utilities face growing stockpiles, declining domestic coal prices, and increasing renewable energy generation.

A new report notes recent improvements in Chinese air quality but warns that the westward expansion of some major industries is contributing to worsening air pollution in provinces not adequately covered under the current plan to cut air pollution. A separate report by Greenpeace East Asia notes that provinces in western China now dominate the list of regions approving new coal power plants. In South Africa, a new report warns of the heavy death toll caused by poor air quality, with Eskom's fleet of coal power plants a significant contributor. Another report flags that South African exporters face a growing economic risk as more countries and trading blocs impose levies on emissions-intensive imports.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 India's US$80 billion coal-power boom is running short of water

India plans to spend nearly US$80 billion on water-hungry coal plants by 2031 to power growing industries like data centre operations, but the vast majority of these new projects are planned for India's driest areas, according to a power ministry document, write Krishna N. Das and Sarita Chaganti Singh in Reuters.

 

 Carbon capture projects promise a climate fix — and a fossil fuel lifeline

Japanese companies are involved in proposed carbon capture and storage projects in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand, with governments promoting the expensive technology as a key element in their emissions reduction plans, writes Nithin Coca in Mongabay.

 

 US coal and gas plants were closing. Then Trump ordered them to keep running

The grid operators that draw power from the plants said they never asked for them to remain open, write Claire Brown and Harry Stevens in the New York Times.

 

 Coal mining fear sparks unexpected conservation boom in South Africa's Mpumalanga province

Fearful of open-cast mining's devastating impacts, a growing number of South African landowners are opting to designate part of their properties as private protected areas for biodiversity conservation, writes Fred Kockott in the Daily Maverick.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 South Korean election offers the prospect of accelerated coal phase-out: Lee Jae-myung, the Democratic Party of Korea's candidate, won the Presidential election with 49.42 per cent of votes cast, comfortably defeating Kim Moon-soo from the conservative People Power Party, who polled just over 41 per cent of votes. Lee will face significant challenges during his five-year term, including a slowing economy, the impact of US tariffs on certain exporters, and political tensions that persist after President Yoon Suk Yeol declared martial law in December 2024. Yoon was subsequently impeached. Lee has backed phasing out coal generation by 2040, the expansion of renewables and a reduced role for imported gas generation. South Korea currently has 41,195 megawatt (MW) of operating coal capacity, with an additional 1050 MW under construction, according to Global Energy Monitor's Global Coal Plant Tracker. Coal generated 28.4 per cent of the country's electricity in 2024. The Australian Department of Industry, Science and Resources estimates South Korea imported 92 million tonnes of coal in 2024, making it the world's fourth largest thermal coal importer. Ahead of the election, Solutions for Our Climate, a South Korean NGO, called on the government to support green steel production, convert coal plants to solar power with storage capacity by 2035, and triple renewable energy generation capacity. (Guardian, Argus, Solutions for Our Climate)

 

 Canadian study warns mines could trigger fish population "collapse": A study by scientists from the Alberta government and the University of Alberta warns that fish in Crowsnest Lake, downstream from two shuttered coal mines, have high selenium concentrations that exceed guidelines. Crowsnest Lake is downstream from the Tent Mountain and Grassy Mountain coal mines, which have been closed since the early 1980s. Australian billionaire Gina Rinehart's Northback Holdings recently won approval from the Alberta government for further exploration within the Grassy Mountain lease area. The study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, states that weathering waste rock from mountaintop removal coal mines presents "an acute threat to downstream fish populations, decades after mining ends". The study warns that prolonged exposure to high levels of selenium could cause "complete reproductive failure and even population collapse". (CBC, Biorxiv)

 

 Report says cleaner air could save 38,000 South African lives a year: A joint report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air and Greenpeace South Africa estimates that PM2.5 fine particle pollution caused about 42,000 deaths in 2023 in South Africa. The report states that if South Africa met its national air quality standard, there would be approximately 9300 fewer deaths a year. The report estimates that if South Africa met World Health Organisation standards, the death toll would be cut by 72 per cent to 3,200 a year. Coal-fired power plants are the most significant contributors to PM2.5 pollution. However, Eskom's lobbying power has resulted in it winning extended exemptions from pollution standards and delaying the retirement of coal plants until the 2030s and beyond. The groups called on the government to introduce the real-time publication of emissions data and impose health impact penalties or a 'polluter pays levy' on large industrial emitters and coal-fired power plants. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 Taiwanese legislature backs call for faster coal phase-out: The Taiwanese parliament has supported a nonbinding resolution moved by the Chinese Nationalist Party and Taiwan People's Party MPs, which calls for the shutdown of 5500 MW of coal capacity at the Taichung power plant by 2028. The parties argued that the coal units could be closed earlier to reduce pollution, as two new gas units at Taipower's plant are scheduled to be commissioned in 2026. The two opposition parties control the 113-seat legislature, but Taiwan's President, Lai Ching-te, is from the centre-left Democratic Progressive Party (DPP). DPP MP Chuang Jui-hsiung accused the two parties of "ruthless politicking". The government's current plan is to progressively retire the coal units through 2034 as Taipower commissions new gas units. (Taipei Times, Focus Taiwan)

 

 South African court offers hope of hearing over coal mine: The Pietermaritzburg High Court has directed Tendele Coal Mining and other parties in the case to meet agreed-upon deadlines regarding the expansion of the Somkhele coal mine in KwaZulu-Natal. Local community organisations and environmental justice NGOs welcomed the court order, which also granted leave for the applicants to seek an expedited hearing. The groups oppose the expansion of the mine into three adjoining villages. The groups argue that Tendele has not complied with a 2022 judgment requiring compliance with environmental and community safeguards, as well as the resettlement of families within 500 metres of the mine. The Mfolozi Community Environmental Justice Organisation wants the court to freeze the company's mine expansion until it has complied fully with the 2022 judgment. (The Witness)

 

 
 "The grid operator wasn't asking for this plant to be kept online. The utility that owns and operates the plant wasn't asking for the plant to be kept online, the state wasn't asking for the plant to be kept online,"

said Dan Scripps, the chair of the Michigan Public Service Commission, on President Trump's directive to keep the 1420 MW J.H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan operating.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The 380 MW unit at EnergyAustralia's Yallourn brown coal power station in Victoria will be offline for at least two weeks after the collapse of an air duct. The unit is slated to close in 2028.

 

 India: A Delhi court dismissed charges against the former secretary of the Ministry of Coal, H C Gupta and two other officials over the allocation of the Mahuagarhi coal block in Jharkhand to JAS Infrastructure Capital (JICPL). The court convicted JICPL and its director of fraudulently obtaining the coal block by misrepresenting facts in its application.

 

 US: The Trump administration approved the expansion of Signal Peak Energy's Bull Mountains coal mine in Montana. The approval extends the mine's life by up to nine years and allows for the production of an additional 57 million US short tons (51.7 million tonnes) of coal.

 

 "Companies can now recover their investment in transitioning to predominantly renewable energy — using solar, wind and batteries — in less than two years,"

said Mujtaba Haider Khan from Reon Energy, a renewable energy supplier in Pakistan.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Chinese coal imports slumped in May: Chinese coal imports in May declined by 18 per cent compared to the same period in 2024 and were down 4.7 per cent compared to April, according to the General Administration of Customs. The slump in imports comes as increased renewable energy generation, a decline in power demand by key sectors of the economy, and growing domestic coal production. For the January to May period, Chinese coal imports totalled 188.7 million tonnes, an 8 per cent decline from the same period in 2024. Several weeks ago, the National Development and Reform Commission, a powerful central agency, urged power utilities to prioritise domestic coal purchases and boost stockpiles by 10 per cent to 215 million tonnes by June 10 to support local coal producers. A surge in domestic coal production following the 2021 blackouts has triggered a sustained decline in domestic prices and growing stockpiles at ports and power plants. (Reuters, Reuters)

Report finds China keeps approving new coal plants in 2025: China approved 11,290 MW of new coal plants in the first quarter of 2025, according to an analysis of data by Greenpeace East Asia. The latest data reveal that since 2021, 289,000 MW of new coal capacity has been approved, almost double the 145,000 MW during the 2015-2020 period of the 13th Five-Year Plan. Wind and solar capacity now exceed installed coal capacity by 32,000 MW. In 2025, western provinces dominate the list of new coal plant approvals, with Inner Mongolia approving 10,640 MW and Gansu just over 10,000 MW. A new report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) found that the national average concentration of PM2.5 fine particle air pollution declined by 5 per cent in the first quarter of 2025 compared to the same period in the previous year. However, the report finds that PM2.5 fine particle air pollution levels exceeded national air quality standards by 18 per cent in the first quarter, and almost three-quarters of provincial regions exceeded their compliance targets. CREA also noted the declining air quality in western provinces, which is attributed in part to the relocation of steel and metal processing plants. CREA proposes the inclusion of western and central provinces in the country's air quality governance framework, as well as accelerating the deployment of clean energy in coal-dependent provinces. (Greenpeace East Asia, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

Report highlights risk to South African exporters to carbon shock: A report by Net Zero Tracker has warned that South Africa's economy is very exposed to trade shocks if it fails to decarbonise the supply chains of major export sectors ahead of the European Union's (EU) Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms (CBAMs) coming into effect in 2026 and the UK's scheme in 2027. The schemes impose a carbon price on imported emissions-intensive products, including steel, aluminium, and cement, to prevent unfair competition with producers covered by domestic carbon price schemes. Net Zero Tracker notes that South Africa exports products worth approximately US$135 billion to 139 countries with net-zero targets and that approximately 422,000 jobs currently depend on exports to jurisdictions with active or incoming CBAMs. Key exposed sectors include minerals and basic metals, the automotive industry, and agricultural products. The Net Zero Tracker is a collaboration between four groups, including the UK-based non-profit, the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit. (EyeWitness News, Net Zero Tracker)

Pakistan's solar boom undercuts Chinese-backed coal plants: Pakistan is undergoing a rapid transition to a renewables-based electricity system, but the switch is mainly driven by consumers, with grid regulators struggling to catch up. In the first three months of 2025, Renewables Now, a Pakistan-based think tank, estimates that 4900 MW of new grid-connected solar capacity was installed, along with an unspecified amount of behind-the-meter capacity. BNEF estimates that Pakistan imported 22,000 MW of solar panels in 2024, as consumers responded to a 155 per cent increase in electricity prices over the previous three years. Renewables Now estimates consumer solar prices halved in 2024. It also states that 89 per cent of China's US$13.7 billion investments in Pakistan power projects are tied to 6600 MW of coal power plants. A further 1620 MW of Chinese-backed coal projects have been proposed. The group notes that imports of Chinese solar panels are cannibalising power sales from Chinese-backed coal plants. The group estimates that of the 39,000 MW of solar panel capacity imported over the past five years, only 4900 MW is grid-connected. The surge in solar capacity triggered a 10 per cent decline in electricity sales from the grid in the 2023 financial year and a further three per cent decline in 2024. The government plans to cut payments for solar electricity exports, but industrial users, such as Lucky Cement, have turned to wind, solar, and battery storage to reduce the amount of electricity they buy from the grid. In 2024, Pakistan's electricity system had a total installed capacity of 46,000 MW. (Financial Times, South China Morning Post, Renewables First [Pdf], Dialogue Earth)

The costs of US coal power continue to rise: A report by Energy Innovation (EI) estimates that 95 per cent of the 162 US coal plants operating in early 2025 are more expensive to run than new local solar, wind, or energy storage facilities within 45 kilometres. The report estimates that between 2021 and 2024, the costs of coal-based electricity increased by 28 per cent, almost twice the rate of inflation. EI, a US-based clean energy think tank promoting a clean energy transition, estimates that US consumers will pay US$6.2 billion more in 2024 for the same amount of electricity than they did three years earlier. The original Coal Cost Crossover report, released in 2019, found that 62 per cent of US coal plants generated electricity at prices higher than those of wind and solar, a gap that increased to 72 per cent and 99 per cent in the 2021 and 2023 updates respectively. The report notes that solar, wind, and energy storage accounted for 93 per cent of the new resources added to the grid in 2024. EI says regulators can accelerate the transition by updating interconnection study rules for new capacity and prioritise existing coal plant grid connections for new local renewable generation. (Forbes, Energy Innovation Policy & Technology, Energy Innovation Policy & Technology [Pdf])

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Fossil fuel emissions outlook report 2025: assessing the climate and public health risk of Malaysia's fossil fuel assets, RimbaWatch and the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, June 2025. (Pdf)

This 36-page report provides an overview of Malaysia's heavy reliance on oil and gas production. The report notes that the country's National Energy Transition Roadmap aims to phase out coal generation by 2050, with renewable energy accounting for 70 per cent of capacity. However, the plan fails to reduce fossil fuel production in line with the goals of the Paris Agreement.

The long term will be decided now: Why climate risk demands system-level action from investors, Sierra Club, June 2025. (Pdf)

This 32-page paper presents the case for why global heating poses a systemic financial threat to the global economy and argues that traditional sustainable investing focuses too narrowly on the risk of climate impacts on individual companies.
