title: CoalWire 568, June 19, 2025
excerpt: South Korea’s last coal mine; Indian coal stockpiles mount; big fall tipped for Chinese coal imports.
content:
June 19, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Analysis by Global Energy Monitor suggests that China's capacity payments scheme has provided financial support to power utilities but done little, if anything, to support more flexible generation and lower reliance on coal power. With the rapid expansion of new coal capacity in China driving the growth of new coal mining, an industry association has forecast a decline in imports this year of between 50 and 100 million tonnes. A fall of this magnitude would hit Indonesian and Australian exporters. In India, the state-owned coal mining company, Coal India, faces mounting stockpiles as cooler-than-expected weather and increased renewable capacity combined to undermine coal generation.

In South Korea, two state agencies are considering the future of the state-owned Korea Coal Corporation as the country's last coal mine nears closure. In Australia, four coal mining company executives face court over their role in dismissing suggestions by a whistleblower about the falsification of coal quality certificates to boost the value of exports. A South Korean power utility, Korea East-West Power Co., Ltd., had flagged concerns about coal quality in March 2020 before the TerraCom scandal became public. In the US, a bill before the Senate, backed by the Trump administration, proposes removing tax credits for new wind, solar, and battery projects. The latest Lazard report on US generation costs notes that even without subsidies, new wind and solar generation is cheaper than competitors.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 The incredible inefficiency of the fossil energy system

Today's fossil energy system is incredibly inefficient: almost two-thirds of all primary energy is wasted in energy production, transportation, and use before fossil fuel has done any work or produced any benefit, write Daan Walter, Kingsmill Bond, Amory Lovins, Laurens Speelman, Chiara Gulli and Sam Butler-Sloss from RMI.

 

 China's 'capacity payments' boosted coal plant revenue by up to eight per cent

An analysis of the US$14.9 billion allocated in the first year of China's capacity payments scheme reveals most coal plant owners received a revenue boost of about five to eight per cent, but there is no clear evidence of reduced generation, writes Mingxin Zhang from Global Energy Monitor in Carbon Brief.

 

 Indonesia downgrades clean energy ambitions in new power plan, bets big on fossil fuels

Indonesia's new power development plan outlines a stark pivot back to fossil fuel reliance, undermining previous clean energy goals and raising concerns among environmental analysts and energy transition advocates, writes Gusty Da Costa in Indonesia Business Post.

 

 World's largest banks pledged US$869 billion to fossil fuel firms in 2024, new report finds

Two-thirds of the biggest 65 banks increased financing by US$162 billion from 2023 to 2024, walking back climate promises, writes Oliver Milman in The Guardian.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australian coal company directors face court over coal test scandal: In 2020, a TerraCom whistleblower alleged that the company pressured ALS, a coal testing laboratory, to falsify coal export certificates in order to overstate calorific values. ALS later confirmed that over 13 years, between 45 per cent and 50 per cent of all coal export certificates were "manually amended without justification". Subsequently, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) launched legal action against TerraCom and its key executives for breaches of the Corporations Act, alleging that the company failed to take reasonable steps to ensure statements made to the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) were not false or misleading. In late May, TerraCom informed the ASX that it had reached an agreement with ASIC to pay A$7.5 million (US$4.85 million) for an agreed breach of the Corporations Act and pay A$1 million (US$650,000) for the regulator's legal costs. The Federal Court of Australia has not yet approved the agreement. However, the deal has not prevented ASIC's case against two TerraCom executives and two board members from proceeding. ASIC told the court that the directors should have sought an investigation into claims by a whistleblower of coal quality certificate tampering before informing the ASX in April 2020 that no customers had raised concerns. ASIC told the court that the South Korean power utility, Korea East-West Power Co., Ltd., had raised concerns about coal quality in March 2020. (The Australian [paywall], TerraCom [Pdf])

 

 South Africa's transition plan moves ahead despite delayed coal closures: The Climate Investment Fund has approved US$500 million for South Africa's updated coal transition plan, which defers the decommissioning of Eskom's 1200 MW Hendrina, 600 MW Grootvlei, and 1600 MW Camden coal plants until 2030. The decision enables South Africa to submit detailed costings for proposed projects for approval by the trust and opens the door to an additional US$2.1 billion in funding from other funders, including the World Bank and the African Development Bank. The retreat of the US government from a range of climate initiatives, including the Just Energy Transition program, cast a shadow over the future of South Africa's proposed plan. In May 2024, the then Minister for Forestry, Fisheries, and the Environment, Barbara Creecy, granted Eskom's request to permit the Hendrina, Grootvlei, and Camden plants, along with two other old power stations, to operate at current, weaker air pollution standards until March 31, 2030. (News24)

 

 UK backs coal tip program, but councils say more funds required: Chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the UK government would provide 118 million (US$158 million) to the Welsh government over the next three years to "keep coal tips safe". Hours before the announcement, four Welsh councils told the UK House of Commons Welsh Affairs committee that the proposed funding would only "scratch the surface" of the need to monitor and rehabilitate high-risk coal tips left after mines closed. The Welsh Government had previously requested 600 million (US$806 million) for the work. Mark Williams of Caerphilly council said it has 205 tips within its boundaries and 89 on its land. He stated that inspections cost around 15,000 per year for each tip and that current funding is inadequate to cover the costs of proper remediation. A Welsh government review classified 360 of the 2573 coal tips as having "the potential to impact public safety" and earlier this year passed legislation creating the Disused Tips Authority for Wales. Nicola Pearce from Neath Port Talbot Council said that it spent about 12 million (US$16 million) making one coal tip safe. The council has 617 coal tips in its area. (BBC, South Wales Argus, Wales Online)

 

 Scientific paper says coal and steel pollution affecting oceans: A paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences suggests that iron particles emitted from industrial processes, including the burning of coal and steelmaking, are altering the marine ecosystem in the Pacific Ocean north of Hawaii. Increased iron levels stimulate the growth of phytoplankton in the North Pacific Transition Zone in spring, but this has the effect of depleting other nutrients, which triggers a crash later in the season. Phytoplankton are the base of the food web and are crucial in supporting fish populations. The study notes that iron emitted from industrial processes has a characteristic isotope signature that distinguishes it from naturally occurring iron, which primarily originates from dust transported from desert regions. The authors state that the study implies that the supply of dissolved iron to the North Pacific surface waters has increased by over 50 per cent since preindustrial times. The study states that steel production and coal combustion in East Asia had increased more than threefold since 1997 when global satellite ocean colour observations commenced. (University of Hawai'i News, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences)

 

 Trump moves to axe pollution standards for coal plants: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin announced proposals to repeal greenhouse gas emissions standards for the power sector under the Clean Air Act and rescind amendments to the 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS), a change that would revert emissions standards to the those adopted in 2012 standards by the Biden administration. Zeldin stated that the MATS rule particularly affects coal plants in Florida, Illinois, Kentucky, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, North Carolina, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, Texas, West Virginia, and Wyoming and would cost the power sector approximately US$120 million per year. Data in the journal Science revealed that between 1999 and 2020, deaths caused by pollution from coal plants declined by 97 per cent among Medicare recipients, who are mostly over 65 years old. An assessment by AP found that the rules Zeldin wants to eliminate could prevent about 30,000 deaths and avoid approximately US$275 billion in social and environmental costs every year they are in effect. "The costs will be borne by the American people who will breathe dirtier air and those around the world suffering from climate change. The benefits will go to a very small group of donors," said Charles Harper from Evergreen Action. (AP, Guardian, Environmental Protection Agency)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Canada: Glencore's Elk Valley Resources said it is cutting 140 staff jobs from its four metallurgical coal mines in British Columbia due to "challenging market conditions".

 

 Canada: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith was challenged at a public meeting attended by 500 people over her decision to support Northback Holdings' proposed Grassy Mountain coal project.

 

 China: Chinese exporters shipped three cargoes of metallurgical coal to Indonesian customers, which analysts view as a signal to Australian exporters and a trial of the Chinese supply chain.

 

 Kazakhstan: Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov discussed Shandong Energy's proposed joint venture with QazaqGaz to establish a coal gasification plant in the Karaganda region. The joint venture has proposed a plant with a projected annual capacity of 2 billion cubic meters of gas.

 

 New Zealand: Bathurst Resources deferred filing its application for fast-track approval for its 4.6 million tonne Buller mine project until November. The company initially planned to submit its application in mid-June. "Every gust of public pressure brings it closer to collapse," said one environmentalist.

 

 Sweden: Volvo will use SSAB Zero steel in key components of its forthcoming electric cars. Volvo estimates steel accounts for about 25 per cent of emissions in the production of its new vehicles.

 

 UK: The UK government has confirmed the allocation of a 500 million (US$671 million) grant to Tata towards the cost of building a new electric arc furnace at its Port Talbot steelworks. Tata plans to commence work on the new furnace in July, with the first production slated for 2027.

 

 US: Despite a court order, the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health's lung screening program for coal miners has not fully resumed operation. The program lacks sufficient funds to operate a mobile X-ray unit and does not have contract workers to read chest X-rays.

 

 US: The Public Utilities Commission of Ohio has commenced hearings into three cases related to the US$61 million House Bill 6 scandal in which FirstEnergy bribed a state legislator and a regulator to subsidise loss-making coal and nuclear power plants.

 

 US: The Department of the Interior has proposed rescinding the 2024 changes to the Ten-Day Notice Rule, which allows citizens to request federal inspections when state regulators fail to act on environmental and public safety violations.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Unsubsidised US renewables still cheaper than new-build gas, nuclear: US-based financial services firm Lazard estimates the unsubsidised cost of the most inexpensive new utility-scale solar and onshore wind projects with storage to be about US$50 and US$44 per megawatt-hour (MWh), respectively. The 18th edition of the firm's Levelized Cost of Energy report estimates the average cost of operating a coal plant in the US is US$73 per MWh. Lazard says unsubsidised utility-scale solar and onshore wind remain the most cost-effective forms of new-build energy generation in the US. It notes that the cost of a new combined cycle gas turbine "has reached a 10-year high", with shortages and long delivery times "expected to continue driving steep" increases in the cost of electricity from new gas plants in the near term. The firm also noted that there have been "sharp declines" in the cost of battery energy storage systems. The firm did not estimate the cost of power from small modular reactors but calculated the cost of new-build conventional nuclear, based on the estimated costs of two most recent units at the Vogtle nuclear plant in Georgia, at US$169 per MWh and US$228 per MWh, respectively. (Renewables Now, Lazard, Lazard [Pdf])

US bill before Senate would slash rollout of solar, wind and batteries: The Trump administration's budget bill would slash tax credits for new wind, solar and battery projects, increase energy costs and undermine clean energy jobs, according to modelling by Energy Innovation (EI), a US climate policy think tank. The bill passed the House of Representatives by just one vote. EI estimates the bill would increase wholesale electricity prices by 50 per cent due to reduced clean energy capacity, which put downward pressure on prices. The report estimates the House bill would reduce new electricity capacity by 120,000 MW by 2030 and 330,000 MW by 2035 compared to current policies. EI estimates that the bill would result in 37,000 MW less solar capacity, including 4000 MW of rooftop capacity, by 2030 and 79,000 MW less wind capacity. The report estimates the changes would also reduce new battery storage capacity by 9000 MW. The bill also proposed reducing federal coal royalties from 12.5 per cent to 7 per cent. Combined with changes in oil and gas royalties, the federal government would collect about US$10.5 billion less in revenue between 2025 to 2035 compared to current policies. The draft Senate version of the bill extends support for geothermal, nuclear, and hydropower projects that begin construction by 2033 but phases out the tax credit for new wind and solar projects built after 2026. (Forbes, E & E News, Energy Innovation [Pdf])

Indian coal generation declines as solar surges: Indian solar generation surged by 32.4 per cent over the January to April period compared to the same period last year, while coal generation remained flat. Over the same period, coal generation increased by just 0.21 per cent. Coal generation in India typically peaks in the January to April period before hydro generation increases with the onset of monsoonal rains. Continued solar installations suggest that coal generation could decline in 2025 for the first time since 2020. Over the last year, India's solar capacity increased by about 30 per cent, with an estimated 13,000 MW installed in the first five months of 2025. Indian solar capacity now stands at about 111,000 MW. (Reuters, SolarQuarter)

Indian coal generation declines as solar surges: Indian solar generation surged by 32.4 per cent over the January to April period compared to the same period last year, while coal generation remained flat. Over the same period, coal generation increased by just 0.21 per cent. Coal generation in India typically peaks in the January to April period before hydroelectric generation increases with the onset of monsoonal rains. Continued solar installations suggest that coal generation could decline in 2025 for the first time since 2020. Over the last year, India's solar capacity increased by about 30 per cent, with an estimated 13,000 MW installed in the first five months of 2025. Indian solar capacity now stands at about 111,000 MW. (Reuters, SolarQuarter)

Coal industry group says Chinese coal imports set for big fall in 2025: Xuegang Li, the vice president of the China Coal Transportation and Distribution Association, told an industry conference that coal imports could decline by between 50 and 100 million tonnes in 2025. China imported 542.7 million metric tonnes of coal in 2024, spurred by low international prices. Li said that emissions restrictions would undercut demand for low-calorie Indonesian lignite and that the decline in coal imports this year "will exceed expectations". In the first five months of 2025, coal imports declined by eight per cent compared to the same period in 2024. A decline of 100 million tonnes in 2025 would represent an 18.4 per cent decrease. Li said China's coal production capacity might increase by 70 to 80 million tonnes in 2024 after a decline in production last year. Declining demand has caused Australian and Indonesian coal prices for the grades preferred by Chinese buyers to fall by 37 per cent and 25 per cent, respectively. Li suggested that China's coal consumption could peak in 2027 or 2028. (Mining.com, MSN)

Uncertain future for Korea coal company after closure of last mine: South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance and the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy have not finalised an agreement on the future of the state-owned Korea Coal Corporation (KOCOAL) after the loss-making Dogye Mine in Gangwon province closes at the end of June. KOCOAL decided in 2022 to close its three remaining coal mines by 2025 to cut financial losses to the state budget. The two ministries need to resolve the outstanding 2.5 trillion won (US$1.8 billion) debt of KOCOAL, rehabilitation liabilities and whether to merge it with the Korea Mine Rehabilitation and Mineral Resources Corporation. (ChosunBiz)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Steelmakers face crunch-time on coal: critical risks in blast furnace relining decisions, Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility, May 19, 2025. (Pdf). (The media release on the report is here.)

The 27-page report finds that more than 60 coal-based blast furnaces owned by 13 major steelmakers require major relining decisions by the end of 2035.

Exposed: Japan's five largest investors delay clean energy transition, Market Forces, June 11, 2025. (Pdf) (The media release on the report is here.)

This 45-page report reveals that Japan's five largest institutional investors — Mizuho Financial Group/Dai-ichi Life, Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Holdings, Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Nomura Holdings, and Nippon Life Insurance — are investing in companies that are expanding their production of coal, oil, and gas.

Banking on Climate Chaos, Rainforest Action Network, BankTrack and others, June 2025. (Pdf)

This 66-page report reviews the financial support by the world's top 65 banks to more than 2,700 fossil fuel companies. The report includes case studies on Adani's Carmichael coal mine, Elk Valley Resources in Canada and the JSW Utkal Steel plant in India.

Indonesia's RUPTL outlines faster growth in fossil fuel use, downgrades ambition for clean energy, Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air, June 2025. (Pdf)

This 12-page briefing paper provides an overview of Indonesia's recently released power development plan for 2025-2034. The final plan backs away from proposals in its 2023 Just Energy Transition Partnership plan for a significant expansion in wind and solar generation.

title: CoalWire 569, June 26, 2025
excerpt: Ireland exits coal power; China’s solar and wind surge; Saskatchewan defies Canada’s coal exit plan.
content:
June 26, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

China's astonishing rate of solar and wind installations since January, ahead of scheduled changes to incentives, suggests that coal power generation could decline over the next year. With new installations expected to slow for the remainder of 2025, solar and wind manufacturers will seek new policy support. In Ireland, coal generation at the Moneypoint coal plant has finally come to an end, curtailing a market for the controversial Cerrejon mine in Colombia. As mines close, decisions are required about what comes next. A new Global Energy Monitor report estimates that abandoned coal mines could host up to 300 gigawatts (GW) of solar capacity by 2030.

While the falling cost of solar and wind generation is rapidly reshaping the electricity market, some governments are attempting to stall the inevitable decline of coal generation. In Canada, Saskatchewan announced its plan to defy federal regulations requiring the closure of coal plants by 2030 and instead extend the life of existing lignite plants. In the US, a coalition of groups and the Michigan government have launched a legal challenge against the Trump administration's order to keep the 1.56 GW J.H. Campbell coal plant operating for another 90 days.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 How black lung came roaring back to US coal country

Modern US coal miners are contracting black lung disease at younger ages and rates not seen since the 1970s. For 20th-century miners, it could take decades to develop severe black lung, but now just a few years of exposure to silica and coal dust can be enough, writes Kate Morgan in The New York Times.

 

 Coal loophole undermines bank pledges to cut fossil fuel funding

Financial institutions that restrict support for thermal but not metallurgical coal projects don't acknowledge that some metallurgical coal is burnt in power stations, write Natasha White and Aaron Clark in Bloomberg.

 

 Coal shadow hangs over new World Heritage plan for South Africa-Mozambique coastline

The Mozambique government is investigating a proposal to build a new deep-water coal export harbour in the heart of the area it wants included on the World Heritage list, writes Tony Carnie in the Daily Maverick.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Coal power comes to an end in Ireland

Coal power generation has ceased at Ireland's 915 megawatt (MW) Moneypoint power station. Over the last decade, much of the coal burned at the state-owned Electricity Supply Board's plant came from the controversial Cerrejon mine in Colombia. The three 305 MW coal units were commissioned between 1985 and 1987 to reduce reliance on expensive imported heavy fuel oil generation and to cater for increased electricity demand. The plant remains available to operate at the direction of EirGrid as an oil-fired plant until 2029. The end of coal generation has made Ireland the 15th country to achieve a coal-free electricity mix, with Italy and Spain set to join the ranks in the next few months. However, Ireland is contemplating the construction of 2 gigawatts (GW) of new gas plant capacity, in large part to cater for the rapid growth of data centres. The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres account for more than 20 per cent of the country's electricity demand. Friends of the Earth Ireland said the government should block the development of further data centres, increase support for batteries, renewables, and demand reduction to ensure the country transitions to a fossil-free grid. (Irish Examiner, Beyond Fossil Fuels)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Report says space for 300 GW of solar on abandoned coal mines: A Global Energy Monitor report estimates that converting closed coal mines to solar farms could add up to 300 GW of solar capacity by 2030. GEM identified 312 surface coal mines closed since 2020 that cover more than 2000 square kilometres (km²) and could host up to 103 GW of solar capacity. A further 3,731 km² of land could become available with the closure of mines by the end of 2030, potentially hosting an additional 185 GW of solar capacity. China is already backing coal-to-solar conversions, with 90 projects operating and a further 46 under consideration. The report estimates that Australia, the US, Indonesia, and India account for almost three-quarters of the global potential for coal-to-solar transitions. (Guardian, Global Energy Monitor, Global Energy Monitor [Pdf])

 

 Western Balkans coal plants continue to breach pollution limits: CEE Bankwatch's annual review of pollution from coal power plants in the Western Balkans has found that sulphur dioxide (SO2) emissions in 2024 remain far higher than allowed under the provisions of the Energy Community Treaty. The review found that coal plants included in the National Emissions Reduction Plans (NERP) submitted by Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Serbia collectively emitted six times more SO2 than allowed, with emissions of the pollutant declining only marginally since 2018. The report found that dust emissions from the plants listed in the NERP were 1.9 times the permitted level. Additionally, it revealed that despite the requirement for small polluting plants to close by the end of 2023, units in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Serbia are operating illegally. While the Energy Community Secretariat has launched cases against the three countries, the governments allow the plants to continue operating. (BNE Intellinews, CEE Bankwatch)

 

 Chinese ministry inspections highlight air pollution breaches: China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment reports that inspections revealed that authorities in Wuhai, Inner Mongolia, had allowed the illegal addition of more than 2.2 million tonnes of coking capacity since 2021 and failed to ensure that other coking plants met emissions standards. The ministry also reported that nitrogen oxide emissions from Wuhai Xinhua Kaiyancheng Coal Coking Company exceeded the annual pollution limits for three consecutive years and the company had illegally disposed of waste outside the plant. The inspection team also found that a company in Shandong province had produced 670,000 tonnes of crude steel since 2022 from two unapproved electric arc furnaces. Inspections are also underway in major coal-producing provinces of Shanxi and Shaanxi. (China Daily)

 

 US coke company pleads guilty to bypassing pollution controls: The now-defunct Erie Coke Corporation pleaded guilty to conspiracy to violate the Clean Air Act by venting raw coke oven gas to the atmosphere in breach of the environmental permit for its plant in Erie, Pennsylvania. The Environmental Protection Agency's investigation of the plant found that company employees removed caps on top of the coke oven batteries, allowing combustion gases to bypass the plant's environmental monitoring system between October 2015 and December 2019. The company submitted emissions monitoring data, knowing that it did not reflect the actual amount of emissions. The company accepted a plea deal that included paying a US$700,000 fine, a level the Department of Justice (DOJ) stated was set "in part based on the funds currently available" as the company ceased trading in 2019. As part of the plea deal, the DOJ dropped six other felony charges against the company. Sentencing is scheduled for October 7. Two company employees were also charged with criminal offences. Anthony Nearhoof, the former plant superintendent, has yet to face trial, while David Stablein, the plant supervisor, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to bypass pollution controls at the plant, with sentencing scheduled for July 11. No executives were charged, with Erie Coke CEO Paul Saffrin signing a statement that the company's board of directors agreed to the plea deal. Benedictine Sister Pat Lupo, the co-chair of Hold Erie Coke Accountable, said she didn't think the agreement "was very fair at all".(GoErie, US Attorney's Office, Western District of Pennsylvania)

 

 Legal challenge against Trump order to keep coal plant open: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has requested a rehearing by the US Department of Energy (DOE) on its May 23 order directing Consumers Energy to keep the 1.56 GW J.H. Campbell coal plant operating for another 90 days. Nessel argues that the DOE's order does not identify a credible emergency and claims that it will impose "unnecessary costs' on ratepayers, generate avoidable pollution and intrude on the powers of Michigan and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to regulate the electric grid. The Chair of the Michigan Public Service Commission estimated that keeping the plant online for 90 days could cost up to US$100 million, due to limited investments following the 2021 decision to close the plant by the end of May. A coalition of 10 environmental groups also filed a request for a rehearing on the DOE's decision. The agency must respond to the request within 30 days. The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis notes that the DOE's order assumes consumers will cover the operating losses of the plant, that short-term coal supplies are available, and that redeployed or retired staff will be available to return to the plant to ensure its safe operation. (Michigan Advance, Sierra Club, Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis)

 

 Philippines mine expansion approved: The Philippines Department of Environment and Natural Resources has approved Semirara Mining and Power Corporation's (SMPC) application for a 852-hectare expansion of its Molave-Narra coal mine. The 291 billion peso (US$504 million) proposal is to exhaust the existing Molave and Narra pits and then proceed to the new Acacia pit, which contains approximately 80 million tonnes of coal reserves. The company exports approximately 60 per cent of its current production to nearby countries, including China, South Korea, and Brunei. The expansion will enable SMPC to increase output from the current 16 million tonnes per year to approximately 20 million tonnes per year. The Amlig Antique Alliance, a coalition of 40 civil society groups, called for the cancellation of the expansion and a transition to ecotourism and agriculture. The alliance stated that the local community of Caluya remained the fourth poorest town in the province. (Philstar, Manila Times, Semirara Mining and Power Corporation [Pdf])

 

 
 "Nationwide, one in 10 working miners is now estimated to have black lung. In the heart of the central Appalachian coal fields, it's one in five. Often, their disease is more severe, the progression faster,"

writes Kate Morgan in the New York Times.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Market Forces has criticised AustralianSuper, a major Australian superannuation fund, for its A$395 million (US$257 million) stake in Whitehaven Coal, despite the fund claiming to be committed to net-zero emissions.

 

 Australia: Peabody Energy locked out about 160 permanent employees without pay for a week after they took limited one-hour stoppages in support of a new work agreement at the Metropolitan Mine in New South Wales.

 

 China: The investigation report into five deaths in May 2024 at the Xing'an coal mine owned by the Heilongjiang Longmay Group found that the accident was caused by inadequate fire prevention and poor safety management.

 

 US: The Bureau of Land Management and the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement have called for public comment by July 7 on their proposal to approve an "emergency federal coal lease and mining plan" over 800 acres (324 hectares) at the Falkirk Mine in North Dakota. The proposed lease area contains about 11.7 million US short tons (10.6 million tonnes) of lignite.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

China smashes solar and wind installation records: National Energy Administration data reveal that China added 92.9 GW of new solar capacity in May, boosting the total installed capacity in the first five months of 2025 to 197.85 GW. New policy restrictions affecting rooftop solar and utility-scale projects spurred installations before the changes took effect. While analysts anticipate a significant slowdown in the rest of 2025, the production of solar and wind components has become a substantial element of China's manufacturing sector. However, the industry could face consolidation and an easing of the price wars between producers. NEA data indicates that China's solar capacity at the end of May was 1.08 terawatts (1080 GW), up 56.9 per cent on the year before. China's solar and wind capacity is now greater than the combined capacity of coal and gas plants. (PV Magazine, OilPrice.com)

Saskatchewan defies federal 2030 coal closure deadline: The Saskatchewan government plans to defy federal regulations adopted in 2016, which require all coal plants to close by 2030 or when the plants reach 50 years of operation, whichever comes first. While Saskatchewan had previously agreed to comply with federal regulations, Jeremy Harrison, the Minister Responsible for the state-owned power utility SaskPower, wrote to employees informing them that the government had decided to extend the life of the Boundary Dam, Poplar River, and Shand lignite plants. Harrison claimed that wind and solar can't replace 'baseload' power and that the government is aiming to replace the 1.5 GW of lignite capacity with equivalent nuclear capacity. SaskPower said it plans to begin work this year on restoring to service the mothballed 150 MW lignite-fired Unit 4 at the Boundary Dam plant and that "in the years to come, all coal units at Boundary Dam, Poplar River and Shand" plants will be upgraded. Coal accounted for just under one-quarter of SaskPower's generation in 2024-25, with extended maintenance at the 293 MW Unit 6 at the Boundary dam plant, as well as the 630 MW Poplar River plant and the 300 MW Shand plant. The federal government's agency responsible for climate policy, Environment and Climate Change Canada, has not yet responded to the Saskatchewan decision. (CBC, SaskPower [Pdf])

Report finds reliance on private finance distorts transition funding flows: An analysis of a decade-long dataset reveals that every public dollar of concessional finance attracts 4-7 times less private investment than anticipated, according to a report by Oil Change International and a coalition of NGOs. Major institutions, such as the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the International Energy Agency, promote 'blended' public and private finance as a central vehicle to support the energy transition. However, Oil Change International found that the countries of the Global North and China are the largest recipients of just energy transition finance. The report states that the remaining 69 per cent of the world's population received just 15 per cent of transition finance in 2023–2024. The report argues that most international packages supporting the energy transition rely on "weak" financial incentives to attract private funding. The report states that the strongest examples of successful just transition projects include subsidies, support for community and publicly owned projects, and the regulation of banks and industry. Oil Change International, Oil Change International [Pdf])

Report says Indonesian coal industry faces tough transition: A report by Energy Shift Institute warns that Indonesia needs to wean itself off its reliance on the coal industry for revenue, export income, and jobs, as key importers such as India and China reduce imports and diversify their sources of supply. In 2024, Indonesia's coal production increased by eight per cent over the previous year to 836 million tonnes. Indonesia, the world's largest exporter of thermal coal, sold 530 million tonnes of thermal coal into the global seaborne market in 2024, with just under half of it going to China. Chinese imports of low-grade lignite from Indonesia have slumped in 2025. However, Indonesia's domestic coal capacity and new captive coal plants are projected to expand by about 40 per cent by 2030. The Energy Shift Institute stated that 12 selected Indonesian coal companies could afford to invest in diversification from their healthy balance sheets. The report stated that Indonesia's reliance on coal as its primary export commodity renders it vulnerable to fluctuations in export prices and market shocks with the sector heavily dependent on a small number of high-volume mines. "Most Indonesian coal-mining companies lack credible diversification or transition strategies despite global pressure," the report states. (Associated Press, Energy Shift Institute, Energy Shift Institute [Pdf])

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Steel giant scraps plans for two projects in Germany: ArcelorMittal has dropped its plan to convert existing steel plants at Bremen and Eisenhuettenstadt to utilise hydrogen despite the German government's pledge of 1.3 billion (US$1.4 billion) in subsidies. ArcelorMittal announced plans to build a direct-reduced iron and electric arc furnace plant at Bremen in March 2021, with the aim of phasing out coal-based blast furnace operations at the site by 2030. The company attributed its decision to drop its plan to high electricity costs, weak domestic demand for steel and a high volume of imports. The German Ministry of Economy stated that Salzgitter, ThyssenKrupp, and Stahl-Holding-Saar are proceeding with their projects to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in steel production. (Reuters, Luxembourg Times, Clean Energy Wire)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

"The risks of fossil fuel dependence in Indonesia's Electricity Supply Business Plan (RUPTL) 2025–2034", Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis, June 23, 2025.

This article provides a concise summary of Indonesia's recently finalised power development plan for 2025-2034.

The Battle of Doongmabulla Springs, BBC, June 20, 2025. (This documentary is available in the UK via the BBC's iPlayer and the BBC World Service YouTube channel elsewhere.)

This 76-minute documentary follows the struggle of Adrian Burragubba and his family against the development of the Carmichael coal mine by Bravus Mining, a subsidiary of Adani. The documentary examines the threat posed by the mine to the culturally and environmentally significant Doongmabulla Springs.

How Public Finance Can Supercharge the Just Energy Transition, Stamp Out Poverty, Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, Christian Aid and others, June 2025. (Pdf)

This 28-page paper describes how public finance can support a just and equitable energy transition. The report includes case studies on how public finance has accelerated the expansion of renewable energy in India, China, and Brazil.

Solar electricity every hour of every day is here and it changes everything, Ember, June 2025. (Pdf) (The executive summary is here.)

This 47-page report examines the potential of solar panels paired with batteries to deliver continuous electricity. The report also analyses how close a sample of cities can get to having solar power all day, every day of the year.

title: CoalWire 570, July 3, 2025
excerpt: Russian mine suspends production; insurance policies hit coal sector; Bangladesh eyes axing capacity payments.
content:
July 3, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The US budget bill before the House of Representatives aims to reverse many of the policy gains made by the climate movement of recent years and stall the rollout of new solar and wind capacity. Fossil fuel suppliers, helped by reduced federal royalties, stand to be one of the beneficiaries in the energy sector of the proposed budget. While the Trump administration seeks to prop up struggling mining companies and power utilities hooked on coal plants, other countries are looking to cut their exposure to expensive fossil fuel imports. A senior advisor to the Bangladesh government has flagged the need to cut generous capacity payments for coal and gas plants.

 

Reduced Chinese and India imports of low and mid-grade coal from Indonesia are a new shock to the world's biggest thermal coal exporter. In Russia, a major coal mine in the Kuzbass region has slashed its workforce in response to a financial crisis. While many major insurance companies have been slow to cut their support for new coal projects, a study by Swiss researchers found that insurers with restrictive polices cut the number of insured coal mines by 16 per cent.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 A coal miner's daughter takes on DOGE to protect miners' health

Since 1970, more than 75,000 miners have died of black lung disease. Now, researchers working to prevent those deaths get layoff notices, writes Meg Duff in Capital & Main.

 

 Coal mining made my Navajo community sick for decades. Reviving it hurts us all

The so-called 'Big Beautiful Bill' currently making its way through Congress is anything but beautiful for our tribal community, writes Robyn Jackson, the Executive Director of Diné C.A.R.E. in USA Today.

 

 The clean energy takeaways of the US budget bill

The clean energy industry managed to notch some tiny wins, but largely failed to change the fate of wind and solar tax credits, writes Maeve Allsup in Latitude Media.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Russian mine closes: Officials from the Kemerovo regional government reported that production has ceased at the Spiridonovskaya underground mine in the Kuzbass coalfield due to financial constraints. The Kuzbass coalfield accounts for about 60 per cent of Russia's hard coal production. The mine employed about 900 people, but employees had not been paid in over a month, according to Andrei Panov, the head of the Kemerovo regional government. In late May, the managers of Shakhta Spiridonovskaya, the company that owns the mine, announced the layoff of 760 workers, with approximately 130 workers retained to maintain the mine. The mine, which first began operating in 1965, has a long history of closures, ownership changes, re-openings, and safety violations. Earlier this year, regulators suspended the mine's operation for 90 days due to a series of safety violations. Russian coal exporters have been hit by the collapse of sales to the European market, high freight costs for exports from eastern ports to the Asian market and the impact of stricter sanctions imposed after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In May, President Putin agreed to a series of measures to support coal producers, including reduced and delayed payment for freight costs to export terminals. (Moscow Times, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Coal plants as major contributor to India's fine particle air pollution: A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimates that ammonium sulphate is responsible for 34 per cent of India's PM2.5 fine particle pollution. Ammonium sulphate forms when sulphur dioxide reacts with ammonia. CREA estimates that the concentration of ammonium sulphate is 2.5 times higher within 10 kilometres of coal power plants, but remains a significant contributor across state boundaries. The report states that with 60 per cent of India's sulphur dioxide emissions originating from coal plants, cutting PM2.5 fine particle pollution requires the installation of flue-gas desulphurisation (FGD) units on coal plants. A recent report revealed that only 44 of the 537 coal units in India have installed FGD plants. Indian power utilities have lobbied the government to delay the deadlines for installing FGD units, which were announced in 2015. Meanwhile, the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser has recently proposed scrapping the requirement altogether. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf)

 

 Forest clearing begins for Adani mine: With a heavy police presence, clearing of thousands of trees started on June 26 for the establishment of the Gare Palma Sector II coal block in Chhattisgarh. The Chhattisgarh Association for Justice and Equality said that police detained seven villagers, a local Congress MP and environmentalists protesting against the tree felling. Tree felling continued on June 27 near the villages of Mudagaon and Saraitola despite 1000 people protesting against the operation. The Adani Group will operate the mine for the Maharashtra State Power Generation Company, which has three coal plants with a combined capacity of 3980 MW in nearby districts. The coal block, which has an estimated coal resource of about 655 million tonnes, was allocated to MAHAGENCO in 2015. (The Wire)

 

 US budget bill passes Senate with anti-renewables provisions intact: The US Senate voted 51-50 for a broad-ranging budget bill that defunds a range of crucial climate programs, provides a subsidy for metallurgical coal exports, and phases out tax credits for new solar and wind projects. The bill revokes the Biden administration's moratorium on coal leasing on federal lands and reduces the royalty rate from 12.5 per cent to 7 per cent. The bill also creates a tax credit for metallurgical coal equal to 2.5 per cent of production costs. The original bill proposed ending tax credits for solar and wind projects after 2027. However, the Senate modified this provision to allow tax credits for projects that commenced construction within one year of the bill's passage. The US House of Representatives has begun debating the Senate version of the bill. The House leadership wants the Senate bill passed as it is, but with a 3-seat majority in the House, divisions within the Republican ranks are likely over some of the bill's provisions. (Guardian, Utility Dive, S&P Global)

 

 US court rules in favour of Oakland coal port developer: The California Court of Appeal has upheld a January 2024 decision by Alameda Superior Court Noel Wise that reinstated the lease to developer Phil Tagami and his associates for the construction of the Oakland Bulk and Oversized Terminal in West Oakland, which included provision for coal exports. The City of Oakland had declared the agreement for the terminal terminated in 2018 due to a lack of progress on the project. Wise overturned that decision, but the City of Oakland appealed the decision to reinstate the lease to the California Court of Appeal. However, Wise rejected OBOT's claim for US$159.6 million in compensation for lost profits. Part of the original proposal was for the state of Utah to invest US$53 million in the port, providing another option for Utah coal producers to access the Asian market. Following the revelation of the plan to ship coal through the terminal, the Oakland City Council approved an ordinance banning the handling and storage of coal within the city limits of Oakland. (The Oaklandside, No Coal in Oakland)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Australian Securities and Exchange Commission has commenced legal action against Tahmoor Coal, a subsidiary of Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance, over failure to lodge its 2024 annual report.

 

 Australia: Peabody Energy has extended the lockout of workers at its Metropolitan underground coal mine in New South Wales until July 6. The company locked workers out of the mine on June 18 after they took industrial action for one-hour, which is protected under workplace law.

 

 Australia: Synergy, the power utility owned by the West Australian state government, plans to spend A$278 million (US$183 million) over the next three years subsidising loss-making coal plants. The government has also provided A$260 million (US$171 million) to keep Griffin Coal viable, enabling it to supply the privately owned Bluewaters power station until mid-2026.

 

 India: Adani Group Chairman Gautam Adani met with Odisha Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik to discuss future projects, including a coal gasification plant.

 

 Montenegro: The draft National Energy and Climate Plan for Montenegro proposes that the 225 MW Pljevlja lignite plant could keep operating until 2041. The plan is open for public comment until August 6.

 

 South Africa: The Mpumalanga High Court has rejected a bid by a couple accused of being part of an illegal coal mining syndicate to release part of the 52.5 million rand (US$2.9 million) frozen by the Asset Forfeiture Unit.

 

 South Korea: The closure of the state-owned Dogye coal mine leaves the privately owned Gyeong-dong Sangdeok mine as the country's last coal project. The government is hoping to close it down by 2030.

 

 South Africa: Exxaro Resources announced it plans to cut some jobs at its loss-making Leeuwpan thermal coal mine in Mpumalanga province. The mine, which employs approximately 600 people directly, primarily produces coal for domestic customers, including Eskom, with less than one-third of its output exported in 2024.

 

 US: We Energies announced it intends to delay the closure of the Oak Creek units 7 and 8 in Wisconsin from the end of 2025 until the end of 2026. The two units have a combined capacity of 610 MW. Clean Wisconsin criticised the decision, stating the units were first supposed to close in 2023.

 

 US: Coal ash spilled from rail wagons into the Vermilion River in southern Louisiana.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Bangladesh looks to scrap capacity payments provisions: The chief adviser to the interim Bangladesh government has confirmed it wants to scrap capacity payment clauses in power purchase agreements with independent power producers. The previous Hasina government, which was ousted from power in August 2024, entered into power purchase agreements with generous capacity payments for plants that are now underutilised. The International Monetary Fund estimated that 1000 MW of excess coal plant capacity could cost US$240–300 million a year. With an estimated surplus capacity of approximately 11,680 MW in the 2023-24 financial year, the losses of the Bangladesh Power Development Board have increased significantly. Bangladesh also wants to renegotiate the coal pricing formula outlined in the 2017 power purchase agreement with Adani Power for electricity from its 1600 MW Godda power plant in Jharkhand. However, Adani insisted it would only renegotiate the coal price if Bangladesh paid its outstanding debt. The Bangladesh government estimates the payment of US$437 million in June would clear its admitted debt, with Adani arguing it is liable for an additional US$500 million. Much of the difference between the company's and the government's estimates of the amount still owed relates to calculations of coal costs and plant capacity. (Daily Observer, Deccan Herald, Business Standard)

Report says insurance company policies impact coal sector: A study by researchers from the Swiss Finance Institute and the University of Zurich found that insurers with policies restricting financial support for coal projects had an impact on the sector. They noted that insurers with restrictive polices cut the number of insured coal mines by 16 per cent, insured 56 per cent less volume of coal and made continued coverage 13 per cent less likely. "Affected mines reduce output, cut employment, and are abandoned more often in subsequent periods," the study concluded. However, the study found that most policies "often remain vague" by excluding only specific projects but not carbon-intensive clients. The study notes that policies with restrictions on coal emerged after 2017 and are more common among European insurers. The report found that some companies expanded coal coverage despite their earlier policy commitments. (Insurance Asia, Swiss Finance Institute)

Australian corporate regulator sues coal utility for market manipulation: The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has launched legal action against Delta Power & Energy, the owner of the 1320 MW Vales Point coal plant in New South Wales, alleging the company manipulated the market for electricity futures contracts between September and October 2022. ASIC alleges that Delta placed orders for electricity futures contracts on 30 occasions shortly before the market close "for the improper purpose of affecting the daily settlement price for those quarterly futures contracts". ASIC alleges the company's bidding was aimed at boosting revenue from an electricity offtake agreement it had with Shell Energy Retail. ASIC argues that manipulating energy markets "has the potential to create a commercial benefit at the expense of others in the market" and result in higher energy prices. In late September, the then-owners of Delta, Trevor St. Baker and Brian Flannery, a coal investor, agreed to sell the company to Sev.en Global Investments, a private Czech firm owned by billionaire Pavel Tykac. In a media statement, Delta said the ASIC allegations occurred before Sev.en Global Investments took control of the company. (Australian Financial Review [paywall], Australian Securities and Investments Commission)

India increases imports of Russian coal cargoes: India's total thermal coal imports increased in May to 17.4 million tonnes, up 10 per cent on the month before and were at the highest level since June 2024. Indian imports of Russian thermal coal increased in May to 1.3 million tonnes, up 10 per cent from the year before and a 52 per cent jump from April. The increase in imports from Russia, which supplies about 7.5 per cent of India's imports, comes as buyers opt for higher calorific value cargoes at discounted prices. Indonesia remains the largest exporter to India. The early onset of the monsoon will boost Indian hydro generation and suppress demand for thermal coal imports over summer. (Economic Times)

Indonesian coal producers eye domestic sales as the global market cools: Indonesian coal producers, hit by declining exports of low- and medium-calorific coal grades to China and India, are turning their focus to sales to captive coal plants tied to new mineral smelters as a more profitable option than the regulated local power sector. Chinese coal producers have increased production and increased imports from Russia and Mongolia. Indian coal producers have also increased domestic production, and coal traders have boosted purchases of higher-grade cargoes from Mozambique, Colombia, and Kazakhstan. The Indonesian Coal Mining Association (APBI) has seized on the downturn to call on the government to scrap measures that coal producers oppose, such as the requirement to retain a portion of their foreign exchange earnings in Indonesia and the establishment of an export floor price for export sales. The government rejected the industry's call to scrap the measures. (Asia News Network)

Indian banks continue to back coal: A report by Climate Risk Horizons, an Indian research NGO, found that between 2016 and 2023, the state-owned State Bank of India and the privately held ICICI provided US$15.2 billion in loans for coal projects and US$13.56 billion in coal underwriting. The report estimates that public banks in India provided about 75 per cent of the total coal loans, while private banks financed around 83 per cent of the total underwriting. The group found that only three Indian banks – Federal Bank, RBL Bank, and Suryoday Small Finance – have policies that restrict coal lending. The report found that 33 other Indian financial institutions have no restrictions on supporting coal projects or companies and are heavily exposed to the sector, with approximately 25–35 per cent of their loans connected to coal as of October 2023. The peak in coal lending occurred in 2017, with loans declining from US$5.37 billion to just US$189 million in 2023. The report notes that electricity generated by coal plants under construction is likely to cost between 6.19 rupees per kWh and 7.24 rupees per kWh. Climate Risk Horizons estimates that renewables firmed with batteries can deliver round-the-clock power for between 3.5 to 4.5 rupees per kWh. (The Wire, Climate Risk Horizons)

Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf)

title: CoalWire 571, July 10, 2025
excerpt: China’s solar and wind boom set to continue; Polish renewables pass coal generation.
content:
July 10, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The different paths pursued by China and the US regarding wind and solar generation are striking. Where analysts expected a significant slowing in new wind and solar installations in the second half of the year, the research arm of the grid operator disagrees. The State Grid Energy Research Institute projects the installation of an astonishing 380 gigawatts (GW) of solar and 140 GW of wind capacity in 2025. For comparison, the entire US fleet of coal plants has a combined capacity of about 184 GW.

In the US, days after the passage of his One Big Beautiful Bill Act, President Trump issued an executive order to "eliminate" tax credits and other support for solar and wind energy. Where the bulk of China's new generation capacity is solar and wind, Trump is intent on recarbonising US generation. In Europe, the latest data reveals a continued decline in coal production and power generation. Even in coal-heavy Poland, it appears likely that renewable energy generation surpassed coal power for the first time.

CoalWire will take short break and be back on July 24.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Inside China's power play: Understanding the institutions behind Africa's energy projects

The future of Chinese-backed power generation in Africa is not only a story about what China brings to the table, but about how African actors shape the terms of that engagement, writes Adjekai Adjei in the China-Global South Project.

 

 China's coal heartland fighting for a greener future

With the lowest GDP growth in the country and a local economy that is heavily reliant on coal mining, Shanxi's fate in China's green future is uncertain, writes Amy Hawkins in The Guardian.

 

 US withdrawal leaves energy transition funding gap in Southeast Asia

The US withdrawal in March from a Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP), a multilateral climate financing programme that promised US$45 billion for Indonesia, South Africa and Vietnam, has come as a reminder to South-east Asian countries that they cannot just rely on external financing, writes A. Anantha Lakshmi in the Financial Times.

 

 Putin faces a coal crisis in Russia

Mechel, one of Russia's top mining companies, has become the first coal producer to get government aid in a deepening crisis for an industry hit by plummeting global demand and sanctions due to Vladimir Putin's war on Ukraine, writes Brendan Cole in Newsweek.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 President Trump orders end of support for solar and wind: President Trump issued an executive order "to eliminate subsidies for unreliable" wind and solar power projects following the passage of his 887-page One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The executive order directs the Secretary of the Treasury to "terminate" production and investment tax credits for wind and solar projects and implement restrictions on Chinese renewable energy components. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which narrowly passed the Senate and was signed into law by Trump on July 4, phases out clean energy tax credits included in the Biden administration's Inflation Reduction Act. The legislation also stripped funding for environmental justice programs, and reduced royalty rates on coal produced from federal lands. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Department of Energy and three other federal agencies all revoked binding regulations implementing the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) process for environmental reviews of proposed projects. The agencies also removed all references to considering climate change, environmental justice, and other environmental issues in undertaking reviews under NEPA. (President Trump, The White House, Utility Dive, Inside Climate News)

 

 First Nation group seeks review of Alberta coal decision: The Siksika Nation has filed an application for judicial review of the Alberta government's decision to lift the provincial moratorium on new coal mining projects. The Siksika Nation said that the provincial government failed to consult with it before lifting the moratorium, which opens the door for new coal mines on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains. In its application, the Siksika Nation stated that the Eastern Slopes "are among the last lands where Siksika can meaningfully exercise its Treaty rights and access critical resources that support its livelihood, and must be protected against further mining development". In May 2020, the Alberta government lifted the moratorium, but after a public backlash, largely reinstated it. Following the backflip, five coal companies filed legal claims for a combined C$15 billion (US$11 billion) in damages. Two companies, Evolve Power and Atrum Coal, informed their shareholders that they have reached agreements to settle the claims. Nigel Bankes, an emeritus professor of law at the University of Calgary, said the public has not been informed about any government compensation payments or what, if anything, the companies are giving up. "Are they returning to the Crown all of their coal rights as part of the deal?". (CBC, Siskia Nation, CBC)

 

 

 Polish coal generation slides to record low: Forum Energy, a Polish climate policy think tank, estimates that renewables generated 44.1 per cent of the country's electricity in June, probably the first time it has surpassed coal power. The group estimates that coal supplied 43.7 per cent of the country's electricity in June. The group estimates that for the April to June quarter, coal generation slumped to 46.2 per cent, down 10.2 per cent from the same period the previous year. Solar capacity has increased by 23.3 per cent over the last year to 23 gigawatts (GW), while wind capacity has increased by 6.9 per cent to 11 GW over the same period. The European Commission, which says it is on track to reach its 2030 target of a 55 per cent emissions reduction compared to a 1990 baseline, has proposed a 90 per cent reduction by 2040. Poland's Minister for Climate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, described the proposed 2040 target as "unrealistic and unacceptable" and stated that "as a country, we are not ready". Poland has long opposed European Union climate policy, but the centre-left coalition government elected in December 2023 supports an increased role for renewable energy. However, it has failed to implement crucial energy sector reforms. Following the May Presidential election, in which conservative candidate Karol Nawrocki won, the situation remains unchanged. The Polish President has the power to veto legislation. (Financial Times, Forum Energii, European Commission, Notes from Poland)

 

 Welsh Conservative MP touts coal sales as part of coal tip clean-up plans: Welsh Conservative Shadow Cabinet Secretary for Climate Change and the Environment, Janet Finch-Saunders, criticised the Labor government's 118 million (US$160 million) commitment to clean up old coal tips in Wales as "insufficient". Finch-Saunders suggested that where making old coal tips safe required removing remaining coal, the "site owners should be permitted to sell that coal to offset the costs". In South Wales, Energy Recovery Investments Ltd has proposed mining coal from two coal tips in Bedwas, with part of the proceeds to fund the restoration of the tips. Coal Action Network (CAN) wants the UK Government's ban on new coal mines extended to include 'remining' old coal tips. CAN argues that "if coal tip remediation is allowed to be used as a smokescreen for new coal mining, it'll contribute to fuelling the climate change that's threatening the stability of all coal tips". (Pembrokeshire Herald)

 

 Indian panel approves coal plant expansions, delays two others: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) Expert Advisory Committee has approved Adani Power's proposed 1320 MW expansion of the Lanco Amarkantak Power plant in Chhattisgarh. Adani bought the plant in September 2024. The committee also approved proposals by NLC India for an 800 MW expansion of its 2.4 GW pit-head Talabira Thermal Power Project in Odisha and a 350 MW expansion of the GMR Group's 1.05 GW Kamalanga power station in Odisha. The committee recommended changes to the terms of reference for the environmental assessment of two other coal plants – NTPC's proposed 800 MW expansion of the 1600 MW Darlipali coal plant in Odisha and a doubling of JSW Energy's 1.8 GW coal plant in Champa district. The committee deferred consideration of a proposal to amend the environmental licence for Jindal Power's existing 2.4 GW plant at Raigarh in Chhattisgarh. (MoneyControl)

 

 
 "From a market perspective, there probably is no demand for any new sources of coal There is more than enough coal production capacity available at the current time to meet market demand,"

said Rob Godby, economics professor at the University of Wyoming, speaking on the Trump administration's lifting of the moratorium on new federal coal leases in the Powder River Basin.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: A former coal miner has launched a A$1 million (US$650,000) damages claim against Anglo American over the trauma caused by the May 2020 underground explosion at the Grosvenor coal mine in Queensland.

 

 Australia: The Fair Work Commission has ordered BHP to pay approximately 2200 contract workers at its Saraji, Peak Downs, and Goonyella Riverside mines in Queensland the same pay rate as directly employed workers. The Mining and Energy Union, which brought the case, estimates that contract workers are entitled to an annual increase of approximately A$30,000 (US$19,600).

 

 Australia: Australian Pacific Coal has appointed administrators after defaulting on a A$174 million (US$113.7 million) loan. The company operates the underground Dartbrook thermal coal mine in the Hunter Valley, New South Wales.

 

 Bulgaria: A subsidiary of the state-owned Bulgarian Energy Holding reported a 52 million (US$60.9 million) loss in 2024 for the 1602 MW Maritsa East 2 lignite plant compared to a profit of 29 million (US$34 million) in 2023.

 

 India: Adani Power has completed the purchase of the 600 MW Butibori coal plant in Maharashtra from Vidarbha Industries Power, a subsidiary of Reliance Power. The purchase price was 40 billion rupees (US$466 million).

 

 South Africa: Eskom announced the return to service of Unit 4, an 800 MW unit at the Medupi power station. An explosion at the unit in August 2021 caused severe damage, requiring significant repairs.

 

 Turkiye: Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief with the Kahramanmaras 3rd Administrative Court against the construction of two new 344 MW units at the 2460 MW Afsin-Elbistan lignite power plant.

 

 US: Court documents reveal that power utility DTE Energy contributed US$100,000 to a dark money group that opposed Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer's COVID-19 lockdown policies.

 

 US: The Department of the Interior has approved a permit for Hurricane Creek Mining to produce up to 1.8 million US short tons (1.6 million tonnes) from a lease on Bryson Mountain in Tennessee.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Chinese agency forecasts wind and solar boom to continue in 2025: The State Grid Energy Research Institute, the research wing of China's national grid management agency, forecasts the addition of 380 GW of solar and 140 GW of wind capacity in 2025. After the release of recent National Energy Administration data revealing the addition of 197.85 GW of new solar capacity in the first five months of 2025, analysts predicted a slowdown in installations as new policies on rooftop solar and reduced incentives for utilities took effect. The latest estimate suggests that new wind and solar capacity installations will reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector over the next year, as clean energy outstrips electricity demand growth. However, the State Grid institute estimates China will add 127 GW of new thermal power capacity in 2025. While the institute doesn't distinguish between coal and gas capacity, it is likely that about three-quarters will be from coal projects. (China Daily, Taiyannews, State Grid Energy Research Institute [Chinese])

European Union coal production and use falls: Coal production in the European Union (EU) in 2024 declined by 12 per cent to 242 million tonnes compared to the year before. Of the 306 million tonnes of coal consumed in the EU in 2024, lignite accounted for approximately 199 million tonnes, representing a 10 per cent decline from the previous year. Hard coal consumption fell by 13.8 per cent to 110.9 million tonnes, with 45 million tonnes of domestic production and the remainder imported. The US and Australia accounted for 25 per cent of coal imports each, with most of the remainder coming from Colombia, South Africa, and Kazakhstan. Russian coal imports collapsed by 98 per cent between 2021 and 2023 due to sanctions imposed after the full invasion of Ukraine. Eurostat estimates that between 2018 and 2024, EU hard coal consumption declined by 51 per cent and lignite by 47 per cent. (Euronews, Ecopolitic, Eurostat)

Study says many countries could hit climate goals by axing fossil fuel subsidies: A report by the Centre for European Economic Research (ZEW) estimates that one in three countries could meet their climate goals by removing subsidies for coal, oil, and gas. The study estimates that Germany accounts for approximately 60 per cent of fossil fuel subsidies in the European Union, with around 41 billion (US$48.3 billion) provided in 2023. The International Monetary Fund estimates that direct fossil fuel subsidies account for about 1.3 per cent of global economic output, with the indirect social and environmental costs adding a further 5.8 per cent. ZEW estimates that the implicit subsidies from coal include about US$2 trillion in the health and environmental impacts of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and PM2.5 fine particle pollution. (Reuters, ZEW, ZEW [Pdf])

Western Australian coal company plunges further into the red: Griffin Coal, a private company that supplies coal to the 466 MW Bluewaters power station, has reported a further A$800 million (US$523 million) loss, bringing its total debt to $2.4 billion (US$1.57 billion). The Western Australian government has budgeted to provide an additional A$49 million (US$32 million) in subsidies to Griffin Coal this year, bringing the total taxpayer financial support to the company to A$308 million (US$201.3 million) since 2022. WA Premier, Roger Cook, told a recent parliamentary committee hearing that financial backing for Griffin would not extend beyond the end of June 2026. Unit 2 at the power plant generates about seven per cent of the electricity in the Southwest grid, with the other unit contracted to provide the bulk of its power to the Boddington Gold Mine. The plant is jointly owned by Kansai Electric Power (KEPCO) and Sumitomo Corporation, but it has faced financial challenges over the last decade. (ABC News)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

10 Key Principles for a Feminist and Just Energy Transition, Friends of the Earth International, July 2025. (Pdf)

This 41-page report sets out 10 principles to guide a feminist and community-based just energy transition.
