title: CoalWire 572, July 24, 2025
excerpt: Queensland rejects coal mine; Chinese coal imports fall again; Indian gov’t scraps sulphur dioxide standards for most coal plants; US study on port coal dust.
content:
July 24, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Farmers and community groups have welcomed the rejection of Fox Resources' application for a coal exploration licence near Bundaberg. Not surprisingly, the proposal by a small exploration company to establish a mine on prime agricultural land near a major regional city sparked widespread public opposition.The decision of the conservative Queensland government to reject the proposal stands in contrast to its support for Whitehaven's far larger Winchester South project in a sparsely populated, semi-arid inland area. Whitehaven's project is currently subject to a legal challenge by two environmental groups.

The spillover effects of China's domestic energy policy continue to reshape the global energy transition and coal markets. A surge in domestic coal production has suppressed domestic prices to the point where the National Energy Administration has ordered inspections to curb loss-making overproduction. Whether this will rekindle demand for coal imports from the global market remains unclear. A new analysis reveals how the growth in China's clean energy exports, particularly in solar technologies, is driving lower global emissions. China's dominance in key clean energy technologies comes as the US and India attempt to prolong the life of coal mines and lower the costs of coal power by scrapping or delaying pollution controls. In the US, the Trump administration has exempted six more coal units from pollution controls on mercury and other emissions. In India, the government has exempted more than three-quarters of the country's coal power units from the requirement to install flue gas desulphurisation equipment to cut sulphur dioxide emissions.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Caught between a fossil fuel past and a green future, China's coal miners chart an uncertain path

As the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter shifts to cleaner energy, some families in China's major coal-producing provinces fear being left behind, writes Amy Hawkins in The Guardian.

 

 Why is China's air pollution shifting west?

Air pollution is increasing in areas not designated as crucial for pollution control, as steel and coal-to-chemical industries have been migrating towards energy-rich western, central and southern China, writes Qiu Chengcheng from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air in Dialogue Earth.

 

 Critics fear Trump will use a flawed Department of Energy report to push a pro-coal agenda

Grid experts say the Department of Energy's new forecast of significant blackout risks by 2030 misuses data to justify the Trump administration's push to force dirty plants to stay open, writes Jeff St John in Canary Media.

 

 Polish power: new President, same old problems?

The growth of wind and solar capacity in Poland is likely to slow after the election of right-wing Karol Nawrocki as the country's next President, writes Hubert Put in Montel.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Queensland Government rejects proposed coal exploration lease: The Queensland Attorney-General, Deb Frecklington, announced that the government has denied Fox Resources' application for a mineral development licence for a metallurgical coal project near Bundaberg. Frecklington said she considered an assessment report by the Department of Natural Resources and Mines and determined the project was not in the public interest. Fox Resources first applied for a licence in 2019 for over 7800 hectares of agricultural and residential land, but attracted opposition from the Bundaberg Council, farmers, and environmentalists. The decision to reject the application in April 2022 by the then Minister for Resources, Scott Stewart, was set aside after the Queensland Supreme Court ruled in favour of an appeal by the company. Fox Resources said it will review the latest decision and consider potential legal action. (ABC News, Queensland Attorney General, Fox Resources [Pdf])

 

 Legal hearing commences against Australian coal mine: An expected seven-week hearing has begun on a legal challenge by the Australian Conservation Foundation (ACF) and Mackay Conservation Group against Whitehaven Coal's proposed Winchester South open-cut coal mine. ACF estimates that the project would contribute approximately 583 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions over its proposed 28-year lifespan, clear at least 2000 hectares of wildlife habitat, and extract large quantities of groundwater. Whitehaven plans to produce up to 17 million tonnes of thermal and metallurgical coal a year from six mine pits. The groups are seeking a court ruling to block the state government from granting a mining lease or environmental authority for the project. Whitehaven Coal currently operates six coal mines in New South Wales and Queensland, with a production target of 35 to 39.5 million tonnes in 2025. (ABC News, Australian Conservation Foundation)

 

 US study finds coal dust at port spikes with bulldozer use and high winds: A Johns Hopkins University study found that air pollution in residential areas adjoining the CSX Curtis Bay coal export terminal in Baltimore was 2 to 2.8 times higher downwind when bulldozers were operating in the coal stockpile than when they weren't. The study analysed data collected at 10 air monitoring stations for every minute between July 5, 2022, and July 16, 2023, as well as from a camera that detected bulldozer activity. The study concluded that strategies to prevent dust emissions from the stockpiles and when bulldozers are in use "appear warranted". In December 2021, a methane gas explosion on a conveyor belt shattered windows and blanketed nearby houses in coal dust. Following the explosion, residents and environmental groups urged the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) to deny the renewal of the terminal's operating permit. MDE renewed the permit, but the community continues to urge regulators to cut dust emissions. The United States exported more than 97 million tonnes of coal in 2024. The CSX site can export up to 14 million US short tons (12.7 million tonnes) of coal a year and predominantly caters for coal from mines in Pennsylvania and West Virginia. (CBS News, Air Quality, Atmosphere & Health, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health)

 

 Trump exempts six more coal units from air quality standards: President Donald Trump issued a new executive order exempting six coal power units from compliance with pollution limits set in the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (MATS) until July 9, 2029. While pollution equipment is available to meet the standards, the order claimed compliance is not possible as the tougher 2024 standards required technologies "that do not yet exist in a commercially viable form". The order specifically exempted the three units at Tri-State Generation and Transmission Association's 1880 megawatt (MW) Cardinal plant in Ohio and City Water, Light and Power's 446 MW Unit 2 and 512 MW Unit 3 at the Craig plant in Colorado. The order also exempted the Cardinal Operating Company's Unit 4 at the 230 MW Dallman plant in Illinois from the MATS standard. Earthjustice, an environmental law NGO, said that Trump's order, combined with other proclamations exempting chemical and other companies from clean air standards, allows major polluters to sidestep clean air standards in at least 30 states and US territories. In a separate development, the US Environmental Protection Agency announced that it would allow power utilities at least an additional year to inspect their coal ash waste sites and install groundwater monitoring systems. (Politico, The White House, Earthjustice, US Environmental Protection Agency)

 

 Indian agency exempts most coal units from sulphur dioxide controls: India's Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has exempted an estimated 78 per cent of India's 537 coal units from the requirement to install a flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) system to cut sulphur dioxide (SO2) emissions. In a post on X, a social media platform owned by Elon Musk, the ministry claimed that "current exposure levels provide no credible evidence to suggest that SO2, under prevailing ambient conditions, is a major public health concern". Category A coal plants within 10 kilometres of the National Capital Region or cities with of population of more than 20 million were initially required to have FGD units installed by 2017. The new deadline is December 30, 2027. Other coal units in highly polluted areas, designated as Category B areas, may only have to install FGD units by December 30, 2028, if recommended by a committee of experts. Categories A and B areas each account for about 11 per cent of the country's coal units. A recent Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) report estimated that about 60 per cent of India's SO2 emissions originate from coal plants. Sulphur dioxide in the atmosphere reacts with ammonia to create ammonium sulphate, which CREA estimates is responsible for 34 per cent of India's PM2.5 fine particle pollution. Indian power utilities have lobbied the government to delay the deadlines for installing FGD units, which were announced in 2015. Sunil Dahiya from the Delhi-based think tank EnviroCatalysts said the decision "takes us back ten years" in controlling S02 emissions. (The Hindu, The Wire)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Independent MP Andrew Wilkie expressed concern that the Australian Securities and Investments Commission may abandon further investigation of allegations of the falsification of coal export samples after a recent loss in a case before the federal court.

 

 Bosnia and Herzegovina: Elektroprivreda BiH abandoned its plan to co-fire the 740 MW Tuzla coal power plant with waste after the Tuzla City Council demanded the cancellation of the trial. Tuzla is the third-largest city in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

 

 Canada: The mothballed Donkin coal mine in Nova Scotia is up for sale by Kameron Collieries, a subsidiary of the US-based Cline Group. The mine was mothballed in July 2023 after the Department of Labour issued a stop-work order. The undersea mine is allowed to resume production.

 

 India: The Bombay High Court has directed government agencies to respond by September 11 to a petition by residents of Vasco, challenging plans by the Mormugao Port Trust to expand coal capacity to 42 million tonnes per year by 2035, from the current 10.6 million tonnes per year.

 

 Pakistan: The Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company (SECMC) has secured funding from a consortium headed by the Meezan Bank to expand production from the Thar Block II lignite mine from 7.6 million tonnes a year to 11.2 million tonnes a year. The expansion will cater for the conversion of the 660 MW Port Qasim Lucky power station from imported coal to Thar lignite.

 

 Russia: A fire spread over a 200 metre long section of the 23 kilometre long coal conveyer that connects the East Mining Company's Solntsevsky mine to the Shakhtersk export terminal on the coast of Sakhalin Island in eastern Russia.

 

 UK: David Lewis, the sole director of the company which operated the controversial Ffos y Fran mine in Wales, initially received a conditional caution from police over an assault on Robert Davies, a solicitor who testified in a court case involving Lewis's companies and another party. Charges against Lewis were laid but subsequently dropped.

 

 US: The reduction in the royalty rate from 12.5 per cent to 7 per cent for coal from federal leases would cut payments to Wyoming by approximately US$50 million per year. One-third of the federal coal royalty is allocated to the Wyoming School Foundation Program, with the remainder going to the state's general fund.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Chinese coal imports slump to two-year low in June: China's coal imports fell in the first half of 2025 to 221.7 million tonnes, down 11 per cent compared to the same period last year. The latest data from the General Administration of Customs revealed coal imports of 33.04 million tonnes, down 8 per cent from May and 26 per cent lower than in June 2024. The decline in imports, especially of lower-grade coal, comes as Chinese domestic coal production increased by six per cent. Indonesian coal exporters have borne the brunt of the decline in imports, with 90.98 million tonnes shipped to China in the first half of the year, a 12 per cent decrease from the same period last year. In June, Chinese imports of Indonesian coal slumped by 30 per cent compared to a 17 per cent, 15 per cent, and 24 per cent decline for cargoes from Russia, Mongolia, and Australia, respectively. (Mining Weekly, Economic Times)

Chinese agency announces checks on coal mine overproduction: The share prices of Chinese coal mining companies surged after social media posts revealed a July 10 announcement by the National Energy Administration of inspections to investigate potential overproduction by coal mines in eight major coal-producing provinces. The notice, which Bloomberg confirmed as authentic, stated that inspections would run until August 15 and penalise any coal companies producing more than 110 per cent of approved capacity. The notice stated that "the oversupply situation has created a distorted market", reflecting the concern of coal industry lobby groups that overproduction by some industry players has resulted in record production and has driven domestic coal prices to a four-year low. (Mining.com, Reuters)

Chinese clean energy exports reduce global emissions: Lauri Myllyvirta from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimates that Chinese exports of clean energy technologies, including solar, wind, and batteries, in 2024 reduced global greenhouse gas pollution by approximately 220 million tonnes, or 1 per cent. In the first year, the emissions reduction from the clean energy exports exceeded the embedded carbon content from the manufacturing process. Myllyvirta estimates that the emissions reductions over the lifetimes of the exports could be about four gigatonnes of carbon dioxide. The single most significant contributor to the emissions reductions is the export of solar panels. (Carbon Brief)

Russia announces US$800 million in tax breaks for coal companies: Russia's Finance Ministry announced a tax break of about 63 billion roubles (US$804.08-million) this year for coal mining companies as the sector flounders with rising costs, the impact of sanctions and softening export demand and prices. The ministry announced that companies could defer royalty payments until the end of November and tax debts incurred before June 1, 2025. The measure followed a directive from President Vladimir Putin to support the coal sector and a warning earlier this year by the government that up to 30 coal mining companies were at risk of bankruptcy. (Mining Weekly)

Glencore seeks approval for expansion of Canadian coal mine: Elk Valley Resources (EVR), a subsidiary of Glencore, has submitted a revised proposal to extend the life of its Fording River mine by about 35 years until the early 2060s. If approved, the extension would maintain the current rate of mining production at 9 million tonnes per year and produce an additional 280 million tonnes of coal over the extended period. Casey Brennan from Wildsight, a Canadian NGO, said water pollution from EVR's four mines in the valley must be addressed and environmental liability securities are in place before any expansion is considered. Last year, the Canadian and US governments agreed to an International Joint Commission investigation into water pollution, particularly selenium emissions, from Glencore's Elk Valley mines. The pollution from the mines affects First Nations, downstream communities, and waterways in Montana and Idaho. (Vancouver Sun, British Columbia's Environmental Assessment Office)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Global Cement and Concrete Tracker, Global Energy Monitor, July 2025.

Global Energy Monitor has launched the Global Cement and Concrete Tracker, which features data on over 3500 plants, including all those proposed or under construction since 2018. Many cement plants include facilities to make clinker which typically relies on coal or oil to achieve high temperatures.

Phasing out coal-fired electric power generation: implications for public health: a case study in Canada, World Health Organization, July 2025. (Pdf)

This 8-page brief provides an overview of Canada's implementation of its plan to phase out all coal generation by 2030, as well as the public health benefits of this policy.

Decarbonising the Coal-based Thermal Power Sector in India: A Roadmap, Centre for Science and Environment, June 2025. (Pdf)

This 172-page report proposes that the introduction of emission intensity standards for India's current coal fleet, along with the adoption of a 20 per cent biomass co-firing target, could reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector by 32.4 per cent by 2031-32.

US Coal Industry Trends, Congressional Research Service, June 30, 2025. (Pdf)

This 17-page paper provides a brief overview of US coal production and employment trends and reviews the actions of the second Trump administration. The paper concludes it is uncertain whether recent policy announcements will slow the decline of coal power plants.

title: CoalWire 573, July 31, 2025
excerpt: Slump in new coal mine capacity; Czech mine to close; Australian court overturns mine approval.
content:
July 31, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The latest Global Energy Monitor update on coal mining revealed that the capacity of new mines commissioned in 2024 fell to the lowest level in a decade. While this is welcome news, the report also notes that there are 830 more projects across 30 countries at various stages of consideration. In the Czech Republic, the country's last hard coal mine, the CSM project near the Polish border, will finally close this year. In New South Wales, a court ruling overturned the approval of a 22-year extension to the Mount Pleasant coal mine.

The advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice on national responsibility to act on climate change may lend additional weight to future legal challenges against fossil fuel projects. The court specifically noted that the production and consumption of fossil fuels "may constitute an internationally wrongful act attributable to that state" and flagged the potential vulnerability of states to reparations. While the Trump administration continues to try and assist the ailing coal industry, the latest data from the US Energy Information Administration suggests a short-term jump in coal power generation in the US this year and a fall by just as much next year as old plants close and renewables increase. The US government's hostility to climate action may also be a factor in the decision of Chubb, a major US insurer, to backtrack on its policy and reinsure a coal power plant in Vietnam.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Indonesian coal plant's seawater permit imperils marine life, fishing communities

Indonesia's marine ministry has granted the operator of the 1.9 gigawatt (GW) Batang coal plant permission to use vast amounts of seawater for cooling, prompting concerns from marine experts over the impact of heated discharge on coastal ecosystems and fisheries, writes Basten Gokkon in Mongabay.

 

 These companies avoided clean-air rules. It took a single email

At least 15 coal plants sought exemptions from environmental rules using a new Trump administration system to fast-track requests, according to documents released under the Freedom of Information Act, writes Maxine Joselow in the New York Times.

 

 Capped Alabama coal ash pond still polluting groundwater 7 years after closure, lawsuit claims

The coal ash lagoon at Alabama Power's Plant Gadsden was supposed to be a model for how to close ash ponds by covering them in place, a process utilities insisted would protect human health and the environment from toxic contaminants in the ash. Now, groundwater monitoring data and a federal lawsuit are challenging that contention, writes Dennis Pillion in Inside Climate News.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Report reveals new coal mine capacity in 2024 was lowest in a decade: Global Energy Monitor's update to the Global Coal Mine Tracker revealed that coal mines with about 105 million tonnes capacity were commissioned in 2024, down 46 per cent on 2023 levels and the lowest level in a decade. However, projects with a combined capacity of 2.27 billion tonnes a year are under consideration, with 1.35 million tonnes of proposed new capacity in China. Thirty-five coal mine expansions are currently under construction, with a further 850 new mines, restarts and expansions under consideration across 30 countries. (Reuters, Global Energy Monitor, Global Energy Monitor [Pdf])

 

 International Court of Justice ruling highlights role of fossil fuels: An advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice stated that the production and consumption of fossil fuels "may constitute an internationally wrongful act attributable to that state", endorsed the Paris Agreement goal a limiting global heating to a 1.5 degrees temperature above pre-industrial levels and suggested those adversely affected could be entitled to "reparations". The case began as an initiative of students in Fiji and was backed by the government of Vanuatu, the Pacific Islands Forum and the United Nations. While the opinion is not binding on governments, it could be influential in corporate, government and legal decision-making, according to Dr Joana Setzer from the London School of Economics and Political Science's Grantham Institute. "This has far-reaching implications: it signals that states could be in breach if they fail to control emissions from companies they license, subsidise or oversee. This will place greater pressure on states to halt any new fossil fuel projects and introduce stricter regulations on the sector," she said. (Carbon Brief, United Nations, International Court of Justice)

 

 New South Wales court overturns mine approval: The New South Wales Court of Appeal has overturned the NSW Land and Environment Court's (LEC) dismissal of an appeal by Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMS HEG) against MACH Energy's proposed 22-year expansion of the Mount Pleasant coal mine. In 2022, the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) approved the company's plan to double coal production to 21 million tonnes a year and extend operations from 2026 to 2048. DAMS HEG appealed this decision, but the LEC dismissed their challenge. However, the Court of Appeal found that the LEC had not considered the impact on the local environment of scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions from burning the coal from the mine overseas. The Court of Appeal decision requires the NSWLEC to consider whether it can impose conditions to minimise Scope 3 emissions associated with the project. If not, the IPC will reconsider the project. MACH Energy said it would review the judgment. (Guardian, ABC News, NSW Court of Appeal)

 

 Czech coal company shuts country's last hard coal mine: The Czech Republic's state-owned coal company, OKD, will close its underground CSM hard coal mine near the Polish border by the end of 2025. CSM is the country's last remaining hard coal mine and was scheduled to close in 2023. However, Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the surge in gas prices prompted the government to extend the operating life of the three 200 MW coal units at CEZ's Detmarovice power plant. Those units closed earlier this year, leaving the mine operating at reduced capacity to supply some district heating plants and the iron and steel industry. (TVP World)

 

 Canadian NGO highlights selenium risk from mine expansion: Wildsight, a Canadian environmental group, welcomed Elk Valley Resources (EVR) engagement with First Nations groups over the proposed to extend the life of the Fording River mine by 35 years and produce an additional 280 million tonnes of coal. EVR is a subsidiary of Glencore. Wildsight warned that the expansion would convert large swathes of Castle Mountain into terraced mine pits and generate about 3 billion cubic meters of waste rock. Simon Wiebe from Wildsight said that the waste rock "will leach selenium into our waterways for decades into our waterways for decades, if not centuries". Castle Mountain also provides winter foraging for threatened bighorn sheep and hosts stands of endangered whitebark pines. An earlier version of the plan with a larger footprint was rejected in 2023 by British Columbia's Environmental Assessment Office. (Wildsight)

 

 Colombian President warns Glencore over coal exports to Israel: Controversy erupted after the Colombian Labor Minister Antonio Sanguino said union members at the port of Puerto Nuevo reported that the bulk carrier Fortune left on July 24 with a cargo of coal for Israel. Prodeco, a subsidiary of Glencore, owns and operates both the port and the Cerrejon coal mine. In August 2024, Colombian President Gustavo Petro issued a formal decree banning coal exports to Israel but with an exemption for contracted shipments and cargoes approved by the customs agency. Following the latest shipment, Petro accused officials of undermining the ban and vowed that "not a tonne" of coal would leave for Israel. Petro also threatened to change Glencore's Cerrejon mining concession agreement unless the company complied with the ban. However, Glencore said that Cerrejon's "last shipment of coal was some two weeks before the decree came into effect". Ship-tracking websites report that the Fortune is due to arrive in the Israeli port of Hadera on August 14. (Reuters, Jerusalem Post, Middle East Monitor)

 

 
 "Failure of a State to take appropriate action to protect the climate system from GHG [greenhouse gas] emissions — including through fossil fuel production, fossil fuel consumption, the granting of fossil fuel exploration licences or the provision of fossil fuel subsidies — may constitute an internationally wrongful act which is attributable to that State",

stated [pdf] the International Court of Justice in an advisory opinion on countries responsibilities to act on climate change.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Dartbrook Mine, a joint-venture between Australian Pacific Coal and Tetra Resources, has retrenched 100 mine workers, representing two-thirds of its workforce. The company has debts of more than A$800 million (US$521 million), with administrators recently appointed to operate the company.

 

 Canada: A study has found that coal mines, roads, towns, and reservoirs affect the ability of grizzly bears to move across their range in search of food. The study analysed 20 years of tracking data from over 100 grizzly bears in southern British Columbia and Alberta.

 

 New Zealand: Climate activists have blocked coal from leaving Bathurst Resources Stockton Mine by occupying a bucket on the company's aerial ropeway.

 

 Philippines: The Department of Energy (DOE) confirmed that the 2020 moratorium on new coal plants does not include Meralco's proposed 1.2 GW Atimonan coal plant. Community groups have opposed the project since Meralco announced the proposal in 2015.

 

 Russia: State-owned Gazprombank's Centre for Economic Forecasting estimates that Russian coal exports to China fell by 25 per cent between January and June. Exports to China in the April to June period fell by 34 per cent compared to the same period in the preceding year.

 

 UK: A Welsh council rejected a proposed housing development because of concerns about the potential effect of coal mine gas emissions on residents. A planning inspector upheld the decision.

 

 US: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel and a separate coalition of advocacy groups have filed legal challenges against the Department of Energy's order to keep the 1.56 GW J.H. Campbell coal plant operating for another 90 days.

 

 US: The Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement granted the bankrupt South Fork Coal Company permission to haul coal from its Rocky Run Surface Mine through the Monongahela National Forest in West Virginia.

 

 "My judgment on this is that this company is absolutely set up to never make taxable profit The related-party transactions are so big and wild and all over the map that this company will never make a profit on paper and will never pay a cent of tax,"

said Jason Ward from the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research on Adani's Carmichael mining operations in Australia.

 
 

Companies + Markets

US coal consumption tipped to rise this year, then fall in 2026: The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates US coal consumption could increase by six per cent in 2025 due to increased electricity demand, followed by a similar decline in 2026 as coal plant retirements take effect and renewables capacity grows. About 90 per cent of US coal production is consumed in the domestic power sector. The EIA estimates coal production could increase by 1.5 per cent in 2025 to 519.9 million US short tons (471.6 million tonnes), followed by an 8.6 per cent decline in 2026 to 475.1 million US short tons (431 million tonnes). Higher domestic gas prices, following historic lows at the end of 2024, spurred an 18 per cent increase in coal generation in the first quarter of 2025. The agency estimates coal plants will drop from a 17 per cent share of electricity generation in 2025 to 15 per cent in 2026, despite forecasting a 2.2 per cent increase in electricity generation in 2025-26. (US Energy Information Administration)

Alberta paid C$143 million to settle coal licence compensation claim: Atrum Coal, a small Australian coal exploration company, agreed to drop its legal action against the Alberta government in return for C$142.8 million (US$103.75) in compensation and the surrender of its Elan Coal leases. The government will hold C$6 million (US$4.36 million) pending the satisfactory rehabilitation of the company's exploration sites. Atrum said the Elan leases contain a hard coking coal resource of about 486 million tonnes and had sought C$3.5 billion (US$2.54 million) in compensation. In May 2020, the Alberta government lifted the moratorium on coal exploration on the Eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, but after a sustained public backlash, largely reinstated it in 2022. Following the backflip, five coal companies filed legal claims for a combined C$15 billion (US$10.9 billion) in damages. Several weeks ago, two companies, Evolve Power and Atrum Coal, informed shareholders that they had settled claims against the government. Evolve stated it was seeking C$1.75 billion (US$1.27 billion), but the final settlement amount for the claim is not public. After the province lifted the moratorium again late last year, the Siksika Nation applied for judicial review. Environmental Defence criticised the government for its policy flip-flops. (CBC, Environmental Defence, Atrum Coal [pdf])

Analysts tip Adani's Australian coal project may never pay tax: Analysis of corporate records filed by Adani entities for its Australian coal subsidiaries reveals the company pays little corporate tax due to complex intra-company charges. According to the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research, Adani's Australian mining subsidiaries may never pay any tax. Adani Mining, the company that operates the Carmichael coal mine in Queensland, reported a A$461.7 million (US$301 million) loss in the year to March 2025. The Bowen Rail Company, which transports the coal from the mine to the export terminal, reported a A$41.8 million (US$27.2 million) loss in the year to March. The Abbot Point coal terminal, which another Adani subsidiary operates, has not yet filed its latest return but reported a A$3.3 million (US$2.15 million) loss in the year to March 2024. A Guardian Australia analysis found that the Adani subsidiary operating the port paid corporate tax of less than A$4 million (US$2.61 million) in just one of the 10 years since 2011, when it entered into a 99-year lease for the port. Adani Mining paid the Queensland government A$78.6 million (US$51.22 million) in the year to March 2025 in royalties on state-owned coal. The losses reported by Adani's Australian subsidiaries are mainly due to payments to other Adani entities for interest on loans, lease expenses and other services. Adani Mining and Bowen Rail Company are subsidiaries of the Singapore-registered Adani Global Pte Limited, which reported a $US71.1 million (A$109 million) profit for the year to March 2025. (Guardian, Australian Financial Review [paywall])

Chubb reinsures Vietnamese coal plant despite policy commitment: Chubb has backtracked on its climate policy and became the lead reinsurer for Nghi Son 2 Power, which owns and operates the 1.2 gigawatt (GW) Nghi Son 2 coal plant in northern Vietnam. Nghi Son 2 Power is a consortium owned by Marubeni, Korea Electric Power Corporation and Tohoku Electric Power Company. In 2019, Chubb released a climate policy that ruled out providing insurance cover for companies generating more than 30 per cent of their energy from coal. The March 2025 version of the policy rules out providing coverage for the construction and operation of coal plants, "new risks" for companies producing more than 30 per cent electricity from coal and states that it "began phasing out coverage of existing risks exceeding this threshold at the start of 2022 (accounting for the viability of alternative energy sources in the impacted region)". Global Energy Monitor estimates that the Nghi Son 2 plant could emit up to 175 million tonnes of carbon dioxide over 25 years. Chubb and Nghi Son 2 Power did not respond to requests for comment. (The Bureau of Investigative Journalism, Chubb [Pdf])

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 China is on track to fall short of its electric arc furnace target: A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) finds that production from China's electric arc furnace (EAF) sector languishes at just 10 per cent of steel production. In 2022, the government set a 2025 target of 15 per cent of steel production from electric arc furnaces to reduce reliance on the coal-intensive blast furnaces. Achieving the target would reduce China's greenhouse gas emissions by about 160 million tonnes and require a 60 million tonnes reduction of steel from blast furnaces. The average global share of EAF steel production is 30 per cent. CREA stated that the EAF sector has been impacted by high electricity costs and unreliable scrap supply, resulting in low plant utilisation rates and the mothballing of mills, with some companies declaring bankruptcy. Despite recent policy changes to ease restrictions on the use of imported scrap metal, imports fell by half in 2024. Steel production accounts for about eight per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, with China accounting for about half of global steel production. (Reuters, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

GenCost 2024-25: Final report, CSIRO, July 2025. (Pdf)

This 135-page report is the latest assessment by the CSIRO, the Australian government's science agency, of the comparative electricity generation costs of a range of technologies. The report finds the firmed costs of solar and onshore wind are the lowest source of new generation, with small modular nuclear power costing two or three times as much by 2030.

links.text: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

title: CoalWire 574, August 7, 2025
excerpt: International Energy Agency tips renewables set to overtake coal power; appeal over life extension for Canadian lignite plants.
content:
August 7, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Two new International Energy Agency reports point to the rapid growth in new solar and wind capacity and the prospect that renewables will overtake coal as the largest source of electricity "by 2026 at the latest". One of the reports also suggests a marginal one per cent increase in coal demand this year and a decline in the export market in 2025 and 2026. The latest Chinese data, which reveals the installation of 212 gigawatts (GW) of solar in the first half of 2025, indicates that new renewables generation is outpacing the growth in electricity demand. In the Philippines, the increase in solar and wind capacity is gradually eating into the dominance of coal generation. Coal India, which produces about 80 per cent of India's domestic coal, reported a decline in demand, partly attributable to milder summer weather.

While solar and wind continue to undercut the viability of coal power, some governments are delaying the closure of old plants. In Alberta, civil society groups have applied for judicial review of the provincial government's decision to extend the life of three aging lignite power plants. A new Canadian study also sheds further light on the long-term selenium pollution from closed coal mines in the McLeod River basin in Alberta. In South Africa, the government's decision to exempt eight Eskom coal plants from pollution control standards imposes a huge health toll on local communities.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Battle to breathe: How air pollution in Emalahleni is affecting people's health

Emissions from power stations and dust from coal mines in South Africa's "energy mecca" are making many people in the area sick, writes Susan Segar in Spotlight.

 

 Pinpointing Pollution: The Mpumalanga town where South Africans suffer most

The South African government recently exempted eight Eskom coal plants from the obligation to comply with minimum pollution control standards, depriving ordinary men, women and children in Mpumalanga province of their constitutional right to an environment that is not harmful to their health, writes Ethan van Diemen in the first of a three-part series published in the Daily Maverick.

 

 Adani claims its export program helps contribute to sustainable energy – but experts say that's 'wilful disinformation'

An Adani claim that its Australian coal exports are advancing the United Nations' sustainable development goals has been denounced by leading scientists, write Jonathan Barrett and Graham Readfearn in The Guardian.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Legal challenge against Canadian province's lignite plan: Citizens for Public Justice (CPJ) has filed an application with the Court of King's Bench seeking judicial review of the decision of the Saskatchewan government to extend the life of its three coal plants beyond 2030. The Saskatchewan government plans to defy federal regulations adopted in 2016, which require all coal plants to close by 2030 or when the plants reach 50 years of operation, whichever comes first. Jeremy Harrison, the Minister Responsible for the state-owned SaskPower, announced in mid-June that the utility will revive the mothballed 150 megawatt (MW) lignite-fired Unit 4 at the Boundary Dam plant. Harrison said that all coal units at the Boundary Dam plant, the 630 MW Poplar River and the 300 MW Shand plants will be upgraded. Coal accounted for just under one-quarter of SaskPower's generation in 2024-25. CPJ, the Saskatchewan Environmental Society, and three individuals stated that Harrison's decision was made without sufficient public consultation, is inconsistent with federal clean energy regulations, and breaches the rights of future children under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. (CBC, SaskToday, Citizens for Public Justice, Citizens for Public Justice [Pdf])

 

 Alberta study finds selenium pollution long after coal mine closures: A peer-reviewed study in Environmental Pollution found that monitoring data revealed selenium concentrations exceeded guideline levels for the protection of aquatic life decades after the closure of three coal mines in the McLeod River basin in Alberta, Canada. The mines closed in the early 2000s, with one fully rehabilitated and another 60 per cent reclaimed. Samples from six locations revealed that 98 to 100 per cent of testing samples found selenium concentrations exceeded guideline levels. High levels of selenium pollution can cause deformities and adversely affect the reproductive capacity of fish and birds. The authors also found higher concentrations of ions, nutrients, and heavy metals downstream of the mines and noted that nickel levels were 200 times higher downstream from the mines than in water upstream. The paper stated that the only population of the endangered Athabasca rainbow trout in the eastern Rockies is found in the McLeod River, noting that, with a declining population, the species is likely to become extinct. The authors conclude that current mine rehabilitation standards are insufficient to achieve the stated objective of restoring old mine sites to pre-existing quality. (CBC News, Environmental Pollution)

 

 Lukewarm interest for latest Indian coal block auction: India's Ministry of Coal announced the successful sale of just seven of the 22 coal blocks offered in the 12th round of commercial coal auctions. The ministry received 41 bids for eight coal blocks, with the sale of just seven blocks. The ministry rated three of the sold coal blocks as "fully explored" with a combined potential production capacity of 5.25 million tonnes a year. One of the areas, the 306 million tonne Mahuagarhi coal block in Jharkhand, was sold to the state-owned Damodar Valley Corporation. The utility operates six coal plants with a combined capacity of 6976 megawatts (MW), with coal projects in the pre-construction phase with a further combined capacity of 5320 MW. Since 2020, the government has auctioned 131 coal blocks with a nominal production capacity of 277 million tonnes a year. (Ministry of Coal [Pdf])

 

 Indian agency approves clearing of part of Hasdeo forest for coal mine: The Chhattisgarh forest department has recommended the allocation of more than 1740 hectares of the Hasdeo Arand forest to Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Ltd (RVUNL) for the Kente Extension coal mine. RVUNL, the state-owned power utility of the Rajasthan government, has contracted Adani to develop and operate the mine. The forest agency estimates that Adani could clear about 450,000 trees in the biodiversity-rich Hasdeo Arand forest for the mine expansion. Alok Shukla, Convener of Chhattisgarh Bachao Andolan, said the affected area is within the catchment area of the Chornai River and is near the Lemru Elephant Reserve. (The Week)

 

 New South African mine approved: The South African Department of Mineral Resources and Energy has approved Richtrau 253's proposed open-cut coal mine near Panfontein despite concerns by residents about pollution and the effect on the nearby Vaal River. Richtrau 253 is a subsidiary of Liketh Investments, which first proposed a mine near Panfontein in 2014 and has been involved in other coal proposals in South Africa and Kenya. Residents had only 20 working days to lodge appeals against the July 2 decision. (The Citizen)

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Bowen Coking Coal has entered voluntary administration after BUMA Australia, the former operator of the Burton Coal Complex, sought A$15.3 million (US$9.9 million) in unpaid invoices and the Queensland Revenue Office rejected a request for deferred royalty payments.

 

 Australia: Climate Integrity filed a complaint with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission against a pro-coal advertisement by NSW Mining, a mining industry lobby group. The complaint argues the "Coal is needed for energy security" ad constitutes misleading and deceptive conduct under the Australian Consumer Law.

 

 Montenegro: The government awarded a 24.5-year concession to Rudnik Uglja for exploration and mining at four lignite deposits in Pljevlja municipality.

 

 New Zealand: Protesters blocked the coal bucket way from Bathurst Resources Stockton mine for nine days.

 

 UK: Barclays has terminated its membership of the UN Environment Program's Net-Zero Banking Alliance that required members to align their financial services to achieving net-zero emissions targets by 2050 or earlier.

 

 US: The Bureau of Land Management will auction a 1070-acre (433-hectare) federal coal lease adjoining North American Coal's Freedom Mine in North Dakota. The proposed sale contains an estimated 18.3 million US short tons (16.6 million tonnes) of recoverable lignite.

 

 US: The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection has ordered Bluestone Coal Corporation, a company owned by Republican US Senator Jim Justice, to explain why the permit for the Poca mine should not be suspended or revoked due to repeated permit violations.

 

 US: The derailment of a loaded CSX coal train in St. Albans, West Virginia, caused the suspension of the Amtrak service between Huntington and New York City.

 

 US: Michigan utility Consumers Energy revealed in its quarterly report that complying with the Trump administration's order to keep the 1.56 GW J.H. Campbell coal plant online cost US$29 million between May and June 2025.

 

 US: The Ohio Consumers' Counsel and the Ohio Manufacturers' Association Energy Group have called on the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio to audit the US$237 million paid in subsidies in 2024 and 2025 for the 1955-vintage 1303 MW Clifty Creek plant in Indiana and the 1086 MW Kyger Creek coal plant in Ohio.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

IEA forecasts coal demand to plateau in 2015 and 2026: The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that the rapid growth in wind and solar capacity is likely to drive renewable generation to exceed coal power "by 2026 at the latest". The agency's Electricity Mid-Year Update 2025 estimates that favourable wind and rainfall conditions could result in renewables exceeding coal generation this year. The IEA forecasts that wind and solar will account for about 90 per cent of the increase in global electricity demand to 2026, with renewables likely to reach 36 per cent of global power generation compared to coal power's share of 32 per cent. The IEA's Coal Mid-Year Update estimates a marginal increase in global coal demand in 2025 to 1180 million tonnes, primarily due to import demand from Asia, with Chinese imports increasing by 14 per cent in 2024 to a record 548 million tonnes. The agency suggests a decline in coal consumption in 2025 of one per cent in China, a two per cent fall in Europe and a seven per cent increase in the US. The IEA estimates a decline in the coal export trade in both 2025 and 2026, with the most significant downturns in Indonesia and Russia. (Carbon Brief, International Energy Agency, International Energy Agency [Pdf])

China's solar surge continues: China's National Energy Administration data for the first half of 2025 revealed that solar power generation increased by 43 per cent compared to the same period the year before, with wind generation rising by 16 per cent year-on-year. Wind and solar generation was 23.7 per cent of total power consumption in the first half of 2025, up from 20 per cent in 2024. New wind and solar generation was greater than the increase in electricity demand. China's solar capacity reached 1100 GW with 212 GW of new capacity installed in the first half of 2025, a 54 per cent year-on-year increase. Rooftop solar now accounts for about 44.8 per cent of installed solar capacity, with the distributed sector accounting for 70 per cent of new capacity installed in the first half of 2025. However, solar generation increased at a lower rate than installed capacity, suggesting ongoing issues with curtailment due to transmission bottlenecks. (PV Magazine, Sina (Chinese), National Energy Administration [Chinese])

Clean energy growth undercutting coal generation in the Philippines: Coal power generation in the Philippines is on track to fall for the first time since 2008 after a 5.2 per cent decline in the first half of 2025. While some analysts sought to attribute the decline to an increase in gas generation, the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis said eight coal units with a combined capacity of 1.4 GW were offline for more than 30 days in the first quarter of 2025. Most of the outages were planned. Increased hydro generation, along with the addition of more than 1 GW of solar capacity in 2024, boosted renewable generation. The Department of Energy has launched an auction for up to 10.5 GW of new renewables capacity, including 1100 MW of solar-plus-storage projects. A June 2025 BNEF analysis of electricity generation costs of new capacity in the Philippines estimated new solar at US$35 to US$72 per megawatt-hour (MWh) compared to $87-117 per MWh for coal capacity and $87-105 per MWh for a combined-cycle gas turbine. BNEF estimates that solar with a four-hour battery will be competitive with new coal and gas units this year, with onshore wind being the second cheapest source of power generation after solar by 2028. (Reuters, Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis, Bloomberg NEF)

Coal India pitches big boost in production as profits and demand falter: Coal India reported a 20 per cent fall in profit to 87.43 billion rupees (US$998 million) for the three months to the end of June 2025 due to a fall in demand and lower prices. An earlier-than-normal monsoon resulted in a 3 per cent decline in coal generation. Coal India's latest data indicates a 6 per cent fall in coal production and a 5.5 per cent decline in offtake sales in the April to July period compared to the year before. Coal India said it has set a target of 900 million tonnes of coal sales in the 2025/26 financial year, an 18 per cent increase on the year before. The company is pursuing the development of two new pit-head coal plants: a 1600 MW project in Odisha and, in a joint venture with the Damodar Valley Corporation, a 1600 MW plant in Jharkhand. (Reuters, Economic Times, Coal India [Pdf])

Anglo American and Peabody Energy head to court over stalled takeover: Peabody Energy is preparing to seek arbitration with Anglo American over its agreement to buy four metallurgical coal mines in Queensland for US$3.78 billion. Anglo American suspended production at the underground Moranbah North mine following a fire on March 31. Peabody Energy stated in its quarterly report released on July 31 that there was "still no credible timetable on resumption of sustainable longwall production" four months after the fire. Peabody said the uncertainty about restarting operations constitutes a 'material adverse change' under the November 2024 purchase agreement and informed investors it has not negotiated a revised deal. Executives from Anglo and Peabody separately told investors on July 31 that they disagreed on whether the fire and suspension of mine production constituted a 'material adverse change'. The original agreement covered the purchase of the Grosvenor, Moranbah North, Aquila, and Capcoal mines, with a fifth, the Dawson mine, slated to be sold to the Indonesian mining company BUMA. Part of Peabody's original offer was a payment of US$450 million if Anglo American's mothballed Grosvenor underground mine resumed production and operated for two years. The mine was closed after a June 2024 fire. (Australian Financial Review [paywall], Peabody Energy)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 US steel company eyes converting transition grant for coal and gas: The Chairman, President and CEO of Cleveland-Cliffs, Lourenco Goncalves, told investors on a July 21 call with investors that he is in discussions with the US Department of Energy on the possible "revamping" the Middleton steelworks in Ohio "using beautiful coal, beautiful coke, beautiful natural gas". In March 2024, the US Department of Energy announced it was considering providing up to US$500 million in funding under the Biden administration's Inflation Reduction Act to phase out the use of coke, build two electric arc furnaces and replace an existing blast furnace with a 2.5 million tonnes per annum "hydrogen-ready" direct reduced iron (DRI) plant. After the election of President Trump, Goncalves said that the plan had been scrapped and attributed the change to the higher-than-anticipated cost of hydrogen production. (Manufacturing Dive, Cleveland-Cliffs [Pdf])

 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Global coal phaseout: Tracking coal plant retirements, Global Energy Monitor, July 2025.

This post features data visualisations on the status of the global coal power plant phaseout.

title: CalWire 575, August 14, 2025
excerpt: China lowers power forecast; rapid decline in hospitalisations after US coke plant closure.
content:
August 14, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The latest Chinese electricity forecasts suggest electricity demand growth this year will be lower than previously estimated. Combined with the China Electricity Council's projected increase in new solar capacity installed in 2025, greenhouse gas emissions are likely to be lower than expected. A new analysis suggests that China's recent boom in new coal plant construction could be a final surge before a long decline. In India, the government continues to pursue an expansion of both renewables and coal power generation. In South Africa, the country's largest thermal coal exporter projects a significant fall in profits due to reduced demand and prices driven mainly by changes in Chinese and Indian demand.

In the US, a new study highlights the dramatic decline in hospital admissions following the closure in 2016 of a coke processing plant in Pennsylvania. The removal of subsidies for two 1955-vintage coal plants in Ohio has finally come into effect. However, the projected boom in US power demand for data centres for AI and cryptocurrency overshadows the scheduled retirement of other old plants. A new report highlights that the concentration of proposed data centres in a small number of US states could have profound impacts on local water supplies. Data centres often require large volumes of water directly for cooling and indirectly for increased electricity generation from thermal power plants.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Why China is still building new coal – and when it might stop

While China's coal power construction boom looks, at first glance, like a resurgence, it currently appears more likely to be the final surge before a long downturn, write Qi Qin and Lauri Myllyvirta from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air in Carbon Brief.

 

 Fool's Gold: When 700 gigawatts of data centres come knocking 

The rush to build, and power, data centres offers an unprecedented opportunity for utilities, and an extraordinary risk - and ratepayers are unwittingly caught in the middle, writes Jeremy Fisher from the Sierra Club.

 

 Data centres in Western US states suck water and power

From simple searches to ChatGPT, the big digital buildup in the US threatens the grid and water supplies, writes Jonathan Thompson in High Country News.

 

 Borneo killing linked to coal industry stays unsolved as the Indonesian Vice-President visits village

More than eight months after the bloody killing of an Indigenous elder in eastern Borneo, police in Indonesia have yet to name a suspect, while community leaders in the country's coal heartland continue to demand justice, writes Muhibar Sobary Ardan in Mongabay.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 US study finds health improvements after coke plant closure: A study by researchers at New York University, the University of Pittsburgh and the Allegheny County Health Department found a dramatic long-term decline in respiratory and cardiovascular emergency room visits and hospitalisations after the January 2016 closure of DTE Energy's Shenango coking plant in Pennsylvania. Coke production involves baking high-grade coal in ovens, resulting in significant emissions, including PM2.5 fine particle pollution, greenhouse gases, sulphur dioxide and benzene. The study found a 41.2 per cent decline in paediatric asthma emergency department visits and a 20.5 per cent decline in weekly respiratory hospital visits immediately after the closure of the plant. The researchers also found that emergency department visits continued to decline over the longer term by four per cent per month. The study compared hospital admissions for the three years before and after the closure and compared the trends with a control site 130 miles (209 kilometres) away in an urban area in Pennsylvania without a nearby coke plant. (Inside Climate News, American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine)

 

 Ohio coal plant subsidies authorised by scandal-tainted bill finally end: From August 14, Ohio utility customers will cease paying subsidies to Ohio Valley Electric Corporation (OVEC) for the 1955-vintage 1303 MW Clifty Creek plant in Indiana and the 1086 MW Kyger Creek coal plant in Ohio. The Ohio legislature passed the scandal-tainted House Bill 6 in 2019, legislation that guaranteed subsidies for the two coal plants and a nuclear plant. After federal prosecutors charged the then speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives and others over their roles in a US$61 million bribery scandal, the subsidy for the nuclear plant was revoked, but left the coal subsidies intact. The Ohio Manufacturers Association recently estimated regulated utility customers could have paid an additional US$413 million in subsidies through to 2030. While the subsidies have ceased, two cases before the Ohio Supreme Court challenge the validity of the authorisation by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) of subsidy payments made in 2018, 2019 and 2020. OVEC, a joint venture between American Electric Power, Duke Energy, and AES Ohio, plans to operate the plants until 2040. (Canary Media)

 

 US seeks to curtail International Energy Agency clean energy emphasis: The US Secretary of Energy, Chris Wright, told the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA), Fatih Birol, to revise its energy forecasting scenarios to reflect the Trump administration's emphasis on fossil fuels rather than clean energy, or the US would withdraw from the agency. The US provides about 14 per cent of the IEA's budget. Wright has publicly criticised IEA scenarios that suggest oil and gas demand has peaked. The IEA has agreed to reinstate its Current Policy Scenario in this year's World Energy Outlook report, a scenario dropped in 2021 in favour of the Stated Policies Scenario. Fossil fuel industry lobbyists and Republicans say the Stated Policies Scenario overstates the role of clean energy sources. (Politico, Bloomberg)

 

 New Zealand company's bid for fast-track review of mine rejected: The New Zealand Ministry for the Environment has rejected an initial application by Stevenson Mining for fast-track approval of its proposed 144-hectare Te Kuha Mine on the west coast of the South Island. In late 2024, the conservative New Zealand government passed legislation allowing designated projects to bypass the normal assessment process. The ministry said Stevenson Mining's application did not meet seven of the required criteria, including failing to identify what other approvals would be necessary. The company had not consulted with relevant agencies, including the Buller District Council, the Ministry for the Environment and the Department of Conservation. Adam Currie from 350 Aotearoa said it was "pretty incredible" that the company had not undertaken the basic steps. The company can submit a fresh application. The Environment Court ruled against the project in April 2023, the third court case since 2017 that Stevenson Mining had lost on the proposed metallurgical coal mine. (Radio New Zealand)

 

 UK coal company launched legal action against UK government: West Cumbria Mining (WCM), the company that unsuccessfully sought approval for the proposed Whitehaven metallurgical coal project, has launched legal proceedings against the UK government in the International Centre for Investment Disputes (ICSID). Details of the case are not yet public, but WCM and Woodhouse Investment, a real estate business that employs only one person, filed a case with ICSID on August 8 seeking to commence arbitration proceedings against the UK government. WCM, a subsidiary of the privately-owned Australian company EMR Capital Investment, applied in February 2023 for a three-year mining licence to extract up to four million tonnes of coal a year. In mid-September 2024, the High Court ruled in favour of the appeal brought by Friends of the Earth (FOE) and South Lakes Action on Climate Change and overturned planning permission for the mine. Global Justice Now said that investors in the Whitehaven project are now using the UK's investment treaty with Singapore to sue the government. Chris Rowley of South Lakes Action on Climate Change said it was hard to see "what valid grounds West Cumbria Mining might have, and worrying that this might all take place behind closed doors". (Inside Climate News, Global Justice Now, International Centre for Investment Disputes)

 

 Controversy over Malaysian coal concession reporting: Police in Sabah state have launched an investigation of the online news site MalaysiaNow following a news report alleging that the Sabah Mineral Management (SMM), the state mineral licensing agency, awarded a coal exploration licence to Bumi Suria over 70,000 hectares of forest within the Kalabakan and Gunung Rara reserves. MalaysiaNow reported that the police are investigating the use of leaked internal SMM documents and a possible breach of communications legislation. SMM rejected the claim that it had granted an exploration licence and threatened to sue the news site for defamation. (MalaysiaNow)

 

 Indonesia changes mine plan system after coal mine controversy: Bengkulu Provincial Prosecutors' Office arrested a former mining inspector as part of an investigation into coal mining by PT Ratu Samban Mining (RSM). Prosecutors allege that a Budget Activity Plan (RKAB) submitted by RSM was inappropriately approved, allowing the company to mine coal from 2022 to 2023 without an authorised reclamation plan in the RKAB or payment of a rehabilitation bond. Two RSM officials were previously arrested, along with six others from two other companies. Government officials allege that up to 500 billion rupiah (US$30.3 million) of coal was extracted from the mine. The Minister for Energy and Mineral Resources, Bahlil Lahadalia, announced in early July that annual approval of work plans for mines will be required, compared to the previous three-yearly interval between reviews. (Indonesia Business Post, VOI.id, Jakarta Post [paywall])

 

 
 "This pollution mix [from a coke plant] is far more toxic than everyday pollution It's like coal-fired power plant particles, but on steroids,"

said George Thurston, a professor in New York University's School of Medicine.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The High Court of Australia has rejected an appeal by Helensburgh Coal, a subsidiary of Peabody Energy, against decisions by the Federal Court and the Fair Work Commission that found the sacking of 90 workers in 2020 did not meet the "genuine redundancies" provision of the Fair Work Act.

 

 New Zealand: Climate activists protested outside ANZ branches against the bank's support for Bathurst Resources, New Zealand's largest coal mining company.

 

 US: Two workers died and 10 were seriously injured in an explosion at US Steel's Clairton coke plant in Pennsylvania.

 

 US: Arizona Public Service (APS), a subsidiary of PinnacleWest Capital Corporation, announced it has abandoned its plan for 65 per cent clean electricity by 2030 and 100 per cent by 2050. APS said it will delay the closure of the 1.5 GW Four Corners coal plant from 2031 until "no later" than 2038.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Chinese agency lowers 2025 estimated electricity demand growth: The China Electricity Council (CEC), which tracks electricity generation, has reduced its 2025 electricity demand forecast and upgraded the likely solar capacity growth. The CEC's original projection for electricity demand growth was 6 per cent, but actual growth in the first half of the year was 3.7 per cent. The agency is suggesting 5-6 per cent demand growth in the second half of the year, suggesting annual growth in the range of 4.5 to 5 per cent. With the installation of about 210 GW of solar capacity in the first half of the year, the CEC is now projecting 310 GW of new capacity in 2025. The CEC estimates that by the end of June, China's total installed power generation capacity increased by 18.7 per cent year-on-year, with wind and solar accounting for about 90 per cent of the new capacity. (Lauri Myllyvirta [LinkedIn], China Electricity Council [Chinese])

Indian government seeking site for 30 GW more coal or lignite plants: India's Minister of State for Power, Shripad Yesso Naik, told India's lower house on August 7 that the Ministry of Power is seeking potential sites for the development of 30.9 GW of new coal and lignite plants by 2034-35. Naik informed the house that, in addition to the 38.9 GW of projects under construction or classified as financially stressed assets, contracts have been issued for a further 15.4 GW of coal and lignite plants. At the end of June, coal and lignite plants accounted for 223 GW of the country's 485 GW of total installed capacity. Naik said that India has 158.45 GW of renewable capacity under construction and a further 62 GW in pre-construction stages with the aim of completion by 2029-30. (Economic Times)

Adani wins auction for new 2400 MW coal plant in India: Adani Power, a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises, said it has won the auction to build, own and operate a new 2.4 gigawatt coal plant at Pirpainti in Bihar state. Adani Power was one of four reported bidders on the project, along with JSW Energy, Torrent Power, and Bajaj Group's Lalitpur. Adani said its winning bid to supply 2.27 GW of power to the North Bihar Power Distribution Company was 6.075 rupees per kilowatt-hour (6.9 US cents per kWh). The Pirpainti project was first proposed almost 20 years ago, but the original 1.32 GW project encountered public opposition and stalled. Adani said that it plans to have the first 800 MW unit commissioned within 48 months and the US$3 billion plant completed within five years of the finalisation of the contract. In a separate development, the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation is seeking 400 acres (162 hectares) area of land near Kalmeshwar as a site for Adani's proposed coal gasification project. (Deccan Herald, Mining Weekly, Adani Enterprises, Times of India)

Coal India production slowed by utilities reliance on stockpiled coal: Coal stockpiles at Indian power plants fell by 13 per cent in July as power utilities delayed purchases from state-owned Coal India, which supplies over three-quarters of the country's coal. In the first half of 2025, 22 GW of new wind and solar capacity were added to the grid. Coal power generation in July fell for the fourth month in a row due to an early monsoon, a 22 per cent increase in hydro generation and a 14.4 per cent surge in renewables generation such as wind and solar. While electricity demand grew by 1.8 per cent in July, coal generation fell by 4.2 per cent to 64.3 per cent, down from 68.3 per cent the year before. (Reuters)

Court win for Texas's anti-ESG lawsuit against major financial firms: A Eastern District Court of Texas judge denied an application by US index fund managers BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street to dismiss a lawsuit brought by 10 Republican states that alleged the funds violated federal antitrust law by restricting support for coal companies. Judge Jeremy Kernodle ruled that "at this stage in the proceeding, the court must assume that Plaintiffs' allegations are true", but dismissed three state-based consumer protection claims against BlackRock brought by Louisiana and Nebraska. The November 2024 lawsuit by the states alleged the three funds held significant stakes in nine major publicly traded coal companies, including more than 25 per cent of Peabody Energy, Arch Resources, CONSOL Energy, Alpha Metallurgical Resources, Black Hill Resources and Warrior Met Coal. The lawsuit alleges that the climate policies of the three financial firms reduced coal supply and increased prices, allowing the investors to "produce extraordinary revenue gains". Victor Flatt from Case Western Reserve University said that while the case may still result in a finding that there was no anti-competitive behaviour between the three firms, the decision may "give pause to companies seeking to work together to reduce GHGs [greenhouse gas emissions] in specific industries". (ESG Dive, Eastern District Court of Texas)

South African exporter announces profit slump with fall in global prices: Thungela Resources, South Africa's largest export coal producer, announced it projects an 85 per cent decline in interim profits in the first half of 2025 due to a slump in export thermal coal prices and reduced demand from China and India. Thermal power generation in both China and India has been lower than expected in part due to increased solar and wind generation and lower summer temperatures. Thungela was founded in June 2021 when Anglo American spun off its South African coal projects. The company bought the Enhsam coal mine in Queensland in September 2023 and now owns seven mines and has a 23 per cent stake in the Richards Bay Coal Terminal. The company produced 17.7 million tonnes in 2024. Average prices for coal shipped through the Richards Bay coal terminal have fallen by 14 per cent in the first half of the year, with Australian export prices down 11 per cent. The company will release its half-year results on August 18. (DevilsDiscourse)
