title: CoalWire 576, August 21, 2025
excerpt: US ups demand growth forecast for data centres; Eskom seeks solar deals with industrial customers.
content:
August 22, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

There are many striking parallels between the narratives used to promote ever-expanding fossil fuel supply and use over the last two decades and the hype about Artificial Intelligence (AI). Fossil fuel lobbyists promoted increased coal use as inevitable for decades to come, touted its supposed technical and economic superiority, insisted there were no viable alternatives and downplayed the health, economic and environmental costs. As each buttress to these narratives eroded, the fossil fuel industry became more politically isolated and its growth prospects faltered. 

The sector has now seized on the current boom in data centre proposals as a lifeline to justify prolonging the life of old coal plants and the construction of new fossil fuel plants. RMI challenges these claims. Google, which once backed a 100 per cent clean energy by 2030 target for its operations, has offered its support for the Trump administration's energy agenda.

The US government's Energy Information Administration has upped its electricity demand forecast to account for projections of accelerating AI use and data centre power consumption. New data centres built by tech companies such as Amazon and Microsoft could also push electricity prices higher for other consumers. A new US report highlights the potential economic costs imposed on other consumers by delayed coal closures. Scepticism about the economic viability of many AI companies has become more pronounced in the last few months, with even tech industry boosters warning it could be a bubble about to burst. In such an event, power utilities could end up with a lot of capital invested in stranded or underutilised plants.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Big Tech's AI data centres are driving up electricity bills for everyone

Electricity rates for individuals and small businesses could rise sharply as Amazon, Google, Microsoft and other technology companies build data centres and expand into the energy business, write [gift link] Ivan Penn and Karen Weise in the New York Times.

 

 Reality check: We have what's needed to reliably power the data centre boom, and it's not coal plants

A range of clean, resilient solutions can help us meet the electrical needs of our growing digital economy while saving Americans money, write Gabriella Tosado, Ashtin Massie and Joe Daniel from RMI.

 

 Why Poland is clinging to coal, despite the economic and environmental costs

Although the rhetoric of Poland's most recent governments has differed – the conservative Law and Justice party were more openly coal-friendly, whereas the ruling coalition, at least during the election campaign, presented itself as more climate-conscious – the results have been strikingly similar, writes Alicja Ptak in Notes from Poland.

 

 The growing criminalisation of climate and environmental protests

Driven by a combination of state and corporate actors, the repression of climate and environmental protest is a worldwide phenomenon that takes place across the Global North and South, writes Oscar Berglund from the University of Bristol.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Trump administration delays silica dust rule again: The implementation of the silica dust rule to reduce the risk of black lung disease has been delayed until at least October 17, pending the outcome of negotiations between the National Sand, Stone and Gravel Association (NSSGA), the federal Department of Labor and the Mine Safety and Health Administration. The silica dust rule reduced the allowable level of silica dust exposure for coal miners from 100 micrograms per cubic meter (g/m3) to 50 g/m3 of air during an eight-hour shift. The rule also mandates free medical screenings for workers to detect black lung early. The new standard was finalised in April 2024 and set to come into effect in April 2025. However, the NSSGA launched legal action in the federal court to block the rule, arguing that the compliance costs were too high. The court said the parties to the action will provide an update on settlement discussions on October 10. Recent studies have indicated that up to 20 per cent of coal miners in central Appalachia have black lung disease. (West Virginia Watch)

 

 Explosion on coal ship as it left US port: The US Coast Guard reported an explosion occurred on the W-Sapphire, a bulk carrier loaded with coal, just after it left CSX's coal export terminal in Baltimore. The crew of 23 were uninjured, and the ship returned to an anchorage. Video of the incident revealed an explosion in a forward hold. A US Coast Guard investigation report released in February revealed that an unnamed coal ship had two explosions in forward cargo holds on November 27, 2024, when it was 100 nautical miles off the coast of Virginia. The report suggested the likely case was methane emissions from the coal, combined with poor ventilation and found "highly elevated levels" of methane in five other cargo holds that were "an immediate threat" to the safety of the ship. In a separate development, a CSX coal train of 28 loaded wagons derailed in Enfield, North Carolina, causing Amtrak to cancel 11 passenger services from Miami to New York. (WBALTV, WAMR, WRAL)

 

 Glencore coal mine threatens key koala habitat: Lock the Gate has called on the federal Minister for the Environment, Murray Watt, to suspend consideration of further coal mine projects that affect the habitat of the koala population of the Northern Bowen Basin until a thorough assessment of the area has been completed. In a single night in mid-June, a Lock the Gate survey team using drones equipped with a thermal imaging camera found 13 koalas in trees within the 600 hectares of habitat Glencore wants to clear as part of the proposed expansion of the Hail Creek mine in Queensland. Lock the Gate said that 24 coal projects include plans to clear 10,614 hectares of koala habitat with Whitehaven Coal accounting for two-thirds of the area. University of Queensland ecologist Dr Bill Ellis said the survey findings "confirm that this koala population is likely of national significance". (Guardian, Lock the Gate)

 

 Call for court probe into West Bengal coal project: The Calcutta High Court has asked the West Bengal government to respond within two days to a petition calling for a court-ordered investigation of the Deocha-Pachami-Dewanganj-Harisingha (DPDH) coal mining project in West Bengal. The Ministry of Coal allocated the coal block, one of India's largest, to the West Bengal Power Development Corporation (WBPDCL) a decade ago, triggering sustained community opposition. The project affects 18 villages comprising about 3000 households, with one-third from tribal communities. Residents argue that promises of jobs and compensation for affected families have not been honoured, while tribal communities opposing the project complain of government repression. While the area is estimated to contain a resource of about 2.1 billion tonnes of coal, developing an open-cut coal mine requires the removal of a thick basalt cap. WBPDCL is also investigating the potential for underground coal gasification in areas where mining is considered uneconomic. (The Hindu)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Afghanistan: The state power utility Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat signed a memorandum of understanding with 77 Company and Zularistan for 160 megawatts of new coal capacity.

 

 Australia: The Queensland Government agreed to defer royalties on Adani's Carmichael coal mine in return for the company spending A$50 million (US$32.1 million) to expand the mine and supporting infrastructure. The details of the repayment schedule for royalties are not public.

 

 Australia: Queensland Premier David Crisafulli has rebuffed lobbying by the Queensland Resources Council to lower the coal royalty rate introduced by the former Labor government in 2022.

 

 New Zealand: Two protesters have ended their three-week occupation of coal buckets in an aerial cableway at Bathurst Resources Denniston mine. Bathurst Resources has applied for fast-track approval to expand its mine.

 

 South Africa: After years of delays due to a lack of funding, MC Mining has commenced initial mining at its Makhado open-cut project. The company is aiming to sell 880,000 tonnes of coking coal a year.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

US agency forecasts jump in US electricity demand growth rate: The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) latest Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) estimates US electricity demand could grow by 3 per cent in 2025 and 4.5 per cent in 2026, primarily driven by increasing data centre demand. The EIA's July STEO forecast projected annual electricity demand growth of 2.2 per cent in 2025 and 2026, a significant increase from the 0.8 per cent average electricity demand increase between 2020 and 2024. The EIA's latest forecast estimates that US thermal coal exports could decline by 7 per cent in 2025 to 47 million US short tons (42.6 million tonnes) and fall a further 5 per cent in 2026 to below 45 million US short tons (40.8 million tonnes). The agency estimates US metallurgical coal exports could fall by 13 per cent in 2025 to 50 million US short tons (45.3 million tonnes) and remain near that level in 2026. (US Energy Information Administration)

Google head backed Trump administration's energy agenda: Ruth Porat, the President and Chief Investment Officer of Google and its parent company Alphabet, offered a glowing endorsement of the Trump administration's emphasis on coal, gas and nuclear power to cater for electricity demand for data centres. At the conference, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum criticised the tech industry for its support of a "climate extremist agenda" and extolled the benefits of "incredibly clean" coal plants and supported new gas plants to cater for data centre demand. Porat was asked about Burgum's comments later that day. "I thought Secretary Burgum's comments were fantastic [B]ecause I think it is very clear that to realise the potential of AI, you have to have the power to deliver it," she said in a previously unreported recording of the April conference. In 2020, Google pledged to source all of its electricity from carbon-free projects by 2030. Google did not respond to questions on Porat's comments. (DeSmog)

Delayed closure of US fossil fuel plants could cost consumers billions: An analysis by energy consultancy Grid Strategies estimates that electricity consumers could pay between US$3.1 billion and US$5.9 billion a year if the US Department of Energy blocks the retirement of all coal and gas plants scheduled to close before the end of 2028. Grid Strategies estimates that 115 units across 54 plants with a combined capacity of 34.9 gigawatts (GW) could close by the end of 2028, covering the term of President Donald Trump. The study estimates that a Trump administration mandate to keep plants open could increase electricity costs "by tens if not hundreds of millions of dollars per year in most states". Earthjustice, Environmental Defense, NRDC and the Sierra Club commissioned the study. (Earthjustice, Grid Strategies [Pdf])

Eskom seeks solar agreements with major industrial customers: Eskom, South Africa's state-owned power utility, has issued a request for proposals from major industrial customers for 291 MW of solar capacity commissioned after December 2027. The utility is offering power purchase agreements of between 5 and 25 years and aims to build an in-house renewables business with 2 gigawatts (GW) of permitted projects by 2027 and 32 GW by 2040. The announcement comes as the government moves to split Eskom into three separate businesses - generation, transmission and distribution. A 2023 government bailout of Eskom was conditional on the utility not taking on new debt on generation projects. South Africa currently has about 14 GW of installed wind and solar capacity, comprising about 6 GW contracted through the government's scheme for independent power producers and 7 GW of rooftop solar. Anton Eberhard from the University of Cape Town noted that South Africa needs to deliver clean energy to attract foreign investment from major companies. "These agreements enable businesses to align with global sustainability standards, reduce carbon footprints, and green their supply chains, enhancing competitiveness," Eskom stated in its announcement. (Financial Post, Eskom, Energy Intelligence)

Peabody Energy abandons deal to buy Anglo American coal mines: Peabody Energy announced it has terminated its November 2024 agreement to buy coal mines in Queensland from Anglo American. The US$3.78 billion agreement to purchase the mines had been scheduled to take effect in April 2025, but a major fire on March 31 shuttered the Moranbah North mine. The mine was intended to produce 5.3 million US short tons (4.8 million tonnes) of metallurgical coal in 2025. Peabody said the mine costs about US$45 million per month in its current state and that there is "no timetable for the resumption of longwall production at forecasted volumes and costs". Anglo American said that it intends to seek damages for wrongful termination of the agreement and is progressing approvals to resume operations at the Moranbah North mine. As part of the original deal, Peabody reached a separate side agreement to sell the Dawson Mine to Indonesian company PT Bukit Makmur Mandiri Utama. Peabody has also cancelled that agreement. Through the purchase of the Anglo American mines, Peabody aimed to boost its role in metallurgical coal exports and expand its operations outside the US market. Peabody currently has five metallurgical coal and three thermal coal mines in Australia. It also has one metallurgical coal mine in Alabama in the US, as well as three major thermal coal mines in the Powder River Basin and six smaller projects. The company's total coal production in 2024 was 118 million US short tons (107 million tonnes). (Mining.com, Peabody Energy, Anglo American)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 POSCO eyes Indian steel plant as NGOs warn banks over Korean mills: POSCO, the world's eighth-largest steel producer, announced a heads of agreement with JSW Steel to establish a 6 million tonnes a year steelworks in the northeastern state of Odisha in India. The South Korean company, which produced almost 38 million tonnes of steel in 2024, said the next step will be a feasibility study to determine the proposed site. In October 2024, POSCO announced a memorandum of understanding to establish a 50:50 joint venture project with JSW Steel for the development of Indian steel projects. In a separate development, a coalition of 21 NGOs has urged 17 major banks to reject any involvement in financing POSCO's proposed relining of two coal-based blast furnaces at steelworks in South Korea at Pohang and Gwangyang. BankTrack and Solutions for Our Climate estimate that the life extension of the blast furnaces could emit 137 million tonnes of carbon dioxide over a 15-year life, delay the transition to steel production using electric arc furnaces, and contradict the banks' climate policies. (POSCO, BankTrack [Pdf])

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Power corrupts: Cleaning up America's biggest industry, Bloomsbury Publishing, June 2025. (Hardcover US$45; Ebook US$36.)

In this 192-page book, author Richard Munson argues that as new technologies have undermined the business model of US power utilities, some have resorted to underhanded schemes to extract taxpayer and ratepayer-funded subsidies for coal and nuclear plants.

links.text: Power corrupts: Cleaning up America’s biggest industry

title: CoalWire 577, August 28, 2025
excerpt: US city bans coal storage after 2029; Canadian coal company fined over coal dust pollution.
content:
August 28, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

In a surprise win for residents of Portland, Maine, the city council voted to ban all transport and storage of more than a ton of coal within the city after December 2029. There are mixed signals on the energy transition elsewhere in the US. The US Energy Information Administration estimates 2025 will be a boom year for new utility solar projects and the deployment of batteries. However, the Trump administration's recent policy changes do not augur well for the sector. In the last week, the administration has moved to fast-track a new coal lease on federal lands in Montana, renewed an order extending the life of a retiring coal plant, and blocked the construction of a nearly complete wind farm off the off the coast of Rhode Island.

There are similar competing trends in China. The recent surge in solar capacity has helped drive power sector emissions lower, but China continues to build and approve new coal plants, as well as expand the coal-to-chemicals sector. As anticipated, the rate of solar installation has slowed after recent policy changes, but there may be a silver lining to this cloud. A new report reveals the rapid increase in sales of Chinese solar panels across Africa.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Fire still burning for custodians in fight against mine

Wangan and Jagalingou custodian Gurridyula Gaba Wunggu has kept a sacred fire burning since the group reoccupied their homelands at the Adani Carmichael coal mine in 2021, writes Keira Jenkins in the National Indigenous Times.

 

 As mining companies write their own rules, people pay the price

Canada is letting coal mining companies off the hook for polluting British Columbia and Alberta watersheds with selenium, writes Lorne Fitch, a past adjunct professor and biologist with the University of Calgary, in The Tyee.

 

 'Hopelessly insolvent': how 'saviour of steel' Sanjeev Gupta's global empire unravelled

Last week, the High Court of Justice in London ruled that Speciality Steel UK, a key subsidiary of Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Group, was "hopelessly insolvent" and should enter compulsory liquidation. It is a decision that reverberated through Gupta's global empire of steel and coal operations, write Jasper Jolly and Jonathan Barrett in The Guardian.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 US city orders coal storage to be removed by 2030: The Portland City Council voted to require all coal that is transported or stored within the city to be stored under a "permanent covering" as of January 1, 2027. The council also voted to ban the transport or storage of more than one ton (907 kilograms) of coal in the city in Maine from December 31, 2029. Residents campaigned for the closure of the open-air coal stockpile at Sprague Energy's Cassidy Point terminal and had proposed a referendum on the coal phase-out ordinance later this year. Instead, the council voted to adopt the ordinance. Sprague Energy supplies about 40,000 tons (36,287 tonnes) of thermal coal a year to the Nine Dragons Paper Company's pulp and paper mill in Rumford. (Maine Public, Portland City Council [Pdf])

 

 Chinese solar drives decline in power sector emissions: Carbon dioxide emissions from China's power sector fell by three per cent in the first half of 2025 in response to the 212 gigawatts (GW) surge in solar installations. However, analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) suggests new coal plant capacity could increase by between 80 GW and 100 GW this year. CREA notes a 20 per cent increase in the amount of coal processed for synthetic fuels and chemicals in the first half of the year, a sector that has added three per cent to China's annual greenhouse gas emissions since 2020. Coal use in the power industry fell by 3.4 per cent in the first half of the year. (Carbon Brief)

 

 New Chinese coal power capacity hits a nine-year high: An analysis reveals that China commissioned 21 GW of new coal power capacity in the first half of 2025, the highest amount completed in the last nine years. The report by CREA and Global Energy Monitor estimates more than 80 GW of new coal capacity will be commissioned in 2025. The report estimates that construction commenced on 46 GW of new coal power projects in the first half of the year, with permits granted for another 25 GW. The recent surge in new solar and wind projects pushed the share of coal generation down to a nine-year low of 51 per cent. Only 1 GW of coal capacity was retired in the first half of the year, well short of the 14th Five-Year Plan goal of retiring 30 GW by the end of 2025. (Deutsche Welle, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Trump administration orders utility to keep operating Michigan coal plant: The Department of Energy (DOE) issued an emergency order directing the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) and Consumers Energy to continue operating the 1.42 GW J. H. Campbell coal plant in Michigan until November 10. Consumers Energy had scheduled the plant to close in May, but the DOE ordered it to remain online until August 21. Consumers Energy revealed that it cost US$29 million to keep the plant operating over 38 days in May and June 2025. A consultancy report by energy consultancy Grid Strategies, commissioned by the Sierra Club and other NGOs, estimated that it could cost approximately US$140 million per year to keep the plant operating. The Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel and a separate coalition of advocacy groups have filed legal challenges against the DOE's first emergency order. Days before DOE's latest order, the US Bureau of Ocean Energy Management directed Orsted to cease all work on the 80 per cent complete 704 MW Revolution Wind project off the coast of Rhode Island. (Utility Dive, Sierra Club, Department of Energy, Guardian)

 

 Canadian coal company fined over coal dust pollution: British Columbia's Ministry of Environment and Parks has fined Conuma Resources C$13,000 (US$9391) for breaching provincial dust emission standards 32 times over 18 months in 2023 and 2024 at its Brule metallurgical coal mine in north-eastern British Columbia. The standard for total particulate emissions compliance is a maximum concentration of 1.75 milligrams per decimetre squared per day, averaged over a month. Acting as the Director of the Environmental Management Act, Stephanie Little, found that Conuma Resources exceeded the limit by between 4 per cent and 375 per cent. In her decision, she wrote that 19 of the 32 breaches exceeded the allowable limit by more than 50 per cent. In June 2024, the ministry fined Conuma Resources C$45,850 (approximately US$33,430) for violating environmental regulations between 2020 and 2023 at the mine. The ministry found that the company breached the requirement to monitor water emissions into fish-bearing streams on 406 occasions between October 21, 2020, and January 1, 2023, and had failed to submit monthly reports, water quality monitoring data, and C$4750 (US$3,465) for excessive dust emissions. (Business in Vancouver, Government of British Columbia)

 

 Alberta regulator cancels public hearing on coal mining plan: The CEO of the Alberta Energy Regulator (AER), Rob Morgan, a former oil and gas executive, cancelled an October 21 public hearing on Summit Coal's proposed Mine 14 near Grande Cache. Summit Coal, a subsidiary of the Australian company Valory Resources, has proposed the development of an underground mine that would produce approximately 1.3 million tonnes of metallurgical coal annually for up to 15 years. Morgan's decision to cancel a hearing approved by commissioners reflects the opposition by Summit Coal to a public forum on the mining plan and its impacts. The Alberta Wilderness Association and the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society said Morgan's decision sets a precedent where companies opposed to a public hearing on a mining project "can avoid the process altogether". (Globe and Mail [paywall], Alberta Wilderness Association, Alberta Energy Regulator [Pdf])

 

 South African opposition challenges legality of coal mine in reserve: The Democratic Alliance (DA), the main opposition party in the South African parliament, has written to the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Minister, Gwede Mantashe, urging his department direct Baobab Mining and Exploration to suspend work on the proposed Makhado metallurgical coal project. The proposed mine is in the Vhembe Biosphere Reserve. The DA argues that, under the National Environmental Management Act, a legal appeal lodged in June 2021 against the environmental authorisation for the project suspends the approval. It also argues that the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act requires all mines to have a valid environmental authorisation. The Gauteng High Court has not decided on the appeal. Baobab Mining and Exploration is a subsidiary of the Australian-headquartered MC Mining. The company stated that it holds all required permits. (Mining Weekly, Democratic Alliance, MC Mining)

 

 
 "Industry can't capture enough selenium to meet meaningful standards, but it has captured the provincial government,"

writes Lorne Fitch, a past adjunct professor and biologist with the University of Calgary.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Bangladesh: Yongtai Energy, a Chinese energy company, has called for an investigation into the coal procurement process for the 1.32 GW Patuakhali coal plant operated by a joint venture of Rural Power Company and NORINCO International.

 

 China: Seven coal miners died in an accident at Fujian Guangfeng Mining's underground Shuijingkeng mine in Fujian province.

 

 Germany: RWE has commissioned the 34.2 megawatts (MW) Aldenhoven wind farm on part of the Inden lignite mine.

 

 Poland: JSW has received approval to extend the operation of the Borynia coking coal mine until 2042. The concession contains an estimated 40 million tonnes of coking coal and 80 million cubic meters of methane.

 

 Romania: The European Commission has approved a proposal for state-owned power utility CE Oltenia to shift its lignite power plants and mines slated for closure into a separate subsidiary.

 

 South Africa: Civil society groups have called on the South African government to ban coal exports to Israel.

 

 US: A mine worker died in an accident at Marfork Coal's processing plant in West Virginia.

 

 US: A US Bankruptcy Court judge has approved a liquidation application by White Forest Resources. South Fork Coal Company, a subsidiary, has ceased mining operations at its Rocky Run Surface Mine in West Virginia.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

US solar sector booms: The US Energy Information Administration estimates that 33 GW of utility-scale solar could be commissioned in 2025, just over half of the 64 GW of new generation capacity likely to be added. The current record for new generation capacity is 58 GW added in 2022, of which 57 GW was gas capacity. The EIA estimated that 12 GW of solar was added in the first half of the year, with just over one-quarter of that in Texas. After solar, 5.9 GW of battery storage was added in the US in the first half of the year, with about 19 GW estimated for the whole year. New wind capacity, however, is languishing, with a forecast of about 7.9 GW in 2025. The EIA stated that 600 MW of coal-generating capacity was retired in the first half of the year, with an additional 5.6 GW likely to close in the remainder of 2025. (US Energy Information Administration)

Saskatchewan budgets to keep old lignite plants operating: The Saskatchewan government has allocated C$900-million (US$650 million) over four years to refurbish SaskPower's three ageing lignite plants. This will allow their operation beyond the federal government's 2030 coal phase-out deadline. SaskPower's three plants, the Shand, Poplar River and Boundary Dam power stations, have a combined capacity of 1.6 GW. In June, the Saskatchewan government announced its intention to defy the federal regulation phasing out coal generation and extend the life of the lignite plants until the completion of a small modular reactor or conventional nuclear plant in the 2030s. SaskPower Minister Jeremy Harrison recently stated that the primary driver for the decision was energy security through the utilisation of a local energy resource, rather than converting the plants to run on gas imported from the US and Alberta. In 2024-25, SaskPower sourced less than one per cent of its electricity from solar and 10 per cent from wind generation. Coal accounted for a 24 per cent of SaskPowers electricity, with gas generation holding a 41 per cent share. (Globe and Mail [paywall])

Serbian utility forced to self-finance new lignite mine: International banks have refused to finance the construction of the Radljevo lignite mine, according to Dusan Zivkovic, the general manager of Serbia's state-owned power utility, Elektroprivreda Srbije (EPS). Zivkovic said EPS will finance the construction of the new mine from internal funds. Funding for the new mine is one of the factors contributing to a 16.6 per cent decline in profits to 233.8 million in the first half of 2025, compared to the same period the year before. The new mine is to supply lignite for the 350 MW B3 unit at the Kostolac power station, which came online in December 2024. (Balkan Green Energy News, Global Energy Monitor)

US agency accelerates approval of new Powder River Basin lease: The Bureau of Land Management issued a 43-page final environmental impact statement for the Navajo Transitional Energy Company's (NTEC) proposed West Antelope III coal lease. NTEC's lease application covers about 3500 acres and is estimated to contain about 441 million US short tons (400 million tonnes) of thermal coal and could extend the life of the current Antelope mine by a decade. Cloud Peak Energy applied for the lease in August 2015 but entered bankruptcy in May 2015. NTEC bought Antelope Coal in March 2021 and requested the revival of the lease application. BLM will hold a public hearing on the project on September 3 in Wright, Montana. In early August, the Department of the Interior approved an extension of the West Antelope II mine to access an additional 14.5 million US short tons (13.1 million tonnes) of coal on federal land. (WyoFile, Bureau of Land Management)

India has launched a new round of coal block auctions. The Ministry of Coal has initiated the auction of 14 new coal blocks, including four in each of Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh, and three in Jharkhand. The ministry said that 10 of the coal blocks are full explored and ready for "immediate development". That latest auction also includes three coal blocks that failed to sell in earlier auctions, with one in each of Odisha, Jharkhand and Madhya Pradesh. (Ministry of Coal [Pdf], MSTC [Pdf], MSTC [Pdf])

Indonesia abandons floor price for coal exports: The Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources has abandoned the requirement for exporters to sell coal at or above a government-determined benchmark price. Earlier this year, the Minister for Energy, Bahlil Lahadalia, promulgated a regulation setting an official floor price that would be revised twice a month. Coal exporters and lobby groups, including the China Coal Transportation and Distribution Association, opposed the floor price, arguing that it was a less responsive to market conditions and set a price higher than justified. While the August 8 decree will leave exporters free to negotiate the sale price, the government will retain the benchmark price for royalties and taxation purposes. (Reuters, Mining.com)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Indian court seeks advice on options with coal-based sponge iron plants: The National Green Tribunal (NGT), India's environmental law court, has requested the Indian Institute of Technology-Kharagpur provide advice about a petitioner's request to reduce pollution from coal-based rotary kilns used in India's sponge iron sector. In 2024, India produced approximately 51 million tonnes of sponge iron. The petitioner is seeking an order to direct a shift to the use of cleaner technologies to reduce greenhouse gas and other emissions. The court requested IIT-Kharagpur's report within eight weeks. (New Indian Express, Down to Earth)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Decarbonising China's cement industry, Climate Analytics, August 2025. (Pdf)

This 109-page report reviews policies and regulations adopted in the European Union and Germany to cut greenhouse gas emissions from cement production and recommends measures for China's sector.

The first evidence of a take-off in solar in Africa, Ember, August 2025. (Pdf)

This report analyses Africa's imports of Chinese solar panels. The report notes a 60 per cent increase in solar panel imports to Africa in the year to June 2025. The report estimates that 25 countries in Africa imported about 15 GW of solar panels.

links.text: The first evidence of a take-off in solar in Africa

title: CoalWire 578, September 4, 2025
excerpt: Canadian regulator upholds C$800,000 fine; Korea drops probe into Indonesian coal plant bribe.
content:
September 4, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Anglo American, one of the world's largest mining companies, boasts on its website that it wants to "contribute to a healthy environment, create thriving communities and build trust as a corporate leader". However, a new ruling has revealed that an Anglo American subsidiary in Canada knowingly breached selenium emissions standards year after year at a mothballed metallurgical coal mine. The company then brazenly claimed it shouldn't be fined and argued that the C$810,000 (US$589,000) penalty was excessive. It is worth bearing in mind that a single mine haul truck costs several times more than that penalty.

In India, a new report found that cases brought by local communities exposed to pollution from coal plants to the National Green Tribunal rarely result in significant improvements on the ground. In the US, a new study reviewing air pollution data from the boundaries of coke and steel plants found many breached regulatory standards. In Australia, a new study found high levels of methane emissions from an unsealed coal exploration drill hole. There are likely to be 130,000 more drill holes in Queensland coal basins with an unknown number remaining unsealed.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 The biggest miner held on to its coal for too long

BHP faces rising costs and falling demand as coking coal loses ground to cheaper, cleaner steelmaking alternatives, writes David Fickling in Bloomberg.

 

 China and India account for 87 per cent of new coal-power capacity so far in 2025

China and India accounted for 87 per cent of the new coal-power capacity put into operation in the first half of 2025, whereas other regions continued to move away from coal, write Christine Shearer and Lucy Hummer from Global Energy Monitor in Carbon Brief.

 

 Censured Sumatra coal plant blamed for sickening children in Indonesia's Bengkulu

Residents and civil society groups blame respiratory illnesses experienced in the local communities on pollution from the 200 MW PT Tenaga Listrik Bengkulu coal plant in Indonesia operated by PowerChina, writes Elviza Diana in Mongabay.

 

 Trump, with tariffs and threats, tries to strong-arm nations to retreat on climate goals

President Trump is not only working to stop a transition away from fossil fuels in the United States, he is pressuring other countries to relax their pledges to fight climate change and instead burn more oil, gas and coal, writes Lisa Friedman in the New York Times.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Canadian regulator rejects appeal by Anglo American subsidiary: British Columbia's Environmental Appeal Board has dismissed an appeal by Peace River Coal (PRC) against a C$809,700 (US$589,000) penalty imposed in September 2021 for excessive selenium pollution. The penalty was imposed for breaches of selenium discharge limits between 2016 and 2019 from the mothballed Trend-Roman metallurgical coal mine. PRC, a subsidiary of Anglo American, was also penalised for failing to submit mandatory quarterly and annual reports. The original decision found that at one mine site, PRC breached weekly selenium discharge limits for all of 2016, 2017, and 2018, as well as in 42 of 52 weeks in 2019. The company did not dispute that it had breached permit standards for selenium, but argued against any penalty or, alternatively, that the fine was excessive. The company did not challenge that it had failed to submit the required reports. Maureen Baird, the chair of the board's appeal panel, stated the penalty was large in order to "satisfy the goals of encouraging compliance and deterring others". In 2023, the Ministry of Environment notified PRC that it faces a separate C$4.4 million (US$3.2 million) penalty for other breaches of selenium emission standards. (Business in Vancouver, Environmental Appeal Board [Pdf])

 

 US court blocks Duke Energy bid to pass coal ash costs on to customers: The Indiana Court of Appeals has overturned an Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission decision allowing Duke Energy to recover approximately US$88 million from customers for coal ash management costs between 2019 and 2023 and US$238 million for projected costs between 2024 and 2030. Duke Energy argued customers should pay for the costs of complying with Environmental Protection Agency coal ash management rules adopted in 2015. The appeals court ruled in favour of the Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana that Duke Energy could not retrospectively charge customers for the expenses and directed the commission to reconsider or dismiss Duke Energy's application. In Indiana, Duke Energy operates the 3.34 GW of coal capacity at the Gibson Generating Station, 1.06 GW of coal units at the Cayuga Generating Station and the 804 MW Edwardsport plant. (Indiana Capital Chronicle)

 

 Study finds little redress for Indian communities hit by coal pollution: A study by Vikalp Social Organisation of eight coal-related cases before India's National Green Tribunal found a lack of effective implementation of court rulings to mitigate damage from coal operations, with compensation awarded to individuals or communities often stayed by higher courts. In only one case had the affected community received any compensation. In most cases, the court ordered measures to mitigate the impacts on communities and appointed an expert committee to develop a detailed remediation plan. However, implementation of measures is often delegated to regulators or committees. The report argued that while strict enforcement of measures could reduce the pollution impacts of coal plants on local communities, a critical element is strengthening regulatory agencies and involving local communities in ensuring the implementation of measures. (Outlook India, Down to Earth, Vikalp Social Organisation [Pdf])

 

 Study finds major methane link from coal exploration drill holes: University of Queensland researchers found that a single coal exploration drill hole in the Surat Basin in Queensland vented about 235 tonnes of methane in a year. The researchers set up a trailer-based sensor in a farm paddock to continuously monitor emissions from a single drill hole over seven days and six nights in variable weather conditions. The monitoring project was the first long-term assessment of methane emissions from a coal exploration drill hole in Australia. The authors estimate the hole has been leaking methane for about 20 years. A 2014 study by the Australian government estimated that there were about 130,000 abandoned exploration drill holes in the Surat and Bowen basins. In the study published in the journal Science of the Total Environment, Associate Professor Phil Hayes and Dr Sebastian Hoerning note that it is unknown how many of the wells in the state are adequately sealed. They state that the study demonstrates the need for a larger sample of exploration drill holes "to understand the frequency and rates of emissions, to investigate emissions from other holes, such as water bores, and further investigation of emission dynamics considering geological characteristics and nearby activities". (Guardian, Science of the Total Environment)

 

 South Korean agency drops investigation into Hyundai bribe in Indonesia: The Seoul Central District Prosecutors' Office announced that it has abandoned the investigation of Hyundai under the International Anti-Bribery Act for paying 550 million won (US$395,000) to win a US$727 million construction contract for the 924 MW Cirebon 2 coal plant in Indonesia. The prosecutor said the investigation confirmed company employees paid bribes to the local governor, who sought 1.7 billion won (US$1.22 million) to suppress protests by residents and civil society groups. The prosecutor said it was difficult to establish the 'intent to obtain undue advantage' under the International Anti-Bribery Act, stating that the company had no choice other than to pay the bribes to ensure the safety of its staff. The Indonesian Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) successfully prosecuted the former Cirebon regent, Sunjaya Purwadi Sastra, who received six bribes from Hyundai. In July, the Indonesian Supreme Court upheld his conviction. Hyundai initially insisted it had not paid bribes but, in 2019, confirmed a broker made the payments. (The Chosun Daily)

 

 US mine manager pleads guilty to operating mine while fire burned: Timothy Parsons, the former manager of Foresight Energy's underground MC #1 Mine in Illinois, has pleaded guilty to conspiring to cover up an underground fire. The Department of Justice stated that, following the initial efforts to extinguish a fire ignited by a cutting torch on August 12, 2021, Parsons and others failed to activate the firefighting and evacuation plan and notify the US Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA). Instead, mining continued over three shifts along with "ad hoc firefighting efforts" until MSHA ordered the mine evacuated after receiving an anonymous tip-off about the fire. In the following days, mine officials secretly entered the mine twice to "assess the fire and manipulate the conditions underground so that MSHA would allow mining to resume". Foresight Energy operates three coal mines in the Illinois Basin. (Kentucky Lantern, US Department of Justice)

 

 
 "PRC [Peace River Coal, a subsidiary of Anglo American] was aware it was not in compliance with the permit from 2017 and the continuous nature of the exceedances over the three-year period in 2017, 2018 and 2019 suggests that in the absence of regulatory action there was no urgency for PRC to become compliant,"

wrote Maureen Baird, the chair of the British Columbia Environmental Appeal Board in a decision rejecting the company's argument it should not be penalised for breaching selenium emission standards.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Bangladesh: The state-owned Coal Power Generation Company rejected a 63,300 tonne shipment of Indonesian coal imported for the 1200 MW Matabari coal plant. The utility stated that the cargo was contaminated with mud and numerous stones, including some weighing up to 30 kg.

 

 Estawini: The Minister for Commerce, Industry, and Trade, Manqoba Khumalo, stated that Japan has expressed interest in sourcing metallurgical coal from Estawini. Metallurgical coal exports from Estawini have declined due to a downturn in South Africa's steel and other energy-intensive industries.

 

 Germany: The Federal Network Agency announced [German] that, as Germany has already exceeded its 2028 target of reducing coal capacity by 8.7 GW, it will not order the shutdown of additional capacity this year.

 

 India: The MP Power Management Company, a Madhya Pradesh state-owned utility, has awarded contracts to Torrent Power for the construction of a 1600 MW coal plant and another to Adani Power for an 800 MW coal plant.

 

 Philippines: The cash-strapped South Korean utility KEPCO announced it plans to sell its 60 per cent stake in SPC Power Corporation, which owns and operates the 221 MW Naga power station in Cebu province.

 

 Romania: The Romanian Minister for Energy, Bogdan Ivan, said the government wants to amend its National Recovery and Resilience Plan to delay the closure of the remaining coal plants from 2025 to 2030.

 

 US: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin signed an agreement approving Wyoming's coal combustion residuals (CCR) program. The plan is open for public comment for 60 days. If approved, it will be the fifth state coal ash management plan approved by the EPA.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

China imposes restrictions on coal production: An official from China Coal Energy, the country's third-largest coal producer, told analysts last week that the government has imposed production limits to prevent a further decline in domestic coal prices. Chinese coal production increased by about 5 per cent in the first half of the year compared to 2024, with prices falling by up to 30 per cent in some parts of the country by the end of June. Mysteel, a consultancy firm, stated that 54 of 153 coking coal mines in Shanxi, with a combined production capacity of 61 million tonnes, have either halted or are curtailing production. Shanxi is the largest coal-producing province in China. In its report to investors on the first half of 2025, China Shenhua said that it expects the growth of coal production will slow in the remainder of the year and imports to decline. (Reuters, China Shenhua [Pdf])

Report finds explosion at Queensland coal unit due to poor management: A report into the failure of state-owned CS Energy's 460 MW Unit 3 at the Callide coal plant found that the collapse of a large piece of hardened ash into the furnace ash system caused an incident that "posed a credible risk of serious harm". There were no injuries from the incident, but the report stated that the fall of the hardened ash, known as clinker, triggered a series of events that resulted in an explosion "that exceeded the boiler's design threshold" and "caused notable equipment damage". The unit was offline for repairs from April 4 to June 1, 2025. The investigation also found that equipment used to dislodge clinker during normal operations was faulty and noted poor coal quality monitoring and control processes. Just days after the explosion at Unit 3, the conservative Queensland government announced plans to delay the closure of Units 1 and 2 from 2028 until 2031. The Queensland Conservation Council (QCC) stated that delaying the closure of the increasingly unreliable units would cost taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars. QCC wants the government to prioritise new renewables backed by storage. (Renew Economy, CS Energy [Pdf], Queensland Conservation Council)

Declining export coal prices hit Russian producers: Russian coal producers suffered a combined loss of US$2.3 billion in the first half of 2025, according to data released by Rosstat, the government statistics agency. The agency estimates that two-thirds of Russian coal companies recorded losses so far this year, and the Ministry of Energy estimates that up to 27 coal companies are facing bankruptcy. A sharp decline in the price of exported coal, a stronger rouble against the US dollar and international sanctions have combined to undermine the viability of major mining companies. Mechel informed investors that revenue fell by 26 per cent in the first half of the year to 206 billion roubles (US$2.6 billion) and reported a net loss of 40.5 billion roubles (US$460 million), more than double the loss recorded in the first half of 2024. The company stated that its coal business "came under serious pressure" due to falling coking coal prices and an oversupplied market. Mechel said that it has decided to suspend production of "unprofitable types of products", but has not provided details. In July, the Finance Ministry announced that companies could defer royalty payments until the end of November and tax debts incurred before June 1, 2025. (The Moscow Times [Russian], The Insider, Mechel [Russian])

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Report finds US coking plants breach air pollution limits: A report by the Environmental Integrity Project (EIP) found that 17 out of 20 US steel-related plants it reviewed violated Clean Air Act standards at some point in the last three years and that 10 were continuously noncompliant. EIP reviewed fenceline air monitoring data of plants in Alabama, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. The group found that US Steel's Clairton Coke Works in Pennsylvania reported a six-month average benzene level eight times California's threshold for long-term exposure, and the Gary Works steel mill in Indiana reported a six-month average concentration of chromium that was more than twice the California standard. In mid-2024, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) amended the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants to require the monitoring of emissions at the plant's fenceline, with the changes scheduled to take effect on July 7, 2025. In response to steel industry lobbying, the Trump administration has extended the compliance deadline for coking plants by two years. In early July, the EPA delayed the new emissions standards for iron and steelworks by two years. (Canary Media, Environmental Integrity Project)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

The Northern Sea Route: Russia's industrial and political expansion, its environmental costs, and Arctic shipping risks, Bellona Foundation, July 2025. (Pdf)

This 74-page report reviews the environmental and political risks associated with Russia's promotion of the Northern Sea Route along the Arctic coast. In 2024, exporters shipped 316,000 tonnes of coal via the route.

links.text: The Northern Sea Route: Russia’s industrial and political expansion, its environmental costs, and Arctic shipping risks

title: CoalWire 580, September 18, 2025
excerpt: Solar surge in Hungary and Poland; Indian pollution control suppliers call for pollution policy change.
content:
September 18, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The latest government data shows Chinese manufacturers have produced 550 gigawatts (GW) of solar capacity in the year to date, with August production up by almost a fifth on a year ago. China's prodigious solar production capacity is not only reshaping the domestic power sector but is also underpinning rapid shifts in the renewable capacity of many countries. A new report by the climate think tank Ember highlights the dramatic increase in solar capacity in Hungary and Poland and the corresponding decline in coal generation. Another report outlines the extensive overseas investments of Chinese companies in new energy technologies and materials. While Germany was a global pioneer of the solar sector, the new conservative government is pondering slowing down the transition to renewables and keeping coal plants operating longer until new gas plants are available. 

A new report by the Global Climate and Health Alliance highlights the profound health impacts of pollution from fossil fuel production and burning. In the Philippines, a news report tracks a family that moved to avoid COVID-19 infection risks only to encounter the effects of pollution from two coal plants and other industrial facilities. In India, major flue gas desulphurisation equipment suppliers are lobbying the government to reverse its recent decision to exempt most coal units from a decade-old standard to cut sulphur dioxide emissions.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 The clean coal myth

Arguments that the dirtiest of fossil fuels can be transformed into something clean and sustainable only betray the coal industry's desperation, writes Tracey Davies, the executive director of Just Share, a South African NGO, in Business Live.

 

 Mining companies leave many Queensland farmers' land barren and broken. When they go belly up, who pays for rehabilitation?

The failure of Bowen Coking Coal, which is now in receivership, to rehabilitate the Bluff coal mine in Queensland highlights the broader problem of the increasing area of unrehabilitated mined land, writes Joe Hinchcliffe in The Guardian.

 

 'It's not safe here anymore': Life in a small Philippine coal town

Teresa Calion moved with her asthmatic father to Kiragon in Mindanao in 2021, in the expectation that cleaner air and a smaller population would keep him safe from COVID-19. Now she fears two nearby coal plants have caused his increased asthma attacks, write by Carmela S. Fonbuena and Bobby Lagsa for the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Solar surge in central Europe displacing coal and gas: Solar power generation in the Central European countries of the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia has surged from 5 terawatt hours (TWh) to 29 TWh over five years to the end of 2024. The almost six times increase in solar generation compares to the 2.5 times growth across the European Union over the period. Solar generation in Hungary has nearly doubled over the past five years and now accounts for almost one-quarter of the country's electricity. Over the same period, the share of coal generation in Hungary fell from 12 per cent to 6 per cent, with gas generation declining from 25 per cent to 19 per cent. In Poland, coal generation fell by almost 19 per cent, while solar and wind generation increased by eight and five per cent, respectively, over the five years. In the Czech Republic, coal's share in power generation fell by 7 per cent, but the increase in solar generation increased by just 2.8 per cent over the five years. (CEEnergy News, Ember)

 

 German government looks to soften coal transition goals: A report commissioned by the Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy has recommended significant changes to policies supporting a transition away from coal power generation, including slowing the growth of renewables to a level "we actually need" to reach 80 per cent of electricity consumption by 2030. The review was a commitment of the April 2025 coalition agreement between the conservative Christian Democratic Union, the Christian Social Union and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The energy policy review estimates electricity demand will decline, recommends the abolition of solar feed-in tariffs, backs the introduction of a capacity market and supports a faster rollout of smart meters. Agora Energiewende, an energy think tank, said slowing the growth of renewables to match lower electricity demand would send the wrong signal to businesses. Greenpeace said the government was ignoring the economic and other costs of global heating and wanted to use a narrow focus on energy transition costs as a way to justify weakening current policy measures. Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently flagged reducing clean energy rollout and delaying the closure of further coal capacity until the commissioning of new gas plants. Legislation passed in 2020 set a deadline for phasing out coal generation by the end of 2038, with the previous coalition government aiming to bring the deadline forward to 2030 if possible. (Clean Energy Wire, Argus)

 

 Documents reveal long-term pollution from Queensland coal mine: Documents released to Local the Gate under freedom of information legislation revealed that BHP likely knew for up to 15 years that its Blackwater mine was polluting environmentally sensitive waterways before taking action. The documents reveal that a 2022 Queensland Environment Department compliance report found that a review of satellite imagery suggested long-term sediment pollution of adjoining land and creeks in the Fitzroy River Basin that ultimately flow into the Great Barrier Reef Lagoon. The report said "it is reasonable to expect that BHP Coal was aware of these releases". BHP commenced remediation work after a warning was issued in 2022. In April 2024, BHP Mitsubishi Alliance sold the Blackwater metallurgical coal mine to Whitehaven Coal. However, following an anonymous tip-off to Lock the Gate, the environment department initiated another site investigation that found the problem remained. The department issued a warning to Whitehaven. BHP is one of the world's largest private mining companies and plans expansions of the Peak Downs, Saraji East and Caval Ridge mines. (ABC News, Lock the Gate)

 

 US utility lobbying for more money for 70-year-old coal plants: American Electric Power (AEP) is seeking Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) approval for an "accounting deferral" that would authorise the recovery of an additional US$35 million from Ohio consumers for losses incurred on two 1955 vintage coal plants. PUCO staff, the Ohio Consumers' Counsel, the Ohio Environmental Council, and the Ohio Manufacturers' Association all oppose the proposal. Earlier this year, the Ohio legislature revoked legislated subsidies to Ohio Valley Electric Corporation (OVEC) for the 1303 MW Clifty Creek plant in Indiana and the 1086 MW Kyger Creek coal plant in Ohio. OVEC is a joint venture between AEP, Duke Energy and AES Ohio. Last year, West Virginia regulators refused permission to charge consumers above-market rates to cover the costs of the two plants. An analysis of Synapse Energy Economics data by West Virginia Public Broadcasting suggested that customers in West Virginia and Virginia are currently paying tens of millions a year more for power from the two plants supplied by AEP under long-term contracts to Appalachian Power. Devi Glick from Synapse Energy Economics said AEP is trying to keep charging for the plants for "as long as they're allowed to". (Signal, Louisville Public Media)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 India: Congress leader Jairam Ramesh accused the Adani Group of clearing forested land in breach of the Forest Rights Act for the Dhirauli coal mine in Madhya Pradesh.

 

 Pakistan: President Asif Ali Zardari attended the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between MFTC Coal Gasification & Manufacturing and a consortium of Sino Sindh Resources and Shanghai Electric for the development of a coal gasification project in Thar province.

 

 US: The West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection issued two violations against South Fork Coal Company over the failure to prevent sediment discharges into waterways and for failing to obtain approval to cease operations. White Forest Resources, the parent company, is in liquidation.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Chinese coal restrictions bite as solar panel production surges: The latest Chinese government data indicates coal production of 390.5 million tonnes in August, a 3 per cent decline compared to the year before but a 2.5 per cent increase on July. Coal power generation increased by 2.2 per cent in August, in part due to a 9.9 per cent decline in hydro generation. Solar and wind generation in 2025 is up 46.2 per cent and 35.2 per cent respectively. Chinese government officials have spoken of the need to curtail overproduction and price wars in key economic sectors, including coal mining. Major coal producers, including China Coal Energy and Shenhua, recently said that the growth of coal production will slow in the remainder of the year and imports will decline. Reuters reports that an Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region Energy Bureau internal document said they suspended production at 15 mines that exceeded their approved capacity by more than 10 per cent in the first half of the year. The latest data indicates that the production of solar cells increased in August by 17 per cent year-on-year to 70 GW. Solar panel production over the January to August period reached 550 GW. (Reuters, National Bureau of Statistics of China [Chinese], Reuters)

Report says Indonesian power plan needs an overhaul: A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) urges the Indonesian government to revise the recently released Electricity Supply Business Plan 2025-2034 (RUPTL) to incorporate greater near-term renewable capacity. The plan backs 16.6 GW of new coal and gas power capacity but lowers the target for renewable power capacity from 20.9 GW to 18.6 GW in 2030. The report says the government should align the RUPTL with the Just Energy Transition Partnership's Comprehensive Investment and Policy Plan 2030 targets and a 1.5-degree scenario pathway. It also highlights major financial and regulatory issues that bedevilled the implementation of the previous power plan, such as the need to renegotiate take-or-pay clauses in power supply agreements with independent power producers to manage coal plant overcapacity. In August, government officials announced a plan to build 100 GW of solar capacity, with 80 GW paired with 320 gigawatt hours of battery systems across more than 80,000 villages. A further 20 GW of utility-scale projects are proposed as part of the scheme. CREA said that achieving the project will necessitate integrating it with national targets and upgrading the transmission network beyond the main Java grid. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)

Vietnamese ministry pitches tax exemption for foreign coal plant owners: In a September 7 memo seen by Reuters, Vietnam's Ministry of Finance proposed exempting the foreign operators of seven coal power plants from the requirement to pay the global minimum corporate tax rate of 15 per cent. In a move to minimise corporate tax evasion, more than 140 countries agreed in 2021 to an Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) proposal to ensure a minimum 15 per cent corporate tax on companies with an annual global turnover of more than 750 million (US$883 million) from 2024. Vietnam's parliament voted in November 2023 to implement the 15 per cent minimum corporate tax from January 1, 2024. The ministry argues that the proposed exemption would "ensure a stable investment environment" and would comply with the OECD guidelines, with Vietnam forgoing US$426 million in revenue over the next two decades. The ministry notes that Kepco and Marubeni, which own the 1.32GW Nghi Son 2 coal plant, would otherwise be liable to pay US$190 million by 2047. Other potential beneficiaries of the proposed exemption are Mitsubishi, Sumitomo, AES, and China Southern Power Grid. The ministry argues that imposing the 15 per cent minimum tax "would expose the Vietnamese government to the risk of having to pay compensation that exceeds the tax revenues". (Reuters)

US agency lowers electricity demand growth forecast: The US Energy Information Administration's (EIA) latest Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) has reduced its projected US electricity demand growth rate to 2.3 per cent in 2025 and a further 3.0 per cent increase in 2026. The EIA's electricity demand forecasts this year have been volatile. At the start of the year, the administration estimated electricity demand growth at 1.5 per cent in 2025, with an estimate in July of a 3 per cent increase in 2025 and 4.5 per cent in 2026. The average US electricity demand increase between 2020 and 2024 was 0.8 per cent. The EIA estimates coal generation could increase by nine per cent in 2025 compared to the year before, the first annual increase in coal generation since 2021. The agency attributes the growing demand for power to the growth of data centres and industrial customers. The EIA estimates coal consumption will total 439 million US short tons (398 million tonnes) in 2025, a 7 per cent increase compared to 2024, with cold winter temperatures driving a 13 per cent increase in coal consumption in the first half of the year, but with a 1 per cent increase in the second half of 2025. The agency estimates US coal production will increase by 10 million US short tons (9 million tonnes) in 2025 to 520 million US short tons (470 million tonnes) before declining in 2026 to 490 million US short tons (445 million tonnes). (Utility Dive, US Energy Information Administration)

Indian government think tank pitches carbon capture subsidies, coal gasification: A senior official with NITI Aayog, an influential Indian government policy think tank, suggested the national government could offer between 50 per cent and 100 per cent of the cost of selected coal-based carbon capture and storage (CCS) projects. Speaking at an Indian Chamber of Commerce coal summit, Rajnath Ram, an advisor to NITI Aayog, said the national plan aimed to support the deployment of CCS technology at coal power plants. Globally, CCS has proven extremely expensive for coal plants, incurs a significant energy penalty and requires increased water consumption. Separately, NITI Aayog recently convened a workshop on the potential for coal gasification projects based on domestic coals that can have an ash content of between 25 per cent and 45 per cent. The workshop concluded that the Indian government should provide financial support to ensure the viability of projects and allocate the coal supply. The workshop included representatives from government-owned equipment suppliers, coal companies such as Coal India and private companies, including Jindal Steel and Power and Larsen & Toubro. Professor Martin Grabner from the Fraunhofer Institute for Ceramic Technologies and Systems in Germany addressed the workshop on possible technologies appropriate for Indian coals. (Reuters, NITI Aayog)

Indian flue gas equipment suppliers call for clarity over pollution policy: Major companies supplying flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) units for India's coal power plants are lobbying the government to change its recent decision exempting about 78 per cent of India's 537 coal units from the need to install the pollution control equipment. The requirement to install FGD units to cut sulphur dioxide emissions was first announced in December 2015 to take effect in 2017, but power utilities successfully lobbied the government to delay the deadline on several occasions. GE and Thermax, amongst others, want the government to apply the exemption to proposed new coal units. A recent analyst's report estimated that contracts have been entered into for FGD units on a further 102 GW of coal capacity, and the tender process is underway for installation on an additional 79 GW of capacity. In July, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change announced the decision and claimed that "current exposure levels provide no credible evidence to suggest that sulphur dioxide, under prevailing ambient conditions, is a major public health concern". A recent Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air report estimated that about 60 per cent of India's sulphur dioxide emissions originate from coal plants. (Economic Times)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Cradle to Grave: The Health Toll of Fossil Fuels and the Imperative for a Just Transition, Global Climate and Health Alliance, September 2025. (Pdf) (The report is also available in French, Portuguese and Spanish. The media release on the report is here, and a guide to Frequently Asked Questions on the report is here).

This 149-page report provides a detailed global overview of the health consequences of fossil fuels from pregnancy to old age.

China's Green Leap Outward: The rapid scale-up of overseas Chinese clean-tech manufacturing investments, Net Zero Policy Lab, September 2025. (Pdf)

This 17-page brief provides a concise overview of the more than US$220 billion in global investments by Chinese companies in energy transition projects from solar, electric vehicles, wind, battery manufacturing, green hydrogen and nickel processing.

links.text: National Bureau of Statistics of China [Chinese],
(Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air)
