title: CoalWire 579, Septmber 11, 2025
excerpt: China’s renewables boom reshaping transition; US judge rejects coal ash challenge.
content:
September 11, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The stark contrast in energy policy trajectories between China and the US has gained increasing attention in the last few weeks. For its part, China is pursuing an ambitious expansion of both renewables and coal generation capacity. A new report by Greenpeace East Asia sketches out a scenario which could result in China's greenhouse gas emissions peaking this year: an end to new coal plants, high-efficiency electrification to lower demand growth and better integration of renewables. A report by Ember highlights the effect of exports of wind and solar in rapidly transforming some national grids. In contrast, the Trump administration has embarked on policies to expand the role of fossil fuels and undercut future growth of renewables and curtail projects under construction. But it is not a one way street. Some court decisions, such as a judge rejecting a challenge against coal ash management standards, have slowed the administration's policy onslaught. In the Netherlands, a significant pension fund has terminated a contract with BlackRock, an asset management firm that has backtracked on its support for ESG policies in the face of attacks by Republican states.

Other countries are also looking to bolster support the long-term role of coal power. In Turkiye, the government has floated a plan to guarantee the purchase of coal power to spur the construction of new coal plants. In the Philippines, the government is contemplating exempting captive power projects from its October 2020 moratorium on new coal plants. In India, the Adani Group has won a temporary court order constraining the reporting of five Indian journalists on controversies about the company's coal mines and power plants.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 In one small town, a coal plant may hold the key to the Philippines' dirty energy exit 

Government officials are stalling on plans to shut down the 232 megawatt (MW) STEAG Mindanao coal plant, citing security of supply arguments that climate change activists insist have no basis in science, writes Carmela S. Fonbuena for the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism.

 

 Wyoming's massive new federal coal tract not likely to draw high bids

State and coal industry officials want an area with about 440 million US short tons (399 million tonnes) of coal offered for sale, but opponents warn the lease won't benefit public coffers like years past, writes Dustin Bleizeffer in WyoFile.

 

 Plan to expand coal production in Pakistan's Thar region has sparked strong opposition from local communities

The anguished voices rising from Thar's villages should serve as a stark reminder that Pakistan's coal ambitions are exacting an unacceptable human cost, writes Nasir Jamal in Dawn.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Report says Chinese emissions could peak this year with right policies: A report by Greenpeace East Asia suggests Chinese power sector emissions could peak at 5.2 billion tonnes in 2025 in a scenario with increased clean energy deployment, no new coal plant capacity and what it terms as "high-efficiency electrification" that lowers electricity demand growth rates. The report assessed four scenarios for the 2025–2035 period to test the impacts of growth rates, an accelerated rollout of renewable against baseline scenarios aligned with national targets but reliant on coal generation. Greenpeace East Asia recommends the need for a high-level policy to control new coal projects and accelerate replacement capacity to 2030, and increased flexibility in managing interregional electricity flows. The group recommends shifting the role of renewables from following "passive grid followers" to having an enhanced role in a high-renewables power system. (Climate Change News, Greenpeace East Asia)

 

 Chinese energy policy driving global transition, says report: A report by Ember, a UK energy policy NGO, argues that the rapid growth of renewables in China will cut domestic greenhouse gas emissions and is helping other countries leapfrog reliance on fossil fuels. Ember estimates that 91 per cent of new wind and solar projects globally generate electricity cheaper than fossil fuel plants. Chinese manufacturers produce about 80 per cent of the world's solar panels and 60 per cent of wind turbines. The report said that Chinese companies filed about three-quarters of global clean energy patents in 2022, up from just five per cent in 2000. China's role in exporting large volumes of solar capacity is rapidly transforming the power grid in some countries. Ember said that since 2018, Chinese solar exports to Namibia, Senegal, Cambodia, Afghanistan and Pakistan have been larger than the national grid as of 2023. Brazil has imported about 90 GW of solar panels that account for about one-third of the current capacity of the current grid capacity. (New York Times, Ember)

 

 US court dismisses utility appeal over coal ash rule: US federal court Judge Michael Watson upheld a 2022 US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) decision rejecting a request by American Electric Power for more time to comply with coal ash management rules for its 2.4 GW Gavin coal plant in Ohio. In 2015, the EPA rejected the company's request to continue adding coal ash to unlined impoundments, stating that about 40 per cent of the coal ash in a 314-acre (127 hectares) ash pond was in contact with groundwater. Earthjustice estimates that the two ponds, a landfill, and two potential ash dumps contain more than 67.3 million cubic yards (51.5 million cubic metres) of coal ash, with monitoring data revealing pollutants including arsenic, cobalt, lead, lithium, and molybdenum all well in excess of allowable levels in drinking water. AEP Ohio argued that the original 2015 guidelines requiring the prevention of liquids migrating into or out of coal ash dams did not apply to groundwater. Watson rejected AEP's claim. (WOUB, Earthjustice)

 

 Adani launches legal action to muzzle Indian journalists: Adani Enterprises has won an interim Indian court order restricting five Indian journalists and three websites reporting on the Adani Group. The five are the leading independent journalists in India documenting controversies over Adani's coal mines and power plants. The order named the websites of journalist Paranjoy Thakurta, Adani Watch published by the Bob Brown Foundation, an Australian environmental NGO, and Adanifiles, published by GetUp, an Australian civil society group. The company told the court that the company's Australian operations "aimed at securing vital resources for India got strained and delayed and repeatedly hindered, pushing back development timelines due to the interference of such reporters, activists and organizations". The order directed the journalists and websites to remove articles and social media posts that are "incorrect and unverified and prima facie defamatory". The Bob Brown Foundation, which publishes the Adani Watch website, said that as it wasn't informed of Adani's court application, it hadn't been able to file a defence. A further hearing is listed for October 9. (Business Standard, Bar and Bench, Scroll, Adani Enterprises [Pdf], Bob Brown Foundation)

 

 Italy likely to delay coal closures beyond end of 2025: The Minister for Energy, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, said Enel's Civitavecchia and Brindisi coal plants will continue operating beyond the end of the year despite the previous goal of ending coal generation by the end of 2025. Each of the plants includes 1.98 GW of coal capacity. In October 2017, Italy announced the goal of closing all coal capacity by the end of 2025. As recently as November 2023, Enel confirmed its intention to meet the target. Pichetto cited the war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East as the reasons to delay the closure of coal plants. (Reuters)

 

 Complaint lodged with the European Commission over Bulgarian plants: Greenpeace Bulgaria and Za Zemiata (For the Earth) have filed a complaint with the European Commission alleging Bulgarian government agencies failed to enforce European pollution limits on four coal plants. The groups argue that between 2018 and 2023 emissions from the 630 MW Bobov Dol plant, the 200 MW Brikel plant, the 105 MW Republika plant and the 908 MW Maritsa 3 plant exceeded European Union standards. The complaint argues that regulators have not enforced permit conditions on air and water emissions or the use of prohibited fuels. Beyond Fossil Fuels said that Daniela Toneva, an environmentalist campaigning against pollution from the Bobov Dol plant, was recently the target of harassment, with paint poured over her car and a rock thrown through the window of her house. (Balkan Green Energy News)

 

 
 "Bluntly, coal ash disposal threatens perhaps our most precious natural resource: water,"

wrote Judge Michael Watson in his decision dismissing a challenge against the US Environmental Protection Agency's regulation of coal ash storage regulations.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The federal Minister for Environment, Murray Watt, approved an 18.8 million-tonne expansion of Glencore Australia's Ulan mine in the Hunter Valley in New South Wales.

 

 Colombia: The value of coal exports in July was US$479.8 million, a 45.8 per cent fall compared to the year before. Declining global coal prices and a ban on sales to Israel have hit Colombian coal exports.

 

 India: State-owned Coal India announced it is investigating repurposing abandoned coal mine sites for data centres.

 

 US: The US House of Representatives voted in favour of a resolution overturning a Bureau of Land Management rule blocking new coal leases on federal land in Montana's Powder River Basin. The resolution requires the support of the Senate and President Trump to come into effect.

 

 "If the only way to keep this industry alive is for the federal government to basically give away coal for free, how does that make any sense?"

asked Emma Jones from the Sierra Club on Republican plans to offer new federal coal leases.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Dutch pension fund axes BlackRock contract over sustainability: PFZW, a Dutch pension fund that holds 248 billion (US$290 billion) of assets for more than 3 million healthcare workers, terminated its contract with BlackRock to manage 14 billion (US$16 billion) in assets for the fund. PFZW said that it had appointed new managers who it believed were "best positioned" to implement its new investment strategy. Over the last few years, BlackRock and other US asset managers have backtracked on their support for companies aligning operations with the Paris Agreement goals and stricter environmental, social and governance (ESG) standards. Republican states and the Trump administration have targeted ESG and climate policies. BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street are currently defending a lawsuit brought in November 2024 by 10 Republican states that alleged the funds violated federal antitrust law by restricting support for nine publicly traded coal companies they hold stakes in. (Financial Times)

Putin says coal exporters should focus on domestic market: President Vladimir Putin told the annual Eastern Economic Forum that coal exporters faced "tough" conditions in the global market but that they should switch their focus to domestic sales. "If the domestic market consumes the amount we need, and we can use it efficiently, then there will simply be no difficulties with the external market conditions that have such an impact on the industry," he said. Russian coal producers suffered a combined loss of US$2.3 billion in the first half of 2025, according to the government statistics agency. Russia exported about 136 million tonnes of thermal coal in 2024, making it the world's third-largest exporter of thermal coal. It also exported about 43 million tonnes of metallurgical coal to the global market in 2024 and ranks as the fourth largest exporter of coking coal. Russian producers have suffered from a sharp decline in the price of exported coal, a stronger rouble against the US dollar and the impact of international sanctions. Global export prices are forecast to plateau for the next few years. (Economic Times, Interfax)

Philippines gov't considers exempting captive projects from moratorium: The Philippines Department of Energy (DOE) Secretary Sharon Garin said the agency is "evaluating" requests by unnamed companies to exempt new captive power plants from the government's moratorium on new coal plants. In October 2020, the then-Philippines Secretary of Energy, Alfonso Cusi, announced a moratorium "on endorsements for greenfield coal power plants" but said that it did not affect proposals that had permits or were potential expansions on the sites of existing plants. Since then, DOE issued certificates exempting Meralco's proposed 1.2 GW Atimonan coal plant and the 73 MW Toledo project from the moratorium. In September 2024, the DMCI Power Corporation, a power utility, lobbied for an exemption from the moratorium for small coal units outside the main grid. DMCI is also the largest coal producer in the Philippines and is developing two new nickel mines. (Manila Bulletin, Manila Standard)

Bangladesh agency orders utility to cancel coal supply tender: The Power Division of Bangladesh's Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources has directed the Rural Power Company and NORINCO International Power consortium to cancel a proposed five-year coal supply contract "due to irregularities and flaws in both the technical and financial evaluation processes". The consortium operates the 1320 MW Patuakhali imported coal plant. Rezaul Karim, the Chairman of the Bangladesh Power Development Board, said that an uncompetitive coal tender would drive up the cost of electricity. The power division cancelled the tender for 1.3 - 4 million tonnes of coal a year after an investigation report suggested tender specifications favoured Singapore-based Yongtai Energy. The division ordered a new tender process for a two-year coal supply agreement that would allow smaller suppliers to compete. (The Business Standard)

India pursues battery trial at coal plants: The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) is working with NTPC to trial the installation of approximate 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of battery storage systems at the sites of 11 coal plants. CEA chairman Ghanshyam Prasad said the trial aimed to test storing coal-generated electricity during periods of high solar generation to avoid shutting coal units down and facing capacity shortfalls during the evening load peak. The CEA recently proposed lowering the technical operating minimum for coal plants to 40 per cent of installed capacity in a bid to cater for increased renewable generation. NTPC, a state-owned utility that generates about one-quarter of the country's electricity, said it preferred a 55 per cent operating minimum. NTPC's Director of Operations, Ravindra Kumar, said sustained operation at low utilisation levels could cut the 25-year lifespan of a plant by about one-third due to increased wear, especially on boilers and turbines designed for higher loads. (Reuters)

NGO says fuel rebate could cover construction cost of Australian mine: Lock the Gate estimates that Whitehaven Coal could recover more than A$1.3 billion (US$860 million) in diesel fuel rebate from the Australian government over the lifetime of the proposed Winchester South mine in Queensland. The estimated construction cost of the mine is A$1 billion (US$660 million). The fuel tax is levied at A$0.516 per litre (US$0.34 per litre) on all diesel and petrol. The levy was initially tied to the upkeep of roads, with primary industries able to claim a 100 per cent rebate if their operations are off-road. Based on data in the environmental impact statement on the Winchester South project, Lock the Gate estimates Whitehaven Coal would consume about 85 million litres of diesel a year, with the company eligible for a rebate of about A$44 million (US$29 million) a year. Tim Buckley from Clean Energy Finance recently proposed capping the diesel fuel rebate at A$50 million (US$33 million) a year per company, which would leave the bulk of the farming and fishing industry unaffected. (Renew Economy, Lock the Gate)

Turkish government unveils incentives for coal generation: The Turkish Minister for Energy, Alparslan Bayraktar, announced that the government will initiate a scheme to purchase electricity at a fixed rate from coal plants until 2030. Speaking at a mine in western Turkiye, Bayraktar said that the government will provide incentives for the establishment of new coal plants to replace retiring units and to increase total installed coal capacity. He said the government is considering a possible purchase guarantee scheme that could run until 2045. Turkiye has 21 GW of operating coal capacity that generated about 35 per cent of the country's electricity. A further 690 MW of new coal capacity is under development. (Reuters)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

The climate crisis—culprits and liability: contribution of South Korea's top ten emitting corporates to climate loss & damage, Solutions for Our Climate, September 2025. (Pdf) (Media release here, and the Korean version of the report is here.)

This 38-page report finds that steelmaker POSCO is South Korea's largest greenhouse gas emitter, followed by five subsidiaries of state-owned Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO).

Hidden impact of Australian coking coal in steelmaking, Ember, September 2025. (Pdf)

This 52-page report finds that Australia's underreporting of coal mine methane emissions has implications for major steel producers' assessments of greenhouse gas emissions in their supply chain, especially ArcelorMittal, Nippon Steel and POSCO.

title: CoalWire 581, September 25, 2025
excerpt: Clean energy undercuts Indian emissions growth; Colombia to host fossil fuel treaty conference.
content:
September 25, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Colombia's announcement that it will host the first international conference on the proposed Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty early next year could refocus global attention on current plans to increase fossil fuel production. The latest Production Gap report, released by the Stockholm Environment Institute and others, highlights the worrying trend of major fossil fuel-producing countries heading in the wrong direction. The Sierra Club's latest assessment of the performance of 75 utilities highlights a similar trend in the US power sector.

While these reports paint an alamining picture, there are strong countervailing forces. In India, power sector emissions declined in the first half of the year, partly due to the rapid expansion of clean energy capacity. In Indonesia, the head of the country's coal industry lobby group recently expressed alarm that solar power poses a threat to export markets.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 The US Department of Energy's emergency orders create a moral hazard

The US Department of Energy's use of emergency orders blocking the retirement of old coal plants could trigger a vicious cycle where a reliance on government compensation replaces the need for good business and planning practices, ultimately jeopardising the grid's reliability, writes Jennifer Danis from the Institute for Policy Integrity at New York University School of Law in Utility Dive.

 

 Indonesia's clean energy future is at the centre of a supply struggle between the US and China

The race to replace coal in Indonesia, the world's largest coal exporter, has become a contest between the US and China. At stake is not only Indonesia's climate future, but also which superpower sets the terms for the next generation of energy in the developing world, writes Aniruddha Ghosal for the Associated Press.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Colombia to host conference on treaty to phase out fossil fuels: The Colombian government, with the support of Vanuatu, will hold the first international conference on a treaty to phase out fossil fuels. The conference is scheduled for April 2026. The proposed Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty aims to support the rapid expansion of renewable energy, prevent the expansion of the coal, oil, and gas sectors, and equitably phase out existing fossil fuel production. The proposal has the backing of 16 countries and a broad coalition of civil society groups. In July, an advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice stated that the production and consumption of fossil fuels "may constitute an internationally wrongful act attributable to that state" and suggested those adversely affected could be entitled to "reparations". The case originated as an initiative by students in Fiji and was supported by the governments of Vanuatu, the Pacific Islands Forum, and the United Nations. (Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative)

 

 Clean energy growth undercuts Indian power-sector emissions: India's power sector coal consumption and carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1 per cent in the first half of 2025 and by 0.2 per cent in the year to the end of June. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) said government data indicated that almost two-thirds of the decline in fossil fuel generation is due to lower electricity demand growth, 20 per cent to an increase in faster growth in low-carbon non-hydroelectric generation, and 15 per cent to increased hydroelectric generation. Lower electricity demand growth was due to a combination of cooler-than-normal summer temperatures and slowing industrial demand. In the first half of the year, 25.1 GW of low-carbon electricity was installed, representing a 69 per cent increase over the same period in 2024. (Carbon Brief)

 

 Indonesia suspends 190 coal and other mining operations: Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM) has suspended the operations of 190 mining companies due to their failure to submit financial guarantees for post-mining rehabilitation. Many of the mines affected are coal operations in East and Central Kalimantan. Deputy Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources, Yuliot Tanjung, stated that some permits were suspended as operators exceeded the production limit set in their company work plan. The companies had failed to respond to three warning letters issued between December 2024 and August 2025. The ministry said the suspension will remain in place until the affected companies provide a reclamation plan and submit a financial guarantee. (Mysteel, Antara, Jakarta Globe)

 

 Report finds increase in fossil fuel production planned by 2030: The latest "Production Gap" report states that estimated global coal production levels in 2030 could be 500 per cent higher than the median pathway consistent with the Paris Agreement goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C above pre-industrial temperatures. The report said estimated coal production in 2040 and 2050 could be 1220 per cent and 2500 per cent higher than a Paris Agreement-compliant pathway. Over the last two years, projected coal production in 2030 is seven per cent higher than the last estimate two years ago. The report by the Stockholm Environment Institute, Climate Analytics, and the International Institute for Sustainable Development estimates coal, oil, and gas production in 2030 could be double the amount consistent with limiting warming to the 1.5C Paris Agreement goal. The report said that countries should aim for "a near total phase-out" of coal production and use by 2040. (Euronews, Stockholm Environment Institute [Pdf])

 

 Adani Power secures land for new coal plant at a nominal rate: Adani Power will pay just one rupee per acre per year for approximately 1020 acres (413 hectares) of land, or about US$11.50 per year, for its planned 2.4 GW greenfield coal plant at Pirpainti in Bihar. The Bihar State Power Generation Company entered into a 25-year contract for Adani Power to build, own and operate the plant. Farmers opposed the project when it was first proposed in 2014, raising concerns about the amount of compensation for the loss of productive agricultural land, including mangoes and lychees. While the land for the coal plant has been acquired, landowners complain that productive farmland was misclassified as barren, resulting in lower compensation levels. The Bhagalpur district already hosts the 2340 MW Kahalgaon lignite plant operated by state-owned NTPC. A new study by researchers from Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi has found that the Bhagalpur district is already one of four hotspots for PM2.5 fine particle pollution in Bihar. (The Wire)

 

 California Supreme Court clears way for coal export terminal: The California Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal by the City of Oakland against a lower court ruling that the city could not terminate the lease for the proposed Oakland Bulk and Oversized Terminal in West Oakland. The City of Oakland terminated the agreement for the terminal in 2018 due to a lack of progress on the project. In the original ruling, Judge Wise allowed Phil Tagami and his partner Mark McClure two and a half years to commence construction of the project. Part of the original proposal was for the state of Utah to invest US$53 million in the port, providing another option for Utah coal producers to access the Asian coal export market. Following the revelation of the plan to ship coal through the terminal, the Oakland City Council approved an ordinance banning the handling and storage of coal within the city limits of Oakland. Tagami stated that the project still requires additional permits, but the first shipments could depart the port in 2028. Ted Franklin from No Coal in Oakland said the group's campaign will now pivot to focus on informing potential investors that the project "will face stiff community resistance and potential legal challenges". (Cowboy State Daily, The Oaklandside, No Coal in Oakland)

 

 
 "I believe solar power is becoming a real threat to us. Beyond that, we are also competing with other renewable energy sources, not just solar,"

said Priyadi, the chairman of the Indonesian Coal Mining Association.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The New South Wales Environment Protection Authority fined Rix's Creek Pty Limited, a subsidiary of Bloomfield Collieries, A$30,000 (US$19,800) over the discharge of saline groundwater from an uncapped borehole.

 

 Australia: Synergy, the West Australian state-owned utility, has recorded a write-off of A$521.8 million (US$343 million) on its coal fleet. The plants now have a book value of zero.

 

 Australia: The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) confirmed that the eastern states' National Electricity Market set a new record for renewables generation, reaching 77.19 per cent on September 22. AEMO said accommodating higher levels of renewables will require reducing coal generation during the middle of the day.

 

 New Zealand: State-owned utility Genesis Energy announced it will buy 240,000 tonnes of coal over two years from BT Mining, a joint venture between Bathurst Resources and Talley's Energy, for the 1.2 GW Huntly Power Station.

 

 Poland: JSW estimates that metallurgical coal production from its Borynia-Zofiowka mine will decrease by approximately 156,000 tonnes in 2025 due to a fire that occurred on September 12.

 

 US: Work can restart on the near-completed 704 MW Revolution Wind offshore wind farm near Rhode Island after a federal court judge granted an interim injunction preventing the Trump administration from enforcing an order to halt work on the project.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

India cuts coal tax rates with aim of reducing power costs: India's Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council has abolished the 400 rupee per tonne (US$4.50) compensation cess on coal and increased the GST rate on coal from 5 to 18 per cent. The coal tax was first introduced in 2010 at a rate of 50 rupees (US$0.56) per tonne to provide funding for new renewable energy projects. The tax was initially referred to as a clean energy cess and was subsequently increased to 200 rupees (US$2.25) per tonne in March 2015 and to 400 rupees (US$4.50) per tonne in March 2016. Legislation passed in July 2017 established the GST scheme, abolished the Clean Energy Cess and replaced it with a GST Compensation Cess at the same rate. Assocham, an industry lobby group, has recently argued for the abolition of the levy as a way to reduce power costs and boost energy-intensive industries. The Ministry of Coal estimates that the abolition of the GST compensation cess and the increase in the GST rate will result in an average reduction in the price of power sector coal of around 260 rupees per tonne. The ministry also argues that the change will favour domestic coal producers and boost import substitution. (Business Standard, Ministry of Coal, S&P Global)

Report finds US utilities downgrade fossil fuel retirement plans: A Sierra Club report scores the performance of 75 US utilities clean energy transition plans at just 15 out of 100, three points lower than the last review two years ago. The Dirty Truth report reviewed utilities plans to retire coal plants by 2030, eschew new gas plant capacity before 2035, and boost clean energy to replace fossil fuel generation and cater for demand growth. The report found that the utilities reviewed currently plan to retire only 29 per cent of their coal capacity by 2030, with one-third awarded a lower coal score than five years ago. The review finds that only 17 of the 75 utilities plan to end coal generation before 2030, and 16 utilities have backtracked on their previous climate commitments. The report found that while 65 per cent of utilities improved their clean energy scores in the past five years, 69 per cent also planned to increase gas capacity. The utilities propose building 151 GW of new gas capacity, up from 51 GW planned two years ago. The report said that planned clean energy projects account for just over half of current coal and gas generation, before accounting for expected load growth. Only three of the 75 utilities scored an A ranking: the Public Service Company of Oklahoma, Entergy New Orleans, and Xcel Energy Minnesota. (Canary Media, Sierra Club [Pdf])

US agency calls for funding bids for new plants and grid capacity: The US Department of Energy has launched a request for information process as part of its Speed to Power initiative, aiming to accelerate new "large-scale" generation and grid projects. The initiative aims to cater for an increase in electricity demand, primarily driven by data centres. The deadline for the request for information is November 21, 2025. The American Energy Alliance, an offshoot of the pro-fossil fuel Institute for Energy Research (IER), claims that the Trump administration will keep 38 coal plants online that would otherwise close by 2028. IER does not disclose its funding sources. However, in the past, it has received funding from Peabody Energy and ExxonMobil. The US Energy Information Administration recently trimmed its projected US electricity demand growth rate from 3 per cent in 2025 to 2.3 per cent and from 4.5 per cent in 2026 to 3.0 per cent. The Sierra Club stated that Santee Cooper announced in its latest power plan update that it intends to delay the closure of the 1.26 GW Winyah coal plant in South Carolina from 2028 to 2033 or possibly 2035. (Reuters, US Department of Energy)

Indian securities regulator closes two Adani cases, but more remain open: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has dismissed two allegations made against Adani Group companies, including stock manipulation and undisclosed party transactions. The allegations were raised in January 2023 by Hindenburg Research, a now-defunct US-based short-seller. The share prices of Adani Power and Adani Enterprises surged after the news. However, a source told Reuters that more than a dozen other allegations against Adani Enterprises, Adani Ports, Adani Energy and Adani Power remain under investigation, with SEBI yet to decide whether to dismiss the claims or impose a monetary penalty. The remaining cases relate to allegations that the companies classed shareholders as public when they are related parties. Earlier this year, Reuters reported that around 30 Adani subsidiaries had applied to SEBI to settle some regulatory charges. (Reuters)

German utility sells Datteln 4 hard coal plant: Uniper has agreed to sell the 1.05 GW Datteln 4 coal power plant in North Rhine-Westphalia to ResInvest Group, a Czech commodities trading and investment company. The Datteln 4 plant was proposed in 2006 but wasn't commissioned until 2020 due to legal challenges and technical faults. The sale of the plant was a condition of the European Commission's December 2022 ratification of a financial bailout of Uniper by the German government. The bailout followed the disruption of energy markets triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the impact on gas and coal prices. Uniper did not disclose the sale price, but Reuters reports that a source suggested the plant's value could be around 1 billion (US$1.2 billion), less than its 1.5 billion (US$1.8 billion) construction cost. ResInvest's Polish subsidiary, RE Polska, bought the 226 MW Chorzow and the 330 MW Skawina coal plants in February 2025. (Reuters, Uniper)

Australian coal companies push for royalty cuts after mine closures: The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) said recent coal mine closures in Queensland reflected the shift in global coal prices. IEEFA said mines that were previously uneconomic restarted to take advantage of the surge in metallurgical coal prices to more than US$600 per tonne following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. BHP Mitsubishi Alliance (BMA), Anglo American and QCoal have announced mine closures in the last week, with the state's coal industry seizing on the job losses to argue for a reduction in the royalty rates introduced by the state government in 2022. The scheme introduced a progressive royalty rate of 7 per cent below $100 per tonne, with a series of increments that increased with the sale price. For coal sales of more than A$300 per tonne, a coal producer pays seven per cent up to A$100, 12.5 per cent on the next A$50, 15 per cent on the next A$25, 20 per cent on the next A$50, 30 per cent on the next A$75 and 40 per cent on the amount over A$300 per tonne. Metallurgical coal export prices have returned to approximately US$200 per tonne. "They're using what is a natural market-driven phenomenon to make some political hay", said Rod Campbell from the Australia Institute. (Guardian)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Perverting justice: The criminalisation of land and environmental defenders in Asia, Human Rights Watch, September 2025. (Pdf)

The 19-page report explores the increasing criminalisation of land defenders with a special focus on the Philippines, Indonesia, India and Vietnam.

Measuring Transition: AMNS: Tracking Technology Transition in the Indian Steel Sector, Carbon Tracker, September 2025. (Pdf)

This 28-page report finds a lack of transition planning by AMNS India, a joint venture between global majors ArcelorMittal and Nippon Steel, and the fourth-largest steel producer in India.

links.text: Perverting justice: The criminalisation of land and environmental defenders in Asia
Measuring Transition: AMNS: Tracking Technology Transition in the Indian Steel Sector

title: CoalWire 582, October 2, 2025
excerpt: AI drives US power prices higher; China’s new climate targets; US bailout for old coal.
content:
October 2, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

China's much-anticipated announcement of its new climate targets drew a mixed response. While some aspects were well received, the overall renewables target for the domestic power sector was remarkably unambitious. Slowing installation of new wind and solar capacity was expected after mid-year policy changes. The upside is that Chinese suppliers are catering for the the transformation of the power sector in many other countries. The rapid growth in solar capacity in Brazil is just the latest example.

In the US, the latest announcement by the Trump administration of a US$625 million funding package to support the upgrading of old coal units has garnered significant coverage, but beyond its symbolic value, it may do relatively little to offset the long-term decline of US coal generation. A more critical factor is how much of the touted expansion of data centre capacity actually materialises. A new assessment of US power prices finds that data centres are imposing big price hikes on residential customers. Increasingly, financial analysts and commentators are questioning the economic viability of substantial investments in a sector where there are few signs of profitability. If the US AI bubble bursts in the short term, a key driver keeping old coal units online could evaporate.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 AI data centres are sending power bills soaring

Wholesale electricity costs are as much as 267 per cent more than they were five years ago in areas near data centres in the US. That's being passed on to customers, write Josh Saul, Leonardo Nicoletti, Demetrios Pogkas, Dina Bass and Naureen Malik in Bloomberg.

 

 Religion at a crossroads in Indonesia as Islamic groups bid to operate large-scale mines

In 2024, the then-President Joko Widodo decided to allow Indonesia's two biggest Islamic organisations, Nahdlatul Ulama (NU) and Muhammadiyah, to operate large-scale mines. The recent revelation that a senior NU cleric is on the board of a nickel producer, has rekindled debate over the organisation's move into mining, writes Ramadani Saputra in Mongabay.

 

 Getting to greener steel

While cutting methane emissions in the steel supply chain will not produce green steel overnight, it could reduce the sector's emissions by the equivalent of a billion tonnes of carbon annually, and at little cost, write Gernot Wagner from Columbia Business School and Roland Kupers, an advisor on the United Nations' International Methane Emissions Observatory, in Project Syndicate.

 

 A coal-burning steel plant may thwart Cleveland's climate goals

Cleveland has big ambitions to reduce its planet-warming emissions. But a massive steelmaking facility run by Cleveland-Cliffs is the city's largest source of greenhouse gas emissions. Advocates argue that the company should replace its outdated blast furnaces with cleaner technology, writes Kathleen M. Kowalski in Canary Media.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Chinese president announce new targets to mixed reception: President Xi Jinping told the United Nations climate summit in New York that China will cut greenhouse gas emissions to 7-10 per cent below peak levels by 2035, increase solar and wind generation capacity to more than 3600 gigawatts (GW) by the same year and increase the non-fossil share of the primary energy mix to 30 per cent. As of June 2025, China had 1673 GW of wind and solar capacity, well in excess of the 2030 target of 1200 GW. China's commitments drew a mixed response, with some welcoming the inclusion of all economic sectors and all greenhouse gases in the commitment to an absolute reduction in emissions. However, Xi did not specify the peak year baseline against which emissions reductions would be measured, while the wind and solar capacity target implies a slowing rollout. In announcing the targets, Xi said China would be "striving to do better". Climate Action Tracker, a project of Climate Analytics and Brave New Climate, described the new targets as "disappointing" and "overly conservative" and said China has the potential to decarbonise faster. "We expect China to update these 2030 targets alongside setting targets for 2035, in order to maintain momentum for climate action before 2030," said Climate Action Tracker. (Climate Action Tracker, Carbon Brief, Carbon Brief)

 

 US government unveils funding package to subsidise ailing coal plants: The US Department of Energy has announced a US$625 million funding package to support extending the life and viability of coal plants, with US$350 million earmarked for recommissioning or upgrading old coal units and US$175 million for coal power projects in rural communities. The package also includes US$50 million for the installation of wastewater management systems and US$25 million to adapt coal units to operate on gas as well. It is unclear whether the announced funding will be in the form of loans or grants. The Sierra Club said the announcement came as the Trump administration sought to block cleaner, cheaper renewable energy projects, has removed funding for clean tech projects and delayed the enforcement of regulations aimed at reducing pollution affecting local communities. In a separate announcement, the Bureau of Land Management announced plans to open up to 13.1 million acres (5.3 million hectares) of federal land for coal leases. The agency also stated that it has reduced the royalty rate on coal from federal land to 7 per cent and is easing approvals for mines in Montana, Wyoming, Tennessee, and other states. The Trump administration has promoted the need to keep coal plants operating to cater for booming data centre demand. While some utilities have delayed planned closures, the Energy Information Administration projects continued retirements. In 2024, coal plants accounted for 15 per cent of the electricity generated in the US. (Utility Dive, Guardian, Reuters, Department of Interior, Sierra Club)

 

 US study finds heavy metal pollution from unlined Alabama coal ash dam: Researchers from the University of Alabama and Texas A&M University found arsenic and cadmium in water and sediment samples downstream from Alabama Power's Plant Barry in Alabama breached US drinking water standards. The study, published in Science of the Total Environment in June, examined heavy metal contamination near the outfall from the coal ash dam during the dry season, the wet season, and following a flood in March 2023. The unlined coal ash dam contains approximately 17 million cubic metres of coal ash generated at the 3.34 gigawatt (GW) plant. The study found that "a significant contribution" of arsenic and cadmium from coal ash in suspended sediments and surface water at the discharge point of the plant, especially during the dry season. The researchers found cadmium in suspended sediments as high as 4.2 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg), exceeding the 2.2 mg/kg observed in sediments following the December 2018 Kingston coal ash disaster in Tennessee. The study also found arsenic in suspended sediments as high as 44.6 mg/kg. Arsenic is not allowed in drinking water, while the federal standard sets a maximum of 0.005 milligrams of cadmium per litre. (AL.com, Science of the Total Environment)

 

 Final unit at South African plant online, 17 years after work started: Seventeen years after construction first commenced on the 4.8 GW Kusile coal plant in August 2008, Eskom announced that the final 800 MW unit has entered commercial operation. The Kusile plant was initially estimated to cost 80 billion rand (US$4.6 billion), but the final cost ballooned to more than 233 billion rand (US$13.5 billion) due to technical flaws, corruption, and construction delays. In November 2022, a poorly designed flue gas ducting on Unit 1 collapsed, which also forced Units 2 and 3 offline until Eskom completed repair work in late 2023. The cost overruns on the Kusile plant and the World Bank-backed 4.6 GW Medupi plant forced Eskom to seek a bailout from the South African government. South African civil society groups opposed the plant due to its economic impacts, pollution, water demand, and greenhouse gas emissions. Eskom said both plants have a design life of 50 years. (Tech Central, Mining Weekly, Eskom)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Brazil: Distributed solar capacity reached 40 GW in June 2025, up from less than 1 GW in 2018. Distributed solar accounted for 43 per cent new generation capacity added over that period.

 

 China: Three mine workers died in a tunnel collapse at an underground mine in the city of Ankang in Shaanxi province. Five other workers escaped.

 

 India: Nine construction workers died when the framing for a roof of a coal storage shed collapsed at the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board's (TNEB) Ennore Thermal Power Station. Two 660 MW coal units are under construction at the site.

 

 South Africa: The Anglican Church of Southern Africa has backed calls for a ban on coal exports to Israel.

 

 US: California became the seventh US state to pass legislation banning investor-owned utilities from funding utility political activities or membership fees for industry groups that undertake political activities. The bill is yet to be signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom.

 

 US: The US Department of Energy's Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy has added "climate change," "green", "energy transition", and "decarbonisation" to its growing "list of words to avoid".

 

 Vietnam: Heavy wind and rain with Typhoon Bualoi triggered the collapse of the roof of the coal warehouse at the 1.2 GW Vung Ang II coal plant.

 

 "Two trillion dollars in annual revenue is what's needed to fund computing power needed to meet anticipated AI demand by 2030. However, even with AI-related savings, the world is still US$800 billion short to keep pace with demand,"

states Bain & Co's Global Technology Report.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Deutsche Bank warns about the US AI financial bubble: While the US government is promoting the extension of ageing coal plants as necessary to cater to growing electricity demand for data centres, Deutsche Bank has warned about the economic risks to the US economy from the massive capital expenditures required to support AI companies. Goldman Sachs estimates that approximately US$368 billion has been spent on AI-related projects in 2025. In a recent research note, Deutsche Bank warned that without the capital expenditure on AI infrastructure, the US economy would "be close to, or in, recession this year". AI investment in the US is closely tied to seven major technology companies – Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet (the parent company of Google), Meta, chipmaker Nvidia, and Tesla. Bain & Company, a financial services firm, estimates that, based on current trends, the AI sector could require approximately 200 GW of new power capacity by 2030, with about half of that capacity located in the US. Torsten Slok from Apollo Management warned that equity investors "are dramatically overexposed to AI". (Fortune)

Auditor refuses to endorse report of Polish metallurgical coal producer: PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) has declined to approve JSW's latest financial report for the six months to June 30 2025. JSW is Poland's largest metallurgical coal producer. PwC told the state-owned company that it did not have confidence in the assumptions used by JSW to ensure it has sufficient financial liquidity to continue operating over the next six months. JSW's financial model assumed favourable efficiency gains, as well as decisions by third parties, including wage negotiations with trade unions, support from social security agencies for deferring social security contributions, and government support for rescheduling loan debt and a tax refund. JSW warned that without favourable decisions, it could run out of cash within six months. The company reported a net loss of 2.09 billion zloty (approximately US$574 million) in the first half of 2025, representing a significant improvement over the same period in 2024. JSW cited declining European steel production, lower prices, exchange rate fluctuations, and increasing competition from Indonesian suppliers. While Indonesia is the world's largest thermal coal exporter, there are only seven metallurgical coal producers with production in 2025 estimated to reach almost 12 million tonnes. (Mining.com, JSW)

Zimbabwe signs agreement to upgrade six old coal units: The Zimbabwean government has signed a US$455 million, 15-year concession agreement with Jindal Africa to upgrade six coal units, which have a combined capacity of 920 MW. The coal units, owned by the Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Authority (ZESA), have suffered from protracted breakdowns and technical faults. Negotiations over proposals to refurbish the units have been ongoing for the last eight years, with the Indian government offering funding for the project in 2018. Reports suggested that Jindal and ZESA agreed in August 2024 to refurbish the six units and signed a memorandum of understanding to construct four new 300 MW coal units, expanding the plant's capacity to 2 GW. With the Kariba hydro project suffering from prolonged drought conditions, Zimbabwe has relied heavily on power imports from South Africa. (Africa News Agency, Reuters, Global Energy Monitor)

Study flags need for better transition planning for some Chinese cities: Researchers from North China Electric Power University in China and the University of Maryland in the US estimate that about 10 per cent of the 292 Chinese cities assessed would be "severely affected" by a transition away from coal. A pre-print study published in IScience found that approximately 60 per cent of employment and tax revenue losses in the worst-affected cities would be caused by plant closures in other provinces. The most affected cities are in Shanxi, Shaanxi, Inner Mongolia and other northern regions. The authors found that continued construction of new coal power plants would only increase the impacts on already vulnerable cities. The authors suggest that cities with rich renewable energy potential should focus on developing these industries and ensuring early job training in advance of coal plant closures. For other cities, the study suggests exploring new economic growth drivers and investing in technology upgrades for both coal mining and power stations to reduce their labour intensity gradually. The study also suggests retrofits to some coal plants to increase their ability to operate flexibly. The authors also flag the option of mothballing plants after 20 years of operation. (iScience)

Report says India looking beyond Australian met coal suppliers: S&P Global estimates China's metallurgical coal imports could decline by about 100 million tonnes a year by 2035, creating an opportunity for Indian steel producers to reduce reliance on Australian exporters, according to a report by the Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis (IEEFA). Australian metallurgical coal exports have declined since 2019, with shipments to India falling since 2021. While analysts expect Indian metallurgical coal demand to increase significantly over the next decade, buyers have turned to cheaper Russian cargoes. Other exporters, such as those in Mozambique, Canada, and the US, are also targeting the Indian market. Indian coal producers are also once again investing in overseas metallurgical coal projects, such as JSW Steel's push for the Minas de Revuboe concession in Mozambique. IEEFA stated that Australian exporters fail to recognise that the Indian government intends to increase domestic metallurgical coal production, following a similar approach to reducing imports of thermal coal. (Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Green power transmission development in India, Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis, September 2025. (Pdf) (The executive summary is here.)

This 27-page report estimates that more than 50 GW of renewable energy capacity is currently unable to meet rising electricity demand due to inadequate transmission planning and integration.

"Who will foot the bill? The opportunity cost of prioritising nuclear power over renewable energy for the case of Finland", Energy, November 15, 2025.

This paper finds Finland's stated support for tripling nuclear power capacity by 2050 could cost 71 per cent more than the alternative scenario of optimised renewable energy capacity.

Coal mining in NSW: key statistics, Parliament of New South Wales, September 2025. (Pdf; a spreadsheet with the key data is available here.)

This paper identifies all coal mines in NSW that are currently operational or have the potential to become operational in the future, along with their current and proposed life expectancy.

title: CoalWire 583, October 9, 2025
excerpt: Renewables eclipse coal power; US plant retired; scathing Polish audit on mine wastewater pollution.
content:
October 9, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The data revealing renewables eclipsed global coal power generation for the first time illustrates the accelerating transformation of the power sector. One statistic in particular stands out from Ember's new report: at least 29 countries now generate more than 10 per cent of their electricity from solar and wind, up from 11 countries four years ago. Even in the US, old coal plants continue to close, with reports revealing that the 459 megawatt (MW) Merrimack plant in New Hampshire closed several weeks ago, three years earlier than previously announced.

Elsewhere in the US, utilities such as Duke Energy are seeking to defer the retirement of old coal units and build new gas capacity, in large part due to the increase in power demand required for new and proposed data centres. The plans to delay coal closures and build new gas plants, though, hinge on when the AI investment bubble bursts. In the meantime, there is little doubt that the boom in data centre power demand is pushing up power prices for other consumers. Cost-shifting to consumers takes other forms too. A US water industry lobby group argues that a Trump administration proposal to delay compliance with new coal plant wastewater standards will simply shift costs to utilities responsible for meeting water quality standards. In Poland, a recent government audit report revealed that inadequate conditions in environmental permits have allowed the pollution of two major river systems with saline wastewater from coal mines.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Trump is reviving large sales of coal from public lands. Will anyone want it?

While the Trump administration pushes ahead with auctions of federal land leases containing hundreds of millions of tonnes of coal, industry analysts doubt that the market exists for increased production, write Matthew Brown and Mead Gruver for the Associated Press.

 

 Energy bills are soaring in America's coal capital

Electricity prices in coal-heavy West Virginia have increased at nearly twice the national rate over the last 15 years, with almost one out of five customers of the leading utility company behind on monthly bills, writes Ivan Penn in the New York Times.

 

 Anguish for residents as Thailand's most polluting coal plant gets new lease of life

Thailand has announced it will delay the decommissioning of two lignite units at the 2.4 gigawatt (GW) Mae Moh power plant, prompting fears among communities who have dealt with health problems linked to the plant for decades, writes Gerald Flynn in Mongabay.

 

 Philippine tribes revive reforestation to defy coal mining expansion

Secrecy surrounds the ownership of the coal mine near the village of Ned on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao. The mine has faced opposition from local Indigenous residents, farmers, and church and community organisations in the area, citing environmental and health concerns, writes Bong S. Sarmiento in Mongabay.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Private utility closes the last coal plant in New Hampshire:

Granite Shore Power, a private power utility, announced that the 459 megawatts (MW) of coal capacity at the Merrimack plant in New Hampshire closed on September 12. The two coal units at the site, the first commissioned in 1960 and the second eight years later, were the last coal units operating in the New England region. Granite Shore Power had previously said that the coal units would cease operating in June 2028 as part of a settlement agreement with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Conservation Law Foundation, and the Sierra Club. Granite Shore Power failed to win a contract with ISO-New England, the region's grid operator, in the capacity auction for 2026-27. Kendra Ford from 350 New Hampshire welcomed the end of coal generation but said there is a need to support the affected workers at the plant, many of whom live in the township of Bow. The company stated that it may install solar capacity and batteries at the site to supplement the continued operation of two small kerosene-fueled peaker units. (Concord Monitor, WBUR)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Renewables eclipse coal generation in first half of 2025: In the first half of 2025, renewable electricity surpassed coal power for the first time, driven by a 31 per cent increase in solar generation compared to the same period in the previous year. In its half-yearly review of global electricity production, Ember estimates that solar's share of generation surged to 8.8 per cent in the first half of 2025, up from 6.9 per cent the year before. While global electricity demand increased by 2.6 per cent in the first half of 2025, the rise in solar and wind generation exceeded the increase. Coal generation declined by 0.6 per cent in the first half of 2025, primarily due to the rapid expansion of clean energy capacity in India and China, as well as cooler summer temperatures in India. China accounted for 55 per cent of the growth in solar generation, with the US and Europe accounting for 14 per cent and 12 per cent respectively. The report notes that at least 29 countries generated more than 10 per cent of their electricity from solar in the first half of the year, up from 11 countries in the same period in 2021. Seven countries — Hungary, Greece, the Netherlands, Pakistan, Spain, Australia and Germany — generated 20 per cent or more of their electricity from solar in the first half of 2025. (Guardian, Ember)

 

 US water industry alarmed at plan to delay pollution standards: The American Water Works Association (AWWA), a group representing more than 4300 US water utilities, has objected to the proposal by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to delay wastewater emission compliance deadlines for coal plants. "We believe it to be inappropriate for one industry to place its pollution burden on somebody else to then have to clean up and address," said Adam Carpenter from the AWWA. "It's much more effective to address it at the source." On September 29, the EPA proposed allowing coal plants more time to comply with seven deadlines in the 2024 effluent limitations guidelines, including the requirement for zero discharge of wastewater from flue gas desulfurisation (FGD) units and water used to transport bottom ash from boilers to storage sites. The current standard requires coal plants to eliminate specific sources of discharges by 2029 or, by December 31, 2025, to commit to ceasing coal burning by 2034. Public comment on the proposal is open until November 3, 2025. The EPA stated the changes could cut costs for power utilities by between US$30 million and US$200 million per year and could help "strengthen America's position as the AI capital of the world while bolstering industrial competitiveness". (PoliticoPro, US Environmental Protection Agency, Sierra Club)

 

 

 Residents raise alarm over coal dust from South African export terminal: Residents living near the Richards Bay coal export terminal have complained that coal dust pollution coats surfaces inside their houses. Sandy Camminga from the Richards Bay Clean Air Association said residents experience respiratory diseases due to breaches of municipal air quality regulations by the Transnet National Ports Authority. In a report released in mid-September, Transnet acknowledged that "increased community complaints" about dust emissions threaten the company's social licence to operate. Transnet stated that it aims to reduce complaints about air quality by 30 per cent by the end of the year. In a comment article in the Zululand Observer, the editor noted that Transnet's commitment was "to reduce complaints – not emissions! – by 30 per cent". About 52 million tonnes of coal were exported through the Richards Bay coal terminal in 2024. (IOL, Zululand Observer, Zululand Observer, Zululand Observer)

 

 Polish audit report finds flawed limits for mine wastewater emissions: A recent report by the Polish government's Supreme Audit Office found that existing water permits for coal mines in Silesia lack effective constraints on saline mine water emissions, with only about 18 per cent of wastewater treated before discharge. The audit report estimated that 733 million cubic metres of saline wastewater, containing approximately 6 million tonnes of salts, was discharged into the Odra River Basin and Vistula River Basin between 2020 and 2023. The audit concluded that companies did not breach legal limits, as their environmental permits allow the discharge of water "containing any levels of chloride and sulphate into rivers." It stated that the salinity level in mine emissions was higher than that of the Baltic Sea. The report concluded that mining companies have little financial incentive to install desalination plants, as the wastewater fee is only 250 zloty (US$69) per day to discharge at a rate of one cubic metre per second, and the charge has not increased since 2018. The Polish government faced public uproar after hundreds of tonnes of fish died in the summer of 2022 due to high salinity levels in the Oder River. (Supreme Audit Office)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The owners of the 1.68 GW Gladstone coal power station have notified the Australian Energy Market Operator that the plant will close in March 2029. The plant, which was slated to close in 2035, is contracted to supply electricity to Rio Tinto's nearby Boyne Island aluminium smelter and two alumina refineries until 2029. Rio Tinto has a 42 per cent stake in the plant.

 

 Australia: The owners of the 1.68 GW Gladstone coal power station have notified the Australian Energy Market Operator that the plant will close in March 2029. The plant, which was slated to close in 2035, is contracted to supply electricity to Rio Tinto's nearby Boyne Island aluminium smelter and two alumina refineries until 2029. Rio Tinto has a 42 per cent stake in the plant.

 

 Canada: The Alberta Wilderness Association and the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society have filed a legal challenge against the decision of Alberta Energy Regulator CEO Rob Morgan to cancel a public hearing on Valory Resources's proposed Summit coal mine.

 

 Germany: Activists occupied an excavator at RWE's Hambach lignite mine in a protest against clearing part of the Hambach forest for the expansion of the mine.

 

 US: The Navajo Transitional Energy Company (NTEC) offered US$186,000 to lease federal land with an estimated 167 million US short tons (152 million tonnes) of coal adjoining the company's Spring Creek mine in Montana. NTEC was the sole bidder for the lease.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Loophole obscures shareholders in Australian fossil fuel projects: A report by Global Energy Monitor (GEM) reveals that the use of nominee companies operated by JP Morgan, Citibank, and HSBC Bank obscures the real ownership of 51 fossil fuel projects in Australia. The fossil fuel projects of the three nominee companies accounted for more than 22 million tonnes of Australia's annual greenhouse gas emissions. Nominee companies are employed to appear in official company documents as shareholders and may provide other services, but don't actually own the shares. A draft bill to establish a public beneficial ownership register of shareholders is before the Australian parliament, but it does not seek to regulate nominee shareholders. GEM warns that the lack of mandatory disclosure of the beneficial owners of public and private companies leaves the real ownership of "fossil fuel interests largely opaque". GEM's Global Energy Ownership Tracker monitors asset-level ownership chains of 48,000 energy assets, including coal mines and power plants. The Greens spokesperson on economic justice, Nick McKim, said that a beneficial owner registry with teeth would make nominee companies redundant. The Guardian sought comment from the Treasury, the Treasurer's office, Citibank, HSBC and JP Morgan, but received no responses prior to publication. (Guardian, Global Energy Monitor)

New Zero Banking Alliance collapses: The Net Zero Banking Alliance (NZBA), launched in April 2021 as a project convened by the United Nations Environment Programme, has collapsed following a spate of resignations after the election of President Donald Trump. The alliance sought voluntary commitments by its 150 bank members to align their lending practices with achieving the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting the global temperature increase to 1.5 degrees. Following Trump's election in November 2024, JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley, Wells Fargo, and Goldman Sachs announced their resignations from the group. Their departures were followed this year by European banks, including HSBC and Barclays, as well as Japanese banks. Lucie Pinson from Reclaim Finance said that the collapse of NZBA contributed little to curtailing the expansion of fossil fuels and said its purpose was "to create the illusion of measures in order to ward off the risk of regulation". Reclaim Finance's recent 'Banking on Business as Usual' report found that 65 of the world's largest banks allocated US$1.3 trillion to sustainable power sources, such as solar and wind and related infrastructure between 2021 and 2024. Over the same period, the banks provided US$3.2 trillion to fossil fuel projects. The report found that the French bank La Banque Postale was the only one surveyed that applied strong restrictions on fossil fuel projects, including coal plants. (Guardian, BankTrack, Reclaim Finance [Pdf])

Duke Energy pitches plan to delay coal closures to cater for data centres: In its 2025 plan for the Carolinas, Duke Energy proposes postponing the retirement of the dual coal and gas units at the 2.2 GW Belews Creek plant in North Carolina by four years to the end of 2039 to cater for the possibility of replacing it with new nuclear capacity. The utility also said that it is considering extending the life of the 658 MW Unit 3 and 660 MW Unit 4 at the Marshall plant in South Carolina, each of which can be co-fired with coal or gas. Duke proposes delaying the closure of the two units from the end of 2031 to 2033. It is also considering delaying the closure date of the 546 MW Cliffside Unit 5, another dual-fuel unit, from the end of 2030 to 2032. Duke Energy downgraded its forecast for new solar capacity, discounted wind generation as not viable before 2040, and increased its proposed gas and battery capacity. The utility said its proposal to delay coal closures is in response to North Carolina's cancellation of its 70 per cent interim carbon reduction goal, the easing of federal regulations, and accelerating demand growth. Duke Energy estimates electricity demand could increase by terawatt-hours (TWh) over the next 15 years, compared to a 10 TWh increase over the last 15 years. Meech Carter from the North Carolina League of Conservation Voters Foundation said much of the electricity demand increase is due to data centres. (Reuters, Inside Climate News, Duke Energy, Duke Energy [Pdf])

Financial analysts warn of risks with data centre investment bubble: An increasing number of financial analysts are warning of an investment "bubble" in data centres and Artificial Intelligence, and the risk of significant economic fallout, especially in the US. The rapid increase in estimated electricity demand is driving utilities to plan for delaying the closure of coal units. However, analysts point to the massive overvaluation of companies in the tech sector, some of which have negligible revenue streams and are increasingly relying on private equity funding. "I wouldn't touch this stuff now," said Dario Perkins from TS Lombard, a financial services firm. Morgan Stanley Wealth Management estimates that since OpenAI launched the ChatGPT large language model in late 2023, shares in the data centre and AI sector have accounted for about 75 per cent of S&P 500 returns. The sector also accounts for about 90 per cent of capital expenditure growth over that period. Julien Garra from MacroStrategy Partnership said the costs of training each generation of large language models are rising exponentially, but with a rapidly diminishing gain in accuracy. (Morningstar, Australian Financial Review [paywall], Axios, Union of Concerned Scientists)

Eskom 'profitability' achieved with government bailout, price hikes: Eskom's financial statement for the year to the end of March 2025 reveals a pre-tax profit of 23.9 billion rand (US$1.39 billion), a dramatic turnaround from the R25.5 billion (US$1.48 billion) loss the year before. Eskom management boasted that the first profit in eight years demonstrated that the utility is "increasingly a sustainable, investable company ready to compete in a liberalised, competitive energy market". However, further down in its report, Eskom noted that the utility's auditor expressed concern about its viability in light of its "dependence on government support, uncertainties related to operational assumptions and regulated revenue by NERSA, as well as growing municipal arrear debt and energy losses". Eskom recorded higher revenue, in part due to a 12.74 per cent increase in the standard tariff and lower interest repayments after a 64 billion rand (US$3.72 billion) government bailout. Increased plant availability and newly commissioned generation capacity brought an end to rolling blackouts that have plagued consumers for years. Eskom's debt is 373 billion rand (US$21.7 billion). Journalist Nick Hedley wrote that Eskom is "miles from being 'sustainable' and 'investable'" and noted that without state support, the utility "can't come close to serving its debts". (News24 [paywall], Eskom)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Malaysia unveils plan to cut steel industry emissions: Malaysia's Minister for Trade, Tengku Zafrul Aziz, unveiled a 10-year roadmap to transition to lower carbon emissions from the country's steel industry. The roadmap proposes carbon pricing as a measure to address the high level of emissions from the steel sector. Zafrul stated that the country's steel industry could experience significant overcapacity by 2030, with a projected production capacity of up to 40.8 million tonnes and domestic demand of just under 15 million tonnes. Zafrul proposed that Southeast Asia should collaborate on a common decarbonisation pathway to face changing market conditions. (Reuters)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

"The Perfect Storm Fueling Pakistan's Solar Boom", World Resources Institute, October 2025.

This article provides a concise overview of the dramatic increase in Pakistan's rooftop solar capacity over the past few years, which is on track to generate approximately 20 per cent of the country's electricity by 2026. A key driver in the transition was the high cost of power from imported coal and gas plants.

Connection costs: Loophole costs customers over $4 billion to connect data centers to power grid, Union of Concerned Scientists, September 2025. (Pdf)

This 8-page brief reveals how millions of electricity consumers in Illinois, Maryland, New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia will pay approximately US$4.3 billion for electricity infrastructure projects approved in 2024 to benefit data centres. This is in addition to an estimated US$9.3 billion in data centre electricity costs that customers supplied by PJM Interconnection, a network operator servicing 13 US states, will pay between June 2025 and June 2026.
