title: CoalWire 584, October 16, 2025
excerpt: Russian coal losses mount; US coal auction postponed, Bank of England flags financial risks of AI.
content:
October 16, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Russia and the US are both struggling to revive their declining coal mining sectors. In Russia, the international response to the invasion of Ukraine deprived exporters of access to traditional markets in Europe, with alternative Asian importers only buying shipments at heavily discounted rates. Accessing Asian markets to the east came at the cost of far higher transport costs. The recent decline in global thermal coal prices has piled further pressure onto exporters. As the war drags on, Russian coal companies are incurring mounting losses and shuttering some mines.

In the US, the Trump administration sought to sell federal coal leases in the hope of boosting production. One auction drew only one unsatisfactory bid, and another auction was postponed. A key justification promoted by utilities for extending the life of old US coal units is the projected increase in electricity demand growth required to support new data centres. Across the Atlantic, a key Bank of England committee has warned of the growing financial risks stemming from the overvaluation of US tech sector stocks.

In the Canadian province of British Columbia, the environmental regulator fined Elk Valley Resources C$3.6 million for more than 170 breaches of water pollution standards at its metallurgical coal mines. In South Africa, a new report highlights the lack of high-quality methane emissions data to underpin the development of a strategy to cut pollution from existing mines, let alone abandoned projects.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 The tycoons behind the Philippines' dirty energy

Tycoon-led conglomerates hold the power to accelerate—or obstruct—the Philippines' shift to clean and affordable electricity, writes Carmela Fonbuena from the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism.

 

 After Spain's blackout, critics blamed renewable energy. It's part of a bigger attack

A report by an expert panel of European grid operators on the April 2025 blackouts that affected Spain and Portugal has found that a voltage surge triggered the crisis, not a power grid with too much wind or solar, writes Julia Simon in NPR.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Canadian coal company fined C$3.6 million over wastewater pollution: The British Columbian Ministry of Environment and Parks fined Elk Valley Resources Operations C$3.6 million (US$2.6 million) for breaching the maximum selenium levels 47 times and nitrate limits 126 times between 2018 and 2022, and the failure to meet deadlines for the construction and operation of three water treatment plants. The ministry imposed the penalties on Teck Coal over the operation of its five metallurgical coal mines in the Elk Valley. The chair of the Ktunaxa Nation Council, Kathryn Teneese, said the fines confirmed a pattern of non-compliance by the company. Simon Wiebe, a spokesperson for Wildsight, an environmental NGO, said the penalties were far from the level required to act as a deterrent. In July 2024, Teck sold its Elk Valley Resources subsidiary to Glencore. (Business in Vancouver, Ministry of Environment and Parks [Pdf])

 

 Mongolian prosecutor says 88 people convicted on coal sector charges: The Mongolian Prosecutor's Office reported that a high-level working group oversaw investigations of 124 cases involving allegations of improper conduct in relation to coal mining, export, transportation and procurement. In late 2022, allegations of corruption in the country's booming coal trade with China, along with growing inequality and inflation, sparked mass mid-winter protests. In the wake of the protests, the government was under increasing pressure to act on allegations of corruption affecting high-level officials. The prosecutor's office filed charges against 108 individuals and three entities for offences including abuse of power and official position, bribery, illicit enrichment and money laundering. Of the 88 found guilty, 80 have been fined, five sentenced to serve prison terms, and 63 banned from holding public office for two to seven years. In 2023, the government also initiated selling coal produced by the state-owned coal mining company, Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi, via an online auction system operated by the Mongolian Stock Exchange to eliminate direct sales contracts. In 2024, Mongolia exported about 56 million tonnes of metallurgical coal, all of which was sold to companies in China. (The Star)

 

 South African study says data gap on coal mine methane emissions: A study by University of Cape Town researchers and Swaniti Global identified the urgent need for more accurate methane emissions data on South African mines. While South Africa is the world's seventh-largest coal producer, the country's official 2022 estimate of methane emissions is only 0.06 million tonnes. Estimates by the International Energy Agency, Global Energy Monitor and satellite data suggest methane emissions could be 7 to 14 times higher than the government estimate. The large gap between estimates reflects the lack of on-site measurements, a lack of fine-resolution satellite data and the lack of information on emissions from abandoned mines. The study identifies the lack of financial incentives to address methane emissions as a significant barrier and notes the potential to include mitigation strategies as part of just energy transition planning. The report notes that while six coal companies – Seriti, Exxaro, Thungela, Glencore, Sasol, and African Rainbow Minerals – produce more than 70 per cent of South Africa's coal, few disclose methane emissions data or have indicated interest in potential mitigation projects. (Mail & Guardian, Swaniti Global [Pdf])

 

 Alabama suspends methane monitoring to protect homes: Kathy Love, the director of the Alabama Surface Mining Commission, notified the federal Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement (OSME) that she has "indefinitely suspended" any requirement for methane monitoring plans above the Oak Grove Mine near Birmingham in Alabama. In March 2024, a gas explosion killed 74-year-old homeowner W.M. Griffice and seriously injured his grandson in the house above the mine, with Love later acknowledging in correspondence that the blast was "likely" caused by the ignition of methane produced by the mine. In December 2024, OSME issued a notice to the commission, requiring action to address the lack of methane monitoring. Earlier this year, Love informed mining companies in the state that they must submit plans by March 31 specifying measures taken to monitor methane gas in and near houses above their mines. This deadline was extended to September after the Alabama Mining Association objected to the requirement. In recent correspondence, Love wrote that she is seeking a formal review of OSME's notice, which she claimed is "not warranted or adequately supported and therefore should be withdrawn". (Inside Climate News)

 

 US coal miners protest delay in rule aimed at cutting black lung disease: Coal miners and supporters rallied outside the Washington DC office of the Department of Labor in protest at the delay in implementing a rule to cut the rising rate of black lung disease in the coal industry. In April 2024, the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) finalised the silica dust rule that reduced the allowable level of silica dust exposure for coal miners from 100 micrograms per cubic meter (g/m3) to 50 g/m3 of air during an eight-hour shift. The rule also mandates free medical screenings for workers for the early detection of black lung disease. The standard was due to come into effect in April 2025, but was delayed after the National Sand, Stone and Gravel Association (NSSGA) filed a legal challenge, arguing that the compliance costs would be too high. The National Mining Association said it supports the lower limit but wants to see a greater role for ventilators and personal protection equipment in meeting the limit, an approach rejected as ineffective by unions and lung health groups. The MSHA is negotiating with the NSSGA over the rule and sought to block unions and health groups from intervening in the court proceedings. (New York Times, Politico, Appalachian Voices)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Bundaberg residents have called on the Queensland government to cancel Fox Resources coal exploration lease after the company went into administration owing more than A$14 million (US$12.8 million).

 

 Australia: The conservative Queensland government unveiled an energy policy roadmap that assumes the completion of no new solar or wind capacity by 2030, beyond projects already under construction, contracted by Rio Tinto to supply its Gladstone aluminium plants or supported by the federal government.

 

 China: The government is on track to convert more than seven million households in northern China from using coal for heating to electric or gas by the end of October.

 

 Poland: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the government would unveil a plan aimed at saving "at least a significant part" of JSW, a state-owned metallurgical coal company.

 

 Poland: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the government would unveil a plan aimed at saving "at least a significant part" of JSW, a state-owned metallurgical coal company.

 

 US: Omaha's Republican Attorney-General has filed a lawsuit aiming to block Omaha Public Power District's plan to retire two coal units in 2026 and replace them with gas capacity. The units were commissioned in 1963 and 1968.

 

 US: John Quintrell, the owner of Kentucky coal company Civil LLC, pleaded guilty to federal charges of failing to collect and pay US$22 million in income and payroll taxes.

 

 US: Coalitions of NGOs and industry groups are urging regulators to reject the Midcontinent Independent System Operator's proposal to recover the cost of the continued operation of the 1.56 gigawatt (GW) J.H. Campbell plant in Michigan. The plant was due to close on May 31, but the Department of Energy ordered its continued operation.

 

 US: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law a bill blocking utilities from charging customers for their lobbying and PR campaigns.

 

 "War is bad for most of the Russian businesses, if not all of them. But the coal sector is in really deep shit,"

one of Russia's top businessmen told the Financial Times.

 
 

Companies + Markets

Russian coal industry losses mount: In the first seven months of 2025, Russia's coal industry recorded losses of 225 billion roubles (US$2.8 billion) due to declining export coal prices and rising transport costs. While exporters sought to counter the European Union ban on imports of Russian coal by switching exports to the Asian market, they did so by offering significant discounts on the global prices. The Financial Times estimates that coal was discounted by about 60 per cent in early 2022, just after the invasion of Ukraine, but is now about 20 per cent cheaper than global prices. Russian thermal coal transport costs rose from approximately 50 per cent of the sale price to 90 per cent as the rail network operator prioritised higher-value cargo, such as oil. While Russia succeeded in occupying coal mines in the Donbas region, private companies are turning the loss-making projects back over to the occupation governments. Pavlo Kukhta, Ukraine's former deputy Minister of the Economy, estimates government subsidies reached about US$1 billion a year before the war but ended after Russian forces seized the mines. "Now the industry is collapsing", he said. (Financial Times)

Bank of England flags risks of AI data centre bubble: The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee has warned that global financial markets are vulnerable to a "sharp market correction" as, on some indicators, share market valuations "appear stretched, particularly for technology companies focused on Artificial Intelligence (AI)". In the minutes of its latest meeting, the committee warned that equity valuations are "comparable to the peak of the dot com" boom and that equity markets are "particularly exposed should expectations around the impact of AI become less optimistic". Harris Kupperman, the founder of Praetorian Capital, a US-based hedge fund, said that he mistakenly underestimated the rate at which AI data centres would depreciate, making the financial prospects of the investments even more dire than he had previously thought. He said that he had initially assumed a depreciation of the data centres over 10 years, but after discussions with more than two dozen senior executives in the data centre sector revised the estimated rate of depreciation to "three to ten years, at most". In his most recent blog post, Kupperman said that the graphics processing units burn out quickly and are rapidly made obsolete by new designs. He also wrote that "changes to cooling systems, chip and racking designs, power systems, and even overall layouts, mean that the buildings themselves are likely depreciating quite rapidly as well". (Reuters, Bank of England, Futurism)

US agency suspends coal auction for Montana lease: The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) rejected a US$186,000 bid by the Navajo Transitional Energy Company (NTEC) for a 1262-acre (510-hectare) federal coal lease adjoining the Spring Creek mine in Montana. The proposed lease area contains an estimated 167 million US short tonnes (152 million tonnes) of thermal coal. BLM postponed the auction for an indefinite period. The Department of Interior said the auction was delayed because NTEC's bid didn't meet the requirements of the Mineral Leasing Act, which requires lease sales to reflect fair market value. An auction scheduled two days later for a lease over 3508 acres (1419 hectares) of land containing an estimated 365 million US short tons (331 million tonnes) of recoverable thermal coal in Wyoming was also postponed, with the department stating it would announce a new date. Trump administration officials blamed the lack of industry interest on the policies of the Obama and Biden administrations. The Sierra Club said that, faced with declining domestic demand, there is limited interest in expanding operations beyond current mines. (Reuters, WV News, Sierra Club)

Taiwanese utility imposes three-year ban on Glencore coal subsidiaries: Taiwans state-owned power utility, Taipower, has imposed a three-year ban on importing coal from two Glencore subsidiaries, Ulan Coal Mines and Mount Owen and HVO Coal Sales, a joint venture between Glencore and Yancoal. Yancoal is a subsidiary of the Yankuang Group Company, a Chinese state-owned mining company. The ban will remain in place until October 1, 2028. The decision affects five six-year-long contracts Taipower had entered into with the companies: three with HVO and two with Ulan Coal Mines. Taipower alleged that marketing managers for the three coal companies cited the annual reference price between Glencore and Tohoku Electric Power, which Taipower and other utilities in Southeast Asia use as a reference price for contract renegotiations. Taipower stated that the reference price had not been finalised at the time and argued that the marketing managers had misled them during the negotiations. Glencore, which has unsuccessfully challenged Taipower's December 2024 notification, said it disputes the utility's allegations and will pursue further legal action. (Argus)

NGO report urges tightening multilateral bank coal policies: A review of the coal lending policies of multilateral banks notes that the World Bank, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) lack some of the specific commitments included by the British International Investment and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank. Recourse, an international NGO working to reform global financial institutions, notes that policy loopholes allowed the IFC to provide indirect support for state-owned power utility PLN's Java 9 and 10 coal power plants in Indonesia. Each plant has a capacity of 1 GW. PLN has also received large loans from the ADB. Recourse note that IFC's Green Equity Approach states explicitly that it does not cover captive coal plants powering mining projects, smelters, cement or chemical industries. In Indonesia, IFC has supported private sector banks backing nickel smelters reliant on captive coal capacity, such as on Obi Island. (Recourse)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 US EPA backtracks on plan to delay coke oven pollution rule: The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has abandoned its bid to overturn a 2024 rule imposing new emissions limits on coke ovens, following a legal challenge by Earthjustice and the Environmental Integrity Project, which represents a coalition of community groups. In May 2024, the US EPA announced new emissions standards for coke ovens, which emit pollutants including mercury, arsenic, lead and benzene. Metallurgical coal is baked in the ovens to produce coke for use in steel production. The coke rule also required steel plants with coke ovens to monitor emissions at the fenceline of the plant and take action when pollution exceeds federal limits. In July this year, the EPA proposed delaying the deadline for compliance with the new rule until July 2027. The lawsuit argued that the EPA published its revised rule without allowing affected communities to object to the extension. The EPA chose not to defend the lawsuit but informed the court that companies could meet the original deadline. (Lakeshore Public Media, Earthjustice, Environmental Protection Agency)

 

 Swedish green steel seeks fresh funding: Stegra aims to raise an additional 975 million (US$1.1 billion) in equity, loans and from strategic partnerships to complete the construction of its hydrogen-based steel plant in northern Sweden. Stegra, formerly known as H2 Green Steel, is building a 690 MW electrolyser powered by renewables, a hydrogen-based direct reduction iron plant and two electric arc furnaces and other facilities. Stegra is aiming to commission the plant in the second half of 2026. In June 2024, the European Commission approved Sweden's 265 million (US$286 million) grant for the plant, and earlier this year, the company insisted the project was "fully funded". (Reuters)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Hard to abate: a justification for delay? The potential for reducing emissions from the iron and steel and cement sectors, Climate Analytics, October 2025. (Pdf)

This 63-page report dissects the use of the 'hard-to-abate' label as justification to delay action to cut emissions in the steel and cement industries. The report argues that while there are technical challenges, the decarbonisation of these sectors is highly achievable with existing and emerging technologies.

 

Bob Wyss, Black gold: The rise, reign, and fall of American coal, University of California Press, September 2025. (Hardcover US$28.95.)

This 312-page environmental history documents the growth of the US coal industry, the conflict with labour unions, the power of the mining industry in shaping public policies, its environmental legacies and current decline.

Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on April 28 2025, Expert Panel on the Grid Incident on April 28 2025, October 2025. (Pdf)

This 264-page report provides a technical account of the blackouts that affected Spain and Portugal in April 2025. The panel said a final report will establish the root causes of the incident.

Australian thermal coal producers are losing their growth markets, Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis, October 2025. (Pdf)

This 10-page briefing paper provides a concise overview of trends affecting coal demand in Southeast Asia and the implications for Australian coal exporters.

Black gold: The rise, reign, and fall of American coal
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on April 28 2025
Australian thermal coal producers are losing their growth markets

title: CoalWire 585, October 23, 2025
excerpt: Kenyan court blocks coal plant; another US coal auction scrapped; Venezuelan exports suspended.
content:
October 23, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The long campaign by Kenyan civil society groups against the country's first proposed Lamu power project has finally come to an end after a court upheld a lower court decision overturning the environmental permit for the project. The US government has encountered another setback in its plan to boost coal production by auctioning off federal coal leases. The Department of the Interior abandoned two Utah lease auctions after failing to attract bids that met the requirements of the Mineral Leasing Act.

In Venezuela, coal exports have ground to a halt after US military strikes on boats in the country's territorial waters. Venezuela's President Nicolas Maduro promoted the revival of mothballed coal mines for exports to offset the financial impact of US sanctions on the country's oil exports. The country's mines have a long history of major social and environmental effects. Despite the spectacular decline in solar prices, the Turkish government could spend US$8.7 billion over four years to subsidise power burning domestic coal. In Indonesia, a new report highlights the significant social and environmental impacts caused by the boom in nickel processing plants, which is driving the construction of numerous captive coal plants.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 China helped Indonesia build one of the world's biggest, youngest coal fleets. It's still growing.

Indonesia is one of the few countries still building new coal power plants, with Chinese companies playing a large role despite a pledge by Beijing to halt such support, writes Nicholas Kusnetz in Inside Climate News.

 

 Rail expansion plans spark clash between coal and tiger conservation

As the Indian government presses on with its plan to double an existing railway line between Goa and Karnataka for coal transport, it has clashed with conservationists over a 26-kilometre stretch cutting through two wildlife sanctuaries in the Western Ghats, which are known tiger habitat, writes Pamela D'Mello in Mongabay.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Campaigns

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Kenyan groups celebrate court ruling against coal plant

The chairperson of the Save Lamu campaign, Somo M. Somo, welcomed the decision of the Environment and Land Court rejecting an appeal by Amu Power against a lower court decision revoking an environmental license for the proposed 1.05 gigawatt (GW) Lamu coal power plant. "Justice for Lamu is justice for the planet. This ruling shows that when communities are heard, the law protects both people and nature," Somo said. In 2019, the National Environmental Tribunal revoked the environmental permit for the plant. Residents, farmers, and environmental groups objected to the pollution impacts of the proposed plant on farms, the climate, and the nearby Lamu Old Town World Heritage site, with Save Lamu and a coalition of NGOs challenging the permit for the plant. In the latest decision, Judge Francis Mwangi Njoroge supported the initial tribunal decision, stating that "public participation was not conducted in accordance with the amended provision of law". The court found "there was a failure to have a proper analysis of the location and project alternatives." Amu Power is a joint venture between Centum and Gulf Energy Ltd. (Kenyan News Agency, Daily Nation, Mining.com, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Venezuelan government push to expand coal exports: The sinking of five boats in Venezuelan waters by the US government has triggered the suspension of coal exports and coal mining operations, according to Reuters. Coal exports are exempt from US sanctions, prompting President Nicolas Maduro's push to revive coal production and diversify sources of export income as US sanctions curtail oil sales. In December 2024, production resumed at the Paso Diablo and Mina Norte mines operated by Carboturven, a joint venture between the state-owned Carbozulia and the Turkish company Glenmore Dis Ticaret Ve Madencilik A.S. Maduro also approved the development of a new mine in Falcon state in the country's north. In the first quarter of 2025, coal production reached three million tonnes, with Maduro pushing for exports of 10 million tonnes this year. Sociedad Homo et Natura, a Venezuelan environmental non-profit, said the coal mines have resulted in heavy metal pollution of the Guasare River and have a long history of displacing indigenous communities. "They are trying to get their hands on everything they can," said Lusbi Portillo, the coordinator of Sociedad Homo et Natura. (Reuters)

 

 Subsidence hits villages near Bangladesh underground coal mine: Thirteen villages near the Barapukuria coal mine have been affected by significant land subsidence, according to the Basat Bari Rakkha Committee, which represents local communities. Abul Kalam Azad from the committee said that the western side of the village of Patrapara had subsided by 30 to 35 feet (9 to 10 metres) and 1 to 1.5 feet (0.3 to 0.5 metres) on the eastern side. Subsidence has caused significant structural damage to houses and affected farms and roads in the area. At a media conference, the villagers warned of increasing protests unless the company took action to address their demand for compensation for damaged properties, access to drinking water and jobs for the youth of families affected by subsidence. The mine, the only coal mine in Bangladesh, is operated by Barapukuria Coal Mining Company (BCM), a subsidiary of the state-owned Bangladesh Oil, Gas and Mineral Corporation (Petrobangla). Abu Tayeb Farazi, the managing director of BCM, said compensation will be available once funds are released. The mine commenced production in 2005 and supplies coal to the Barapukuria power station. (Dhaka Tribune)

 

 Report finds Indonesian nickel boom comes at a cost: A report by Climate Rights International (CRI) found patterns of widespread air and water pollution, health impacts and dangerous working conditions in Indonesia's nickel mining and processing sectors. The researchers interviewed 93 people working in, and living near, nickel mines and smelters in Southeast Sulawesi, Central Sulawesi, and North Maluku provinces. Farmers and residents reported forced relocations and, for those who spoke out, threats from security forces. The number of nickel smelters in the country has surged from 2 in 2016 to more than 60. Data from the Global Energy Monitor estimates that there is 11.6 GW of captive coal capacity with nickel plants, with an additional 5.5 GW under construction and 1.5 GW in the pre-permit stage. The plants do not provide electricity for local communities. CRI reports that captive coal plants are not subject to individual environmental impact assessments and do not report greenhouse gas emissions. Residents also complain of the lack of information about new projects. One resident living near the Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park was informed that the company was constructing a canteen. "It turned out to be a coal plant," she said. (Globe and Mail, Climate Rights International, Climate Rights International [Pdf])

 

 Indian court rules forest rights can be revoked for coal: The Chhattisgarh High Court ruled against Hasdeo Arand Bachao Sangharsh Samiti and other civil society groups that challenged a decision by a district-level committee to revoke community forest rights allocated in 2013 to villagers of Ghatbarra in the Hasdeo Arand forest. The court ruled that the district could rescind the rights granted after the allocation of the area in 2012 to state-owned Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Limited (RVUNL). Adani Mining is the mining operator for RVUNL of the Parsa East and Kete Basen coal mines. Jairam Ramesh, the general secretary of the Congress party and a former Minister for Environment, said the judge's statement that the allocation of forest rights does not interfere with state rights to minerals over minerals underneath the forest is "a strange perversion of logic and justice". Ramesh said that forest rights grant villagers access to forest produce, which cannot be separate from the land. "The Court has now made this right conditional on Government policy. This is a dangerous verdict that undermines the entire foundation of the Forest Rights Act," he said. (The Hindu, The Hindu)

 

 
 "We are poor communities that live by [goat] herding, and the animals are dying from the [coal] dust We live in extreme poverty surrounded by coal wealth,"

said an Indigenous person from La Guajira in Venezuela.

 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Coronado Curragh, a subsidiary of Coronado Global Resources, was fined A$80,000 (US$52,000) for the death of Clark Peadon, a mine worker crushed by a dragline at the Curragh mine in Queensland in November 2021. The Mining and Energy Union said the fine was not enough.

 

 China: Chinese imports of coal from Mongolia surged to 9.29 million tonnes in September, up 33 per cent on the year before and the highest monthly amount since 2015.

 

 India: The Delhi High Court ruled that revenue obtained from a coal block secured by alleged misrepresentation and fraud is considered proceeds of crime under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.

 

 "The process violated Articles 42 and 69 of the Constitution, which guarantee every Kenyan the right to a clean and healthy environment Public participation, environmental protection, and respect for constitutional rights cannot be overlooked in pursuit of unsustainable projects," 

said Judge Francis Mwangi Njoroge, who rejected the appeal of Amu Power.

 
 

Companies + Markets

US abandons another coal lease auction: The Department of the Interior rejected a bid by a subsidiary of Wolverine Fuels LLC for two coal leases in the Manti-La Sal National Forest in Utah because the bids did not meet the requirements of the Mineral Leasing Act. The legislation requires companies to pay a fair market price for federal coal. The two leases contain about 6.5 million US short tons (5.9 million tonnes) of coal. The abandoned sale is the third cancelled auction after the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) rejected a US$186,000 bid by the Navajo Transitional Energy Company (NTEC) for an estimated 167 million US short tonnes (152 million tonnes) of thermal coal in a lease adjoining the Spring Creek mine in Montana. Another auction for a lease containing an estimated 365 million US short tons (331 million tonnes) of recoverable thermal coal in Wyoming was also recently postponed. (Associated Press)

Turkiye plans billions in subsidies for plants burning domestic coal: A report by Ember, a climate policy think tank, estimates that the Turkish government could provide up to US$8.7 billion over four years to 2030 to subsidise coal power generation utilising domestic coal. In September, the government announced that power utilities will be eligible from 2026 to receive US$75 per megawatt hour (MWh) for 60 per cent of the electricity generated from domestic coal. Ember said US$75 per MWh is 12 per cent above the average electricity sales price (US$67 per MWh) over the past year and 36 per cent higher than the US$55 per MWh cost of power from domestic coal plants. Ember argues funding would be better directed to supporting grid upgrades and facilitating new solar capacity to help reach Turkiye's target of 120 GW of wind and solar capacity by 2035. (Turkiye Today, Ember)

Report says A$398m royalty underpayment from Adani's Australian mine: An analysis by the Australia Institute estimates the Queensland government may have been underpaid over the last three years by about A$398 million (US$258 million) in royalties on coal from Adani's Carmichael mine. The institute analysed corporate and government data and found that in 2023, Adani sold coal from the Carmichael mine for about A$102 per tonne (US$66 per tonne) at a time when the expected market price would have been about A$282 per tonne (US$183 per tonne) even after allowing a 30 per cent discount because of the low coal quality. In August 2025, the Queensland Government and Adani settled an ongoing legal dispute that commenced under the previous government regarding royalty payments on coal from the mine. The exact details of the matters in dispute remain secret. An Adani spokesperson said that the analysis relied on incorrect assumptions and "mismatched data". (Guardian, Australia Institute, Australia Institute [Pdf])

Report queries potential for carbon credits in Philippines coal transition: A report by Reclaim Finance and the Center for Energy, Ecology and Development (CEED) questions the effectiveness of two pilot carbon credit schemes in the Philippines promoted as helping finance the early retirement of coal plants. The report argues that both the 270 MW SLTEC power station on Luzon Island and the 232 MW Mindanao STEAG plant were already slated for early retirement before Carbon Transition Offsets (CTO) were available. The groups query how backers can quantify the impact of a new revenue stream on coal unit retirements and highlight the risk that additional funding may extend the life of coal plants. The Monetary Authority of Singapore's Transition Credits Coalition (Traction) and the Rockefeller Foundation's Coal to Clean Credit Initiative (CCCI) developed the CTO pilot scheme. Verra, a non-profit certifier of carbon offsets, released a methodology in May outlining options to allow the creation of "high-integrity transition credits" to allow the financing of coal plant retirements. (Reclaim Finance)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Coal Mine Methane Data Tracker, Ember, October 2025.

This tracker includes data on country-by-country coal mine methane emissions, projections and production data. A video explaining the tracker is available here.

US Pension Proxy Guidelines Tracker, Sierra Club, 2025.

This interactive tracker rates the proxy voting guidelines issued by major US public pension funds, including their policies on political lobbying, climate resolutions and just transition policy.

Steel Climate Impact 2025: An International Benchmarking of Energy and GHG Intensities, Global Efficiency Intelligence, October 2025. (Pdf)

This 40-page report details the energy and greenhouse gas intensity of steel production in the largest steel-producing countries and regions. It also includes a separate breakdown for blast furnace-based production and the electric arc furnace sector.

The Indian Steel Majors: Measuring Transition, Carbon Transition Analytics and Carbon Tracker, October 2025. (Pdf; registration required.)

This 22-page report assesses the transition performance of the major Indian steel producers, JSW Steel, Tata Steel, JSPL, and ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel India.

links.text: Steel Climate Impact 2025: An International Benchmarking of Energy and GHG Intensities
The Indian Steel Majors: Measuring Transition

title: CoalWire 586, October 30, 2025
excerpt: Morocco sets 2040 coal end date; Saskatchewan says extending life of coal plants is a ‘bridge’ to nuclear; Mongolian political turmoil after change on mineral royalty rates.
content:
October 30, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

Morocco's announcement that it plans to phase out coal by 2040 is welcome news ahead of the next global climate conference. Morocco said that it wants international financial support to accelerate the retirement of its four coal plants, but will still aim for the 2040 end date even without additional assistance.

A new report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air suggests that China, India, and Indonesia could peak their coal power use this decade by expanding support for clean energy. For China and India, which have already made substantial progress in building new wind and solar capacity, the policy and practical challenges are less formidable than in Indonesia, a major thermal coal exporter to both countries. Indonesian coal producers have flourished in a booming Asian market but face an uncertain future as prices fall and growth slows.

Meanwhile, Mongolia's government faces turmoil over changes to coal royalties that could undermine its ability to fund infrastructure projects and social welfare policies. The proposed change comes on top of public protests against growing inequality and corruption scandals in the coal industry. In Canada, the Saskatchewan governments wants to extend the life of ageing coal plants to 2050 as a "bridge" to new nuclear capacity. For decades, utilities have touted coal plants as reliable suppliers of electricity. The latest counterpoint is the 12-year-old 932 MW Sandy Creek plant in Texas. After an as yet unexplained breakdown in April, the plant is likely to remain offline until March 2027.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Coal plants emitted more pollution during the 2018 US government shutdown, while regulators were furloughed

As soon as the 2018 US government shutdown began, coal-fired power plants started producing about 15 per cent to 20 per cent more particle pollution. And as soon as the government reopened and inspections resumed, pollution levels dropped, write Ruohao Zhang from Penn State University, Huan Li from North Carolina A&T State University and Neha Khanna from the State University of New York in The Conversation.

 

 Debt problems that dogged Sen. Jim Justice as West Virginia's governor continue to nip at his heels

The trail of debts — and claims made trying to collect them — that dogged Jim Justice well before he became West Virginia's two-term Republican governor has ballooned since the former billionaire became a US senator earlier this year, writes John Raby in AP.

 

 The terrible price of speaking the truth and the human cost of justice delayed

Five years after the assassination of Fikile Ntshangase, an environmental activist who challenged a coal mining expansion that has displaced and continues to displace communities near the Hluhluwe-iMfolozi Game Reserve in South Africa, no one has been arrested for her murder, writes Kirsten Youens in Daily Maverick.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Morocco sets 2040 end date for coal plants: In its latest national climate plan, Morocco committed to phase out coal use in the power sector by 2040, subject to adequate international support for the early closure of plants and the "management of contractual commitments". Morocco's Nationally Determined Contribution submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change said that without international support, it would provide an "unconditional commitment" to ending the use of coal by the 2040s. Morocco has four coal plants with a combined capacity of 4.1 gigawatts (GW). The 1.39 GW Safi coal plant was commissioned in 2018 and is 50.7 per cent owned by Nareva, a subsidiary of Al Mada, the holding company of King Mohammed VI, with the Japanese trading company Mistui holding a 30 per cent stake. Morocco has also committed to tripling renewable energy capacity to more than 15 GW by 2030, upgrading the grid and adding new storage capacity. (Climate Home News, Powering Past Coal Alliance, Morocco [Pdf, French])

 

 Report says China, India, and Indonesia could peak emissions soon: A report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) said greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector in China, India and Indonesia could peak this decade if they continue and extend their support for clean energy generation. In China, power sector emissions have fallen since early 2024. However, the recently stated target of 3600 GW of solar and wind capacity by 2035 implies installing just 200 GW of new wind and solar per year, down from 360 GW in 2024, a level that would be unlikely to cover the projected increase in demand and reduce fossil fuel generation unless growth rates slow. CREA estimates Indian emissions could peak if it meets its 2030 target to install 500 GW of non-fossil generation capacity, but this requires 50 GW of new clean generation capacity as year for the rest of the decade. In Indonesia, achieving President Prabowo's 100 GW solar goal would see emissions peak and then fall, but questions remain about the ability to implement a scheme focussed on small-scale installations in rural areas. Indonesia's latest power development plan downgraded the role of new clean energy capacity, and the potential for rooftop solar was constrained in 2024 by the imposition of a limited annual quota for new installations. The report notes that as clean energy generation increases, there is likely to be increased political resistance from well-entrenched coal mining and power utilities. (CREA)

 

 US coal unit to be offline for two years after a serious failure: The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) said the 932 MW Sandy Creek plant in Texas will remain offline until March 2027 after a major breakdown in April. The plant was commissioned in May 2013 after years of community opposition and legal challenges by the Sierra Club. ERCOT initially said that the unit would remain offline until June 1, 2026. The nature of the damage to the plant, which commenced operation in 2013, has not been disclosed. The Institute for Energy Economics & Financial Analysis (IEEFA) said the plant was shut down in February, a common time for maintenance work ahead of peak summer loads, and restarted on April 22. The unit suffered a severe failure late on April 23 and has not restarted since. IEEFA said the extended outage would impose considerable costs on the owners and highlighted the reliability risks of fossil-fuelled power plants, as well as the need for more wind, solar and battery capacity. (IEEFA, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 Mongolian government in turmoil over royalty rate change: Mongolia's Constitutional Court ruled that a parliamentary vote to oust Prime Minister Zandanshatar Gombojav was unconstitutional, upholding President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa's veto of the dismissal. The trigger for the motion to dismiss Zandanshatar was a switch from levying mineral royalty rates on international benchmark prices to lower domestic prices. The change would significantly reduce government revenue, particularly from coal exports to China, while boosting mining companies' profitability. In 2024, Mongolia exported about 80 million tonnes of coal, with about 90 per cent of it transported to China. In a mid-September analysis, the International Monetary Fund noted that coal exports fell "markedly" in the first half of 2025 and that producers experienced a "sharp" price decline. Reduced coal royalty income will undermine the country's financial ability to invest in infrastructure and key social policy initiatives. The government also faces continued public pressure to implement integrity measures following protests in 2022 over corruption in the coal industry, which the Independent Anti-Corruption Agency confirmed involved high-level officials. (Reuters, Government of Mongolia, International Monetary Fund)

 

 Polish utility reaches agreement with unions on redundancy package: The state-owned power utility PGE has reached an agreement with unions on a 250 million zloty (US$69 million) package for workers affected by the impending closure of 908 MW of coal units at the Dolna Odra. Two coal units will cease operation by the end of this year, with two other units scheduled for retirement in August 2026. PGE agreed to give those opting to continue working priority for positions elsewhere within the group's operations. Workers within four years of retirement are guaranteed 80 per cent of their salary, while workers opting for voluntary redundancy are eligible for payments of up to 400,000 zloty (US$110,000) each. (Notes from Poland)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: The Mining and Energy Union has urged SIMEC, a subsidiary of Sanjeev Gupta's embattled GFG Alliance, to restart its Tahmoor mine, which has been mothballed since February or sell the project. Rstar, a labour-hire contractor that employs 250 workers at the mine, said it can no longer afford to pay them.

 

 India: Farmers protesting at South Eastern Coalfields Limited Gevri mine in Chhattisgarh said police baton-charged people peacefully calling for employment, rehabilitation, and compensation for the impacts of the mine on their land.

 

 India: NTPC, which generates about one-quarter of India's electricity, has agreed with Engineers India Limited to develop a coal-to-synthetic natural gas plant. NTPC proposes processing high-ash coal from its mines.

 

 Japan: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and President Trump signed a trade agreement in Tokyo that notes a multi-year deal between Tohoku Electric Power and the Global Coal Sales Group to buy more than US$100 million worth of thermal coal. The Global Coal Sales Group is the marketing subsidiary of Signal Peak Energy, a Montana coal producer.

 

 Philippines: The Secretary of Energy, Sharon Garin, said the Department of Energy will sign an implementation agreement with Singapore by February 2026 on a transition credit mechanism to retire coal-fired power plants.

 

 US: The South Carolina Occupational Safety and Health Administration dropped a US$3,500 fine against Santee Cooper after a bulldozer driver died in a collapse of a coal mound at the 1260 MW Winyah Generating Station. Santee Cooper said the contractor who employed the man reported the death but agreed to report future incidents jointly.

 

 US: More than a dozen loaded coal wagons in a 53-car CSX train derailed in Providence Forge, Virginia. Coal from the derailed wagons spilled onto the tracks and into a creek. An unknown amount of diesel also spilled from two locomotives.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Report says Chinese investors top support for metallurgical coal projects: A report by the German NGO Urgewald estimates that major financial institutions provided almost US$52 billion in support for the expansion of metallurgical coal projects between 2022 and 2024. Urgewald said the support comprised US$22 billion in loans and underwriting and US$30.2 billion in securities from institutional investors. The largest investors are three US-headquartered financial management firms: Vanguard, BlackRock, and State Street. The report notes that 201 banks financed metallurgical coal project developers, with Chinese institutions accounting for US$14.7 billion, or 67 per cent of global funding, and US firms providing US$3 billion. The report found that the largest lenders for metallurgical coal projects are China Everbright, CITIC, CSC Financial, and Jefferies Financial Group. (Mining.com, Urgewald [Pdf])

New South African power plan touts 'clean coal' demonstration plant: South Africa's latest Integrated Resource Plan (IRP 2025) was gazetted on October 24 and proposes a 'clean coal' demonstration plant by 2030 as a "potentially cheaper and more efficient" alternative to the installation of flue gas desulphurisation units on Eskom's coal plants. The plan envisages the retirement of 8 GW of old Eskom coal plants by 2039 and the installation of 34 GW of onshore wind, 25 GW of utility-scale solar, and 8.5 GW of storage. It also envisages 16 GW of distributed generation, mostly rooftop solar. The plan anticipates 6 GW of new gas plants by 2030, potentially rising to 16 GW by 2039. The plan sets a minimum load factor of 50 per cent for the new gas plants in a bid to underwrite the cost of new gas infrastructure for industrial customers. The plan also proposes between 5.2 GW and 10 GW of new nuclear capacity by 2039, a technology long backed by some unions and the ANC, despite the prohibitive costs. Energy consultant Clyde Mallinson estimates the government's heavy emphasis on gas and nuclear generation could result in electricity prices 60 per cent to 70 per cent higher than an alternative plan based on renewables. "In today's terms, that's roughly R250 billion (US$15 billion) per year in wasted money," he said. (News 24, BusinessTech, Department of Mineral Resources and Energy)

Canadian provincial government unveils plan to keep coal going to 2050: The Government of Saskatchewan unveiled a power development plan centred on refurbishing all operating and mothballed coal and lignite plants to extend their lifespans to 2050. The Saskatchewan First Energy Security and Supply Plan backs the construction of two 300 MW GE-Hitachi small modular reactors near Estevan, the city that hosts the current Shand and Boundary Dam coal plants and the Estevan mine. The plan also envisages the potential development of large-scale nuclear plants. The plan proposes refurbishing the 139 MW Units 4 and 5, which were mothballed in 2021 and 2024, respectively, and extending their lifespans to 2050. The plan proposes upgrading the 284 MW Unit 6 at the Boundary Dam plant, which was scheduled to close in 2027, and operating it until 2050. The plan also proposes extending the life of the two 291 MW units at the Poplar River plant to 2050, from their scheduled retirement dates of 2031 and 2033. "That (coal) is going to be the bridge by which we get to that nuclear future," said Jeremy Harrison, the Minister responsible for SaskPower, the state-owned power utility. In June, the Saskatchewan government announced its intention to defy the federal regulation phasing out coal generation by 2030. At the time, the Saskatchewan government said only that the life of the coal units would be extended to coincide with the completion of a small modular reactor or a conventional nuclear plant in the 2030s. "(Global News, Saskatoon StarPhoenix, Government of Saskatchewan [Pdf])

Canadian provincial government settles coal leases compensation claim: The Alberta government agreed to pay C$95 million (US$68 million) to Evolve Power to settle a C$1.75 billion (US$1.27 billion) legal claim over the cancellation of two coal leases on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains. As part of its settlement, Montem Resources, a subsidiary of Evolve Power, agreed to surrender the Chinook and Greenfield coal leases but has retained the Tent Mountain lease. At Tent Mountain, the company wants to redevelop an old flooded mine pit as part of a pumped hydro project. A spokesperson for Energy Minister Brian Jean said the government "has no intention to further lease" the rights the company surrendered. In May 2020, the Alberta government lifted the moratorium on coal exploration on the Eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains, but after a sustained public backlash, largely reinstated it in 2022. Following the backflip, five coal companies, including Evolve Power, filed legal claims seeking a combined C$15 billion (US$10.9 billion) in damages. In July, the Alberta government paid Atrum Coal, a small Australian coal exploration company, C$142.8 million (US$103.75) in compensation for surrendering its Elan Coal leases. (CBC, Evolve Power)

European Commission approves delay in Romanian coal plant closures: The European Commission approved Romania's request to delay the closure of 900 MW of coal capacity across three plants until the end of 2029 due to delays in building replacement gas capacity. Romania's Minister of Energy, Bogdan Ivan, said two other coal plants will continue operating until the end of August 2026. Romania's original National Recovery and Resilience Plan included a commitment to retire 1.76 GW of coal capacity by the end of 2025. Two combined-cycle gas plants with a combined capacity of 1.33 GW are proposed in the same towns as the 660 MW Turceni lignite plant and the mothballed 315 MW Isalnita coal plant. (Romania Insider, Balkan Green Energy News)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

title: CoalWire 587, November 6, 2025
excerpt: China’s overseas coal plant spree slows; Japanese utility accelerates coal plant closure; coal ships identified as major threat to endangered Indonesian dolphin
content:
November 6, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

The latest review of China's qualified ban on new overseas coal plants indicates a continued decline in proposed projects, but the loophole allowing support for new captive coal plants remains. Many of the 14 new Chinese-backed coal power projects under construction are captive plants. In Japan, J-Power, one of the largest power utilities, announced the retirement of two coal units a year earlier than planned. In Indonesia, government officials said they intend to exclude coal barges from tributaries of the Mahakam River in a late bid to save the critically endangered Mahakam dolphin. In Canada, a federal agency has ordered an assessment of the likely impacts of extending the Fording River mine in British Columbia, one of four Elk Valley mines that have caused a major selenium pollution problem.

In Poland, the government said it will table a bill to ease the process of coal mine closures and provide some support for affected workers. It is a measure that is vulnerable to the veto power of the country's pro-coal president. In South Africa, the government's latest power plan proposes a central role for the most expensive new generation options – coal, gas and nuclear – at the expense of a far greater role for the cheapest options of solar, wind and batteries.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Alberta's big payouts to spurned Australian coal miners

The Alberta government has paid C$238 million (US$169 million) to two Australian coal mining companies to settle compensation claims over mining licences on the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains. Taxpayers face more such hits, writes Andrew Nikiforuk in The Tyee.

 

 For years, residents opposed the Atimonan coal plant in the Philippines. It's been greenlit anyway.

The Philippines Department of Energy recently exempted the proposed 1.2 gigawatt (GW) Atimonan power project from the country's moratorium on new coal plants despite opposition from community groups and the Catholic church, writes Iya Gozum in Rappler.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 More Chinese-backed overseas coal plants cancelled in 2024: The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) and the People of Asia for Climate Solutions (PACS) estimate that new overseas coal plants backed by China declined from nearly 50 GW in 2024 to 31.4 GW as of July 2025. The groups estimate companies cancelled 16.4 GW of new capacity in 2025 and 4.1 GW of new plants commenced operation in 2024. Since President Xi Jinping's September 2021 pledge to end China's financing of overseas coal projects, CREA estimates proponents cancelled a total of 59.3 GW of projects. The report notes that 14 new Chinese-backed coal power projects are under construction with a combined capacity of 12.1 GW. Most of these projects are captive coal projects in Indonesia, India, Laos, Zimbabwe, and Zambia, serving industrial projects backed by private Chinese companies. CREA and PACS argue that the 2021 policy should be updated to include captive coal projects and that a specific government agency should be assigned responsibility for ensuring the implementation of Xi's policy. (Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air [Pdf])

 

 Japanese utility brings coal closures forward: J-Power, one of the largest Japanese utilities, announced plans to close the two 250 MW coal units at the Takasago Thermal Power Station by the end of the 2028 financial year, which runs until the end of March 2029. The two units commenced operation in July 1968 and January 1969 respectively. J-Power said the closure was part of its plan to retire "inefficient" coal units and achieve greenhouse gas emission reductions of 46 per cent from a 2013 baseline. J-Power President Hitoshi Kanno said the 700-MW No. 3 unit at Takehara and the 1 GW No. 1 unit at Matsuura are candidates for future closure. These units were commissioned in 1983 and 1990. In May 2024, J-POWER said the two units would be retired by the end of the 2030 financial year. (Reuters, J-Power [Pdf])

 

 Coal ships identified as major threat to endangered Indonesian dolphin: Indonesia's Minister of Environment, Hanif Faisol Nurofiq, said coal shipping is a major threat to the future of the critically endangered Mahakam dolphin. Nurofiq said the environment ministry is working with the Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries "to halt coal transportation through tributaries" of the Mahakam River. Only 64 individual Mahakam dolphins remain, and they are now primarily confined to tributaries of the Mahakam River. Several years ago, environmental groups proposed that the government designate a conservation area in the Mahakam catchment, including the known dolphin habitat. (Antara)

 

 Canadian metallurgical coal project called in for further assessment: Following a review of Elk Valley Resources (EVR) 's proposed 35-year extension to the life of the Fording River mine, the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC) decided the project requires further assessment. EVR, a wholly owned Canadian subsidiary of Glencore, has proposed a new mine on Castle Mountain to produce about 10 million tonnes of coal a year from 2030. The IAAC said that, after an initial round of public comment, further assessment of the project is required, including potential impacts on fish, migratory birds, water pollution, and the exercise of Indigenous rights. Simon Wiebe from the environmental NGO Wildsight said the Elk Valley "has already sacrificed more than enough". An earlier version of the proposal, when Teck Coal owned the Fording River mine, was rejected by the Ktunaxa Nations due to concerns about water pollution. The mine, along with three other EVR projects in the valley, has caused high levels of selenium emissions that flow across the border into the US. (Vancouver Sun, Wildsight, Impact Assessment Agency of Canada)

 

 Israeli government agencies push to extend life of Hadera coal plant: Israel's Electricity Authority wants a three-year life extension for the coal units at the state-owned Orot Rabin power station in Hadera, despite a pledge to close them in 2025. The Independent Systems Operator, which operates the grid, suggested keeping the units online for another 10 years as an option. The four coal units at the plant were commissioned in the early 1980s and have a combined capacity of 1500 MW. In August 2016, the then Minister for Energy, Yuval Steinitz, said the coal units would close by June 2022, with the government backing their conversion to operate on gas from as yet undeveloped gas fields. Studies estimate the power plant causes between 50 and 250 annual premature deaths a year. A member of Hadera city council recently told a parliamentary committee that coal dust from the plant covers houses and cars in the nearby residential area of Hefsiba. "We can only imagine what it does for their lungs, their life expectancy," he said. In Malta, human rights organisations called on the government to block a Maltese-flagged ship allegedly readying to transport a 170,000-tonne cargo of coal to Israel. (Times of Israel, MaltaToday, Global Energy Monitor)

 

 South African power plan pursues life extensions for old coal plants: The Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) recently launched by the Minister for Electricity, Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, assumes life extensions for many old Eskom coal plants from 50 years to 60 years. The IRP suggested the life extensions are required as "it may be onerous" to add other new generating capacity to fill the gap of retiring plants. The IRP also assumes coal plants will operate at a capacity factor of 68 per cent, far higher than if 50 GW of new wind and solar is added by 2030 and the government presses ahead with a competitive electricity market. Climate and energy writer Nick Hedley argues that the IRP estimates 28.7 GW of new solar, 43 GW of wind and 8.2 GW of energy storage, far less than independent least cost electricity modelling suggests is necessary, with higher prices forced on consumers as a result of assumed high utilisation of expensive new gas plants and nuclear capacity. (News24 [paywall])

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: Liberty Primary Metals Australia (LPMA), a subsidiary of Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance, which operates the Tahmoor metallurgical coal mine in New South Wales, has entered voluntary administration. LPMA has more than A$100 million (US$65 million) in outstanding debts, including A$30 million (US$19.4 million) in royalties owed to the NSW government.

 

 Australia: BHP has agreed to transfer 3700 hectares of its Mt Arthur mine lease to allow Malabar Resources to extend the operation of its Maxwell underground metallurgical project. In return, BHP will store tailings in disused parts of Malabar's Maxwell underground site.

 

 India: A Delhi court dismissed charges against the former Secretary of Coal, H C Gupta and joint secretary K S Kropha over the allocation of the Fatehpur East coal block in Chhattisgarh to R.K.M. Powergen. The court also dismissed charges against the company's director and managing director.

 

 Indonesia: The government is backing the development of a coal-based Dimethyl Ether (DME) plant in East Kutai, East Kalimantan, and is assessing two gasification technologies for the project.

 

 Philippines: Aboitz Power has agreed to buy a 25 per cent stake in Van Phong Power from Sumitomo for about US$220 million, subject to regulatory approval. Van Phong Power owns the 1.3 GW Van Phong power station in Khanh Hoa province in southern Vietnam.

 

 North Korea: The US State Department wants a UN Security Council committee to impose sanctions on seven ships suspected of illegally exporting North Korean coal and iron ore to China.

 

 US: A federal court order against three coal companies owned by the family of West Virginia Republican Senator Jim Justice allows the seizure of property worth US$150,000 to settle unpaid premiums into a union retiree health benefit plan.

 

 US: Consumers Energy said it had cost more than US$80 million to keep the 1.56 GW J.H. Campbell plant in Michigan operating since its scheduled May 31 closure. The Trump administration issued an emergency order to keep the coal plant operating.

 

 US: Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved Duke Energy's plan to convert two 531 MW coal units at the Cayuga Generating Station to burn gas. Duke Energy also reached a settlement agreement with Reliable Energy, a group representing Indiana coal producers, for a feasibility study on the operation of the retired coal units by third parties.

 

 US: The Virginia Department of Environmental Quality confirmed that the derailment of a CSX train resulted in 4000 gallons (15,140 litres) of diesel fuel and about 4000 US short tons (3629 tonnes) of coal spilling into wetlands next to the Chickahominy River in Virginia.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Polish bill to ease coal closures faces uncertain future: The Polish government has agreed to submit a bill to parliament to provide state funding for the decommissioning of coal mines, transfer closed mine sites to local authorities or state utilities and guarantee severance payments of 170,000 zloty (US$46,100) for affected workers. The Minister for Energy, Milosz Motyka, said the bill will also include provisions to prevent the diversion of state subsidies from cutting coal production to underwriting operating costs. The bill's adoption is far from certain. While the government has a majority in parliament, legislation is subject to the veto power of pro-coal President Karol Nawrocki. (Notes from Poland)

Bangladesh dispute with Adani Power on track for international tribunal: Muhammad Fouzul Kabir Khan, a key adviser to Bangladesh's interim government, said it remains committed to negotiations with Adani Power over disagreements on a 25-year power purchase agreement for power from the 1.6 GW Godda plant in Jharkhand and will only proceed to arbitration "if needed". Adani Power has indicated it wants to pursue arbitration. Anonymous Bangladesh Power Development Board sources said the company has requested the board nominate a mediator, an indicator that Adani Power intends to file a case before the Singapore International Arbitration Centre. The power agreement was signed in 2017 by the government led by Sheikh Hasina, who was deposed in August 2024 by a public rebellion against her autocratic rule. In a separate development, the Indian government approved Adani Power's bid to connect its 1.6 GW Godda coal plant in Jharkhand to the national grid via a new transmission line. The Godda plant is in a Special Economic Zone that provides Adani with favourable tax concessions. The Bangladeshi government appointed a committee to review all power sector contracts entered into by the Hasina government, including Adani Power's. (Reuters, Business Standard, Times of India)

Adani says it won a coal power tender for Assam: Adani Power executives told investors during a quarterly earnings call that the company had submitted the lowest bid for a new 3.2 GW coal power tender for Assam. Adani executives told investors that the company plans to expand its thermal power portfolio from 18 GW to 41.87 GW by 2032, with 23.72 GW of new projects. The company said that construction is well advanced on brownfield expansions, including the Mahan Phase-II, Raipur Phase-II, and Raigarh Phase-II, each with a capacity of 1.6 GW. Adani Power told investors it is pursuing new power purchase agreements in Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and West Bengal. (Economic Times, Indian Express, Adani Power)

Kentucky court decision on Oakland coal terminal case faces review: The City of Oakland will appeal against a decision by Kentucky bankruptcy court Judge Joan A. Lloyd that the City of Oakland is liable for damages caused by the cancellation of a contract for the development of a new port facility. Lloyd scheduled a hearing with the parties for December 2, 2025, to address the amount of damages. Weeks before the Oakland City Council cancelled the contract, developer Phil Tagami had subleased 19 acres of land to Insight Terminal Solutions (ITS) for the development of a coal terminal as part of the larger project. In a separate case, Alameda County Superior Court Judge Noel Wise ruled that the Oakland City Council had wrongly cancelled the lease but rejected Tagami's application for US$159.6 million in damages, finding it based on "speculative and unreliable" estimates of lost profits. The City Attorney's Office said Lloyd's ruling is "subject to an independent review of a federal district judge", and the Oakland Council looks forward to the outcome. Ted Franklin, from No Coal in Oakland, said Lloyd "appears to pick and choose which parts of prior legal decisions to adopt and which to discard" and that opposition to the potential development of a coal terminal continues. (The Oaklandside, Maritime Executive, No Coal in Oakland)

US government announces funding for coal conversion projects: The US Department of Energy (DOE) has approved a US$1.5 billion loan to Wabash Valley Resources to support the development of a US$2.4 billion coal-to-ammonia fertiliser plant in Indiana. The proposal is to convert local coal and petroleum coke into 500,000 tonnes of ammonia per year at a gasification plant built in 1994 and mothballed in 2016. The loan was tentatively approved during the Biden administration as a petcoke-fuelled plant with carbon capture and storage (CCS). The latest DOE announcement states the plant will process coal and petcoke, but does not mention CCS. Several days later, the department announced a funding opportunity for up to US$100 million to support upgrades to existing coal plants. DOE said the funding priorities are upgrades to enable fuel switching between coal and gas, improvements to wastewater management systems, and the adoption of coal- and gas-cofiring systems. Michelle Solomon from Energy Innovation, an energy policy think tank, says the funding won't go far. "Those types of retrofits for a single plant can cost hundreds of millions of dollars," she said. (Inside Climate News, US Department of Energy, US Department of Energy)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Hyundai presses ahead with Louisiana steel plant: Hyundai Motor Group is continuing with its plan to build a new US$6 billion steel plant in Louisiana despite a Trump administration policy change removing tax credits for green hydrogen production and a recent raid by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement on the company's battery plant in Georgia. Hyundai Steel plans to build an electric arc furnace by 2029, with a capacity of 2.7 million tonnes of steel per year to supply Hyundai and Kia car plants. The company plans to produce direct-reduced iron using hydrogen derived from gas. The company has proposed switching to green hydrogen from 2034. (Canary Media)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Emissions Gap Report 2025: Off Target, United Nations Environment Program, November 2025. (Pdf)

This 76-page report estimates that, if countries fully implement the emissions-reduction commitments in their Nationally Determined Contributions, the global temperature increase would be 2.3-2.5C above pre-industrial levels. Implementing current government policies would result in a 2.8 C increase in the global temperature.

Closing in on no new coal: the final push, E3G, October 30, 2025. (Pdf)

This 18-page briefing paper outlines progress on securing international commitments to no new coal plants and identifies remaining challenges to moved past coal power.

Integrated Resource Plan: October 2025, South African Department of Electricity and Energy, October 2025. (Pdf)

This 64-page document outlines the South African government's preferred electricity strategy to 2030 and beyond.
