title: CoalWIre 588, November 13, 2025
excerpt: Legal challenge against Saskatchewan’s coal plan; Chinese power sector emissions remain flat; South African energy minister urges coal industry to speak up.
content:
November 13, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

With global climate negotiations underway in Brazil, there has been a spike in international media coverage of possible pathways to reduce rising greenhouse gas emissions. The International Energy Agency's (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2025 estimates that coal use will fall before 2030 under current policies, and even sooner if the Paris Agreement's goal of limiting global heating to a 1.5C increase is taken seriously. National commitments to emissions reductions are one thing, but overcoming the lobbying power of entrenched incumbents is another. A Reuters feature highlights how the investment of a Brazilian business family rescued an old, struggling coal plant in Brazil from closure. In South Africa, the minister for the power sector wants the coal mining sector to be more vocal in demanding policies that serve their interests.

In China, the latest data indicates that greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector have remained flat, underpinned by the astonishing deployment of new wind and solar capacity. In Canada, residents and environmental groups are seeking a judicial review of the provincial government's June 18 decision to continue operating coal plants in defiance of the federal government's coal phase-out deadline of December 31, 2029.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Why coal still clings on in renewable energy powerhouse Brazil

One of Brazil's last coal plants roared back to life in July after a powerful business group owned by Wesley and Joesley Batista invested millions to keep its turbines turning in the southern mining town of Candiota, writes Leticia Fucuchima in Reuters.

 

 Karen community fighting corn and coal for clean air in northern Thailand

Northern Thailand is affected by hazardous air pollution from burning agricultural waste from maize farms. Even as some communities ban maize cultivation to fight haze, new coal projects threaten to undo their gains, writes Gerald Flynn in Mongabay.

 

 Rise in Chinese off-grid coal plants in Indonesia belies pledge to end fossil fuel support

A surge in the supply of Chinese-backed coal-fired power plants built to supply electricity to Indonesia's fast-growing nickel mining and processing sector is undermining Beijing's efforts to dial back support for fossil fuels, writes Jeff Hutton in Mongabay.

 

 Deep in Trump country, coal miners with black lung say government is suffocating the 'working man'

Retired miners with black lung disease are demanding that President Donald Trump implement a rule lowering the exposure limit for silica dust to reduce the incidence of the disease, writes Margie Mason in the Associated Press.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Chinese power sector emissions remain flat in third quarter of 2025: Chinese power-sector carbon dioxide emissions CO2 emissions were flat in the third quarter of 2025, despite electricity demand growth surging to 6.1 per cent, up from 3.7 per cent in the first half of the year. Solar generation increased by 46 per cent and wind by 11 per cent compared to the same period the year before. In the first nine months of 2025, China added 240 GW of solar capacity and 61 GW of wind projects. While power sector emissions plateaued, a 10 per cent increase in carbon dioxide emissions from the plastics and other chemicals sectors offset the declines in the cement and steel industries. While steel production fell by three per cent in the third quarter, emissions declined by only one per cent, as most of the decline was absorbed by the lower-emissions electric arc furnace sector rather than the emissions-intensive, coal-based blast furnace sector. (Carbon Brief)

 

 International Energy Agency points to decline in coal before 2030: The International Energy Agency's (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2025 Current Policies Scenario (CPS) estimates that coal use will fall before 2030. The IEA estimates that the CPS scenario would lead to global heating of almost 3 C above pre-industrial levels by 2100 compared to the IEA's Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) scenario which equates to global heating of about 1.65 C. In the NZE scenario, unabated coal generation declines rapidly and is all but eliminated in the 2030s. The report estimates that, under the NZE scenario, PM2.5 fine particle pollution, sulphur dioxide, and nitrogen oxides emissions would plummet by almost 80 per cent in emerging and developing economies, primarily due to reduced coal power generation. It also estimates that coal-sector employment would decline by 60 per cent under the NZE scenario. The IEA estimates that coal production accounted for more than half of the 120 billion tonnes of raw materials from fossil fuels and critical minerals mined in 2024. (Guardian, International Energy Agency)

 

 South African energy minister urges coal industry to speak up: South Africa's Minister for Electricity and Energy, Kgosientsho Ramokgopa, said the coal industry's voice was "missing" in the debate over the recently announced Integrated Resource Plan (IRP). "You must defend your bread when it is threatened. But you kept quiet, and now everyone in the country thinks coal must die," said. Ramokgopa was speaking at a forum organised by FFF Carbon, a lobby group that describes its role as serving the "techno-intellectual needs of the multidisciplinary fossil fuel and energy community" in Africa. Ramokgopa told the conference that the coal industry is struggling to recruit young engineers and scientists because it is "perceived as 'dirty'". "We need to fund research demonstrating that coal is not a threat to civilisation or humanity," he said. The IRP recently released by Ramokgopa extends the lifespans of many old Eskom coal plants from 50 to 60 years and proposes the construction of a 'clean coal' demonstration plant by 2030. (Mining Weekly)

 

 Legal challenge filed against coal expansion plan of Canadian province: Three residents of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, along with the Saskatchewan Environmental Society and Citizens for Public Justice, have requested judicial review of the provincial government's June 18 decision to continue operating coal plants after the federal government's coal phase-out deadline of December 31, 2029. The application also requested an interim stay of the Saskatchewan government's direction to state-owned power utility SaskPower to extend the life of its coal fleet. The provincial government filed a motion requesting that the court reject the application. Justice R.S. Smith adjourned the hearing and will determine whether the court can hear the case and the government's motion to strike the proceedings. The provincial government recently proposed extending SaskPower's three coal plants, with a combined capacity of 1.14 GW, to operate until 2050. (SaskToday, Saskatchewan Environmental Society, Saskatchewan Environmental Society [Pdf])

 

 US regulator delegates permits for coal ash management to North Dakota: The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin has approved North Dakota's application for accreditation of its coal ash management standards. The Trump administration has delayed compliance deadlines for coal ash standards and given states greater responsibility for managing sites. North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong said the state "has regulated coal combustion residuals effectively for more than 40 years". Environmental groups disagree. Earthjustice said the EPA decision is a "huge mistake". The group said there are 16 coal ash landfills and ponds at eight North Dakota coal plants with about 67 million cubic yards of coal ash stored. Ten of these storage sites lack impermeable liners to prevent the migration of toxic heavy metals into groundwater. Monitoring data show that 9 of the state's 10 coal plants have groundwater contamination exceeding federal drinking water standards. (E & E News, Earthjustice, Environmental Protection Authority)

 

 Indian utilities team up for 1.6 GW coal plant expansion: Coal India (CIL) has entered into a 50:50 joint venture agreement with the state-owned Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) to build a 1.6 GW expansion of the 500 MW Chandrapura coal plant in Jharkhand. DVC owns six coal plants with a combined capacity of 6.5 GW and has proposed an 800 MW expansion of the Durgapur DVC power station at the Durgapur steel mill site in West Bengal. CIL said that the joint venture company may also pursue the development of other coal plants and renewable energy projects. (Financial Express)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: In an appeal before the High Court of Australia, the former New South Wales Labor ministers Eddie Obeid and Ian Macdonald, along with Obeid's son Moses, argued their convictions for conspiracy to commit misconduct in public office should be overturned. The Obeids netted A$30 million (US$19.7 million) from the Mt Penny coal lease awarded by Macdonald.

 

 India: Hundreds of people attended a public meeting opposing coal handling at Mormugao port in Goa and the expansion of rail capacity to facilitate increased coal transport through the state.

 

 US: Ranchers and environmental groups appealed to the Supreme Court of Montana against a District Court ruling upholding a water pollution permit for the 62.3 million US short tons (56.5 million tonnes) AM5 expansion of Westmoreland Coal Company's Rosebud mine.

 

 US: One coal miner died and another was seriously injured at an Alliance Resource Partners mine in West Virginia.

 

 US: A search is underway for a miner missing after water flooded into the current mine workings after breaching an old mine wall at Alpha Metallurgical Resources Rolling Thunder mine in West Virginia.

 

 US: Xcel Energy and the state of Colorado and Xcel Energy have requested that the Colorado Public Utilities Commission approve a one-year delay to the December 2025 closure of the 396 MW Unit 2 at the Comanche Generating Station. Xcel Energy said the delay is required while repairs are underway on the 857 MW Unit 3 at the plant.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

Report says one-third of Asian coal plants could earn transition credits: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) estimates that about one-third of coal plants across 15 Asian countries could generate high-quality 'energy transition credits' equal to about one gigatonne in annual emissions reductions. The scheme, first floated in May 2023, proposes allocating credits to power plant owners who publicly commit to no new coal capacity and to permanently reducing coal-fired greenhouse gas emissions. MAS argues that the credits would help finance the early retirement of coal plants and drive greater reliance on renewables. A recent report by Reclaim Finance and the Center for Energy, Ecology and Development (CEED) questioned the effectiveness of two pilot carbon credit schemes promoted as helping finance the early retirement of coal plants in the Philippines. (The Edge, The Straits Times, Monetary Authority of Singapore)

Indonesian sovereign wealth fund eyes coal gasification investment: Rosan P. Roeslani, the CEO of the Indonesian government's sovereign wealth fund, Daya Anagata Nusantara (Danantara), said the agency is considering investing directly in a coal gasification project that would produce dimethyl ether (DME) as a substitute for imported liquefied petroleum gas. A coal gasification plant is one of 18 energy and mineral projects under consideration by Danantara. A consortium between PT Bukit Asam, PT Kaltim Prima Coal and the US-based Air Products and Chemicals previously proposed a DME plant. In March this year, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto directed the National Energy Resilience and Downstream Task Force to pursue the development of four coal gasification projects in Kalimantan and Sumatra. However, the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis estimated DME would cost 42 per cent more than the equivalent amount of energy from LPG. The push for coal gasification projects comes as Indonesian coal exports face an uncertain future, and global prices have fallen. (Indonesia Business Post)

Japanese traders forecast Chinese steel exports to hit met coal prices: Executives from major Japanese commodities traders Mitsubishi and Itochu estimate a high level of Chinese steel exports will undercut metallurgical coal and iron ore prices for at least the next six months. A sharp downturn in China's domestic construction sector has spurred steel producers to boost exports. Keita Ishii from Itochu said that Chinese steel exports to the Middle East and Africa have increased, limiting the impact of tariffs and anti-dumping measures imposed by other countries. In 2024, China produced just over 1 billion tonnes of steel, with exports jumping by almost 23 per cent to 110.7 million tonnes. According to Chinese Customs Service data, Chinese steel exports in the first ten months of 2025 increased by 6.6 per cent to 97.7 million tonnes. In March this year, the Chinese government announced plans to reduce steel industry overcapacity as part of its 'anti-involution' measures to curb excessive price competition between producers. (The Business Times, GMK Center)

US government designates metallurgical coal as 'strategic' mineral: The US Geological Survey has added metallurgical coal to the US government's list of critical minerals. The designation opens up the possibility of policy support, such as fast-tracked permitting and subsidies for metallurgical coal producers. The Trump administration's One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a provision for tax credits for US companies that produce metallurgical coal. The Sierra Club and a coalition of climate and environmental groups opposed the designation, arguing that most US metallurgical coal is exported and does not meet the Energy Act's criteria for critical minerals. The groups also noted that, as metallurgical coal is sometimes burnt as a fuel in thermal coal plants, it is prohibited from being classified as a critical mineral. (Mining.com, Sierra Club)

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Resources

Photo Essay: Coal miners with black lung fight Trump administration rollback of safety protections, AP, November 8, 2025.

This photo essay documents the recent protest by coal miners and their supporters against the Trump administration's delay in implementing a new silica dust rule to reduce the incidence of the deadly disease.

title: CoalWire 589, November 20, 2025
excerpt: South Korea to close almost two-thirds of coal fleet by 2040; US coal trader to let coal terminal lease lapse.
content:
November 20, 2025
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Editors Note

As the global climate negotiations draw to a close, South Korea's announcement that it has joined the Powering Past Coal Alliance is significant. The announcement came as a legal case brought by South Korean farmers against the state utility Korea Electric Power Corporation has come to the fore. South Korea's commitment to close almost two-thirds of its non-captive coal-fired power plants by 2040 represents a shift in the country's energy strategy and is a powerful signal to other Asian countries. However, the decisions on the closure dates of the other one-third of the country's coal units will be crucial. South Korea, like Japan, has touted ammonia co-firing as one strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from coal plants. Two recent accidents in the US with ammonia production and distribution highlight some of the risks with the technology.

Meanwhile, the head of Indonesia's Just Energy Transition Partnership bemoaned the lack of international funding for the closure of coal plants. The financing pitch comes as the Indonesian government is drafting changes to its renewable energy targets to allow for a greater role for new grid-connected coal capacity.

 
 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Features

 

 

 
 
 
 
 South Korean growers sue state power utility, blaming climate change for crop damage

Rice farmer Hwang Seong-yeol and four other South Korean growers have sued the state utility Korea Electric Power Corporation and its power-generating subsidiaries, alleging their reliance on coal and other fossil fuels has accelerated climate change and damaged their crops, writes Kim Tong-Hyung in the Associated Press.

 

 A new unifying issue: just about everyone hates data centres

Recent US election results and evidence from states reveal misgivings about the growth of AI and the ramifications for energy costs and the environment, writes Dan Gearino in Inside Climate News.

 

 Ottawa's double standard leaves Saskatchewan free to continue burning coal

The Canadian government can't have it both ways—celebrating its supposed leadership of the Powering Past Coal Alliance while signing side deals that enable provinces such as Saskatchewan to keep burning coal in contravention of its own laws, writes Maryo Wahba from the Citizens for Public Justice in The Energy Mix.

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Top News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 South Korea sets 2040 end date for two-thirds of coal fleet: South Korea announced it plans to close about two-thirds of its fleet of non-captive coal plants by 2040 and has joined the Powering Past Coal Alliance, an international coalition aimed at accelerating the transition from coal generation. Kim Sung-hwan, the Minister for Climate, said the coal phaseout "is not only necessary for the climate but also beneficial for energy security, corporate competitiveness and job creation". South Korean government data indicates there are 61 operating coal units, excluding captive plants, with 40 units scheduled to close by 2040. The government will finalise the closure dates of the remaining 21 units in 2026 after detailed assessment and public consultation. South Korea's coal fleet has a combined capacity of 39.1 gigawatts (GW). Solutions for Our Climate described the proposed coal phaseout as "far from sufficient", pointing to recent research that said that South Korea needs to retire all coal power plants by 2035 to meet the upper limit target of a 61 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions included in its Nationally Determined Contribution report to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. In 2024, South Korea imported about 91 million tonnes of thermal coal, mainly from Indonesia, Russia and Australia and accounts for about 7 per cent of global thermal coal imports. (The Korea Times, Guardian, Powering Past Coal Alliance, Solutions for Our Climate)

 

 Dozens hospitalised after US ammonia leak: Dozens of people were hospitalised, and more than 500 evacuated, after a parked tanker truck leaked anhydrous ammonia. Four people were in a critical condition after the accident in Oklahoma. The week before, an anhydrous ammonia leak resulted in a major explosion at the CF Industries hydrogen and ammonia plant in Mississippi. The two incidents, while not directly related to the power sector, highlight the risks associated with ammonia transport and production. Ammonia, which is made by combining hydrogen and nitrogen, is primarily used as a key ingredient in fertiliser production. However, ammonia could have an expanded role as an energy carrier over long distances for reprocessing into hydrogen near the point of use. Hydrogen proponents envisage its use as a transport fuel, co-firing in fossil-fuel power plants, and in industrial sectors such as steel. Others see a negligible role for hydrogen in the transport and power sectors, and point to the safety risks and economic hurdles to transporting large volumes of ammonia. (Guardian, NBC News)

 

 Indonesia highlights funding challenge for coal closures: Mr Paul Butarbutar, the head of the secretariat for Indonesia's Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP), said that to date, contributing governments have not provided finance to support the closure of 6.7 GW of coal plants by 2030. A JETP progress report in October stated that US$2.85 billion in loans and equity and US$186.9 million in grants have been allocated to grid upgrades, renewable projects, energy efficiency projects, and the electrification of transport. The JETP was announced in late 2022 with the aim of allocating US$20 billion to accelerate the retirement of coal plants. Since then, the US has withdrawn from the partnership. "If there is no one really willing to jump in to finance the coal phaseout, then we will have to think about whether phaseout is actually the best option," Butarbutar said. In a separate project, the Asian Development Bank's Energy Transition Mechanism has earmarked about half the US$2.56 funding to Indonesia to support the closure of the 660 MW Cirebon-1 plant east of Jakarta. (Reuters)

 

 NSW court approves order overturning expansion of Glencore mine: The New South Wales (NSW) Land and Environment Court overturned the New South Wales government's approval of Ulan Coal's proposed 18.8 million tonnes expansion of the Ulan thermal coal mine. Ulan Coal is a subsidiary of Glencore, the world's largest thermal coal exporter. The proposed expansion would allow the mine to continue operating until 2035. Ulan Coal acknowledged that the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure had failed to make the climate change impacts of the proposed expansion a mandatory consideration. The company agreed with the Mudgee District Environment Group (MDEG) to a consent order that set aside the department's approval. Glencore said it intends to modify its application and resubmit it for fresh approval. Anita O'Hart from Johnston Legal, who represented the environment group in the case, believes the decision may affect 18 coal mine expansion projects under consideration in NSW. (Brisbane Times)

 

 Municipal authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina protests power plant pollution: The state-owned power utility, EPBiH, shut down two units of the 450 MW Kakanj lignite plant after Mirnes Bajtarevic, the mayor of Kakanj municipality, protested the plant's contribution to extreme air pollution levels. The utility agreed to operate only Unit 6, the 110 MW unit that supplies the district heating scheme. In 2022, Bankwatch revealed that Unit 5 commenced operating illegally after breaching the European Union's Large Combustion Plants Directive 20,000 operating hours threshold for plants operating after January 1, 2018, without the installation of pollution controls. EPBiH entered into contracts for the installation of desulphurisation equipment on Units 6 and 7, with completion scheduled for the end of the year. (Balkan Green Energy News)

 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 News

 

 

 
 
 
 
 Australia: A coalition of environmental groups has called for an investigation after recent test results revealed dissolved salt levels four times above the recommended water quality target. The sample was collected downstream from Energy Australia's Mt Piper Power Station and Centennial Coal's Western Coal Services mine site.

 

 Australia: Rio Tinto, a major iron ore producer, has scrapped its A$215 million (US$139 million) BioIron research project that aimed to achieve a 95 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions in converting iron ore to iron.

 Germany: The European Commission has approved a 1.75 billion (US$2 billion) compensation payment by the German government to LEAG for the closure of coal-fired power plants.

 

 Indonesia: The Jawa-9 and Jawa-10 coal units at the Banten Suralaya plant have begun commercial operation. Each unit has a capacity of 1 GW.

 

 Nepal: Water in the Tinau River became unusable for domestic and other uses after a landslide pushed waste from abandoned coal mines into the waterway.

 

 New Zealand: The Greens announced that they would revoke permits for any coal project approved under the conservative government's fast-track approvals law. The next national election is due by the end of 2026, and the Labour Party would likely require the Greens' support to form a minority government.

 

 US: A majority of the House of Representatives' Democratic members are urging US Energy Secretary Chris Wright to cease extending the order requiring the operation of Consumers Energy's 1.56 GW J.H. Campbell coal plant. Since May, the plant's operation has cost Consumer Energy US$80 million, or more than US$615,000 per day.

 

 US: Resource workers found the body of Steve Lipscomb, the foreman missing for four days, after water flooded into mine workings at Alpha Metallurgical Resources Rolling Thunder underground mine in West Virginia.

 

 
 

Companies + Markets

US coal terminal to close in 2026: Midwest Energy Resources Company, a subsidiary of DTE Electric Company, announced it will not renew the lease for the Superior coal terminal at the Port of Duluth-Superior due to the rapid decline in coal demand. The terminal commenced operations in 1976, spurred by increased demand for low-sulphur coal following the Clean Air Act, which introduced measures to reduce sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions from US coal-fired power plants. The volume of coal handled by the terminal peaked at 22 million US short tons (20 million tonnes) in 2008 but has since declined by 75 per cent. Midwest Energy's lease with Koch Industries expires on June 30, 2026. "As the lease is coming due, there just isn't a business case to continue moving coal through there," said Jayson Hron, a spokesperson for the Duluth Seaway Port Authority. (Wisconsin Public Radio, Global Energy Monitor)

Indonesian minister tips production cut to support prices: Indonesia's Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources, Bahlil Lahadalia, said the government will aim to reduce coal production in 2026 in a bid to support export prices. Indonesia's HBA thermal coal benchmark price has fallen from US$114.43 in November 2024 to US$103.75 per tonne in November 2025. The September edition of the Australian government's Resources and Energy Quarterly projects Indonesian thermal coal exports could fall from 549 million tonnes in 2024 to about 514 million tonnes this year and remain at a similar level in 2026. The dominant factor in the decline in exports in 2024 was a sharp downturn in Chinese imports. In 2024, Indonesia produced about 836 million tonnes of coal. Mining companies supplied about 140 million tonnes to state-owned power utility PLN to satisfy their Domestic Market Obligation (DMO). The DMO requires coal producers to provide at least 25 per cent of production to PLN at US$70 per tonne, a price set well below the export market price to limit the impact on electricity prices. Coal exporters argue that the US$70 per tonne rate has not changed since 2018, and that the government should raise it. The Indonesian Mining and Energy Forum wants coal allocated for captive coal plants supplying smelters excluded from the DMO obligation. The Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR) has expressed concern that the government is drafting amendments to significantly weaken the 2022 regulation promoting renewable power projects and expand the role of new coal projects. IESR said mooted changes include allowing new coal power plants in the name of system stability and supporting new fossil fuel projects if paired with renewables. (Antara, VOI, Jakarta Post [paywall], Institute for Essential Services Reform)

US utility wants consumers to pay corporate costs: FirstEnergy, the utility at the heart of the Ohio coal and nuclear subsidy scandal, is seeking approval from the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) to recoup US$108 million in misclassified expenses from Ohio electricity consumers. A 2022 Federal Energy Regulatory Commission audit suggested that First Energy may have misclassified corporate costs, such as advertising and lobbying expenses, as construction costs. Utilities are allowed to earn a rate of return on construction costs, but generally corporate costs cannot be recovered from consumers. FirstEnergy consumers have already paid a heavy price for FirstEnergy's initial success in the US$61 million 2019 scandal, which forced bailouts for two coal and two nuclear plants. Before the legislature repealed the subsidy for the two coal plants earlier this year, consumers had paid more than US$500 million to Ohio Valley Electric Corporation (OVEC) for the 1303 MW Clifty Creek plant in Indiana and the 1086 MW Kyger Creek coal plant in Ohio. OVEC is a joint venture between AEP, Duke Energy and AES Ohio. (Ohio Capital Journal, Energy and Policy Institute)

 
 
 
 Green Steel Transition

 

 

 
 
 
 Minister flags support for British Steel plant: Ahead of the release in December of the UK government's steel strategy, Business Secretary Peter Kyle said he supports the transition to electric arc furnace production at British Steel's Scunthorpe steel plant. In April, the UK government passed legislation ordering the Chinese steel company, Jingye, to keep the plant's blast furnaces operating to avoid the loss of 2700 jobs. Jingye bought British Steel in 2019 and reportedly rejected a government offer of 500 million (US$658 million) in support to keep the mill operating. While the government is under pressure from unions and opposition parties to keep the carbon-intensive blast furnaces operating to maintain primary steel production, most analysts consider the only option to stem the financial losses is to switch to electric arc furnace production. In 2022, Tata Steel cut 2500 jobs at its Port Talbot mill as it transitioned production to electric arc furnaces. (Guardian)
